paragraphs.text: “The proverbs of Solomon the son of David, king of Israel” [1].

The name of Solomon appears in three parts of this book (Prov 1:1; 10:1; 25:1). The ancient commentators regarded the whole book as the work of Solomon the Wise. It is said in (1 Kgs 4:32): “He spake three thousand proverbs: and his songs were a thousand and five,” and some scholars still take this view.

The word “proverb,” as we saw before, means in Hebrew “to rule” or “to govern” a matter, and some see that it means “to present a thing or a person by what resembles it.” It is as though this is the book in which Solomon the Wise presents the life of faith as God governs it in us and through us in practical reality.

Solomon mentions his name, his descent from his father David and his office as king of Israel, in order to declare his longing that we imitate him and become sons of peace, belonging to the Son of David, the true King, and become through Him kings and priests to God His Father (Rev 1:8).
Solomon points to himself in verse 1 as the king, the son of David. And we look to Wisdom Himself, the Son of David, the King of kings, and by acquiring Him we carry wisdom within us.

* He is a wise son of a wise father; therefore he added the name “David,” who begot Solomon. From childhood he learned the Holy Scriptures, and he received his authority neither by lot nor by violence, but by the judgment of the Spirit and by a divine decree.
St. Hippolytus

2 To know wisdom and instruction; to perceive the words of understanding; 3 To receive the instruction of wisdom, justice, and judgment, and equity; 4 To give subtilty to the simple, to the young man knowledge and discretion. 5 A wise man will hear, and will increase learning; and a man of understanding shall attain unto wise counsels: 6 To understand a proverb, and the interpretation; the words of the wise, and their dark sayings. 7 The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction.

Verses 2-6 tell us why Solomon wrote these proverbs. In brief, these proverbs support us in practicing wisdom in a practical way, so that we enjoy true success and lasting happiness. When a young man is concerned about his life, wants to walk as is fitting, recognizes his own ignorance, and longs to learn and to enjoy knowledge, then he receives knowledge, understanding and discernment.
Ten words are used in verses 2-4 which seem to be synonyms. Certainly there is a relationship among them, but these synonyms differ from one another. Among these words are:

A. Wisdom, chochmah: in the Bible it means “the ability to use knowledge rightly.” It is used 37 times in this book alone, and it is a word of importance in the Bible. Perhaps wisdom means not only the divine knowledge by which we can discover the best end of man’s life and how we can reach it by fitting ways, but it also means the heavenly teaching by which we discover ourselves as we come to know God, so that wisdom guides us into all truth and forms true religion in its entirety. Wisdom brings us into true and practical knowledge, for there are many people gifted with extraordinary intelligence and having knowledge, but they lack wisdom, and so they misuse knowledge.

Wisdom is the subject and the aim of God’s school. And wisdom in the Old Testament means Jesus Christ for the contemporary believer. “But of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption” (1 Cor 1:30).

When you come to know the Lord Christ, you reject playing with folly and corruption, and you become wise. And when you receive the Lord Christ into your life, you enter into new experiences of knowledge and are truly reckoned wise.

B. Instruction, musar: it appears 26 times in the Book of Proverbs. The literal meaning is teaching or correction by discipline, as in (Prov 13:24): “He that spareth his rod hateth his son: but he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes” (cf. Prov 3:11; 22:15).

Discipline here is for teaching and not for punishment and vengeance (Eph 4:14; 2 Pet 1:6). For God, in His love for the sinful man, hands him over for a time to the fruit of his works, not to take vengeance on him, but that he may taste the bitterness and death that sin brings, and so come to himself and return to God his Savior, who lifts him out of sin; thus the soul is reformed. This is what we also should do, as fathers or leaders: to carry a spirit of love and self-giving even toward the one we discipline. For sadly, criminals are sometimes thrown into prison to be reformed, while we punish our children with anger and violence. We discipline criminals to reform them, while we punish our children as though we were taking vengeance on them. This is a kind of confusion, and a failure of our hearts to open wide to the new generations.
C. Knowledge: it is true and useful information. The verb “to know” is used about a thousand times in the Old Testament.

The Bible affirms that faith is not opposed to knowledge, for faith is offered to man as a rational being who is eager to enjoy true knowledge. St. Clement of Alexandria says: “Here are the observations that form our gnosis (knowledge): first contemplation, then the fulfillment of the commandments, and finally the instruction given by the righteous. When these things are realized in a person, he becomes a gnostic (one who has knowledge).”
D. Understanding: the believer who receives the Lord Christ, “Wisdom,” into his life and responds to discipline receives an understanding of God’s plan for his life.
* Understanding is the eye of the soul; therefore the word “Israel” means: “the one who sees God, that is, the one who understands God.
St. Clement of Alexandria E. Justice: it is righteousness, and means walking uprightly.

F. Judgment (truth): it means to pass judgments or take wise decisions, as children of God fulfilling His will. Every day the believer stands at a crossroads to decide where to go in his life. This needs divine help and heavenly wisdom.
G. Equity: it means spiritual integrity. Here it points to a principle rather than a way of behavior.

The children of God are not subject to rulings, but are given principles to guide them on the way. As it is said in Rom 14:22: “Happy is he that condemneth not himself in that thing which he alloweth.” The believer carries strong inner feelings that lead him toward the truth, though he realizes that many times he is walking on eggshells, and he needs inner help to lead him so that he does not fall.

H. Discretion (discernment): it means discerning between the good and the evil, the precious and the worthless, the beneficial and the harmful. Believers enter God’s school so that they may become God’s children: wise, righteous and honored.
“To know wisdom and instruction; to perceive the words of understanding” [2].

He begins with knowledge to affirm the link of faith with knowledge; then he links wisdom with instruction. If wisdom is God’s school, which translates true knowledge into upright behavior (practical wisdom), the believer will not attain this without bowing to God’s disciplines, which straighten the soul and develop understanding. The believer needs teaching, training and refinement, and by this he receives a true understanding of God’s plan for him.

* As for wisdom and instruction [2], it is said that wisdom is the knowledge of all human and divine things and of their causes; therefore whoever is a practicing theologian knows wisdom. “Howbeit we speak wisdom among them that are perfect: yet not the wisdom of this world, nor of the princes of this world, that come to nought: But we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, even the hidden wisdom, which God ordained before the world unto our glory” (1 Cor 2:6, 7).
St. Basil the Great “To receive the instruction of wisdom, justice, and judgment, and equity” [3].

Here he clarifies the preceding statement, affirming that the purpose of wisdom is to receive discipline with joy, to obtain knowledge that satisfies the heart and mind, and righteousness, which is walking in a spirit of uprightness, and to acquire truth and equity.

Thus the wise man reveals the living relationship between the divine Teacher and the believing disciple. For the Teacher’s aim is not merely the acquiring of noble behavior, but the enjoyment of divine knowledge, righteousness and heavenly truth in an integrated, upright life that touches the whole being of the believer: his heart, mind, will, feelings and all his behavior, hidden and visible. It is the disciple’s enjoyment of the icon of his divine Teacher, Wisdom Himself!

St. Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, sees that these divine gifts of knowledge, justice, judgment and equity transform the soul into a garden full of spiritual fruit, or into a bride who bears the beauty of her bridegroom.
* How delightful is this garden whose fruits represent the beauty of the Bridegroom!
He is the true light, the true life, the true righteousness, and so on, as Wisdom says.

When a person comes to possess these qualities through good works, he looks upon the cluster (of virtues which) belongs to his conscience, and sees the Bridegroom there, reflecting the light of truth by his pure life.
St. Gregory, bishop of Nyssa “To give subtilty to the simple, to the young man knowledge and discretion” [4].

The word “discretion” in Hebrew appears in the plural, “counsels,” and it is used of the pilot of a ship who holds the rudder in his hand, moving and steering it as he wishes. So by wisdom the believer becomes the leader of his thoughts and the steersman of his inner life, guiding the ship of his life by the Holy Spirit of God in the royal way.
The word is also used of the tending of sheep, where a man tends all his energies and abilities like a flock that listens to him.

Adam Clarke sees that the word “simple” is used in more than one sense. It means the plain-hearted, those who walk with clarity and openness, who show outwardly what they are inwardly. Here simplicity carries the meaning of innocence, absence of guile, and not harming others. But since very few people came to carry this trait, the word was misused and turned into the idea of foolishness, lack of wisdom and inexperience. Here the word is used in the latter sense.
“A wise man will hear, and will increase learning; and a man of understanding shall attain unto wise counsels” [5].

These proverbs were written not only for the young but also for the wise, for it is fitting that they grow in wisdom by being ready to be taught. It is fitting that they be willing to listen and not content with themselves. For even in guiding others they need to hear and learn. As St. Ambrose says, all humanity needs to learn; God alone teaches and does not need to learn.

A person in humility bows to listen to the voice of wisdom, feeling the need for constant growth in knowledge. Thus he says with St. Paul the Apostle: “He speaks wisdom among them that are perfect” (1 Cor 2:6). And as the Lord Christ says, that to him who has, it is given and he has more; so the wise man, by his longing to learn, increases in wisdom, and the fool, by his refusal to learn, increases in ignorance and folly.
“To understand a proverb, and the interpretation; the words of the wise, and their dark sayings” [6].

If wisdom cries out on the high places and goes down into the markets to offer the free invitation of salvation in simplicity to every person, she nevertheless keeps some hidden mysteries, which she presents as a gift to those who are earnest in seeking them and asking for them from God.

God does not scatter pearls on the ground, and the precious jewels He hides from human eyes so that they may seek them and find them. Gold and pearls and everything precious are sought in mines and in the depths of the earth, and petroleum is extracted from the depths. So God hides His mysteries so that we may realize that they are worth seeking by study with prayer. As the Lord Christ says: “Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have life.”

The call of the Book of Proverbs to us today: Dig! Study deeply, so that you may declare to God your earnest longing to enjoy the gift of wisdom and understanding, and He will reveal to you the mysteries of His word.”
What does he mean by dark sayings (chidoth)? Some believe that he means by this the parables that our Lord Jesus Christ presented.
After reviewing the purpose of wisdom, he presented to us the motto of the whole book, which is:
“The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction” [7].
This verse is the key to the book. I have already pointed to the meaning of “the fear of the LORD.”
Here there is a contrast between the fear of the Lord, which urges the believer to learn, and folly, which does not want to learn from wisdom but rejects it as it rejects instruction.

The first foundation that must be laid for erecting the spiritual building is the fear of the Lord. What destroys it is the madness of relying on one’s own will, with unwillingness to learn, along with disobedience and the rejection of all counsel and all discipline. Besides knowing what is good and what is evil, which the fear of the Lord achieves, one must submit to the order God has set, by governing the will and sanctifying it through submission to parents, true leaders and counselors.
What is the relationship between the fear of the Lord and true wisdom?

Are there not among the atheists, or at least among those who deny the faith, some who have attained high degrees of knowledge? We do not deny that some of those who ignore the existence of God, and even blaspheme His name and despise His word, have high knowledge of many languages, or are well versed in scientific knowledge, or have obtained academic degrees in philosophy, politics, history and so on. This knowledge may be useful, and sometimes it harms if it drives a person to pride and arrogance even against the Creator Himself. But true fear supports a person in his relationship with God and with his brothers, and even with his body and soul, and opens before him the doors of hope in heavenly things, so that he lives in a spirit of joy and exultation; by this a person is reckoned truly wise.

* If the law brings fear, then the knowledge of the law is the beginning of wisdom, for a person cannot be wise without the law. Whoever despises the law is not wise, and is therefore reckoned wicked.

St. Clement of Alexandria * The arrogant and wrathful person becomes the prey of his successive passions through the loss of wisdom; therefore the prophet says: “There is no soundness in my flesh; my wounds stink and are corrupt because of my foolishness” (Ps 38:3, 4), showing that all sins begin with folly. So the virtuous man who has the fear of the Lord understands more than others, and as the wise man says: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” [7]. If the one who fears the Lord receives wisdom, and the wicked man does not have this fear, then he is deprived of true wisdom. And when he loses what is called true wisdom he becomes more foolish than others. Yet many admire the wicked, thinking that they are able to wrong and harm others, and they do not know that we must truly reckon these to be more wretched than all men, these who, while they think they are harming others, strike themselves with the sword. It is a work of extreme folly for a man to strike himself without knowing it, thinking that he hurts others while he is killing himself.
St. John Chrysostom * “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom”; the awareness of sin leads to repentance, and God grants His compassion to those who repent.
St. Irenaeus * (The philosophers) say that God must not be feared, for in their view all things are free and without any rule governing them.
Why is God not to be feared, unless because He does not exist?
If God does not exist, then truth does not exist either..
But where God exists, there is the fear of God, which is the beginning of wisdom.

And where the fear of God exists there is earnestness, honorable and balanced diligence, with careful watchfulness, a respected attachment (to holy service), a fellowship together full of trustworthiness, offering good service, submission (to authority), devout listening, humble running, a united Church, and God is in all things.

Tertullian Many of the Fathers see the believer’s need of the fear of the Lord, especially at the beginning of the way, for it is the guide of the body and the soul, with the mind and all the faculties, to walk in the royal way, to carry the person across into the divine presence, and to enjoy living fellowship with God. Therefore St. Gregory of Nazianzus warns us against beginning our spiritual life with contemplation of divine things without being bound by the fear.

* It is fitting for us not to begin with contemplation and leave the fear (for contemplation without restraint may perhaps drive us toward recklessness), but we must be established and purified, and become light through fear, and so be lifted up to the heights. For where there is fear the commandments are kept, and where the commandments are kept there is purity of the body, which is the cloud that covers the soul and hides from it the sight of the divine ray. And where there is purity there is illumination, and where there is illumination the desires of those who long for great things are satisfied, and for the greatest of things, that is, God, who surpasses all greatness.

St. Gregory of Nazianzus If the Book of Psalms was called in Hebrew “Tehillim,” that is, “the exultations,” because it is the book of the soul that exults in the Lord even in the midst of its sufferings and sorrows, then the expression “the fear of the LORD” is often repeated in it. For the fear of the Lord is linked with joyful shouting, and so the psalmist says: “Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling” (Ps 2:11). And in Psalm 115:11 true believers are called those who fear the Lord: “Ye that fear the LORD, trust in the LORD”; and it is said of the Lord Christ Himself, the incarnate Word of God: “And the spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the LORD, and his delight shall be in the fear of the LORD” (Isa 11:2, 3). It is as though the prophet invites us to share in this feature by our union with the Word, so that we carry the spirit of the fear of the Lord with delight and joy.
“But fools despise wisdom and instruction” [7].

The word “fools” means the wicked, that is, the wicked in their hearts, in their thoughts and in their ways, those who rely on their own will and are hardened, unwilling to listen to any advice. And just as the wise man wants to learn eagerly, so the fool is the one who cannot bear to hear guidance that leads him toward true success and happiness.

paragraphs.text: 8 My son, hear the instruction of thy father, and forsake not the law of thy mother: 9 For they shall be a crown of grace unto thy head, and chains about thy neck. 10 My son, if sinners entice thee, consent thou not. 11 If they say, Come with us, let us lay wait for blood, let us lurk privily for the innocent without cause: 12 Let us swallow them up alive as the grave; and whole, as those that go down into the pit: 13 We shall find all precious substance, we shall fill our houses with spoil: 14 Cast in thy lot among us; let us all have one purse: 15 My son, walk not thou in the way with them; refrain thy foot from their path: 16 For their feet run to evil, and make haste to shed blood. 17 Surely in vain the net is spread in the sight of any bird. 18 And they lay wait for their own blood; they lurk privily for their own lives. 19 So are the ways of every one that is greedy of gain; which taketh away the life of the owners thereof.
“My son, hear the instruction of thy father, and forsake not the law of thy mother” [8].

The seven chapters are addressed to “my son.” This expression is used about 15 times. In these chapters we hear the heartbeats of a father who wants the best life for his son. It is the voice of the spiritual father, as it is the voice of the parents, that is, the voice of the Church and the voice of the family church.

It is fitting for us to realize that the relationship between the true teacher and his disciple is the relationship of a father to his son. Teaching in the early Church was an episcopal work, or a fatherly work. Teaching is not merely the presentation of doctrines and teachings, but the presentation of a living experience of the new life in Christ Jesus, which the disciples experience with their fathers.

Abraham, Isaac and Jacob were called “fathers” (patriarchs), or the fathers of Israel [(Gen 1:24) LXX, (Ex 3:13; Deut 1:8; Acts 3:13; 7:2, 12; Rom 4:12, 16; 2 Pet 3:4)]. According to Jewish tradition the official title of the scribes was “father.” And in the Church of the New Testament, at the martyrdom of St. Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, the Jews and the pagans cried out: “This is the father of the Christians.” And when Pope Athanasius the Apostolic referred to St. Dionysius of Alexandria, St. Dionysius of Rome and others, he used the word “the Fathers.”

Teaching and discipleship were inseparable from one another. Through true fatherhood the bishops and priests looked on teaching not as the fruit of theoretical doctrines, but as the fruit of their fatherly love, repeating the words of St. Paul: “For in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel” (1 Cor 4:15).
* When a person learns from the mouth of another, he is called the son of the one who teaches him, and the other is called his father.
St. Irenaeus * Speech is the son of the soul; therefore we call those who teach us our fathers.

St. Clement of Alexandria He refers here to the parents, and not to the father alone. Mothers and grandmothers have played a principal role in every age, down to our present age. Many great men enjoyed the wealth of blessings they learned at their mothers’ knees. Among these great mothers and grandmothers are Hannah, the wife of Manoah, the mother of Lemuel, Lois and Eunice, Mother Dolaji, St. Rebecca and St. Monica.

Not only is it fitting for children to honor their parents, but it is fitting for fathers also to realize their responsibility for teaching and training their children. The parents are supposed to have the fear of the Lord, able to offer the best counsel to their children, and to present to them an exact example of the godly life. For the counsel of the parents is in vain if their own conduct is not upright.

Usually the father gives instructions and imposes discipline, but he is not always present in the midst of the family because of work, while the mother is often within the doors; therefore the order of the family is bound up with her, and it is she who presents the law to her children.

paragraphs.text: “For they shall be a crown of grace unto thy head, and chains about thy neck” [9].
This phrase appeared in the Septuagint: “So thou shalt receive a crown of grace for thy head, and chains for thy neck” (LXX)

Respect and filial obedience create honor, glory and spiritual beauty in the life of the wise son. Obedience grants the adornment of grace to his head as a crown and a diadem, and golden chains and pearls.

The children of the nobles and aristocrats used to put a chain around their necks to distinguish them from the rest of the people. And here the Book of Proverbs directs our eyes to the fact that whoever listens to his father and accepts his disciplines becomes a nobleman among the noblemen.
* The crown is also made of a marvelous material.. of the tender mercies of God, for the psalmist says: “Bless the LORD, O my soul, who crowneth thee with mercy and compassion” (Ps 103:2, 4).
And it is made also of glory: “Thou hast crowned him with glory and honour” (Ps 8:6); “With blessing Thou hast crowned us as with a shield” (Ps 5:12) LXX.
And also of grace: “Thou shalt receive a crown of grace upon thy head” (Prov 1:9) LXX.
See this crown, which among many crowns surpasses the others in grace.

St. John Chrysostom In the Song of Songs we see the bride having adorned her neck with chains of obedience and of service to others, and it is said of her: “Thy cheeks are comely with rows of jewels (like a dove), thy neck with chains” (Song 1:9). A man’s neck without adornment often points to the coarseness of human nature, but if it is adorned with the gifts of the Holy Spirit it becomes a symbol of spiritual beauty and gentleness in bearing with others... These are the ecclesiastical chains (the collar or necklace). Our neck once bore shame and disgrace because of our disobedience and pride, but now it bears the yoke of Christ and accepts His obedience, and so it has come to bear surpassing spiritual beauty.
* “How beautiful are thy cheeks, as the cheeks of a dove, thy neck with chains” (Song 1:9)...
Let us interpret the neck of the bride... as pointing to the souls that have received the yoke of Christ, who says: “Take my yoke upon you... for my yoke is easy” (cf. Mt 11:29-30).
It was called “neck” because of its obedience.
And her neck has become beautiful as with chains, and truly it is so.
For if the disobedience of transgression made it formerly deformed, the obedience of faith has now made it beautiful and wonderful...
Submission and obedience were called a neck, because the neck is said to receive the yoke of Christ and to offer the obedience of faith as a treasure.

Her neck, that is, her obedience, is Christ. For He Himself first was obedient unto death (Phil 2:8), and as by the disobedience of one man, that is Adam, many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one, that is Christ, shall many be made righteous (Rom 5:19).
Thus the adornment of the Church and her chain is the obedience of Christ.

entries.section: 3. A warning against association with destructive groups (gangs)

paragraphs.text: Origen “My son, if sinners entice thee, consent thou not” [10].

Verses 10-19 indicate that life is full of enticements. Here we notice groups (gangs) of young people at the corners of the roads calling a young man to take part with them in an armed robbery. The wicked are zealous to deceive others so that they walk the destructive way. Sinners love company in sin, and they have a very tempting style. Therefore it is fitting for young people to be extremely careful.

He says: “Consent thou not.” They cannot cause you any harm unless you join them of your own full will. For God’s eternal purpose for man is that he exercise freedom of will, or rather that the will, which is essentially free, cannot be compelled by any power to do a certain thing. Satan himself cannot lead a person into sin unless the person agrees to it. St. John Chrysostom says that no one can harm a person unless the person harms himself.

entries.section: 3. A warning against association with destructive groups (gangs)

paragraphs.text: “If they say, Come with us, let us lay wait for blood, let us lurk privily for the innocent without cause” [11].

This is the method of the wicked in all ages, which is to call others to join them in their practice of evil against the innocent. They find their pleasure not only in persecuting the godly, but also in making many others partners with them in this violence.

This saying applies to the Jewish people, who devoted all their energies, especially at the level of the religious leaders, to kill the Lord Christ, the innocent, who alone is without sin. They wanted to kill Him and seize His possessions, that is, the Church, not in order to enrich themselves with her, but to destroy her.
* He (the wise man) understood these things of the people of the Jews, and their particular crime of shedding the blood of Christ, since they thought that His citizenship was on earth only.

St. Hippolytus * What we read in Proverbs about the wicked who say, “Let us lurk privily for the innocent...” is not a mystery that cannot be understood. It needs no effort to interpret, since it applies to Christ and to what He possesses, that is, the Church. Indeed the parable in the Gospel about the wicked husbandmen shows that our Lord Jesus Christ Himself said something like it: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and let us seize on his inheritance” (Mt 21:38).
St. Augustine * Accept my advice, my friend, and be slow in doing evil and quick in your salvation. For readiness for evil and slowness in doing good are equally bad.
If you are called to rebellion, do not hasten to it.
And if it is to apostasy, leap away in flight.
If the company of the wicked says to you: “Come with us, let us lay wait for blood, let us lurk privily for the innocent without cause” [11], do not incline to them even with your ears.
By this you gain two great benefits: the other person comes to know his sin, and you deliver yourself from the company of the wicked.

If the great David says to you: “Come, let us rejoice in the Lord,” or another prophet says: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord,” or the Lord our Savior Himself says: “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest,” or “Arise, go, and thou shalt shine with splendor, and glisten more than snow, and be whiter than milk, and shine more than sapphire,” let us neither resist nor delay.

St. Gregory of Nazianzus “Let us swallow them up alive as the grave; and whole, as those that go down into the pit: We shall find all precious substance, we shall fill our houses with spoil” [12, 13].
They “hasten like death, where the earth is split open and swallows them suddenly.”

It seems that he is referring here to the destruction of an entire city, as though the wicked were saying: “Let us destroy the man and the woman and the child, and then we will stretch out our hands and carry off all their possessions and gain great spoil.”

The destructive groups liken themselves to the earth that split open to swallow Korah and his company, who offered strange fire (Num 16:30, 33), or to what is said in the Psalm: “Let death come suddenly upon them, let them go down quick into hell: for wickedness is in their dwellings, and among them” (Ps 55:15). So they swallow every person who accepts their counsel, offering a fire strange to God; instead of the fire of divine love they kindle the fire of evil and violence.

Perhaps he is referring here to the destructive groups as graves that open continually to swallow souls dead through evil without ever being satisfied! Therefore it is fitting for us to cry with the psalmist: “Unto thee will I cry, O LORD my rock; be not deaf to me, lest thou be silent to me, and I become like them that go down into the pit” (Ps 28:1). “My bed is among the dead, like the slain that lie in the grave, whom thou rememberest no more, and they are cut off from thy hand” (Ps 88:5). They want his portion to be with the devil, of whom it is said: “But thou art cast out of thy grave like an abominable branch, and as the raiment of those that are slain, thrust through with a sword, that go down to the stones of the pit; as a carcase trodden under feet” (Isa 14:19).

They will never point to the negative results of their crimes, but rather present what seem to be rewards and advantages. This is the tempting road of sin. Satan highlights what seems good, and leaves the dark side with its ugliness hidden, to be discovered too late.

entries.section: 3. A warning against association with destructive groups (gangs)

paragraphs.text: “Cast in thy lot among us; let us all have one purse” [14].

How can they cast his lot among them so that he knows his portion, and at the same time all of them have one purse? In simplicity they assure him of two things. First, that he will be as one of them; they will not wrong him in anything, but he will receive his portion by lot like them. And at the same time he will not be left in need of anything, since they have one purse, from which each takes according to his need.

entries.section: 3. A warning against association with destructive groups (gangs)

paragraphs.text: “My son, walk not thou in the way with them; refrain thy foot from their path” [15].

This verse points to two ways or paths, and this reminds us of the two ways of life as given in Psalm 1, the way of the righteous, which the Lord knows and loves, and the way of the wicked, which leads to the pit.
After describing the continual enticements of the wicked, the wise man gives his son good counsel and a warning, giving three reasons for it.
· The first reason for his warning is:

entries.section: 3. A warning against association with destructive groups (gangs)

paragraphs.text: “For their feet run to evil, and make haste to shed blood” [16].

His words here carry a tone of speed. The two verbs “run” and “make haste” sound the bell of “emergency.” The prophet Isaiah used the same two expressions in 59:7 when describing the wicked: “Their feet run to evil, and make haste to shed blood.” So also St. Paul in Rom 3:15: “Their feet are swift to shed blood.”
· And the second reason for his warning is:

entries.section: 3. A warning against association with destructive groups (gangs)

paragraphs.text: “Surely in vain the net is spread in the sight of any bird” [17].

Solomon the Wise uses this proverb in a special sense. The wicked lie in wait in secret to trap the innocent. By this alone they hope to destroy them and seize them, because if their plans are known, the innocent will take their guard against them. For the nets are spread in vain before the eyes of the birds that a man wants to catch.
· And the third reason for his warning is:

entries.section: 3. A warning against association with destructive groups (gangs)

paragraphs.text: “And they lay wait for their own blood; they lurk privily for their own lives” [18].

The wicked reap what they sow. Those who lie in wait lie in wait for themselves, where they fall into the trap. And those who attack in hidden places only attack themselves. Evil plans explode and bring evil news to the criminals, while good news is given to the one who resists these deeds.

entries.section: 3. A warning against association with destructive groups (gangs)

paragraphs.text: “So are the ways of every one that is greedy of gain; which taketh away the life of the owners thereof” [19].
Solomon the Wise warns us against trying to get rich by violence or deceit. For covetousness is the sin of every hour.

* You are a captive of your money and a slave to it; you are bound with the chains and fetters of covetousness; you whom Christ once loosed have come into harsher bonds. You keep your money, which, while you keep it, does not keep you.

St. Cyprian the Martyr In brief the wise man presents us with a picture of the evil friend, summed up in the following points: 1. A flatterer who entices his friend [10]: outwardly he seems gentle, but inwardly he offers poison. 2. Within him is violence: “Let us lay wait for blood” [11]. 3. He plans [12]. 4. He is greedy [13]. 5. He sets a snare for himself without knowing it.

20 Wisdom crieth without; she uttereth her voice in the streets: 21 She crieth in the chief place of concourse, in the openings of the gates: in the city she uttereth her words, saying, 22 How long, ye simple ones, will ye love simplicity? and the scorners delight in their scorning, and fools hate knowledge? 23 Turn you at my reproof: behold, I will pour out my spirit unto you, I will make known my words unto you. 24 Because I have called, and ye refused; I have stretched out my hand, and no man regarded; 25 But ye have set at nought all my counsel, and would none of my reproof: 26 I also will laugh at your calamity; I will mock when your fear cometh; 27 When your fear cometh as desolation, and your destruction cometh as a whirlwind; when distress and anguish cometh upon you. 28 Then shall they call upon me, but I will not answer; they shall seek me early, but they shall not find me: 29 For that they hated knowledge, and did not choose the fear of the LORD: 30 They would none of my counsel: they despised all my reproof. 31 Therefore shall they eat of the fruit of their own way, and be filled with their own devices. 32 For the turning away of the simple shall slay them, and the prosperity of fools shall destroy them. 33 But whoso hearkeneth unto me shall dwell safely, and shall be quiet from fear of evil.

In (Prov 1:20; 8:1; 9:3) Wisdom presents an invitation. It is as though both wisdom and folly seek followers for themselves, but in general we see wisdom making her call openly in the streets, and in the squares and entrances of the city, while folly and the inclination to evil are hidden and secret. Wisdom stands crying with a loud voice in important strategic places so that everyone may hear her voice.
“Wisdom crieth without; she uttereth her voice in the streets” [20].

Here wisdom appears as a person, and her voice stands in contrast to the voice of the deceitful wicked, those who were referred to earlier in verses [10-19]. This voice is heard in every place, in public and private places, in the streets as in the private room.
“She crieth in the chief place of concourse, in the openings of the gates: in the city she uttereth her words, saying:
How long, ye simple ones, will ye love simplicity? and the scorners delight in their scorning, and fools hate knowledge?” [21-22].

Man often complains that God speaks to him from His heavens, not feeling human weakness and not touching life on earth. But here we find the wisdom of God coming down to the chief places of the markets, at the entrances of the gates, where people carry on their social relations. At the entrances of the city gates the leaders used to gather for judgment (Prov 31:23; Ruth 4:11; Job 29:7), and at the heads of the markets the merchants and the people gather together for commercial dealings. It is as though the wisdom of God meets people in the reality of life, in the councils of judgment as in the markets, to lead them to practical truth. The wisdom of God incarnate, Jesus Christ, came down to us and dwelt among us as one of us.
Since Solomon the Wise showed how dangerous it is to listen to the voice of the devil, he declares here the danger of not listening to the calls of Christ as the wisdom of God.

The Book of Wisdom points to four kinds of fools, of whom we spoke in the introduction (Prov 20-21), and here the Lord Christ calls three of them: 1. The simple or the ignorant, pethayim: these cannot distinguish accurately between truth and falsehood, because they lack the ability to discern. They can easily be deceived because they are naive, and it is easy to influence them in good matters as in evil. 2. The scorners: proud and mocking people, who turn everything into a jest. They laugh at wisdom and make light of her counsel. In their view nothing is holy or serious. When someone warns them of the evil they are committing they say: “This will not happen to us.” 3. The fools: they hate learning, and carry a deep hatred of godliness. By their own will they are ignorant of wisdom, and live according to their desire. They do not care at all whether a thing is good or evil. All that matters to them is: “What does it profit me in this matter?” 4. The rebels: they hate wisdom so that it can be said that they are unbelievers and revolutionaries.
“Turn you at my reproof:
behold, I will pour out my spirit unto you, I will make known my words unto you” [23].
The phrase “Turn you at my reproof” can be understood in two ways.
The first perhaps means: Since you did not want to listen to my call, return now and listen to my reproof. I pour out my Spirit upon you so that you may discover my judgment that comes upon you.
And the second meaning is: Turn back and repent at my reproof. I pour out my Spirit upon you to help you in your repentance.
“Because I have called, and ye refused; I have stretched out my hand, and no man regarded” [24].
“But ye have set at nought all my counsel, and would none of my reproof” [25].

It is a catastrophe that God wants us to be wise and we do not want to. Man’s rejection of divine wisdom makes him stubborn, and he even becomes as though he were an irrational being. In ancient times Israel rejected God (Isa 1:4; 5:24), and in the New Testament they rejected the Savior (Mt 23:37). He spreads out His hands continually (Isa 65: 2).
“I also will laugh at your calamity; I will mock when your fear cometh” [26].
“When your fear cometh as desolation, and your destruction cometh as a whirlwind; when distress and anguish cometh upon you” [27].
It seems that these words and those that follow concern those described earlier in verses 10-19, those who refuse to turn back from their evil ways until they fall into the grasp of divine justice.
The laughter here carries no trace of cruelty or vengeance, but is symbolic language that reveals the folly of the man who mocks Almighty God, and so is like an insect mocking the flame of a fire.

They have come to the doors of entering into suffering from the requirements of the law. They must die, because their crimes have become against them, and justice leaves them in the hands of their iniquities, which know no mercy. Their ruin becomes like a tempest, like the blowing of an opposing wind.
Truly the love of Christ and the divine promises, mingled together with His reproofs, ought to be the concern of everyone.

Now sinners live the easy life, but their catastrophe is coming. Now God is ready to listen to their prayers, but afterwards they will cry in vain. Do we still despise wisdom? Let us listen diligently and obey our Lord Jesus Christ, that we may enjoy peace and confidence in God, be freed from evil in this life, and enjoy eternal glory.
“Then shall they call upon me, but I will not answer; they shall seek me early, but they shall not find me” [28].
* Many call upon Him, but not in truth.

St. Augustine If God loves sinners, it is for their repentance, their sanctification and their glory by returning to Him; therefore He refuses to listen to sinners who persist in not repenting, as He did with Israel (Deut 1:45; Isa 1:15). They seek Him early not to enjoy Him, but to obtain temporal blessings without enjoying Him; therefore they will not find Him, for whoever finds wisdom finds life and blessing (Prov 3:13; 8:17, 35). By rejecting their prayers He urges them to return to Him, that they may find in Him their resurrection from death, their eternal glory, their lasting joy and their inner satisfaction.
“For that they hated knowledge, and did not choose the fear of the LORD” [29].
The present life is a period of testing, but in eternity life becomes fixed and permanent without change; there the guilty remain guilty forever.

May no one harden his heart because of God’s longsuffering, for if he dies in his sins he will no longer be with God. And when the unquenchable fires close upon him he will not ask for mercy, for he sees clearly and feels that his hope of salvation has been utterly cut off.
“Therefore shall they eat of the fruit of their own way, and be filled with their own devices” [31].

Every person is to determine his choices in life, but he is not free to choose the results of these choices; what he sows, that he reaps (Gal 6:7; Prov 18:20; 31:31; Isa 3:10). We often hear of God who takes vengeance or who puts to death. He speaks with us in our human language. But God, who is all love and the giver of life, has no pleasure in the death of the sinner, but that he turn and live. The one who takes vengeance or puts to death is in fact our sins, which bring their fruit. When God removes His grace from us He lifts His mercies, and since we persist in not responding to Him, we drink from the cup of our works.
“For the turning away of the simple shall slay them, and the prosperity (wealth) of fools shall destroy them” [32].
This testimony became against them, when, in their wealth and in what they thought was safety for them, they were easily drawn to the fruit of their iniquities and lost their lives.
* For it is under the symbol of the Edomites, who allowed themselves to be defeated by the abundance of their wealth.

Those who rejoice in the success of this world are rebuked with the words: “Which have appointed my land into their possession with the joy of all their heart and mind” (Ezek 36:5). It is noticed in these words that they were rebuked severely, not only because they rejoice, but because they rejoice with all the heart and mind. Therefore Solomon says: “For the turning away of the simple shall slay them, and the wealth of fools shall destroy them” [32]. Paul counsels us, saying: “They that buy, as though they possessed not; and they that use this world, as not using it” (1 Cor 7:30, 31).
Father Gregory (the Great)
“But whoso hearkeneth unto me shall dwell safely, and shall be quiet from fear of evil” [33].

Among the surpassing gifts of God is inner security, for we find in Him a fortress for our depths, and so we are in Him as in dwellings of peace. This is what He promised before: “And my people shall dwell in a peaceable habitation, and in sure dwellings, and in quiet resting places” (Isa 32:18). The secret of this tranquility is the overflow of His spiritual goods upon us together with our release from the captivity of sin: “And the tree of the field shall yield her fruit, and the earth shall yield her increase, and they shall be safe in their land, and shall know that I am the LORD, when I have broken the bands of their yoke, and delivered them out of the hand of those that served themselves of them” (Ex 34:27).

Whoever listens to the voice of wisdom, preferring it to the enticements of the wicked, dwells safely, that is, he comes to be in complete safety, and is quiet from fear of evil, enjoying the wealth of the righteousness of Christ and His protection of him.
* What is truly good is seen to be delightful, and produces tasty fruit: tranquility of soul!
It is said: “But whoso hearkeneth unto me shall dwell safely, and shall be quiet from fear of evil” [33]. “Trust in God with all thy heart, and all thy mind upon God.”

St. Clement of Alexandria * “And we desire that every one of you do shew the same diligence to the full assurance of hope unto the end... Whither the forerunner is for us entered, even Jesus, made an high priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec” (Heb 6: 11-20). In the same way Paul the Apostle, full of wisdom, says: “But whoso hearkeneth unto me shall dwell safely, trusting in hope”..

To the expression “dwell” the word “trusting” was beautifully added, showing that whoever receives rest enjoys hope in what he hopes for; therefore it was added: “and shall be quiet from fear of evil.”
St. Clement of Alexandria
Give me Yourself

1 My son, if thou wilt receive my words, and hide my commandments with thee; 2 So that thou incline thine ear unto wisdom, and apply thine heart to understanding; 3 Yea, if thou criest after knowledge, and liftest up thy voice for understanding; 4 If thou seekest her as silver, and searchest for her as for hid treasures; 5 Then shalt thou understand the fear of the LORD, and find the knowledge of God. 6 For the LORD giveth wisdom: out of his mouth cometh knowledge and understanding. 7 He layeth up help for the upright: he is a buckler to them that walk uprightly. 8 He keepeth the paths of judgment, and preserveth the way of his saints. 9 Then shalt thou understand righteousness, and judgment, and equity; yea, every good path.

In this passage [1-9] Solomon the Wise speaks with the believer as with his spiritual son, urging him to listen to the word of God which he utters, to hide it as a treasure in his depths, to incline his ear to it, and to open his heart to it so that it may settle in him. By this he enjoys the fear of the Lord and receives the knowledge of God, is fortified with the spiritual weapons of God, and walks the upright royal way.
“My son, if thou wilt receive my words, and hide my commandments with thee...” [1].

“Solomon” speaks as a teacher with his disciple, reckoning him his son, since he offers him his heart full of love together with a word of teaching. And St. Clement of Alexandria says: “Every person who learns submits to his teacher as a son.”
Would that before we offer our words to others we offered our hearts full of love for them, and aflame with true longing for their salvation and glory.

The father asks his son to receive his words and to hide his commandments. This is the first lesson in the school of this life, which is the son’s acceptance of and response to the words of his parents. It is as though he answers sincere fatherly love with practical filial love. Not only that he respond to him, but that he hide it in his heart with all care and concern as the most precious and best of treasures. The living believer stands from time to time looking toward his inner treasure, contemplating the treasures he has acquired and stored up, admiring them as divine gifts at work in his daily life.

Solomon the Wise counsels us to hide the commandments of the parents, those which are without doubt in complete harmony with the commandments of the Holy Bible. We hide them in our hearts, so that when we fulfill them our conduct proceeds mingled with the inner feelings of the heart, and we fulfill them with our full freedom and great joy, and not like one who practices them under compulsion, as one fulfilling a duty he is bound to. Whoever puts the commandment in his heart fulfills it with his heart, and his heart accompanies him wherever he goes, and so he finds his delight in the will of his heavenly Father.

The believer hides in his heart the commandment of God, his precious treasure, the most precious thing in his life, the center of love and life, and the place of safety, so that the enemy cannot break in upon him to seize it from him. We hide the commandment of God, and then no sin can hide in the heart or creep into it, for darkness cannot find a place where light is. Perhaps the wise man asks us to hide the commandment in our heart so that we may meditate on it and be occupied with it, and our spiritual stomach digest it. For just as food that is not digested does not benefit the body at all, so whoever hears the commandment and does not meditate on it and occupy himself with it, his soul does not benefit from it.
Anthimus, bishop of Jerusalem, gives three reasons for hiding the word of God in the heart:

[A - He hides the word of God in his heart who is warned against error, not only in outward action but also in hidden thought. Such a one avoids not only fornication but also the perversion of his desire and its hidden inclination...
B - And also he who hides in his heart the mysteries of the faith and does not disclose them to unbelievers, acting by His saying: “Neither cast ye your pearls before swine.”

C - Likewise he who hides the sayings of God in his heart lest the birds of the air snatch them, I mean by them the demons fallen from heaven, so that they do not rob him of them by doubt or pride or evil thought...]

* He who does not receive the teachings of God superficially and outwardly but hides them in his heart until his thought and also his intentions are set straight, becomes free of sin before God, who sees what is hidden, for he commits not only adultery but also every evil desire. This verse corresponds to the words: “My son, if thou wilt receive my words, and hide my commandments with thee, so that thou incline thine ear unto wisdom” (Prov 2:1, 2).
St. Didymus the Blind * If we do not hide the sayings of God in our heart as we hide a jewel, the wicked one comes and snatches it (Mt 13:19).

St. Athanasius the Apostolic * He asked first for divine help, lest the words of God hidden in his heart be hidden without fruit, where works of righteousness do not follow them. Therefore after saying this he added: “Blessed art thou, O Lord, teach me thy righteousness” [12].

Because I have hidden Your words in my heart so that I might not sin against You, who gave me the Law, grant me also the blessing of Your grace, so that by doing what is upright I may learn what You have commanded...

St. Augustine It is good for a person to study the Holy Bible with the aid of some study references and commentaries, but there is no book that can take the place of the word of God. Therefore it is fitting for the believer to have his quiet sitting with the word of God, asking God to let him taste it in his depths so that he may live it in his daily life wherever he is.

Relying on previous studies is beneficial, especially the writings of the Fathers on the Holy Bible, since their lives were an open practical Gospel; but if a person does not meet the Word personally, these studies become dry, without renewed spiritual fruit.
“So that thou incline thine ear unto wisdom, and apply thine heart to understanding; Yea, if thou criest after knowledge, and liftest up thy voice for understanding” [2, 3].

The wise man urges us to devote all the senses of the body and its members, together with the soul, to seeking to learn wisdom, knowledge and understanding. This is what we seek with all our energies, listen to, and carry into our hearts. We incline our ears, open our hearts and cry with our tongues until the wisdom of God enters into our depths, into the mind as into the heart. She grants us understanding and satisfies our hearts.

Let us cry to God with our tongues as with our inner voices, for God is pleased with the cries of the heart, and He alone is the giver of wisdom. The Apostle Peter expressed the longing of believers for divine wisdom, saying: “As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby” (1 Pet 3:2). When the baby sees his mother preparing the bottle of milk he moves with all the members of his body, with his tongue and hands and feet and head, etc., to express his desire to nurse. So we, as children of God, declare our eagerness for the milk of the Word, crying out to Him.

Prayer, especially for the enjoyment of divine knowledge, is the language of the soul’s longing toward God. It is the interpreter of the heart’s yearning. Therefore St. Augustine distinguishes between one who offers by his prayer a voice and one who offers a meaningless noise. He says that when we pray without love our prayers are a noise in which God has no pleasure. On the contrary, He is pleased with the prayer that carries a meaningful voice, since it carries love with it. Therefore the psalmist often uses the expression “voice” when speaking of prayer:
“I cried unto the LORD with my voice” (Ps 3:4).
“My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD” (Ps 5:3).
“And he heard my voice out of his temple” (Ps 18:6).
“With my voice I call; therefore have mercy upon me” (Ps 27:7).
“Hear my voice, O God” (Ps 64:1).
“Attend to the voice of my prayer” (Ps 66: 19).
* Who can doubt that the cries raised to the Lord in the sound of prayer are in vain if they are uttered with the voice of the body and not with the voice of the heart that is fixed in God?!

But if they proceed from the heart they escape the notice of men, if through bodily weakness the person is silent, yet they do not escape the notice of God. Therefore when we cry to the Lord with the voice of the body, where circumstances require it, or in silence, we must cry from the heart.

* He says “the voice of my prayer” (Ps 140:7); that is, the life of my prayer, or the soul of my prayer, and not merely the sounds of my words, but what gives the words life. For every other noise that has no life can be called sounds and not words.

Words belong to those who have souls, that is, to the living; but how do many pray to God while they have no understanding worthy of God and no upright thoughts toward Him? Such people may have the sound of prayer but cannot have the intelligible voice, because there is no life in their prayers.

* The cry to God is not made with a bodily voice but with the heart. Many have silent lips yet cry out with the heart, and many offer noise with their lips while their hearts have become unable to offer anything. Therefore if you cry to God, cry to Him from within, where He hears you.
* The mouth speaks through the mediation of words; and the heart speaks through the mediation of its desires. Your prayer is the desire of your heart.
* God does not seek words but your hearts.
* With the heart we ask, with the heart we seek, and at the voice of the heart the door is opened.
* He who prays with desire praises in his heart even if his tongue is silent. But if (a person) prays without longing he is dumb before God even if his voice reaches the ears of men.
St. Augustine “If thou seekest her as silver, and searchest for her as for hid treasures” [4].

The search for wisdom is compared to the search for silver and other precious metals in deep mines. Wisdom, like these treasures, is not found by chance by a passer-by, but the matter requires enormous efforts and discovery and digging. So it is fitting for us to search for the salvation of our souls with burning zeal, as the lover of money searches for wealth. And we should be ashamed of ourselves if our longing for salvation and for the enjoyment of wisdom as true wealth is less than our search for the wealth of the world. Let us search for wisdom with unparalleled diligence, burning desire and great patience.

It is noticed that the word “treasures” here means the possession of what is hidden in the earth and in caves, and it can also mean the precious metals and precious stones found in mines. How do we seek them? By digging the mines until we reach them in the bowels of the earth.

* God does not want us to listen to the words and phrases in the Holy Bible carelessly, but with great attention. This is what moved the blessed David to put the title “for understanding” in many places of his psalms. As he says: “Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law” (Ps 119: 18, 130). And after him his son also came to show the necessity of seeking wisdom as silver, and of trading in it as more precious than gold (Prov 2:4; 3:14) [He also quoted: “Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me” Jn 5:39]. When the Lord urges the Jews to search the scriptures, He urges us all the more to search. For He would not have said this if it were possible to grasp the scriptures completely as soon as we read them. No one searches for what is plain and in his hands, but he searches for what is hidden in shadow, which we must find by searching. So, to urge us to search, He calls it “the hid treasure” (Prov 2:4; Mt 13:44). These words were said to us so that we may not apply the words of Scripture slackly or carelessly, but with great precision. For if someone listens to what is said in the Scriptures without searching for the spiritual meaning but accepts the literal meaning, he thinks things unworthy of God, such as that He is wrathful and furious, and what is worse than this.
St. John Chrysostom “Then shalt thou understand the fear of the LORD, and find the knowledge of God. For the LORD giveth wisdom: out of his mouth cometh knowledge and understanding.
He layeth up help for the upright.
He is a buckler to them that walk uprightly” [5-7].

In the Book of Proverbs Solomon the Wise affirms the close relationship between wisdom and the fear of the Lord. We have already seen that the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, and at the same time whoever attains understanding and enjoys knowledge and wisdom perceives the fear of the Lord and touches it practically. The fear of the Lord is not the motto of the Book of Proverbs alone, but the motto of the whole Holy Bible. St. Ambrose says that the house of wisdom can be built only if the fear of God is deeply established in the soul.

The search for truth must always be accompanied by a walk in the truth that we find. By this God gives His godly ones renewed concepts of the truth, and an ever-increasing living experience of the power of truth.
* I want to have a fitting fear founded on reason and understanding... so that we may not have fear without understanding, nor understanding without fear.

Origen sees Solomon the Wise as saying that wisdom proceeds as though from the mouth of God to be directed toward the ears of the believer, and goes out to his heart as to his mind, and there it settles, where his will, his senses and his feelings, and therefore his words and his conduct, are sanctified.

God is the fountain of all wisdom, knowledge and understanding, and the truly wise and understanding are channels through which God pours out wisdom on many. Divine wisdom is a buckler for the people of God who walk uprightly, or a help for them to obtain victory. For as we hold fast to wisdom and keep her, she holds fast to us and keeps us.
* For those who are justified by philosophy, knowledge leads them to godliness as a help for them.

St. Clement of Alexandria Origen comments on what is in the Septuagint: “They shall find a divine sense” for the Hebrew text: “and find the knowledge of God” [5], explaining that just as the body has its own senses for temporal things, so the soul of the believer enjoys divine senses that concern heavenly things.
* To learn from the Holy Scriptures that there is a divine sense other than the senses of the body, read only what Solomon the Wise says: “Thou shalt find a divine sense” [5].

* Lest it be thought that our saying that rational things are not known by the senses is unsound, Solomon the Wise used an example, for he says: “Thou shalt find also a divine sense,” showing by this that these rational things are not sought by a bodily sense, but by another particular sense which he calls “divine.” It is fitting for us to look through this sense at every one of the rational beings that we reckon to be heavenly. By this sense the words we utter are understood, and by it our phrases which we write are weighed. For the divine nature knows those thoughts that go on within us while we are silent.
* (Solomon) knew that there are two kinds of senses within us: mortal senses, which can be corrupted and are human, and the others immortal and rational, which he calls “divine.”

By this divine sense, not the sense of the two eyes but the sense of the pure heart, which is the mind, God is seen by those who are worthy of it. For certainly you will find in all the Holy Scriptures, old and new, the expression “heart” repeated in place of “mind,” that is, the rational faculty.
Origen St. Augustine comments on the phrase “out of his mouth (face) cometh knowledge and understanding” [6], saying:

* True faith and sound teaching declare that both graces are from God. The Holy Bible says: “Out of his face cometh knowledge and understanding,” and in another book it says: “Love is of God” (1 Jn 4:7).
* “For the LORD giveth wisdom: out of his mouth cometh knowledge and understanding” [6]. From Him they receive the very desire for knowledge, when it is joined (wedded) to godliness.
St. Augustine “He layeth up help for the upright: he is a buckler to them that walk uprightly.
He keepeth the paths of judgment, and preserveth the way of his saints” [7, 8].

God Himself keeps the paths of judgment, which are the paths of His righteousness, so that His believers may walk in them under His care and protection. And it is He who preserves the way of His saints who keep their covenant with Him. It is as though God, who grants wisdom, knowledge and understanding, also gives victory to His believers and protects them as they walk in His way.
“Then shalt thou understand righteousness, and judgment, and equity; yea, every good path” [9].

By saying “then” he makes clear that God, who is the giver of all these gifts, when we respond to His gifts in a spirit of fear, grants us more understanding to perceive the law of His justice, truth and righteousness. It is as though wisdom enters our depths and enlightens our mind to perceive the will of God and the mysteries of His work.

10 When wisdom entereth into thine heart, and knowledge is pleasant unto thy soul; 11 Discretion shall preserve thee, understanding shall keep thee: 12 To deliver thee from the way of the evil man, from the man that speaketh froward things; 13 Who leave the paths of uprightness, to walk in the ways of darkness; 14 Who rejoice to do evil, and delight in the frowardness of the wicked; 15 Whose ways are crooked, and they froward in their paths: 16 To deliver thee from the strange woman, even from the stranger which flattereth with her words; 17 Which forsaketh the guide of her youth, and forgetteth the covenant of her God. 18 For her house inclineth unto death, and her paths unto the dead. 19 None that go unto her return again, neither take they hold of the paths of life. 20 That thou mayest walk in the way of good men, and keep the paths of the righteous. 21 For the upright shall dwell in the land, and the perfect shall remain in it. 22 But the wicked shall be cut off from the earth, and the transgressors shall be rooted out of it.
When we listen in the fear of the Lord and ask Him for wisdom, knowledge and understanding, we enjoy these gifts in our depths, and they bring us the following gains:

entries.section: First: delight of heart and inner happiness with satisfaction of mind

paragraphs.text: 10 When wisdom entereth into thine heart, and knowledge is pleasant unto thy soul; 11 Discretion shall preserve thee, understanding shall keep thee, “When wisdom entereth into thine heart, and knowledge is pleasant unto thy soul” [10].

As we incline our ears and cry with our mouths to God, the doors of our hearts open to receive divine wisdom and heavenly knowledge, and the commandments of God become no burden on the soul, and the yoke of Christ becomes light and sweet to the soul. The wisdom of God gives the soul joy, for in its reception of wisdom it finds union with Christ, the wisdom of God. This union is in itself a reward which the believer enjoys as a pledge of the heavenly reward. By divine wisdom the believer realizes that the aim of his life is to glorify God and to delight in Him.

entries.section: Second: it delivers man from the paths of the wicked

paragraphs.text: 12 To deliver thee from the way of the evil man, from the man that speaketh froward things; 13 Who leave the paths of uprightness, to walk in the ways of darkness; 14 Who rejoice to do evil, and delight in the frowardness of the wicked; 15 Whose ways are crooked, and they froward in their paths:

“Discretion (discernment) shall preserve thee, understanding shall keep thee: to deliver thee from the way of the evil man, from the man that speaketh froward things; who leave the paths of uprightness, to walk in the ways of darkness” [11-13].
The Book of Proverbs teaches us that the people of God must be careful of two dangerous persons: the wicked man, and the foreign, corrupt woman.
A. The wicked man, who gives God his back and not his face, walks in his way by his own will, independent of God, feeling that he has no need of Him.

B. The adulterous woman, who upsets the balances, turning love into lusts, the body, God’s good creation, into an instrument of temporary pleasure, and the wide heart into selfishness! She puts on the mask of love, affection and cheerfulness, with lips dripping honey... and hides in her depths a poison deadly to the soul and a two-edged sword. She is a skilled hunter of foolish souls that bear the image of simplicity.

We see in the wicked man independence from God, and in the adulteress we see the corruption of the godly religious life. And as the Book of Revelation reveals to us that the kingdom of the Antichrist in the last ages will bear these two marks, it calls it “Babylon the Great, the mother of harlots.”

When wisdom has entered our hearts and become the object of our delight, we are not quickly deceived, but become watchful, able to avoid evil company and not to share in their evil conduct. In other words, wisdom leads us away from the way of the wicked and keeps us from their world and its enticements.

When wisdom reigns over the heart and controls the mind, she keeps them against every corruption, inner or outer. She draws from us every desire or inclination toward the way of darkness, since we realize that this way is neither comfortable nor safe.

We saw in the first chapter how the wicked find their delight in committing sin as in enticing others to commit it. The role of wisdom is the sanctification of the heart, the mind and the senses, so that she keeps the believer from fleshly lusts and temporal enticements, and the body and the soul together respond to the work of the Holy Spirit of God.

As we love divine wisdom we enjoy the mind or discernment which keeps the believer in his entirety and makes him able to take wise decisions that deliver him from the snares of the wicked. Thus the believer enjoys a life guarded on all sides, escaping the corruption that is in the world through lust.
“Who rejoice to do evil, and delight in the frowardness of the wicked.
Whose ways are crooked, and they froward in their paths” [14, 15].

Just as true believers rejoice in the living gifts of God, especially wisdom, knowledge and understanding, the wicked rejoice to do evil and delight in lying; but there is a difference between an inner joy that grows and is perfected in heaven, and a temporary one that turns into bitterness and sorrow.
While the way of the Lord is called straight and safe, the ways of the wicked are crooked, turning right and left from the straight way, full of tempests that shatter the soul.

entries.section: Third: it keeps the believer from the snares of corrupt women

paragraphs.text: 16 To deliver thee from the strange woman, even from the stranger which flattereth with her words; 17 Which forsaketh the guide of her youth, and forgetteth the covenant of her God. 18 For her house inclineth unto death, and her paths unto the dead. 19 None that go unto her return again, neither take they hold of the paths of life.
“To deliver thee from the strange woman, even from the stranger which flattereth with her words; which forsaketh the guide (leader) of her youth, and forgetteth the covenant of her God” [16, 17].

By the foreign woman here is meant “the adulterous woman,” for God established a special law for the Israelite woman who practices prostitution, that she goes out automatically from Israel. It is as though “the foreign woman” here means the woman who came from the Gentiles practicing prostitution in the midst of Israel.

The flattering adulteress, hechelikah, is the one who offers sweet, gentle words. The Hebrew word means a slippery tongue that utters words like smooth oil. While the wicked try to entice others in a spirit of greed (Prov 1:11-19), the adulteresses try to entice them with fleshly lusts.

Though the adulteress is gentle in her sweet words, she is unfaithful to the one she loved and married in her youth; she forgets her covenant with him as she breaks her covenant with her God. Treachery and betrayal are in her nature even in her dealings with those nearest her, and even with God Himself. She pledged before God to marry her man, to leave her father’s house, and to submit in a spirit of faithfulness to the one she chose as her guide in her youth, who loves her and gives himself for her, and she submits to him in the Lord.

Here Solomon the Wise links married life with entering into a covenant with God, because marriage too is a covenant which God Himself establishes between the spouses, and He is a witness and judge of this holy covenant. St. Gregory of Nazianzus says, in his apology for his absence from the wedding celebration of Olympias and Nebridius: “Despite my illness I share your celebration, as I join the hands of the bride and groom together in the hands of God.”

entries.section: Third: it keeps the believer from the snares of corrupt women

paragraphs.text: “For her house sinketh (inclineth) unto death, and her paths unto the shades (the dead)” [18].

Although wisdom, like folly, has been symbolized by two women, it is clear that the speech here is not figurative, but means the adulterous woman, and the warning against her is clear and explicit, for she draws the one she entices into her house, that is, into eternal death, and walks with him in the ways of the dead, so that he smells no scent of life. This is what drives the true believer to flee from fornication, avoiding the adulterous woman whatever it costs him. While a man walks with her to her house, he is gradually descending toward eternal death, sharing with her the destructive way of sin. It is clear that the word “death” here does not mean the death to which all are subject but the eternal destiny.
“None that go unto her return again, neither take they hold of the paths of life” [16].

Fornication hastens a person, bringing him down to the way of death with no return. That is, whoever falls into the snares of fornication with a certain person finds it difficult, even impossible, to be delivered from it, unless the surpassing grace of God intervenes to support him and grant him the spirit of true repentance. Therefore many of the Fathers advise whoever falls into the sin of fornication not to meet the one with whom he fell, and not to go to the place where he committed the sin, declaring by this his sure desire and his response to the Holy Spirit of God, the giver of repentance, forgiveness and sanctification.

entries.section: Fourth: it brings him into the way of the good

paragraphs.text: “That thou mayest walk in the way of good men, and keep the paths of the righteous.” [20].

The gifts of wisdom do not stop at the negatives, such as keeping from the ways of the wicked and delivering the believer from corrupt women, but present what is positive, which is bringing a person into the way of the good. For Christ, “the wisdom of God,” carries believers and brings them in to Himself as “the Way.” In Him the believer meets the holy men of God, and enters the company of the fathers, prophets, apostles and all the saints, and even shares the heavenly ones in their praise and love!

entries.section: Fifth: he dwells safely in the land from which the wicked are rooted out

paragraphs.text: “For the upright shall dwell in the land, and the perfect shall remain in it.
But the wicked shall be cut off from the earth, and the transgressors shall be rooted out of it.” [21, 22].

Under the Mosaic Law the righteous received their reward, which was the safe land of Canaan. In the New Testament these gifts have become a symbol of heavenly spiritual gifts. The believer, though he does not receive a material land as a reward for his righteousness in Christ Jesus, sees all the earth, which belongs to the Lord and to His Christ, become his. He lives on it hidden in Christ, the King of heaven and earth, to reign with Him. He says with the Apostle Paul: “As having nothing, and yet possessing all things.” And he sings with David the prophet, saying: “Whatsoever he doeth shall prosper. The ungodly are not so: but are like the chaff which the wind driveth away... For the LORD knoweth the way of the righteous: but the way of the ungodly shall perish” (Ps 1:3-6).
In the epistle of St. Clement of Rome to the Corinthians he asks them to live in uprightness, in a spirit of unity and kindness so that they may enjoy this divine promise, for he says:

[Not a little harm comes upon us, but we come into great danger, if in impulsiveness we yield to the enticements of men who aim at stirring up strife and sedition in order to draw us away from what is good.

Let us be kind to one another after the pattern of the tenderness of the mercies and the kindness of our Creator, for it is written: “The good in heart shall dwell in the land, and the perfect shall remain in it, but the disobedient shall be cut off from the face of it.”]
Let me acquire You and carry You in my bosom

entries.section: 1. Obedience is the way to favor in the sight of God and man

paragraphs.text: 1 My son, forget not my law; but let your heart keep my commandments: 2 For length of days, and long life, and peace, shall they add to you. 3 Let not mercy and truth forsake you: bind them about your neck; write them upon the table of your heart: 4 So shall you find favor and good understanding in the sight of God and man.
“My son, forget not my law; but let your heart keep my commandments.
For length of days, and long life, and peace, shall they add to you” [1].

The wise Solomon begins by revealing obedience as the way of wisdom. Perhaps the speaker here is Solomon as a spiritual father and guide, or the speaker is “Wisdom,” that is, “the Lord Christ.” In any case, obedience is a participation with the Lord Christ in His nature: “[He] became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” (Phil 2:8). As we abide in Him as members of His body, we bear the spirit of obedience to God, to His commandment, to His servants, and to those who lead us in the Lord. We even find sweetness in practicing obedience toward those who are younger than we are or less than we are in knowledge, so long as it is “in the Lord.” St. Pachomius wept and mourned for a time in repentance because he had not obeyed the words of his spiritual son Theodore. The latter was responsible for the clothing store and asked his father to exchange his worn-out garment for a new one, but the father refused... Yet he regretted his disobedience to his son!

In brief, Solomon calls his disciple with a tender fatherly spirit, asking him to remember the law of his spiritual father, indeed the law of the Lord which his father speaks. He should repeat it constantly in his depths and on his tongue so that he does not forget it, and he should practice what he remembers so that it may be kept all the more within the heart. It is as though he says to him: “I do not ask only that you remember it in your mind and keep it by heart, but what is more important is that you engrave it on your heart and practice it. In this way the commandment enters the heart, not so that the heart may lock it up like a precious jewel that must merely be hidden away, but so that it may reign over the heart and lead it in the royal way, and bring it into the very bosom of God.” Thus the heart acquires the “wisdom of God,” the Lord Christ, the Giver of all treasures and riches, bearing a share in the nature of His sweet obedience.

In the Midnight Prayer we repeat what the prophet David says: “Your word I have hidden in my heart, that I might not sin against You” (Ps 119:11). We also continually repeat what was said of the young priest Ezra: “For Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the Lord, and to do it, and to teach in Israel statutes and judgments” (Ezra 7:10).

When we hear: “For length of days, and long life, and peace, shall they add to you” [1], we do not desire to remain on the face of the earth, even though that is a good divine gift, but we ask for the lengthening of our fruitful days. Many remained alive even after their death; their life story, their prayers and their words remained at work in the lives of people. Though they died, they work through the grace of God that was given to them.

The wise man says, “years of life,” because some live “years of death.” Perhaps the days of their sojourn on earth extend to tens of years, but they are years of death, bearing neither life nor love; their presence on earth is like their absence...
