As for peace, the believer asks for the “peace” of the inner heart, even if fire surrounds him on every side, so that he practices, with the three young men, their praise while in the furnace of fire.
By obedience in the Lord, springing from the heart, we walk the royal way, the way of mercy and truth.

entries.section: 1. Obedience is the way to favor in the sight of God and man

paragraphs.text: “Let not mercy and truth forsake you: bind them about your neck” [3].

By saying, “forsake you not,” it is clear that he is not speaking of two mere characteristics, but of a personal relationship with mercy and truth, who here in reality are the divine Hypostasis of the Word, who desires neither to leave us nor to be left by us.

Our Christ is the Way. When we acquire Him, we bear the spirit of love, mercy and kindness, this Spirit who walks in the truth without deviating to the right or to the left. In our love we bear the truth, and in our holding fast to the truth we practice love. For love without truth turns into a looseness that kills the soul as well as others, and truth without love begets anger that corrupts the eyes. True love is the other side of truth, and true truth is the other face of love!

When we practice mercy and truth, the commandments that seem exceedingly heavy, and at times impossible, turn into a precious and beautiful necklace with which the neck of the soul is adorned as a heavenly princess, as happened with Joseph in the house of Potiphar (Gen 41:41). Therefore he says: “bind them about your neck” [3].

The two commandments of mercy and truth enter into the depths, and there they are engraved on the two tablets of the heart, so that events cannot incline the believer to one side or the other, but he walks uprightly. Therefore it is said: “write them upon the table of your heart” [3].

St. John Chrysostom comments on the saying, “Let not mercy and truth forsake you” [3], saying that our relationship with God and His commandments is not a temporary relationship for a short period, but that we hold fast to mercy and truth continually without interruption and never leave them, so that they do not leave us, for we need them at all times.

* It is fitting for us to please God not once, but continually. He who enters a race, if he runs ten laps and stops running the last distance, loses all that he has done. So we too, if we begin good works and then become negligent, lose all that we have done and spoil everything.

Listen to the profitable counsel: “Let not mercy and truth forsake you” [3]. He does not say, do this once, or twice, or three times, or ten or a hundred times, but “let them not forsake you,” showing that we are the ones who need them, and not they who need us. He teaches us that we must exert all effort to keep them with us.

* Let us obey them now, not for one day, nor for three days, but the wise man says: “Let not mercy and truth forsake you.” He did not say: “once or twice.” As we know, the virgins had oil that remained with them to the end (Mt 25:3, 8). So we too need much oil, that we may be like the green olive tree in the house of the Lord (Ps 52:8).

St. John Chrysostom — The two commandments of mercy and truth are placed around the neck so that they may be the object of our sight and we never ignore them, and they are engraved on the tablet of the heart so that they may absorb all our feelings and reign over our senses; we feel them with our hearts as we see them with our inner eyes.

entries.section: 1. Obedience is the way to favor in the sight of God and man

paragraphs.text: The fruit of obedience, which brings us into this way, is: “So shall you find favor and good understanding in the sight of God and man” [4]. God is pleased with us and grants us holy understanding more and more, and although some oppose us, many honor us and seek our counsel.

Thus the wise man urges us to strive, by the grace of God, to cling to mercy and truth continually until we reach perfection. In the discourse of the blessed Clement on virginity, he spoke of the necessity of ceaseless, continual striving to attain perfect virtue, and that virgins should not stop at the outward appearance of virginity.

* It is fitting for all virgins of both sexes who have truly resolved to keep virginity for the sake of the Kingdom of Heaven, each one of them, to be qualified for the Kingdom of God in everything. For it is not by eloquence, nor by fame, nor by position, nor by origin, nor by beauty or strength, nor by length of life that we reach the Kingdom of Heaven, but we obtain it by the power of faith, when a man shows the works of faith. For whoever is truly righteous, his works bear witness to his faith; he truly believes, with great faith, perfect faith, faith in God, a faith that shines in good works, so that the Father of all is glorified in Christ.

Now those who are truly virgins for the sake of God submit to the One who says: “Let not mercy and truth forsake you: bind them about your neck. So shall you find favor and good understanding in the sight of God and man” [3, 4].

St. Clement of Rome — Finally, by saying, “Let not mercy and truth forsake you,” he calls us to be in their constant company, for they are two faithful friends whose continual companionship we need. Rather, they are one Friend, the Person of the Lord Christ, “the Mercy and the Truth,” to whom we hold fast, saying with the bride who strove to seek Him, found Him, and held Him and would not let Him go (Song 3:4). She clung to Him as to her own Bridegroom alone, saying to those around her: “I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that you stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please” (Song 3:5).

entries.section: 2. Trust in God makes straight the paths of man

paragraphs.text: “Trust in the Lord with all your heart; and lean not unto your own understanding.
In all your ways acknowledge Him, and He shall direct your paths” [5, 6].

These are the most important commandments, connected with our faith in God, the Source of all good things, the Lover of mankind, the almighty and wise heavenly Father who cares for us even in small matters, who promises and fulfills His promise to us. It is fitting for us to trust in the Lord with all our hearts, for He wishes to give us what is best and is able to do so. Those who know themselves realize that their understanding, without divine help, is like a broken reed: if they lean on it, they fail. Therefore it is fitting that we plan nothing except what is in harmony with the divine commandment, asking God for His counsel, as we ask Him to sanctify our thought and lead our conduct. Truly, whoever relies on his understanding, his experience and his abilities without divine help is foolish!

In all our ways, whether private, family, or related to work or the society around us, it is fitting that we acknowledge God as our Leader, so that we submit to Him and declare our joy in fulfilling His will and commandments. Then He directs our ways and makes them straight, and we live in peace and happiness, rightly dividing His word in our lives (1 Tim 2:15).

We acknowledge Him as our Leader at the beginning of every way we walk, accompanying us throughout our journey, speaking with us and we with Him without interruption, and bringing us across to the end. Then we say with the two disciples of Emmaus: “Did not our heart burn within us, while He talked with us by the way, and while He opened to us the scriptures?” (Lk 24:22).

entries.section: 3. Humility grants healing to soul and body

paragraphs.text: 7 Be not wise in your own eyes: fear the Lord, and depart from evil. 8 It shall be health to your navel, and marrow to your bones.
We cannot practice obedience, nor enjoy trust in the Lord, by any way other than humility. Therefore he says:
“Be not wise in your own eyes.
Fear the Lord, and depart from evil. It shall be health to your navel, and marrow to your bones” [7, 8].

The wisdom that God gives us grants not only healing to the soul alone, but also offers a special blessing to the body, so that a person enjoys healing for his navel, that is, for the hidden sicknesses of his belly, and it becomes a hidden marrow within his bones, that is, for the frame of his body, or for his bodily strength. When we honor the Lord with a spirit of humility, He comes to us as a Physician for our souls and bodies, working in our hidden depths to give us life, growth and strength.

The wise man points to the healing of the navel because the believer regards himself as an embryo in the womb of the Church his mother, whose spiritual growth is not yet complete. He does not receive food by his mouth or by any other organ, but enjoys life and growth through the umbilical cord, which reveals God’s work with him through the Church. Without this divine work the embryo dies and is not born. So without divine wisdom the soul dies and has no existence in the heavenly places.
“Honor the Lord with your substance, and with the firstfruits of all your increase: so shall your barns be filled with plenty, and your presses shall burst out with new wine.” [9, 10].

In the Old Testament the believers offered the firstfruits, that is, the firstborn of the flocks and the firstfruits of the crops at harvest time. They offered them in the temple of God on the day of Pentecost (Num 28:26). By this they declared their longing to offer to God everything they possess, honoring the Lord with all their hearts and from their possessions, their works and their money. He declared to His people that the whole earth is His, and for this reason the commandment came confirming that they should not sell the land forever, for it belongs to God (Lev 25:23). So the believer feels that he has received the land of his heart from the hands of God, as the people of Israel received the land of Canaan. We are not content to offer God the chief place in the heart, but we hand the whole heart over to Him, to receive it anew from His hands as faithful stewards of what is His!

The New Testament warns us against expecting God to reward us with material blessings in return for our godliness (1 Tim 6:3-6). For God does not want to hire Christians, since He does not want them to be hired servants, but sons of His, in the likeness of the Lord Christ, in love, holiness and purity. He wants us to seek Him for His own sake, not that He may give us bodily or material gain. The reward of obedience to God is clinging to Him, enjoying a deeper union with Him, and His dwelling within us (Jn 14:15-18, 21-31). He also wants us to be content with what He supplies to us and not to covet what is more (1 Tim 6:6).

entries.section: 5. Accepting the Lord’s chastening is a practical exercise of sonship

paragraphs.text: “My son, despise not the chastening of the Lord; neither be weary of His correction: for whom the Lord loves He corrects; even as a father the son in whom he delights.” [11-12].

The Apostle Paul quoted this passage in his Epistle to the Hebrews to link the Lord’s chastening with sonship to Him, saying: “And ye have forgotten the exhortation which speaketh unto you as unto children, My son, despise not the chastening of the Lord, nor faint when you are rebuked of Him: for whom the Lord loves He chastens, and scourges every son whom He receives. But if ye be without chastisement, whereof all are partakers (that is, in chastisement), then are ye bastards, and not sons” (Heb 12:5-8).

The Apostle presents the following truths: 1. The believer receives every affliction as chastening from the Lord and not from men, for God chastens out of His nature as “God is love,” confirming His nature that radiates love upon us however severe the chastening may seem. Any chastening, even if it comes from a tender heart, is counted severe when compared with divine chastening. The Lord chastens according to what He sees for our edification and as much as we can bear! 2. If we receive chastening without thanksgiving, it turns into a bitter rebuke and we faint. It is as though what befalls us of troubles depends on our view of divine chastening: the view that springs from a filial heart sees edification in chastening, and his soul rejoices, while the grumbler sees in it a bitter rebuke. 3. All sons are partakers in chastening... without it a man is an illegitimate son (one of the bastards)!

God in His fatherly love sometimes visits us with afflictions and sicknesses for our edification, to make us wise and good. As for us, since we realize our sonship to Him, we do not collapse before trials, however heavy they are or however long they last. We never despair and never sin, but we wait for the salvation of the Lord with thanksgiving.

God does not scourge the sons of Satan; He strikes His own sons. For the coming of chastenings is a good witness that you belong to Him, as Eliphaz the Temanite says in his speech with Job during his trial: “Behold, happy is the man whom God corrects: therefore despise not the chastening of the Almighty: for He makes sore, and binds up: He wounds, and His hands make whole. He shall deliver you in six troubles: yes, in seven there shall no evil touch you” (Job 5:17-19).

* The words: “My son, depart not from the chastening of the Lord” are addressed to the free will of man. The Lord said: “I have prayed for you, that your faith fail not” (Lk 22:32), so that man may lean on grace.

St. Augustine — * He teaches us to give thanks and rejoice more and more when we are counted worthy of chastening. He says: “Whom I love I chasten.” How blessed a servant you are, since the Lord cares to correct you! He condescends and is angry with you! He does not deceive you by hiding His rebukes!

In all cases we must bind ourselves to the duty of patience, whether the trials come because of our faults, or proceed from the snares of the enemy, or are rebukes from the Lord. For the reward of this duty (patience) is great, namely happiness. For who is it that the Lord calls happy but the patient one, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

entries.section: 5. Accepting the Lord’s chastening is a practical exercise of sonship

paragraphs.text: Tertullian, the scholar — * Thus the chastening of wisdom (“for whom the Lord loves He corrects” [12]) causes pains in order to bring understanding and to restore peace and immortality.

St. Clement of Alexandria — * If God rebukes the one He loves, and rebukes him with the aim of correcting him, so the brethren, especially the priests, do not hate those they rebuke but love them, for the sake of their correction. For God also foretold through Jeremiah, pointing to our own time, saying: “And I will give you pastors according to My heart, which shall feed you with the food of chastening” (Jer 3:15).

St. Cyprian — * Rebuke is bringing sin forward and setting it before the person. This kind of teaching is necessary in the highest degree, because of the weakness of faith of many... God uses the language of pain and blows that belongs to rebuke while offering His consolations through Solomon, hinting in a hidden way at His love toward the sons who respond to His teaching. “My son, despise not the chastening of the Lord...” “A sinful man will flee from reproof” (Sir 32:21). Therefore the Scripture says: “Let the righteous correct me and reprove me, but let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head.”

St. Clement of Alexandria — * Hear the words of David: “It is good for me that I have been afflicted, that I might learn Your statutes” (Ps 119:71). And another prophet says: “It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth” (Lam 3:27). And again: “Blessed is the man whom You chasten, O Lord” (Ps 94:12). And another says: “Despise not the chastening of the Lord” (Prov 3:11). And again: “If you come forward to serve the Lord, prepare your soul for temptation” (Sir 11:1). As the Lord Christ also said to His disciples: “In the world you shall have tribulation, but rejoice” (Jn 16:33).
And again: “You shall be sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy” (Jn 16:20). And again: “How narrow is the gate” (Mt 7:14). Do you see how affliction is praised everywhere?!

St. John Chrysostom — * Let the sick be advised that they realize they are sons of God when they are scourged with the whips of chastening. For if God did not aim to give them an inheritance after their correction, He would not care to instruct them by sorrows. Therefore the Lord says to John through the angel: “As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten” (Rev 3:19; Prov 3:11). It is also written: “My son, despise not the chastening of the Lord, nor faint when you are rebuked of Him: for whom the Lord loves He chastens, and scourges every son whom He receives” (Heb 12:5, 6). The psalmist says: “Many are the afflictions of the righteous: but the Lord delivers him out of them all” (Ps 33:20). Likewise blessed Job cries out in his grief and says: “If I am justified, I will not lift up my head, for I am full of dishonor and beholding my humiliation” (Job 10:15).

Let the sick be told that if they believe the heavenly city to be their city, they need to endure labors in this city as those who are in a foreign land. For if stones must be struck with the axe outside so that they may be set in the building of the temple of the Lord without the sound of the axe, so also we are now struck with whips from without so that afterwards we may be set in inner places, without the blows of chastening, in the temple of God.
In the end these blows remove what is unprofitable and unnecessary, and through the unity of love alone we are joined together in the building.
Father Gregory (the Great)
* Now God punishes in anger the sons of wrath, but He punishes (chastens) in mercy the sons of grace.
St. Augustine

entries.section: 6. Seeking wisdom is the way of blessedness, wealth and glory

paragraphs.text: 13 Blessed is the man who finds wisdom, and the man who gets understanding. 14 For the merchandise of it is better than the merchandise of silver, and the gain thereof than fine gold. 15 She is more precious than pearls, and all your jewels cannot equal her. 16 Length of days is in her right hand; and in her left hand riches and glory. 17 Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace. 18 She is a tree of life to those who lay hold upon her, and blessed is the one who holds her fast. 19 The Lord by wisdom has founded the earth; by understanding has He established the heavens. 20 By His knowledge the depths are broken up, and the clouds drop down the dew.
“Blessed is the man who finds wisdom, and the man who finds understanding” [13].
It is fitting for the believer to seek wisdom, to labor in searching for her, and to ask the Lord to acquire her, for she grants the blessed life, and offers him true and lasting riches and glory.

He says “blessed”... because the enjoyment of wisdom makes us partake of union with the Father in His Son by the Holy Spirit. This new life is a participation in the divine life, which is worthy of being called blessed. The Lord Christ opened His Sermon on the Mount with the call to enjoy this blessed life, repeating the word “blessed...” (Mt 5). For God created us to experience this blessed life, which we receive in its full form in the life to come.

The wise man sees that the earnest search for wisdom is like a business or a serious venture which the believer undertakes in order to gain profit. Believers are investors looking for spiritual gains.

The wise man compares wisdom and the gains she brings with worldly ventures and the wealth they bring, affirming that precious jewels and the treasures of the earth cannot be compared with true divine wisdom. The former are temporal and passing, while the latter is eternal. The former is the enjoyment of some gifts, while the latter is the possession of the Giver of gifts and Creator of all. Truly blessed is he who finds the Lord Christ, who is Wisdom, leading us by His Holy Spirit in our daily life.
“For the merchandise of it is better than the merchandise of silver, and the gain thereof than fine gold”

entries.section: 6. Seeking wisdom is the way of blessedness, wealth and glory

paragraphs.text: She is more precious than pearls, and all your jewels cannot equal her” [14-15].
This very phrase is among many phrases through which spiritual investors exercise their right of choice; from this we exercise this right as free people, relying on the riches of God’s grace.
“Take my instruction, and not silver; and knowledge rather than choice gold. Wisdom is better than pearls, and all the jewels cannot equal her” (Prov 8:11).
“Better is little with the fear of the Lord than great treasure with disgrace. Better is a meal of herbs where love is than a fatted ox and with it, silver” (Prov 15:16, 17).
“My fruit (the fruit of wisdom) is better than gold, yes, than fine gold; and my revenue than choice silver” (Prov 8:19).
“Better it is to be of a humble spirit with the lowly, than to divide the spoil with the proud” (Prov 16:19).
“He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that rules his spirit than he that takes a city” (Prov 16:32).
“Better is a dry morsel, and peace with it, than a house full of sacrifices with strife” (Prov 17:1).
“Better is the poor that walks in his integrity than he that is perverse in his lips, and is a fool” (Prov 19:1).
“A good name is better than great riches, and good favor better than silver and gold” (Prov 22:1).
“Open rebuke is better than secret love” (Prov 27:5).

* Wisdom proclaims: “Blessed is the man who finds wisdom, and the mortal who sees understanding, for from her goes forth righteousness, and her tongue carries law and mercy” [13, 16 LXX]. For the Law and the Gospel are both the work of the one Lord, who is mercy, because in Him is our salvation.

St. Clement of Alexandria — The psalmist says: “The law of Your mouth is better to me than thousands of gold and silver” (Ps 119:72). And St. John Chrysostom asks: Was St. Peter poor when he had neither gold nor silver to give to the lame man?
* This means: better for me is the Law that proceeds from Your mouth, which is Christ. I despise the shining pieces of gold and silver so that I may delight in the law of Your mouth and enjoy it.

We can say that the “law of the mouth” is the order of the words that come from the mouth of God: the first words were spoken to beginners, while the following words were spoken to those who had received the first, until they reach perfection.
Origen, the scholar — * The prophet says that for him the law of the mouth of God is better than all the desires of the world, referring to the desires by the shining pieces of gold and silver.

St. Augustine — * By the allegorical interpretation, silver represents the intellect, and gold indicates the spirit. So although there are thousands of pieces of gold and silver which those who dispute with the wisdom of the world use in the schools of philosophy, yet he who lives the divine wisdom and divine truth says: “The law of the mouth of the Lord is better for me.” Truly, only the Law that proceeds from the mouth of God can offer true gain to those who hold fast to it.

St. Didymus the Blind — Thousands of gold or silver may be lost or stolen or endanger the life of their owner, but the law of the mouth of the Lord offers a riches that is firm forever, which no one can take away from us.

St. Clement of Alexandria uses the previous phrase [13] in directing women who busy themselves with piercing their ears to put very costly “earrings” in them, and with putting special cosmetics for adorning the eyes, explaining that the ear’s listening to the voice of wisdom is natural and more precious than all jewels, and that the opening of the eyes to see divine and holy things is true beauty, where the believer sees what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man.

* Do not let your ears be pierced contrary to nature, so that “earrings” may be attached to them and hang from them. For it is not fitting to compel nature to do what is contrary to it. And there can be no ornament that adorns the ear better than the teaching that finds a natural path in the passages of hearing.

The anointing of the eyes with the Word and the piercing of the ears with the commandment make a man a listener and a contemplator of divine and holy things, and the Word declares true beauty: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard” (1 Cor 2:9).

entries.section: 6. Seeking wisdom is the way of blessedness, wealth and glory

paragraphs.text: St. Clement of Alexandria — “Length of days is in her right hand; and in her left hand riches and glory; out of her mouth proceeds righteousness, and her tongue carries law and mercy” (Septuagint) [16].
* The adornment of her right hand is the extension of generations, where the Word says: “Length of days is in her right hand.”
And in her left hand is the wealth of precious virtues with the splendor of glory: “in her left hand riches and glory” [16].
Solomon then speaks of the fragrance of the bride’s mouth, which gives off the good fragrance of righteousness:
“Out of her mouth proceeds righteousness (Septuagint)” [16].

St. Gregory of Nyssa — Some of the Fathers see that the right hand here refers to the eternal good things and glories, while the left hand refers to temporal blessings on earth. Therefore the bride sings in the Song, saying: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me” (Song 2:6). This is the living voice of the Church, which seeks the eternal glories as a right hand that embraces her, but is not much occupied with temporal blessings.
* The Church says in the voice of the elect: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me” (Song 2:6).
The left hand of God means the abundant good things in the present life, which the Church places under her head to press upon them because of her exalted love.

But the right hand of God embraces her, for in her complete consecration she is enveloped with eternal blessings. Therefore Solomon says again that length of days (eternity) is in her right hand, while in her left hand are riches and glory [16].

By speaking of riches and glory as placed in her left hand, he showed in what manner we look to them. Therefore the psalmist says: “Save me by Your right hand” (Ps 17:7). For he did not say “by Your hand,” but “by Your right hand,” to point by the right hand to the eternal salvation that he seeks. Again it is written: “Your right hand, O Lord, dashes the enemy in pieces” (Ex 15:6), for the enemy, though flourishing in God’s left hand, is shattered in His right hand, because the wicked are often exalted in the present life, but the coming of the eternal blessings (on the great day of the Lord) condemns them.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
In the Septuagint it reads, “her tongue carries law and mercy,” and St. Augustine comments on this phrase, saying:
* Thus concerning the wisdom (of God) it is said: “her tongue carries law and mercy.” The Law that condemns the proud, and the mercy that justifies the humble.

* We do not nullify the Law through faith, but we establish it (Rom 3:3), for fear leads to faith. Thus surely the Law brings about wrath, so that God’s mercies may give grace to the sinner, who is terrified and turns to the fulfillment of the righteousness of the Law through Jesus Christ our Lord, who is the wisdom of God of whom it was said: “her tongue carries law and mercy.”
By the Law she frightens, and by mercy she helps.
The Law was given through His servants, but mercy He offers Himself.

The Law was like the staff of Elisha (2 Kgs 4:29 etc.) sent to raise the widow’s son, and it failed to raise him. “For if there had been a law given which could have given life, verily righteousness should have been by the law” (Gal 3:21). But mercy was like Elisha himself, who bore the type of Christ; and by his giving life to the dead he was linked to a great mystery, as with the New Testament.
* When it is said: “Let us love one another,” this is law! And when it is said: “For love is of God,” this is grace!
For the tongue of the wisdom of God carries law and mercy. Therefore it is said in the Psalm: “He who gives the Law also gives blessings” (cf. Ps 84:6).

entries.section: 6. Seeking wisdom is the way of blessedness, wealth and glory

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine — “Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace” [17].

Wisdom is not only a treasure, which we acquire by acquiring the Creator of treasures, but she also bears a kind of fatherhood or parenthood: she carries believers like little children, that they may lean upon her breast, and she walks with them on the royal way, where believers enjoy heavenly blessings and surpassing peace.

entries.section: 6. Seeking wisdom is the way of blessedness, wealth and glory

paragraphs.text: She is a tree of life to those who lay hold upon her, and blessed is the one who holds her fast” [18].
Thus Wisdom invites us to climb upon her as a tree of life, from which the fruits of the Spirit are plucked, and so we practice the blessed life.

If wisdom is a tree of life, then the lazy and the slack will not enjoy her fruit. She is a free divine gift offered to the soul that longs to enjoy her and strives to obtain her. She is the Person of Christ, who desires to offer Himself to us, but by our slackness we deprive ourselves of Him.

* Some affirm that the prophet Isaiah referred to these days of the tree of life as the present time of the Church of Christ, and that it was foretold of Christ Himself that He is the tree of life, because He is Wisdom, of whom Solomon says: “She is a tree of life to all who embrace her.”

* Rightly it was said of (Wisdom): “She is a tree of life to those who lay hold upon her.” As there was one tree in the material paradise, so there is another tree in the spiritual paradise. The one gives strength to the senses of the outer man and the other to the inner man.

St. Augustine — * The prophet Solomon teaches us what this tree of life is, in his exhortation concerning wisdom. She is a tree of life to all who lay hold upon her and lean upon her. This tree is living, not only living but even more guided by reason, meaning that she yields fruit not randomly nor out of season, but in her season. This tree is planted by the streams of water in the region of the Kingdom of God, that is, surely in Paradise, in the place where the stream springs up and divides into four rivers.

St. Hilary of Poitiers — * For the tree of life is the Wisdom born before all. “She is a tree of life to those who lay hold upon her,” as the prophet says, “and he who holds her fast is blessed.” She is a tree planted by the streams of water, “that yields her fruit in her season,” meaning that teaching, love and discernment are offered from her storehouses in due season to those who come to the waters of salvation.

He who does not believe in Christ, and does not understand that He is the first foundation and the tree of life, and cannot show God his tabernacle adorned with the best fruits, how can he keep the feast? How can he rejoice? Does he not desire the good fruit of the tree? Let them understand the words of our Lord Jesus Christ, how they become more delighted than the sons of men.
Father Methodius — “The Lord by wisdom has founded the earth.

entries.section: 6. Seeking wisdom is the way of blessedness, wealth and glory

paragraphs.text: By understanding has He established the heavens” [19].

* Solomon attributes all the elements of creation to the power of wisdom, and adorns her with many names, for by wisdom, prudence, perception, knowledge, understanding and the like he means the same thing.

St. Gregory of Nyssa — * If God is the Source of wisdom and life, and is so called, as it is said in Jeremiah: “They have forsaken Me, the fountain of living waters” (Jer 2:13); and also in the Book of Baruch: “You have forsaken the fountain of wisdom” (Bar 3:12), this requires that life and wisdom are not foreign to the essence of the Fountain, but are proper to Him, and were never non-existent, but always existent. Now the Son is all this, He who says: “I am the life” (Jn 14:6), “I wisdom dwell with prudence.” Is it not an error to say that the Son was not at some time? For this means that the Fountain was at some time dry and void of life and wisdom. What recklessness! For God promises those who fulfill His will that they become like an unfailing fountain, saying by Isaiah the prophet: “And satisfy your soul in drought, and strengthen your bones: and you shall be like a watered garden, and like a spring of water, whose waters fail not” (Isa 58:11), and although the “Fountain of wisdom” is so called, you insult Him as one barren who does not bear His wisdom?!

The teachings (of the Arians) are vain, for the truth bears witness that the Fountain of the wisdom of God is eternal, and if the Fountain is eternal, wisdom must be eternal. For in her all things were created, as David says in the Psalm: “In wisdom have You made them all” (Ps 104:24), and Solomon says: “The Lord by wisdom has founded the earth; by understanding has He established the heavens” [19]. This Wisdom is the Word, “All things were made by Him; and without Him was not any thing made that was made” (Jn 1:3).

entries.section: 6. Seeking wisdom is the way of blessedness, wealth and glory

paragraphs.text: St. Athanasius the Apostolic — “By His knowledge the depths are broken up, and the clouds drop down the dew” [20].
In wisdom He was resolved to cleave the great deeps to bring water to the earth, and by it He established the laws of nature so that the earth might enjoy the dew and the rains.

If God cares for the needs of the earth, which He created for man, and gave it the waters of oceans, lakes and rivers, and poured upon it rains from above, how would He not care for man? In His love He gives us, in our depths, waters flowing in the heart like rivers of living water, which turn the dryness and wilderness of the heart into the fruitful paradise of God. He also rains upon the heart the dew and showers of the Spirit, that the heart may enjoy all sweetness and rest.

21 My son, let not them depart from your eyes: keep counsel and discretion: 22 So shall they be life unto your soul, and grace to your neck. 23 Then shall you walk in your way safely, and your foot shall not stumble. 24 When you lie down, you shall not be afraid: yes, you shall lie down, and your sleep shall be sweet. 25 Be not afraid of sudden fear, neither of the desolation of the wicked, when it comes. 26 For the Lord shall be your confidence, and shall keep your foot from being taken.
If God cleaves in our depths rivers overflowing with sweet water, and rains upon us with the grace of the Spirit, He warns us against pride and against not seeking counsel, saying:
“My son, let not them depart from your eyes.
Keep counsel and discretion.
So shall they be life unto your soul, and grace to your neck.
Then shall you walk in your way safely, and your foot shall not stumble.
When you lie down, you shall not be afraid: yes, you shall lie down, and your sleep shall be sweet.
Be not afraid of sudden fear, neither of the desolation of the wicked, when it comes.
For the Lord shall be your confidence, and shall keep your foot from being taken” [21-26].

The words “let not depart” are repeated in this book (Prov 3:21; 4:21), and they mean the abiding of wisdom within the heart so that it does not turn aside from the truth, but the heart sails like a ship in the course of the royal way. St. Clement of Alexandria used this expression in his speech about women: “Do not wear showy fashions lest you slip away from the truth.”

When the believer sets the Lord’s commandment and His wisdom before his eyes, trusting in the riches of His free grace, and seeks a spiritual guidance for his life in the Lord, he walks in the safe way, enjoying the following blessings:
· The life of the soul, so that it is not dead and without feeling.
· Honor in the eyes of God, where he becomes the object of His delight.
· He walks in safety despite the enemy’s opposition to him, for with the bronze feet of Christ (Rev 1:15) he tramples down every opposing stone.

· He does not fear the anxieties of the near or distant future, for he knows that his life is in the hands of a loving, wise and almighty God, and that every moment of his life is regulated by the hand of his heavenly Father.

· When he lies down he enjoys deep sleep, not the sleep of laziness and slackness, but the sleep of trust and assurance in God’s work with him. He knows that God cares for him even in his dreams, and he finds them heavenly and sweet. Many, when they sleep, fear that they will not wake, but the true believer sleeps assured that if he wakes and finds himself in the presence of the Lord he will sing: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready.” And if he wakes to find himself in this world, he glorifies God in everything.

27 Withhold not good from those to whom it is due, when it is in the power of your hand to do it. 28 Say not unto your neighbor, Go, and come again, and tomorrow I will give; when you have it by you. 29 Devise not evil against your neighbor, seeing he dwells securely by you. 30 Strive not with a man without cause, if he has done you no harm.
“Withhold not good from those to whom it is due, when it is in the power of your hand to do it” [27].

What does he mean by “those to whom it is due”? Not everything we have is ours, but the needy have a share in what is in our hands. When you give it to them, you have only given them their right, of which we were merely guardians. We are stewards over what belongs to the poor; when we give them what is theirs we are counted faithful stewards, with no merit to us except in the faithfulness we practice by the grace of God.
“Say not unto your neighbor, Go, and come again, and tomorrow I will give; when you have it by you” [28].
Since the time is short and evil, let us hasten to do good to those who ask for it, lest death come upon us or upon them and we lose our opportunity to enjoy doing good with them.
“Devise not evil against your neighbor, seeing he dwells securely by you.
Strive not with a man without cause, if he has done you no harm” [29-30].

He asks us not to bear a spirit of quarrel and strife, for just as some bear a spirit of love to embrace everyone if possible, others bear a spirit of quarrel and find their pleasure in strife with many.
According to the Law it is fitting for us to treat others on a sound basis, so that we do not wrong them, but in the era of grace we rise to treat them as God treats us.

31 Envy not the oppressor, and choose none of his ways. 32 For the perverse is an abomination to the Lord: but His secret is with the upright. 33 The curse of the Lord is in the house of the wicked: but He blesses the habitation of the just. 34 Surely He scorns the scorners: but He gives grace to the humble. 35 The wise shall inherit glory: but fools bear dishonor.
“Envy not the oppressor, and choose none of his ways.
For the perverse is an abomination to the Lord.
But His secret is with the upright” [31-32].

It is fitting for us not to envy the oppressor nor imitate him, because by this we become an abomination in the eyes of the Lord. But he who walks uprightly finds in God a friend who speaks with him even about His surpassing divine secrets.
Truly, many throughout the ages envy the rich even if they are oppressors, but in the end they discover that God condemns the wicked rich, as the psalmist says (Ps 37).

Asaph almost slipped away from the faith, because he envied the wicked their success. “For I was envious of the proud, when I saw the peace of the wicked, for there are no pangs in their death, and their body is fat; they are not in the toil of men, and with men they are not afflicted” (Ps 73:3-5). But when he drew near to the sanctuaries of God, and looked to the end of their life, he realized “how they became a desolation suddenly” (Ps 73:19). He cried out: “Whom have I in heaven but You? And with You I desire nothing upon earth” (Ps 73:25), and he ended his psalm with the words: “But it is good for me to draw near to God: I have put my refuge in the Lord God, that I may declare all Your works” (Ps 73:28).
Though the oppressor obtains many temporal blessings, he bears an abomination before the Lord, while the righteous or upright in heart comes to know the surpassing mysteries of God.
“The curse of the Lord is in the house of the wicked: but He blesses the habitation of the just.
Surely He scorns the scorners: but He gives grace to the humble.
The wise shall inherit glory: but fools bear dishonor” [33-35].

With God there is no curse, but He is the source of every blessing. But the wicked person, determined on evil, since he insists on being estranged from God, deprives himself by his own will of the source of blessings, and so falls into the curse, which takes place with divine permission as the fruit of the evil work. Therefore it is figuratively called “the curse of the Lord.”

* As it is written: “God resists the proud, and gives grace to the humble” (Prov 3:34; 1 Pet 5:5; Jas 4:6). Now this grace is a gift from God. But the greatest of gifts is the Holy Spirit Himself, and so He was called “grace.”

St. Augustine — The wise are united with the Lord Christ, the wisdom of God; in the waters of Baptism they become children of God, and therefore it is said of them that they inherit glory as a personal right of theirs, since they are sons. But the fools deprive themselves of enjoying it, and consequently of partaking in His glory, and so they come into eternal shame.
* (The wise) not only receive (glory) but inherit it.

Likewise the wicked, even if they become great, become great only to receive a greater dishonor. And just as a man does not honor his wicked colleague if he exalts himself, but rather humiliates him, by declaring his shame before the enemy, so God glorifies the wicked person (for a time) in order to show his shame all the more. Pharaoh (in the days of Moses) became great only so that the world might condemn him.
St. Hippolytus
Carry me to You, O Royal Way
* Carry me to You, O divine Wisdom; I will walk in You and by You to the bosom of Your Father, turning neither to the right nor to the left.
You are the safe Royal Way!
* Let me hear Your voice in my depths, and in humility let me bow down to listen to every spiritual counsel.
Let me learn obedience that I may be like You. You, the Creator of all, bore obedience to Your Father; carry me, that I may enjoy the fellowship of glorious obedience!
By obedience You are pleased with me, and I find favor even in the eyes of men!
* On whom shall I lean but on You?!
Your bosom is full of tenderness and wisdom!
I lean upon it, and my soul is at peace; I rest and enjoy Your leading!
* Who will remove my haughtiness?
Who will give me the spirit of humility?
You alone, O Physician of souls and bodies!
Let me be humbled, that I may become like an embryo carried in the womb of Your Church, my mother!
Through the navel I am nourished by Your precious Blood, and so I am fed and grow and my image is completed.
I become in truth Your icon!
I bear Your deep humility in my soul!
* You have given me Yourself as a way in which I walk.
I enter and find You giving even Yourself to Your enemies!
Grant me the spirit of giving and generosity, that I may possess You, my precious treasure!

* In the midst of the way You chasten me with Your love; You chasten me not to take vengeance on me, but that I may enjoy Your surpassing fatherhood, and that my depths may be renewed and formed by Your Holy Spirit!
* Bring me in and hide me in You, that all along the way I may gather the fruits of wisdom with true riches and glory.
I enter and feel the warmth of Your love.
I walk in safety and assurance.
Even in my sleep my dreams, enclosed in You, are sweet to me.
* I thank You, O Way, Truth and Love.
For as I enjoy Your love, I love every brother and sister of mine.
I offer love and kindness with every good thing.
I offer my heart, which is Yours, that they may enjoy You.
I offer them from what You have given me, O You who are all love and wisdom.
So let Your blessing rest upon me in this world!
And let me experience the fellowship of Your glory here as in the age to come!

1 Hear, you children, the instruction of a father, and attend to know understanding. 2 For I give you good doctrine, forsake not my law. 3 For I was my father’s son, tender and only beloved in the sight of my mother. 4 He taught me also, and said unto me: Let your heart retain my words: keep my commandments, and live. 5 Get wisdom, get understanding: forget it not; neither decline from the words of my mouth. 6 Forsake her not, and she shall preserve you: love her, and she shall keep you. 7 Wisdom is the head; therefore get wisdom: and with all your getting get understanding. 8 Exalt her, and she shall promote you: she shall bring you to honor, when you embrace her. 9 She shall give to your head an ornament of grace: a crown of beauty shall she deliver to you.

The wise Solomon affirms the need to acquire wisdom from God through obedience to the commandment, with prayer and supplication, and the acceptance of the counsel of parents and spiritual leaders, presenting himself as an example to them, as he says:
“Hear, you children, the instruction of the Lord, and attend to know understanding.
For I give you good doctrine, forsake not my law.
For I was my father’s son, tender and only beloved in the sight of my mother” [1-3].

The wise Solomon comes to his disciples as to sons of his, so that they may be able to receive his words, which sometimes carry rebuke or reproof. His parents loved him and therefore taught him, and for his part he was attentive and obedient to them. It is as though he says:

“What I received from my parents I offer to you. They gave me the teachings of wisdom mingled with love toward me. So listen to me as I listened to them; listen so that you may receive, together with the commandments, fatherly love.”

He said this to show them that what he received from his parents and offers to them are exceedingly precious teachings. By this he draws their attention so as to find a way by which he may penetrate to their hearts.
The wise Solomon, as a son who obeyed his parents, now teaches his children not by commandments only, but also by his life as an example to them. As St. Athanasius the Apostolic says:

* The righteous father brings up (his children) well when he is diligent in teaching others in harmony with his own good conduct, so that he is not ashamed when he hears the objection: “You therefore which teach another, teach you not yourself?!” (Rom 2:21), but rather he is like the good servant who saves himself and wins others. Then the grace he received is doubled, when he hears: “Well done, good and faithful servant: you have been faithful over a few things, I will make you ruler over many things” (Mt 25:21).

Pope Athanasius the Apostolic — The wise man declares that he offers them good doctrine and a law, and as St. Hippolytus says: [It is fitting for us to note that he calls the law a good gift, with regard to the man who takes gifts into his bosom uprightly.]
This good doctrine is realized by two things: “hearing the instruction of the Lord,” as though instruction were a teacher to whom we listen, and “attending to know understanding.”
“He taught me also, and said unto me:
Let your heart retain my words.
Keep my commandments, and live.
Get wisdom, get understanding.
Forget it not; neither decline from the words of my mouth” [4-5].

* By saying, “and I shall live,” he does not ask for ordinary length of life, but asks for a life pleasing to God. Therefore he says: “and I will keep Your words,” because keeping the words of God and doing His commandments are true life and the cause of eternal life.

Anthimus, Bishop of Jerusalem — * The word “and I shall live” suggests a movement of life in the future. For I am not thinking of the present life, since he says “I shall live,” and this is certainly in keeping with the true life.

Let us hear St. Paul as he speaks of himself and those like him: “Our life is hid with Christ in God. When Christ, who is our life, shall appear, then shall you also appear with Him in glory” (cf. Col 3:3).
Let us understand “I shall live” as belonging to the future, and also “I hide Your word,” that this will be a reality, not in a mirror nor in an enigma.
Origen, the scholar — * I do not feel that I fulfill Your commandments without reward; give us the reward of this: a happy, immortal life that I may live and keep Your words.

St. Didymus the Blind — * Who can deny that the gift of life is a work of divine majesty? It is written: “Quicken Your servant.” Thus He gives life to one who is a servant, that is, man, who had no life before, but received it as a gift to him.
St. Ambrose — “Forsake her not, and she shall preserve you: love her, and she shall keep you” [6].

By saying “forsake her not,” he personifies wisdom, presenting her as a guardian and friend, for if you do not forsake her, she remains faithful in guarding you, and if you love her, she undertakes to protect you.

When St. Gregory of Nyssa speaks to virgins of both sexes, he asks them to accept the counsel of the wise Solomon, so that they love wisdom as a helper and companion to them, for she also gives love as the wedding garment without which the wedding of the soul with the Lord Christ will not take place. He sees in divine wisdom a Bridegroom for the soul, who satisfies its depths and fills it with joy.

* If a man accepts the advice of Solomon and cares for the helper and companion, that is, true wisdom, of whom it was said: “love her, and she shall keep you,” “honor her, and she shall embrace you,” by this he prepares himself in a fitting way for such love, so that he may celebrate the wedding with the consecrated guests, wearing a garment without stain. Then he is not cast out when he sits at the celebration for not having put on the wedding garment.
It is also clear that what is said here concerns men and women on an equal footing, that they may move toward the wedding.
St. Gregory of Nyssa — “Wisdom is the head (the foundation); therefore get wisdom: and with all your getting get understanding” [6].
Christ, the Head of the Church and her Foundation, is Wisdom; whoever acquires Him enjoys wisdom and understanding, where he grasps the surpassing mysteries of God and His plan for our salvation.
Let us acquire wisdom as the foundation for building the Kingdom of Heaven within us. She is our eternal treasure, our lasting account, and the cause of fellowship in heavenly glory.

How different our wisdom and understanding are from the wisdom and understanding of the wicked! For our wisdom is based on living, practical faith, while the wicked may have faith with theoretical knowledge, but they do not bear the experience of union with God in His Son by the Holy Spirit, the practical living faith through which we practice our true sonship to God.

When the Lord Christ becomes our Head, and He is the divine Wisdom, He takes over the leadership of our life, and we practice wisdom in our worship in church as in our private room, in our work as on the road, in our dealings with loved ones as with opponents, in our fellowship with the heavenly ones as with the believers who are still striving... The Lord Christ governs all our aspirations, our glances and our conduct, even our dreams! We see everything through Him, and we see Him transfigured before us in everything.
“Exalt her, and she shall promote you: she shall bring you to honor, when you embrace her” [8-9].

Some see that the word “exalt” here means “strengthen.” If wisdom is a free divine gift, and is the possession of the Lord Christ Himself, the wisdom of God, then He does not dwell in a slack or careless heart, but He strengthens His dwelling in us by living striving and the enjoyment of holy virtues, that we may embrace Him not with mere words but with practical, living love. We exalt wisdom and strengthen her in us, as the virtues surround her on every side, and then wisdom exalts us and strengthens us. She exalts us in the eyes of God as in the eyes of the heavenly and the earthly, so that even the demons fear us, for we are hidden in Christ, the true Wisdom.

* What does “exalt her (strengthen her)” mean? That is, fence her around with holy thoughts, for you need a strong defense, where there are many things exposed to danger, like possessions. But if it is in your power to exalt her, and if it is within your ability to practice virtues that honor the knowledge of God, these become fortresses for her. As an example, whoever maintains the practice (of virtue), the love of study and the rest of the chain of virtues honors wisdom, and the reward is that you are honored by clinging to her and embracing her in the splendor of heaven.

St. Hippolytus — * Philosophy was a preparation, making ready the way for him who becomes perfect in Christ. Solomon says: “Exalt her, and she shall promote you: she shall bring you to honor, when you embrace her. She shall give to your head an ornament of grace: a crown of beauty shall she deliver to you” [8-9]. When wisdom is strengthened with the garment of philosophy and by good use, you protect her from the attack of the sophists.
St. Clement of Alexandria — “She shall give to your head an ornament of grace: a crown of beauty shall she deliver to you” [9].

Wisdom makes of the believer a prince or a king who bears on his head a crown of grace and fellowship in glory, and he sings, saying: “[He] has made us kings and priests unto God and His Father” (Rev 1:8), or she makes of the soul a queen crowned with surpassing heavenly glory and beauty.

entries.section: 2. Wisdom and the life of uprightness

paragraphs.text: 10 Hear, O my son, and receive my sayings; and the years of your life shall be many. 11 I have taught you in the way of wisdom; I have led you in right paths. 12 When you go, your steps shall not be straitened; and when you run, you shall not stumble. 13 Take fast hold of instruction; let her not go: keep her; for she is your life.
The wise Solomon speaks of the positive way of wisdom, saying:
“Hear, O my son, and receive my sayings; and the years of your life shall be many” [10].

Listening to holy counsel is the beginning of the positive way of wisdom, where in a spirit of humility the believer obeys, walking in the commandment. The fruit of this way is “many years of life,” or length of days. This is a general principle or general fruit, which cannot be applied literally to all believers, since some children and youths were martyred in the prime of their lives, yet they did not die, for they are still in Paradise practicing worship and interceding for the salvation of the world. The saying here is entirely true if taken in the spiritual sense.

As for the literal side, we know that evils in general, especially anger, adultery and the like, affect a person’s bodily and psychological health besides the spiritual, which makes him lose his inner peace and exposes him to many diseases. Even if his life on earth is long, it is counted as nothing. But from wisdom springs harmony between body, soul and spirit, so that the person walks with moderation and a spirit of balance, which gives him resistance against many diseases. Sound, living and practical faith is a powerful master not of the spirit alone but also of the body as well as of the psychological side.

entries.section: 2. Wisdom and the life of uprightness

paragraphs.text: “I have taught you in the way of wisdom; I have led you in right paths [11].

In tender fatherhood Solomon comes to his hearers as a teacher and guide, opening the inner eyes of his disciples so that they may see the way of truth, and taking them by the hand to lead them into the paths of uprightness. In this he bears a shadow of the work of the Lord Christ, whom the Fathers of Alexandria like to call “the Teacher” or “the Trainer.” St. Clement of Alexandria recorded for us a book on this matter which he called “The Trainer, Paedagogos,” in which he showed how the whole world needs the Lord Christ as teacher and physician, and that He leads His believers in the way of perfection until they bear His image in themselves. He taught humanity by His Incarnation, His dwelling in their midst and His crucifixion, that they might know Him and possess Him, and He renews their nature by His Holy Spirit.

The Scripture presents various examples of teachers, among them: 1. The prophet Moses: the first leader of the people of God, who taught the people of God the divine law, and asked fathers and mothers to teach their children (Deut 4:5). The living leader creates living leaders, and each generation asks the next to lead those who come after it. 2. Bezalel and Aholiab: two skilled and gifted craftsmen who were called to teach others the making of the tabernacle (Ex 35:30-35); the skilled leader is the one who trains others to become skilled and to work with him. 3. The prophet Samuel: the last judge of the people of Israel before the establishment of the monarchy, who counted slackness in prayer and in teaching the people to be a sin against God Himself, for he says: “Moreover as for me, God forbid that I should sin against the Lord in ceasing to pray for you: but I will teach you the good and the right way” (1 Sam 12:23). 4. David: he was not able to build the temple, but he prepared his son Solomon to build the temple and to set up its furnishings (1 Chr 28:9-21); the teacher or leader is the one who rejoices in the success and growth of his disciples more than in his own. 5. Solomon: known for the wisdom he received as a gift from God, which he used to teach his people to be wise in everything. 6. Ezra: a scribe and priest who was committed not only to keeping the Law but also to teaching it to others (Ezra 7:10). 7. Barnabas: one of the teachers among the believers of Antioch (Acts 13:1), who had an effective influence on Saul of Tarsus after his acceptance of the faith (Acts 9:26-30). 8. Gamaliel: a famous Jewish rabbi, who was the teacher of Saul of Tarsus in his youth and had an influence on him in living according to the Law literally, until he met the Lord Christ and realized the need for a new spiritual view of the Law. 9. Paul: perhaps the most effective teacher of the early Church because of his extraordinary gifts. He taught in the Roman world and confronted philosophical ideas, especially Greek. 10. Priscilla and Aquila: a family who turned their house into a church, and taught a gifted, eloquent young man named Apollos the way of the Lord (Acts 18:20). 11. Apollos: a teacher of powerful influence, an Alexandrian, whose teachings paved the way for the acceptance of the Gospel in Ephesus (Acts 18:24-26). 12. Timothy: a young man whom St. Paul led to Christianity, who became a bishop (1 Tim 1:3; 2 Tim 4:2). 13. Titus: another young man whom St. Paul also led to Christianity and who became bishop of the Church in Crete (Titus 2:1-15).

entries.section: 2. Wisdom and the life of uprightness

paragraphs.text: “When you go, your steps shall not be straitened; and when you run, you shall not stumble” [12].

When the believer bears wisdom within him, he walks in his daily life with a spirit of clarity and uprightness, without fear of the future. Therefore we find him, not only in his worship but also in his daily work, walking with wide steps, working without ceasing, running with joy under the shadow of God’s surpassing care.
Walking with wide steps and running without stumbling carry the upright conduct, where the believer knows neither malice nor deceit, and does not waste his time or his work in crooked ways.

entries.section: 2. Wisdom and the life of uprightness

paragraphs.text: “Take fast hold of instruction; let her not go: keep her; for she is your life” [13].

By instruction (discipline) is meant not merely good conduct, or nobility in dealing with others, but clinging to the Lord Himself. What the wise Solomon says here he repeats in the Song of Songs in the voice of the bride, who held her heavenly Bridegroom and did not let him go until she brought him into the depths of her soul and was united with him (Song 3:4).

entries.section: 3. Guarding oneself against the wicked and evil

paragraphs.text: 14 Enter not into the path of the wicked, and go not in the way of evil men. 15 Avoid it, pass not by it, turn from it, and pass away. 16 For they sleep not, except they have done mischief; and their sleep is taken away, unless they cause some to fall. 17 For they eat the bread of wickedness, and drink the wine of injustice. 18 But the path of the just is as the shining light, that shines more and more unto the perfect day. 19 The way of the wicked is as darkness: they know not at what they stumble. 20 My son, attend to my words; incline your ear unto my sayings. 21 Let them not depart from your eyes; keep them in the midst of your heart. 22 For they are life unto those that find them, and medicine to all the body. 23 Keep your heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life. 24 Put away from you a froward mouth, and put far from you perverse lips. 25 Let your eyes look right on, and let your eyelids look straight before you. 26 Make level the path of your feet, and let all your ways be established. 27 Turn not to the right hand nor to the left: remove your foot from evil.
After speaking about the positive side of the way of wisdom, the wise man speaks to us about the negative side, which is guarding oneself against the wicked and evil.

The wise captain of a ship does not have complete familiarity with all the rocks of the ocean and the reefs and the dangerous regions, but he studies with all precision the straight course, and knows its directions, and understands its details, and so he sails with assurance. So the man of God turns aside from the rugged ways of the wicked, and does not waste his time being occupied with them, but is occupied with the way of truth, and knows its features and all its details as he walks in it with assurance.
“Enter not into the path of the wicked, and go not in the way of evil men.
Avoid it (shun it).
Pass not by it, turn from it, and pass away” [14-15].

Let us flee from clinging to the wicked in their sinful conduct. Let us avoid their ways, and not flatter them at the expense of our salvation, but let our souls be earnest in closing every door that leads us into sin. Let us not pass along with the wicked in their way out of courtesy to them, or out of a desire to satisfy bodily lusts or to obtain material or moral gains. If we notice that we have come near to it, let us turn our back to it and return from it, clinging to the Lord. Let us pass away from it quickly so that we do not fall into snares.

St. Hippolytus sees that the wise man advises us to keep away from the way of the heretics who in their wickedness corrupt the teachings, as well as from those who are perverse in their conduct, whom he calls the evil men.
* The heretics are “the wicked,” and those who rebel against the Law are the evil men; he commands us to keep away from their ways, which are their works.

St. Hippolytus — Since the way of the heretics is shining with vain philosophies, and the way of the evil men is also alluring with its bodily pleasures and its material and moral gains, therefore the wise man powerfully asks us not merely to keep some distance away from these ways, but to turn our backs on them completely. For the way of the righteousness of Christ is light, while the way of evil and iniquity is darkness; and there is no fellowship between light and darkness, between righteousness and corruption, between truth and falsehood.
We need a leader who directs our life in a direction opposed to evil, namely the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of Christ, who is able to carry us to where Christ is seated!
The wise man continues his speech about the wicked, saying:

entries.section: 3. Guarding oneself against the wicked and evil

paragraphs.text: “For they sleep not, except they have done mischief; and their sleep is taken away, unless they cause some to fall” [16].

The heretics, and likewise the evil men, do not rest until they ensnare as many souls as they can in the snares of heresies or the nets of corruption. They spend the nights of their lives without sleep in order to push every person they can toward their way.

entries.section: 3. Guarding oneself against the wicked and evil

paragraphs.text: “For they eat the bread of wickedness, and drink the wine of injustice” [17].

Their food is stolen bread, and their drink is the wine of violence. Two characteristics accompany the wicked: theft or dishonesty, and violence or injustice. Here he does not mean theft in its narrow sense, for the wicked person may embezzle the glory of God or rob the truth by distorting its image. As for injustice, they sometimes present it through sweet words full of gentleness and kindness in appearance.

entries.section: 3. Guarding oneself against the wicked and evil

paragraphs.text: “But the path of the just is as the shining light, that shines more and more unto the perfect day. The way of the wicked is as darkness: they know not at what they stumble” [18-19].

The upright way is distinct from the sinful way. The first way leads to the high city of God, where the Lamb of God, who lights it, is found; therefore the way is radiant and bright, bearing rays of heavenly glory with which it enlightens the minds of those who walk in it, so that they say: “Let me die the death of the righteous, and let my last end be like his!” (Num 23:10). But the way of the wicked bears the marks of its end, namely the kingdom of darkness.

The word “path” came in the plural in the Septuagint: “the paths of the just.” If the truth is one way, the Person of the Lord Christ, He draws believers to Himself by many ways. Truly all must have one faith, but each has his own gift. One person meets the Lord with a spirit of constant worship, another with a spirit of love and giving to others, and a third with a spirit of service and preaching, as St. Paul the Apostle says: “There are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit. And there are differences of ministries, but the same Lord. And there are diversities of operations, but it is the same God who works all in all. But to each one is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the profit of all: for to one is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge by the same Spirit...” (1 Cor 12:4-9).

* The way of truth is one, but in it is an ever-flowing river, from which streams overflow on every side. Therefore the inspired word says: Hear, O my son, and receive my sayings, and you shall have many ways of life. I have taught you in the way of wisdom, so your springs will not run dry, those that overflow from the earth itself. There are not only various ways of salvation which the righteous man uses, but (God) adds many other ways for the righteous, for he says: “The paths of the just are as the shining light” [18].
St. Clement of Alexandria — When St. John Cassian spoke about our imitating others, he warned us against being attached to one person, since there is no perfect person in whom are all the virtues.

The wise man likens the paths of the just to the earth upon which the Sun of Righteousness has shone, and which continues to send forth its rays until the light increases and reaches the peak. But the way of the wicked is one from which the Sun of Righteousness is hidden, therefore darkness prevails over it, and those who walk in it stumble.

* He says: “Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven” (Mt 5:16). Nothing is so full of light as the most exalted conversation. And as one of the wise says: “The paths of the just are as the shining light” (Prov 4:18) LXX, and they shine not for themselves alone, kindling the flame of their (illuminating) works, and not only for the sake of righteousness, but they also shine upon their relatives.
St. John Chrysostom — “My son, attend to my words; incline your ear unto my sayings.
Let them not depart from your eyes; keep them in the midst of your heart.

entries.section: 3. Guarding oneself against the wicked and evil

paragraphs.text: For they are life unto those that find them, and medicine to all the body” [20-22].

The wise man returns to ask his son to consecrate all the members of his body and his energies to the enjoyment of wisdom, so he asks him to incline his ears, and to look to her with his eyes continually, and to bring her into the depths of his heart. He asks him to store her in the midst of his heart so that she may move all his energies, desires, longings, words and conduct.

entries.section: 3. Guarding oneself against the wicked and evil

paragraphs.text: “Keep your heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life” [23].

Just as impure blood enters the heart and then leaves it purified through the arteries to nourish the whole body from the top of the head to the soles of the feet, so the righteousness of Christ enters the depths of the heart to crown the whole inner and outer being of man.
What we keep in our heart reigns over our thoughts, our words and our conduct, whether it is the righteousness of Christ or evil.

* Let us keep our hearts, and let us keep our mouths, for it is written of both. In this place we are commanded to beware of our mouth, and in another place it was said to you: “Keep your heart with all diligence.” If David takes heed, will you not take heed?!
If Isaiah had unclean lips, for he said: “Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips” (Isa 6:5); if the prophet of the Lord had unclean lips, how shall we have clean lips?
St. Ambrose — * Keep your heart with all diligence, that is, not in secret, for thoughts must be shown and works revealed. Use your hands in work, and your heart in meditation in prayer.

St. Mar Ephrem the Syrian — * Let us be on our guard with all care, as it is written: “Keep your heart with all vigilance.” For our enemies are fearsome and crafty, the evil spirits, against whom we wrestle, and as the Apostle says, we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places. How many they are in the air around us! For they are not far from us.
Pope Athanasius the Apostolic

entries.section: King Solomon and the scientist Harvey

paragraphs.text: Some see in the saying of the wise Solomon, “Keep your heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life” [23], that he preceded the scientist Harvey, who made the great discovery of the circulation of the blood that is accomplished by the heart; this discovery which brought about a revolution in medical thought. Here we find Solomon speaking calmly and with certainty, using this scientific fact to reveal a spiritual truth. Just as the heart is the center of the bodily system, from which life issues, so the heart, or the inner man, is the center of the spiritual life1.

entries.section: King Solomon and the scientist Harvey

paragraphs.text: “Put away from you a froward mouth, and put far from you perverse lips” [24].
What is a froward mouth but anger, condemnation and rashness in speech, while perverse lips mean slander and the distortion of facts.
“Let your eyes look right on (uprightly), and let your eyelids look straight before you.

entries.section: King Solomon and the scientist Harvey

paragraphs.text: Make level the path of your feet, and let all your ways be established” [25-26].

The work of the men of the Old Testament was to prepare the way so that believers might walk it with a spirit of strength and victory, with souls strengthened by the spirit of living hope. St. John the Baptist, who came in the spirit of Elijah to prepare the way for the Lord, cried out, saying: “Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make His paths straight. Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low; and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough ways shall be made smooth; and all flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Lk 3:4-6).

Thus the wise Solomon shares with the rest of the men of the Old Testament in preparing humanity to receive the Lord, so that it may walk in straight paths with strong feet able to cross the Royal Way, in which you never find a lame person! He does not walk it who limps between God and Belial, nor between fervent spirituality and deadly literalism, nor between heaven and earth, but in it the Gospel of Christ, the Giver of heavenly joy, is revealed!

* For the sake of learning, it was well said of Solomon: “My son, do nothing without counsel, and when it is accomplished you will not regret it” (Sir 32:24). And also: “Let your eyelids be before your steps” [25]. For truly our eyelids go before our steps when good counsels govern our actions. For he who neglects to look ahead, and closes his eyes when he wants to go forward to work during his journey, does not go forward to work looking ahead, and so soon falls, since he does not take heed with the eyelids of the eye of counsel to perceive where he must place the foot of his knowledge.
Father Gregory (the Great)
* He whose thoughts are free from passion looks uprightly, and his judgment is sound, not swayed by outward appearances. When he says, “Let your eyes look right on,” he means the insight of the soul.
St. Hippolytus — Finally the wise man says:

entries.section: King Solomon and the scientist Harvey

paragraphs.text: “Turn not to the right hand nor to the left: remove your foot from evil” [27].
He warns us against walking in crooked and deviating ways, whether on the right side or the left, for the straight Royal Way is the way of moderation.
* It is truly fitting for us to walk the Royal Way and not to deviate to one side of it, whether to the right or to the left, as the Book of Proverbs says.

St. Gregory of Nazianzus — * Solomon, the wisest of men, warns us not to deviate to the right side or the left side. So do not exalt yourself because of your virtues, nor be puffed up because of the spiritual heights you have reached, deviating toward the right. And do not sway toward the way of vices, toward the left, boasting of what is shameful (Phil 3:19).
St. Hippolytus — * Virtue occupies a middle position; it is said that mature courage is the way between recklessness and cowardice.

St. John Cassian — * Deviation to the right is that a person deceives himself and says that he is without sin. And deviation to the left is that a man surrounds himself with his sins, thinking that he will suffer no harm and will not be punished.
St. Augustine — And in the discourse of St. John Cassian on “how vainglory attacks the monk from the right and from the left,” he says:

* Whoever aspires to go forward on the Royal Way “by the armor of righteousness on the right hand and on the left,” must, according to the teaching of the Apostle, pass “by glory and dishonor, by evil report and good report” (2 Cor 6:7, 8).
He proceeds carefully to direct his straight course amid the tossing waves of trials. And with caution he holds the rudder, so he gives the Spirit of the Lord, and spreads His fragrance around us.

We know that if we deviate a little to the right or the left, the ship of our life is soon shattered upon the rugged rocks. Therefore the wise Solomon warns us, saying: “Turn not to the right hand nor to the left” (Prov 4:27). That is, do not praise your virtues before yourself, nor boast of your spiritual achievements on the right, nor turn to the way of vices toward the left, choosing for yourself some of these vices, using the words of the Apostle: “glorying in your shame” (Phil 3:19).
For when the devil cannot stir up vainglory in a man by means of his good appearance and the elegance of his dress, he tries to produce it by means of unkempt garb and dirty, neglected clothing.
And if he cannot make a man fall by pride, he makes him fall by humility.
And if he cannot drive him toward self-exaltation by the grace of knowledge and eloquence, he drags him down under the weight of silence.
And if a man fasts openly, the pride of conceit and vanity attacks him, and if he hides it, scorning the boasting it brings, he falls prey to the very sin of pride.

And so that the stain of vainglory may not drive him, he avoids prolonging his prayers in the sight of the brethren, but because he practices them in secret, with no one noticing him, he does not escape the pride of conceit.
St. John Cassian
Carry me in the way of wisdom
1 My son, attend unto my wisdom, and bow your ear to my understanding: 2 That you may regard discretion, and that your lips may keep knowledge.

Every person has two ears in his depths that listen to one voice or another; whoever does not listen with his ears to the voice of wisdom will inevitably listen to strange voices such as the voice of the deceiving adulteress. Therefore, before warning us against this destructive voice, he presents to us the wise, constructive, fatherly voice.

The wise man repeats this call so that the believer may listen and incline his ears, as well as his heart, to the voice of his spiritual father, and keep discretion, and gain a knowledge that his lips speak.
“My son, attend unto my wisdom.
Bow your ear to my understanding, that you may regard discretion, and that your lips may keep knowledge” [1-2].
He calls us to enjoy the living spiritual experiences which the spiritual father lives in the Lord.

St. John Cassian spoke, in the fourth book of the “Institutes,” in chapters 9 and 10, about the obligation of novices in monasticism not to rely on their own discernment, and not to hide any of their thoughts from the experienced elder who looks after them. In this way Satan cannot destroy the novice, unless he seduces him by pride and the concealment of his thoughts. The obedience of novice monks should be complete, so that they cannot leave their cells, nor go to attend to their natural needs, without permission. They obey with confidence and certainty and without hesitation as though the command came from heaven.

* Whoever has a good mind, and in humility with longing imitates sincerely what he sees, whether through teaching or by following what he sees in the Fathers, instead of being occupied with argument, in this way the knowledge of everything is established in him by practical experience. But those who begin their learning with argument will not enter into the goal of truth... Therefore our enemy (Satan) easily drives them far from the knowledge of the Fathers, until the beneficial and useful matters seem to them unnecessary, even harmful. In this way the cunning enemy plays shrewdly, making them hold stubbornly to their own opinion, convinced that what fills their unclean minds of errors is good, true and holy.

Abba Piamun — * It is written: “My son, attend unto my wisdom, bow your ear to my prudence, that your thoughts may be kept” [1]. For truly there is nothing like the heart that tries to flee (from wisdom), which fails us when it slips away with evil thoughts. Therefore the psalmist says: “My heart has forsaken me” (Ps 40:12).
Father Gregory (the Great)

The wise man asks his spiritual son to listen, and also asks him to incline his ear to his understanding.
