If listening indicates the desire to learn and readiness to obey, then the inclining of the inner ear indicates the secret, hidden relationship, for whoever inclines his ear to hear the whispers of another declares his longing to hear private, unannounced words. Together with his ear, a person offers his heart and all his feelings and senses.

The wise man used the expression “bow your ear to my understanding,” perhaps drawing on his father, who loved to commune with God, saying: “Incline Your ear unto me” (Ps 17:6). For the Father inclined His ear to humanity by the descent of His Son to us, speaking with us and we with Him as in a secret personal relationship, which the heart hears and the soul responds to with all its hidden energies.

So that we may not listen to the voice of the adulteress woman or deceiving sin, let us incline our ear to our heavenly Beloved, saying: “The voice of my beloved! Behold, he leaps upon the mountains, skipping upon the hills” (Song 2:8).
St. Clement of Alexandria sees in verse 2, “that you may regard discretion, and that your lips may keep knowledge,” a revelation of the Christian view of culture or secular knowledge, for he says:

* He advises us indeed to use secular culture, but not to linger and spend (long) time in it. For what is given to every generation in a beneficial way and at suitable times is an elementary training for the word of the Lord. For indeed, some who fell into the snares of the handmaids despised their accompanying philosophy, and grew old. Some fell through music, others through mathematics, others through grammar, and the majority through rhetoric.

St. Clement of Alexandria — The prophet Malachi used the expression “keeping knowledge with the lips,” saying: “For the priest’s lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of the Lord of hosts” (Mal 2:7). It is as though the mouth of the living believer becomes like a treasury of knowledge under the guard of wise lips, which bring out of these treasures as needed and in the measure fitting for the edification of souls.

3 For the lips of a strange woman drop as an honeycomb, and her mouth is smoother than oil: 4 But her end is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a two-edged sword. 5 Her feet go down to death; her steps take hold on hell. 6 Lest she should ponder the path of life, her steps sway, and she does not perceive it. 7 Hear me now therefore, O you children, and depart not from the words of my mouth. 8 Remove your way far from her, and come not nigh the door of her house: 9 Lest you give your bloom unto others, and your years unto the cruel: 10 Lest strangers be filled with your strength; and your labors be in the house of a stranger; 11 And you mourn at the last, when your flesh and your body are consumed, 12 And say, How have I hated instruction, and my heart despised reproof! 13 And have not obeyed the voice of my teachers, nor inclined my ear to them that instructed me! 14 Were it not for a little, I would have been in all evil in the midst of the company and congregation.
If the lips of the believer who listens to the voice of wisdom keep knowledge, then from the lips of the dissolute woman flow sweet words, soft as oil.
“For the lips of a strange woman drop as an honeycomb, and her mouth is smoother than oil.
But her end is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a two-edged sword” [3-4].

We have already spoken in this book about the strange woman, that she means a Gentile adulteress woman, because according to the Law an Israelite woman caught in adultery was stoned. Therefore some wicked women came and dwelt in the midst of Israel. Perhaps it also means the Israelite woman who falls secretly into adultery, for she is counted a stranger and foreign because she has separated herself from the divine covenant and lost her belonging to the holy people.

Her words are outwardly sweet as honey, and inwardly exceedingly bitter as wormwood; outwardly soft as oil, and inwardly like a deadly two-edged sword. Some see that the end bitter as wormwood and the two-edged sword are the venereal diseases from which many who fall into adultery suffer. Perhaps God allowed this so that through what befalls the body man may realize the gravity of what befalls the soul. If the world was shaken some years ago by the discovery of the disease of AIDS, which is often transmitted through wrongful bodily relations, humanity will be shaken when many lose their eternity and their heavenly glory and their fellowship with the heavenly ones because of enslavement to unclean bodily lusts.
By the lips and the mouth here are often meant the kisses that stir up evil, together with deceitful, passionate words.

The wise man looks at the wicked woman with her mouth of soft lips as a dangerous enemy standing holding a two-edged sword. Every pair of lips is like the edge of a sword, wherever the sword is directed it cuts and destroys... such is the mouth of the wicked woman.

* One offers this advice: “Do not notice the beauty of the strange woman, and do not meet a woman who is addicted to adultery. For the lips of the adulteress drop honey, which for a time seems soft to your throat, but afterward you find it more bitter than wormwood, and sharper than a two-edged sword. For the adulterous woman does not know how to love but hunts; her kisses are full of poison, and her mouth is a harmful narcotic. If this does not appear at once, she must be avoided all the more, because she conceals this destruction and seals this death and does not allow it to appear at the beginning.

St. John Chrysostom — * The features of the adulteress appear acceptable. I know that, for the Scripture says: “The lips of a strange woman drop as an honeycomb” [3]. For this reason I bear all this labor, that you may not have experience of this honey, for it immediately turns into wormwood. So also the Holy Scripture says: “That which for a time is soft to your throat, but afterward you find it more bitter than wormwood, and sharper than a two-edged sword” [3, 4] [LXX].
St. John Chrysostom — * Thus man deprived himself of the fruits of good things and filled (his belly) with the fruit that brings destruction through disobedience.
St. Gregory of Nyssa — “Her feet go down to death.
Her steps take hold on hell.
Lest we should ponder the path of life, her steps sway, and she does not perceive it” [5-6].

He began his description of the adulterous woman with her lips that drop poisoned honey, which she has anointed with the oil of deceit to draw every heart to her. Whoever listens to her goes down to the depths below, “her feet go down to death,” and does not rise to the summits of the high mountains and the firm hills, so he is unable to perceive the voice of his true Beloved. He loses his ability to sing, saying: “The voice of my beloved! Behold, he comes leaping upon the mountains, skipping upon the hills” (Song 2:8). As St. Gregory of Nyssa comments on this wonderful canticle, saying that the bride, having been awakened in many ways, reached the summit of happiness. Her Bridegroom spoke with her through the Fathers and the prophets, through the mountains and the hills, and now He has come to her Himself to speak with her mouth to mouth and face to face.

The danger of the adulterous woman is that her movements sway to the right and to the left, or her steps are unsteady, and so she draws the heart of the one who is joined to her to where he does not know. What is certain is that she takes the one joined to her with her into the kingdom of death.

At the beginning she appears as a serpent spreading her venom; her vain lusts form her whole being, her movements and her words, to bring souls down to death sooner or later. Clinging to her hastens the body to destruction and casts the soul into eternal death. She draws the heart and the mind away from contemplating the way of eternal life, not openly but by deceit, and with the passing of time the one who clings to her forgets the day of judgment, so his soul does not long for the crowns of glory, nor does it fear the fire of Gehenna.

The apparent marks of the way of sin are: passion, love, sweetness, pleasure, a life of luxury, indulgence and looseness... shining names attractive to man, so he thinks that life without them has no taste, while the true hidden marks of this way are death, hell and eternal destruction. As the wise man places this great day before the eyes of his disciples he says:
“Hear me now therefore, O you children, and depart not from my words” [8].
* Good, he has begun to fear the day of judgment.
May he reform his life by fear, and watch against his enemies, that is, his sins.
May he begin to set out toward the inner life again and put to death his members which are upon the earth, as the Apostle says.
St. Augustine — “Remove your way far from her, and come not nigh the door of her house” [9].
The wise man offers us this advice, which is to keep away from the way of sin and not to approach the entrance of its house, lest we fall into its snares.

* This advice which the author of Proverbs offers us: “Remove your way far from her, and come not nigh the door of her house” [8] concerns the adulteress. I wish to repeat the same thing concerning the love of money. For by entering gradually into it you fall into a sea of madness and cannot get rid of it easily. So you are like one in a storm: you struggle as much as you can, yet you do not easily reach deliverance from it. For after you fall into the evil pit of covetousness you destroy yourself and all that you possess (Acts 8:20).
Thus my advice is that we must be on guard from the beginning, and avoid small evils, for great evils come out of these.
St. John Chrysostom — “Lest you give your bloom (your honor) unto others, and your years unto the cruel” [9].

In the literal sense the wise man warns the person whom sin deceives, especially adultery, lest the husband discover what this fallen man does with his unfaithful wife, and so he loses his honor before him, indeed before the whole community, and is condemned to death, or falls under punishments that embitter his life. Spiritually, what is more serious is that what a person commits is known to heaven, so he loses his place there, and has no portion among the heavenly ones and the saints. He loses his splendor, which it was fitting for him to possess through his constant meeting with God and his fellowship with the heavenly ones, and so he plunges with the devil and his hosts into humiliation, shame and dishonor.

When a person is negligent with himself and approaches sin or stands beside its door, he loses his self-respect and forgets his dignity in the Lord, and hands over the rest of his life to the enemy of good. Sin, especially adultery, often seems gentle and kind, but it subjects us to a violent, tyrannical master, and destroys the soul and its true dignity.

* Who are strangers to us but the perishing spirits who have been separated from the company of the heavenly ones? And what is our dignity but that, although we are bodies of clay, we were created in the image and likeness of our Maker?! Or who is cruel but the apostate angel who inflicted upon himself the pain of death through pride, and has not ceased to bring death upon the human race although he himself is lost?! Therefore he who was created in the image and likeness of God and devoted the seasons of his life to the pleasures of the perishing spirits gives his dignity to strangers.
Father Gregory (the Great)
“Lest strangers be filled with your strength; and your labors be in the house of a stranger.
And you mourn at the last, when your flesh and your body are consumed” [10-11].

Evil is like a violent storm that blows and shatters everything. When a person commits sin, especially adultery, he thinks he is enjoying a kind of satisfaction instead of deprivation, not knowing that he is handing over his strength to the enemy of good, and handing over all he owns to a stranger’s house, not only in the spiritual aspect but even in material matters, since his life often ends in bitterness. He loses much of his possessions and loses the health of his body.

Perhaps he means here that when the matter of the adulterer is discovered he is obliged to provide for the woman with whom he fell into adultery, and for the child born of her, for life; in this way strangers are filled with his strength and his labor is in a stranger’s house.
“And say, How have I hated instruction, and my heart despised reproof! And have not obeyed the voice of my teachers, nor inclined my ear to them that instructed me!
Were it not for a little, I would have been in all evil in the midst of the company and congregation” [12-14].

The matter is not, as some think, a field for amusement, but it is truly dangerous, for what a man sows, that he also reaps. Perhaps we now see how societies groan from the fruits of the dissoluteness that was sown in the hearts of the new generations, and so reaped bitterness and destruction.
According to the Mosaic Law the adulterer is exposed to stoning to death (Deut 22:22), but what is more serious is that a person loses eternal life.

Although he is in the midst of the company and congregation, that is, in the midst of the Church of the Old Testament or the New Testament, he has deprived himself of her peace and joy, and has isolated himself from her by not listening to the voice of his spiritual father, his guide and teacher. He refused chastening and rebuke, and so lost his membership in the Church even if he carries it outwardly.

* Whoever relies on his own opinion, even if he is a saint, is deceived, and the danger of his deception is greater than the danger of the beginner who has handed his guidance into the hand of another. The former is like a ship’s captain who threw himself into a boat without sail or oar in the middle of the sea, relying on his skill and the art of his management. The latter, that is, the beginner, is like one who has no experience in sea travel, and asks a skilled sailor to take him aboard his ship, which is furnished with all its necessities and needs.

Let none of you be deceived and flee from the gentle yoke of obedience, resolved to hold fast to his own opinion in spiritual matters such as fasting and prayer and other signs of faith and asceticism, thinking that by this he is saved!!
John Chrysostom — * Obedience... is the denial of the self, the death of the will, the grave of passion, the resurrection of humility...

Obedience is the death of the members of the body and of the passion of the soul, and that is with pain for the beginner, at one time with pain and at another without pain for the intermediate, while the perfect feels no pain unless he does something according to the passion of his soul...

So those who wish to bear the yoke of Christ on their necks, and place their burdens on the necks of others (their fathers or spiritual guides), their way is to reject their own passions and do what they see to be in accord with the will of God.

* Without a guide there is no safety. From obedience comes humility, and from humility comes healing from the passions. For it is written that in our humility the Lord remembered us and delivered us from our enemies.

John Chrysostom — * How happy is he who puts his will to death and leaves the management of his soul to the one whom God has given him as father and teacher, for his place will be at the right hand of Jesus Christ the Crucified.

* He who obeys his father once and disobeys him another time, obeys him in one thing and disobeys him in another, is at one time building and at another time tearing down, and so his labor is in vain.
* He who obeys his spiritual father at one time and disobeys him at another is like one who at one time puts good water on his sick eyes, and at another time puts hot lime on them.

The Fathers said that singing the Psalms is a weapon, prayer is a safeguard, pure tears are a washing, and virtuous obedience is a testimony, so without confession and obedience sinners are not saved.

* The way of obedience is the shortest of paths, though it is the most difficult. And there is only one way in which, whenever we walk, we go astray: it is what we call “reliance on the self and on our own personal will.”

* Obedience is a plea before God. If you are asked by Him: Why did you do this? You answer Him: “You, O Lord, commanded obedience, and I did what You commanded,” and so you answer Him and are justified.

Traveling on this ship is safe from shipwreck. A man travels while he sleeps, just as a man travels in a ship asleep and is not obliged to manage it, because its manager is present. Such is the state of the man who walks under obedience: he travels toward heaven and perfection while he sleeps, without toil or thought of what he ought to do. For the superiors are the managers of this ship and the ones who keep watch for him. I swear that it is no light matter but is very great. For man crosses the sea of this world upon the arm and forearm of another!! This is the great grace which God does with the one who walks under obedience.
St. John Climacus

15 Drink waters out of your own cistern, and running waters out of your own well. 16 Let not your fountains overflow outward, channels of water in the streets. 17 Let them be only your own, and not strangers’ with you. 18 Let your fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of your youth, 19 The loving hind and pleasant roe; let her breasts satisfy you at all times; and be ravished always with her love. 20 And why will you, my son, be ravished with a strange woman, and embrace the bosom of a stranger? 21 For the ways of man are before the eyes of the Lord, and He weighs all his paths.
“Drink waters out of your own cistern, and running waters out of your own well” [15].
In ancient times the owners of houses and fields prized the wells they dug and the cistern they excavated as exceedingly special and precious possessions (2 Kgs 18:31; Jer 38:6).

Here he points to faithfulness in married life, where the two spouses are joined together in the Lord, so each of them drinks from his own cistern, where he sees the waters of love in the heart of the other party, counting it his cistern and his deep well and his fountain.

The wise man here presents a lofty and holy view of conjugal love, at a time when speaking of the bodily relations between spouses was considered shameful and disgraceful. Here he declares that marriage is sanctified by God, so each of the spouses feels esteem for the other and sanctity in the passionate feelings, and even for his own body and the body of the other. The Apostle Peter speaks to husbands, saying: “Giving honor unto them as being heirs together with you of the grace of life; that your prayers be not hindered” (1 Pet 3:7).

Whoever seeks passion or lustful love, or hands over his body to one other than (his wife or her husband), lets his fountain overflow outward and squanders his waters in the streets; he loses what is his, since he hands the waters of his love over to a stranger.

It is noticed that the word “well” or “cistern” in Hebrew is in the singular, as though the wise Solomon, who for political reasons fell into polygamy, makes clear here the attachment of a person to one wife, whom he regards as his one fountain, as she regards her husband as her one fountain... God created Eve alone for Adam, and he is to be hers.
* Isaiah says: “Ho, every one who thirsts, come to the waters” (Isa 55:1). And Solomon urges us: “Drink waters out of your own vessel”...

The philosopher Plato, who learned from the Hebrews, commands husbands not to drink or take water from others, but to dig first in their own land (attachment to the wife alone), which is said to be virgin land.

St. Clement of Alexandria — * If you look in impurity, desiring your neighbor’s wife, your portion will be with the adulterers... Leave your fountain to yourself and drink water from your own well. Let your fountains be yours alone and let no other drink with you. Seek the purity of your body as you ask it of the other party. For as you do not want the wife of your youth to be defiled with another man, do not defile yourself with another woman, the wife of another man.

Mar Ephrem the Syrian — * Let the fountain of your waters (your wife) be yours alone and not strangers’ with you... Then do not concern yourself with a foreign river (another woman), nor with delighting other women more than your wife. Lest, if you are carried off to another place, you practice the law of uncleanness with the other party as well.
St. Gregory of Nazianzus — And the inner fountain is the overflow of divine love which the Holy Spirit causes to burst forth in us.
* Good, then, are these waters, which are the grace of the Spirit.
Who will give me this fountain for my breast?
Let it spring up within me, let Him who gives eternal life overflow upon me.

Let this fountain overflow upon me and not outside of me. For Wisdom says: “Drink waters out of your own cistern, and running waters out of your own well; let not your fountains overflow into the streets.”
How shall I keep this water so that it does not overflow and run far away?
How shall I keep the vessel so that the crack of sin does not strike it, and the waters of eternal life leak out of it?
Teach us, O Lord! Teach us as You taught Your disciples, saying: “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal” (Mt 6:19).

St. Ambrose — If the wise man speaks here of the purity of the married, his speech also applies to the purity of teaching. The teacher who preaches what others say without having experienced it in his practical life does not drink from the waters of his cistern, nor enjoy the waters of his well. It is fitting for us to drink from the fountains of our inner hearts, where the Holy Spirit overflows with His waters in them, so we are watered and overflow upon others.
* Open the porch of your heart to the Word of God, who says to you: “Open your mouth and I will fill it!”

St. Ambrose — * All who do not love God are strangers and antichrists. Though they come to the churches, they cannot be counted among the children of God, and the fountain of life does not belong to them.
That a man be baptized is possible even for the wicked; that a man prophesy is possible for the wicked!
St. Augustine — “Let not your fountains overflow outward, channels of water in the streets.
Let them be only your own, and not strangers’ with you” [16-17].

What does he mean by the one who overflows with his waters outward and casts the channels of water into the streets? He is that fool who does not care about the value of water in remote regions, and so squanders it by sprinkling it in the streets.

Some see here a picture of some men in ancient times who did not sanctify family life, so the man was not content with one wife to care for with their children, but all that occupied him was satisfying his lusts with more than one wife, and pleasing them all by having children from him... so that sometimes he does not know the names of his children because of their great number, and therefore does not offer them the spirit of fatherhood or care for their upbringing and salvation.

Perhaps he means that whoever drinks from the outside fountain, that is, from other than his wife (or her husband), pushes the other party to give himself or herself over to adultery. While the man drinks from a fountain that is not his, he loses his own fountain (his wife), who gives her feelings and perhaps her body to another. In this way he sins against himself and against his life partner.
* When anyone diverts the energy of his thoughts to evil, he has squandered the overflow of waters upon strangers.

As long as we water the path of our life, in which thorns spread, with the waters of evil thoughts, the good plants dry up and perish, because their roots are not refreshed by the moisture of good thoughts.
St. Gregory of Nyssa — “Let your fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of your youth” [18].
“The loving hind and pleasant roe; let her breasts satisfy you at all times; and be ravished always with her love” [19].

* The Word of God is living, and the soul that receives Him is living. This kind of water overflows from God, for the Fountain Himself says: “For I proceeded forth and came from God” (Jn 8:42). The bride has an overflow of water within the well of her soul, so she becomes a treasury for this living water that flows from Lebanon (Song 4:15).
St. Gregory of Nyssa — Let the spouses walk in a spirit of simplicity with love, for as the infant is satisfied from his mother’s breasts, so the spouses are satisfied from their mutual love.

The likening of the wife to the loving hind and the delighting roe points to the purity of love and the swiftness of response between them. The hind signifies purity of body, and the delighting roe swiftness of movement.
The wise Solomon used similar words in the Song of Songs (Song 2:9, 17; 4:5; 7:3).
“And why will you, my son, be ravished with a strange woman, and embrace the bosom of a stranger?” [20].

The verb here in the original means that a person wanders or goes astray until he becomes a captive. So it is with one who falls into the snares of an adulteress (a stranger) or the wife of another man. He thinks she is attached to him and loves him, and does not know that she is taking him captive in the cords of sin that destroy freedom.
“For the ways of man are before the eyes of the Lord, and He weighs all his paths.
His own iniquities shall take the wicked himself, and he shall be held with the cords of his sin.
He shall die without instruction; and in the greatness of his folly he shall act recklessly” [21-23].

He asks us for inner and outer purity, so that we are not ravished by a strange woman through our hidden glances or thought, and do not embrace a stranger by practical conduct. For God looks at man and knows his hidden secrets and his outward actions. As the Apostle says: “Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in His sight: but all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of Him with whom we have to do” (Heb 4:13).

Whoever falls into sin binds himself with its cords, and drinks from its cup, and eats its deadly fruits. For sin carries its wages within itself, where it enslaves him, humiliates him and destroys him.
* You harm no one; rather every man is bound by the cords of his sin. (See Ps 7:15-16; 57:6).

St. Augustine — * “Let them fall into the snare (which they set)... a grave recompense, there is no justice greater than this! They hid a snare so that I would not know it, so that the snare which they do not know might catch them... The wicked is bound by the cords of his sin, therefore the wicked are deceived by that with which they wish to deceive others. Then harm comes upon them when they wish harm to others. Therefore it is said: “Let the net that they hid catch them, and let them fall into their own snare.”

He is like one who prepares a cup of poison for another, and forgets that he will drink from it himself, or one who digs a pit to make his enemy fall into it in the darkness, forgetting that he himself will first walk on the road in which he dug and fall...
St. Augustine — * The very pleasures we enjoy become torment to us, and the delights and pleasures of the flesh turn into tormentors of the one who produced them.
St. John Cassian
22 His own iniquities shall take the wicked himself, and he shall be held with the cords of his sin. 23 He shall die without instruction; and in the greatness of his folly he shall act recklessly.

He concludes his speech here with the end of the reckless “fool” who does not control himself. It is noticed that the word “self-control” occurs 42 times in this book, and the word “fool” is repeated 40 times; so those who do not control themselves live in a spirit of folly and ignorance, and those who walk in folly lose their control of themselves.
The summary of this chapter is that whoever bows himself before bodily lusts loses his self-control and lives in stupidity.
The divine teaching concerning bodily relations:

This chapter affirms that every relationship into which a young man falls before his marriage has its effect on his home in the future; for purity keeps a man in his home to drink from his good fountain. Wrongful relationships destroy the young man’s inner peace and rob him of the sanctity of the view of married life, especially in bodily relations, so he drinks bitterness and loses the sweetness of family life.
Let me incline my ear to Your voice,

entries.section: 1. Rashness in standing surety for others (irresponsible conduct)

paragraphs.text: My son, if thou be surety for thy friend, if thou hast stricken thy hand with a stranger, thou art snared with the words of thy mouth, thou art taken with the words of thy mouth. Do this now, my son, and deliver thyself, when thou art come into the hand of thy friend; go, humble thyself, and make sure thy friend.
Give not sleep to thine eyes, nor slumber to thine eyelids.
Deliver thyself as a roe from the hand of the hunter, and as a bird from the hand of the fowler." [1-5].

In the previous chapter the wise Solomon warned the young man against confusing pure love, which builds up the personality and supports the soul, with lust, which destroys the whole being of man: body, soul and spirit. Here he warns the young man against hasty, unwise love, in which a person stands surety for another without regard for counting the cost. The wise man warned against this conduct several times (Prov 11:15; 17:18; 20:16; 22:26; 27:13). According to Jewish law, a surety who is unable to pay the debt of the one for whom he stood surety is liable to have his property confiscated, and even to be sold as a slave for the creditor's account.

A young man often comes forward as surety for another out of pride and self-confidence in himself and his means, without deliberation. Therefore the wise man asks him to be humble, to cast himself down, as it were, at the feet of the debtor and ask him to pay what he owes. He did not ask him to cast himself down at the feet of the creditor so that he might forgive the debt or postpone it for the debtor, but at the feet of the debtor so that he might pay what he owes. This shows that he is speaking of a pledge given for a merchant who is able to pay, not for a poor man who needs a loan out of necessity.

Some think that the practice of standing surety developed and increased among the Jews at that time, so that some wealthy young men specialized in conducting surety transactions between individuals of their own people and strangers, their aim being to take the greatest possible amount of interest. In this they were swept along by greed, but their lives ended in bankruptcy, indeed in utter ruin. So the warning here is not against humane action and generosity in giving surety, but against wrong commercial dealings.
The wise Solomon presents to us the following principles concerning standing surety for others:

First: do not be hasty in standing surety for another, for although this surety is given by a word of the mouth, the believer is bound by the word he utters. This haste is reckoned a snare in which a person falls. Some say that a man's lips are a snare in which he falls through his own words. Therefore it is fitting for the believer to devote his energies to controlling the tongue more than the other members, and to put a bridle on it. We need the work of the Holy Spirit, who sanctifies the tongue.
* An unbridled tongue is a dangerous snare, and needs a strong bridle. Therefore one of them said: "A man's lips are a strong snare set for him, catching him by the words of his mouth."
Let us control this member more than all the other members.
Let us bridle it, and keep away from it words of violent reproach, coarse and foolish expressions, a wounding manner, and the evil habit of swearing.
St. John Chrysostom * Much talking is a throne of vanity...
Much talking is a sign of ignorance.
* The friend of silence draws near to God, and as he converses with Him in secret he is enlightened by His light.

St. John Climacus Second: if you stand surety for a person, do not take the matter lightly, but it is fitting that you neither sleep nor rest, exerting every effort so that the debtor may pay the debt for which you stood surety. In this way you free yourself from the obligation, and you will be like the roe hastening from the hand of the hunter, or like the bird flying far from the snare.

It is observed that the words "hand" and "hunter" in Arabic, as in Hebrew, are "sayyad, yad"; and that the word "hand" is common to both words, since through his ignorance he falls captive into the hand of the hunter and does not escape from it.
Ben Sirach encourages the believer to treat his brother with love combined with wisdom, saying:
"A good man will be surety for his neighbor, and he who has lost all sense of shame will fail him...
Suretyship has ruined many men of means, and tossed them about like the waves of the sea.
It has driven powerful men into exile, so that they wandered among foreign nations.
The sinner who rushes into suretyship in pursuit of gain rushes into his own judgment.
Help your neighbor according to your ability, and take care for yourself lest you fall" (Sir 29:14-20).

Once again we affirm that the wise Solomon does not command us not to stand surety, but to act with wisdom, whatever the motive for it. There is a Jewish (rabbinic) proverb: "When the fool goes to the market, the merchants rejoice."

6 Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise: 7 Which having no guide, overseer, or ruler, 8 Provideth her meat in the summer, and gathereth her food in the harvest. 9 How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard? when wilt thou arise out of thy sleep? 10 Yet a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep: 11 So shall thy poverty come as one that travelleth, and thy want as an armed man.

St. John Chrysostom sees that man, who was created in the image and likeness of God, is brought low by sin until he descends to the point where animals and insects become better than he in many matters. The wild beasts, such as lions, when they gather together support one another, and none of them attacks the other; but man, when he gathers with his brother, often has a spirit of jealousy and envy arise between them, which sometimes drives them to commit murder. Man also loses his speech, his diligence and his wisdom, so that he needs to learn these from the ant. As the wise Solomon says:
"Go to the ant, thou sluggard.
Consider her ways, and be wise.
Which having no guide, overseer, or ruler,
Provideth her meat in the summer, and gathereth her food in the harvest.
How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard?
When wilt thou arise out of thy sleep?" (6-9)
The wise man asks the sluggard to go to the ant so that he may learn many things from it, among them:

A. Although there is no leader or general manager, the ants know how to work together for the good of the community (team work). The ants preceded man in organized, collective work, without struggle over positions of power or authority.

B. The ant does not need a leader to compel it to work, but works by an inner instinct without outside pressure, whereas man often works, not out of his inner faithfulness, but out of fear of others, lest he lose his wage or his dignity.

C. Ants prepare their food in the spring, the summer and the autumn, so that they may sleep and rest in the time of winter. They work as long as it is the time for work, and keep on working for long periods, so that when the time comes in which they cannot work they find beside them what they may eat. They do not know sleep in the times of work, but labor diligently without slackness. So it is fitting for us to work while it is day, so that when night falls we may rest.
Among the insects there is none so truly diligent and constantly working as the ant; even the bee, which gathers nectar from the flowers, is not as ever-moving and ever-working as the ant.

D. The wise Solomon did not mention the ant's care for its young: it carries the young one before its growth is complete and brings it out of the hole and places it at the entrance, to be exposed to the light of the sun and benefit from it. And when it senses that rain is coming, it carries it back inside the hole, and puts a very small stone so that water does not seep in to its young. Truly the ant is counted a wonderful and living example for man of tireless work together with care for the little ones.

Some in the early ages were ashamed to be taught by a woman, even if this woman was the mother, as St. Augustine confessed, saying to God: "You were speaking to me through my mother's mouth, but I was not listening to You, because You were speaking to me through the mouth of a woman." And St. John Chrysostom marvels at those who refuse to be taught by some women, such as mothers, while man has descended to the level at which he needs to learn from a small insect like the ant.

* If you are ashamed to have a woman as your teacher, flee from sin; then you will be able to ascend to the wisdom that God gives you. As long as you sin, the Holy Scripture sends you not only a woman but an irrational creature, and sometimes a lowly one! Truly it is not shameful that it sends you as a pupil to an ant, while you are honored with reason.

* We say: Notice how a being lower than you is full of zeal and watchfulness! Therefore receive from these insects (animals) the best counsel in work, and marvel at your Lord, not only because He created heaven and earth, but also because He created the ant. For although it is small, it offers proof of the greatness of God's wisdom. Look how the ant behaves with prudence, and how God planted in this small body a desire to work without ceasing!
St. John Chrysostom * Be prudent, imitate the ant as the Scripture says: "Let it be stored up in summer lest you hunger in winter."
Winter is the last day, the day of judgment.
Winter is the day of rebellion and bitterness.
Gather what will be yours in the future, or else you will perish because you are neither prudent nor wise.
St. Augustine St. John Cassian almost devoted a whole discourse to the necessity of work and not being idle, even for those living in solitude:

* (The Apostle Paul), like a skilled and experienced physician, tries to heal by performing surgery with a spiritual weapon, saying: "That ye withdraw yourselves from every brother that walketh disorderly, and not after the tradition which he received of us" (2 Thess 3:6). So he commands them to avoid those who devote no time to work, and to cut them off like members of the body disfigured by the sores of idleness and emptiness, lest the disease of slackness and laziness pass gradually to the healthy parts of the body, like some deadly contagious diseases.

When the Apostle speaks of those who do not work with their hands, and eat their bread in quietness, he urges us to avoid them. Listen to the kinds of blame and rebuke with which he assails them at the outset. First, he calls them "disorderly," and also, "not after the tradition." In other words, he describes them as stubborn because they do not walk according to his direction, and as unseemly because they do not keep the proper, fixed times in their going out, their visits and their conversations. For the person who is not orderly is certainly exposed to all these faults.

"And not after the tradition which he received of us": by this he rebukes them as being in some way rebellious and scoffers, who have made light of the teaching they received from him and did not take care of it, and did not follow what they remembered he had taught them not in word only but also by actually practicing it... "For yourselves know how ye ought to follow us" (2 Thess 3:7).

The Apostle piles up an enormous heap of reproach and blame when he affirms that they did not heed what still remained in their memory. And those who learned it not only by oral instruction, but also received it in his own person as an example in work which must be imitated.
St. John Cassian

12 A naughty person, a wicked man, walketh with a froward mouth. 13 He winketh with his eyes, he speaketh with his feet, he teacheth with his fingers; 14 Frowardness is in his heart, he deviseth mischief continually; he soweth discord. 15 Therefore shall his calamity come suddenly; suddenly shall he be broken without remedy.

If the sluggard is condemned for his laziness even though he practices no evil, how much more will be the condemnation of one who practices evil, especially baseness! For such a man does everything in an affected manner, plotting craftily against others; a man like this loses his innocence by withdrawing from the way of the Lord, and so destroys himself.
The wise man presents seven deeds marked by deceit, which the foolish man practices.
"A naughty person, a wicked man, walketh with a froward mouth, he winketh with his eyes, he speaketh with his feet, he teacheth with his fingers.
Frowardness is in his heart.
He deviseth mischief continually.
He soweth discord.
Therefore shall his calamity come suddenly.
Suddenly shall he be broken without remedy" [12-15].
The word "base" in Hebrew means literally "a man of Belial," that is, the worthless man who is good for nothing, because his dealings are with false words.
The base man is marked by the following characteristics:
A. A wicked man: the Hebrew word means an apostate man, separated from God and opposing Him. He uses his mouth to pervert the truth, walking in crookedness.

B. He speaks not only with his tongue, but he presses into service, if possible, all the members of his body to express the crookedness, or deviation from the truth, that he carries within him. His mouth speaks crookedly, his eyes wink in mockery, his feet move to speak what accords with his corrupt heart, and his fingers point toward what he wishes to accomplish.

In the East the feet and the fingers are often used as a means of expressing certain thoughts, especially in the presence of persons from whom a man wishes to hide what he is communicating to another; so instead of speaking with the tongue he speaks by the movements of his feet and fingers, without those present realizing what the person means. Some merchants are also known to have done this when entering into the conclusion of deals in the presence of others: they sit on the ground and place a piece of cloth over their thighs, and express what they are saying through the movements of their fingers. In the same way the Brahmins convey religious secrets to their disciples while hiding their hands in the folds of their garments; thus they teach with their fingers. This was known among the ancient Romans, and the classical writers described it.

Some think that Simon Peter could not speak to the Lord Christ to ask who would betray Him, so he made a sign to Him, speaking with him in the language of gestures, for it is said: "Simon Peter therefore beckoned to him, that he should ask who it should be of whom he spake" (Jn 13:24).
Corrupt girls and dancers used to use their feet to express what they wished to say. Some think that the wise Solomon most likely meant these corrupt women when he spoke of the base and wicked man.
C. Frowardness is in his heart: if the outward members of his body are devoted to evil, the secret of this is the heart, which carries falsehoods instead of the truth.

Whoever carries the Lord Christ, the Truth Himself, in his heart, all the members of his body are sanctified; and whoever carries the devil, the liar and the father of liars, all the members of the body are used to practice his evil works and deceits.
* Purity of heart means purity of the eye with which we behold God, and without doubt our concern for purity of heart increases in proportion to the greatness of what we see with the heart.

St. Augustine * For the sake of purity of heart we ought to do everything and endure everything, and not cling to our relatives, our land (our possessions), our (earthly) honor, our position, the delights of the world and all kinds of pleasures...

We ought to do everything or seek anything for the sake of purity of heart. For its sake we seek solitude... and for its sake we fast and keep vigil and bear toils and nakedness and study, and acquire all the other virtues, so that we may prepare our hearts and keep them from all evil poisons, and thus ascend to the perfection of love...

So the things that come second in importance, such as fasting, vigil, renunciation of the world and meditation on the Holy Bible, these we must do looking to the chief goal, which is "purity of heart," which is "love." We must not lose this chief virtue because of fulfilling another virtue.

So if we do not carry out one of these other virtues for a compelling reason, no harm comes to us, so long as the chief virtue is present. It is not permissible for us to carry out a work that would cause us to lose this goal which we are discussing, but we strive for it whatever it may cost.

Abba Moses D. He devises evil without ceasing: he is not only deceived by the devil, but bears his mark, and urges all those around him to practice the works of the devil. Day and night, even in his dreams, he is occupied with practicing the works of his father, the devil.
E. He soweth discord: Father Gregory (the Great) says concerning the directions we should give to those who sow discord:

[There is a difference between the counsels given to the sowers of discord and to the makers of peace. The sowers of discord are advised to realize whom it is that they follow. It was said of the tares sown among the good wheat that an enemy did this (Mt 13:28), that is, a base angel... As the wise Solomon says, he is a base person, a man of no use, who walks with a froward mouth, and winks with his eyes, and stamps with his feet, and speaks with his finger, and devises evils without ceasing, with a heart in which are falsehoods, and sows discord.

Yes, the one about whom he wishes to speak is a sower of discord. He is called first base, because after the manner of the proud angel he first falls within himself by turning his thought away from the face of his Creator, and afterward sows discord outwardly. Rightly also is he described as winking with his eyes, speaking with his finger and stamping with his feet. For the watchfulness of the inner man keeps his outer members controlled in their order. Whoever loses the steadiness of his thought also falls outwardly into unseemly movements, and by his outward movements shows that he has no settled roots within. Let the sowers of discord hear what is written: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God" (Mt 5:9). And on the other side, let them realize that if the peacemakers are called children of God, those who oppose this (sowing discord) will certainly be called the sons of the devil.]
Truly the base or deceitful man sows discord even between husband and wife, to destroy the spirit of love and unity.
As for the end of the base man, it is to fall into sudden calamities; he is broken, and there is no healing for his breaking.

Perhaps he alludes here to the deceitful man who becomes deceived, especially by the sin of adultery, and so is suddenly exposed to stoning, according to the Mosaic Law, and his bones are broken, and there is no one to heal their breaking, or to have mercy on him as he is in the pit while stones rain down on his body from many.

entries.section: 4. Seven things abominable to the Lord

paragraphs.text: 16 These six things doth the LORD hate: yea, seven are an abomination unto him: 17 A proud look, a lying tongue, and hands that shed innocent blood, 18 An heart that deviseth wicked imaginations, feet that be swift in running to mischief, 19 A false witness that speaketh lies, and he that soweth discord among brethren.
The following statements describe the "man of Belial," and correspond to what was declared earlier in (verses 12-15), affirming that the gravest of sins is sowing discord among brothers.
"These six things doth the LORD hate: yea, seven are an abomination unto him.
A proud look, a lying tongue, and hands that shed innocent blood.
An heart that deviseth wicked imaginations, feet that be swift in running to mischief, a false witness that speaketh lies, and he that soweth discord among brethren" [16-19].

Some ask: "If God is love, does He bear hatred or aversion?" He is love, and by His love He hates hatred and aversion, and does not accept evil. In the book of Ecclesiastes He instructs us: "A time to love, and a time to hate" (Eccl 3:8). And in Deuteronomy it is said: "Neither shalt thou set thee up any image; which the LORD thy God hateth" (Deut 16:22). And in the Psalms: "Thou lovest righteousness, and hatest wickedness" (Ps 45:7), and in the book of Revelation: "But this thou hast, that thou hatest the deeds of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate" (Rev 2:6). Some compare God's fatherhood, which is full of love, to a father who loves his little child, but when he sees a poisonous snake wanting to kill him he hates it and kills it. So God, in His love for us, hates sin, which spreads its poisons in us.

The wise man presents to us a list of the things which the Lord hates. They are sins that cause above all harm to human life, as though whoever harms his brother wrongs God Himself, who desires the rest of mankind and seeks their peace and growth.
Let us look at this list not to condemn others, but to discover our own faults and repent of them in a spirit of humility, with prayer and supplication and avoiding every door to evil.
These sins are:

A. A proud look: these are the eyes of the proud, for a man exalts himself over his brothers instead of looking at them with looks of sympathy and tenderness and eagerness to give. This is the first of the things that God hates, and Satan fell into this sin (Isa 14:13, 14). And he does not cease to urge every person to claim divinity and not to trust in God, thinking he has no need of Him. Therefore the Lord says to Job: "Look on every one that is proud, and abase him; and tread down the wicked in their place" (Job 40:12). And David the prophet cries out: "LORD, my heart is not haughty, nor mine eyes lofty: neither do I exercise myself in great matters, or in things too high for me" (Ps 131:1). And God says in Isaiah: "To this man will I look, even to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word" (Isa 66:2).

* There is no fault that destroys and plunders all the virtues, and strips a man of all righteousness and holiness, like the evil of pride, which is like a dangerous plague that attacks the whole man, and is not content with destroying a part of him or one member, but destroys the whole body by its deadly effect. Pride strives to cast a man down by a destructive fall, and immediately shatters those who have reached the summit of the virtues.
With any other fault it is content to cause within a wound of limited extent; even if it resists some of the virtues, it is directed mainly against one virtue only and attacks it in particular.

To make my meaning clear: gluttony, the desires of the belly and delicious dishes destroy the virtue of chastity (self-control). Greed and covetousness stain or blemish purity or cleanness. And anger does away with patience. Therefore the man who is enslaved to one of these sins lacks some of the virtues... The person is simply deprived of one of the virtues when he yields or submits to the vice (or iniquity) that opposes it with its enticements, but he can preserve his other virtues. But when this vice once takes possession of a wretched soul, it is like some predatory (ravening) beasts that demolish the lofty citadel of virtue, and utterly destroy and demolish the city, so that the vices rise up together to demolish and throw into confusion the fortresses of holiness.
The yoke of slavery to pride is harsh and painful, and by its tearing cruelty it strips the soul and overcomes every power of virtue.

St. John Cassian B. A lying tongue: it cannot utter the truth, and bears no kindness or sincere gentleness toward the brothers. This is the second thing that the Lord hates. Lying is a mark of the enemy of good, the devil, who is marked by lying along with pride; his work is to spread this spirit among all men, so that David the prophet cried out, saying: "I said in my haste, All men are liars" (Ps 116:11), and he also cries out, saying: "Deliver my soul, O LORD, from lying lips, and from a deceitful tongue" (Ps 120:2).

C. Hands that shed innocent blood: man also bears the spirit of treachery and betrayal, like Judas the traitor. This is the third thing that God hates, namely violence and injustice, and the enemy of good was called a murderer from the beginning.

D. A heart that deviseth wicked imaginations: the fourth thing that God hates is the thoughts of evil that come from the defiled heart. For it lays false foundations for untrue imaginations and builds much upon them, setting up a building of falsehoods with which it distorts the image of its brothers and drives them into injustice.

E. Feet that be swift in running to mischief help a man to commit iniquity out of covetousness. When the heart is corrupted it draws the whole body toward evil, and the feet hasten to practice it. As Isaiah the prophet says: "Their feet run to evil, and they make haste to shed innocent blood: their thoughts are thoughts of iniquity; wasting and destruction are in their paths. The way of peace they know not; and there is no judgment in their goings: they have made them crooked paths: whosoever goeth therein shall not know peace" (Isa 59:7, 8).

F. A false witness that speaketh lies causes injustice to fall upon the innocent. Sadly, this sin which God hates has become common today; how easy it is for someone to hire a false witness who speaks lies.

G. He that soweth discord among brethren, whether at the level of the individual, or of families, or of societies, and sometimes between nations. If the peacemakers are called children of God (Mt 5:9), then the sowers of discord are called children of the devil.
These seven sins which God hates are like a mirror into which a man looks and discovers his weakness; then he hastens to God, confessing his sins and asking Him to cleanse him.

20 My son, keep thy father's commandment, and forsake not the law of thy mother: 21 Bind them continually upon thine heart, and tie them about thy neck. 22 When thou goest, it shall lead thee; when thou sleepest, it shall keep thee; and when thou awakest, it shall talk with thee. 23 For the commandment is a lamp; and the law is light; and reproofs of instruction are the way of life.

The divine commandment supports the believer so that he does not fall into the preceding sins; therefore he must keep this commandment which his father teaches him, and store it in the depths of his heart and bind it to his whole being. As it is written in the book of Deuteronomy:

"And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart: and thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up. And thou shalt bind them for a sign upon thine hand, and they shall be as frontlets between thine eyes. And thou shalt write them upon the posts of thy house, and on thy gates" (Deut 6:6-9; cf. Deut 11:18-20).
"My son, keep thy father's commandment, and forsake not the law of thy mother.
Bind them continually upon thine heart.
Tie them about thy neck.
When thou goest, it shall lead thee; when thou sleepest, it shall keep thee; and when thou awakest, it shall talk with thee" [20-22].

The wise man does not cease to remind his disciple to hear the commandments of his father and hold fast to the law of his mother (Prov 1:8), who present to him the word of God or the divine commandment.
What does the commandment offer him?
A. Inner satisfaction: he binds it continually upon his heart, and it satisfies all his feelings and emotions, and he does not suffer from inner emptiness.

B. True honor: it is an honor and glory to him, with which he encircles his neck as a sign of his kingship and of his sonship to God his heavenly Father. He writes it on the tablets of his heart or binds it to himself, and it regulates the center of his love, his feelings and his emotions, and all his thoughts, words and conduct come forth in harmony with the divine commandment.

C. A divine gift: here he personifies the law or commandment, presenting it as a teacher or trainer of the soul, a guardian of it and a friend; the commandment accompanies him as he walks the road of life, and guards him in his sleep, and converses with him in love, so that he feels neither isolation nor emptiness.

D. Heavenly guard: the true believer will not go to any place without seeking the guidance of the divine commandment. And he will not give sleep to his eyes unless he takes shelter under its wings. And when he awakes he enters with it into a conversation of love, through prayer and the study of the Holy Bible, and his whole being is filled with joy and satisfaction. He gives the firstfruits of his day, the early morning, to God, where he meets Him, speaking as a son with his father, and holds fast to the divine promises to plead for His heavenly mercies.
E. Inner enlightenment:
"For the commandment is a lamp; and the law is light; and reproofs of instruction are the way of life" [23].

The commandment illumines our depths, so that we see the truth about ourselves and realize our constant need of the Savior. We also discover the work of the Holy Trinity in us and are filled with hope, and our eyes are opened to the knowledge of the divine will and the understanding of the divine mysteries. Thus we accept every discipline from the Lord and count it beneficial to our depths, for it draws us away from the pleasures of sins and their enticements to walk in the way of eternal life; it draws us away from the deceits of the evil one to receive divine truth and purity.

24 To keep thee from the evil woman, from the flattery of the tongue of a strange woman. 25 Lust not after her beauty in thine heart; neither let her take thee with her eyelids. 26 For by means of a whorish woman a man is brought to a piece of bread: and the adulteress will hunt for the precious life. 27 Can a man take fire in his bosom, and his clothes not be burned? 28 Can one go upon hot coals, and his feet not be burned? 29 So he that goeth in to his neighbour's wife; whosoever toucheth her shall not be innocent. 30 Men do not despise a thief, if he steal to satisfy his soul when he is hungry; 31 But if he be found, he shall restore sevenfold; he shall give all the substance of his house. 32 But whoso committeth adultery with a woman lacketh understanding: he that doeth it destroyeth his own soul. 33 A wound and dishonour shall he get; and his reproach shall not be wiped away.
He returns to the sin of adultery, of which the wise Solomon has often spoken, and which some call "the sin of the age." Strangely, many drink this sin like water, and count it a kind of love!
How many marriages, among the young or the old, have been destroyed by a third party, a man or a woman, who came in to rob the spouses of their unity.
"To keep thee from the evil woman, from the flattery of the tongue of a strange woman" [24].
By realizing the wisdom of God and accepting His disciplines we are kept from the sweet and deceitful tongue of the adulterous woman, so as to receive the firm words of God, which are full of truth.
The words of the evil woman carry desires mixed with poison, but the words of the Lord are love full of eternal life. Therefore we listen to the tongue of the Lord, not the tongue of wicked women.
"Lust not after her beauty in thine heart; neither let her take thee with her eyelids" [25].
The wise Solomon presents to us his bitter experiences, for he fell into the snares of the beauty of women, and so turned aside to the worship of idols and shared in their abominations.
The care of women to beautify their eyes and the lashes of their eyelids so that the eyes appear wide and attractive is an ancient matter in the East.

It is not the beauty of a woman nor her care for her appearance that is the secret of man's fall, but the deviation of the heart. Therefore the wise man says: "Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life" (Prov 4:23). Sin begins in the heart, therefore he warns us: "Lust not after her beauty in thine heart."

* Do not let the desire for beauty overcome you. For many nets and snares are set by Satan. Looking at an adulteress is a snare set for the one who loves her. (The corruption of) our eyes is nets set for us, as it is written: "neither let her take thee with her eyelids." Therefore we set nets for ourselves, and we fall into them and are entangled. We bind ourselves with chains as it is written: "for every one is bound with the cords (ropes) of his sins."
St. Ambrose The blessed Clement of Alexandria wrote in his discourse "On Virgins":

* Therefore we do not permit any person whatever to sit (for long periods) with a married woman, and still more not to live in one house with a maiden who has offered her life as a vow, nor to sleep where she sleeps, nor to be her constant companion. For this is a thing that those who fear the Lord abhor and hate.
St. Clement of Rome "For by means of a whorish woman a man is brought to a piece of bread: and the adulteress will hunt for the precious life" [26].

In the Septuagint, the Vulgate and the Syriac it reads: "For the hire of a harlot is a single loaf of bread." It is as though the man hires the harlot at a paltry price, a loaf of bread, but does not realize that she draws another price, his own precious soul. A person thinks that sin is very cheap and costs him nothing, while he loses his inner life and his eternal salvation.
"Can a man take fire in his bosom, and his clothes not be burned?
"Can one go upon hot coals, and his feet not be burned?
So he that goeth in to his neighbour's wife.
Whosoever toucheth her shall not be innocent" [27-29].

To be lax with the sin of adultery is to play with fire: his lust blazes up as a fire that burns his clothes so that he becomes naked in shame, and it scorches his feet so that he tastes bitterness and cannot complete the journey of his life as is fitting for him, and it also burns every longing for purity, so that he is not innocent in the eyes of God and men.

* Let us flee from (this fire of lust) although it follows us, not only running behind us but also within us. Let us take heed with all diligence lest, while we flee from it, we carry it within us. For we would rather only flee, but if we do not cast it completely out of our minds we have rather held on to it and not let it go.

Let us leap and pass over it, lest it be said to us: "Walk in the flame of your fire which you have kindled" (Isa 50:11). For just as one who takes fire into his bosom burns his clothes, so one who walks on burning coals must needs have his feet scorched, as it is written: "Can one go upon hot coals, and his feet not be burned?" [28].
St. Ambrose * Evil lust is like a flame and fire. Does fire burn a garment, and the lust of adultery not burn the soul?!
St. Augustine * If the eye falls upon a person, at least do not let the inner affection follow it. For looking is not a sin, but a man must be careful that it not become a source of sin.
Let the bodily eye look, and let the eye of the heart be closed, and let humility of mind remain.

We have a Lord who is strict and forbearing... The Lord says: "Whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart" (Mt 5:28). He did not say: "Everyone who looks commits adultery," but "whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her." He condemns the inner lust, not the glance.

St. Ambrose * Lest you say: What harm is there in the eyes, since the look is not necessarily corrupting? He shows you that lust is a fire and that the body is like a garment. The latter can be an easy prey, for lust is tyrannical. The harm does not occur within only, but extends and goes forth until it finds an outlet outside. For whoever looks at a woman, even if he flees from the temptation, is not completely pure from lust.

And why should a man remain in toil when it is in his power to avoid it and be freed from it? See what Job says: "I made a covenant with mine eyes not to think of another's wife." So he knows the danger of corruption. And for the same reason Paul subdued his body and brought it into bondage. And in a symbolic way, whoever allows an impure thought to dwell in his heart keeps a fire in his bosom. And whoever practices sin in deed walks on coals and destroys himself.

St. Hippolytus If a thief cannot justify himself before the law even if he stole in order to eat because he was hungry, what excuse is there for the adulterer who commits the sin and destroys his own soul?!
"Men do not despise a thief, if he steal to satisfy his soul when he is hungry.
But if he be found, he shall restore sevenfold; he shall give all the substance of his house.
But whoso committeth adultery with a woman lacketh understanding.
He that doeth it destroyeth his own soul.
A wound and dishonour shall he get; and his reproach shall not be wiped away" [30-33].

People pity the poor man who steals in order to eat, but the law does not acquit him; it requires him to restore sevenfold what he stole, and if he has not the means to pay, he is sold as a slave (Ex 22:1-4; Lev 25:39).

* The thief is a grave offender, but the adulterer is graver than he. For the former acts so for a pitiable reason, yet at the same time need constrains him to it, whereas the latter has no necessity constraining him; rather his madness makes him rush into the pit of iniquity.

St. John Chrysostom Whoever commits adultery with a married woman is exposed not only to shame but also to death [33]. Among the Romans, if a man was caught committing this act, the husband had the right to hold to the law and kill him, so that the adulterer is in disgrace and loses his life.
"For jealousy is the rage of a man: therefore he will not spare in the day of vengeance.
He will not regard any ransom; neither will he rest content, though thou givest many gifts." [24-25].

Here he speaks of the jealousy of the husband whose wife the adulterer has violated; he takes vengeance for his dignity and honor, and does not ask for a ransom however great, but demands the death of the adulterer.
Let me act in the spirit of wisdom and love,

1 My son, keep my words, and lay up my commandments with thee. 2 Keep my commandments, and live; and my law as the apple of thine eye. 3 Bind them upon thy fingers, write them upon the table of thine heart. 4 Say unto wisdom, Thou art my sister; and call understanding thy kinswoman: 5 That they may keep thee from the strange woman, from the stranger which flattereth with her words.

As is his custom, the wise Solomon calls us to listen to the voice of the commandment and to concentrate on it, for the divine commandment presented to us by our fathers and guides is more precious than all the treasures of the earth. Its blessings are as follows:
First: a source of life. "My son, keep my words, and lay up my commandments with thee."

By saying "Keep... lay up my commandments," he affirms that we must be occupied with the Holy Bible, not to be read hastily, but to be stored in the depths of the heart, so that the word of God becomes daily nourishment for the soul and an inseparable part of our life.
"Keep my commandments, and live" [1, 2].

The divine commandments are spirit and life (Jn 6:23); they raise the soul from death to give it the new life in Christ Jesus. They transform the carnal man into a spiritual man, that he may enjoy the spiritual body instead of the natural (1 Cor 2:14) and enter into the Kingdom of God, which flesh and blood cannot inherit (1 Cor 15:50). This is accomplished by the commandment, which presents to him the person of "the divine Word." For the commandment is not merely an order for excellent moral conduct or a prohibition of vice, but a living encounter with the person of the Lord Christ, the Word of God, who said: "I am the life," and "I am the resurrection." Without Him the soul remains in the tomb of sin, bearing the odor of corruption, until it hears the divine voice: "Lazarus, come forth," and the Lord commands His disciples (His priests) to loose its bands, and the soul enjoys the new life.
When we open the door of the heart to the Lord Christ, the word of God who gives life, He dwells in us, and sin flees and cannot remain.

The commandment of the Gospel is the axis of the life of every Christian. Therefore, when St. John Cassian spoke in his book the Institutes about the monastic life in Egypt as an ideal Christian life, he called monasticism an evangelical or Christian life that revolves around the Gospel of the Lord Christ.

Bishop Ignatius Brianchaninov says: [The holy monks of old call the monastic life a life according to the commandments of the Gospel. St. John Climacus defines the monk thus: "A monk is one who is led by the commandments of God alone, the word of God, at all times, in every place, and in every matter." The monks under St. Pachomius the Great were bound to keep the Gospel by heart, so that it might always be before the eyes of the mind and be imprinted on the soul, so that it might fulfill it easily and successfully. The blessed Elder Seraphim said: "We must thus train ourselves that our mind may meditate on the law of the Lord, which becomes the leader of our life and the regulator of it"... The Holy Spirit teaches and leads the true servants of God who have become His.]
Second: a source of light and spiritual insight. "Keep... my law as the apple of thine eye" [2].

It is the inner insight, by which we look to see God in His glory, and perceive heaven with all its hosts, and by which we have a sound view of mankind and all creation, as of the body and temporal life. If the commandment is broken we remain in darkness and lose sight. If the eye is very precious in a person's life, its pupil is the most precious thing a person cherishes. The word "pupil" came in Hebrew to mean a very tiny man, a "mini man." So the text would be: "my law as a little man in thine eye." When a person draws near to look into another person's eyes, he sees his own image imprinted on them. Here the father advises his son to draw very near to the commandment, so that the image of the commandment may be imprinted on his eyes, and the commandment shine forth in them, so that he sees everything through the commandment. The same expression is used in (Deut 32:10; Ps 17:8).

Origen sees in the Lord Christ's address to the holy soul, His bride: "Thou hast doves' eyes" (Song 4:2), an indication of her nearness and cleaving to the Holy Spirit, so that His image appears imprinted on the pupils of her eyes, to see everything through the Holy Spirit.

Concerning this expression it is said: "The eyeball, and in its center the pupil, has been called the apple because its shape is round. Because of its great value and for the sake of its strict protection, the two eyelids surrounding it close automatically when there is the slightest possibility of danger; therefore it has become a symbol of what is very precious and must be guarded with care. So it is fitting for us to take care of the commandment and surround it with our whole being, lest we break it and be exposed to spiritual blindness. It seems very small like the pupil of the eye, but it is exceedingly precious: without it we do not see the open gates of heaven, and at the same time it can easily suffer grave damage."
Third: a support for worship and work. "Bind them upon thy fingers" [3]

Thus whenever you lift up your arms in prayer you speak with God through His commandment, which is full of divine promises. And if you stretch out your hands to work, you do everything through it, so that your work is holy. The commandment is bound about the neck as an indication of the mark of kingship and the surpassing honor that we receive through it, and it is bound on the fingers to support us in our prayers and our practical conduct.

Some of the Jews were accustomed to put some texts of the Holy Bible in a leather case and bind it on their foreheads or their arms during prayer. The leather case was bound around the left arm with seven straps, and then the strap was wound seven times around the middle finger.

Some think that binding them on the fingers is realized in many ways, among them engraving them on rings. Kings and great men used to engrave their names on rings, and when the king trusted a person he gave him his ring to seal every royal command with it. So in place of our names we engrave the commandment of God on the fingers, to seal our thoughts, our words, our deeds and our prayers with the seal of the commandment, so that they carry heavenly power.
Fourth: preserving feelings and emotions. "Write them upon the table of thine heart" [3]

It is not enough to bind the commandment on the arm and the finger; it must be bound to the heart. It establishes the Kingdom of God within you, and so preserves and sanctifies every emotion, feeling and sensation, and all your works come forth from a heart pure and faithful to God. Thus the commandment is bound to our whole inner being and is not merely an outward ornament in which we take pride before men.
Fifth: entering into a relationship of kinship. "Say unto wisdom, Thou art my sister; and call understanding thy kinswoman" [4].

Although the book of Proverbs is concerned with the fitting and wise conduct of the believer in all aspects of his life, yet through its lines it brings the believer into the encounter with "the incarnate Wisdom of God," so that the soul may accept union with Him and share His nature, and practice the new, risen life. It is occupied with the Bridegroom dwelling in its depths and converses with Him in a spirit of love and joy. Thus its conduct changes, not in its outward appearance only, but in its hidden roots.

Through wisdom we are made worthy to belong to the heavenly family, and so we count our Christ as the firstborn Brother, who is the Creator, the Savior and the Almighty and wise Lord. When the soul calls to wisdom: "My sister, my kinswoman," it bears a kind of respect for wisdom together with intense nearness to her, and enters with her into a kinship resembling "blood kinship," and has a special boldness before her.

The calling of wisdom "my sister" points to a marital union, for the word brother or sister is sometimes used for a husband or wife (Gen 20:2, 12; 26:7; Song 4:9, 10, 12; 5:1, 2). If adultery comes to a person as a woman who wishes to unite with him to satisfy his fleshly lusts, Wisdom truly comes forward as the Bridegroom of the soul, uniting with her eternally, to satisfy all her needs on a joyful heavenly level, so that the believer lacks nothing! When Wisdom came incarnate, many adulterers and tax collectors gathered around Him, who truly found what satisfied their inner depths, and left corruption, not by compulsion, nor in repression, but with a true joy that cannot be expressed!

The personification of Wisdom here is important, for it prepares the way for (chapters 8 and 9), where Wisdom comes forward as a being who invites us to her own banquet, which is the banquet of the eternal wedding.
Sixth: protection from the deceit of evil. "That they may keep thee from the strange woman, from the stranger which flattereth with her words" [5].

After presenting the commandment in its positive work, where it gives the soul life, enlightenment, true worship and holy work, and preserves and sanctifies feelings and emotions, and brings us into belonging to heaven, it also, on the negative side, keeps us from the deceits of the evil enemy, especially through the words of the flattering adulteress. It alone is able to protect us from the shame of defiled relationships with a wicked strange woman. For none will keep a man from the folly of the adulteress except the Lady (Wisdom).

entries.section: 2. Warning against the wiles of the adulteress

paragraphs.text: 6 For at the window of my house I looked through my casement, 7 And beheld among the simple ones, I discerned among the youths, a young man void of understanding, 8 Passing through the street near her corner; and he went the way to her house, 9 In the twilight, in the evening, in the black and dark night: 10 And, behold, there met him a woman with the attire of an harlot, and subtil of heart. 11 (She is loud and stubborn; her feet abide not in her house: 12 Now is she without, now in the streets, and lieth in wait at every corner.) 13 So she caught him, and kissed him, and with an impudent face said unto him, 14 I have peace offerings with me; this day have I payed my vows. 15 Therefore came I forth to meet thee, diligently to seek thy face, and I have found thee. 16 I have decked my bed with coverings of tapestry, with carved works, with fine linen of Egypt. 17 I have perfumed my bed with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon. 18 Come, let us take our fill of love until the morning: let us solace ourselves with loves. 19 For the goodman is not at home, he is gone a long journey: 20 He hath taken a bag of money with him, and will come home at the day of the new moon.

Since the wise Solomon tasted the bitterness of marriage to pagan women, and his feet slipped into the worship of their pagan gods, he was therefore occupied in this book with the good wife, for he closed it with the most wonderful song in which he praises the good wife. And in order to reveal her importance, he spoke in the body of the book of three kinds of wicked wives, to prepare for this song by presenting the negatives first. These three kinds, the opposite of the good wife, are:
* The adulterous, unfaithful woman (Prov 2:16-17; 7:5, 10-11; 22:14; 30:20).
* The quarrelsome and sulky woman (Prov 21:9, 19; 25:24; 27:15).
* The woman beautiful in form but without wisdom or discretion (Prov 11:22).

The wise Solomon presents to us a tragic story in which he declares the role of the adulterous woman as she snares a foolish young man in her trap. In this story the wise man appears himself as an eyewitness of an event he watched through the window of his house, when he saw a foolish young man void of understanding hunted by a married woman who seduces him to commit sin. What he saw is an example among countless numbers of simple ones who fall every day into the deceit of evil.

He says: "For at the window of my house I looked through my casement" [6]. The wise man speaks as an eyewitness, presenting a practical, realistic account. The wise man himself looks out secretly to see the tragic scene of the unfaithful wife who plays the part of a harlot hunting the simple. Perhaps by this scene he reminds us of what was carved on pieces of ivory in many regions of Phoenicia, namely the goddess Ashtoreth looking out of the window. Her worship was linked with adultery, as priestesses devoted themselves to this work in the pagan temples. What a difference between the wise man who looks out in bitterness in order to cry out, guide and rescue, and the goddess who looks out to find her pleasure in the corruption of people's lives and their eternal perdition.
