The wise man describes the young man who fell into the cords of this adulteress as follows:

entries.section: 2. Warning against the wiles of the adulteress

paragraphs.text: First: "void of understanding" [7], that is, he has trivial thinking; wisdom has no place in his depths, and he does not seek it with any seriousness.

entries.section: 2. Warning against the wiles of the adulteress

paragraphs.text: Second: "passing through the street" [8]; he has no serious aim in his life, but passes along the road wandering idly, occupied with nothing important in his life. Perhaps this trait is among the most dangerous, that a person be empty of mind and heart and without work, like one who loiters in the streets without aim. As St. John Cassian says: "He who works is attacked by one demon, but he who does not work is attacked by all the demons."
Third: "Passing... near her corner, and he went the way to her house" [8]. He does not guard against falling, nor does he flee from danger; he is like one who drives his car through a red light.

We can say that he missed the way, for his inner lusts drew him toward the place of sin. We do not blame the sinful woman as much as we blame the young man who went to her door to meet her so that she seduced him. Sin lay hidden in his heart, so he responded to the call of the evil outside.

entries.section: 2. Warning against the wiles of the adulteress

paragraphs.text: Fourth: he walks "in the twilight, in the evening, in the black and dark night" [9]. He does not know the light, nor walk by day, nor enjoy the rays of the Sun of Righteousness. He also walks outside the circle of Christ, where there is darkness of heart and mind. Verse 9 contains five Hebrew words, all of which mean "darkness," to affirm that the adulteress does not bring the one she snares only to the end of his day, but into the very darkness. For if the adulteress has submitted to the authority of "the prince of darkness," she finds her pleasure in capturing others with her, so that all may live with her in the humiliation of darkness. It is said in the Gospel according to our teacher John the Beloved: "Men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil" (Jn 3:19), "I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life" (Jn 8:12).
The wise man presents to us an exact description of a woman who incites a young man to sin, her lust inflamed:

entries.section: 2. Warning against the wiles of the adulteress

paragraphs.text: First: she wears "the attire of an harlot" [10], to stir up thoughts in those around her inclined toward evil. She is married, but with boldness, without modesty or shame, she seeks evil, and uses all the methods of the world to entice.
Second: "subtil of heart" [10]; what she says and how she behaves differ from what she harbors in her depths. No sign of divine grace appears on her.

entries.section: 2. Warning against the wiles of the adulteress

paragraphs.text: Third: "She is loud and stubborn" [11]. She does not have the grace of inner quiet or balance in her conduct, but is full of clamor and noise. She knows no inner rest; however many sweet words she offers or however cheerful her face, she is always in a state of anxiety and clamor. As Isaiah the prophet says: "There is no peace, saith the LORD, unto the wicked" (Isa 48:22; 57:21). She is also obstinate, hard-headed and violent, and knows no control of her feelings and conduct. As it is said: "Israel slideth back as a backsliding heifer" (Hos 4:16).

Fourth: "her feet abide not in her house" [11], for she finds her pleasure in the streets and public squares, not in her house, contrary to what the Apostle Paul advises the young women, saying: "To love their husbands, to love their children, to be discreet, chaste, keepers at home, good, obedient to their own husbands, that the word of God be not blasphemed" (Titus 2:4, 5).

entries.section: 2. Warning against the wiles of the adulteress

paragraphs.text: She does not stay in her house, but runs in the streets to set her nets and hunt the simple and the foolish. "Now is she without, now in the streets, and lieth in wait at every corner" [12]. Sin is very easy to come by; it throws itself upon every person in order to attract him. The wise man portrays the adulteress as having a house, not a home; she has a building but not a family that enjoys its warmth, and she does not shed on them her love and care. She may have a husband and children, but they have no place in her heart, nor in her thoughts. She finds her pleasure in going out of her house to set her nets and hunt the simple. Therefore the Apostle advises the young women to be "chaste, keepers at home, good" (Titus 2:5).

entries.section: 2. Warning against the wiles of the adulteress

paragraphs.text: Fifth: she bears the image of love and gentleness in her dealings: "So she caught him, and kissed him" [13]. She embraces him with her arms and kisses him with her mouth, and the young man thinks he is happy and has found what satisfies him, and does not realize that she offers him lust, not love.
Sixth: she bears the image of religiosity.
"With an impudent face said unto him:
I have peace offerings with me; this day have I payed my vows. Therefore came I forth to meet thee, diligently to seek thy face, and I have found thee" [13-15].

She pretends to be religious, offering peace offerings, which are voluntary sacrifices (Lev 7), and she invites him to share with her in a religious meal. Thus he thinks that he has not sinned, for he has found one who is religious, and who offers him love along with the food. She snares him by deceit and draws him through his belly.

* When the stomach is filled with all kinds of food, the seeds of lust are generated, and the mind, when it is weighed down with food, cannot keep the control of its thoughts. For the mind is made drunk not only by wine but also by the abundance of kinds of food, which weaken it and rob it of all its power and capacity for pure, clean contemplation.

St. John Cassian * Just as the ear of purity is the product of the seed of sweat in fasting, so excessive fullness causes dissolution and excess produces defilement. But if the belly is left hungry and humbled, shameful thoughts will not rush into the soul.

St. Isaac the Syrian Perhaps she wanted to express to him how much she cared for him: she made a vow to God for his sake that He might give him health and safety, and now she invites him to share in this special banquet of the vow. She is more occupied with his health and peace than with herself!

We often fall into troubles because of our concentration on outward appearances, so that we wear the mask of religiosity to hide a corrupt heart, or as St. Augustine says, that we find in the Church some who wear sheep's clothing, but inside them are the hearts of ravening wolves. When a king was being chosen according to God's heart, the Lord said to Samuel: "Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature... for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart" (1 Sam 16:7).

If the wicked woman hunts the young man by the deceptive outward appearance, the young man surrenders himself to adultery not only through his laxity with the causes of sin, but also through his arrogance and love of vainglory.
* Vainglory is the servant of adultery.
* The man who boasts of his practice of virtue is allowed to fall into adultery. And he who is full of imaginations because of his wisdom is allowed to fall into the dark nets of ignorance.

St. Isaac the Syrian Some interpret this verse as meaning that the woman seduces the young man by being ceremonially clean, so that she thinks that whoever clings to her in bodily relations is not defiled, although this opinion is not acceptable. Others see that she makes clear to him that she is clean from "the monthly sickness." For whoever lies with a woman in her menstruation is unclean seven days (Lev 15:24). Or perhaps she makes clear to him that he may be joined to her without fear, since she is not exposed to pregnancy. In any case, she links adultery with worship, which was known among the Phoenicians in their worship of the goddess Ashtoreth, and the Law warned against this. Also by her saying: "this day have I payed my vows" she means that she has offered peace offerings, and according to the Law she may eat from the sacrifice on the day on which the sacrifice was offered and the day after. It is as though she says to him: "I have an abundance of delicious food for us to enjoy." Thus she draws him by the lust of his belly. For she knows that she can hunt his heart through his stomach.

She pretends that she came out to seek his face, and did not cease searching until she found him! These are words of deceit, for she is not seeking a particular person but seeking what is for herself, to satisfy her emotions or instincts, and in his folly the one who has fallen a victim in her hands thinks that he is the very important person sought by her. She confuses his concepts so that he does not distinguish between love and lust.
Seventh: she invites him to enjoy a marital night.
"I have decked my bed with coverings of tapestry, with carved works, with fine linen of Egypt.
I have perfumed my bed with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon.
Come, let us take our fill of love until the morning.

entries.section: 2. Warning against the wiles of the adulteress

paragraphs.text: Let us solace ourselves with loves" [16-18].
Besides her moral dissolution and the inflaming of her fleshly lusts, this woman is marked by betrayal of her husband and unfaithfulness.

She uses every sensory means to attract this foolish young man: the luxurious, soft bed, the precious linen, and the alluring perfumes. She wants to attract him with all the senses: he sees the provocative clothes and the bed spread with coverings of tapestry, and hears the sound of her invitation since she sought him and searched for him until she found him, and feels her affection until morning, and tastes the sweetness of her lips, and smells the perfumes. Thus sin enters us through the five senses, therefore the Holy Bible is concerned with sanctifying these senses, not destroying them, but raising and directing them to be satisfied with what is for building, not tearing down.

Sadly she invites the young man to sin with her on her bed, which she shares with her husband, and so offers him what belongs to her bridegroom for the account of evil. We offer the heart to the kingdom of darkness instead of the kingdom of light, and turn our mind into a stage for evil instead of the manifestation of heaven in it, and squander our emotions, feelings and sensations instead of sanctifying them.
Eighth: the circumstances are prepared for the pleasure of love; nothing lacks for them except his consent and response to her.
"For the goodman is not at home.
He is gone a long journey.
He hath taken a bag of money with him.

entries.section: 2. Warning against the wiles of the adulteress

paragraphs.text: And will come home at the day of the new moon" [19-20].

It is as though she invites him to spend the night with her without fear, for her husband will not return to his house until the appearance of the crescent, or the new month. Is this not the enticement of sin to the soul, so that it brings it in as into a pitch-dark night, and offers it every reassurance as though the Bridegroom of the soul were absent and would not return until the day of judgment!

In the same spirit Potiphar's wife called Joseph to sin with her, for her husband was absent, but he believed that the eyes of God were watching him, for he said to her: "How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" (Gen 39:9).

entries.section: 3. The folly of the one who falls into her nets

paragraphs.text: 21 With her much fair speech she caused him to yield, with the flattering of her lips she forced him. 22 He goeth after her straightway, as an ox goeth to the slaughter, or as a fool to the correction of the stocks; 23 Till a dart strike through his liver; as a bird hasteth to the snare, and knoweth not that it is for his life.

In folly the young man fell, whom he described as void of understanding [7], trivial in his thinking and walking through life without aim. He became like an ox led to the slaughter, like a fool led to punishment, and like a bird hastening to the snare. He acts without awareness, for the woman drew him with the fetters of his lust without his realizing that the price is his whole life or his soul.
"With her much fair speech she caused him to yield, with the flattering of her lips she forced him.
He goeth after her straightway, as an ox goeth to the slaughter, or as a fool to the correction of the stocks.
Till a dart strike through his liver.
As a bird hasteth to the snare, and knoweth not that it is for his life" [21-23].
Perhaps he means here that the man will come one day and discover what the young man has done, and will strike their liver with the dart and sentence them both to death.
And even if the husband does not discover the truth, the two of them will not be able to justify themselves before divine justice, and their portion will be eternal perdition.

Adultery is the shortest road to destruction, whether at the hand of the husband who discovers the crime, or because of the venereal diseases under whose weight the adulterer falls, or the mental and psychological confusion, and what is more important, eternal ruin and deprivation of fellowship in the heavenly life.
Hearken unto me now therefore, O ye children, and attend to the words of my mouth:
Let not thine heart decline to her ways, go not astray in her paths.
For she hath cast down many wounded: yea, many strong men have been slain by her. Her house is the way to hell, going down to the chambers of death." [24-27].

Truly "many strong men have been slain by her," although we have been given power to overcome her, and those who are with us are more than those who are against us; but by being lax with small things we fall into great ones. Therefore the voice of the Lord to Lot was: "Escape for thy life." The Fathers were concerned with this divine principle.

St. Piamun the Great says: "It is good to avoid the causes of sin. The man who approaches the opportunities of sin is like a person sitting on the edge of a cliff; the enemy can hunt him easily whenever he wishes."

And St. Isaac the Syrian says: "Our falling into various sins is caused not by the sins in themselves but by our weakness, whereby our nature falls easily. Therefore there is urgent need to beware of them."
* Whoever does not withdraw by his own will from the causes of the passions, sin draws him against his will.

The causes of sin are wine, (wicked) women, wealth, and excessive concern for the health of the body. These things are not sins by their nature... For this reason it is fitting for a person to be on guard against them with great care.
* Beware of small things so that you do not fall into great things.
Do not be slack in your work, lest you be put to shame when you stand in the midst of your companions, and be without provisions on your journey, and be alone by the side of the road.
St. Isaac the Syrian Who is this unfaithful wife who hunts souls to bring them down to death?!

If this chapter can be interpreted literally concerning the falling of young men into the sin of adultery, it can also apply to many sins that present themselves as maidens hunting the soul from its Bridegroom, so that it loses its union with God. If the wise Solomon reveals here the nets of the adulterous woman for hunting the foolish, then all sins set their varied nets in one form or another, especially the deceitful teachers who use every attractive means to corrupt the faith of the simple.

Some see that it refers to the apostate churches that bear the name of the Lord Christ but offer false teachings. She betrays her Bridegroom, and does not cease working without interruption to draw souls by every means from the house of the true Church. She carries every philosophical beauty and offers many means of luxury, so that believers leave the narrow way of the cross and enter the broad way which pushes them to eternal perdition.
* You have seen how great is the harm of the adulteress!

Do not allow lust to rise up, for its death is eternal. As for her words and her sweet speech and her wounds, by her sins she kills those who submit to her. Her evil has many forms that lead to descent into hell. As for "the chambers of death," they mean either death or its storehouses. How then can one escape from it?
St. Hippolytus

entries.section: Then I shall settle in my eternal home!

paragraphs.text: * Let me keep Your commandments as the apple of my eye.
It is exceedingly precious; without it I lose sight, and live in darkness!
Let me bind it on the fingers of my soul as a unique ring!
With it I seal all my thoughts, my words and my deeds.
Let it not depart from my eyes, nor be taken away from before me.
* Let me carry You within me, O Wisdom of God, and be united with You, O Bridegroom of my soul.
You alone satisfy my whole being!
You are near to me!
Deep within me, You carry me into the depths of Your hidden divine mysteries.
And You lift me up to the throne of Your grace.
* With You I fly as if to heaven, so the snares of the adulteress will not close upon my feet, nor will my heart fall into her hidden nets.
* What do I see in this deceiver?
She is a stranger by race.
But I have become Your son!
She flatters with her words, but You put truth in my mouth.
She is an unfaithful adulteress, who knows no faithfulness, but in You I become faithful to the end.
She is void of understanding because she resists You, O Wisdom of God; but by Your grace I become wise.
She wears the garments of a harlot, glittering and alluring, but I hide myself in You, O my eternal wedding garment.
I put You on, and so I bear Your surpassing righteousness!
She is loud and finds her pleasure in noise, * but I meet You with calm of soul and stillness of heart.
She is exceedingly stubborn and obstinate, but I long to bear Your obedience.
In her house her feet abide not, but I see in the heavens an open door.
I see You carrying me to the bosom of Your Father; there Your fiery Spirit carries me, and I settle as in my eternal home.
* The adulteress roams outside, in the streets, and at every corner.
But I enter into the depths, and enjoy my heavenly home.
My soul will not roam among the enticements of the world and its passing pleasures.
She catches others and kisses them with her mouth, opens her heart like a wolf to devour whoever clings to her.
Give me a heart that knows no enmity and bears no hatred, but melts with love even toward those who oppose it.
She is deceitful even in the appearances of religiosity, but I cry out to You: remove from me Pharisaism, and give me inner purity of heart!
* Yes, whenever I see sin embodied in one form or another, my heart is kindled the more, longing to set out to You, for in You alone my depths find rest.
Carry me to Yourself, O desire of my heart!
1 Doth not wisdom cry? and understanding put forth her voice?

In (chapters 8 and 9) Wisdom appears as a person who performs 19 acts to draw us to Himself, dealing with us by every means: 1. He cries out without ceasing (Prov 8:1-3). 2. He stands to meet us (Prov 8:2). 3. He calls us, crying to all the sons of men (Prov 8:4). 4. He speaks with us (Prov 8:4). 5. He rebukes (Prov 8:5). 6. He hates lying (Prov 8:7). 7. He disciplines (Prov 8:10). 8. He finds practical knowledge to give to the believer (Prov 8:12). 9. He hates false words (Prov 8:13). 10. He gives true counsel and sound judgment (Prov 8:14). 11. He gives kings, great men, rulers and nobles honor together with justice (Prov 8:15, 16). 12. He loves (Prov 8:17). 13. He leads in the ways of truth (Prov 8:20). 14. He gives generously and fills the storehouses of His believers (Prov 8:21). 15. He rejoices with gladness (Prov 8:31). 16. He delights and takes pleasure in the sons of men who love Him (Prov 8:31). 17. He builds Himself a house by His incarnation, and hews out pillars (Prov 9:1). 18. He prepares a sacrificial food and a mystical table (Prov 9:2). 19. He sends out His servants and maidens to invite mankind to His banquet (Prov 9:3-6).

If folly or sin appears as a woman subtil of heart, stubborn and unfaithful, who loves to hunt the soul and entice it by every means in order to bring it down to eternal perdition, then the Wisdom of the eternal God does not stand with folded hands, so to speak; He does not cease to cry in every place, and though He is the Creator He comes down to His creation, and He, the Wisdom beloved of the Father, finds His delight in the sons of Adam, offering them fellowship in the heavenly life and the enjoyment of the blessed life.
"Doth not wisdom cry (call out)? and understanding put forth her voice?" [1]

In former times the divine command was given to Isaiah the prophet: "Cry aloud, spare not, lift up thy voice like a trumpet, and shew my people their transgression, and the house of Jacob their sins" (Isa 58:1). And the Levites used to read the blessings and the curses with a loud voice (Deut 27:14).

Wisdom calls continually and cries out so that all may hear her voice, to declare the will of God and His plan concerning man. She declares this through nature, which bears witness to God's providence; and she spoke most clearly through the fathers, the Law and the prophets. But the difficulty lies in man's refusal to listen to the divine voice.

If sin does not cease to entice, the Wisdom of God calls without ceasing. As the Apostle Paul says: "God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son, whom he hath appointed heir of all things, by whom also he made the worlds" (Heb 1:1, 2). At last the divine Wisdom, the Lord Christ, came crying out Himself and giving His voice directly. He offered us His speech, not in words only, but in practical self-giving love on the cross, and He gave us His Holy Spirit to carry us in Him, so that we hear His voice through our union with Him and our continual renewal, to become a living icon of Him.

In this chapter it stands out that Wisdom is the one who goes after man and searches for him and invites him to receive her, but she does not compel him. Contrary to what many imagine, that God is secluded in His heavens and man seeks Him and tries to please Him, we see God through Wisdom coming down to man, seeking him in the streets and in every place, for He takes the initiative in love.

2 She standeth in the top of high places, by the way in the places of the paths. 3 She crieth at the gates, at the entry of the city, at the coming in at the doors. 4 Unto you, O men, I call; and my voice is to the sons of man. 5 O ye simple, understand wisdom: and, ye fools, be ye of an understanding heart. 6 Hear; for I will speak of excellent things; and the opening of my lips shall be right things. 7 For my mouth shall speak truth; and wickedness is an abomination to my lips. 8 All the words of my mouth are in righteousness; there is nothing froward or perverse in them. 9 They are all plain to him that understandeth, and right to them that find knowledge. 10 Receive my instruction, and not silver; and knowledge rather than choice gold. 11 For wisdom is better than rubies; and all the things that may be desired are not to be compared to it.
"She standeth in the top of high places, by the way in the places of the paths.
She crieth at the gates, at the entry of the city, at the coming in at the doors" [2, 3].

The Wisdom of God, or His Word, calls in the house of the Lord, which used to be set up on the tops of high hills, and which stood at the crossroads as a center for the surrounding villages; the Hebrew expression beith neithiboth nitstsbabah came to mean "the house established by the roads." Although we hear the voice of God wherever we are and under all circumstances, yet God speaks to us most in His house, for the Holy Bible is the book of the Church, and the Church is the Church of the Book. In the Church we meet the Lord Christ, the Wisdom of God, and acquire Him and live by Him... we hear His voice within us!
The wise Solomon presents to us three places in which we meet the divine Wisdom:

A. "In the top of high places," that is, on the high elevations, for Moses the prophet received the Law on the summit of Mount Sinai, and the Lord Christ gave His sermon on the mount. So we too are called to go up with the Lord Christ as with Peter, James and John, and see Him transfigured on Mount Tabor. We ascend always and do not settle at the foot of the mountain, and we say with the psalmist: "Unto thee do I lift up my soul..." Our souls are lifted up to be united with the Crucified One on the mount of Golgotha! There we hear the unique divine voice, the voice of practical self-giving love, the divine commandment in its most wonderful form!

Wisdom stands at the summits of the heights and mountains, for the call is public. The Lord Christ, who is Wisdom, was lifted up on the cross on Mount Golgotha, where Jews and Gentiles saw Him, to declare His practical self-giving love, stretching out His hands to embrace everyone without exception. He is the lover of all mankind, the Savior of the world!
Even though He came down to the foot of the mountain to meet the simple multitudes, He calls from the summits so that all may see Him and hear Him, and no one has an excuse for refusing the call.

B. "By the way in the places of the paths": Wisdom stands at the crossing of all roads, so that all may come to Him, from the east and the west, and from the north and the south. He is the Savior of the whole world! So the Church opens the doors of her heart to every person!

At the meeting of the roads the Lord Christ stands where He finds man in perplexity not knowing which way to turn, and He leads him in the royal road. He overshadows him as a cloud that protects him by day, and as a pillar of light that dispels the darkness through Him. It was said of the foolish: "The labour of the foolish shameth them, because he knoweth not how to go to the city" (Eccl 10:15); therefore the Wisdom of God stands and meets them to bring them into His house, the house of heavenly Wisdom.

The Hebrew expression "beith nethiboth nitsabah" means "the house established by the road," and by it is meant "the house of God," whether the tabernacle of meeting or the temple in the Old Testament, and the Church in the New Testament, where the house of God is at the meeting of the roads, and man can reach it.

If the house of God is the place of worship where believers meet as sons of God and practice their worship through their sonship to God, it is also a place of preaching, in which the Lord Christ speaks to the world through His servants so that all may realize the surpassing love of God. The Church is the place where divine Wisdom meets mankind, where Christ offers Himself to all.

C. "At the gates... at the coming in at the doors": there the elders of the city used to gather to judge the cases of the people, as though divine Wisdom wished to present Himself to everyone who has a complaint, or who is in distress, for He alone is able to restore peace to the soul.

When the Wisdom of God became incarnate and became man, He went about doing good in every place. He proclaimed His message in the temple as in the synagogues, and on the tops of mountains, and on the shores of the seas, and in the villages, as in the roads of the cities and in the houses. His disciples received this spirit, and walked as their Teacher walked, seeking sinners wherever they were found, and presenting the voice of truth in every place.

Wisdom cries at the gates of the entrance and its doors to meet those who go in and out. If the Lord Christ is "the Door," then His disciples and apostles and all His servants must cry out in truth of the Gospel in Him, to reveal its treasures offered to mankind, and the truth, that all may enjoy it.
Would that we did not stand with the Lord only on the high summits, nor speak of Him only inside the church building, but carry Him to every person, and go to him to offer him "the royal door."
* When they hold fast to righteousness in innocence they are not ashamed; this is preaching at the door.
And who is this who preaches at the door?
He who preaches in Christ, for Christ is the door by which we enter into that city...

Therefore those who speak against Christ are outside the door, for they seek their own honors, not the honor of Christ. But he who preaches at the door seeks the honor of Christ, not his own honor. Therefore he who preaches at the door says: "Do not trust in me, for you do not enter through me but through the door." But those who ask men to trust in them want them not to enter by the door; so we do not wonder if the door is shut before them and in vain they knock and it is not opened to them.
St. Augustine "Unto you, O men, I call; and my voice is to the sons of man" [4].

The word "men" here, ishim, means those who have wealth and power, so divine Wisdom calls those in authority as responsible leaders and also lifts up His voice to all the sons of men. He calls the rich as well as the poor to walk in wisdom. He calls all the sons of Adam, for the Lord Christ tasted death for every person, presenting the Gospel of salvation to the whole world. As the Apostle Paul says: "Even the righteousness of God which is by faith of Jesus Christ unto all and upon all them that believe: for there is no difference" (Rom 3:22).
St. Augustine declares the universality of salvation for the world without distinction or partiality, saying:
[Christ came to the sick and found all to be so. Therefore let no one boast of his health, lest the physician stop treating him... He found all sick.

But there are two kinds of the sick flock; one kind came to the physician and clung to Christ and began to hear Him and honor Him and follow Him, and was changed... The other kind was fascinated by the sickness of evil and did not realize its sickness; this kind said to His disciples: "Why eateth your Master with publicans and sinners?" (Mt 9:11). And He who knew them and their state answered them: "They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick."]

After affirming the universality of the call, he returns to direct his call especially to the foolish and ignorant, for whoever discovers his sins or realizes his folly and ignorance finds his healing in the Savior.
"O ye simple, understand wisdom: and, ye fools, be ye of an understanding heart" [5].

He directs his words to the simple (the foolish), pethaim, whom sweet words and the enticements of sin have deceived, so that they fell into the pit of evil, and he also speaks to the fools, kesilim, by whom he means the dull who in their ignorance have stiffened the neck and lost feeling.
He opens the door of hope before the deceived and the ignorant by their receiving Him as wisdom and understanding!

D. The blessings of the call. The purpose of the call of the Wisdom of God is that, since He finds His delight in the sons of men, He desires to give them Himself, that they may obtain riches, honor, wisdom, knowledge and success in all aspects of life, as He offers a love that is received only by one who responds to it with love... Therefore He emphasizes His promise: "I love them that love me."

Since Solomon has made clear that the call has never ceased and that it is universal for all mankind, especially those whom sin has deceived and ignorance has shattered, he tells us of the blessings of this call, saying:
"Hear; for I will speak of excellent things; and the opening of my lips shall be right things" [6].

Why is it fitting for them to hear? Because what the Lord Christ utters is not worthless matters, but excellent things, negidim, that is, surpassing things, which have priority in man's life, higher than all other matters. He teaches things that touch their eternal dignity and their surpassing and everlasting glory.
When He opens His lips, uprightness, meysharim, flows from them, that is, the things that correct our mistaken concepts and turn crooked ways into straight ways.

The speech is addressed to the foolish and the ignorant [5], those who through their ignorance have become trivial, but the wise One speaks on weighty matters that lift them out of what they are in so that their lives become valuable.
"For my mouth shall speak truth; and wickedness is an abomination to my lips" [7].
The Lord Christ speaks the truth that knows no falsehood and is not mixed with lying!
"All the words of my mouth are in righteousness; there is nothing froward or perverse in them" [8].

The truth, betsedek, that comes out of His lips is practical truth, or righteousness mixed with justice in His dealings with His Father and with mankind; He gives to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's. His words reveal truthfully the relation of man to God his God and to his neighbor as to himself. This truthfulness carries justice and uprightness, and there is no trace of deceit or deviation in it, and it does not tolerate reinterpretation, or lead to crookedness, but on the contrary:
"They are all plain to him that understandeth, and right to them that find knowledge" [9].

Whoever is concerned for the salvation of his soul and the enjoyment of true knowledge perceives the mysteries of divine wisdom, and God's plans become plain and right before him; and whoever enjoys knowledge, that is, knows himself as he ought, sees uprightness even in the disciplines of the Lord, and touches God's promises as true and faithful.

St. John the Beloved wept much because no one was found worthy to open the book and read it, or to look on it. But one of the elders said to him: "Weep not: behold, the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David, hath prevailed to open the book, and to loose the seven seals thereof" (Rev 5:5). Now that the seals of the book have been loosed, God's plan has become plain to His believers; they perceive its mysteries and taste the pledge of the glory He has prepared for them.
All that the Lord Christ declares is exceedingly precious:
"Receive my instruction, and not silver" [10].
"And knowledge rather than choice gold" [10].

Why does God repeat the call that we receive the disciplines that come from Him rather than silver? Fathers according to the flesh often cease to discipline their children, either because they despair of correction, or because they feel they are angering their sons; but our heavenly Father will not cease to discipline us because He always hopes for our salvation, however great our stubbornness; and on the other hand, His love is eternal, and He does not seek to appease us here at the cost of our fellowship with Him in eternal glory.
"For wisdom is better than rubies; and all the things that may be desired are not to be compared to it" [11].

Knowledge is the food of the soul; without it the soul faints and dies! The wise man says that knowledge is better than pure gold. Some compare mankind that is occupied with gold and wealth without divine knowledge to a group who were shipwrecked in the middle of the ocean, and when they found a barren island they went down to it and were saved, but became completely isolated from all the world. They had grain and food, so they began to eat and drink, and when one of them discovered very rich gold mines they rejoiced, and began to extract gold until they became very rich and gave no heed to farming. Winter came and the food ran out, with an abundance of gold, but what good was gold to them? They fainted from hunger, and at last died in the midst of heaps of gold. This is the state of one who rejects divine knowledge because he is occupied with wealth.

12 I wisdom dwell with prudence, and find out knowledge of witty inventions. 13 The fear of the LORD is to hate evil: pride, and arrogancy, and the evil way, and the froward mouth, do I hate. 14 Counsel is mine, and sound wisdom: I am understanding; I have strength. 15 By me kings reign, and princes decree justice. 16 By me princes rule, and nobles, even all the judges of the earth. 17 I love them that love me; and those that seek me early shall find me. 18 Riches and honour are with me; yea, durable riches and righteousness. 19 My fruit is better than gold, yea, than fine gold; and my revenue than choice silver. 20 I walk in the way of justice, in the midst of the paths of truth, 21 So that I cause those that love me to inherit substance, and I fill their treasures.

Since the Wisdom of God presents a general and public call to all mankind to acquire Him, He reveals His work in the lives of those who have acquired Him, where He declares Himself to them and within them.

entries.section: First: He gives intelligence and good management

paragraphs.text: "I wisdom dwell with prudence, and find out knowledge of witty inventions" [12].

When the Wisdom of God dwells in us, intelligence dwells with Him, and He gives the believer sincere thought and conscious understanding. All intelligence or skill is from the Lord. Man has invented many ways of management, but the Lord gives all the ways that build up. Man's own intelligence destroys because it lacks goodness, but that which God gives builds.

On the other hand, He gives him practical, experiential knowledge which he calls "knowledge of witty inventions, mezimnoth emsta." Whenever a person bears spiritual wisdom, it is translated in his inner life and his outward conduct into practical plans that are righteous and holy in the Lord. Intelligence is the ability to think skillfully, but wisdom carries with intelligence practice; wisdom leads man to act in a fitting, godly manner. This is the positive side of the work of wisdom; the negative side is the wise man's hatred of evil and folly.

entries.section: Second: He gives the fear of the Lord that rejects evil

paragraphs.text: "The fear of the LORD is to hate evil: pride, and arrogancy, and the evil way, and the froward mouth, do I hate" [13].

Wisdom overflows on those who acquire her not only with intelligence and good management but she reigns over the feelings and emotions of the heart, so that the believer hates four things: evil, pride, arrogance and deceit. In other words, if the fear of the Lord is the head of wisdom, then through wisdom we enjoy the fear without which we would not love righteousness and goodness and hate sin and evil.

Fear of punishment may oblige us not to sin, but it may generate more longing toward sin, for "Stolen waters are sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant" (Prov 9:17). But the fear of the Lord, which rests on the boldness of love and the realization of our sonship to God, makes us hate sin, not out of fear of punishment, but out of love for God our Father, as we see in sin a wound to the love of God, who does not accept darkness.

Man, whose nature has been corrupted after the Fall, has come to incline to sin and be drawn to it despite his awareness of its danger to his life; therefore he needs the Wisdom of God, the Savior, to renew his nature by His Holy Spirit, and give him an inner hatred of sin.
The men of the Old and New Testaments have cried out because of man's inclination to evil:
"The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?" (Jer 17:9).

"As it is written, There is none righteous, no, not one: there is none that understandeth, there is none that seeketh after God. They are all gone out of the way, they are together become unprofitable; there is none that doeth good, no, not one" (Rom 3:10-12).

It is impossible for man to hate evil unless he loves goodness; and since hatred of evil leads man to forsake the evil way, and love of goodness leads him to do what is right in the eyes of God, and that by the action of the Holy Spirit who gives hatred of evil and love of goodness, this in turn kindles in us the fear of the Lord.

If the fear of the Lord represents a deep goodness in the heart that leads it away from evil, and even gives it a hatred of evil, then this inner work has a practical translation in outward conduct by rejecting pride and arrogance and the uttering of lies.

In the account by Pope Athanasius the Apostolic of St. Abba Anthony the Great he says: [Since his soul was free from disturbances, his outward appearance was calm; so out of the joy of his soul he bore a cheerful countenance; and from the movements of his body the state of his soul could be perceived, as it is written: "A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by sorrow of the heart (the countenance) is broken" (Prov 15:13).

entries.section: Third: He gives the ability to give counsel

paragraphs.text: "Counsel is mine, and sound wisdom.
I am understanding; I have strength" [14].

Since Wisdom, our Lord Jesus, has counsel and also the ability to give right thought and wise management of matters with understanding, He gives the one who acquires Him the ability to give counsel in turn to others. Therefore the godly believer becomes a spiritual counselor even in his silence, but the wicked man is unable to give good, effective counsel, even if he speaks well and has long experience.
The Lord Christ, the Wisdom of the Father (1 Cor 1:14), the source of wisdom, not only overflows upon us, but stirs up in us springs of living water that overflow upon those whom we meet.
He says "I have strength," lest we think that the quiet godly life is weakness and resignation, when it is the very enjoyment of strength.
Pope Athanasius the Apostolic comments on this phrase, saying:

* Being the very Wisdom of the Father... He Himself is the living Counsel of the Father and His power and the Creator of all things which the Father saw to be good. This is what He says of Himself in Proverbs: "Counsel is mine, and sound wisdom, I am understanding, I have strength." ("For Christ is the power of God, and the wisdom of God") (1 Cor 1:24). Here He changes the expression and says: "I am understanding" and "I have strength." When He says: "Counsel is mine," He Himself is the living Counsel of the Father, as the prophet also teaches us that He became "the Angel of great counsel," and was called the good pleasure of the Father.
Pope Athanasius the Apostolic

entries.section: Fourth: He gives the spirit of kingship and authority

paragraphs.text: Since the Lord Christ possesses "Wisdom" in us, He makes us not slaves but kings, so that we bear His mark in us, bearing the spirit of kingship that does not accept slavery to any passion, and we are not terrified before temporal events, nor fear any creature, but we bear the freedom of the glory of the children of God. We have authority over our thoughts, our feelings, our emotions and our senses, as over our outward conduct, so that we walk as sons of heavenly kings, with surpassing wisdom from above.
"By me kings reign, and princes decree justice.
By me princes rule, and nobles.
Even all the judges of the earth" [15-16].

Thus the King of kings, "the Wisdom of God," raises up from His people kings and great men and rulers and nobles and judges. When He asks them to walk in a spirit of humility, it is that they may bear His humility in them, and so become great in the eyes of God, and in the eyes of heaven and men. He came to restore man, shattered by sin, to the glorious kingship!

God in His love for mankind identifies Himself with the suffering, and so is called the Father of the fatherless and the Judge of the widows; He searches for the outcast, and upholds the wretched, and raises the humble, and cares for those who have no one to ask after them. If He has raised up kings, rulers, nobles and judges, it is to work on behalf of all these; He raised them up not for any merit in them, but to work on behalf of the whole community, especially the oppressed and the needy... So it is fitting for one who is in a position of responsibility to realize that he received it from the hand of God to work on behalf of the community in a spirit of love and humility.

* The divine speech on this matter is clear, for the Wisdom of God speaks thus: "By me kings reign, and great men rule the earth." But it is not to be understood by this that they are wicked and ungodly kings, but courageous kings.
St. Augustine

entries.section: Fifth: they become the object of heaven's love!

paragraphs.text: "I love them that love me; and those that seek me early shall find me" [17].

Since "Wisdom" presents Himself to mankind, declaring that He is counsel, sound wisdom, understanding and strength, whoever acquires Him perceives the mysteries of the Father, and comes to know His will, and bears power from Him, and so lives in this world as God's steward, bearing the icon of heaven, and bearing witness to the surpassing work of God. Now He affirms two grave and complementary principles:

The first principle is the sanctity of human freedom, for He does not thrust Himself into a person's life without his choice, affirming: "I love them that love me." He is all love; He opens His arms on the cross to the whole world, and His breast is wide for every human being to lean upon, but not all receive Him!
Let us love Him, and we shall realize that He loved us first!
Let us throw ourselves on His breast, and we shall find it prepared for us!
Let us long for Him, and we shall touch His surpassing longings toward us.
His love for us is not the fruit of our love for Him, for He loved us first.
He took the initiative in love before we knew; while we were enemies He reconciled us to God His Father.
But our love is the key to our knowledge of His standing and overflowing love for all mankind.
The second principle, which completes the former, is our commitment to seek Him early that we may find Him. What does it mean: "and those that seek me early shall find me"?

Seeking early here carries the concept of priority, for He gave our salvation and renewal a special priority, and the Father offered His beloved Son as a sacrifice of love for our sake. It is as though He says: "Man first!" If this is the wondrous divine work, is it not fitting that we seek Him early, saying: "God first" in our daily life, and in our inner thoughts, and in our family conduct, etc.

In every action, hidden and manifest, let God be the center of our thinking; let us seek Him early, for He sought us early, and placed us at the summit of His concern, He who is the Creator of heaven and earth!

Let us seek Him early and give Him the best of our times to meet with Him, so that He is not at the end of the list, so that we worship Him in the leftovers of our time. It is fitting for us to give special attention to our meeting with Him, so we run to Him in the early morning, and offer Him the first day of the week (Sunday), and prefer meeting with Him to any human ties or courtesies. God is above all!
Let us seek Him early and remember our Creator in the days of our youth, offering Him the firstfruits of our life that He may sanctify the whole life.

entries.section: Sixth: He gives us Himself as treasure, glory and satisfaction

paragraphs.text: "Riches and honour are with me; yea, durable riches and righteousness.
My fruit is better than gold, yea, than fine gold; and my revenue than choice silver" [18-19].
Usually the wise become rich and honored in the eyes of men, but this principle does not have many exceptions.

What the wise Solomon speaks of here is not material wealth, nor temporal honor, nor the filling of the belly, but something greater, the enjoyment of the person of the Lord Christ, in whom is our sufficiency!

There is a wealth, glory and satisfaction that fills the being of the wise man, which the whole world cannot take from him, nor the powers of darkness, nor the events of the future, because all this will not be able to separate the wise, godly believer from the person of the Lord Christ, in whom we have treasure, glory and satisfaction. The wise man repeats with St. Paul the Apostle: "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?" (Rom 8:25).

* If we must distinguish between one who is counted rich because his possessions are many and he is weighed down with gold like a filthy purse, and the righteous man who alone is full of grace, for grace has its own order, observing the proper and beautiful measures in arrangement and distribution.
St. Clement of Alexandria "I walk in the way of justice, in the midst of the paths of truth.

entries.section: Sixth: He gives us Himself as treasure, glory and satisfaction

paragraphs.text: So that I cause those that love me to inherit substance, and I fill their treasures" [20-21].
Who is this who walks in the way of justice and dwells in the midst of the paths of truth but the Son of Man, our Lord Jesus Christ, so that He carries us in Himself, and we enjoy what He has?!

* As if the Son of Man were walking in the midst of the seven lampstands (Rev 1). It is said that He is in the midst of the seven churches, and as Solomon said: "I walk in the way of justice," the Eternal One, the fountain of kingship.

Father Victorinus If the rich man seeks to satisfy his soul with possessions, the wise man, who acquires wisdom, has his soul satisfied by walking in the way of justice and moving in the midst of the paths of truth. In justice and truth together with love he finds what satisfies his depths, so that his inner storehouses are filled with joy and exultation with surpassing peace and goodness.

Temporal blessings give the belly a temporary satisfaction which hunger soon follows, but divine righteousness gives the inner storehouses satisfaction and fullness, which the Spirit of God lifts up to heaven as an eternal credit on our account. David the prophet expressed this in a wonderful way, saying: "Thou fillest their belly with thy hid treasure: they are full of children, and leave the rest of their substance to their babes. As for me, I will behold thy face in righteousness: I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness" (Ps 17:14, 15). What a man draws from temporal gifts is a gift from God, but a temporary gift that satisfies the belly, and what remains of it he leaves as an inheritance to his children, offering them his perishable leftovers. But he who walks in the way of justice in the midst of the righteousness of the Lord Christ has his inner man formed, and becomes by the Holy Spirit an icon of Christ, in His likeness. This is his eternal credit that fills his heavenly storehouses... which no thief will steal, and no moth corrupt!

22 The LORD possessed me in the beginning of his way, before his works of old. 23 I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning, or ever the earth was. 24 When there were no depths, I was brought forth; when there were no fountains abounding with water. 25 Before the mountains were settled, before the hills was I brought forth: 26 While as yet he had not made the earth, nor the fields, nor the highest part of the dust of the world. 27 When he prepared the heavens, I was there: when he set a compass upon the face of the depth: 28 When he established the clouds above: when he strengthened the fountains of the deep: 29 When he gave to the sea his decree, that the waters should not pass his commandment: when he appointed the foundations of the earth. In this chapter the person of the Lord Christ shines forth with all power, as the Wisdom of God, who calls all mankind to acquire Him and to enjoy His surpassing possibilities. Now He reveals Himself as one with the Father, the Creator of the world, who is concerned for the salvation of His creation that has become corrupt, and who finds His delight in calling sinners to salvation.
"The LORD possessed me (possessed Me) in the beginning of his way, before (for the sake of) his works of old" [22].

The Arians concentrated on the phrase "The LORD possessed me in the beginning of his way, before his works of old" [22], to claim that the Lord Christ, although He preceded all creation, is in their view "the first of creation," whom the Father created alone, and who carried out the work of creation. They relied in this on the word "possessed me" and translate it "created me." Therefore the Fathers of the Church, headed by Pope Athanasius the Apostolic, took pains to interpret this phrase and link it with the rest of the whole passage [22-31]. I shall try to present the thought of the Fathers briefly in an appendix devoted to this chapter.
Now I present a simple interpretation of the passage.

While the Arians misunderstood this phrase, many of the Fathers found in it a living and wonderful picture of the love of the Father, who by Wisdom planned our salvation before our creation. From the beginning He planned the divine Incarnation, that the Wisdom of God, or His Word, the divine Hypostasis inseparable from Him, might become man for the sake of mankind, to be "the first of his works," that is, "the firstborn among many brethren" (Rom 8:29); "the beginning, the firstborn from the dead" (Col 1:18). It is as though the divine Wisdom here presents His surpassing promise that His eternal Father is with Him planning our salvation before our creation, and as though His plan precedes our existence as a sign of His concern for us and His surpassing eternal ability to accomplish the plan of His love toward us.
The following is to be observed in this verse:

First: although some Fathers, such as St. Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, affirm that the Hebrew word does not mean "created me" but "acquired me, possessed Me," some, such as Pope Athanasius the Apostolic, did not refrain from using the Greek word ἔκτισεν, which means "created me," yet he affirms that it is not the same word that was used in the creation of the world.
Second: the book of Proverbs is a symbolic book, so we do not pick up a word from it and separate it from the Holy Bible to interpret it theologically.

Third: the word "created me" does not confuse us, for the Wisdom of God, the Second Hypostasis, became Word, taking a created body... and He truly became man and a servant without changing, for He is still God blessed forever.

Fourth: this expression "created me" cannot refer to the essence of the hypostasis of Wisdom, because in the same phrase it was said: "for his works"; if this Hypostasis had been created for the sake of mankind, then mankind would be better and more important than He. But since creation here means the Incarnation and the plan of salvation, the meaning is entirely different, for the creating is for the sake of the surpassing divine love toward mankind.

Fifth: we do not stumble at the saying "the first of his ways," for by the divine Incarnation the incarnate Hypostasis took the place of Adam; for as by Adam's fall human nature was corrupted, so by the victory of the new Adam and His righteousness, victory and righteousness came to mankind. This is what the Apostle Paul expressed, saying: "Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned... Nevertheless death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over them that had not sinned after the similitude of Adam's transgression, who is the figure of him that was to come... For if through the offence of one many be dead, much more the grace of God, and the gift by grace, which is by one man, Jesus Christ, hath abounded unto many" (Rom 5:12 etc.).

Thus our first father Adam lost his position as firstborn, and the incarnate Wisdom of God took his position, so that He leads us as firstborn to His heavens, and we enjoy fellowship in His glory. The Only-Begotten Son, to whom the angels bow down, became firstborn for us: "For unto which of the angels said he at any time, Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee? And again, I will be to him a Father, and he shall be to me a Son? And again, when he bringeth in the firstbegotten into the world, he saith, And let all the angels of God worship him" (Heb 1:5-7).

He became firstborn for us by His Incarnation, He before whom the angels bow down, and who alone is called the Only-Begotten Son, and of whom it was said: "Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever..." (Heb 1:8).

Sixth: in the same passage the wise Solomon spoke of Him: "I was by him as a craftsman (manager)"... How can the maker or Creator be at the same time a thing made or a creature? Does He create Himself? Especially since it was said of Him: "All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made" (Jn 1:3).

Seventh: by saying "for his works," it is clear that He does not mean the creation of His essence, but the plan of the divine Incarnation, because the work comes after the existence of the being and not the reverse. So here the expression "created me" refers to the work and not to the existence of His essence. The Holy Bible has used the expression of creation for work in many places, among them:
"Create in me a clean heart, O God" (Ps 51:10); the psalmist does not ask God to create in him a new being, but to work in him and renew his heart.

"For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works..." (Eph 2:20). This does not mean that we had died in the body and then He created us again, but that He renewed our nature, which had become as though dead, and re-created it in Christ Jesus.

By comparing (Rom 13:14; with Eph 4:24) it appears that we put on Christ in the sense of His work of salvation: "Put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ" (Rom 13:14), "Put on the new man, which after God is created" (Eph 4:24).

Since the Lord defines His essence as the Wisdom, the Only-Begotten Son born of the Father, which is different from things that have a beginning and natural creatures, He said in His love for man: "The LORD possessed me in the beginning of his way," as though He were saying: "My Father prepared a body for me, and possessed me for men for their salvation."

For as when John says: "The Word was made flesh" (Jn 1:14), we do not understand that the whole Word became flesh, but that He put on a body and became man. And when we hear: "Christ became a curse for us," "he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin" (Gal 3:13; 2 Cor 5:21), we do not understand simply that the whole of Christ became a curse and sin, but that He bore the curse that was against us (as the Apostle said: "redeemed us from the curse." And as Isaiah said: "He bore our sins," and Peter wrote: "bare them in his own body on the tree" (Gal 3:13; Isa 53:4; 1 Pet 2:24)); so when it is said in Proverbs: "created me," it is not fitting for us to understand that the whole Word is by nature a creature, but that He took a created body and that God (the Father) created Him for our sake, preparing for Him the created body, as it is written that for our sake we may in Him be renewed and deified.
What has deceived you, you who in ignorance call the Creator a creature?

Pope Athanasius the Apostolic * Again, Wisdom herself speaks of the mystery of the assumed body and says: "The LORD created me." Although the prophecy here is of things to come, yet because the coming of the Lord had been determined beforehand, He did not say "will create me" but "created me," so that men may believe that the body of Jesus, born of the Virgin Mary, happened once and not many times.

St. Ambrose When the Wisdom of God speaks of His Incarnation to accomplish the plan of salvation of mankind, He opens the way of salvation and is the firstborn who carries mankind to enter with it into His glories. Thus He called Himself: "I am the way" (Jn 14:6).

For Christ does not wish only to present Himself to those who have completed the journey, but to be Himself the way for those who are beginning the journey, determined to take a body. Therefore the expression came: "The LORD possessed me in the beginning of his way," meaning that those who wished to come must begin their journey in Him.

St. Augustine * Again, as the wise Solomon said in Proverbs: "possessed me." And he said "the beginning of the way" of the glad tidings that lead us to the Kingdom of Heaven, not that He is created in essence and being, but He became "the Way" according to the economy. For the two words "made" and "created" came to bear the same meaning. He was made the way, and the door and the shepherd and the angel and the flock, and also the high priest, and the apostle; other names are used in other senses.
St. Basil the Great "I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning, or ever the earth was" [23].
"When there were no depths, I was brought forth; when there were no fountains abounding with water" [24].
"Before the mountains were settled, before the hills was I brought forth (begot me, LXX)" [25].
"While as yet he had not made the earth, nor the fields, nor the highest part of the dust of the world" [26].
"When he prepared the heavens, I was there: when he set a compass upon the face of the depth" [27].
"When he established the clouds above: when he strengthened the fountains of the deep" [28].
"When he gave to the sea his decree, that the waters should not pass his commandment: when he appointed the foundations of the earth" [29].
The divine Wisdom affirms that He existed before the following things:
* All creation [22].
* The existence of the earth [23].
* The depths of the fountains of water [24].
* The founding of the mountains and hills [25].
* The earth and the dust of the world [26].
* The heavens and the clouds [28].
* The laws of nature [29].
St. Gregory the Theologian found in these passages the wealth of the Creator's love for him, and sang, saying:
[You set up the heaven for me as a roof, and established the earth for me to walk upon.
For me You bridled the sea, for me You revealed the nature of animals, You subjected everything under my feet, and did not leave me lacking anything of the works of Your honor".]
And St. Anthony the Great says:
[The world is preserved by divine providence... for there is no place which this providence does not reach.

Divine providence is the carrying out of the promises of the divine Word, who gives form to the matter of which this world is composed, and is the architect and artist of all this. Things could not have received their beauty were it not for the prudence of the power of the Word, who is the image of God (the Father) and His mind and His wisdom and His providence.]

The plan of salvation is not new, but precedes creation itself; before the Fall God was preparing for man his resurrection, and the divine Wisdom was appointed the Messiah of Israel and Savior of the whole world. He affirmed that not only before the creation of man did He plan redemption, but even before the creation of the world, for He made clear His role in creation. He who loved man and created the world for his sake, before the Incarnation, and offered His life as a ransom for him.
Many of the Fathers comment on what is in the Septuagint: "Before He made the earth, and established the mountains, before all the hills He begot me" [24, 25 LXX].

* In the form of God it was said: "Before the hills He begot me," that is, before every height of created things, and "before the dawn I begot thee" (Ps 110:3) Vulgate, that is, before all times and temporal things. But since (He appeared) in the form of a servant it was said: "The LORD possessed me in the beginning of his way" [22].
Being in the form of God He says: "I am the truth," and in the form of a servant: "I am the way" (Jn 14:6).
For He Himself, being the firstborn from the dead (Rev 1:5), passed over into the Kingdom of God for eternal life for the sake of His Church, being the Head, to make the body also immortal.

St. Augustine * We must ask what is the meaning of saying that God (the Word) was begotten before all ages, and also created for the beginning of the ways of God and for His works. Surely this was said because there was a birth before the beginning of the ages... but when it speaks of a creating at the beginning of the ages for the ways of God and for His works, this applies to the creative cause of the works and ways.

First: since Christ is Wisdom, we must see that He Himself was the beginning of the ways of God's works. I think there is no doubt about this, since He says, "I am the way: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me"... Therefore He was created for the beginning of the ways and works of God, because He is the Way and leads men to the Father..
Second: He was created for the works of God from the beginning of the ages when He submitted Himself to the form of visible creation, bearing the form of a created being.

St. Hilary of Poitiers * Let no one be confused by the words "before the world," and "before he had made the earth," and "before the mountains were settled".. For there is here an allusion to the economy according to the flesh. Although the grace that came upon us from the Savior has now appeared, as the Apostle says, and came when He dwelt among us, yet this grace was prepared even before we existed. Indeed, it was prepared before the foundation of the world, and the reason for it is His wonderful tenderness.
Pope Athanasius the Apostolic "While as yet he had not made the earth, nor the fields, nor the highest part of the dust of the world" [26].
"When he prepared the heavens, I was there: when he set a compass upon the face of the depth" [27].
* The Wisdom of God, by whom all things were made, was there; Wisdom Himself works in holy souls and makes them friends of God, and His prophets, and speaks to us of His works in quietness.
St. Augustine * Let us learn also that the Father was with Him, and He was with the Father when all things were created.
Wisdom says, "When he prepared the heavens, I was with him, when he made the fountains of waters."

And in the Old Testament, when the Father says, "Let us make," He showed that the Son must be worshipped with Him as the maker of all things, since it is said that these things were created by the Son.

St. Ambrose * Who was with Him when He created all existence, if not His Wisdom, who says, "When he made the heaven and the earth, I was with him"? By referring to heaven and earth He refers to all the creatures that are in heaven and on earth. For being present with Him as His Wisdom and His Word, looking to the Father as He created, ordered, and gave order to the universe, and being the power of the Father, He gives power to all things, and as Savior He says, "What things soever he doeth, these also doeth the Son likewise" (Jn 5:29; 1:16). And His holy disciples knew that all things were created by Him and for Him.
St. Athanasius the Apostolic
30 Then I was by him, as a craftsman: and I was daily his delight, rejoicing always before him; 31 Rejoicing in the habitable part of his earth; and my delights were with the sons of men.
"I was by him, as a craftsman (administrator)" [30].

The divine hypostasis of Wisdom affirms His role in creation. As the Evangelist John says: "All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made" (Jn 1:3), and the Apostle Paul says: "By whom also he made the worlds" (Heb 1:2); "For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him, and for him" (Col 1:16).
"And I was daily his delight, rejoicing always before him" [30].

This affirms the relationship of mutual love between the two hypostases, the Father and Wisdom. If the Father planned that the Son should accomplish salvation, it is because the Father's delight is in His Son, and the Son's delight is in His Father. So the redemption accomplished by the Son, "the Wisdom of God," is ascribed to the Father, as the Lord Christ says: "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son" (Jn 3:16). Thus Wisdom's accomplishment of redemption is also a giving up by the Father, who loves Wisdom and is one with Him.
* I am the one in whom He (the Father) delights. Moreover, I was daily His delight before Him.
He rejoiced in the world that He had created, and in the sons of men..
With God is Wisdom, begotten before the worlds, not only present with Him, but ordering the worlds together with Him..

Observe His work in managing and ordering things. The Father by His command is the cause, and the Son manages and orders by carrying out what has been commanded. The distinction between the two hypostases lies in the work belonging to each.

When it was said, "Let us make" (Gen 1:26), creation was made known by the word of command, and when it was written, "I was by him as a craftsman," God declares that He did not make it alone (apart from the Son). For He was His joy before Him.. He rejoiced in the world He made and in the sons of men.

Wisdom tells us the reason for His joy. He rejoices at the joy of the Father, who rejoices at the completion of the creation of the world and of the sons of men. For it is written: "And God saw that it was good" (Gen 1:10, 12, 31).. His Wisdom is a partner with Him in the work and rejoices with Him as He completes the work.
St. Hilary of Poitiers * Is it not counted blasphemy to say that there was a time when the Wisdom of God did not exist?! He said: "I was by him as a craftsman, I was his delight daily."
Or to say that the power of God did not exist, or His Word, or anything else by which the Son is known, or to which the Father points, is this not an error?!
Whoever says that the brightness of the glory of the Father did not exist at some time destroys the original light, which is the brightness....

Pope Alexander of Alexandria * Therefore the eternal brightness shines before Him and exists with Him, in the same existence that has no beginning, and is begotten always, and always shines before Him. He is the Wisdom who says, "I was with him, his delight; I was his delight always before his face..."
St. Dionysius the Great * His Wisdom is the one in whom is His delight always, as in His Spirit. He is one with Him as the soul of God, and stretches out like a hand to form the universe.
The Clementine Homilies "Rejoicing in the habitable part of his earth; and my delights were with the sons of men" [31].

If Wisdom declares that He is the object of the Father's delight, being one with Him and the Creator, then in turn He draws His delight in us, His creation, who disobeyed Him and rebelled against Him.

32 Now therefore hearken unto me, O ye children: for blessed are they that keep my ways. 33 Hear instruction, and be wise, and refuse it not. 34 Blessed is the man that heareth me, watching daily at my gates, waiting at the posts of my doors.

Finally, after Wisdom has declared the plan of His incarnation, which arises from His love and the Father's love for the sons of men, and His desire that we be the object of His good pleasure and delight, He calls us to listen to Him and to receive Him, so that we may enjoy the blessed life.
The Lord Christ says: "Verily, verily, I say unto you, If a man keep my saying, he shall never see death" (Jn 8:51).
"Now therefore hearken unto me, O ye children: for blessed are they that keep my ways" [32].
"Hear instruction, and be wise, and refuse it not" [33].
"Blessed is the man that heareth me, watching daily at my gates, waiting at the posts of my doors" [34].
* He who has the light is watchful, "and the darkness comprehended it not" (Jn 1:5), and he does not sleep, since there is no darkness.
He who is enlightened is wakeful toward God; thus he lives.
St. Clement of Alexandria
"For whoso findeth me findeth life, and shall obtain favour (will) of the LORD" [35].
The Wisdom of God asks us not only to listen to Him but to find Him and possess Him, as the Lord Christ says: "He that believeth on the Son hath everlasting life" (Jn 3:36).

Wisdom offers Himself to the human soul, and it must seek Him and find Him. Here seeking means the will, for Wisdom does not force His way into the human soul without its will; rather, when it seeks Him in complete freedom, it finds Him present. This holy will is also a gift from God, as the Apostle says: "For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure" (Phil 2:13).

* For man it is not good not to will, but by the grace of God he receives help to will, for it is not in vain that it is written: "For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure" (Phil 2:13); and that "the will is prepared of God."
St. Augustine

entries.section: 7. The misery of those who reject the call

paragraphs.text: "But he that sinneth against me wrongeth his own soul:
all they that hate me love death" [36].

The Lord Christ Himself says: "He that believeth not the Son shall not see life; but the wrath of God abideth on him" (Jn 3:36). He also says: "For as the Father raiseth up the dead, and quickeneth them; even so the Son quickeneth whom he will" (Jn 5:20). And the beloved John says: "He that hath the Son hath life; and he that hath not the Son of God hath not life" (1 Jn 5:12).
Let me possess You and enjoy life!
* Your voice resounds in my inner ears.

Let me ascend with You to the summits of the high mountains, to enjoy the splendor of Your glory on Mount Tabor, to delight in Your pure blood on Mount Golgotha, and to experience the company of the angels on the Mount of Temptation.
* When I find myself wandering, I see You standing on the way, waiting for me at the crossroads, carrying me on Your royal road, and bringing me into the bosom of Your Father.
* When my soul groans in distress, at the gates I find You a just Judge!
You hear all the troubles of my soul, and when the world wrongs me, I find You my defender!
* Let me hear Your voice and enjoy Your wisdom.
Your wisdom is the food that comes down from heaven.
It satisfies my soul and waters it.
It gives me a transcendent life, before which all the treasures of the world become very small.
* Let me possess You, O Wisdom of God, my beloved Jesus!
Then I will love goodness and hate all evils.
You give me good counsel and strength with honor.
You fill the storehouses of my soul with blessings that never perish!
* For my sake You became incarnate and became man, that I may meet You as a Savior and a personal friend.
You are the good pleasure of the Father; You have made me the object of Your pleasure and delight every day!
* Let me possess You and possess the light, so that there is no more darkness or night in me, and my eye does not slumber, but I remain watchful.
I enjoy the blessed life, and I receive partaking in the divine nature!
* Yes, whoever finds You finds eternal life!
And whoever sins against You acquires death!
You are my life, my joy, and my glory!

1 Wisdom hath builded her house, she hath hewn out her seven pillars: 2 She hath killed her beasts; she hath mingled her wine; she hath also furnished her table. 3 She hath sent forth her maidens: she crieth upon the highest places of the city, 4 Whoso is simple, let him turn in hither: as for him that wanteth understanding, she saith to him, 5 Come, eat of my bread, and drink of the wine which I have mingled. 6 Forsake the foolish, and live; and go in the way of understanding. 7 He that reproveth a scorner getteth to himself shame: and he that rebuketh a wicked man getteth himself a blot. 8 Reprove not a scorner, lest he hate thee: rebuke a wise man, and he will love thee. 9 Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser: teach a just man, and he will increase in learning. 10 The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding. 11 For by me thy days shall be multiplied, and the years of thy life shall be increased. 12 If thou be wise, thou shalt be wise for thyself: but if thou scornest, thou alone shalt bear it.

The wise Solomon reviews the concern of the Wisdom of God for the heavenly table that He has prepared for His beloved, the sons of men, who are the object of His good pleasure and delight, showing its cost and its effectiveness in their lives. He speaks of the following:

entries.section: A. The house of the banquet

paragraphs.text: Every emperor, king, or head of state takes care to set aside a main part of his palace for holding banquets, especially for emperors, kings, or presidents, and also for statesmen, officials, and others. The banquet hall reveals the person's concern for those he invites, and it also makes known the character of the one who gives the banquet. For this reason the building bears a national character that reveals the civilization of the country, its resources, and so on. But the Wisdom of God did not build a house to invite others to it; rather, He took on our human nature, becoming truly man. The house became not foreign to Him, but His own house. His divinity was united with His humanity without separation and without mixture. So the invitation He extends to us is that we abide in Him and become members of His body. It is an invitation to eternal union with Him!

He opened the doors of His house, that is, His body, not only when He opened His mouth before the crowds in the Sermon on the Mount, nor when He spoke with us on the level of the congregation as well as on the personal level, with each one of us, but when He allowed His side to be opened on the cross to pour out blood and water for us. His side is open at all times so that we may enter into His house and touch the bowels of His fiery love, and so enjoy continual existence with Him and in Him. As the Giver of the banquet Himself says: "Abide in me, and I in you" (Jn 4:15). And the Apostle Paul says: "Your life is hid with Christ" (Col 3:3).
"Wisdom hath builded her house" [1].
The house that the Wisdom of God built is the humanity of the Lord Christ. God's eternal plan prepared the Incarnation so that salvation might be accomplished.

* Let us look at Christ from both sides: the divine Word who became one in Mary with the one He took from Mary. For in her womb the Word formed for Himself a house, just as in the beginning He formed Adam from the earth.. Or rather, as the wise Solomon said plainly, knowing that the Word is called Wisdom: "Wisdom hath builded her house," which the Apostle interpreted, saying: "whose house are we," and in another place he calls us a temple. If it was fitting for God to dwell in a temple made after a certain pattern, built of stones, He commanded the ancient people through Solomon to build it, whereas at the appearing of the truth the pattern ceased (for the truth itself appeared).

Pope Athanasius the Apostolic * But we say that in the first part of the book, where it says, "Wisdom hath builded her house," he points in an obscure way through these words to the preparation of the body of the Lord, for the transcendent Wisdom did not dwell in another's dwelling, but built for Herself a dwelling from the body of the Virgin... Thus we can see in this passage Solomon moved by the spirit of prophecy, delivering to us in it the fullness of the mystery of the Incarnation.

St. Gregory of Nyssa * Here we surely recognize that the Wisdom of God, that is, the Word, who shares eternity with the Father, built for Himself a house, that is, a human body in the womb of the Virgin, and subjected the Church to Him as members to the Head. He slew the martyrs as sacrifices and prepared a table with bread and wine, having established the priesthood after the order of Melchizedek.
