He called the simple and those who lack sense, as the Apostle says: "God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty" (1 Cor 1:27).
St. Augustine * The testimony of St. Gregory of Nyssa in his book Against Eunomius:

"The Word was before all the ages, but the flesh was made in the fullness of time, and no one can say the opposite, that the flesh was before the ages, or that the Word was made in the fullness of time.

Theodoret * Christ, meaning the wisdom and power of God, built a house for Himself, that is, His nature in the flesh which He took from the Virgin, as John says: "The Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." This is as the wise prophet bears witness: the Wisdom who was before the world, the source of life, the Infinite, "the Wisdom of God hath builded her house" by means of a mother who knew not a man, that is, He took the temple of the body.

St. Hippolytus Holy Scripture declares that the Holy Trinity shared in accomplishing the divine Incarnation, or in establishing the house of the banquet, for it devised the plan of salvation, and the divine Wisdom built a house for Himself, and the divine Incarnation was accomplished by the work of the Holy Spirit in the womb of the holy Virgin Mary, who thereby received a unique honor. And the wonder is that the Wisdom of God also builds by His Holy Spirit a house for Himself in us, a dwelling for the Holy Trinity, as He says: "My Father will love him, and we will come unto him, and make our abode with him" (Jn 14:23).
* Just as we read that the Father wrought the mystery of the Lord's incarnation, and the Spirit also, so we read that Christ Himself made His body.
Of the Father it is written: "The LORD possessed me" (Prov 8:22), and in another place: "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law."
And the Spirit wrought the whole mystery, as we read: "Mary was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

St. Ambrose From our inner man He builds a wonderful house of banquet, which the soul calls "his garden," as it speaks to the Wisdom of God, saying: "Let my beloved come into his garden, and eat his pleasant fruits" (Song 4:16). And the divine Wisdom answers her invitation, saying:
"I am come into my garden, my sister, my spouse:
I have gathered my myrrh with my spice; I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey;
I have drunk my wine with my milk:
eat, O friends; drink, yea, drink abundantly, O beloved" (Song 5:1).

This is the house that the Wisdom of God builds in us and counts as His house and His garden, and to it He invites His heavenly friends to eat and drink and rejoice in the fruit of His wonderful Holy Spirit in us.
St. Gregory of Nyssa comments on this invitation which the human soul extends to the One who made a garden of it and turned its depths into a rich banquet, saying:
[Who is this whom the bride invites to her banquet, which bears its own fruits?
For whom has she prepared a banquet from her own (inner) resources?

Who is this whom the bride invites to the banquet she has prepared? None other than the One of whom and through whom and to whom are all things (Rom 11:36). He gives every one their meat in due season (Ps 145:15), He opens His hand and fills all living with His blessings. He came down as bread from heaven (Jn 6:41), and gave life to the world, and made the waters burst forth from His fountain of life. This is the One for whom the bride prepares her table.
The table is a garden planted with living trees.
We are indeed the trees, and the food offered to Him is the salvation of our souls.]

It is the work of the Wisdom of God to tear down the old tent, which is the works of the old man that sin has raised up in us, in order to build a new inner house, renewed every day. "Though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day" (2 Cor 4:16).

This house which the Lord Christ built is His holy Church, in which He presents Himself as a living stone, rejected of men, but chosen of the Father and precious (1 Pet 2:4); He bears us as living stones resting upon Him, built beside one another and united together to become like one tower. As St. Peter the Apostle says: "Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ" (1 Pet 2:5).

entries.section: B. The strength and stability of the house

paragraphs.text: "She hath hewn out her seven pillars" [1].

If the Wisdom of God has built a house for Himself, taking our humanity and making it one with Himself, then He hewed out seven pillars on which to set the building. What are these pillars but His fiery Spirit, one with Him? This Spirit, who cannot be separated from Him, He has given us by building our inner man as a house for Himself, so that we are supported by Him, and He leads us with power to the inexhaustible pastures of Christ and brings us into His eternal Kingdom, granting us strength, victory, and transcendent consolations.
* It is impossible for anyone to receive the grace of God unless he has the Holy Spirit, in whom are all the gifts of God.
St. Didymus the Blind * (The Holy Spirit) is called "the Comforter" because He comforts and gladdens those who are in tribulations.

St. Macarius the Great * When the soul is filled with the fruit of the Spirit, it is fully comforted from sadness, distress, and weariness, and it puts on spaciousness, peace, and joy in God, and the door of love for all people is opened in its heart.

Mar Isaac the Syrian * "She hath hewn out her seven pillars," that is, the sweet fragrance of the all-holy Spirit, as Isaiah says: "And the seven spirits of God shall rest upon him." Some see the pillars as the seven orders upon which creation stands by His holy and inspired teaching, namely the prophets, the apostles, the martyrs, the priests, the solitaries, the saints, and the righteous.
* He means the new Jerusalem and the holy body. And by the seven pillars he means the sevenfold unity of the Holy Spirit resting upon them.

St. Hippolytus * Concerning the dignity of the number seven we have many testimonies, but we content ourselves with a few of the many. For example: seven precious spirits are named, for I think Isaiah likes to call the activities of the Spirit spirits; and the teachings of the Lord are purified seven times, as David says (Ps 12:6); and the righteous is delivered from six troubles, and in the seventh no evil shall touch him. The sinner is forgiven not seven times, but seventy times seven. We can also see this by the opposite (for the punishment of the wicked is praised): vengeance was taken for Cain sevenfold, and when the punishment for the killing of his brother was carried out, it was exacted for Lamech seventy times sevenfold, because he was a murderer according to the Law and was condemned. And wicked neighbors receive sevenfold into their bosom, and the house of Wisdom rests on seven pillars, and the stone of Zerubbabel is adorned with seven eyes, and God is praised seven times a day, and also the barren woman bears seven, the perfect number, in contrast to her whose children are imperfect.
St. Gregory of Nazianzus
"She hath killed her beasts" [2].

What does the Lord Christ offer in His house but His body given up, a sacrifice of love, which the Father smells as a sweet savor, and which He offers to His believers as a transcendent heavenly table?
* This table is the support of our souls, the bond of our mind, the foundation of our hope, our salvation, our light, and our life.
* When you see the table prepared before you, say to yourself:
Because of His body I am no longer dust and ashes, nor a prisoner, but free!
Because of this (body) I hope for heaven, and I receive the heavenly goods, immortal life, the portion of the angels, and converse with Christ!
This body was nailed with nails and scourged, and death no longer has power over it!
It is the body that was stained with blood and pierced, and from it came forth the two fountains that save the world: the fountain of blood and the fountain of water.

St. John Chrysostom As we partake of this unique sacrifice, we long to share with our Christ His sacrificial love, so that we offer sacrifices of love without ceasing. As the teacher Tertullian says: [This sacrifice goes forth from the whole heart, is nourished by faith, observes the truth, enters in innocence and purity, in chastity, and is adorned with love. We must guard it with the greatness of good works, offering psalms and hymns on the altar of God so that we may receive all things from Him.]

With the Apostle Paul we offer the sacrifice of daily suffering and sing, saying: "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress.. As it is written, For thy sake we are killed all the day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter" (Rom 8:25, 26). By the cross of our Lord the ego is slain, and we say: "I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I," boasting that the slain Christ has become alive in us.. and we say: "but Christ liveth in me" (Gal 2:20).

We offer the sacrifice of humility before God (Ps 51:16, 17), the sacrifices of righteousness (Ps 4:5), the sacrifice of the body held in check by the cross of the Lord (Rom 12:1), the sacrifice of praise (Heb 13:15).
* I myself would like to be numbered among her children, that I may be slain by her. I would like to be slain in order to be a son.

But is she a slayer of her children, or a tormentor of them? For I hear God say also in another place: "I will burn them as gold in the fire, and I will try them as silver is refined." Surely it is by the pains of fire and punishments and by the trial of martyrdom for the faith.
The Apostle also knows a kind of slaying which he describes to us: "He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things?"
Behold how the divine Wisdom slays even what is her own!
The only-begotten firstborn Son is slain, who not only lives but gives life to others. I say: He is the Lord Christ who gives Himself for our transgressions.

Tertullian * The phrase "she hath killed her beasts" refers to the prophets and martyrs who were killed in every city and nation by unbelievers for the sake of the truth, and who cry out, saying: "For thy sake we are killed all the day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter."
St. Hippolytus
"She hath mingled her wine" [2].

The ancient Jews, Greeks, and Romans seldom drank wine without mixing it with water, and many ancient writers have dealt with this matter. Some see the mixing of wine with water at a ratio of 3 to 1, others 5 to 1, and Pliny noted that some wines require the addition of 20 measures of water, but the great majority hold that 3 measures of water are added to 2 measures of wine.

Some, however, do not mix wine with water to weaken its strength but mix it with spices or honey or myrrh, or madragora or opium and the like, to increase the sharpness of the wine, so that it not only intoxicates but also stupefies. Perhaps the mixing also refers to blending it with precious kinds of wine so as to bring a man joy and gladness of heart.

The Wisdom of God offers us His pure blood as a spiritual, heavenly drink. As it is said in the Liturgy of Bishop Serapion: [We offer to You this bread.. and this cup.. Make all who partake of it receive the medicine of life, healing for every weakness, support for all progress and virtue, and not judgment upon us.]

* Moreover, the Holy Spirit shows through the wise Solomon the order of the sacrifice of the Lord, pointing to the sacrifice offered of bread and wine. And also concerning the altar and the apostles he says: "Wisdom hath builded her house, she hath hewn out her seven pillars, she hath killed her sacrifices, she hath mingled her wine in the cup, she hath also furnished her table. She hath sent forth her maidens, she crieth upon the highest places of the city, Whoso is simple, let him turn in hither. And as for him that wanteth understanding, she saith to him, Come, eat of my bread, and drink of the wine which I have mingled." He proclaims the mingled wine, and also tells us beforehand with a prophetic voice of the cup of the Lord mingled with water and wine, which is shown to have been fulfilled in the passion of our Lord, of which prophecy was made beforehand.

St. Cyprian * The phrase "she hath mingled her wine" in an earthen vessel means that the Savior unites His divinity with the body like pure wine in the Virgin, born of her as God and man at the same time without mixture between them.

St. Hippolytus * Since they abandon milk, they drink wine that gladdens the hearts of those who are more perfect, who no longer practice childish things. Now they have become able to drink the good things from the cup of Wisdom with their mouths.

St. Gregory of Nyssa The Wisdom of God offers us the cup of wine, which is His blood shed for us for the forgiveness of our sins, and with it the cup of wisdom, that by it we may understand the mysteries of Holy Scripture and receive a spiritual knowledge that is effective in our lives.

* Those who receive symbols from Holy Scripture according to the understanding of the disciples enjoy the hope that the saints truly eat; indeed it will be the bread of life that refreshes the soul with the food of truth and wisdom, enlightens the mind, and makes it drink from the cup of divine wisdom according to the declaration of Holy Scripture.

Origen If wine points to spiritual joy, then as we partake of the holy blood and drink from the cup of wisdom, a true joy is born in us that supports the soul and waters it, so that it does not faint on the path of suffering.

entries.section: E. The order of the banquet

paragraphs.text: "She hath also furnished her table" [2].

By saying that she "furnished" or "prepared" her table, Holy Scripture affirms that this banquet, though free and with its doors open to every human being, is a banquet prepared by the Lord Himself. For long generations He prepared mankind through the fathers and the prophets to enter it. The banquet has its order and arrangement, because the One who prepared it is a God of order and not of confusion (1 Cor 14:32).

entries.section: F. The invitation to the banquet

paragraphs.text: "She hath sent forth her maidens: she crieth upon the highest places of the city,
Whoso is simple, let him turn in hither:
as for him that wanteth understanding, she saith to him,

entries.section: F. The invitation to the banquet

paragraphs.text: Come, eat of my bread, and drink of the wine which I have mingled" [3-5].

Wisdom sent her maidens to the tops of the hills and the heights and the mountains to cry out, for it is a general and public invitation, because God wills that all be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth. It was the custom anciently in some Asian cities that a person would send to those invited a company of maidservants, preceded by some eunuchs, and they would deliver the invitation to the feast.

St. Clement of Alexandria sees these messengers as the prophets who went before the Lord, whom He sent to invite them to the banquet; these are not thieves or robbers, but philosophy was not sent by the Lord, and so it came to steal. He means here the philosophies opposed to the truth and resisting the knowledge of God.

* The phrase "she hath furnished her table" refers to the knowledge of the Holy Trinity that was promised, and also to His precious pure body and blood, which are offered every day as a sacrifice on the divine spiritual table, a perpetual remembrance of the first divine spiritual supper.

St. Hippolytus The cry of the invitation is directed to the one who feels that he is simple, that he may turn aside and enjoy divine wisdom, and the one who feels that he lacks understanding comes forward to enjoy the table of true knowledge.
* In this house of the banquet, those who come from the east and the west find a place for themselves in the bosom of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the Kingdom of Heaven.
Origen

entries.section: G. The effectiveness of the banquet

paragraphs.text: "Forsake the foolish, and live; and go in the way of understanding" [6].

When the believer responds to the public, free call of Wisdom, it is fitting for him to show his response to this call by forsaking foolishness and walking in the way of understanding, through the riches of the grace of God working in him. He asks us to forsake ignorance and the foolish, for whoever keeps company with them necessarily becomes foolish like them.
* That (the table of demons) is a mingling with demons, but this (the table of the Lord) is fellowship with God.
St. Cyril of Jerusalem * The mystical table is the body of the Lord, which supports us against our passions and against Satan.
Truly Satan trembles at those who partake of these mysteries with reverence.
St. Cyril the Great

entries.section: H. The seriousness of the banquet

paragraphs.text: "He that reproveth a scorner getteth to himself shame: and he that rebuketh a wicked man getteth himself a blot.

entries.section: H. The seriousness of the banquet

paragraphs.text: Reprove not a scorner, lest he hate thee: rebuke a wise man, and he will love thee" [7-8].

The philosophers thought that they were without sin and formed a special class immune from error, but the word of God reveals the weakness of human nature and the need of all, even the teachers and leaders, for continual learning.

entries.section: H. The seriousness of the banquet

paragraphs.text: * Is this perhaps the reason that there is no one, even among those who dare to call themselves wise, because they (the philosophers) think that the wise man is without sin? But our Holy Scripture does not say this; it says: "Rebuke a wise man, and he will love thee" [8]. Without doubt, whoever thinks that a man must be rebuked judges that he is a sinner.

In any case, for my part I do not dare to count myself wise even in this sense. It is enough for me to count myself what they cannot deny, that the struggle for wisdom is ascribed to the philosophers, that is, to the lovers of wisdom. For those who practice the love of wisdom do not cease to struggle for wisdom, and these are counted wiser than they.

St. Augustine The invitation is directed to all, but only the man who is serious about the salvation of his soul perceives it. For this reason the scorner, finding in the invitation a rebuke of his carelessness, instead of responding to the call of Wisdom insults the one who offers it to him, and the wicked man who is determined to remain in his wickedness, instead of repenting, ascribes faults and evils to the one who cares for his salvation.

It is not strange that "unto every one that hath shall be given, and he shall have abundance: but from him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath" (Mt 25:29). He who has wisdom increases in wisdom, because he seeks to grow in it, and he loves the one who teaches and rebukes him that he may obtain knowledge. But he who has a spirit of mockery, scorn, and evil grows worse in evil, because he bears hatred toward the one who rebukes or guides him.

entries.section: H. The seriousness of the banquet

paragraphs.text: "Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser: teach a just man, and he will increase in learning" [9].

He did not say, "Give teaching to a wise man," but "Give to a wise man," without specifying what you offer him. For the wise man benefits from everything that is given to him; he is like the bee that gathers honey from every flower.

St. John Chrysostom sees among his people wise men who need him to begin some of his meditations on Holy Scripture with them to open the way, while they complete what he began and add to it, growing in wisdom.

* It would be fitting for us to present all the other points, but this would make the discourse very long, and extend over a very long time. For this reason we stop presenting other points, and leave this matter to you, for it is within your power to have it in your hands. It is within your power to gather these points together at home and examine the differences, and in the same way you will perceive new points. It was said: "Give the beginning of the place to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser" [9 LXX]. The beginning is from us, but the end is with you.
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: I. The way of the banquet

paragraphs.text: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding" [10].

We cannot enter the way of Wisdom unless we seek the fear of the Lord, for it is the beginning of wisdom, and it is also its goal. We begin with the divine fear that accompanies us all along the way until it brings us into the divine embrace. We enjoy a fear mingled with love, not the fear of slaves that casts out love, but the fear of sons who enjoy the spirit of love.

The teacher Tertullian, in his attack on philosophy and the philosophers, says that the philosophers fail to know God, and are doubtful, and fall into confusion because they have lost the fear of the Lord.

entries.section: J. The extension of the banquet

paragraphs.text: "For by me thy days shall be multiplied, and the years of thy life shall be increased" [11].

Wisdom grants a multitude of days and an increase in the years of life. Whether the days of the believer's life on earth are short or long, in the eyes of God they are fruitful and extended, and death cannot destroy them.

entries.section: K. The one who benefits from the banquet

paragraphs.text: "If thou be wise, thou shalt be wise for thyself: but if thou scornest, thou alone shalt bear it" [12].
What a man sows he reaps: if he sows wisdom, he enjoys it, and if he sows mockery and scorn, he harms no one but himself.
* No one shares in the spiritual table except the one who is called by (God), and who listens to the Wisdom that says: "Come, eat."

St. Dionysius the Great He who experiences Wisdom comes to her hungry, seeking her not to receive temporal blessings, but to possess her, and Jesus ben Sirach expressed this in a wonderful poem on the search for Wisdom with which he closed the book, in which he said:
[In my youth, before I went astray, I sought wisdom openly in my prayer.
Before the temple I asked for her, and I will seek her out even to the end.
My heart delighted in her blossom, as in a grape when it ripens.
My foot walked in the straight way.
From my youth I followed her track. I inclined my ear a little and received her.
And I found for myself much instruction.
I made progress by her, and to him who gave me wisdom I will give glory, for I purposed to practice her, and I was zealous for the good, and I shall not be put to shame.
I strove with my soul for her, and I observed the Law with great exactness.
I stretched out my hands to the heights, and I bewailed my ignorances.
I directed my soul to her in purity, and I found her.
With her I gained understanding from the beginning, therefore I shall not be forsaken.
My bowels were stirred in seeking her, therefore I have gained a good possession.]

13 A foolish woman is clamorous: she is simple, and knoweth nothing. 14 For she sitteth at the door of her house, on a seat in the high places of the city, 15 To call passengers who go right on their ways: 16 Whoso is simple, let him turn in hither: and as for him that wanteth understanding, she saith to him, 17 Stolen waters are sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant. 18 But he knoweth not that the shades are there; and that her guests are in the depths of hell.
"A foolish woman is clamorous: she is simple, and knoweth nothing" [13].

If the table of Wisdom was prepared and arranged by God Himself, offering divine resources which the believer enjoys in order to become wise and a possessor of knowledge, and to grow in both, then the table of folly is offered by the foolish woman. Perhaps by the foolish woman he means evil itself. He describes her as follows:
a. Foolish: without wisdom or true knowledge.
b. Clamorous: she causes a clamor that is meaningless and carries no love, but only noise and anxiety.
c. Simple: she acts with stupidity.
d. Haughty: she sits at the door of her house on a seat in the high places of the city, teaching the spirit of pride to whoever clings to her.

e. She calls those who walk in the truth to leave their way and walk after her. "To call passengers who go right on their ways: Whoso is simple, let him turn in hither: and as for him that wanteth understanding, she saith to him, Stolen waters are sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant" [15-17].

f. She seduces, offering sweetness with theft, and pleasure with that which is hidden in evil. While the Wisdom of God builds a house to which He invites us to enjoy a banquet of mutual love, folly calls the young and seduces them to a banquet of stolen waters and secret bread held in the street, without a house.

g. She offers phantoms and death to whoever accepts her hospitality and eats of the secret bread she offers and the sweet stolen waters. "But he knoweth not that the shades are there; and that her guests are in the depths of hell" [18].
A queen who cares for building. A foolish, simple woman.
She prepares a precious banquet. She calls to vain pleasures.
She offers the experience of the royal life. She offers slavery to pleasures.
* You have given me Your body and blood as a heavenly table; let me be satisfied, and rejoice, and grow in the knowledge of You.
I enjoy it and am united with You, O Savior of my soul.
* You have turned my soul into a temple for You, and set up Your altar within me, and proclaimed Your unique priesthood!
Accept my life as a sacrifice of love.
Pour upon it the wine of Your joy, and turn my depths into living sanctuaries.
* Carry me on Your shoulders, for I am foolish and weak!
Take me along Your royal way, that I may enjoy Your companionship.
* Support me, so that I am not drawn to the banquet of folly, nor listen to a strange voice.
Let me not seek passing pleasures, lest my soul descend to the pit.
* Break into my soul and enter into its depths.
Open to me the gates of heaven that I may enter them.
Dwell in my depths, and let me dwell in Your heavens!
You are my portion, my satisfaction, and the gladness of my heart.
"The proverbs of Solomon. A wise son maketh a glad father: but a foolish son is the heaviness of his mother" [1]
At the beginning of chapter ten we read "The proverbs of Solomon," or, as it appears in some old copies of the Vulgate, "The Second Book of Proverbs."
Some regard the preceding chapters (Prov 1-9) as a kind of introduction to the book, revealing the importance of wisdom and its blessings.

In these chapters we listen to Wisdom as she calls us to enter her house, to be united with her, and to live by her, so that we are enlightened in every action and under all circumstances. She also calls us not to listen to folly, for it is deceitful and turns us aside from the way of truth. The preceding chapters did not deal with the problems we face in their details; rather, they set out the broad lines and the spirit in which we should walk. They concentrated in a special way on the young, that they might attach themselves to wisdom and reject folly.

Now with chapter ten he begins to present the proverbs. Each proverb is short, but it has its weight in a person's life. For this reason this section needs a quiet reading, mingled with prayer and with striving to practice the wise life.

Some think that the body of the book begins with chapter ten, where this section deals through proverbs with the situations to which the believer is exposed. Others think that Holy Scripture as a whole, in all its parts (the Law, history, wisdom, and prophecy), is in harmony with this section and closely bound to it, and that these books offer practical examples throughout history that reveal the work of the Wisdom of God in us and its riches, as well as examples of those who reject wisdom and cling by their own will to folly.
Who is the father who is gladdened by his wise son? And who is the mother who grieves over the foolish son?

a. According to the literal interpretation, the wise man here means the father and the mother by blood, for they see in their son their hope in life that he will inherit from them, not only in their wealth and their experience of life, but also in their fellowship with God in Christ Jesus by the Holy Spirit. Without doubt the conduct of the son or the daughter is reflected in the parents' state of mind, but the wisdom of the son fills the father's heart with even more gladness, for he is proud of him, and perhaps turns to him as to a younger brother who shares counsel with him, and he may entrust to him the management of all his property with a glad heart. But the folly of the son or daughter is reflected even more on the mother, because she is more emotional than the father and cannot bear the ruin or loss of her children.

If the wise Solomon speaks to us of the wise son who brings joy to his father, he himself is an example of this (1 Chr 22:12; 2 Chr 1:7-12), and as for the mother who grieves over her son's folly, an example is Rebekah, who tasted bitterness from the folly of her son Esau (Gen 26:34-35; 27:46).

b. Since Solomon appears in this book as a father speaking with every member of his people as his son, the father and mother here are every person who feels an obligation toward those under his charge. Whether he is a king, a ruler, or a teacher, he does not seek to dominate, command, and forbid, but offers fatherhood or motherhood in love, so that all those around him may enjoy the wise life of faith.

c. If every believer in a position of leadership feels a fatherhood or motherhood toward those around him, how much more the bishop and the priest, who enjoy fellowship in the unique priesthood of the Lord Christ. With the Apostle Paul he bears bowels burning with love for the salvation of every soul and for bringing it into the fellowship of the heavenly glories.

* Be obedient to your bishop, and welcome him as a father to your soul... And I also say that bishops must know that they are priests and not lords... It is a bad custom that spreads in some churches that priests are bound to keep silent in the presence of bishops.

St. Jerome d. Evangelical Church teaching is a fatherly work, in which the priest gives not the juice of his thought but his whole life, in order to bring every person out of the corruption of the world into the glory of the children of God. This is what the Apostle Paul meant by his words: "I have begotten you through the gospel in Christ Jesus" (1 Cor 4:15).
* When a person learns from the mouth of another, he is called the son of the one who teaches him, and the latter is counted his father.
St. Irenaeus * The word is the child of the soul; therefore we call those who teach us our fathers... and the one who learns in submission is counted a son.

St. Clement of Alexandria e. Every true believer, under all circumstances and regardless of his age, carries in his depths a kind of fatherhood or motherhood, so his soul longs to see all humanity enjoying the blessed evangelical life that he enjoys.

f. But what is above all this is that we have the heavenly Father, who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim 2:4). If a father desires to make his son happy, offering all his resources, even his health and his time, for his happiness, then the father on his part is happy at his son's success. The happiness is shared between the wise father and the son who walks in wisdom. So God, the source of wisdom, offered His Wisdom (the Son) incarnate and given up for us, to raise up from us wise sons, and to find His pleasure in us as we become His icon and walk after His likeness in the spirit of wisdom. And just as the heavenly Father is pleased with His Son if he walks in the spirit of wise sonship, so the Church, as a mother, grieves over every soul marked by folly, because in her tender motherhood she wishes to raise every human soul to the glories prepared for it. The Church bears us in her womb as her members, who are fit to bear her wisdom, being like the Bridegroom, the Wisdom of God Himself, and sharing in His nature.

In other words, the wise man, though his soul rejoices and exults in God's work in him, God the giver of wisdom, the Lord of heaven Himself rejoices, as do the hearts of his family and all who love him; but if he turns aside to evil in folly, he loses his inner joy and grieves the hearts of many. Thus the wise Solomon uses every means to urge us to enjoy wisdom and to forsake folly.

entries.section: 2. The wise man's wealth of righteousness

paragraphs.text: 2 Treasures of wickedness profit nothing: but righteousness delivereth from death.

Perhaps someone will say: "I seek what is for myself; my father's pleasure does not concern me, and my mother's grief does not pain me. I am not a child; I care for what pleases me." Therefore the wise man affirms that all that a person gathers in his wickedness and folly profits him nothing.
"Treasures of wickedness profit nothing: but righteousness delivereth from evil" [2]

The portion of the righteous is happiness, life, and satisfaction, but the portion of the unbeliever is bitterness, death, and hunger. This righteousness is considered the introduction to all the virtues mentioned in this section.
Wealth that a person acquires by illegitimate means will not last; it quickly vanishes. And at the moment of death it does not support its owner.

The wicked man may be rich, but his treasures do not satisfy his depths, nor do they give him inner peace, so he always feels want. The righteous man, though poor, is made by God to need no one and nothing, and God gives him spiritual and psychological satisfaction with protection from evil. Righteousness delivers its owner from death, since for him it becomes a passage to a meeting with God face to face. The believer sees in the righteousness of Christ a victory over death and a triumph over Hades.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks to us of the wicked rich man who relies on his riches and gathers what he can by improper means, saying: "The partridge broodeth over what it hath not laid; he that getteth riches, and not by right, shall leave them in the midst of his days, and at his end shall be a fool" (Jer 17:11). So the foolish rich man embraces money and possessions, things that God gave to man to share with his brothers, and thinks them his alone; he toils and loses, and at the end of his life, when he leaves behind all that he gathered, he discovers that he was a fool. But the righteous man, whatever troubles and pains he suffers in this life, escapes eternal death.

The story of Esther presents a practical picture fulfilled throughout history: Haman, who had authority and wealth, lost everything, and evil surrounded him, while the godly Mordecai was glorified by God in this world and enjoys eternal glories.

* "Treasures of wickedness profit nothing" (see Prov 10:2). What then? Have not some escaped death by paying money (like one who pays a ransom so that he is not killed or sentenced to death)? Certainly this happens. But they cannot be cleared of sin, and in truth they prepare for themselves a life worse than death. Therefore we must not put our trust in wealth but in virtue... As for righteousness, it not only delivers those who possess it, but also leads many others to desire it, and continually transfers them from death to eternal immortality.

St. John Chrysostom * If a man casts his seed on ground full of thorns and abundant weeds, covered with the refuse of the harvest, he suffers a double loss. He loses his first seed, and he also suffers much toil. Therefore, in order that the divine seed may flourish well in us, let us first remove from our hearts worldly cares and the useless anxiety that makes us seek to be rich, for "we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out" (1 Tim 6:7). For what profit is there in possessing superfluous things? "Treasures of wickedness profit nothing: but righteousness delivereth from death" (Prov 10:2).
St. Cyril the Great
"The LORD will not suffer the soul of the righteous to famish: but he thrusteth away the desire of the wicked" [3]

The Lord does not allow the soul of the righteous to die of hunger, because it is He who feeds it, offering His word, the bread of life. The psalmist says: "I have been young, and now am old; yet have I not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread" (Ps 37:25).

It is not material, psychological, or social resources, or the circumstances surrounding each of them, that satisfy the heart of the righteous or leave the heart of the wicked hungry; rather the heart of the believer is lifted up as to the heavenly table, so that his depths exult in the midst of the tribulations that come upon him, while the depths of the wicked turn into an emptiness with nothing to satisfy it.
The men of God have sung of this satisfaction, and have also warned the wicked of the state of famine, hunger, and thirst that comes upon them. We recall, for example:
As for me, I will behold thy face in righteousness: I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness (Ps 17:15).
The meek shall eat and be satisfied: they shall praise the LORD that seek him: your heart shall live for ever (Ps 22:26).
They shall not be ashamed in the evil time: and in the days of famine they shall be satisfied (Ps 37:19).
My soul shall be satisfied as with marrow and fatness; and my mouth shall praise thee with joyful lips (Ps 63:5).
Blessed is the man whom thou choosest, and causest to approach unto thee, that he may dwell in thy courts: we shall be satisfied with the goodness of thy house, even of thy holy temple (Ps 65:4).
Man did eat angels' food: he sent them meat to the full (Ps 78:25).
O satisfy us early with thy mercy; that we may rejoice and be glad all our days (Ps 90:14).
With long life will I satisfy him, and shew him my salvation (Ps 91:16).
Who satisfieth thy life with good things; so that thy youth is renewed like the eagle's (Ps 103:5).
He watereth the hills from his chambers: the earth is satisfied with the fruit of thy works (Ps 104:13).
The trees of the LORD are satisfied; the cedars of Lebanon, which he hath planted (Ps 104:16).
That thou givest them they gather: thou openest thine hand, they are filled with good (Ps 104:28).
Thou openest thine hand, and satisfiest the desire of every living thing (Ps 145:16).
He maketh peace in thy borders, and filleth thee with the fat of the wheat (Ps 147:14).
A covetous man's eye is not satisfied with his portion; and the wickedness of the wicked drieth up his soul (Sir 14:9).

* "And filleth thee with the fat of the wheat" (Ps 147:14). Note that he did not say "wheat" only, but "the richest fat of the wheat," pointing to great abundance, the most abundant of fruits. For the gifts of God are like this, as you see, exalted and flourishing. He speaks of them here as giving satisfaction from the best kinds of wheat and in overflowing generosity, to show that He does not merely give to you, but satisfies you.
* He gives not merely food, but what is profitable for everyone, what everyone desires, and what satisfies everyone.

St. John Chrysostom * Do you fear that your inheritance will run short if you begin to give generously from it? Where has it ever happened that the resources of a righteous person failed, when it is written: "The LORD will not suffer the soul of the righteous to famish" (Prov 10:3)?
Elijah was fed by the ravens in the wilderness.

And a meal was prepared from heaven for Daniel in the pit, when he was shut in by the king's command to be prey for the lions, and you fear that you will lack bread... The Lord Himself rebuked in the Gospel those who have doubt in their thought and whose faith is weak, saying: "Behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feedeth them. Are ye not much better than they?" (Mt 6:26).

God feeds the birds, offering daily food to the sparrows and to creatures that have no sense of divine things and do not need food or drink. Can a Christian then lack anything?! Can the servant of the Lord lack? Can one who practices good works, and who is dear to the Lord, lack?!

St. Cyprian If God is the supreme eternal Good, then the wealth of this world cannot satisfy the soul that is in the image of its Creator; rather, its union with God, and its enjoyment of His dwelling in it, satisfies it and fills it with joy.
* O my poor soul, what are you seeking?!
If you want wisdom, you will find Jesus, the source and fountain of wisdom, indeed Wisdom Himself!
If you seek strength and power, He is the Almighty!
If you search for pleasure and delight, He is the fountain of true joy!
If you long for intoxication, His love intoxicates the soul!
If you hunger for bread, He is the bread of life!
If you are passionate for riches, He is the Creator of all!
If you want rest, you will find your rest in Him alone...! Receive Him, for you have no one else to satisfy you.
St. Augustine
4 He becometh poor that dealeth with a slack hand: but the hand of the diligent maketh rich. 5 He that gathereth in summer is a wise son: but he that sleepeth in harvest is a son that causeth shame.
"He becometh poor that dealeth with a slack hand: but the hand of the diligent maketh rich" [4]
The wise man is always at work and in motion, gathering riches. The fool is lazy, preferring sleep and slackness to watchfulness and diligence, and his portion is poverty.

God created Adam and set him in Paradise to work, for He blesses the diligent hand, and in His providence allows the slack hand to become poor, for whoever does not work shall not eat. Whoever sows neglect reaps poverty, and whoever sows zeal and diligence reaps blessing and success.

Work and the ability to do it are a gift that God gives to man, so it is fitting for the believer not to stop working as long as he can, and as far as the strength, ability, and talents God gives him allow. The call to work has come as a command of Scripture. The Apostle says: "For yourselves know how ye ought to follow us: for we behaved not ourselves disorderly among you; neither did we eat any man's bread for nought; but wrought with labour and travail night and day, that we might not be chargeable to any of you" (2 Thess 3:7-8). It is as though a serious and practical desire to work accompanies living faith and expresses it.

The land that the farmer does not toil to plow and sow yields thorns instead of grapes or other fruits and crops. The earth, with all its rich resources, does not give us fruits or treasures without work, such as farming, prospecting for mines of precious metals, and fishing... for the earth could not have been fit for life if work had not been practiced.

Most of the governments of the world have recognized the danger of unemployment and idleness for the behavior of society, and so they have counted unemployment the most dangerous enemy that threatens society and robs it of its peace. For work is not only a source of increased production, but also of the growth of man's character and his inner peace.

The joyful message of the Gospel came as a clear call to work without ceasing, by the riches of God's grace, that man may reach the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, that is, that the believer remain striving all the days of his sojourn to taste the sweetness of the inner Kingdom.

* In the beginning God gave us a life free from cares and exempt from toil. But we did not use the gift well; we spoiled our rest and lost Paradise. For this reason He made our life wearisome... Idleness works to corrupt us and causes us many troubles.

* In the beginning you could have worked without toil... because God Himself wanted this, but you did not allow it. For God did not mix work with toil. If man had experienced toil from the beginning, he would not have been afflicted with it afterward as a punishment. In fact you can work and at the same time not reach the stage of hard labor, as in the case of the angels.

St. John Chrysostom * Let us contemplate the fear of God in the lives of these saints. Yes, we find that it is written of Moses and Aaron that they worked and lived with men who walked after their example, and so too Joshua the son of Nun.
A letter attributed to St. Clement of Rome * The good worker receives the wages of his work with boldness, but the lazy and the negligent does not dare to look his employer in the eye.

St. Clement of Rome * Everyone who comes to you in the name of the Lord, receive him (Mt 21:9; Ps 118:26); after that test him and get to know him, so that you may distinguish the right hand from the left.
If the one who comes is a traveler passing through, help him as far as you are able, but he should not stay with you more than two or three days if necessary.
If he wants to stay with you as a craftsman, let him work in order to eat (2 Thess 3:10).
But if he has no trade, then direct him yourselves, so that he does not live among you as an idle Christian.
If he does not want to work, he is a trafficker in Christ (1 Tim 6:5); beware of such people.
The Didache The text in the Septuagint reads: "Poverty brings a man low, but the hands of the diligent make rich"

* It is said: "Poverty makes a man humble" [4 LXX]. And Christ also says: "Blessed are the poor in spirit" (Mt 5:3). Do you grieve because you are on the road that leads to virtue? Do you not know that this gives us great confidence (He cares for us in spite of our poverty)?!
St. John Chrysostom * It is said: "Poverty brings a man low"; by poverty he means stinginess, by which the rich man becomes poor, having nothing to offer to others.
St. Clement of Alexandria "He that gathereth in summer is a wise son: but he that sleepeth in harvest is a son that causeth shame" [5]

Here the wise Solomon blames the one who does not seize the right opportunity for work, for if a man is negligent in the season of harvest, he loses his labor that he did during the sowing. It is as though it is fitting for a man to labor not only in the season of plowing and sowing, taking care of the crop, but also in the summer, the time of harvest. The Lord Christ urged His disciples to work, saying to them: "Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest" (Jn 4:35).

The wise man portrays our life on earth as sons working in our Father's vineyard. It does not befit us to sleep at the time of harvest, and so be counted sons of disgrace and shame; rather we should work and gather, and as the Apostle says: "Redeeming the time, because the days are evil" (Eph 5:16). It is a precious time for work in our Father's vineyard. The Apostle Paul gives us a practical example of working without ceasing, while Demas represents the man who sleeps at harvest time. "For Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world, and is departed unto Thessalonica" (2 Tim 4:10)
"Blessings are upon the head of the just: but violence covereth the mouth of the wicked" [6]

The righteous man walks uprightly, submits to counsel, and obeys commands in the Lord, so his portion is blessedness and safety. The unbeliever walks in crooked ways, deceitful and in inner terror, and his end is destruction.

Although the world cannot bear the righteous, it is only for a time, and these will surely receive many blessings in their depths in this world, and openly in the world to come. But as for the wicked, their mouth, filled with violence, testifies against them and deprives them even of temporal blessings; their mouth condemns them!

The law of the harvest is that what a man sows he reaps, so whoever sows uprightness reaps the blessings of God and the praise of others. But whoever sows the tares of sin, injustice and violence rule his mouth, and his words come forth from a corrupt heart.

entries.section: 6. The memory of the wise man

paragraphs.text: "The memory of the just is blessed: but the name of the wicked shall rot" [7]

The righteous and the wicked both die, but their destiny differs, and even their remembrance differs, for the memory of the righteous remains a blessing to many, while the name of the wicked becomes like a garment eaten by moths. For after nearly twenty centuries we find no Christian who calls his son Judas, but we find many who call him "Paul."

Paul stood alone before a dangerous lion roaring to devour him, the unjust Nero. But he saw the Lord standing before him, whose eternity and remembrance death cannot destroy: "Notwithstanding the Lord stood with me, and strengthened me; that by me the preaching might be fully known, and that all the Gentiles might hear: and I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion. And the Lord shall deliver me from every evil work, and will preserve me unto his heavenly kingdom" (2 Tim 4:17-18).

After the death of the prophet Elisha, when the raiders of Moab cast a man into his grave, and the body touched the bones of Elisha, he revived and stood up on his feet (2 Kgs 13:21). So his memory bore a power that appeared from his bones! And the Lord Christ said of the woman who broke the alabaster flask of ointment and poured it on His head: "Verily I say unto you, Wheresoever this gospel shall be preached throughout the whole world, this also that she hath done shall be spoken of for a memorial of her" (Mk 14:9). And St. Mary said: "For, behold, from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed" (Lk 1:48).

The memory of the righteous remains carrying the sweet fragrance of Christ, and offers blessings through the generations, so we should not be surprised to see St. Gregory of Nazianzus lament his brother St. Caesarius, not denying human feelings, but asking that they be with moderation. He says: [Even in my tears and admiration I must respect the law that governs these things, for this is not foreign to our philosophy. It says: "The memory of the just is accompanied by blessings." And let tears also flow from our eyes, and begin with lamentation, as those who have suffered a great loss (by his death), and so remove from us insensibility and excess.]

* "The memory of the just is praised." He did not say this to mean that our praise helps the departed souls. Rather he said it because those who praise the departed receive the greatest benefit from their remembrance. Therefore, since we gain much benefit from their holy remembrance, let us not despise the words of the wise man, but rather give heed to them.
St. John Chrysostom
"The wise in heart will receive commandments: but a prating fool shall fall" [8]

When the heart of the believer is filled with heavenly wisdom, as the Wisdom of God dwells in him, he bows down before Him with his whole being, and his soul exults in obedience to the divine commandment. But the fool thinks himself wise, and does not want to listen to the divine voice, but in stubbornness insists on his own thought.

Since Abraham, the father of fathers, was wise, "when he was called to go out into a place which he should after receive for an inheritance, obeyed; and he went out, not knowing whither he went" (Heb 11:8). So Abraham and his sons according to the Spirit found joy and gladness in obedience to the commandment.

The man who is wise in his heart turns his knowledge into action, so he receives the commandments and fulfills them, for he longs to hear and obey in the Lord. He thirsts for the word of the Lord like the thirsty land that longs for water to quench it and turn it into a paradise. But the fool in his words brings forth empty words that do not support him but cause him to fall.
"He that walketh uprightly (in simplicity) walketh surely: but he that perverteth his ways shall be known" [9]

The upright man is always secure; he is marked by simplicity, has no two faces or two personalities, and walks uprightly without fear, because there is no place in his life for hypocrisy or craftiness. But whoever perverts his ways, thinking he can hide his deceits, will surely have them discovered and his affair exposed.

Joseph walked uprightly in his father's house, and was a faithful and upright servant in the house of Potiphar the Egyptian, and was faithful even as a prisoner, and so lived in security despite the tribulations that came upon him and pursued him. And at last he sat as the second man in Pharaoh's palace. All this commends him before God, to live forever in the divine embrace in heavenly peace and eternal security.

St. John Chrysostom sees that uprightness here means simplicity, in which the believer lives with a simple mind, not composite or complicated, walking the straight way and not limping between this way and that.

* We do not recommend that we acquire a simplicity without knowledge, so that we yield to everything that is said and are deceived by every deceitful teaching, but we mean by simplicity that whose whole meditation is on virtue, God, and goodness, like the child who knows only one teacher and fears him alone, and carries out only his command, and does not accept the teaching of any other teachers.

So the believer ought to be a child in his conduct with Christ, with His fear ruling his life, and not accept teaching from any other teacher. For childhood is pure by nature, and no tyranny corrupts the mind of the child.

Let us now rejoice in discipleship to Christ in the way He has shown us, and strive to walk in simplicity and be children in order to receive good teaching. And let us be wise as serpents against the enemy who schemes to harm us, and remember at all times the saying of our Lord that whoever does not receive the Kingdom of God as a child will not enter it (Lk 18:7). May the Lord make us worthy of it, to whom be glory for His greatness. Amen.
St. Mar Philoxenos * "Blessed is every simple (upright) soul" (see 11:25 LXX), "He that walketh in simplicity walketh surely" [9].

For this is the cause of all kinds of evil, that many do not know how to apply the commandment uprightly, even the testimony of the Holy Scriptures. So in this case the writer does not mean by (simplicity) the foolish man, or the one who knows nothing, but the one who is free from evil, who is not a doer of evil, for he is wise.

* Was not the Gospel first preached to the shepherds (the simple)? And also to Joseph, who, being simple in mind, did not allow the suspicion of adultery to frighten him into committing a wrong? Did not God choose the simple, men who are sincere by nature? For it is written: "Blessed is every simple soul," and also "He that walketh in simplicity walketh surely" [9].
You say: "True, but prudence is required."
I ask you: "What is simplicity if not prudence?!" For when you do not suspect men, and do not pretend anything, when you have no disturbances and cannot remember the harm!

* Absalom was a deceitful man who stole the hearts of all men (2 Sam 6:15). Note how great his deceit was, for it is recorded that he would come forward and say: "Hath no man judged thee?" wishing to win everyone over to himself. But David was innocent. What then? Look at the end of both. See how the first was full of madness! For since he concentrated wholly on harming his father, he was struck blind in everything, because "he that walketh uprightly walketh surely" (Prov 9:10).

St. John Chrysostom Let the insincere listen to what is written: "He that walketh in simplicity walketh surely" [9]. Truly simplicity of conduct is a guarantee of security. Let them warm themselves with what the mouth of the wise man says: "Deceit flees from the discipline of the Holy Spirit" (Wis 1:5). Let them also hear what the testimony of Scripture affirms: "his strong relationship (his secret) is with the upright" (Prov 3:32), for God's strong dealings are His disclosure of His secrets to human minds by the enlightenment of His presence.

"But he that perverteth his ways shall be known"; in contrast to simplicity, deceit, or walking in a crooked way. The deceitful think that by their experience and skills they are able to deceive others and not be discovered. But "there is nothing hid, which shall not be manifested; neither was any thing kept secret, but that it should come abroad" (Mk 4:22). Judas planned with the Pharisees to betray the Lord Christ, and thought that his affair would not be discovered, but what he did in secret carried a scandal on the level of earth and heaven, and across the centuries.
"He that winketh with the eye causeth sorrow: but a prating fool shall fall" [10]

We have already spoken of the last part of this verse (see [8]). The text in the Septuagint reads: "He that reproves with boldness makes peace." The text in the Syriac agrees with the Septuagint. Whoever rebukes sin faithfully and openly supports the peace of the community more than one who ignores it or does not care about it. For many sinners return to God through a word of rebuke full of frankness and love, especially if the rebuke is joined with a spirit of tenderness and humility. Although rebuke wounds the feelings of the sinner, its being mingled with love and tenderness drives him to sincere repentance.
Winking with the eye points to deceit and cunning, and anciently it pointed to corrupt glances that stir up fleshly desires.

Some think that winking of the eyes indicates that what he utters is other than what he conceals within, or that what he says is other than what he thinks. Others think that the kiss of Judas to the Lord Christ at His betrayal was a kind of deceit like winking of the eye.

St. Clement of Alexandria sees it as a form of adultery, in which a person expresses the desires of his body with his eyes. For the glances and movements of the eye reveal either the inner enlightenment or the hidden desires of the flesh.

* The amorous, mocking glances, which are winks of the eyes, are nothing but the commission of adultery by the eyes, for lust is fought through the eyes. For of the whole body the eyes perish first. "The eye that contemplates the beauty of things gladdens the heart," meaning that the eye that sees uprightly rejoices.

"Winking the eye with deceit gathers woes for men." These practice the effeminacy of Sardanapalus, king of the Assyrians, who sat on his throne with his feet raised up, daintily fingering his purple robe, and rolling the whites of his eyes upward. So do women who practice the same thing, displaying their desire for sin through their glances.
And as Scripture says: "The light of the body is the eye," so the radiance of the light appears through inner enlightenment.
"The adultery of a woman is in the lifting of the eyes" (Sir 26:9).
St. Clement of Alexandria
"The mouth of a righteous man is a well of life: but violence covereth the mouth of the wicked" [11]

The mouth of the wicked is full of violence and deceit, stirring up quarrels, and his portion is punishment and destruction. But the speech of the righteous is a source of rest and knowledge for his hearers, offered in the spirit of love [12]. His portion is the fellowship of goodness with others and the storing up of knowledge and wisdom.

The mouth of the righteous is always spoken through by the Lord who dwells in him, as it was said to the prophet Moses: "Now therefore go, and I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt say" (Ex 4:12). And to the prophet Jeremiah: "I have put my words in thy mouth" (Jer 1:9). Therefore he overflows with living waters, that is, words useful for teaching, comfort, and guidance.

The expression "a well of life" in Hebrew means "overflows in the arteries of life," as though the mouth of the righteous man becomes like the heart that receives the impure blood and beats to pour out pure blood into the arteries of the whole body. So no evil or harmful word comes out of the mouth of the righteous, but he overflows with words of divine life, so that everyone who meets him finds rest and enjoys God's work in him.
The Lord Christ, who dwells in the spiritual man, is manifested in all his words, and presents him as a mystery of life to others.
The spiritual man lives in the likeness of his Lord, so that his whole heart beats with life without ceasing for the life of others and their growth in every aspect of their lives.
The mouth of the righteous is like a well that overflows with sweet water on the surrounding land and waters it, as it quenches the thirst of people, animals, and birds.
As for the last part of the verse, it was discussed earlier (verse 6).

If the mouth of the righteous is like a spring, overflowing with the waters of the Spirit on those around him, turning deserts into gardens full of fruit, the mouth of the wicked is like a sea full of turbulence, casting from its depths salt water on the shores. The sound of its currents never calms, night or day, and not even grass can grow on its shores, and if it overflows with its waters on a cultivated field, it ruins all its crop!
So from every person's mouth comes what overflows from his heart, either sweetness that gives life and growth, or saltiness that destroys life and sends forth death.
This phrase reminds us of the Lord Christ's words to the Samaritan woman: "He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water" (Jn 7:38).
"Hatred stirreth up strifes: but love covereth all sins" [12]

If the wise Solomon has linked wisdom with righteousness, the third of them is love, without which a person loses the spirit of wisdom and divine righteousness. He also links folly with evil, and the third is hatred, for folly and evil have their source in the closing of the heart and its rejection of love, and at the same time they feed hatred and make it grow. Hatred is their cause and their source, and it grows and flourishes by them.

In the spirit of hatred a person remembers past events that stir his soul and urge him to quarrels, and he cannot forget even after tens of years, and cannot forgive the faults of his brothers. But the spirit of love is like beautiful curtains that cover the faults and mistakes of others, and therefore he does not boil inside because of them. If love "beareth all things," keeping the peace of the soul and the unity of the community, hatred stirs up the soul, which stirs up disturbances within, and disputes and quarrels without. Hatred seeks to find an opportunity to stir up enmity, for it finds its pleasure in divisions and quarrels, but love gives harmony and reconciliations, and removes from every soul the evil provocations, so that the person finds his delight in building up his brothers, pouring water on every flame to extinguish it.

Both the Apostle James and the Apostle Peter quoted this phrase. "From whence come wars and fightings among you? come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members?" (Jas 4:1). "For charity shall cover the multitude of sins" (1 Pet 4:8).

* He who has love considers no one a stranger, but considers all as his kin and family, and knows no anger, and is not arrogant, and does not burn with fury, and does not wrong, and does not rob another of his honor, and never counts anyone his enemy except the devil alone.

Mar Ephrem the Syrian * Just as our enemy divides the brothers who are still weak and carnal by a sudden outburst of anger over some trivial causes and earthly matters, so he sows the seed of strife even among spiritual persons on the basis of differences in thought, and from these there certainly arise disputes and struggles with words, which the Apostle condemns... By these our malicious and dangerous enemy sows strife between brothers who were of one mind. For the words of the wise Solomon are true: strife begets hatred, but friendship is a fortress for all who do not fight.
St. John Cassian

13 In the lips of him that hath understanding wisdom is found: but a rod is for the back of him that is void of understanding. 14 Wise men lay up knowledge: but the mouth of the foolish is near destruction.
"In the lips of him that hath understanding wisdom is found: but a rod is for the back of him that is void of understanding" [13]
The speech of the man of understanding supports others, but the fool benefits no one, and succeeds only in drawing punishments to fall upon himself.

He who bears wisdom in his heart as in his mind, wisdom announces its presence through his words, so his mouth is blessed and his lips are a storehouse of wisdom. But the one who is void of understanding, that is, one able to learn who does not want to learn, the rod is his teacher, falling on his back so that he bends down broken. In other words, whoever does not seek wisdom and knowledge from a burning, loving heart prepares his back for harsh blows, and bends down by force and in bitterness.

Perhaps the lives of both Solomon himself and his son Rehoboam illustrate this proverb. The first did not rely on his personal wisdom, but asked wisdom from God, and many came from the ends of the earth to hear his wisdom and benefit. "And there came of all people to hear the wisdom of Solomon, from all kings of the earth, which had heard of his wisdom" (1 Kgs 4:34). But Rehoboam relied on his human wisdom and the counsel of his young friends, and did not consult God, nor accept the counsel of the elders, and because of him the kingdom was divided, and the rod of discipline fell on his back (1 Kgs 12:8-19).
"Wise men lay up knowledge: but the mouth of the foolish is near destruction" [14]

The wise man is skillful: whenever he finds knowledge, he stores it in his depths, especially the word of God, hiding it and guarding it by a godly, holy life, so that when he needs it he finds it not far from him but within him. He lays up knowledge through living, practical faith with prayer and earnest study of the word of God, so that he may enjoy the Lord Christ, the Wisdom of God, and possess Him, saying with the holy soul: "I held him, and would not let him go, until I had brought him into my mother's house, and into the chamber of her that conceived me. I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please" (Song 3:4-5).
The wise man keeps knowledge in order to speak it at the right time, in the right place, in a fitting manner, and to the right person.

Since the wise man understands the value of words, he counts them as jewels that must be stored in a safe place, but the fool does not cease from speech that has no meaning, which brings him near to destruction. You do not know what he will say, because he brings out words without balance, bringing upon himself and others countless troubles.
For the sake of a man's peace and the building up of his brothers, it is fitting for him to think much and speak little, and not utter a word without thought preceding it.

St. Timothy represents the wise man who is rich in true knowledge: "But continue thou in the things which thou hast learned and hast been assured of, knowing of whom thou hast learned them; And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus" (2 Tim 3:14-15). On the contrary, Elymas the sorcerer represents the arrogant fool who destroys himself (Acts 13:6-11).

* St. Paul says: "If ye then be risen with Christ, seek those things which are above." And he adds: "For ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God. When Christ, who is our life, shall appear, then shall ye also appear with him in glory" (Col 3:1-4).

Life according to the flesh disappears in us if our base nature blames us, and then we transfer the ambition of our life from earth to heaven. As the proverb says: "Wise men lay up knowledge" (Prov 10:14). Then we wait for the true life, and Christ appears in us and we are filled with His glory, and are changed into a holy state.

Let us now listen to the words of the Song, as though we had died in the body, so that we are not drawn to words with a fleshly meaning. The person who has died to the passions turns the literal meaning of the words of the Song into pure and undefiled meanings. And since his mind is empty of earthly things, his mind is occupied with the things above, where Christ is, free from passion, sitting on the right hand of the glory of God (Col 3:1). Let us now listen to the words that describe the pure beauty of the bride. May we listen as though we did not share in the nature of the body, but had passed over into the realm of the Spirit.
St. Gregory of Nyssa
"The rich man's wealth is his strong city:
the destruction of the poor is their poverty" [15]

This proverb is not advice that the wise man offers, but a statement of a regrettable reality, in which the rich man sees in his wealth his fortified city, and so is all the more fond of enlarging his possessions, while the poor man, seeing the rich man robbing him of his rights, collapses and has no motive to be delivered from the state of poverty that holds him captive.

Some think that this proverb means that the rich grows richer and the poor grows poorer. That is, the truly rich man strives all the more without ceasing, and the careless poor man persists in his carelessness without commitment or a sense of responsibility.

Many rich people lose their inner peace and live in terror for fear of losing their possessions through theft, so they feel their need of a fortified and safe city in which to put their treasures. Likewise many poor people are crushed by murmuring and discontent.

But from the spiritual side, the wealth of the rich man is his inner city, when his heart becomes the new Jerusalem from above, the icon of heaven, which no sin can slip into and no enemy can assault, so that the person lives rich with the heavens of God revealed within him. The poor man is the one whose eyes do not look to the inner wealth, and so he loses the One in whom we have a treasure.

* Wealth in itself is not an evil thing. "The ransom of a man's life are his riches" (Prov 13:3), for whoever gives to the poor redeems himself; therefore even in wealth there is room for virtue. You are like helmsmen on a great sea: if a man steers his course well he crosses the sea quickly and reaches the harbor, but the one who does not know how to manage his possessions well sinks in his cargo. So it is written: "The rich man's wealth is his strong city" (Prov 10:15).

St. Ambrose * To enjoy anything means to cling to it firmly for the sake of the thing itself. But to use something is to employ what we receive in order to obtain what we need, provided that it is fitting for us to need it.

* Do not think that silver or gold should be blamed because of the greedy, nor food and wine because of gluttons and drunkards, nor female beauty because of adulterers and fornicators. So it is in all other matters, especially when you see a physician using fire in a good way while a murderer uses bread containing poison to carry out his crime.

* When Job lost all his wealth and reached extreme poverty, he kept his soul undisturbed, fixed on God, to show that earthly things had no value in his eyes, but that he was greater than they, and God greater than he. If the men of our day had the same mind, we would not have been so persistently forbidden in the New Testament to possess these things in order to reach perfection. For our possessing such things without being attached to them is something more worthy of praise than not possessing them at all.
St. Augustine
"The labour of the righteous tendeth to life:
the fruit of the wicked to sin" [16]

Perhaps the righteous man has nothing but the toil of his hands; he works in order to eat and live, and finds life and sweetness in his work. But the wicked man spends what he earns on sin, whether by his extravagance or by his stinginess. He squanders every blessing, and lives like one who is dead.

Some think that the righteous man puts his hand to honorable, lawful work that gives life its taste, offering what is for the building up of the community. But the wicked man puts his hand to improper works because they are more profitable, so he offers to others what is for their destruction, and his sins multiply into sins, and he continues in this without ceasing until he destroys himself and others.

* For we remember that we must be thankful to the Lord our God and Creator. We reject no fruit of His works; we use them in moderation and not in sinful excess. For this reason we do not fail to frequent the forums, the markets, the baths, the shops, the workshops, the inns, and all your business, and to keep all our other relations, so as to express our life with you in this world. With you we sail the sea, we enlist in military service, we till the soil and trade, and we sell openly the products of our commerce and our manufacture that you use.
Tertullian Origen says that no one is idle in the house of the wise man.
"He is in the way of life that keepeth instruction (discipline): but he that refuseth reproof erreth" [17]

A person lives as one on a journey toward heaven; the believer, keeping discipline, accepts counsel and so does not turn aside from the way of life. But the wicked man rejects counsel and does not accept discipline, so he goes astray and remains in his error.

* Just as the refiner of gold throws the piece of gold into the furnace so that it endures the fire for a time until he sees that it has been purified, so God permits the testing of human souls by tribulations until they are purified and obtain great benefit...

Let us not be troubled or despair when trials come upon us. For just as the refiner of gold knows the time the gold should be left in the furnace, and takes it out at the appointed time and does not leave it any longer in the fire lest it be spoiled and burned, how much more does God know this. When He sees that we have been greatly purified, He frees us from our trials, lest we be cast down and cast out because of the increase of our evils.

When something comes upon us that we did not expect, let us not murmur or lose heart, but receive it from God, who knows these things exactly, so that He tests our hearts by fire as He pleases, doing this for the benefit of those who are tried. Therefore the wise man commands us to submit to God in all things, for He knows perfectly when to bring us out of the furnace of evil (Wisdom of Jesus 1:1-2).

It is fitting for us to submit to Him always, and to thank Him continually, bearing everything with contentment, whether He grants us blessings or gives us disciplines. For the latter are a kind of blessing.
For the physician is a physician not only when he allows us to bathe (in the baths)... or to go to pleasant gardens, but also when he uses the scalpel and the knife!
And the father is a father not only when he caresses his son, but also when he disciplines and punishes him...!

And since we know that God is more tender than all physicians, it is not for us to inquire into His dealings, nor to demand an account of them from Him, but He does what seems good in His sight. So let us not distinguish whether He frees us from trial or disciplines us, for in both ways He wishes to restore us to health and make us partners with Him, and He knows our different needs, and what suits each one of us, and how and in what way we must be saved...
Let us follow Him wherever He commands us, and not think much about whether He commands us to walk an easy, smooth way or a hard, rough way.
St. John Chrysostom

18 He that hideth hatred with lying lips, and he that uttereth a slander, is a fool. 19 In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise. 20 The tongue of the just is as choice silver: the heart of the wicked is little worth. 21 The lips of the righteous feed (guide) many: but fools die for want of wisdom.
"He that hideth hatred with lying lips, and he that uttereth a slander, is a fool" [18]

The Book of Proverbs is concerned to speak of the sanctification of the mouth and the tongue, comparing the lips of the righteous with the lips of the fool. The first utters holy words, or yields his lips to the Lord Christ who dwells in him, who sanctifies them and uses them for the building up of the speaker's soul and the souls of the hearers. The second expresses what is in his depths of dryness and emptiness, even death; so his words come forth deadly to his own soul and to his hearers.
And in the New Testament St. James gave us his epistle, which some call "the Book of Proverbs of the New Testament," speaking of the danger of the tongue, making clear the following:
Let us be swift to hear, slow to speak" (Jas 1:19).
Whoever does not bridle his tongue is not religious (Jas 1:26).
A man is not counted a true believer unless his works match his words (Jas 2:14-24).
The tongue does great things despite its small size (Jas 3:5).

"The tongue is a fire, a world of iniquity" (Jas 3:6); "an unruly evil, full of deadly poison" (Jas 3:8); "a fountain sending forth either blessing or cursing" (Jas 3:10), a tree bearing a certain fruit (Jas 3:12).
It is fitting that we not use it to swear by (Jas 5:12), and that we always be truthful in what we promise.

This book is concerned with the speech of man in daily life, for it reveals what is in the depths. Speech must be truthful and not false [18], it has its limits [20], so that it becomes precious [20] and satisfying [21].

In this proverb a contrast is presented between the one who hides his hatred by hypocrisy, offering honeyed false words, and the one who declares the hatred in his heart and slanders his brothers. The first is a hypocrite and the second is ignorant and foolish, and it is not fitting for us to choose between this one and that, for both are wicked. The right choice is not to bear hatred at all, neither in our hidden hearts nor in our pure words.
Whoever thinks he can hide his hatred from God, as though God did not perceive what is in his heart or his thought, speaks lies with his lips in a spirit of pride.
"In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise" [19]
"Who will set a watch before my mouth, and a seal of wisdom upon my lips, that I fall not suddenly by them, and that my tongue destroy me not?" (Sir 22:33).

The more we speak, the greater the likelihood of falling into error, and we are drawn into the desire to speak without ceasing. By this we fall into exaggeration in speech, which drives us unconsciously to lying. This habit also leads us to fall into anger and to rush into unrestrained passions, and we are often compelled to apologize. This is the way of ignorance or folly.
Whoever speaks much loses the way of wisdom, but whoever examines every word before he utters it is counted wise, and is able to offer good counsel.
It is fitting for the believer to utter only edifying words, so that he does not give account for every idle word.
* Keep the doors closed, and then evil thoughts will quickly submit to you.
* "In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin." If you have a truly useful word, open your lips. But if there is no need to speak, be silent, for this is better!

St. John Chrysostom * The virtue of silence, especially in church, is very great. Do not let any divine utterance escape you, but listen to it and control your voice, and do not utter with your lips a word that you will later wish to take back. Do not be rash in speech, for truly in a multitude of words there is a multitude of sin.
