* Set a door to your mouth, to be closed when that is necessary. Close it tightly so that no one can make your voice rise in anger, or make you answer ugly words with the like. You have read and heard "Be ye angry, and sin not"; therefore, although we become angry because of our nature and not by our will, our mouths must not utter a single evil word, for fear of falling into sin.
Rather our words must be humble and gentle, and so we subject our tongues to our minds.

Control your tongue by bridling it firmly. Govern it and set it straight with moderation. Weigh the words it utters in the scales of justice, so that if your meanings are serious, your speech will have meaning, and your words will have weight.
Those who obey this become longsuffering, kind, and meek, by controlling their mouths, governing their tongues, thinking before speaking, and weighing their words.
We must behave thus, lest our words, which ought to reflect the beauty of our inner life, show instead evil character.

* When a multitude of words comes, sin finds an entrance, for in this multitude of words that we speak, it is not possible to keep to the limits even in a small degree. And because of lack of prudence, you fall into error. Truly, to express our thoughts without weighing our words as is fitting is in itself a grievous sin.

St. Ambrose Origen sees that Solomon himself did not sin when he spoke many words in dealing with the subjects that appear in the books mentioned in Holy Scripture (Eccl 12:12). Nor did Paul sin when he prolonged his speech until midnight (Acts 20:7-10). For they and others spoke the word of God, who is the one Word who was in the beginning with God (Jn 1:1), the one Word who bears many diverse thoughts that reveal aspects of the one Word. But whoever speaks of matters other than the word of God sins by prolonging his speech. He says: [The saints are not talkative or garrulous, for they hold to the aim that is in harmony with the one Word.]
* Much speaking is a sign of lack of discipline.

St. Mar Ephrem the Syrian * And as the lazy mind falls step by step through not being on guard against idle talk, then it descends and utters harmful speech. We are content first to speak about the affairs of others, then the tongue gnaws away, slandering their lives, and finally we incline to open abuse. Thus, when we sow provocation, quarrels begin and fires flare up at the center of anger, and then the peace of the heart is extinguished. Therefore Solomon says well: "The beginning of strife is the letting out of water" (Prov 17:14); the letting out of water is nothing but the letting loose of the tongue in chatter. On the other hand the wise man says: "The words of a man's mouth are deep waters, and the wellspring of wisdom is a flowing brook" (Prov 18:4). Thus when we let out water, we become a fountain of strife and quarrels. And those who do not control their tongues break harmony. Therefore we read what is written: "As an archer who wounds all, so is he who hires a fool or hires deceivers" (Prov 26:10). Moreover, those who are addicted to much speaking depart altogether from the straight way of righteousness. Therefore the prophet testifies, saying: "A man of tongue shall not be established in the earth" (Ps 140:11). And Solomon also says: "In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise" (Prov 10:19). And therefore Isaiah says: "And the work of righteousness shall be peace; and the effect of righteousness quietness and assurance for ever" (Isa 32:17). This indicates that where there is no restraint of speech, the righteousness of the soul grows cold. Therefore James says: "If any man among you seem to be religious, and bridleth not his tongue, but deceiveth his own heart, this man's religion is vain" (Jas 1:26). Likewise he also says: "Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath" (Jas 1:19). And when he describes the power of the tongue he adds, saying: "But the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison" (Jas 3:8). For this reason the Truth Himself warns us, saying: "Every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment" (Mt 12:36). What is meant here is every idle word that is unjustified and unnecessary and aims at no benefit for godliness. Therefore, if we shall give account for every idle word, we ought to consider the punishment laid up for chatter that is harmful and carries all iniquity.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Guard your tongues. That is, do not speak evil of your brothers. For whoever speaks evil of his brother angers God who dwells in him. What each one does to his fellow, he does to God.
St. Macarius the Great * If you cannot stop the mouth of one who speaks evil of a person, then at least keep your mouth from sharing in this matter.
Mar Isaac the Syrian * It is said of St. Augustine that he composed two lines of verse, which he wrote and hung in the dining room to put an end to the plague of slander. Their translation:

O you who slander the honor of another / and rob the standing of his monastery, / leave this place, flee, / for you shall not share in its good. It happened that some bishops, his friends, sat with him at the table. They began to backbite certain people and to slander them before him. The saint immediately advised them, saying to them: Either you erase these two lines or I will rise from the table.
* If you hear someone slandering another, flee from him as you would flee from a poisonous snake, until he is ashamed and learns not to speak so again.
St. Jerome "The tongue of the just is as choice silver: the heart of the wicked is little worth" [20]

What a person utters often reveals his character and declares what is in his heart. The man who has experienced the heavenly pledge brings forth words that are as though heavenly, and the one who values his precious life brings forth words like silver.

The tongue of the righteous is choice silver because it brings forth the precious treasures in the heart of the righteous, but the heart of the wicked is empty, and his words have no value, revealing the work of the wicked one in the soul.
* The commandments of the Lord are pure commandments, refined by fire, tried on the earth, purified seven times (Ps 12:6).

As silver is refined, so the righteous man is tested, and becomes God's coin and receives the royal image. Or as the wise Solomon says: "The tongue of the righteous is like gold refined by fire," hinting that firmly established and wise teaching is accepted and praised, and it is sufficiently refined on earth, meaning that the soul of the Gnostic (the possessor of spiritual knowledge) is made holy in many ways when it is withdrawn from the earthly fire.

St. Clement of Alexandria Origen sees that gold points to understanding and thought, while silver points to language and the power of speech. Therefore the cherubim are described as being of gold, because they are full of knowledge, and the golden lampstand that was placed in the tabernacle of meeting also points to the natural law that holds the light of knowledge.
The lips of the righteous feed (guide) many: but fools die for want of understanding (wisdom) [21]

The speech of the righteous carries no folly, and no bad word comes out of his mouth, but he offers all that is for the building up of his own soul and the building up of his brothers. He regards his mouth as a consecrated instrument bearing the words of the Lord, which are uttered in a spirit fitting to an ambassador of Christ. Goodness, or the righteousness of Christ declared by the lips of the righteous, feeds the soul with angelic bread as it feeds other souls, and so drives all toward growth; but folly, ignorance, or evil cannot keep its owner alive, for it destroys him with hunger.

Since the Lord Christ, the divine Wisdom, speaks through the lips of the righteous, He offers Himself to the hearers as spiritual food that satisfies souls, while fools speak much to offer, out of the emptiness of their hearts and thoughts, death to their own souls and the souls of their hearers.

Here we see in Samuel the judge and prophet, and Saul the king, a witness to what is said in this proverb, for Samuel's aim was to offer blessing to the thousands of the people, but Saul gained nothing from being chosen king, nor did he benefit from the presence of the great Samuel among the prophets.
"The blessing of the LORD, it maketh rich, and he addeth no toil with it" [22]

The blessing of the Lord alone is able truly to enrich life, but does it really add no toil with it?! How does this agree with what Holy Scripture and practical reality bear witness to, that the tribulations of the righteous are many? The true believer touches the blessing of the Lord in his joys and sorrows, in all the circumstances of his life, so he feels the richness of God's transcendent providence, and perceives God's mysteries and His plan toward him, and does not feel the toil.
"To do wickedness is as sport to a fool: but wisdom is for a man of understanding" [23]

Since the fool does not carry the fear of the Lord in his heart, he cares for nothing, but the wise man has his heart, his thought, his words, and his conduct ruled by the fear of the Lord, and he walks in the spirit of the Holy God.

The Book of Numbers presents to us the character of Phinehas the priest, who was zealous for the holiness of the people of God and the sanctity of the divine holy things, and took a firm stand, by which God turned away His wrath from His people (Num 25:6-13). On the contrary, Balaam was foolish, despite God's declarations to him not to curse the people of God, but love of the gift made him waver, and it reached the point that he was rebuked by the donkey he was riding (Num 22:28).

The fool, or the foolish man, is the one who practices vice and delights in it, counting the harm to his own inner depths and the harm to his brothers as laughter and amusement. He does not care about his eternity as though it were an illusion, and does not care for the comfort and peace of his brothers.

Jesters turn their lives into a kind of amusement, so they utter jests, thinking that they are creating an atmosphere of fun, sometimes using false words, and perhaps wounding some of the hearers under the cover of humor.
But the wise man finds his amusement and delight in his fellowship with God and his enjoyment of new daily experiences on the royal way under the guidance of the Holy Spirit of God who dwells in him.
Let the believer realize that his mouth is God's embassy, speaking the message of salvation, bearing witness to the new life in Christ Jesus, and proclaiming the heavenly life.

* They said to him (St. Abba Anthony): What is the meaning of the Apostle's saying: "Rejoice in the Lord"? He said: [If we rejoice in doing the commandments, this is rejoicing in the Lord; let us rejoice in fulfilling the commandments of the Lord and in the success of our brothers, and let us keep ourselves from the joy of the world and from laughter if we want to be among the special ones of our Lord, for He said that the world will rejoice, and you will weep (Jn 16:20), and He said that woe to those who laugh and blessed are those who weep (Lk 6:21, 25). And it is not written that He ever laughed, but it is written that He was grieved and His eyes shed tears (Jn 11:35).]
St. Abba Anthony the Great * Familiarity, jesting, and laughter are like a fire kindled in reeds, and they destroy.
Abba Agathon * Take care not to open your mouth in laughter, for laughter shows a lack of the fear of God.

St. Abba Isaiah * Because we do not guard against small slips, we fall into great ones. For example, a person's laughing at the wrong time draws another to laugh, and then he says: What harm is there in laughter? Then the fear of God begins to be uprooted from him, and from laughter jesting is born, and from jesting ugly speech, and from these come blameworthy deeds. So the deceiving enemy makes small slips easy for us and from them draws us into great sins.
St. John Chrysostom

24 The fear of the wicked, it shall come upon him: but the desire of the righteous shall be granted. 25 As the whirlwind passeth, so is the wicked no more: but the righteous is an everlasting foundation. 26 As vinegar to the teeth, and as smoke to the eyes, so is the sluggard to them that send him. 27 The fear of the LORD prolongeth days: but the years of the wicked shall be shortened. 28 The expectation of the righteous shall be gladness: but the hope of the wicked shall perish.
"The fear of the wicked, it shall come upon him: but the desire of the righteous shall be granted" [24]

The wicked often appear as jesters who create an atmosphere of fun and joy, and boast of their ability to do so, but their depths are filled with fear and disturbance, and peace finds no place in their depths. In their depths they think that by their jesting they lighten their terrible inner feelings and the burdens of others, but soon their inner fears are realized. As for the righteous, the desire of their heart is the glory of God, the salvation of the world, and the building up of their souls; all these are divine gifts that God offers them freely. It is as though God gives every person the hidden desire of his heart. The fearful wicked man falls into fear, and the righteous man who cares for eternity enjoys it. It is as though in the end a person faces the sum of his inner depths: either he receives unutterable glory, or falls into a shame that cannot be removed.
"As the whirlwind passeth, so is the wicked no more:
but the righteous is an everlasting foundation" [25]

Some regard this verse, together with the preceding verse, as one complete proverb. The wicked man, who bears the image of courage, strength, authority, and happiness, is ruled by fear, anxiety, and gloom, and passes like a whirlwind that no sooner blows than it disappears and becomes as though it had never been. But the righteous man, in the midst of his trials and tribulations, has his inner being filled with great joy, for the Lord grants him the desire of his heart, and makes him like a temple founded on foundations that support him eternally.

The wicked man casts himself under the divine wrath, and the fruits of his evil pass over him like a tornado (a cyclone) that shakes the whole city, sweeps away its buildings, and topples its trees, leaving neither branch nor root but uprooting trees with their roots. But the righteous man, whose soul is founded on eternity, cannot be shaken by all the whirlwinds of the world, for the hairs of his head are numbered by his heavenly Father, and he is hidden in the Rock of Ages and is not moved. The practical example in the Old Testament is the prophet Daniel and those who accused him. Daniel was thrown into the lions' den and spent the most wonderful night he had lived in all the days of his life, while his accusers thought they had succeeded in carrying out their plan, but soon the lions devoured them.

* When the storm blows, the wicked perish, but the righteous, since they avoid it, are saved forever. When temptation attacks, the wicked easily fall into sin. On the other hand, the righteous are saved eternally when they overcome temptation with patience and a soul thankful to God. See how righteousness carries security, for the righteous are saved when they avoid evil, for they take a defensive position and stand firm at all times. On the other hand the wicked fall even when no temptation attacks them at all. Therefore those who are ignorant of God's just judgment sin easily.
St. John Chrysostom "As vinegar to the teeth, and as smoke to the eyes, so is the sluggard to them that send him" [26]

As vinegar spoils the teeth and smoke the eyes, so whoever relies on a sluggard finds that he does not return to those who sent him with the required results, but causes them a state of frustration and great anxiety. As the Lord Christ offers Himself as heavenly bread that the believer eats and lives and is satisfied, sin offers itself as food or vinegar that spoils the teeth.

The Lord Christ gave us the parable of the slothful servant (Lk 19:20-26), who did not trade with the talent given to him, nor even give it to the bankers so that he might benefit from the profit (interest), but buried it in the earth, justifying this by insulting his master, saying: "For I feared thee, because thou art an austere man: thou takest up that thou layedst not down, and reapest that thou didst not sow" (Lk 19:21).
"The fear of the LORD prolongeth days: but the years of the wicked shall be shortened" [27]

Perhaps you will say that many who feared the Lord died as children or young people, like the martyrs Abanoub and the sons of St. Rebecca and Mother Dolagi... Although they died as children, their life in the eyes of the Lord is far longer than that of wicked old men without spiritual fruit. The measure of a person's age in God's eyes is not counted by the time we live but by the work we offer.

The fear of the Lord lengthens a person's days, for the grace of God is added to him, so that a day becomes for him as a thousand years. But the wicked man, deprived of the fear of the Lord, loses his eternity and falls under the judgment of bitter Gehenna.
"The expectation of the LORD is gladness: but the hope of the wicked shall perish" [28]

Besides the blessing that the one who fears the Lord receives, so that every moment of his life is valued as long, fruitful years, the fear of the Lord fills his life with hope of meeting with God and enjoying the fellowship of the glories, so he lives rejoicing in the Spirit and pours out this joy on others.

The righteous man awaits his eternity and the eternity of his brothers with joy in the midst of the pains of this world, but the wicked man's hope is in temporal things which, even if he obtains them, soon pass away. The wicked man who persists in not repenting, even if he hopes for God's mercies, loses this vain hope through his persistence in not repenting and his continual negligence.

It is said of Alexander the Great that he was never satisfied; he wept because he found no other worlds to open and subject to his kingdom, and he died at about 33 years of age, and died almost like a suicide.
And Hannibal, who filled three huge bushels with gold rings taken from those he slaughtered, ended his life by suicide with poison.
Julius Caesar, whose garments were dyed with the blood of a million of his enemies, who defeated 800 cities, was wounded by his dearest friend at the scene of his great triumph.
Napoleon, the feared conqueror, who had been the punisher, spent his last days punished.
29 The way of the LORD is strength to the upright: but destruction shall be to the workers of iniquity. 30 The righteous shall never be removed: but the wicked shall not inhabit the earth.
"The way of the LORD is a fortress to the upright: but destruction shall be to the workers of iniquity" [29]

The believer finds strength in the way of the Lord, seeing in God a fortress and a tower that protects him, and in obedience to Him a renewal of his vitality, and as he works striving, he sings, saying: "The LORD is my strength and song, and he is become my salvation."
The psalmist says:
"The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; my God is my rock, in whom I take refuge; my buckler, and the horn of my salvation, and my refuge" (Ps 18:2).
"The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? the LORD is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?" (Ps 27:1).
"The LORD is their strength, and he is the saving strength of his anointed" (Ps 28:8).
"Bow down thine ear to me; deliver me speedily: be thou my strong rock, a fortress, an house of defence to save me" (Ps 31:2).
"Pull me out of the net that they have laid privily for me: for thou art my fortress" (Ps 31:4).
"The righteous shall never be removed: but the wicked shall not inhabit the earth" [30]

The wicked rejoice, thinking that the earth is their eternal dwelling, but in a moment they leave it, as though they had passed over it like a shadow and had not dwelt in it. Even if they live in palaces they are counted as those in exile or as wanderers without shelter, because their depths do not enjoy stability. But the righteous man sets up his dwelling on an eternal foundation, which death cannot remove; he feels security and stability, even if he is imprisoned.

Holy Scripture presents us with practical examples such as Cain and Abel, for Abel died, but though he died his blood cries out (Gen 4:10)! But Cain lived on the earth as a fugitive, pursued by fear wherever he settled. So also Isaac and Ishmael, the latter wanted to kill Isaac while jesting with him! So also Jacob and Esau.
31 The mouth of the just bringeth forth wisdom: but the froward tongue shall be cut out. 32 The lips of the righteous know what is acceptable: but the mouth of the wicked speaketh frowardness.

The chapter closes with two statements about the tongue [31-32]. Having already presented examples of the wise mouth and the holy tongue, he returns to affirm the importance of sanctifying the mouth and the tongue.
"The mouth of the just bringeth forth wisdom: but the froward tongue shall be cut out" [31]

The mouth of the righteous is like a tree that bears wisdom, growing without ceasing, satisfying the hearts of many, but the tongue that utters lies, a time comes when it is cut off from the world without benefit.
Perhaps by the tongue of lies he means opposition to the true faith, and uttering blasphemy against God or deviation from the true faith.
"The lips of the righteous know what is acceptable: but the mouth of the wicked speaketh frowardness" [32]
The righteous utter what pleases God and gives Him joy, so they offer the truth for the building up of many souls, but the wicked utter destructive blasphemies.
* Do not keep company with the one of harsh tongue or the proud of heart.
St. Abba Paul of Tamoh * If we keep the right faith and keep the body from fornication and the tongue from slander, then by the grace of God we are prospering according to this age.
Abba Bela
Grant me Your heavenly wisdom, and my life will be exalted by Your grace!
* Grant me Your wisdom, O holy Father, that I may walk as Your son, ascend to the heights of loftiness, and You will rejoice in me, O Father wonderful in His love!
* Grant me not to allow my follies to rule over me, nor my foolishness to make me lose my attachment to You, lest Jerusalem above, my mother, grieve because of me!
* Let me possess the righteousness of Christ, and my soul will overflow with satisfaction.
And my heart will be filled with the treasures of Your knowledge.
I do not desire the riches of the world and its treasures.
You are my wealth and the treasures of my soul!
* I will walk by Your Spirit who never ceases to work.
In the spirit of diligence and sincerity I will work with You.
Then my soul will be enriched by You, O Supreme Good.
I will not suffer want or poverty or hunger!
I do not know idleness, nor do I seek the rest of the world, but I rejoice in striving by Your grace, and I find my rest in You alone!
* You give me the spirit of uprightness and simplicity.
I will not turn to the right or to the left.
Then Your blessings will come upon my head.
And deceit and craftiness will find no place in my thought or heart!
* By Your grace I bear Your blessings.
You support me in my sojourn, and keep my memory after my departure!
Here I bow before Your commandment in a spirit of obedience; I rejoice in it as a treasure I hide in my heart.
My soul exults in it, and my whole being is filled with heavenly peace!
* By Your commandment I walk uprightly, and all my senses and emotions are in harmony with my words and my conduct.
My whole being becomes a spiritual harp, upon which Your Holy Spirit plays the symphony of eternal love!
* A fountain will arise in me overflowing with living waters.
And my tongue will be sanctified, speaking only according to Your grace!
My life will become a love that never ceases; I cover the faults of my brothers, and You cover my sins with the blood of the Crucified!
* My mouth overflows with Your wisdom, and my soul exults as the light of Your knowledge shines upon me!
* My life becomes a delightful journey; with every morning my soul sets out as to heaven!
My insight is dazzled by the splendor of Your glory.
And my tongue is silent in amazement before the throne of Your grace!
I long for silence that I may hear Your voice, O Beloved.
And I long for You to speak through me, that my brothers may enjoy Your mysteries with me.
* I know neither jesting nor laughter, and my soul knows neither gloom nor bitterness.
I cherish every second of my life, because You never cease to work in me in Your bounty.
* My soul is filled with Your fear, O Lover of mankind.
Then I grow continually by receiving the abundance of Your wisdom.
I live in security, for I take refuge in Your embrace.
For You are the secret of my joy, my satisfaction, and my eternal peace.

1 A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight. 2 When pride cometh, then cometh shame: but with the lowly is wisdom. 3 The integrity of the upright shall guide them: but the perverseness of transgressors shall destroy them. 4 Riches profit not in the day of wrath: but righteousness delivereth from death. 5 The righteousness of the perfect shall direct his way: but the wicked shall fall by his own wickedness. 6 The righteousness of the upright shall deliver them: but transgressors shall be taken in their own naughtiness. 7 When a wicked man dieth, his expectation shall perish: and the hope of unjust men perisheth. 8 The righteous is delivered out of trouble, and the wicked cometh in his stead. 9 An hypocrite with his mouth destroyeth his neighbour: but through knowledge shall the just be delivered. 10 When it goeth well with the righteous, the city rejoiceth: and when the wicked perish, there is shouting. 11 By the blessing of the upright the city is exalted: but it is overthrown by the mouth of the wicked. 12 He that is void of wisdom despiseth his neighbour: but a man of understanding holdeth his peace. 13 A talebearer revealeth secrets: but he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter. 14 Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety. 15 He that is surety for a stranger shall smart for it: and he that hateth suretiship is sure.

Man practices righteousness in the field of work [1-4], so that the faithfulness of his heart and the sincerity of his intention are reflected in his work. He knows neither cheating nor deceit, whatever the material or moral temptation. He walks like his Creator and Savior, in a spirit of meekness and humility, without greed.
The effect of inner faithfulness extends to the field of personal problems [5-8]: how the righteous man comes out victorious in the midst of problems, troubles and afflictions.
It extends also to the field of government [9-15]: righteous citizens build a joyful society [10], an exalted one [11], pervaded by peace [12-13], and bearing the spirit of victory [14].

entries.section: First: In the field of work

paragraphs.text: "A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight" [1]
The literal translation of the Hebrew expression ba eben shelemak means "balances of stones," since stones were used in the scales.
Many make light of cheating in scales and measures, not knowing that it is an abomination in the eyes of the Lord, who cannot bear cheating and deceit.

* Every work that contains injustice is shameful, even in public affairs. False scales and unjust measures fall under the curse. If cheating in the market or in business brings a man under punishment, can it be overlooked when it is found in the midst of carrying out the duties of virtue?!

* Let each one weigh his words without cheating or deceit. "A false balance is abomination to the Lord." I do not mean that balance which weighs other things. Before the Lord this balance of words is hateful, which falsifies wise dignity while practicing deceit with cunning. God condemns the man who cheats his neighbor with treacherous injustice. He gains no profit from his skillful cleverness. For what does it profit a man if he gain the wealth of the whole world and deceive himself, so that he does not obtain eternal life?

St. Ambrose The disorder of man's scales, standards and concepts If sin has corrupted man's scales, standards and concepts, the incarnation of the wisdom of God has restored to man the truthfulness of his scales, measures and weights, so that man may give everything and every being its due, rendering unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and unto God the things that are God's (Mt 22:21). Through the work of divine wisdom we have been given the possibility of restoring matters to their true scales, such as:

A. The balance between soul and body. God created for man true scales so that he might care for his whole being, working with his body with all its energies and abilities, and with his soul with all its possibilities. The soul takes the leadership of the body, so that man as a whole walks in the royal way. But sin made man lose his scales, and made the body a leader that rides the soul and directs it according to its evil lusts. The scales were upset, so that the rider became the ridden, and the ridden the rider. Therefore the wisdom of God came incarnate, and took our body, and He had a soul as a perfect man, so that in Him the body might be in harmony with the soul, and the two might walk the heavenly way.

By His incarnation, crucifixion, resurrection and ascension He opened the doors of heaven so that the Holy Spirit might dwell in man in his entirety, opening all his doors, to lead soul and body together in the heavenly pastures without conflict.

B. Sin upset man's scales in his view of earth and heaven, so he counted the earth his dwelling as one who will remain in it forever, and looked at heaven as an illusion or a fancy. He was no longer able to realize "Surely man walks about like a shadow" (Ps 39:6), for he counts the earth a reality worthy of all attention, while heaven and the eternal things are secondary matters. But the heavenly coming gave the believer's view a heavenly tinge, so that he sees the earth as if it had become heaven, and thanks God for his reality as a man living on earth, while his heart is in heaven.

C. Sin made man lose his true scales for weighing his spiritual, psychological, intellectual, scientific and social needs... so that he cannot realize the unity of life in order to balance all the aspects of his life, to be faithful in everything and sound in his personality. But when the Creator of soul and body, the unique Physician of man, became incarnate, He restored to life its unity, so that man might succeed in everything, by the work of the Holy Spirit of God, the Spirit of power and victory, not the spirit of failure.

D. The scales of man's thought were upset in his view of his own being, so he was no longer able to sit with himself and look into his inner depths, to discover the Kingdom of God within him, and to realize that God created him to make of him a dwelling for the Spirit of God. Man lost his awareness of his inner man, so that he saw in his life only the perishing of the outward man, without the growth and renewal of his inner man. But in Christ Jesus, who draws our gaze inward, saying to us, "The kingdom of God is within you," we have come to sing with the Apostle Paul: "Though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day" (2 Cor 4:16).

E. Our scales were upset even in our view of God, the world, the body and every heavenly and earthly creature, and our Christ, the incarnate Wisdom, came to offer us His Holy Spirit to grant us new scales through which we realize the following:
* God draws near to us in love; He is a Father even in His chastisements, opening His arms to us.

* The body is a holy talent, a divine gift, having its own sanctity, whether our own body or the bodies of others. So we do not look at it to satisfy fleshly lusts, but as a divine sanctuary in which the Lord delights.

* The world is a bridge by which we cross to the heavenly Jerusalem; we walk upon it as a divine gift. We accept sufferings as a school of philosophy and a way to enter into the fellowship of glory with our suffering Christ, as we also rejoice in every gift and blessing that stirs in us the spirit of thanksgiving and praise to God.
* The heavenly creation, for us, is the society of heaven in which we find friendships that last eternally.
* The earthly creation is talents with which we deal, so that we grow in the life of faithfulness, sharing with our Christ the quality of faithfulness.

F. Sin turned deceit and cunning into human wisdom, and faithfulness and truthfulness into narrowness of mind. Thus the scales were overturned, so that truth became falsehood in man's eyes, and falsehood truth! And the wisdom of God came to offer Himself, "the Truth," given in love through the Cross, which the Jews see as a stumblingblock and the Greeks as foolishness (1 Cor 1:23). In Christ Jesus we realize true wisdom.

G. Man's scales were upset by the spirit of selfishness, in which he sets up the ego as the center of the world, seeking what is his own. And "Love" Himself came to break the ego, in which there is a deadly selfishness, and to live in us Himself, so that our mind is opened and our heart widened, and we bear with our Christ, if possible, all people.

entries.section: First: In the field of work

paragraphs.text: "When pride cometh, then cometh shame: but with the lowly is wisdom" [2]

Creation was formed out of nothing, so in reality it has nothing to boast of before its Creator. Pride is a denial of the work of the Creator, who wishes to honor His rational creation and desires that it grow and be glorified continually. Humility, on the other hand, offers a sacrifice of thanksgiving to God the Creator, and acknowledges His kindness. Pride is a dangerous sign of folly and ruinous foolishness, while humility is a spiritual sign of steadfastness in the heavenly wisdom given to us as a free gift from the Creator.

When Nebuchadnezzar walked in the palace, and said in his arrogance: "Is not this great Babylon, that I have built for the house of the kingdom by the might of my power, and for the honour of my majesty?" (Dan 4:30), he was driven from men to live like the oxen. And when his reason returned to him and he blessed God and praised and honored Him, he says: "My reason returned unto me, and returned to the glory of my kingdom, my honour and brightness" (Dan 4:36).

The proud man shrivels up around himself, and thinks that he is the center of the world and of society, so he demands that all serve and respect him, supposing himself to be something. Then he finds others treating him otherwise than he expects, and he feels humiliation and shame, even in his own eyes. The humble man, however, does not wait for a word of praise, nor expect others to serve him, nor desire it, and behold, he is counted wise, receives honor and is the object of the love of many.
* It is pride that turns a man away from wisdom, and foolishness is the fruit of turning away from wisdom.

* "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." We read in the Holy Scripture of toil for temporal things: "All is vanity and vexation of spirit." The phrase "vexation of spirit," Presumption of spirit, means insolence, pride and arrogance, and it is also customary to say of the proud man that he has lofty spirits, and this is right, because the wind is called a spirit. And so it is written: "Fire and cold, snow and fog, the stormy wind" Spirit of tempest (Ps 148:8). Truly the proud man is called puffed up, as if he were exalted with the wind. And here the Apostle says: "Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth" (1 Cor 8:1)...
Let us understand in truth that the poor in spirit are the humble and those who fear God, that is, those who have no spirit that swells.

In truth, the Beatitudes could not begin with anything other than this beginning, since they are set forth for the attainment of high wisdom: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom" (Ps 111:10), and on the other hand, "Pride is the first of sins" (Sir 10:15).
Therefore let the proud man seek earthly kingdoms and love them, but "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."
St. Augustine * He who loves humility acquires many gifts through humility.
When you seek mercy, you find it among the humble, for humility is the dwelling place of righteousness.
Teaching is found with the humble, and knowledge is the springs of their lips.
Humility begets wisdom and understanding, and the humble acquire prudence...
Sweet is the word of the humble, and his face is radiant, and he laughs and rejoices.
Love is beautiful among the humble, and they know how to manage by it.
The humble fast from all evils, so their faces shine with the goodness of their hearts.
The humble man speaks and speech becomes him, and his lips laugh, yet the sound of his laughter is not heard...

The humble man humbles himself, but his heart is lifted to the heights above. Where his treasure is, there his thoughts are. The two eyes of his face look to the earth, and the two eyes of his mind to the heights above.

St. Aphrahat * Nothing is acceptable to God like a man's counting himself the last of all; this is the first principle of practical wisdom, for the humble man, wounded in his heart, does not love vainglory, nor is he angry, nor does he envy his neighbor, nor resort to any lust.

entries.section: First: In the field of work

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom "The integrity of the upright shall guide them: but the perverseness of the treacherous is their shame" [3]

When a man seeks the truth with an upright conscience, the Holy Spirit of God works in him, leads him, guides him and accompanies him in the way of truth, as happened with Cornelius the pagan centurion. Since he was devout and feared the Lord, God sent him an angel to bid him seek Simon Peter, who would reveal to him the way of his salvation. And when Peter came, while he was speaking with him and with those present, "the Holy Ghost fell on all them which heard the word" (Acts 10:44).

The upright man is faithful to himself as to others, and so he finds his way clear and straight, while the treacherous or the cheat finds his way crooked, and loses the way, since he does not fulfill his mission.

David the prophet sings, saying: "My defence is of God, which saveth the upright in heart" (Ps 7:10). "The righteous shall be glad in the LORD, and shall trust in him; and all the upright in heart shall glory" (Ps 64:10). It is also said: "Light is sown for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart" (Ps 97:11). "The upright shall dwell in thy presence" (Ps 140:13).
* God calls the sincere and truthful upright, those who hide nothing and do not conceal corruption beneath the surface.

Uprightness, as you see, is like this: God looks upon it above all things... Those who speak the truth need no effort, no struggle, no hypocrisy, no cunning, nor anything of the kind, because the truth shines through its own harmony.

In other words, just as deformed bodies need an outward artifice to cover their natural deformity, while natural beauty carries splendor in itself, so also falsehood can be distinguished from truth, and vice from virtue.

entries.section: First: In the field of work

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom "Riches profit not in the day of wrath: but righteousness delivereth from death" [4]
The rich man often relies on his wealth, supposing that it achieves impossibilities for him.

But when the day of death comes, it is for the wicked a day of wrath and anger, and their wealth does not intercede for them, but is rather the cause of their condemnation, because they misused it. At that moment they cannot buy the forgiveness of sins, nor enjoy the divine mercies. The Book of Revelation describes the day of wrath thus: "And the heaven departed as a scroll when it is rolled together; and every mountain and island were moved out of their places. And the kings of the earth, and the great men, and the rich men, and the chief captains, and the mighty men, and every bondman, and every free man, hid themselves in the dens and in the rocks of the mountains; and said to the mountains and rocks, Fall on us, and hide us from the face of him that sitteth on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb: for the great day of his wrath is come; and who shall be able to stand?" (Rev 6:14-17).

* I know why it is written: "Riches profit not in the day of wrath." This is said of the person who does not use his wealth for mercy. Is it not within the power of wealth to be used in time of need? In the hour when your spirit returns to the hands of God, you will understand that the benefit of all your wealth is to use it for mercy. For it was given to you by Jesus Christ, God and the Son of God.

St. Anba Shenouda * (Solomon) leads us toward understanding, especially when he says: "Riches profit not in the day of wrath." For he pours into your heart the knowledge that an abundance of money will not help you on that day, nor remove from you the eternal punishment. And when he says: [The righteous shall inherit the earth] (cf. Prov 2:21), he clearly means the earth which the meek also inherit. For the psalmist said first: "The meek shall inherit the earth" (Ps 37:11) LXX. And afterward the Lord said: "Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth" (Mt 5:4).
St. Basil the Great

entries.section: First: In the field of work

paragraphs.text: Second: Personal problems [5-8]
But the righteous man is saved from eternal death, for he enjoys the fellowship of eternal glory.

* "Many are the afflictions of the righteous (the just), but the LORD delivereth him out of them all" (Ps 34:19). Did He say: "Let Christians be righteous, and then those who hear my word will suffer no afflictions"? God did not promise this, but says: "Many are the afflictions of the just." Rather, when they are wicked their afflictions are fewer, and when they are righteous their afflictions are many. But after few afflictions, or with no afflictions, those (the wicked) go to eternal torment, from which they cannot escape. The righteous, however, after many afflictions come to eternal peace, where they no longer suffer any evil.
St. Augustine "The righteousness of the perfect shall direct his way: but the wicked shall fall by his own wickedness" [5]
The Book often confirms this truth, that righteousness is the believer's support, his deliverer, and his guide amid the afflictions of life, though it uses different words and expressions.
Palestine is known for its rocks and hills, so travelers find hardship in their journeys, but the guide is righteousness, for it leads the believer to eternal glory through the rocks of this life.

entries.section: First: In the field of work

paragraphs.text: "The righteousness of the upright shall deliver them: but transgressors shall be taken in their own naughtiness" [6]
The corrupt man sets nets for himself in which he falls. But for the righteous, righteousness lifts up his feet, and the nets cannot catch him.

* An upright life and faith in God are a great weapon against the demons, who fear fasting, asceticism, night vigils and prayer, quietness and meekness, hatred of silver, boasting and humility, love of poverty and mercy, freedom from anger and the doing of righteousness in Christ, for the demons strive exceedingly not to be defeated. Let us remember in our hearts that the Lord is with us at all times, and the demons cannot do anything to us, and if they see that we are afraid and weak they make fear increase all the more in our hearts by their thoughts. But if they find us rejoicing in the Lord at all times, thinking in our hearts of the good things to come and speaking of the things of the Lord, and thinking: Everything is in the Lord's hand, then the demons can do nothing and have no authority in anything whatever. And if they find the soul fortified with such thoughts they are put to shame at once and turn back, for thus the enemy found Job fortified and steadfast and withdrew from him, when he could not turn his mind from God, and for this he was put to shame.
St. Anba Anthony * I marvel at the cunning of Satan, for though he is corruption and harm itself, he suggests thoughts that seem pure, but the result is a snare rather than a temptation.

St. Athanasius * If it happens that you are exposed to these evils, ask yourself: What are we doing in this world? Our time is short; your end is corruption and you are on the way to the grave. Then say to yourself: What are you doing there? Prostrate yourself before the Lord lest He condemn you to the eternal fire. Resist without truce the enemy who strikes you and destroys your understanding. Blessed are those who cross these dark and terrifying regions, this dreadful night, the desolate places, and this corrupt atmosphere of sin, and arrive at rest and gladness in the joy of the Holy Spirit.

entries.section: First: In the field of work

paragraphs.text: St. Macarius the Great "When a wicked man dieth, his expectation shall perish: and the hope of unjust men perisheth" [7]

When a righteous man dies, his hope turns into a glorious reality, and no fear passes through him, nor does he fall into weakness; but the wicked man, who persists in impenitence in negligence, hoping for God's mercies, loses this vain hope by his death.

Hope is a great blessing for the striving spiritual man, who endures sufferings looking to the eternal glory prepared for him by God freely, but for the wicked, hope represents negligence and laxity. They walk in the way of destruction claiming that they will be saved and enjoy the Kingdom of Heaven, refusing to change their direction toward eternity; the hope of such people is nothing but a tomb.

* When a righteous man dies, hope does not perish. He hopes that his children will walk well, and hopes to receive great things. This statement also carries us over to thoughts concerning the resurrection, or to the generations that will come after us. Or it means that he who was righteous enjoys all these things already, and will enjoy their complete future fulfillment, and will finally enjoy the glory after death.

St. John Chrysostom * My son, before everything do not count yourself as anything, for this is the father of humility. And humility begets teaching, and teaching begets faith, and faith begets hope, and hope begets love, and love begets obedience, and obedience begets steadfastness without wavering.

* My son, hurry and take heed, lest you go astray and become lazy and negligent and be despised in the age to come. For it is written: Woe to the negligent, for their end has drawn near, and there is no helper for them, nor hope of salvation.

entries.section: First: In the field of work

paragraphs.text: St. Anba Anthony "The righteous is delivered out of trouble, and the wicked cometh in his stead" [8]
Often the wicked man sets his snares for the righteous, and behold, he himself falls into them, and the righteous feels God's surpassing care for him.
When the wicked man rejects love and mercy, he throws himself into the hand of justice, and drinks of the cup he prepared for himself, supposing that he was offering it to his brother.

The cross which Haman prepared for Mordecai, Haman was hanged upon (Esth 7:9-10), and the lions' den which the accusers of Daniel planned in order to be rid of him, they and their families were cast into it and the hungry lions devoured them (Dan 6).

The Egyptians shed the blood of the children of the Israelites, and when the Egyptians were thirsty they found blood mingled with the water of the Nile. With the measure that a man measures to his brother it shall be measured to him.

entries.section: First: In the field of work

paragraphs.text: Third: In government [9-15]
"An hypocrite with his mouth destroyeth his neighbour: but through knowledge shall the just be delivered" [9]

The hypocrite speaks other than what he hides within. So he destroys not himself alone, but draws his companion with him. It is as though wise Solomon were calling us to enjoy the spirit of discernment and to flee from the company of hypocrites, lest we perish with them.
* Do not bear ill will toward any man, lest your labors become vain.
* The worship of the man who has the malice of revenge in his heart is vain.
* This is our struggle: that we have no passion in the mouth, nor iniquity or malice in the heart.

Father Isaiah If hypocrites and deceivers perish by their words full of deceit, then the children of God can, by the spirit of discernment, escape the deceit of hypocrites as from the deceit of the enemy of good.

* The soul has a discernment from its rational sense by which it knows the difference between truth and falsehood, as the mouth distinguishes between wine and vinegar, though they are alike in color; so the soul by its rational sense knows the difference between spiritual gifts and satanic fantasies.

St. Macarius the Great * My son, do not speak in anger, but let your speech be with wisdom and knowledge, and your silence also, for our wise fathers' speech was full of wisdom and discernment, and so was their silence.

entries.section: First: In the field of work

paragraphs.text: St. Anba Anthony "When it goeth well with the righteous, the city rejoiceth: and when the wicked perish, there is shouting" [10]

If the hypocrite destroys his neighbor, the righteous man becomes a blessing to the whole city, not only by his guidance and counsels, but also by his prayers and supplications for others, and by the blessing of the Lord working in him. The Lord says: "Run ye to and fro through the streets of Jerusalem, and see now, and know, and seek in the broad places thereof, if ye can find a man, if there be any that executeth judgment, that seeketh the truth; and I will pardon it?!" (Jer 5:1).
As for the wicked, when they die the righteous grieve over their destruction, but they shout for joy at the deliverance of the simple whom the wicked opposed in order to crush them.

entries.section: First: In the field of work

paragraphs.text: "By the blessing of the upright the city is exalted: but it is overthrown by the mouth of the wicked" [11]
The righteous are a blessing not only to themselves and their families, but to the whole city.

St. Anthony the Great presents to us a wonderful picture of St. Pachomius, by whose blessing "the city is exalted," in his talk with the sons of St. Pachomius during their visit to him, when he said to them: [Let not your hearts be pained, my children, for the man of God, the righteous one adorned with every virtue, our father Pachomius, because he has fallen asleep, for you have become with him one body and partakers in the members (that is, the membership), and you have been filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit of God which used to shine within him. And truly I desired to see him in the flesh, and truly I was not worthy of him, especially since the souls which he gathered around him are holy to the Lord of Sabaoth, and these will show forth that they are higher than we, and walk in the way of the Apostles of Christ, which is the holy communion.]

* Pray, then, for the world, for "the eyes of the LORD are upon the righteous, and his ears are open unto their cry" (Ps 34:15). You know well that God hears the prayer of the righteous and that the supplication of a good man has great power, so remember us without ceasing.
St. Anba Serapion, Bishop of Thmuis Just as the city is blessed by the presence of the saints and their prayers, so it is also broken down by the mouth of the wicked, full of blasphemy and lying.

entries.section: First: In the field of work

paragraphs.text: "He that is void of wisdom despiseth his neighbour: but a man of understanding holdeth his peace" [12]
Sometimes silence is the best thing we can do, especially if our words make us lose our peace, or wound our depths, or wrong others.

The foolish man lies in wait for the faults of others and concentrates on their weaknesses, so he despises them, but the wise man covers the weaknesses of his brothers and supports them in every positive aspect for their continual growth and edification.

* There is no work of love better than that a man should not despise his brother, as it is written: "Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thine heart: thou shalt in any wise rebuke thy neighbour, and not suffer sin upon him" (Lev 19:17). Accordingly, if you see your brother continuing in sin and you neglect to warn him so that he may then know his error, his blood will be required of you. But if he repeats the sin and continues in it, he dies in his sin, and it is good for you to heal him with love without wounding him and without scorning him as an enemy.

Abba John the Short * If you pray and no evil thing comes into your mind, you have become free. He who blames his brother, or despises him, or speaks against him before others, or shows anger toward him, is far from mercy. And if a man says that he wants to repent of his sins and he does any of these things, he is a liar.

entries.section: First: In the field of work

paragraphs.text: St. Anba Isaiah "A talebearer revealeth secrets: but he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter" [13]
The faithful man does not disclose the secrets entrusted to him, unless in doing so there is edification for their souls and within the proper limits for the salvation of others, not to expose them.
* Frown at the one who begins to speak against his brother before you, for if you do so you will be guarded before God and before him.

entries.section: First: In the field of work

paragraphs.text: St. Isaac the Syrian "Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety" [14]

Total reliance on one's own judgment is the height of folly, for even the wisest and most devout of men have their grave errors, and sometimes an inability to discern. No man is immune from error. Man needs to seek God's counsel and to resort to a spiritual father or spiritual guide. Rehoboam lost most of the kingdom because he ignored this important truth, and many have suffered grave harm for the same reason.

It is fitting for the believer not to rely on his own idea and feelings, but to consult and discuss in a spirit of humility and a sincere desire to benefit from the abilities and experiences of others.

The Book of Daniel tells us of Nebuchadnezzar's need for a wise counselor from God, and when the secret was revealed to him the king glorified the God of Daniel (Dan 2:46). King Belshazzar also needed a counselor (Dan 5:13).

* Since we all wish to come out of Egypt and flee from Pharaoh, we certainly need another Moses, a mediator from God and before God, who by standing for us between action and knowledge (contemplation) stretches out the arms of prayer to God, until those whom he leads cross the sea of their sins, and overcome Amalek (Ex 17), and raise the banner of victory. For he is deceived who surrenders himself to this way (the monastic way) and imagines that he needs no one to lead and guide him.

St. John Climacus * An elder said: [A rich man distributed all his possessions, freed his slaves and renounced the world, then came to rely on himself, being his own guide, and decided not to be a follower of another nor to learn from one who was older than he, and he fell into hideous impurities and nearly perished had not God by His grace rescued him through repentance, so that he learned by experience that humility is greater than works.]

The Garden of the Monks * If (the believer) does not walk with his guide from the beginning to the end, he will never reach the city. So cast your will behind you and be humble, and you will be saved.

entries.section: First: In the field of work

paragraphs.text: St. Barsanuphius "He that is surety for a stranger shall smart for it: and he that hateth suretiship is sure" [15]

He has already spoken of not being hasty in standing surety for a stranger, without examination and good management, whether as to the truth of his need, the study of his use of the loan, and the ability of the borrower and the surety to repay (cf. Prov 6:1-5).
The wise man is afraid of rashness in standing surety for a stranger who has come to spend a night or a day in order to borrow, with no guarantees of repayment, or no seriousness about repaying.

But our Christ signed with His blood on the wood of the Cross, standing surety for us. He paid the price of our sins, death, and He is able to repay. The Apostle Paul says: "For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that for your sakes he became poor, though he was rich, that ye through his poverty might be rich" (2 Cor 8:9). He became surety for us strangers, to remove our estrangement. "Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God" (Eph 2:19). In His surpassing love He says: "Then I restored that which I took not away" (Ps 69:4), for He paid our debts which He had not borrowed, and so through Him we have become free.

16 A gracious woman retaineth honour: and strong men retain riches. 17 The merciful man doeth good to his own soul: but he that is cruel troubleth his own flesh. 18 The wicked worketh a deceitful work: but to him that soweth righteousness shall be a sure reward. 19 As righteousness tendeth to life: so he that pursueth evil pursueth it to his own death. 20 They that are of a froward heart are abomination to the LORD: but such as are upright in their way are his delight. 21 Though hand join in hand, the wicked shall not be unpunished: but the seed of the righteous shall be delivered. 22 As a jewel of gold in a swine's snout, so is a fair woman which is without discretion. 23 The desire of the righteous is only good: but the expectation of the wicked is wrath. 24 There is that scattereth, and yet increaseth; and there is that withholdeth more than is meet, but it tendeth to poverty. 25 The liberal soul shall be made fat: and he that watereth shall be watered also himself. 26 He that withholdeth corn, the people shall curse him: but blessing shall be upon the head of him that selleth it. 27 He that diligently seeketh good procureth favour: but he that seeketh mischief, it shall come unto him. 28 He that trusteth in his riches shall fall; but the righteous shall flourish as a branch. 29 He that troubleth his own house shall inherit the wind: and the fool shall be servant to the wise of heart. 30 The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life; and he that winneth souls is wise. 31 Behold, the righteous shall be recompensed in the earth: much more the wicked and the sinner.

entries.section: A. A woman's grace brings honor

paragraphs.text: "A gracious woman retaineth honour: and strong men retain riches" [16]

In the Septuagint: "A gracious woman raises honor for her husband, but she who hates righteous things is a throne of dishonor." The meaning is that because of a devout and wise wife her husband is honored, but she who does not care for her eternity and salvation becomes a seat of shame, and everyone who clings to her loses his honor. It is as though the wise man here urges a man to choose a life partner who is gracious and devout.

The strong, or the physically powerful, are often able to work in order to enjoy wealth, as well as to protect it from those who try to rob or seize it. So by grace and meekness a woman can gain honor and esteem in the eyes of many. There is nothing more beautiful in a woman than the touch of grace and the anointing of humility, meekness and gentleness together with wisdom. This is what David the prophet perceived in the person of Abigail, when he said to her: "Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, which sent thee this day to meet me: and blessed art thou, which hast kept me this day from coming to shed blood, and from avenging myself with mine own hand" (1 Sam 25:32-34).

So Ruth the Gentile was able to find grace in the eyes of God, who chose that the Word of God should come incarnate from her seed, and in the eyes of the people. And as Boaz said to her: "For all the gates of my people do know that thou art a virtuous woman" (Ruth 3:11).

* In speaking of the glory of the man, Paul now sets up a balance, so that the man may not boast beyond what is fitting, nor oppress the woman. For in the Lord the woman is not independent of the man, neither is the man independent of the woman. If you ask who came after the other, each is the cause of the other, or rather, not each is from the other, but God is the cause of all.
* The women stood at the Cross, the weaker sex, which appeared stronger, and so all things were completely changed.
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: B. A man's mercy benefits himself

paragraphs.text: "The merciful man doeth good to his own soul: but he that is cruel breaketh his flesh" [17]

What a man does to others he offers to himself; the mercy he practices toward others leads him to enjoy the divine mercies, and gains him inner peace. And he who thinks he is crushing others by his violence is crushing himself without knowing it. The cup we fill for others we are bound to drink ourselves.
* What is purity? It is a heart full of mercy toward all the natures of creation.
* The prayer of the hateful is like seed sown upon a rock. A merciless ascetic is like a tree without fruit.

St. Isaac the Syrian * Be desirous of good things and keep them, a servant pleasing to your Master, a humble disciple of Him who for your sake humbled Himself, an obedient disciple of the Obedient, enduring with the Enduring, longsuffering with the Longsuffering, merciful for the sake of the Merciful, bearing the burdens of your neighbor as He Himself bore your burdens, loving all sincerely as He Himself loved us, following Him in all things until He receives you into His great rest, where "Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him" (1 Cor 2:9).
St. Barsanuphius

entries.section: C. Sowing righteousness gives a true reward

paragraphs.text: "The wicked worketh a deceitful work: but to him that soweth righteousness shall be a sure reward" [18]

The wise man links evil with deceit, and righteousness with faithfulness. For evil carries within it a deception of the soul and of the inner sight, so that the wicked man imagines in sin a joyful life, happiness, wealth or honor. And the righteous man, or the just, sees in faithfulness to God and to himself as to men the secret of his inner happiness. Evil carries within it its corrupt fruit, and righteousness carries within it its reward.

The clear example of this serious contrast is Sennacherib king of Assyria and Hezekiah. The first, in his wickedness, used to reproach God and speak against Him with insolence and arrogance. He says: "As the gods of the nations of other lands have not delivered their people out of mine hand, so shall not the God of Hezekiah deliver his people out of mine hand" (2 Chr 32:17). But devout Hezekiah, the man of prayer, enjoyed deliverance from the hand of Assyria from heaven itself.
The wicked man reaps the deceit with which he thought he was deceiving others, and finds that he is cheating himself. But he who is diligent in sowing the seeds of righteousness finds a sure reward.
"As righteousness tendeth to life: so he that pursueth evil pursueth it to his own death" [19]
True holiness is real life and happiness, but he who runs after evil is only running to end his life.

entries.section: E. Walking without crookedness gives us joy in the Lord

paragraphs.text: "They that are of a froward heart are abomination to the LORD: but such as are upright in their way are his delight" [20]
There is nothing the Lord cannot bear like hypocrisy and crookedness, and nothing the Lord loves like uprightness and holiness.

entries.section: F. Collective action does not justify evil

paragraphs.text: "Though hand join in hand, the wicked shall not be unpunished: but the seed of the righteous shall be delivered" [21]
The wicked joining together does not protect them from the fruit of their evil, but the righteous, they and their seed who walk in their likeness, enjoy divine protection.

entries.section: G. A woman's beauty is in her mind

paragraphs.text: "As a jewel of gold in a swine's snout, so is a fair woman which is without discretion" [22]
A woman often destroys her beauty by her lack of wisdom, so that she is like one who takes a gold ring and puts it in the nose of a sow.
J. Vernon McGee says: [Have you seen a sow walking around with a gold ring in her snout? Well, there are many of them here in... They are beautiful women without discretion.]
If God has given many women bodily beauty, what gives this beauty its dignity and worth is discretion, wisdom and discernment.

Gold signifies the heavenly life that will not corrupt. The true believer is bound to walk with a practical heavenly mind, and if he deviates he is like the sow that wallows in the mire, and so defiles the gold ring in her snout (her nose).

* Although it is believed that virginity is something exceedingly precious and has a divine appearance, yet if the life as a whole is not in harmony with the soul, virginity becomes "a jewel of gold in a swine's snout," or "a pearl trodden under the feet of swine."

St. Gregory of Nyssa * Those whom you indicate do not possess the knowledge which none but the pure possess, but acquire a vain knowledge of which the Apostle speaks, saying: "Avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called" (1 Tim 20:6). Those who appear to receive some kind of knowledge, or those who devote their souls to reading the sacred volumes and memorizing the Holy Scriptures without abandoning fleshly sins, of these it is said in the Book of Proverbs: "As a jewel of gold in a swine's snout, so is a fair woman which is without discretion" (Prov 11:22). For what does it profit a man if he acquires the heavenly adornment of eloquence, and the costly beauty of the Holy Scripture, if he corrupts it by clinging to filthy deeds and evil thoughts, pushing them into unclean ground, or defiling them by wallowing in the filth of his lusts?! The result is that what is an ornament for those who use it well becomes for them not only unable to adorn them but filth and increasing mire, for "Praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner" (Sir 15:9). For it is said to him by the prophet: "What hast thou to do to declare my statutes, or that thou shouldest take my covenant in thy mouth?!" (Ps 50:16). Such souls have not the fear of the Lord in any way, for it is said: "The fear of the LORD is the instruction of wisdom" (Prov 15:33). And yet they try to draw out the meanings of the Holy Scripture by continual meditation on it, and fittingly they are asked in the Book of Proverbs: "Wherefore is there a price in the hand of a fool to get wisdom, seeing he hath no understanding?" (Prov 17:16).

Father Nestor * In brief, if anyone thinks he becomes beautiful by gold, he is less than the gold, and he who is less than gold is not lord over it. But for a person to confess that he is less beautiful than the mine in (the region of) Lydia, how ugly! If gold is spoiled by the filth of a sow stirring up the mire with her snout (her nose), so also these women who luxuriate excessively in their pleasure, exulting in wealth, spoil what is truly beautiful, through the defilement of servility to fleshly lusts.
St. Clement of Alexandria

entries.section: H. The goal of the righteous is good for all

paragraphs.text: "The desire of the righteous is only good.
The expectation of the wicked is wrath" [23]
What the wicked hope for is the harming of others, while the righteous desire good for all; every man receives in himself what he desires for others, and what he seeks for his brother returns to him.

When man's heart is planted in the Lord who is all good, the heart overflows with longing to do good to every man as far as he can. Therefore the psalmist commands us: "Delight thyself also in the LORD; and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart" (Ps 37:4).

Giving in truth is receiving, and generosity in giving is wealth and prosperity, and giving rest to others brings rest to us. The Lord Christ says: "Give, and it shall be given unto you..." (Lk 6:38).

And the Apostle says: "He which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly; and he which soweth with blessings shall reap also with blessings. Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver" (2 Cor 9:6-7).
"There is that scattereth, and yet increaseth; and there is that withholdeth more than is meet, but it tendeth to poverty" [24]

He who cares to give to the poor, God blesses everything to which his hands are stretched, so that he increases in wealth and blessing, but he who refrains from giving because of his stinginess and miserliness loses the Lord's blessing and is counted poor.

* The demons gather secretly against you like the Egyptians, and the devil their chief like Pharaoh, and they besiege you with worries and thoughts that darken your soul and deprive you of seeing the light of the knowledge of Christ.
And these are the thoughts which they begin to stir up in your mind:
Why did you leave the world, where you could easily have become righteous?
Why did you squander your wealth, from which you used to give alms when it was at your side?

Now that you have distributed it hastily and prematurely, perhaps it was given to those who do not deserve it. If you had kept it and invested it wisely, you could now entertain strangers, ease the pains of the weary, clothe the naked, help the monks and solitaries with your gifts, and stand by the widows and orphans; your house would have become a place for all good works; for as long as your money was at your side it helped you to rest and to relieve the pains of others.
St. Philoxenus "The liberal soul shall be made fat: and he that watereth shall be watered also himself" [25]
He who is generous, especially toward the needy and the suffering, in pure love, receives from God a hundredfold of God's mercies in this world.

God is wonderful, for He has given us everything, and also gives us generosity of soul and breadth of heart so that we may use what He has given us in a fitting way, and He returns and repays us a hundredfold because of our response to His gift to us.
Love waters the souls of others, and God in His love waters our thirsty souls.

* "Every blessed soul is simple [25 LXX], does not cling to temporal things, and is not brought low with wings unspread, but shines with the splendor of the virtues, soars in the open air on the twofold wings of love (for God and for the neighbor), and sees how to offer to others that in which it strives, and is not in idle rest, but says in security: 'The Lord gave, the Lord hath taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord, let Him do according to His good pleasure!'"

St. Augustine * He says: "The soul that blesses is made fat, and he that watereth shall be watered also himself" [25]. For he who blesses from without by preaching receives within the fatness of an enlarged (heart), and while he does not cease to water the minds of his hearers with the wine of eloquence, he is all the more refreshed by the multiplied gift...
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* May those who hide the word of teaching within them listen in dread to the voice of divine judgment, so that this dread may remove another dread from their hearts (that is, that the dread of judgment may remove the dread of venturing to teach). And let them know that those who do not put forward their gifts lose them and forfeit them; not only do they lose them, but with the loss the curse falls upon them. And let them hear how Paul was confident that he was innocent of the blood of his brothers inasmuch as he did not delay in the effort of rebuking sins. In this he says: "Wherefore I take you to record this day, that I am pure from the blood of all men. For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God" (Acts 20:26-27). And let them hear also how the angelic voice warns John, saying: "And let him that heareth say, Come" (Rev 22:17), meaning that those who hear His voice in their depths must also raise their voices to draw others to where God calls them. This is lest, if one of them comes forward empty-handed, he finds the doors shut before him. And then he hears the word of Isaiah, who during the ministry of the word closed his lips, although the heavenly light had shone and lit upon him, and who therefore cries out in repentance, rebuking himself, saying: "Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips" (Isa 6:5). And let them hear the words of Solomon which show how the teacher's wisdom increases if he does not hide his gifts through the sin of sluggishness, which say: "The liberal soul shall be made fat: and he that watereth shall be watered also himself" (Prov 11:25). Those who go out to the ministry of teaching distribute its blessings, and so they are filled within and increase. And as long as the teacher continues to water his hearers with the wine of effective spiritual words, the sips of multiplied grace make him drunk. Let them hear how David presented this as a gift from God, and did not hide the gift of teaching which God gave him: "Lo, I have not refrained my lips, O LORD, thou knowest. I have not hid thy righteousness within my heart; I have declared thy faithfulness and thy salvation" (Ps 40:9-10).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* "The sway of his wrath is his destruction" (Sir 1:22), "The wrathful man is not beautiful," for there is nothing more shameful or uglier than a face inflamed with anger.
St. John Chrysostom "He that withholdeth corn, the people shall curse him: but blessing shall be upon the head of him that selleth it" [26]

It is fitting that we not keep the Lord's blessings and gifts to ourselves alone in selfishness, but offer from what we have been given to our brothers. Perhaps what is meant here by hoarding is that a man keeps the wheat and does not sell it, waiting for the price to rise so that he dictates his terms to the buyers.

* May the love of money come to an end, may the lust for (wealth) die... To demand an increase in price is a sign of malice, not of simplicity. Therefore it is said: "He who demands a high price for his wheat, the people shall curse him."

* Solomon the wise rightly says: "He that withholdeth corn leaves it to the nations," he does not leave it as an inheritance, because he who acquires greed does not work for the good of his successors.

St. Ambrose * "He that withholdeth corn, the people shall curse him." He who keeps (the wheat) for himself has no mercy. He does not gather (the wheat) for the sake of mercy. Yet unless he gathers, how can he offer mercy? Is it not also a fact that people bless him who spends and gives? As it is written here and in the pages of the Holy Scriptures?

St. Anba Shenouda Pope Gregory (the Great) holds that he who keeps wheat for himself and hoards it is the one who keeps the holy word of preaching for himself, and keeps silent without profiting by it in the correction of others; such a one deserves the curse of the people.

* Those who are able to teach with great effect, yet hold back out of excessive humility, should learn to infer, from reflection on small matters, how greatly they sin in the greater and more important tasks. Therefore, if they were to hide from needy brothers the money in their possession, they would doubtless cast sadness and grief upon them. Let them consider how deeply they are involved in a great guilt, for by withholding the word of teaching from sinful brothers, they withhold the medicine of life from souls going to death. Therefore the wise man says rightly: "Wisdom that is hid, and treasure that is hoarded up, what profit is in them both?" (Sir 20:32). If a famine were destroying a people, and this people hid their wheat, they would doubtless be heralds and announcers of death. Accordingly, let those who do not come forward to minister the bread of grace which has been granted them, when souls perish of thirst for the holy word, consider the terror of the punishment. Therefore it is also said rightly by the tongue of Solomon: "He that withholdeth corn, the people shall curse him" (Prov 11:26); he who hides the wheat keeps for himself the words of holy teaching. Such a man is struck by the curse, because by the sin of silence he deserves the punishment of all those who could have walked in what is right because of him.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

The righteous man does not rely on material wealth, but on genuine righteousness [28]. He inherits rewards that build his house [29], and sees the fruit of his life in souls he leads to the Lord [30].
"He that diligently seeketh good procureth favour: but he that seeketh mischief, it shall come unto him" [27]

He who strives toward what is good is rewarded according to his sincerity and faithfulness, and finds the favor of others and becomes a cause of their joy. But he who does evil and delights in the troubles of others and in harming them, it returns upon him. As Adonibezek said: "Threescore and ten kings, having their thumbs and their great toes cut off, gathered their meat under my table: as I have done, so God hath requited me" (Judg 1:7). The Apostle says: "Whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap. For he that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption; but he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting. And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not. As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith" (Gal 6:7-10).
St. John Chrysostom says that it is fitting for us to seize every opportunity to do good, for if the opportunity is lost it may not return again.

And Father Marius Victorinus says: [It is not enough to do good, but we must always strive to do good, for many began to do good and stopped, either because they grew tired or strayed from the way. We must not grow weary in doing good, and must continue in it. He also says: [The time is short, and life quickly reaches its end, the end of the world is at the doors. We have opportunity, that is, as long as we are alive or while life still continues in this world.]
"He that trusteth in his riches shall fall; but the righteous shall flourish as a branch" [28]

The Apostle says: "Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy; that they do good, that they be rich in good works" (1 Tim 6:17-18).

The Lord Christ warns us not to imitate the foolish rich man who said: "This will I do: I will pull down my barns, and build greater; and there will I bestow all my fruits and my goods. And I will say to my soul, Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry" (Lk 12:18-19).

* He thought within himself, saying: What shall I do, because I have no room where to bestow my fruits?
