He said, This will I do: I will pull down my barns, and build greater, and there will I bestow all my fruits and my goods. There is no more trivial position than this. In truth he had pulled down his barns, since the secure storehouses on which he depends are the bellies of the poor, not the walls of the barns...

Truly death came, and put out all this luxury, and led him away as a captive with bowed head, groaning with shame, unable to speak, trembling with fear, as though his enjoyment of all this luxury had been a dream.

In the end the rich man was reduced to entreating the poor man, begging him, he who had before lain hungry exposed to the mouths of dogs. The situation was reversed, and all knew who was the truly rich and who the truly poor, and so Lazarus became the richest of all and the other the poorest of all. And as it is in the theater, where the actors enter in borrowed masks as kings, generals, physicians, teachers, sages and soldiers, while in reality they are not so, so in the present life poverty and wealth are nothing but masks. For if you sit in the theater and see one of the actors wearing the mask of a king, you do not count him fortunate for that, nor do you believe that he really is a king, nor do you wish to be like him; but because you know that he is a merchant, or perhaps a rope-maker or a barrel-maker or something of the kind, you do not count him fortunate on account of his borrowed mask or the costume he wears, nor judge his social standing by the cheapness of his other garb, for this is not a sign on which you can rely.

Here too it is the same: sitting here in the world as though in a theater, and looking at the actors on the stage, you see many rich people, but you do not believe that they are really rich, for they are wearing borrowed masks of the rich.
St. John Chrysostom "He that troubleth his own house shall inherit the wind: and the fool shall be servant to the wise of heart" [29]

If he who sows a few seeds reaps much at harvest time, and if from a small spark fires arise which may devour thousands of acres, as happens in forests, so he who sows a few evils and bad habits destroys his house, and perhaps his grandchildren's grandchildren, who imitate him with some exaggeration.
The second part of the proverb refers to the rich owners of power, who think the lives of others are in their hands, but soon collapse before the wise and devout children of God.

Daniel was brought before King Belshazzar, and the latter said to him: "Art thou that Daniel, which art of the children of the captivity of Judah, whom the king my father brought out of Judah?" (Dan 5:13). The same night Belshazzar was slain and the kingdom of Babylon came to an end, while Daniel was honored.
Paul also stood to be tried before King Agrippa, and the king said: "Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian" (Acts 26:28).
"The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life; and he that winneth souls is wise" [30]

Men of God offer the fruit of righteousness as a tree of life, from which sinners pluck and are refreshed and live. They offer not abstract theoretical teachings, but the word of God, the giver of life. In this they win souls for the account of the Kingdom of God.

This is what the children of God seek, imitating the Apostle Paul, who wished to win the souls of all mankind. "For though I be free from all men, yet have I made myself servant unto all, that I might gain the more. And unto the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might gain the Jews; to them that are under the law, as under the law, that I might gain them that are under the law... I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some" (1 Cor 9:19-22).
"Behold, the righteous shall be recompensed in the earth: much more the wicked and the sinner" [31]

If the life we live is full of weaknesses, so that even the righteous and the just who will be rewarded in heaven are not spared from trials and afflictions, because of the weakness of their nature and their falling into sins, how much more must the wicked and sinners who persist in their evils and obstinacy expect eternal troubles and a terrible fate!

* "If the righteous scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear?"... If God gives us anything, He will test our work by it, and who is justified except he who is purer than the sun? He who hates God is wicked. The "sinner" is he who walks in evil.
St. John Chrysostom
By Your righteousness lead me in all my life!
* All the scales have been upset before me because of my sins.
Who but You can restore to me the spirit of sincerity and balance?
In You I know how my soul is sanctified, and my body too!
In You my senses are in harmony with my mind, for my edification and glory!
In You I see everything as holy and blessed!
Take away from me the scales of deceit and false concepts.
* By Your righteousness I imitate You, O You who are meek and lowly in heart.
Pride cannot creep into me and destroy my life with folly.
* By Your righteousness I enjoy the spirit of uprightness, so that I do not turn to the right hand or to the left.
May crookedness not carry me to shame and disgrace!
* By Your righteousness I see You as my wealth and my treasure!
You satisfy me, and water me, and enrich me, and gladden my heart!
I do not rely on the wealth of the world and its treasures, for the world and all that is in it passes away.
And I remain with You in Your embrace forever.
May death not rule over me, and may the enemy of good find no place within me!
* I possess You, and so I possess perfection and security.
I walk in You, and my soul is filled with joy in hope.
You are my reward, my crown, and my glory!
* Let the whole world stand against me, for I am hidden in You, O Conqueror of the world!
The world hates me, because it hates You!
It devises plots against me, and perishes by them itself!
The world crucified You, and its authority was shattered!
It wanted to be rid of You, and the powers of darkness collapsed.
* You establish Your Kingdom within me.
You count me Your holy city.
No evil word is heard in it, nor unseemly jesting.
Rather, words of blessing go forth from my mouth.
There is not a word of contempt for my neighbor, but all hear Your words that give hope.
There is no tale-bearing nor betrayal of secrets, but every word is heard for edification.
* Your righteousness carries within it an inexpressible reward.
By it my soul is transformed into a bride adorned with Your grace.
And my soul is strengthened and made firm, so that the enemy does not steal my wealth; it bears Your icon, and knows nothing but love, tenderness and mercy!
Your righteousness bears fruit in the joyful fruits of the Spirit.
Your righteousness proclaims within me the pledge of eternal life.
Your righteousness makes my way straight, so that there is no crookedness in it; Your righteousness sanctifies my will, my feelings and my longings, so that I seek only good for every human being.
* My soul rejoices with the salvation of every soul.
I desire not only to give of the good things I have, but also to make myself a servant to all, that I may gain the more.
Let me give from what You have given me, for I have no merit in anything!
Let nothing occupy me in all my life but the winning of souls!
"Whoso loveth instruction loveth knowledge: but he that hateth reproof is brutish" [1]

He who accepts discipline desires the truth. But he who hates reproof is like a (brutish) animal that cannot appreciate correction (Prov 10:17). He prefers his unbridled will, even if it is against sound teaching. Acceptance of discipline is a sincere sign of the desire for progress and correction, and therefore of the desire to enjoy true knowledge. The psalmist says: "Let the righteous smite me; it shall be a kindness: and let him reprove me; it shall be an excellent oil for the head" (Ps 141:5). And the Apostle Paul says: "Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby" (Heb 12:11).

He who refuses discipline is like the animal that kicks or bites the one who offers it medicines for healing, because it does not understand what lies behind the pain, but seeks temporary comfort even at the expense of its health and benefit.

* I am obliged to exhort you, and especially to use reproof with you. For just as fire melts wax, so the fear of punishments softens the hearts of sinners, and not only this, but it burns up your sins through your repentance and your return to the Redeemer, and enriches your minds and increases your boldness and your striving.
* This is counsel, not judgment; medicine, not punishment; correction, not torture... a spiritual remedy to heal sinners and keep them from new sins.
St. John Chrysostom * Discipline (or reproof) is a proof of loving care, and it leads to understanding.
The Teacher shows this reproof when He says in Scripture: "How often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!" (Mt 23:37).

Scripture also says: "They went a whoring after idols and stones, and offered their burnt offerings to Baal." It is a great proof of His love, for although He knows the shame of those who rejected Him and that they ran far from Him, yet He urges them to repent... In His care for the people He rebuked them in Isaiah, saying: "This people honoureth me with their lips, but their heart is far from me" (Isa 29:13). And He says also: "But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men" (Mt 15:9). Here His loving care shows their sins and their salvation side by side.
St. Clement of Alexandria

entries.section: 2. The good man and the man of devices

paragraphs.text: 2 A good man obtaineth favour of the LORD: but a man of wicked devices will he condemn. 3 A man shall not be established by wickedness: but the root of the righteous shall not be moved.
"A good man obtaineth favour of the LORD: but a man of wicked devices will he condemn" [2]

The good man obtains grace and benefit from the Lord, because all the goodness in him is not from himself, but is the Lord's gift to him through free grace. And as he submits to Him in obedience, his goodness grows and increases. But the goodness of God is absolute by nature, and does not change.
Some see that the literal translation of the word "favour" is "good will," for it is from the Lord.
We do nothing good by ourselves, but by the will of God we receive this salvation; and we are called (saints) not because we deserve it, but because in that is His good pleasure.

St. John Chrysostom If other things are found called good in the Holy Bible, such as an angel (Tob 5:21; 2 Macc 11:6), or a man (Prov 12:2; Ps 37:23; Mt 12:35), or a servant (Sir 7:21; Lk 19:17), or a treasure (Tob 4:9; Lk 6:45), or a good heart (Jdt 8:28; Wis 1:1; Sir 26:4; Lk 8:15), or a good tree (2 Kgs 3:19; Mt 7:17-19), all these were so called by an inexact use of the word, since the goodness in them is incidental and not essential.
* Christ is the Good that the people were awaiting.
Origen * If you do good you live in God, and those who do good like you live also.

Hermas "A man of devices" does not mean only one who devises plots by deeds and words, but one who carries in his heart or mind the desire to devise plots against his brother, even if he does not accomplish it because of the inadequacy of his means.

The face of the Lord shines on the good man, and so the man becomes steadfast and unshaken (Rom 14:4). But the wicked shall not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous (Ps 1:5). [Cf. Hushai and Ahithophel (2 Sam 15:32; 16:15; 17:23).]

* The righteous man dies in the strength of his simplicity, in complete mastery over his will, with a soul full as of meadows. But the sinner, though he lives in comfort, giving off sweet perfumes, ends his life in the bitterness of his soul, and passes his last day without taking anything of the good things he once enjoyed, carrying nothing but the wages of his evil.

* St. Job answers: Do not think that you are happy while you are immersed in pleasures, because the blows of God have not fallen on you in this life. "The lamp of the wicked shall be put out." It gives light for a time, but it carries no eternal light. And although the world favors such people because they practice the will of God, who has authority over the world (Jn 14:30), yet there usually comes a moment of change in events, when sorrows come from the wrath and anger of heaven, when the wicked are sifted "as stubble before the wind." The unjust are sifted like straw, and the righteous like wheat. Look to the Lord who says to Peter: "Behold, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat: but I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not" (Lk 22:31-32).

entries.section: 2. The good man and the man of devices

paragraphs.text: St. Ambrose "A man shall not be established by wickedness: but the root of the righteous shall not be moved" [3]

* The man who founds his life on evil is like one who builds his house on the sand, as the Lord Christ says, and the rain descends, and the floods come, and the winds blow, and beat upon that house, and it falls, and great is the fall of it (Mt 7:27). But the wise righteous man founds his life on the Lord Christ, the Rock, and the rain descends, and the floods come, and the winds blow, and beat upon that house, and it will not be shaken.

The overflow of rivers, as in the lands of Egypt and Assyria, cannot harm them; rather, those who build on the sand, that is, who practice the wisdom of the world, are the ones harmed. The winds that blow are like false prophets. All these come together in one place and strike the house. But if it is founded on the rock, no harm comes to them, for there is no way of a serpent upon a rock (Prov 30:19).
Origen * Those who hear the words of the Lord are like a wise man who builds on the rock. Those who do not follow the words of the Lord are like a foolish man who builds his house on the sand.

* He who practices virtue becomes able through Christ who strengthens him (Phil 4:13). We receive everything from God, who puts all things in their place. From Him come wisdom, insight and union with all that is good.

* The wicked man cannot accuse God as the cause of his evils and his folly. He makes himself like a fool when he withdraws from what proceeds to him according to nature, and turns aside to what is contrary to nature.

St. Cyril the Great * Jesus speaks of human circumstances and calamities by way of reference to rain, flood and winds, such as false accusations, plunder, death, the loss of family members, insults from others, and all the horrible things in life that a man can speak of. And Jesus says that the soul that follows the way of loftiness does not yield to these disasters that may happen. The secret of this is that the soul is founded on the rock.

The "rock" signifies reliance on the teachings of our Lord Jesus, for His commandments are stronger than any rock. They are founded in calm above all the human waves of life. He who keeps these commandments carefully rises, not only above human beings when they teach them with malice, but even above the demons themselves with their plans.
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: 3. The virtuous woman and the woman who shames

paragraphs.text: "A virtuous woman is a crown to her husband: but she that maketh ashamed is as rottenness in his bones" [4]

It is dangerous to limit virtue to virginity alone. The virtuous woman radiates many qualities, as is stated in (Prov 31). She is truly the crown of her husband. But the foolish and lazy woman causes him shame, and brings him down to old age.

* The crown of the woman must be reckoned her husband, and the crown of the husband is his marriage, for both have the flower of their union, which is the child, truly the meadows of the flesh. The crown of the old is their grandchildren, and the glory of children is their fathers, as it is said (cf. Prov 17:6). Our glory is the Father of all, and the crown of the whole Church is Christ.
St. Clement of Alexandria * When you go to choose a wife, look not only for a companion for you in life, but also for a companion for you in virtue.

It is inevitable that the husband of a corrupt woman perishes with her in her way. Therefore look to virtue, not to money. Then the virtuous wife becomes a crown of glory, because she is strong. But the wicked one is like a worm dwelling in his heart, causing gradual ruin in silence.

What is more dangerous than this? She does not appear outwardly, but this kind of wife injects poison into the wretched soul and destroys it. On the contrary, virtue adorns him who follows it, while evil burdens the wicked man with more hatred.

St. John Chrysostom How great the difference between devout Sarah, who shared her husband's good life, and Job's wife, who asked him to curse God and die! The Apostle Peter says: "Even as Sara obeyed Abraham, calling him lord: whose daughters ye are, as long as ye do well, and are not afraid with any amazement."

* When they (the man and his wife) are in agreement, and their children in good upbringing, and their household in good order, the neighbors smell the sweet fragrance of the harmony, and with them the friends and relatives. But if it is otherwise, everything is overturned and falls into confusion.
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: 4. The thoughts and counsels of the righteous and the wicked

paragraphs.text: 5 The thoughts of the righteous are right: but the counsels of the wicked are deceit. 6 The words of the wicked are to lie in wait for blood: but the mouth of the upright shall deliver them. 7 The wicked are overthrown, and are not: but the house of the righteous shall stand. 8 A man shall be commended according to his wisdom: but he that is of a perverse heart shall be despised.
"The thoughts of the righteous are right: but the counsels of the wicked are deceit" [5]

The thoughts of the righteous are simple and clear, aiming at what builds up the soul and others, so they are upright in the eyes of God and men. Good thoughts are translated into good words and righteous conduct, and are rewarded by God who loves righteousness and goodness. But the thoughts of the wicked are mixed with cheating and deceit at the expense of their neighbors as well as themselves, for they perish because of them..

* Thoughts come from ourselves, since by nature we remember what we do or have done or have heard. Of this the blessed David says: "I have considered the days of old, the years of ancient times. I call to remembrance my song in the night: I commune with mine own heart: and my spirit made diligent search" (Ps 77:5-6). Again he says: "The LORD knoweth the thoughts of man, that they are vanity" (Ps 94:11), "The thoughts of the righteous are right..." (Prov 12:5). And in the Gospel the Lord says to the Pharisees: "Wherefore think ye evil in your hearts?!" (Mt 9:4).
Father Moses * The more you are negligent in watching your mind (your thoughts), the greater the distance becomes between you and Jesus.

Hesychius of Jerusalem * By long observation we have found a difference between the thoughts that come from angels, the thoughts that come from men, and the thoughts that spring from Satan; that difference is:
The thoughts from the angels work to reveal the nature of things and their spiritual meanings. As, for example, they reveal:
For what purpose does gold exist?!
And why is it scattered like sand in the valleys?
And why do they obtain it with great toil and striving?

And how, when it is discovered, it is washed not with water but with fire, and after that is placed in the hands of craftsmen who fashion from it lampstands and censers for the house of God (2 Chr 19:4-21), those vessels which, by the grace of God, the king of Babylon was not able to use for himself (Dan 3:5), while Cleopas offers a heart burning with these mysteries (Lk 32:24).

But the thought that springs from the demons does not know this or understand it, but shamelessly presents only the possession of gold, deluding us with the pleasure and glory that we obtain by acquiring gold.

As for the (mere) human thought, it neither seeks the possession of gold nor yearns to understand the (spiritual) meanings (of its existence and of its use for good...), but presents to the mind the images of gold without lusts or covetousness.
And if a man applies this with his mind to other things (besides gold), he will find the same.

entries.section: 4. The thoughts and counsels of the righteous and the wicked

paragraphs.text: St. Evagrius "The words of the wicked are to lie in wait for blood: but the mouth of the upright shall deliver them" [6]

The wicked cast their words with malice, as though they were nets to catch others and shed their blood. But the upright offer their words to rescue themselves from the nets set for them by the wicked.

The Pharisees tried to trap the Lord Christ with their words, and His answer came to silence them and nullify their wicked schemes. "Then went the Pharisees, and took counsel how they might entangle him in his talk" (Mt 22:15; Mk 12:13; Lk 11:54).
* Keep your tongues from speaking evil of your brothers, for he who speaks evil of his brother angers God who dwells in him. What each one does to his companion he does to God.

* The soul of a man who is not perfect in the virtues is found pure like the sun before an evil word reaches him, but if he hears an evil word or slander, immediately the demons overpower his mind and veil the light from him, and make him wretched because his soul is unsteady and his virtues incomplete.

St. Macarius the Great * An elder said: "The tongue is full of fire and it defiles the whole body, so let him who loves his life spare his tongue. Guard your lips, O man of God, and bridle your tongue, and you will profit from all your labors, for he who keeps his tongue has many honors, and blessed is he who rules over his tongue, for his storehouses (that is, his granaries) are filled with good things."

* An elder said: "If the movements of your tongue are abundant, the pure movements in your heart have been extinguished, but if your tongue is silent and your heart boils with pure movements, blessed are you, for its movement by the Spirit lifts you to the calm of life. Your tongue was silent that your heart might speak, and your heart was silent that the Spirit might speak in it."

entries.section: 4. The thoughts and counsels of the righteous and the wicked

paragraphs.text: The Paradise of the Fathers "The wicked are overthrown, and are not: but the house of the righteous shall stand" [7]

The wicked may flourish, and appear successful and healthy, with children to inherit them and perpetuate their memory, but sooner or later evil sweeps them away, and they lose everything, and their souls perish. But the righteous, though they suffer trials and pains, their house stands.

When bitter trials came upon Job and he lost his sons and daughters at one stroke, his friends thought that this was a true and certain testimony of his grave wickedness and hypocrisy. But Job was glorified and enjoyed the sight of God, and received double what he had lost, and his memory is still alive to this day in heaven and on earth, as though his house were still standing, while as for his friends, the world knows nothing of them.

The two midwives whom Pharaoh asked to kill the male Hebrew children at their birth acted in the spirit of the fear of God; therefore it was said of them: "Therefore God dealt well with the midwives... And it came to pass, because the midwives feared God, that he made them houses" (Ex 1:20-21). As Nathan the prophet said to David the king: "Also the LORD telleth thee that the LORD will make thee an house" (2 Sam 7:11). So when we enjoy the fear of the Lord, God Himself builds for us a spiritual house made by His own hands to dwell in Himself.

* Without the fear of God a house cannot be built. If by the fear of God houses were built by those who committed no sin, but raised their buildings according to the good pleasure of God, what shall we do, who have been taken captive (by sin)? Listen, O sinner: we must fear God in order to avoid sin, but after a loss has occurred to us and our ship has been wrecked, there is another lifeboat, and it is repentance.

St. Jerome Pope Gregory the Great holds that the wicked man, when he is overturned or changed, "is not," not in the sense that he loses his existence or his being, but that he no longer stands in the state of evil in which he was.

The wicked Pharaoh thought he was able to destroy the people of God, so he commanded that their children be cast into the river, and he did not realize that his evil would return upon his family after 80 years and destroy his army, while God works wonders for His people.

* Pharaoh commanded that the children be cast into the river. Had the children not been cast out, Moses would not have been brought into the palace. When the child Moses was safe he was not honored, and when he was cast into the river he became honored. God did that to show the riches of His means and ways.

entries.section: 4. The thoughts and counsels of the righteous and the wicked

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom "A man shall be commended according to his wisdom: but he that is of a perverse heart shall be despised" [8]

Nothing honors a man like heavenly wisdom, for it reflects upon him an inward heavenly splendor, and he carries within him the spirit of truth. All men prefer wisdom, and the world honors prudence and spiritual understanding, even though he who holds to these things is exposed to persecutions and opposition.

But the perverse man, who thinks himself wise and able to reach his goal by crooked ways, is not pleasing to God, and even men discover the truth of his character and make light of him, and mock his crooked manner.

* Heartbreaking and deadly is this poison of the enemy, by which he has blinded many and cast them down suddenly, for he suggests to the soul a false and ruinous thought, so that it imagines it has attained things not attained by most people, and that it excels in fasting. He also suggests to the soul many heroic deeds, and leads it astray by making it forget all its sins so that it feels its superiority over those around it. He steals from its heart the remembrance of its faults, and he does this not for the soul's benefit, but so that it may not be able to utter this healing saying: "Against thee only have I sinned; have mercy upon me" (Ps 51:4, 1), and he does not allow it to say: "I will praise the LORD with my whole heart" (Ps 111:1). Rather, as Satan himself said in his heart: "I will exalt my throne above the stars of God" (Isa 14:13), so he deceives man by turning him toward domination and high positions, and also toward the positions of teaching and boasting of healing. And so the soul perishes by deception, being struck with a wound hard to heal.
Amma Syncletica * Do not receive vainglory into yourself, for you cannot bear its deceit and the madness of its hypocrisy, since it brings deceitful thoughts upon you.

* If you surrender your heart to it in false dreams, it grows more firmly rooted in vain thought until it misleads all who receive the spirit that loves the saying written of it: "When he speaketh a lie, he speaketh of his own: for he is a liar, and the father of it" (Jn 14:8).
Anba Paula of Tamouh
"He that is despised, and hath a servant, is better than he that honoureth himself, and lacketh bread" [v. 9].

He says that the man who appears despised, without reputation or fame, and without the show of greatness and pomp, but who has a servant or slave who renders him humble service, is better than he who glorifies himself and cares for vain greatness and has nothing to live on, not even the necessities. When Saul wished to give his daughter to David as a wife, David did not exalt himself, but said to the king's servants: "Seemeth it to you a light thing to be a king's son in law, seeing that I am a poor and needy man?" (1 Sam 18:23).
The Latin translation (the Vulgate) reads: "Better is the poor man who supports himself than the proud man who lacks bread."
The proverb in general means that it is better for a man to appear poor while his depths lack nothing than a man who is occupied with outward appearances and vainglory and suffers emptiness.

* In these snares the weak fall... for while they are indifferent to their own salvation, and while they themselves need the teaching and guidance of others, they are deceived by the wiles of Satan under the cover of guiding others and urging them to repentance. So if they obtain some gain from their talk with others, they lose their patience in the matters that must be acquired. And so there comes upon them what Haggai the prophet said: "Ye have sown much, and bring in little; ye eat, but ye have not enough; ye drink, but ye are not filled with drink; ye clothe you, but there is none warm; and he that earneth wages earneth wages to put it into a bag with holes" (Hag 1:6). For truly the man who puts his wages in a bag with holes loses all that he seemed to have gained from his talk with others, because of the loss of his self-control and his mental confusion every day. The result is that while he thinks he can acquire great gain by teaching others, he in truth deprives himself of growth, for "There is that maketh himself rich, yet hath nothing: there is that maketh himself poor, yet hath great riches," "He that is despised, and hath a servant, is better than he that honoureth himself, and lacketh bread" (Prov 13:7; 12:9).
Father Abraham * If you clothe yourself with poverty in this world together with humility, you will be with the Son of God in His Kingdom.
* Blessed is the poor and needy who keeps stillness. He will be a friend of God like Abraham, for the Lord does nothing unless He reveals His secret to His servants the prophets (Amos 9:3).
* Let your labor be between you and God, until God makes it manifest at the resurrection and glorifies you for it among all the righteous and the just.
* Do not receive vainglory into yourself, for you cannot bear its deceit and the madness of its hypocrisy, since it brings deceitful thoughts upon you.

* O poor one, acquire patience and be humble, and you will attain this honor. And let your heart think on heavenly things and not on things on the earth. And be confident that the saints will come to you. And imitate the disciples of Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and power forever. Amen.
Anba Paula of Tamouh

entries.section: 6. The mercies of the righteous and the cruelty of the wicked

paragraphs.text: "A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast: but the tender mercies of the wicked are cruel" [v. 10].
The righteous man cannot but be gentle even with animals. But the wicked man becomes a beast of prey when he obtains authority over others. Violence and evil are brothers who work together.

* "A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast." It is a training in human tenderness, when a person becomes accustomed to showing mercy to his fellow men through practicing it on his animals. Surely he who is tender toward animals is all the more inclined to be tender toward his brothers... Do the righteous have compassion on the souls of their animals? Never! For certainly benefits must be conveyed to them, and so much the more should he practice that with his fellow men. God rightly commanded us to care for wounded animals and to return the strayed ones, and not to muzzle the ox (Deut 22:1-4). He asks us to keep animals in complete safety, first for our own sake, and second so that they may serve us. At the same time this is a training in caring for others and doing what is useful to them. Truly he who has compassion on strangers will all the more have compassion on those he knows. And he who is tender to his servants will be all the more tender to his brothers. Perhaps you will say: The animal gives you useful service, but in what does your brother benefit you? I say that he is a greater help to you than it, and that in the sight of God. You can see this when we care for our animals in this way, we do not count it a lowly work. For in doing this we serve not them alone but ourselves also.

St. John Chrysostom * When any man acquires the love of goodness of which we have spoken, by which we become like God, then he is given the tender heart of God, and he prays for those who wrong him, saying in the same pattern: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do" (Lk 23:34).

There is a clear sign that reveals the soul that has not yet been wholly purified of the residue of sin, and it is that it does not grieve tenderly over the faults of others, but judges them like a judge in fierce blame.

But how can he attain perfect purity of heart who does not carry out the commandments which the Apostle sets forth, "Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ" (Gal 6:2), and who has not the virtue of love, which "doth not behave itself unseemly... is not easily provoked... thinketh no evil... beareth all things... endureth all things" (1 Cor 13:4-7)?! For "A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast: but the tender mercies of the wicked are cruel" (Prov 12:10).

So the man (the monk) falls into the very faults for which he cruelly and without gentleness condemns another, for "A wicked messenger falleth into mischief" (Prov 13:17), and "Whoso stoppeth his ears at the cry of the poor, he also shall cry himself, but shall not be heard" (Prov 21:13).

Father Cheremon St. Augustine asks us to have the quarrels of doves and not the kisses of wolves. For doves, even in their quarrel, do not hurt one another, but use their beaks to attack the other's beak without harm, and after the quarrel the doves fly together and eat together in harmony. But wolves, even if you want to kiss them, attack and hurt. So the believer carries tenderness toward all, and the wicked man overflows with violence and cruelty.
* He who uses violence is worse than he who steals.

St. John Chrysostom * You have been commanded to rescue the ass or the ox that has fallen in the mud. Do you see a Christian like yourself, saved by the blood of Christ, cast into the sewer of drunkenness, and wallowing in the mire of dissipation, and you stand silent? Do you pass by and stretch out no hand of mercy? Do you stop at crying out and rebuking, or do you tremble for him?

Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles * If the Law does not allow you to separate the young irrational animal from its mother before it has suckled (Lev 22:27 etc.), how much more must mankind be prepared against violence.
St. Clement of Alexandria
"He that tilleth his land shall be satisfied with bread: but he that followeth vain persons is void of understanding" [11].

The word of God is a field that needs continual tilling (2 Tim 2:15). Every moment we devote to the word of God has its fruit in due time. But he who wastes his time on unseemly things does not enjoy true knowledge, because he does not till the field of the Holy Bible, and so he is deprived of the bread of the word.

It is fitting for the believer to plow the ground of Scripture every day, that he may be satisfied with the heavenly bread. For he who walks in the way of Scripture runs toward heaven and grows in every good work.
Timothy represents the man who grows through the word (2 Tim 3:14-17), and Jehoiakim represents the one who resists the word (Jer 36:22-32).

* It has come to my knowledge that a lazy man took the Holy Bible into his lap from the seventh hour (that is, one o'clock in the afternoon) until sunset and was not able to open it at all, as though he were bound with lead. But Anba Anthony did as the angel showed him: at one time he sat practicing his work, at another he rose to pray persistently, and at another he sat reading the words of God. And he was granted such enlightenment that he said to one of the philosophers of his time: [It is enough for me to contemplate the nature of creatures always, and to recite the sayings of the Lord until the darkness of night.] To this extent he was in touch with God, and his night shone like day, as it is said: "Even the darkness is not dark to thee, and the night shineth as the day" (Ps 139:12).
St. Nilus of Sinai

entries.section: 8. The desires of the wicked are evil

paragraphs.text: 12 The wicked desireth the net of evil men: but the root of the righteous yieldeth fruit.
"The desires of the wicked are evil, and the root of the righteous is profitable" [v. 12 LXX]

The desires of the wicked are evil, as if he overflows with what is in his heart even upon his inward desires and his outward conduct. He is like one who casts nets in every place to catch evils, and he does not know that while he hunts them, they hunt him in their snares.
But the righteous man, being genuine in his thought and principles, moves with balance for the good of all, bears with them in love and does not condemn them.

* There was an honorable man who had a debtor, and he kept asking him for the debt for ten years and he did not answer him, and the creditor bore with him with a good heart. He had a friend, who said to him: "I am amazed at you, how is it that you have not grown resentful toward him, for you have been asking him for a long time and he has not responded?"

He said to him: "You wonder that I have been longsuffering with him for ten years, and behold, God has been asking me for more than fifty years to keep His commandments, and until now I have not responded to Him nor fulfilled His will, and He with a good heart bears with me. So if I, a man, have not responded to God, and He is not angry with me, it is no wonder if a man like me does not respond to me and I am longsuffering with him."

* One of the brothers complained to an elder, saying: "What shall I do, father, for my brother grieves me because he wanders about?" The elder said: "Bear with him, my beloved, for God will bring him back when He sees your patience and your treatment of him with gentleness and mildness, and put away harshness from you, for a devil does not cast out a devil. And by your gentleness and patience he will return, for God brings a man back only by longsuffering, goodness of heart and forbearance."
The Paradise of the Fathers

entries.section: 9. Evil words and the sweet tongue

paragraphs.text: 13 The wicked is snared by the transgression of his lips: but the just shall come out of trouble. 14 A man shall be satisfied with good by the fruit of his mouth: and the recompence of a man's hands shall be rendered unto him.
"The wicked is snared by the transgression of his lips: but the just shall come out of trouble" [v. 13]

Judgment is passed on the wicked on the great day of the Lord through the evil words they uttered. What they carried in their lives of disobedience to the divine commandment, and of lust for evil, condemns them, and they do not escape the nets they set for themselves without knowing it. But the righteous man stands on the great day of the Lord rejoicing; he feels that the troubles, trials and sufferings he endured have become the secret of eternal glory for him.
* And do not keep company with the one who has a harsh tongue, nor with the haughty of heart.

Anba Paula of Tamouh * An elder said: "If a monk reviles his brother by mentioning some of his sins, such as saying to him: O fornicator, or O thief, or O liar, and the reviled one keeps silent and forgives the reviler, and says in himself: Truly I am a sinner, then the sin for which he was reviled and of which he said that he is a sinner is forgiven him, and it comes upon the reviler, because instead of confessing his own sin he exposed his brother's sin, and because the reviled one bore the exposure of his sin it is counted to him as a confession, and because he forgave his brother he obtained forgiveness."

The Paradise of the Fathers * A golden vessel is not used for base things because of its high price, how much more the mouth, which is more precious than gold and coral, so it is not permissible for us to defile it with foul speech, reviling and slander of others.

* Silence is a great growth for a man and rest for his soul. Silence gives the heart constant solitude. Silence brings tears to a man, silence drives away anger, silence is the companion of asceticism, silence begets knowledge, silence guards love, silence does not pain any man's heart nor scandalize anyone, silence does its work without murmuring, silence keeps the lips and tongue and leaves nothing of evil in the heart, silence is the perfection of philosophy, and he who holds fast to silence can hold fast to all good things. He who keeps silence with knowledge has been sealed with the seal of Christ, and he who keeps it will without doubt inherit the Kingdom of Heaven.

entries.section: 9. Evil words and the sweet tongue

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom A man shall be satisfied with good by the fruit of his mouth: and the recompence of a man's hands shall be rendered unto him" [14]

The wise man often concentrates on the tongue, for the righteous man is filled with good things through his sweet, holy tongue for the account of the Kingdom of God, and what he practices returns to him. So by the tongue as by deed man sows, to reap fruit according to what he sowed. "For whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap" (Gal 6:7).
* Silence for God's sake is good, as speaking for God's sake is good.
Father Poemen

entries.section: 10. He that hearkeneth unto counsel is wise

paragraphs.text: "The way of a fool is right in his own eyes: but he that hearkeneth unto counsel is wise" [15]

The foolish man who lacks divine wisdom is self-reliant; he does not seek God's counsel, nor resort to a father or guide. But the wise man in his humility resorts to God, and consults, not clinging to his opinion without fitting dialogue.
* He who relies on his own opinion, even if he is a saint, is deceived, and the danger of his deception is greater than the danger of the beginner who has put his direction in the hands of another.

For the first is like a ship's captain who throws himself into a boat without sail or oar in the middle of the sea, relying on his skill and art of management. The second, that is the beginner, is like one who has no experience of sea voyages, and asks a skilled sailor to take him aboard his ship, which is well furnished with all its necessities and needs.

Let none of you be deceived and flee from the gentle yoke of obedience, determined to cling to his own opinion in spiritual matters, such as fasting and prayer and other marks of faith and asceticism, supposing that by this he will be saved!

St. John Chrysostom * The way of obedience is the shortest of paths, though it is the most difficult. And there is only one way in which, once we walk, we go astray: it is that which we call "reliance on self and on our personal will."

* Obedience is a defense before God. If you are asked by Him: Why did you do this? You answer Him: "You, Lord, commanded obedience, and I did what You commanded," and so you answer Him and are justified.

Voyaging in this ship carries safety from drowning. Man travels while he sleeps, as a man travels asleep in a ship and is not obliged to steer it, because its steersman is present. Such is the condition of the man walking under obedience: he voyages toward heaven and perfection while he sleeps, without toil and without thinking about what he ought to do. For the superiors are the steersmen of this ship and the ones who watch for him. Truly, it is no small matter but very great. Man crosses the sea of this world upon the forearm and arm of another! This is the great grace which God does to him who walks under obedience.

St. John Climacus * Our holy father John began his monastic life with perfect obedience and humility, so that by them he might tear down the roots of sin, and Anba Ammoi disciplined him by the law of the Lord, and all that he taught him he fulfilled and kept the counsel, being very obedient; therefore the grace of God was supporting him.

* St. John used to say to the brothers: "Submit in perfect obedience according to the way of life of our fathers. Receive counsel with faith, and especially with humility, purity, the fear of God, steadfastness in God and occupation with Him; these things are higher than all the virtues and make the soul shine with God by its uprightness." The Fathers have related of him that just as the earth cannot fall, so Anba John the Short could not fall because of the greatness of his humility, for he fulfilled great obedience while under submission to his spiritual father, being aflame with the fire of the Holy Spirit.
The Paradise of the Fathers

entries.section: 11. Restraining the spirit of anger and covering others

paragraphs.text: "A fool's wrath is presently known: but a prudent man covereth shame" [16]

* It behooves us to restrain every movement of anger and soften it under the guidance of discernment (wisdom), so that we do not rush into blind rage, of which Solomon said: "The fool shows all his anger, but the wise man quiets it in the end" (Prov 11:29). That is, the foolish man is inflamed with the passion of anger to avenge himself, but the wise man, because of the maturity of his counsel and his gentleness, extinguishes anger little by little and rids himself of it.

The Apostle says something similar: "Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord" (Rom 12:19). That is, do not allow your hearts to be confined in the straits of impatience and cowardice, so that when any violent storm of anger arises you cannot bear it, but let your hearts be wide, receiving the waves of words of anger in the wide currents of love, which "beareth all things... endureth all things" (1 Cor 13:7). And so your minds are enlarged with longsuffering and patience, and there are in it the depths of faithful counsel, which receives the smoke of anger and destroys it.

The passage can be understood in the following sense: we give place to anger by submitting with a humble and calm mind to the passion of others, and bowing to the impatience of the angry, as though we deserved every kind of wrong (as a discipline for us).

As for those who distort the meaning of perfection of which the Apostle speaks, interpreting "give place unto wrath" as withdrawing from a man in the time of his anger, it seems to me that by this they do not cut off the causes of anger, but stir up the motives of strife. For unless we straightway amend the neighbor's anger by an amendment full of humility, withdrawal provokes the neighbor all the more...

Solomon speaks of a matter like this, saying: "Be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry: for anger resteth in the bosom of fools" (Eccl 7:9). And "Go not forth hastily to strive, lest thou do something to the other when thy neighbour hath put thee to shame" (Prov 25:8). In this he does not blame haste in strife in the sense that he praises delayed strife.

In the same way we must understand the saying: "A fool's wrath is presently known: but a prudent man covereth shame" (Prov 12:16), for it does not mean that the wise man stores up the outburst of anger secretly, but blames the outburst of rash anger... He must hide the outburst for this reason, that when he leaves it for a while he calms the spirit of anger forever. For this is the nature of anger, when room is left for it (that is, we are not hasty with it) it weakens and perishes, but if anger is displayed in a state of rage it burns more and more.

Hearts must be enlarged and opened so that they are not confined in the straits of cowardice and filled with increasing anger, and become unable to receive the commandments of God, by what the prophet calls "enlargement of the heart or exceeding enlargement." For the prophet says: "I ran in the way of thy commandments when I enlarged my heart" (Ps 119:32).

For slowness to anger is wisdom, which we learn from the clear sayings of Holy Scripture, for "He that is slow to wrath is of great understanding: but he that is hasty of spirit exalteth folly" (Prov 14:29). Therefore Scripture says of him who asked the Lord for the gift of wisdom: "And God gave Solomon wisdom and understanding exceeding much, and largeness of heart, even as the sand that is on the sea shore" (1 Kgs 4:29).
Father Joseph The fool in his foolishness exposes others as one better than they, but the wise man covers others.

When Noah became drunk and was uncovered, Ham told his two brothers outside (Gen 9:22). But Shem and Japheth took a garment and laid it upon both their shoulders, and went backward, and covered the nakedness of their father, and their faces were backward, and they saw not their father's nakedness (Gen 23:9).
* Ham the son of Noah brought a curse upon himself, because he laughed when he saw his father's nakedness. But the two who covered their father's nakedness received the blessing.

St. Ambrose * Do not say that so-and-so is bad by nature, and so-and-so is good by nature. For if he is good by nature, can he never become bad, and if he is bad by nature, can he never become good? But now we see the change happening quickly from one state to another... This we have seen not only in the Holy Scriptures, I mean that tax collectors became apostles, the disciple became the betrayer of his Master, harlots became chaste, robbers became victors, astrologers became worshippers of God, unbelievers passed over to true worship... This happened in the Old Testament and the New Testament, and every day anyone can see these things happening... So let no one purpose to rebuke another, saying: O wicked one, given over to the passions of sin.
* If it is counted evil that a man should not see his own sins, his evil is doubled when he sits on the seat of judgment of others while carrying a beam in his eyes.
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: 12. The tongue of the wise and the tongue of fools!

paragraphs.text: 17 He that speaketh truth sheweth forth righteousness: but a false witness deceit. 18 There is that speaketh like the piercings of a sword: but the tongue of the wise is health. 19 The lip of truth shall be established for ever: but a lying tongue is but for a moment. 20 Deceit is in the heart of them that imagine evil: but to the counsellors of peace is joy. 21 There shall no evil happen to the just: but the wicked shall be filled with mischief. 22 Lying lips are abomination to the LORD: but they that deal truly are his delight.

In the following verses [17-22] the wise man speaks of the tongue of the wise and, in contrast to it, the lying tongue of the wicked. The wise speak the truth and do not know lying; this is the delight of God Himself, for He is the Truth who knows no falsehood. The wicked, however, find lying sweet and rejoice in it, and it is an abomination to the Lord, who cannot bear falsehood, lying, deceit or malice.
"He that speaketh truth sheweth forth righteousness: but a false witness deceit." [17]

The tongue often reveals what is in the heart. He who speaks the truth bears witness to the righteousness or justice that is established in his heart. But he who speaks falsehood reveals the crookedness and deceit that are in his heart.

* "Abba Pishoy the deacon said: I once said to our two Roman fathers (Maximus and Domadius): 'If you were in Constantinople now, we would surely find you two to be kings now.' They turned their faces toward me and said to me gently: 'Where is your spirit, brother, that you said this word? We have told you several times, brother Pishoy, that whether you are sitting with us or in your dwelling, you must always hold fast, without ceasing, to the saving name of our Lord Jesus Christ, for in truth, if this most holy name were in your heart, you would not have said this word that you have just uttered. For if we neglect this most holy name, we shall surely die in our sins. Let us hate freedom (in speech), joking and vain words, which scatter all the fruit of the monk. When we were in Syria, people tried to make us happy without letting us think about our sins; but exile and silence, with understanding and the endurance of hardships, these are the characteristics of our race. For hardship begets prayer in purity, and prayer begets the fear of God and love, and this is what makes the man; for surely neither rank nor wealth nor courage is honored before God, but the holy soul that seeks Him and His sacrifice and offering; this is our salvation."
The Paradise of the Fathers * Do not allow the spirit of lying to be found in you, lest the Lord deliver you to destruction.

entries.section: 12. The tongue of the wise and the tongue of fools!

paragraphs.text: St. Abba Paula of Tamouh "There is that speaketh like the piercings of a sword: but the tongue of the wise is health." [18]

He who pours out wounding or even gentle words, under the guise of joking and merriment, is pouring out poisons, and is like one who stabs others with a sword, as he stabs himself. But earnest words that have the touch of the quiet Spirit heal wounds and support others, and also build up his own soul.
* Familiarity, joking and laughter are like a fire that is kindled in a reed and destroys.

Abba Agathon * Because we do not guard ourselves against small slips, we fall into great ones. For example, a man's laughing at a time when it is not the time for laughter draws another into laughter, and then he says: What harm is there in laughing? Then the fear of God begins to be uprooted from him; then from laughter comes joking, and from joking foul speech, and from this come blameworthy deeds. Thus the deceiving enemy makes small slips easy for us, and from them draws us into great sins, and from there leads us to despair. By this gradual progress he draws us into matters in a hidden manner. We must therefore drive away his thoughts from their very beginning, and not be careless about small things, for the enemy lies in wait in them to drag us into great ones. For if he fought us openly, his fighting would be easy for us and his defeat within our reach; but he sets for us ambushes and snares from which we cannot quickly free ourselves.

entries.section: 12. The tongue of the wise and the tongue of fools!

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom "The lip of truth shall be established for ever: but a lying tongue is but for a moment." [19]

He who speaks the truth abides in God, the Truth, and his words become immortal, accompanying him to eternity as a secret of his glory. But the lying tongue clings to the devil, the liar and father of liars, and in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, its lie and deceit are exposed, and its plans are destroyed as its life is destroyed.

entries.section: 12. The tongue of the wise and the tongue of fools!

paragraphs.text: "Deceit is in the heart of them that imagine evil: but to the counsellors of peace is joy." [20]

What a man utters returns to him and works upon his depths more than its effect on others. He who speaks evil reaps in his heart and mind deceit and evil, and he who offers counsel of peace enjoys inner joy in his depths.

entries.section: 12. The tongue of the wise and the tongue of fools!

paragraphs.text: There shall no evil happen to the just: but the wicked shall be filled with mischief." [21]

The wicked exert every effort to trouble the righteous and to inflict harm on him, but their evils return upon them and do the righteous no harm. And the righteous exerts every effort to do good to others, and the first to benefit from these good things is the righteous himself.

entries.section: 12. The tongue of the wise and the tongue of fools!

paragraphs.text: "Lying lips are abomination to the LORD: but they that deal truly are his delight." [22]

Every word we utter, whether for the benefit and good of others or for their harm, God reckons as directed to Himself personally. So He delights in those who speak the truth, and cannot bear lying and deceit.

entries.section: 13. Quietness with knowledge, not ignorance with chatter

paragraphs.text: "A prudent man concealeth knowledge: but the heart of fools proclaimeth foolishness." [v. 23]

The wise man, even if he speaks few words, hides behind them true and honored knowledge; but the fool cries out at the top of his voice, and in chatter reveals the ignorance and folly in his heart. He exposes himself by the multitude of his words.
"The hand of the diligent shall bear rule: but the slothful shall be under tribute." [24]

Many have gifts and abilities, but because they are slack and lazy they gain nothing from their gifts; rather these become a judgment against them, and through their laziness they come into humiliation, like those who are under tribute. For our life on earth is a time for earnest work.

Perhaps the most important of the sins that seem trivial but are destructive is carelessness or laziness, and as St. Cyril the Great says: [Since Paul knows that laziness is the door of destruction, he says: "Woe is unto me, if I preach not" (1 Cor 9:16).]

Let us be sober and watchful, lest our portion be with that woman whom Hermas saw, when he saw the sluggish soul as an old woman, worn out and reclining on a chair, unable to move. When he asked the reason, he was told: [Because your spirit is now an old woman who has lost her strength by reason of your weaknesses and doubts. She has become like old men who have lost hope of renewing their strength, and no longer expect anything except that they will sink into their last sleep. So you have become weak through worldly preoccupations, and have handed your souls over to sluggishness, and have not cast your care upon God (1 Pet 5:7).

* "Wilt thou be made whole?" (Jn 5:6)... The Lord asked (the sick man at Bethesda), not in order to know (whether he wished to be healed), for He had no need of that, but He wanted to show forth the man's perseverance, and that because of it he had left the others and come to Him...
The perseverance of the paralytic is astonishing: for thirty-eight years he had been hoping every year to be healed of his sickness. He continued lying there and did not withdraw from the pool...
Let us be ashamed, beloved, let us be ashamed and sigh over the greatness of our slackness.

For thirty-eight years he waited without obtaining what he longed for, and yet he did not withdraw. He did not fail through any neglect on his part, but through the pressure of others, their violence and their troubles. All this did not make him dull. Whereas we, if we persevere in prayer for ten days for some matter and do not obtain it, our zeal grows slack.
St. John Chrysostom
"Heaviness in the heart of man maketh it stoop: but a good word maketh it glad." [25]
St. Anthony says that just as the body needs its food to sustain and refresh it, so the soul needs joy. But gloom, anxiety and agitation bow the soul down and shatter it.

It is fitting for the believer to rejoice and to make the hearts of others glad with a good word, as the Apostle Paul says: "Comfort the feebleminded" (1 Thess 5:14). And Job says: "How forcible are right words!" (Job 6:25).

entries.section: 16. The two paths of righteousness and evil

paragraphs.text: The righteous guides his companion, but the way of the wicked leads them astray. 27 Slackness catches no game, but the precious wealth of man is diligence. 28 In the way of righteousness is life; and in the pathway thereof there is no death.
"The righteous guides his companion, but the way of the wicked leads them astray." [26]
He who is sincere and pure in heart supports himself as he builds up his brother; but the wicked man tears down his own life and strays from the true way.

entries.section: 16. The two paths of righteousness and evil

paragraphs.text: "Slackness catches no game, but the precious wealth of man is diligence." [27]

He who walks the way of righteousness lives faithful and diligent, while he who walks the way of evil lives slack. The first carries a treasure in his heart, for he is faithful in little, diligent and earnest in his life, and goes from success to success. But the second is lazy, and whatever his possibilities and abilities, he only hunts the wind.

Ruth gleaned the fallen ears all day long until evening (Ruth 2:17), so her story was recorded in the Holy Bible, and she was made worthy to bear Obed, the father of Jesse, the father of David the prophet, from whose seed the Lord Christ came incarnate!
The lazy servant who buried his talent in the earth became worthy of eternal punishment (Mt 25:14-30).

entries.section: 16. The two paths of righteousness and evil

paragraphs.text: "In the way of righteousness is life; and in the pathway thereof there is no death." [28]

The way of righteousness or love shines day by day until the day of the Lord comes, and those who walk in it are made worthy of eternal life. Their bodily death is turned into a passing over to eternity. They sing, saying: "For this God is our God for ever and ever: he will be our guide even unto death" (Ps 48:14).
Truly blessed is the believer who passes through the way of righteousness in the midst of this wicked world, and goes forth with love for all to the city of God, the heavenly Jerusalem.

* That we may not be among the murderers or among the living dead, let us strive to love, not only our friends, but our enemies also. By this we can meet the merciful and compassionate Lord with a simple conscience in keeping with the bond of His pledge.

* The ways of the wicked who think of harm are death (Prov 12:28). "Thou shalt not think harm against thy brother" (Lev 19:18) LXX. And also: [If you see the donkey of one who hates you fallen (in the mire), do not pass by it unless you first lift it up] (cf. Ex 23:5). Everyone must keep in mind that it is not permitted to leave the donkey of his enemy in the mire; how then can a man hate or ignore one created in the image of God? I have noticed in the blessed Job a sincere and perfect love in all faithfulness, even toward his enemies, so that he was able to rejoice and to say to the Lord with a clear conscience: "If I rejoiced at the destruction of him that hated me, or lifted up myself when evil found him, and said in my heart: Well!" (Job 31:29).

* By loving a man who is your enemy you become a friend of God; in truth not only His friend but also His son, as the Lord Himself says: [Love your enemies, do good to them that hate you; this proves that you are the sons of your Father in heaven] (cf. Mt 5:44-45)... Let us strive to act as physicians toward all the wicked. Let us hate their evil deeds, not the people themselves. Let us pray for all the good, that they may always rise to a better life, and for the wicked, that they may quickly enjoy a good life through the medicines of repentance. When we pray for this, He grants it to us also.

* (Stephen) grieved more over their sins than over his wounds. He grieved over their evils more than over his death. He acted rightly; surely there was in their evil conduct what required mourning, while there was nothing in his death to grieve over. Eternal death followed their evil, while life without end followed his death... Would that we loved our brethren in the Church with the same spirit with which Stephen loved his enemies.

Fr. Caesarius, Bishop of Arles * Why should we spend more time in citing the apostolic and evangelical commandments, when the old Law, which is thought to be somewhat lenient, warns against the same thing, when it says: "Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thine heart," and also: "Thou shalt not be wroth against the children of thy people" (Lev 19:17-18). So also it says: [The ways of those who are wroth lead to death] (cf. Prov 12:28). Thus you see that evil is forbidden, not in deed only, but also in the hidden recesses of thought, according to the commandment that calls for the uprooting of evil from the heart, not merely taking vengeance for the wrong done to us, but even thinking about it.
St. John Cassian
Sanctify me, that I may pass over to You
* Who can lead me to You?
Your grace is the guide of my life.
May it extend and work in me with tenderness as with discipline.
* Your Holy Spirit works in my heart as in my mind.
He grants me goodness, so that my depths are filled with love of good for all.
Malice cannot creep into me.
And evil finds no place in me.
* Let me be united with You, and love Your commandment and Your word.
Then my depths will be built upon the rock of Your teachings.
The whirlwinds of the worlds cannot shake me.
The foundations of my soul are not shaken, for they are built upon You, O Rock of ages!
* Your Spirit beautifies my soul and renews it, making of it a beautiful bride, adorned with the fruit of the Spirit.
He makes of it a crowned queen, honored by the heavenly ones.
* Your Spirit sanctifies my thoughts, my words and my deeds, that I may bear witness to Your righteousness and enjoy Your salvation.
He builds a holy temple that death does not destroy, nor time corrupt, but which increases in splendor and glory day by day.
* I have nothing to seek but the divine wisdom.
So I ask You uprightly, that I may pass over to You.
I ask nothing of the world, for You satisfy my whole being!
* Grant me Your love, that I may be tender even toward the dumb animals; even in my contention, let nothing proceed from me but tenderness.
Let violence have no authority over my depths.
Grant me the contention of the gentle dove, not the kisses of the deceiving, ravening wolves.
* My soul groans with love for the sinners.
They set nets for me, and fell into them.
They wanted to snare me, and became the prey of their own evils.
Their plots were turned into a crown of glory for my weakness.
The cup they filled for me, they drank.
And what they sowed, they reaped.
"A wise son heareth his father's instruction: but a scorner heareth not rebuke." [1]

It is fitting for parents to represent the Fatherhood of God and the motherhood of the holy Church, declaring to the child from his birth true and wise love, so that the child grows up in a joyful, heavenly atmosphere and bows in a spirit of obedience, to draw from the wisdom in which his parents live in the Lord. Thus the son, in the spirit of wisdom, accepts the conduct of his parents, full of love even in their firmness and in their discipline of him.

The wise son, in a spirit of need and gratitude, seeks wisdom and help; but the son who does not listen to his parents, in scorn and heedlessness, loses the blessings of wisdom. He walks in arrogance, making light of others, refusing discipline and reproof. In a spirit of self-importance he despises the words of the wise.

* My children, everyone who hears discipline and does not accept it or act on it is losing his own soul, and becomes constantly tormented in soul; his mind is never at rest, and he becomes irritable, sad, gloomy, anxious, grieved and full of thoughts; his soul demands of him to do evil and to speak foul words. For discipline is like the king's highway, on which guards keep watch day and night, so that everyone who walks on it by day or by night is safe! But ignorance, deafness and self-admiration are a rough road that is not traveled, and everyone who walks in it goes astray and grows weary and perhaps perishes, for the haunt of robbers is there! And everyone who walked on the traveled road and happened to stumble in some matter or accident, his excuse was spread out and his remedy at hand; but he who left the king's highway and chose to walk on the rough road has neither excuse nor remedy.
St. Macarius the Great

2 A man eats good from the fruit of his mouth, and the desire of the treacherous is wrong. 3 He that keepeth his mouth keepeth his life: but he that openeth wide his lips shall have destruction. 4 The soul of the sluggard desireth, and hath nothing: but the soul of the diligent shall be made fat. 5 The righteous hates false speech, and the wicked brings shame and disgrace.

The Lord Christ says: "A good man out of the good treasure bringeth forth good things: and an evil man out of the evil treasure bringeth forth evil things. But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment. For by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned" (Mt 12:35-37).
"A man eats good from the fruit of his mouth, and the desire of the treacherous is wrong." [2]

The wise man desires good for all, so his words come from between his lips full of sweetness and tenderness; he eats of them and his soul rejoices. But the wicked man's heart gives forth treachery and deceit, which his words express; he eats of them and his soul hungers all the more for violence and wrong.
In other words, as a man offers his words to others, they become food for him. If he offers his words anointed with grace, he enjoys grace within him; and if he offers evil words, they return to him.
* My son... let your heart be humble, and your mouth always speak the truth.
* Do not slander anyone, lest God hate your prayer. Beware of play and mockery, for it drives the fear of God out of the heart.
St. Abba Anthony the Great * Teach your mouth to say what is in your heart.
St. Abba Poemen "He that keepeth his mouth keepeth his life: but he that openeth wide his lips shall have destruction." [3]
He who guards his mouth guards his life. The spiritually mature man controls his tongue for his edification, and the foolish man destroys himself with his words.

Some see in opening the lips wide, or exaggeratedly, a reference to a man's speaking in a crooked way, where the words carry two meanings, the apparent meaning concealing a hidden meaning that destroys the soul.

And some see that opening the lips wide means not being bound by any set limits for the words one utters, but speaking about everything, at any time and without limit, without balanced thought before speaking.

God gave man two eyes so that he might see, examine and observe closely, and also two ears so that he might hear and listen with long-suffering, but He gave him one tongue so that he might be guarded and brief in his words, especially as the tongue is surrounded by barriers, the lips and the teeth.
* Let your speech be sweet and without loss, for glory and shame come from speech. Love mercy and arm yourself with faith.

* My son, do not make your heart wicked so that it thinks evil, but make it good, and seek goodness and acquire zeal in all good works. Do not raise your voice, and if you go to someone, let the fear of God be in your heart, and guard your mouth that you may return to your place in peace. Do not multiply words before one who is older than you.
St. Abba Anthony the Great "The soul of the sluggard desireth, and hath nothing: but the soul of the diligent shall be made fat." [4]

In spiritual matters as in bodily matters, "if any would not work, neither should he eat" (2 Thess 3:10). He who diligently seeks the truth in the word of God rejoices in the word like one who finds spoil. As the psalmist says: "I rejoice at thy word, as one that findeth great spoil" (Ps 119:162).
It is fitting for us to work diligently: "Consider your ways" (Hag 1:6).
"Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men (Prov 22:29).
"Strive to enter in at the strait gate" (Lk 13:24).
"Wherefore the rather, brethren, give diligence to make your calling and election sure: for if ye do these things, ye shall never fall" (2 Pet 1:10).
"Be diligent that ye may be found of him in peace, without spot, and blameless" (2 Pet 3:14).
"I write unto you, exhorting you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints" (Jude 1:3).

* My son... think on the works of God and do not be lazy, for the prayer of the lazy is vain speech. Strive to keep away from men who lack counsel. If you do virtuous deeds, do not boast and say, I have done them. For if you think that you have done them, you are not wise. It is a shame for you to command others with commands you have not carried out in yourself, for you do not profit from another's work. The wise man knows the way of his conduct, so he does not hasten to speak, but considers what he says and what he does.

St. Abba Anthony the Great * Thus I see you both fallen under this weakness of laziness which the Book of Proverbs describes: "The soul of the sluggard desireth, and hath nothing," and also "The desire of the slothful killeth him" (Prov 13:4; 21:25). For it is not fitting for us to be at ease concerning our temporal needs so long as these needs are necessary and proportionate to our calling. If we think that we can acquire for ourselves great gain from those delights that spring from bodily feelings, shall we not strip from ourselves the consolation of our relatives? Does the saying of our Savior not restrain us, which removes us from all that is attributed to the needs of the body, saying: "If any man come to me, and hate not his father, and mother, and wife, and children, and brethren, and sisters... he cannot be my disciple" (Lk 14:26)?

Abba Abraham * Solomon, the wisest of men, points to this vice in many of his writings when he says: "He that followeth after vain persons shall have poverty enough" (Prov 28:19), either openly or in secret, for the slack man cannot but become entangled. And whoever is pursued by shortcomings never discerns the divine contemplations or the spiritual treasures, to which the blessed Apostle points when he says: "That in every thing ye are enriched by him, in all utterance, and in all knowledge" (1 Cor 1:5).

As for this poverty that befalls the lazy man, that is, the weary one, he also writes: "The sluggard shall be clothed with rags" (Prov 23:21). Surely he does not deserve to be adorned with that garment which no misfortune or corruption will touch, of which the Apostle says: "Put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ" (Rom 13:14), and also: "Putting on the breastplate of faith and love" (1 Thess 5:8), and of which the Lord Himself spoke to Jerusalem by the mouth of the prophet, saying: "Awake, awake; put on thy strength, O Zion" (Isa 51:1).

Anyone overcome by the sleep of slackness or weariness prefers to be clothed not with his work and toil, but with the rags of laziness, quoting (and misusing) phrases from the firm Holy Scripture, without clothing his laziness in a garment of glory and honor, but in a robe of shame and the seeking of excuses. Those are the ones who prefer this laziness and do not wish to support themselves by the labor of their hands, as the Apostle always did and charged us to do, saying that it is written: "Labour not for the meat which perisheth, but for that meat which endureth unto everlasting life" (Jn 6:27), and also: "My meat is to do the will of my Father" (Jn 4:34). But these proofs are rags torn from the firm and solid garment of the Gospel, taken for this purpose, I mean to cover the scandal of our laziness and our shame, instead of providing us with warmth and our being adorned with the splendid and costly garment of virtue; for it is said that the woman mentioned in the Book of Proverbs, who was wrapped in strength and splendor, made garments either for herself or for her husband, so that it is said of her at all times: "Strength and honour are her clothing; and she shall rejoice in time to come" (Prov 31:25).

Solomon returns once more to mention the plague of laziness, saying: "The way of the sluggard is strewn with thorns" (Prov 15:29), that is, strewn with these and other similar defects which the Apostle said earlier spring from idleness. Likewise he says: "The soul of the sluggard desireth, and hath nothing" (Prov 13:4), and the Apostle points to this desiring when he says: "And that ye may have need of no man" (1 Thess 4:12). Finally the Apostle enumerated those plagues which the wise Solomon said are the planting of idleness and weariness, in the passage just mentioned, by saying: "Working not at all, but are busybodies" (1 Thess 4:11). And he adds to this plague another, saying: "And that ye study to be quiet," then "to do your own business, and to work with your own hands, and to walk honestly toward them that are without, and that ye may have need of no man" (1 Thess 4:11).

As for those who walk disorderly and do not obey the commandments, the Apostle charges the earnest children of obedience to withdraw from them, saying: "Withdraw yourselves from every brother that walketh disorderly, and not after the tradition which he received of us" (2 Thess 3:6).
St. John Cassian "A righteous man hateth lying: but the wicked brings shame and disgrace." [5]

The heart committed to the truth becomes a source of practical righteousness in Christ Jesus. It becomes a throne for the Holy One, and hates vain abominations and lying. It finds its happiness in fellowship with God and in glorifying His holy name in the midst of this wicked world that resists the truth. But the wicked man corrupts his depths by his sin, to carry within him the smell of death and stench. He becomes naked in this world, and is cast into outer darkness on the great day of the Lord.
The man of God not only avoids lying, but hates it and cannot bear it.
Beware of lying, for it drives the fear of God out of a man.

St. Abba Anthony the Great * Let us refuse the honor and dignities of the world that we may be rid of vainglory, and let us use the tongue in remembering God and the truth that we may be rid of lying.
St. Moses the Black

6 Righteousness keepeth him that is upright in the way: but wickedness overthroweth the sinner. 7 There is that maketh himself rich, yet hath nothing: there is that maketh himself poor, yet hath great riches. 8 The ransom of a man's life are his riches: but the poor heareth not rebuke.
"Righteousness keepeth him that is upright in the way: but wickedness overthroweth the sinner." [6]

Whoever earnestly desires to walk uprightly in the righteousness of Christ, righteousness keeps him from grave errors, keeps him perfect in the eyes of God, that he may receive fellowship in eternal glory. But as for him who is set on evil, his destruction comes to him from within, from evil, the giver of corruption.
"There is that maketh himself rich, yet hath nothing: there is that maketh himself poor, yet hath great riches." [7]

Some pretend to be rich while inwardly they are poor. This is the sin of vainglory and the love of greatness with hypocrisy. Yet there are those who are rich in their depths, overflowing with good things, and in humility consider themselves poor, in need of God's continual grace and the prayers of others. The rich Apostle Paul says: "As poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things" (2 Cor 10:6), while the Lord rebukes the angel of the church of the Laodiceans, saying: "Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked" (Rev 3:16-17).
This is the work of the nature of the old man which we inherited from our father Adam: with our inner poverty we pretend to be rich!
* The sickness of the rich man is dangerous pride.
The truly great spirit in the midst of wealth does not prostrate itself and fall into this sickness.
The spirit is greater than its wealth and rises above it, not by desiring it, but by despising it.
