Then his mind was opened and he heard a great voice saying to him: These are the souls of the righteous that you saw flying; they passed over into Paradise and were saved, and that tall being is the enemy who envies the faithful, and those whom he seized and prevented from passing over are his followers who followed the lusts of the flesh, so they sank into hell, and this is their judgment. But those whom he was unable to seize as they passed upward are those who did not submit to him.]
When he saw this, and whenever he remembered it, he grew in striving every day to press on toward what was before.

The saint did not want to speak about these visions, but when he spent a long time in prayer, marveling and perplexed, and those who were with him pressed him with questions, he was compelled to speak, as a father who cannot hide anything from his children, and he believed that, as long as his conscience was pure, explaining these matters would benefit them, so that they might know that asceticism had brought forth good fruits, and that visions are often a consolation for their labors.
The Garden of the Monks
20 The poor is hated even of his own neighbour: but the rich hath many friends. 21 He that despiseth his neighbour sinneth: but he that hath mercy on the poor, happy is he.
"The poor is hated even of his own neighbour: but the rich hath many friends" [20].

Since corruption has come upon man, his standards have become material: he hates the poor merely because of his poverty, even if he is his neighbor, and he flatters the rich and loves him for no reason except his wealth. For this reason the divine commandment came to defend the wronged poor, and forbids partiality toward the rich.
"Thou shalt not wrest the judgment of thy poor in his cause" (Ex 23:6).

"If there be among you a poor man of one of thy brethren within any of thy gates in thy land which the LORD thy God giveth thee, thou shalt not harden thine heart, nor shut thine hand from thy poor brother" (Deut 15:7).
"Thou shalt not oppress an hired servant that is poor and needy, whether he be of thy brethren, or of thy strangers that are in thy land within thy gates" (Deut 24:14).

"He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth up the beggar from the dunghill, to set them among princes, and to make them inherit the throne of glory: for the pillars of the earth are the LORD'S, and he hath set the world upon them" (1 Sam 2:8).
"For he shall deliver the needy when he crieth; the poor also, and him that hath no helper" (Ps 72:12).
"Deliver the poor and needy: rid them out of the hand of the wicked" (Ps 82:4).
"Better is the poor that walketh in his uprightness, than he that is perverse in his ways, though he be rich" (Prov 28:6).
"The poor is honored for his work, and the rich is honored for his riches" (Sir 10:33).
"The supplication of the poor reaches the ears of the Lord, and his judgment comes speedily" (Sir 21:6).
"He does not show partiality in judging the poor, but hears the prayer of the wronged" (Sir 35:16).
"And oppress not the widow, nor the fatherless, the stranger, nor the poor; and let none of you imagine evil against his brother in your heart" (Zech 7:10).

"My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons. For if there come unto your assembly a man with a gold ring, in goodly apparel, and there come in also a poor man in vile raiment; and ye have respect to him that weareth the gay clothing, and say unto him, Sit thou here in a good place; and say to the poor, Stand thou there, or sit here under my footstool: are ye not then partial in yourselves, and are become judges of evil thoughts? Hearken, my beloved brethren, Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom which he hath promised to them that love him? But ye have despised the poor. Do not rich men oppress you, and draw you before the judgment seats?" (Jas 2:1-6).

* What benefit comes to you from honoring (showing partiality to) the rich man? Is it because he is better prepared to keep the love of others for him? We do a kindness to those from whom we expect that they will repay us for it. We must think rather of the weak and the needy, because it is on account of these that we hope for the reward from the Lord Jesus, who in the example of the wedding feast (Lk 14:12-13) gave us a general picture of virtue. For He asked us to offer our works rather to those who are not able to repay them to us.
St. Ambrose * All are equal before God; rather the rank of each one is exalted according to his faith, not according to his wealth.
St. Augustine * Many rebuke me, saying: You are always pressing hard on the rich, and they, in turn, press hard on the poor.

Well, I do press hard on the rich, or rather not on the rich, but on those who misuse their wealth. I am not attacking their persons but their greed. To be rich is one thing, and greed is another; to have a surplus is one thing, and covetousness is another.
Are you rich? I do not forbid you this. Be rich. Are you greedy? I threaten you... I will not keep silent.

Do you attack me because of this? I am ready for my blood to be shed, but I want to keep you from sinning. I do not hold hatred toward you, nor do I wage war against you; I want only one thing, the benefit of those who listen to me.

The rich are my children, and the poor too are my children. One womb (Baptism) bore them in great travail. All of them are the offspring of her who bore them in travail. If you heap insults on the poor man, I threaten you, because in this case the poor man suffers no loss such as yours. For he does not fall into error, and the loss that befalls him is merely the loss of money, whereas you, as a rich man, suffer loss in your soul.

St. John Chrysostom * It is said that the governor once wished to see Abba Pimen, but the elder refused, so the governor seized his sister's son and imprisoned him as an evildoer, saying: If the elder comes and asks me about him, I will release him. His sister came to him and knocked at his door weeping, but he did not answer her at all. She reproached him, saying: O hard of heart, O iron of bowels, have mercy on me, for he is my only son and I have no one else! He said to her: Pimen has not begotten children, and she went away. The governor heard of this and said: Even if he asks me by writing, I will release him. But Father Pimen sent to the governor, saying: Examine the young man's case according to the law; if he deserves punishment, let him be punished, and if not, do as you see fit. The governor marveled at his virtue and released the young man.

* It once happened that the governor seized a man from Abba Pimen's native town, and many went to the elder begging him to intercede for his release. He said to them: Leave me three days, and then I will go. Then the saint prayed to the Lord, saying: Do not give me, O Lord, this grace (before the governor), or else they will not let me stay in this place. Then the elder went to intercede with the governor, who answered him: Do you intercede, Father, for a thief? And the elder rejoiced because he had not been granted this grace.

The Paradise of the Fathers St. John Chrysostom says: [He who is not rich in himself cannot be rich, just as he cannot be poor who is not poor in his mind. For if the soul is higher than the body, the less exalted members have no authority by which to influence even themselves, but that which is higher influences them and changes them], as he also says: [Wealth is of no benefit if the soul is poor, and poverty does no harm if the soul is rich.]

St. Cyril the Great comments on the two women grinding at the mill, one of whom is taken and the other left, saying: [It seems that these two women refer to those who live in poverty and hardship, for even among these there is a great difference. Some of them bear poverty with maturity and strength in a virtuous life, while the others have different characters, walking with cunning in a wicked and base life.]
"He that despiseth his neighbour sinneth: but he that hath mercy on the poor, happy is he" [21]

He who despises his brother in pride sins, but he who has mercy on the poor man, since he expects no reward from him, receives a share in the blessed life, because he imitates the merciful God, the God of the poor, of the outcast, of the despised, and of those who have no one to ask after them.
* If the Kingdom of God belongs to the poor, who is richer than they?
St. Ambrose
"Do they not err that devise evil?!
But mercy and truth shall guide them that devise good" [22]
Those who are skilled in evil miss the way, but mercy and truth lead those who care for good in the royal road.
* Nothing makes us equal to God except doing good (mercy).

* Let us bring ourselves, our children and all who are ours to the school of mercy, and let man learn it above all things, for mercy is man... Let us count ourselves as those who are not alive if we do not yet show mercy!

* Love (mercy) is, as it were, the highest of crafts, and a protector of those who practice it. It is dear to God, always standing beside Him and asking Him on behalf of those who desire it, if we practice it in a way that is not sinful...!
It intercedes even for those who hate! Great is its authority even for those who sin!
It looses the chains, dispels the darkness, quenches the fire, kills the worm, and removes the gnashing of teeth.
Before it the gates of heaven open with great assurance, and it enters like a queen, and none of the doorkeepers at the gates dares to ask her who she is, but all receive her at once.
Such also is the case of mercy, for she is truly a real queen, who makes men like God. She is winged and light, with golden wings on which she flies, and by them she greatly delights the angels.
St. John Chrysostom
"In all labour there is profit: but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury" [23]
God does not forget the labor of love, and He does not deprive a man of the fruit of his striving, but he who speaks and does not work walks in the way of poverty and receives nothing.
* To know what is good is not enough for attaining blessedness, if one does not put the good into practice by action! Godliness is the practical beginning of knowledge.

St. Didymus the Blind * Godliness is the beginning (of discernment). It acts as a fountain and source for the perception of divine things according to our inner man, so that we may see the true light, hear the secret divine revelation, be refreshed with the bread of life, receive the fragrance of Christ, and learn the manner of this life. When we have godliness, our senses ally themselves with us, so that our eyes do not see evil and our tongue does not utter it.

St. John Chrysostom * The wisest of men, that is, Solomon, tells you: "Give strong drink unto him that is ready to perish, and wine unto those that be of heavy hearts. Let him drink, and forget his poverty, and remember his toil no more" (Prov 31:6-7). That is, those who have come into the distress of grief and sorrow because of their past deeds, support them abundantly with the joys of spiritual knowledge, like "wine that maketh glad the heart of man, to make his face shine more than oil, and bread which strengtheneth man's heart" (Ps 104:15). These he restores by the strong drink of the word of salvation, lest they be drowned in continual sorrow and fall into the despair that leads to death, lest they be "swallowed up with overmuch sorrow" (2 Cor 2:7). But those who are still in coldness and indifference, not stricken with sorrow of heart, of these we read: "The talk of the lips tendeth only to penury" (Prov 14:23).

Thus we avoid with all possible care being puffed up with vainglory, and in this way we become partakers with the one whom the prophet praises, saying: "He putteth not out his silver to usury" (Ps 15:5). For everyone who distributes the words of God out of love for the praise of men... is like one who gives out his money at usury, and deserves not only to go unrewarded but to receive severe punishment.

Father Nestor * Our Lord Jesus Christ says: "Worthy of his meat" - not everyone at all, however it may be, but the worker only (Mt 10:10), and the Apostle Paul commands that we labor and work with our hands the thing which is good, that we may have something to share with him that needeth (Eph 4:28). It is clear from this that we must work diligently, for it is not permissible for us to make worship a pretext for idleness and for fleeing from responsibility. Rather, we must make it a subject of striving and of great labors, and of patience in hardships, so that it may be given to us also to say: "In weariness and painfulness, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst" (2 Cor 11:27). Such a course profits not only for mortifying the body, but also for practicing love of neighbor, that we may support the needy brethren and provide them with what suffices by the work of our hands, according to what the Apostle taught in the Book of Acts, saying: "I have shewed you all things, how that so labouring (with your hands) ye ought to support the weak" (Acts 20:35). And also: "But rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth" (Eph 4:28). And so you will deserve to hear His saying: "Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world: for I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink..." (Mt 25:34).

And I have no need to describe to you the gravity of the evil of idleness, when the Apostle commanded plainly: "If any would not work, neither should he eat" (2 Thess 3:10). For just as daily bread is necessary for every man, so also toil according to his ability is necessary for him.

Solomon did not write in vain in praise of the diligent woman: "She eateth not the bread of idleness" (Prov 31:27). And the Apostle also says of himself: "Neither did we eat any man's bread for nought; but wrought with labour and travail night and day, that we might not be chargeable to any of you" (2 Thess 3:8), although he had the authority, as a preacher of the Gospel, to live of the Gospel (1 Cor 9:4, 14).

The Lord joins laziness with wickedness, saying: "Thou wicked and slothful servant" (Mt 25:26). Moreover, Solomon the Wise not only praised the worker in the way we have mentioned (Prov 31:27), but also rebuked the sluggard, comparing him to the lowest of animals, saying: "Go to the ant, thou sluggard" (Prov 6:6). Therefore we must fear lest we too be rebuked on the day of judgment, for He who gave us the ability to work asks of us works that suit this ability. For He said: "To whom men have committed much, of him they will ask the more" (Lk 12:48).

And since some shrink from work on the pretext of devoting themselves to prayers and the chanting of psalms, such men should know that everything has its own time, as the Preacher said: for every matter there is a season (Eccl 3:1).

We must work as far as possible in order to share resources with those who lack them... There is no excuse for the lazy man who lives in idleness while he is able to work. Let him imitate those fish that cross the seas in a wonderful way in search of food.
St. Basil the Great
"The crown of the wise is their riches.
The progress of fools is folly" [24]
The wise man is honored with the crown of the wealth of true knowledge, which cannot be taken from him, but the fool increases in folly and loses all honor.
"A true witness delivereth souls: but he that speaketh lies is deceit" [25]

Holy Scripture, in both its Testaments, gave special importance to testimony, so it is not fitting for the believer to utter false testimony, but he bears witness to the truth. On the one hand, as a child of God and His ambassador, he is bound to the truth and hates lying. Moreover, true testimony rescues the innocent who are wrongly accused, whereas false testimony may lead to the killing of the innocent.
The wicked Jezebel used two false witnesses against Naboth the Jezreelite in order to kill him and inherit his vineyard adjoining the royal palace (1 Kgs 21).
26 In the fear of the LORD is strong confidence: and his children shall have a place of refuge. 27 The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life, to depart from the snares of death.
"In the fear of the LORD is strong confidence: and his children shall have a place of refuge" [26]

The Book of Proverbs as a whole carries a hidden thread, namely that the believer needs the Spirit of God, the Holy One, who gives him the fear of the Lord, so that he practices a life of godliness and enjoys great confidence in God, the guide of his life, and finds in Him a refuge from all the attacks of the evil enemy, the lusts of the flesh and the love of the wicked world.

Whoever holds fast to the divine fear is fortified by it, he and his offspring after him, for whoever is faithful to the Lord enjoys God's surpassing care. The fear of the Lord is the steering wheel of the soul, given to us by the Holy Spirit of God, who alone is able to bring us in from glory to glory, and to grant us grace upon grace, through our fellowship with the Lord of glory, the holy Jesus. The fear of the Lord brings us into the royal road, so that we turn aside neither toward sin nor toward self-righteousness. It keeps us from blows on the left and on the right, until we enter into the bosom of the holy heavenly Father.

* The fear of the Lord urges the soul to keep the commandments, and through keeping the commandments the house of the soul is built up... May we fear the Lord and build houses for ourselves, so that we may find shelter in winter, when there is rain and thunder, for whoever has no house suffers great dangers in the time of winter.

Father Dorotheus * The fear of the Lord contains all those requirements (for continual joy). For the man who fears the Lord as he ought and trusts in Him gathers all the sources of happiness and acquires the perfect fountain of delight. Just as a drop of water falling into a wide ocean quickly disappears, so whatever befalls the man who fears the Lord is dissolved and vanishes in the immense ocean of joy.

It is truly a most wonderful thing that, even when there is something that causes grief, you find the man rejoicing. For since there is nothing that brings sorrow, this matter is worth nothing to him compared with his enjoyment of constant joy.

St. John Chrysostom * When you fear the punishment that threatens, you learn to love the reward that is promised. Thus, through the fear of punishment you are careful to walk in the good life, and by walking in the good life you seek a good conscience, until finally, with a good conscience, you no longer fear any punishment. Therefore, if you wish not to fear, learn to fear.

St. Augustine * Fear the Lord and keep His commandments. For by keeping the commandments of God you become strong in every work, and your works become higher than all criticism. Fear the Lord, and then you will do something good.
Hermas The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life, to depart from the snares of death [27]

* Whoever acquires the Lord's fear enjoys the indwelling of the Lord in him, and so he bears a fountain of life overflowing in his depths, which waters many, and his soul is delivered from the snares of death that the enemy sets for it.

* Fear the Lord, and keep His commandments, which strengthen you in all your affairs, so that your works have no equal... Do not fear Satan if you fear the Lord, for your fear of God gives you authority over Satan.
Hermas * He who fears the Lord withdraws from error and directs his ways toward virtue. Unless a man fears the Lord, he cannot renounce sin.
St. Ambrose
"In the multitude of people is the king's honour: but in the want of people is the destruction of the prince" [28]

If a man occupies a position of spiritual, civil or military leadership... let him not be puffed up or proud, for a king is not counted a king without a people, and a prince has no honor without the people around him. The successful leader is the one who wins the crowds by his practical love, his service to them and his humility before them, and so receives honor and glory.

St. John Chrysostom used to say to the priest: "You are the father of all mankind," for his priesthood and his leadership lie in the breadth of his heart toward all mankind. He also required of bishops that they not boast of their positions, for the bishop has no existence as a bishop without the people; his honor lies in the honor of his people.
"He that is slow to wrath is of great understanding: but he that is hasty of spirit exalteth folly" [29]

* If anger dims the eyes, or causes a man to lose his inner sight, then the one who is slow to anger enjoys understanding and perceives the truth, whereas the one who is hasty in his anger increases in folly and ignorance.

* Do you not see the wrestlers, how they train when they fill bags with sand? But you have no need to practice this, for life is full of things that make you train and become strong... For it has been said: "He who is longsuffering abounds in wisdom, but he who is short of spirit is utterly foolish."

St. John Chrysostom * Since everyone knows that "patience" takes its name from suffering and endurance, it is clear by this that no one can be called patient except the one who bears everything that befalls him of troubles without being vexed. Thus Solomon did not praise such a man without reason, when he says: "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city" (Prov 32:16). And also "He that is slow to wrath is of great understanding: but he that is hasty of spirit exalteth folly" (Prov 14:29).

If a man is defeated by a fault and the fires of anger are kindled in him, he must not consider that the bitterness of the insult directed at him is the cause of his sin, but rather the appearance of his hidden weakness, according to the parable of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, in which He spoke of the two houses (Mt 7:24, 26). One was founded on the rock and the other on the sand. He said of both that the storms of rain, the floods and the winds beat upon them equally, but the one founded on the rock and the solid ground was not affected at all by the severity of the blow, while the one founded on the soft, shifting sand collapsed and fell at once, and the cause of its fall certainly was not its collision with the storms and floods, but that it had been built unwisely on the sand.
Father Piamoun
"The life of the flesh is a calm heart, but envy is the rottenness of the bones" [30]

* Let the envious know that if this destructive, hidden envy takes hold of them, they destroy everything that is good and upright within them. Therefore it is said in the Scripture: "The life of the flesh is a calm heart, but envy is the rottenness of the bones" (Prov 14:30).
The flesh here signifies weakness and feebleness, and the bones are nothing but valiant, strong deeds...
Well does the Book of Proverbs say that: "The life of the flesh is a calm heart."

For when we preserve the innocence of the mind, even deeds that seem feeble outwardly are sometimes strengthened. Therefore the book rightly adds: "and envy is the rottenness of the bones." The vice of envy makes deeds that seem impressive in the eyes of men to be as nothing in the eyes of God. The rottenness of the bones that envy causes means that some things, although they seem impressive and effective, end in nothing.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* In all our conduct we need to be free from hidden rancor; this applies even more in the choice of a bishop, whose life is a model for the whole flock. Calm and sober judgment are called for, if you prefer that the one who is above all be chosen by all and heal every dispute. "The meek man is the physician of the heart." The Lord declares in the Gospel that He is the physician of the heart, when He says: "They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick" (Mt 9:12; Mk 2:17; Lk 5:31).
St. Ambrose
"He that oppresseth the poor reproacheth his Maker: but he that hath mercy on the needy honoureth him" [31]

* "He who slanders the poor reproacheth his Maker." Here there are two sins: slander and opposition to the poor man. Why does he reproach his Maker? Surely because He created him, and made him as though he could easily fall under the tongue of the slanderer. "He who truly honors God has mercy on the needy."
If God created the poor man, why is it necessary to show compassion to him?

I have heard many say: Is there any need to show compassion to this poor man, whom God could have kept from being poor if He loved him? How long shall we make sport of our salvation? How long shall we laugh at matters that should make the wicked man, burdened with them, tremble and fear and be terrified? Tell me, who did a kindness to whom: Lazarus or the rich man? This is what truly destroys us, that we slip easily into (wicked) jesting.
St. John Chrysostom
"The wicked is driven away in his wickedness: but the righteous is confident in his death" [32]

In the moments of death the wicked man departs accompanied by the evils he committed, which condemn and reproach him. And the righteous man departs accompanied by his faith, his love and his godliness in the Lord, so he does not fear death, nor is he confused at the meeting with the Judge.

In bitterness Balaam spoke, wishing that he had walked in the spirit of godliness and so departed with the righteous to eternal life: "Let my soul die the death of the righteous, and let my last end be like theirs" (Num 23:10). But Stephen, in the moments of his death, said: "Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of man standing on the right hand of God" (Acts 7:56).
* Death, for those who understand it, is immortality, but for the foolish who do not understand it, it is death.
We must not fear this death, but fear the perishing of the soul, which is ignorance of God. This is what truly terrifies the soul!

* It is impossible for us to flee from death by any means. And since the truly wise know this, they practice the virtues and think of the love of God, and face death without sighs or fear or tears, considering that death is, on the one hand, inevitable, and on the other hand, that it frees us from the diseases to which we are subject in this life.
St. Abba Anthony the Great

entries.section: 25. Nothing hidden that will not be made known

paragraphs.text: "Wisdom resteth in the heart of him that hath understanding: but that which is in the midst of fools is made known" [33]

Wisdom shines forth in the heart of the man of understanding who has the spirit of discernment, and becomes the cause of his inner glory. But the fool reveals by his evil conduct the folly that has reigned in his depths and that he tries to hide.
"Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people" [34]

History bears witness throughout all ages that nations, like individuals, are exalted by righteousness and shattered by the corruption of evil. Even if nations often exalt themselves in their military capabilities, history still bears witness to the power of righteousness and its ability.
What righteousness is is not written in the letters of the Law (that is, the Holy Scripture), but a pure heart is man's righteousness.
St. Abba Anthony the Great
"The king's favour is toward a wise servant: but his wrath is against him that causeth shame" [35]

If kings and rulers look for their ambassadors to be men of wisdom and knowledge, then the King of kings presents the Second Hypostasis, the Wisdom of God, to raise up from the believers wise ambassadors who are fit to bear witness to God, His care and His heavenly glories.
Your fear leads me to the treasure of Your wisdom!
* Let Your fear lead the depths of my heart, and make of my soul the wise bride, who builds her house by the Holy Spirit of God, a holy temple for Him.
* Your fear opens for me the royal road.
I walk in You, and do not turn to the right or to the left.
I go forth to You and enjoy fellowship with You forever.
* Your fear sanctifies my words, so that they bear a spirit of love, tenderness and kindness.
You grant me earnestness in work without ceasing.
* I cling to those who fear You, and rejoice in them.
I learn from them, and join them in praising You!
* Your fear makes of my heart a wedding, and my soul is filled with unceasing joy.
I enjoy the inner treasure and am enriched by it.
* Your fear supports the tent of my life, so that storms and whirlwinds do not shatter it.
Rather, You carry me through in glory, until I go forth to the eternal dwelling.
* Your fear grants me the spirit of discernment, so that the way of death does not deceive me.
I seek the inner joy of the Spirit, not laughter filled with frivolity.
With the spirit of discernment I rightly divide the word of truth.
With the spirit of humility I turn away from evil.
With the spirit of love anger does not creep into my heart.
With the spirit of wisdom I enjoy true knowledge, not folly.
With the spirit of truth I show no partiality to the rich, nor do I despise the poor; with the spirit of holiness I bear no false witness, and I utter no word of lying or guile or deceit.
* Your fear is my refuge; in it I am fortified and settled.
In it I enjoy the fountain of life, and I do not fear death.
In it I desire to serve everyone, and I seek the edification of every human soul.
In it I am clothed with Your divine righteousness, and it supports me all the days of my life, until I pass over and go forth to You, to see You face to face, and to live with You forever!
1 A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger. 2 The tongue of the wise useth knowledge aright: but the mouth of fools poureth out foolishness.
"A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger" [1]
Many have turned from friends into enemies for long years because of hurtful words, while some have won their enemies and made them their friends by gentle, tender words.

Under the cover of defending the truth, or under the cover of frankness and love, we often wound the feelings of our brethren with harsh and violent words. In the Lord Christ's rebuke of the sinful woman He said: "Hath no man condemned thee?... Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more" (Jn 8:10-11). And in His dialogue with the Samaritan woman, He gently asked her to give Him to drink, as one in need of her (Jn 4:7), and when she answered Him: "How is it that thou, being a Jew, askest drink of me, which am a woman of Samaria?" - because the Jews do not deal with the Samaritans - He did not wound her feelings with a single word, although He knew her shameful past and her unseemly present. By His gentleness He won her, and indeed won the whole city of Sychar.

* The mouth of the chaste speaks good things, delights its owner, and gladdens those who hear. Whoever's speech is orderly and chaste, and who is pure in heart, is a son of Christ's inheritance; but whoever's speech is anxious and clouded with anger is a second devil.
* The mouth of the fool overflows with bitterness, kills its owner, and makes drunk those who listen to him.
* He who softens his speech and schemes in order to harm is a second devil.

The Spiritual Elder * Our Lord offered most of His help by persuasion rather than by blame. Gentle rains soften the earth and seep into it completely, while heavy rain makes it hard and ruins the surface of the ground, so that it does not absorb the water. "Grievous words stir up anger" and with it harm occurs. While the harsh word opens the door, anger enters, and on the heels of anger the harm is done.
St. Mar Ephrem the Syrian * He who cannot control his tongue at the time of anger will not be able to overcome even the smallest of the passions.

Father Irais * "Anger destroys even the prudent, and a soft answer turneth away wrath, and a grievous word stirs up anger"; everything depends on your decision, whether to stir up anger or to walk quietly... And if anger destroys even the prudent, how much more does it destroy those of whom it is said that this anger kills the fool? This happens, without doubt, to the prudent because of neglect. But a soft answer turneth away wrath, that is, an answer given with evident humility, without rudeness.
St. John Chrysostom "The tongue of the wise useth knowledge aright: but the mouth of fools poureth out foolishness" [2]

The tongue is the door of the heart, so the wise man brings forth words of knowledge for his own edification and the edification of his brethren, while the fool brings forth words of folly that corrupt his life and the life of his brethren.
The wise man knows what to say, and when, and to what extent; every word has its own weight, and he thinks about it before he utters it.

One of the most wonderful examples is the answer of Gideon, full of wisdom and humility, when the men of Ephraim contended with him sharply because he had not called them when he went to fight the Midianites; he said to them: "What have I done now in comparison of you? Is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the vintage of Abiezer? God hath delivered into your hands the princes of Midian, the raven and the wolf: and what was I able to do in comparison of you?" (Judg 8:2-3). And the writer comments: "Then their anger was abated toward him, when he had said that." On the contrary, when the men of Ephraim took the same attitude toward Jephthah when he fought the children of Ammon, instead of answering in a spirit of humility he rebuked them and entered into war with them, in which forty and two thousand of Ephraim were slain (Judg 12:1-6).

* He who fasts with his mouth from food but does not fast with his heart from rancor and his tongue from vanities, his fast is in vain, for the fast of the tongue is better than the fast of the mouth, and the fast of the heart is better than the fast of the two. The strength of the body is in foods, and the nourishment of the soul is in speech and tales; and just as the greed for many tales is a desire of the soul, so silence is the fruit of impending wisdom. He who removes from his conscience the faults of his neighbor sows peace in his heart. The simple man who is wise toward God is better than the clever man who is deceitful in his conscience. He who has enslaved his belly and his tongue is better than he who has enslaved the lion, and he who has suppressed the word in his heart is better than he who buried his talent in the earth. The man who is stripped of goodness and yet argues about the virtues is no different from the blind man stripped of light who argues about precious stones and the many colors.
St. Isaac the Syrian

entries.section: 2. Concern to please God, not men

paragraphs.text: "The eyes of the LORD are in every place, keeping watch on the evil and the good" [3].

As the wise man invites us to gentle and soft speech so that we may turn away the spirit of anger from him who troubles us, he also declares that our words are the expression of the wisdom and true knowledge in our hearts and thoughts, for what truly concerns us is to please God, not men. With sweet words our depths must be holy, in harmony with the sweetness of the words. For the eyes of the Lord look into our depths.

When Potiphar's wife wanted to draw the young Joseph into sin, he said to her: "How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" (Gen 39:9). In the midst of all the harsh circumstances in which he lived, deprived of his parents and sold as a slave, and with his mistress tempting him, he was aware that the eyes of God were watching him!

Moses the prophet erred when "he looked this way and that way, and when he saw that there was no man, he slew the Egyptian, and hid him in the sand" (Ex 2:12). He did not look up to realize that God saw him! It is fitting for us in all our conduct, even in our worship, to be occupied with God's looking into our hearts and our inner feelings!

* When we gather with the brethren in one place and celebrate the divine sacrifice with the priest of God, we must keep in mind humility and good manners, and not hurl our prayers at random with rude voices nor cast our petitions with violent babbling. Rather, our petition must be offered to God in humility, for God hears our hearts, not our voices.

God, who sees our thoughts, is not reproached by shouts, and as the Lord says: [Why think ye vain things in your hearts?] (cf. Mt 9:4). And in another place He says: [All the churches shall know that I am He who searches the desires and the hearts] (cf. Rev 2:23).
The Martyr Cyprian
"A wholesome (calm, sound, healthy) tongue is a tree of life: but perverseness therein is a crushing of the spirit" [4]

From time to time the wise man returns to speak of the tongue, realizing its gravity, for in its wholesomeness the believer enjoys, as it were, the tree of life, and in its perverseness he loses his life, as his spirit is crushed and murmurs! The tongue can be a blessing that carries a man to the enjoyment of eternal life, and it can be a curse that drives him to eternal punishment.

The sound, healthy tongue is the tongue that makes peace among brethren, while the sick, perverse tongue is the one that makes disputes and divisions among brethren. Abraham says to his nephew Lot: "Let there be no strife... for we be brethren" (Gen 13:8).

* "A wholesome tongue is a tree of life." The tongue that does not sin in speech is marked by health, for the sickness of the tongue is its sin. He who can control his tongue and not sin is filled with the Holy Spirit.

St. John Chrysostom * Be master of your heart and bridle your tongue (Jas 1:26). Take no pleasure in hearing a word against anyone, so that you may have peace with all men, for all the saints of the Lord are in peace, and God dwells in them. As it is written: "Great peace have they which love thy law" (Ps 119:165). Those who love God live in peace with all men.
St. Stephen of Thebes * The monk who does not sin with his tongue is truly a shining star on this earth.
St. Hesychius the Priest
"A fool despiseth his father's instruction: but he that regardeth reproof is prudent" [5]
It is folly for a man to refuse in pride to benefit from the experience of those who have gone before him on the way, whether his parents or his spiritual father.

The man who is careful about the salvation of his soul accepts the rebuke of those who have gone before him and their disciplines, just as he accepts the disciplines of the Lord Himself as his heavenly Father, who cares for the salvation of his soul and for bringing him into the heavenly glories. Accepting discipline willingly is a strong proof of the love of wisdom, and it approves the believer before God.

* True prudence is knowing what you must do and what you must not do. He who acquires it will not hold back from practicing virtuous deeds, and will not be wounded by the deadly arrow of vice. Thus he who understands the words of prudence knows the difference between what is treacherous, built on deceit, and what reminds us of the calm of the better way in which to live our life. This is like the practice of the money-changer, who holds fast what is good and abstains from every appearance of evil (1 Thess 5:21).

Grant such prudence to the builder of his house, so that he lays its foundations on the rock, that is, supports it by faith in Christ, and so is not shaken when the winds, the rains and the storms assail it (Mt 7:25). For through this parable the Lord teaches us to remain steadfast when trials blow, whether their source is human or beyond nature. Besides this, He teaches us not to be ignorant of the necessary things, but to provide ourselves with them for the journey of life, and so to await the coming of the Bridegroom with zealous hearts.

Prudence is the quality by which all things are accomplished through skillful perseverance, and in the same way cunning is the quality by which evil is committed. For prudence can be added to every activity, and even evils can happen in all matters; therefore the name of prudence denotes two realities (the one who uses reason for good or for evil).
Thus he who uses intelligence and skill for the ruin of others is wicked, while he who acts with uprightness and wisdom reveals his goodness; this one acquires the prudence worthy of praise.

Listen diligently to the voice of the prudent soul, and you will know that it contains a center in which sound counsel is given for its own benefit and for the benefit of its neighbor, and is worthy of praise. But the prudence that is used to harm one's neighbor deserves condemnation.

St. Basil the Great * If we sin, God may raise up our enemies against us to discipline us, and accordingly we must not fight them, but call ourselves to account and educate ourselves. And as long as He has let them loose on us because of our sins, then if we fight them He gives them victory over us, and for this reason He commanded us not to take vengeance on our enemies. Let us accept trials as we accept medicines from the physician so that we may be saved, and as we accept discipline from the father so that we may be refined. Therefore the wise man said: "My son, if thou come to serve the Lord God, stand fast in righteousness and godliness, and prepare thy soul for temptation" (Sir 2:1).

St. John Chrysostom * He who quibbles against discipline drives away from himself the fatherly mercies. He who murmurs against trials has them multiplied upon him. He who is not disciplined here and broken by trials is tormented there without mercy.
St. Mar Isaac the Syrian
6 In the house of the righteous is much treasure: but in the revenues of the wicked is trouble. 7 The lips of the wise disperse knowledge: but the heart of the foolish doeth not so.
"In the house of the righteous is much treasure: but in the revenues of the wicked is trouble" [6]

The house of the righteous man, which is his heart, holds a precious, inestimable treasure, namely the fruit of the Spirit: joy, love, peace, etc. (Gal 5:22), whereas the revenues of the wicked, or what they gain from their evils, are hatred, anxiety, turmoil, etc. This is the sum of their evils!
The mark of the righteous is inner joy and the peace that passes understanding, and the mark of the wicked is anxiety and inner turmoil.
The treasure of the righteous is the heavenly Bridegroom, Emmanuel, who dwells by faith in our hearts, and the trouble of the wicked is his deprivation of the heavenly Bridegroom.
The righteous enjoy hearts that have been turned into wedding houses for the heavenly Bridegroom, and the hearts of the wicked are turned into a hell in which the evil enemy dwells.

* The letter "Eta" means "El" in the Hebrew language אֵל, which means "God", for the prophet Isaiah said "Emmanuel" (Isa 7:14), and St. Matthew the Evangelist, the preacher of the joy that cannot be uttered, interpreted it by saying: "Emmanu" means "with us", and "El" means "God" (Mt 1:23).
Let us examine ourselves, then, to see whether God is truly with us. If we are far from evils, and strangers to Satan, who is their source, God is truly with us.
If the desire for good works reigns over us and we delight in them, being accustomed to consider our conduct to be in the heavenly places (see Phil 3:20), God is truly with us.
If we regard all men as equal and all days as alike, God is truly with us.

If we love those who hate us, those who insult us, those who are harsh to us, those who despise us, those who mistreat us and those who trouble us, just as we love those who love us, those who praise us, those who do good to us and give us rest, God is truly with us.
And the sign that a man has reached this degree of perfection is his sense that God is always with him - and He is indeed always with him - and his feeling that he has obtained all this.
Let him rejoice in the Lord who has understood this, and who will understand it, and who has hope of understanding it!
"Eta" means "guide," and the guide is the one who leads.
He leads you to the light, so do not seek the darkness.
He leads you to uprightness, so do not seek falsehood.
He leads you to the truth, so that illusion does not deceive you.
He leads you to peace, so do not seek strife.
He leads you to joy, so do not strive for sorrow.
He leads you to humility, so do not yield to pride.
He leads you to justice, so do not look for injustice.
He leads you to help you bear the insults and humiliations directed against you, so do not seek praise and vainglory.
He leads you to mortification, so do not seek ease and comfort.
He leads you to the right side, so do not place yourself among those on the left.
He leads you to eternal life, so do not seek eternal punishment in Gehenna, the fire that is not quenched.

And the sign of a man's rejecting what ought to be rejected is in his choosing good things, and in never making light of the prayers of the day and the night. Let him rejoice in the Lord who has understood this, and who will understand it, and who has hope of understanding it!
St. Barsanuphius "The lips of the wise disperse knowledge: but the heart of the foolish doeth not so" [7]

The lips of the wise declare the true knowledge in their hearts, which builds up souls and spreads blessing upon the hearers. But the wicked fools utter the folly in their hearts, which profits no one if it does not harm them.
In Paphos Paul and Barnabas spoke with the governor, who sought to hear the word of God (Acts 13:7), but Elymas the sorcerer wanted by his words to turn the governor away from the faith (Acts 13:8).

8 The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the LORD: but the prayer of the upright is his delight. 9 The way of the wicked is an abomination unto the LORD: but he loveth him that followeth after righteousness. 10 Correction is grievous unto him that forsaketh the way: and he that hateth reproof shall die. 11 Hell and destruction are before the LORD: how much more then the hearts of the children of men?
"The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the LORD: but the prayer of the upright is his delight" [8]

Since God seeks purity of heart, He accepts the prayer of the righteous and delights in it, and rejects the sacrifices and offerings of the wicked. God has no need of our offerings, our sacrifices and our worship; He seeks our hearts.

* God has no need of sacrifices, as is very clear in the Holy Scriptures. "I said to the Lord: You are my God, You have no need of my goods" (cf. Ps 16:2), for in accepting or rejecting them He looks only to man's good. God gains no benefit from our worship; rather, we are the ones who gain it.

St. Augustine * Cain did not begin his wickedness when he killed his brother. For even before that, God, who knows the heart, did not look upon Cain or upon his sacrifice. His baseness only appeared plainly when he killed Abel.

Origen * First of all, God accepted Abel's offering because of the purity of his heart, and Cain's offering was rejected (Gen 4:4). How do we know that Abel's offering was accepted while Cain's offering was rejected? And how did Abel sense that his offering was accepted? And how was Cain assured that his offering was rejected? I will try, as far as I am able, to explain this.

You know, my dear one, that the sign of an offering accepted by God is the descent of fire from heaven and the burning of the offering. When Abel and Cain offered their offerings together, the living fire that ministers before God (Ps 104:4) came down and consumed Abel's pure sacrifice, while it did not touch Cain's impure sacrifice. So Abel knew that his offering was accepted, and Cain that his offering was rejected. The fruits of Cain's heart were known afterward, when he was tested and his heart was found full of deceit, when he killed his brother; thus what he conceived in his mind his hands brought forth. But the purity of Abel's heart was the foundation of his prayer.
The beloved prayer is the pure prayer, free from all deceit. And prayer is powerful when the power of God works in it.

My dear one, I have written to you that when a man commits himself to fulfilling the will of God, and it is the main axis of his prayer, the man is exalted in his prayer. I have told you this so that you do not neglect prayer.

St. Aphrahat * We can discover many counsels about other matters also, such as prayer. The Scripture says: Good works are a prayer acceptable to the Lord. The way to prayer is described: if you see a naked man, to clothe him, and not to hide yourself from the members of your household. Then your light shall break forth like the morning, and your garments shall shine speedily, your righteousness shall go before you, and the glory of the Lord shall surround you (cf. Isa 58:7-8).
St. Clement of Alexandria "The way of the wicked is an abomination unto the LORD: but he loveth him that followeth after righteousness" [9]

It is God's delight that man enjoy sonship to Him, and walk as a son of God, according to the Spirit and not according to the flesh. "Because the carnal mind is enmity against God... So then they that are in the flesh cannot please God" (Rom 8:7-8). As was said before, the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the Lord, because their hearts are evil and their ways are evil. It is not fitting for the sinner to offer anything to God unless he offers repentance, that is, returns to God with his heart, and his soul bows in obedience to Him, longing to enjoy His face. So when sinners are justified before the Lord through repentance, and find their delight in Him, and seek Him sincerely, He too delights in their ways, their worship and their spiritual sacrifices.

It is as though God seeks man's heart and the renewal of his inner man and his enjoyment of the work of His Holy Spirit, and then he becomes, wholly, the object of God's delight. Thus the believer can chant with sincerity and assurance: "I will go into thy house with burnt offerings: I will pay thee my vows, which my lips have uttered, and my mouth hath spoken, when I was in trouble. I will offer unto thee burnt sacrifices of fatlings, with the incense of rams; I will offer bullocks with goats" (Ps 66:13-15). As he also says: "If I regard iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me: but verily God hath heard me; he hath attended to the voice of my prayer" (Ps 66:18-19).

* It is clear that the sacrifices were not instituted for their own sake, but to suggest the rest of their way of conduct. When they neglected their principal obligations and busied themselves with nothing but sacrifices, God told them that He would no longer accept them (Amos 5:22; Jer 6:20; Mic 6:6-8).

St. John Chrysostom * God Himself says that He requires obedience to His commandments rather than the offering of a sacrifice to Him. God declares this, and Moses declared it to the people of Israel, and Paul preaches it to the Gentiles. Do what you see to be better... "I will have mercy, and not sacrifice" (Mt 9:13).

St. Ambrose * The knowledge of God is better than offering sacrifices and burnt offerings, for it brings us to perfection in Christ. For through Him and in Him we know the Father, and become rich in justification by faith.
St. Cyril the Great "Correction is grievous unto him that forsaketh the way: and he that hateth reproof shall die" [10]

Some translate it: "Discipline (correction) is dangerous for him who leaves the way," like Ahab, who hated whoever gave him honest advice or told him of his error. Ahab said to Jehoshaphat: "There is yet one man, by whom we may enquire of the LORD: but I hate him; for he doth not prophesy good concerning me, but evil. The same is Micaiah the son of Imlah" (1 Kgs 22:8), and also when he met Elijah he said to him: "Hast thou found me, O mine enemy?" (1 Kgs 21:20), as he also said to him: "Art thou he that troubleth Israel?" (1 Kgs 18:17). Such also was the attitude of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, who, when he heard part of what was in the scroll, "cut it with the penknife of the scribe, and cast it into the fire that was in the hearth, until all the roll was consumed in the fire that was on the hearth" (Jer 36:23). Such kings as these cannot bear the word of God, do not receive men of God, and do not value repentance, but hate the word of truth and honest guidance. Since these hate discipline, they die in their sins.
"Hell and destruction are before the LORD: how much more then the hearts of the children of men?" [11]

In verse 3 the wise man says that the eyes of the Lord keep watch on the evil and the good in every place. Here he affirms that God, the true Light, sees everything, even hell and destruction, where the height of the darkness of death and ruin is; they are before Him and not hidden from Him, so would anything that is in the hearts of men be hidden from Him? As the Apostle says: "All things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do" (Heb 4:13).

What seems invisible to many men, such as heaven, Paradise, Gehenna and hades, are realities seen by God, which He presents to His children by His Holy Spirit, so that they do not see them as imagination, as others think, but see them as facts, and long with all their hearts to cross over into Paradise, to enter heaven, and to be saved from the powers of darkness.

The Lord Christ promised us that His Holy Spirit takes of what is His and gives it to us (Jn 16:15), that is, takes of what is visible to Him and declares it to us, so that we even experience the life of Paradise and taste the earnest of the heavenly things, and do not fear hades, for we have no place in it.

* Let us marvel to what height He has lifted the Church! He lifted her as by a certain device and set her on high, and seated her on a lofty throne, for where the Head is, there the body is also. There is no separation between them, otherwise the body would no longer be a body, nor the Head a head.
* It is possible for us - if we wish - not to be in the body, nor on the earth, but to be in the Spirit, in heaven.
Let us enter into our souls... into heaven, in the Spirit!
Let us remain in the peace and grace of God, and be freed from fleshly things, and so enjoy good things in Christ our Lord.

* It is fitting for you, as you go out from this place, to proclaim that it is a holy place. You go out as men coming down from heaven itself, full of dignity and wisdom, speaking and doing everything with propriety...
Teach those outside that you are in the company of the Seraphim.
Teach them that you are numbered with the heavenly beings, counted in the ranks of the angels, speaking with the Lord, and in the company of the Lord Christ.

And as they look at the beauty of your shining souls, their hearts will be kindled by your good appearance, however dull they may be, for if the beauty of the body entices the one who sees it, how much more does the beauty of the soul and its harmony stir those who behold it and draw them to the same zeal?!
* The Church is higher than heaven and wider than the world.
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: 7. The hatred of scorners for him

paragraphs.text: "A scorner loveth not one that reproveth him:
neither will he go unto the wise." [12]

By this proverb he makes clearer still what was stated in (verse 10). The unserious person, the scorner, cares nothing for the things of the world to come, even though they are firm realities seen before the Lord. What occupies him is his pleasures and his honor, so he hates the one who reproves him, and does not wish to sit with the wise and speak with them. He counts their talk about eternity as imagination, a waste of time and a deprivation of pleasures.

13 A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken. 14 The heart of him that hath understanding seeketh knowledge: but the mouth of fools feedeth on foolishness. 15 All the days of the afflicted are evil: but he that is of a merry heart hath a continual feast.
"A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken" [13]
Divine consolations fill the heart of the spiritual man, and reflect on his face a constant cheerfulness, able to face tribulations.

The spiritual man sees his Christ dwelling in his heart, satisfying him, guiding his life and delivering him from tribulations, and even turning sufferings into glories, as they become a fellowship of sufferings with Him.
Nothing breaks a man like hidden inner sorrow, and his failure to realize the truth of the work of the Lord Christ as his Savior from sins and the bearer of his burdens.

* This joy is not separated from sorrow, for rather it clings to us in a deep way. He who grieves over his errors and confesses them rejoices. Instead of sorrow over sins, joy in Christ is realized... Therefore he says: "Rejoice in the Lord" (Phil 4:4). For this (sorrow) becomes as nothing with the acceptance of a life made worthy of joy.

St. John Chrysostom In (the Long Rules), Question 17 concerned laughter, and St. Basil the Great made clear the necessity of distinguishing between corrupting laughter and laughter in the sense of the soul's joy and exultation in God.

* Those who live under discipline (self-control of the soul) must avoid even such an excessive activity with all care, so that it is used lightly. For indulging in laughter in an uncontrolled and exaggerated way is a sign of excess and a lack of control of one's feelings, and a failure to suppress the frivolity of the soul by using reason firmly. It is not unseemly to bear witness to the merriment of the soul with a cheerful smile, if only it illustrates what is written: "A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance" (Prov 15:13). But coarse laughter, without control of the movements of the body, is not an indication of a soul that has a good, moderate management, or of personal dignity, or of one who rules over himself.

This kind of laughter the Preacher condemns especially as destroying the steadiness of the soul, in the words: "I said of laughter, It is error (madness)" (Eccl 2:2). Again: "For as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fool" (Eccl 7:6). Moreover, the Lord shows that He experienced these necessary emotions that belong to the body, as well as those connected with virtue, for example sorrowing with the sorrowful and compassion for them, but as we know from the story of the Gospel, He never laughed. On the contrary, He declared that those who give themselves over to laughter are unhappy (Lk 6:25).
Let us not allow the word (laughter) to deceive us, for it has two meanings.

For the Holy Scriptures often use it of the joy of the Spirit and the gladness of the feelings that follows good works. For example, Sarah says: "God hath made me to laugh" (Gen 21:6). And there is another saying: "Blessed are ye that weep now: for ye shall laugh" (Lk 6:21). In a similar way the words of Job: "Till he fill thy mouth with laughing" (Job 8:21). All these witnesses to gladness point to the merriment of the soul rather than boisterous merriment. Therefore he who is master of every passion and feels no agitation in his pleasure, or at least shows no outward expressions, but tends to restrain firmly every harmful pleasure, such a one is perfectly chaste, and is in the same truth plainly free from every sin...

If a man flees from all the provocations of sin but falls prey to even one of them, such a man is not chaste. Like one who is not sound in health when he suffers from one single illness. And like one who is not considered a free man if he falls under the authority of any person, regardless of who that person is.
St. Basil the Great "The heart of him that hath understanding seeketh knowledge: but the mouth of fools feedeth on foolishness" [14]

The heart of the man of understanding does not exalt itself over his understanding and knowledge, but thirsts for new depths of knowledge, so he remains always looking at himself as one who looks in a mirror, in a riddle, until he meets the Lord Christ - the Wisdom of God - face to face. His thirst for knowledge and his constant hunger for the truth give him humility along with earnestness and a striving to enjoy new heavenly, divine experiences.

But the mouth of fools overflows with the amusement, jesting and indifference to eternity that are in their hearts, so their words come forth as a pasture of folly, satisfying no one's heart and supporting no one.
"All the days of the afflicted are evil: but he that is of a merry heart hath a continual feast" [15]

He who does not experience the sweetness of salvation has sorrow take possession of his heart, and is captive to gloom, so he lives in misery and wretchedness; but he who tastes the sweetness of fellowship with the Lord Christ has his heart turned into a joyful wedding feast. He rejoices and makes his brethren rejoice with him, as the Lord delights in him, and the heavenly hosts exult in his salvation.

* "Rejoice in the Lord alway" (Phil 4:4). This means that the result of unity in understanding and faith is that they rejoice in the Lord, and that each of them is dear to the others. He says: "Rejoice in the Lord" - this is very little - "and again I say, Rejoice." For when you are united together in heart you rejoice in the Lord, and when you rejoice in the Lord you are united in heart and stand in the Lord.
Marius Victorinus
16 Better is little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure and trouble therewith. 17 Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith.
"Better is little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure and trouble therewith" [16]

Here he sets up a contrast between the fear of the Lord and trouble, as though the fear of the Lord were bound up with true inner surrender and reliance on the Almighty and the enjoyment of inner peace. And deprivation of the divine fear makes a man lose his peace, even if he enjoys treasures of such measure.

There is no basis for comparison between Daniel the captive, without resources, and the company of the wise men and sorcerers, counselors of the greatest king of that time. The first acquired the fear of the Lord, so he refused to eat of the king's delicacies offered to the idols, not for the sake of his bodily health (a diet), but for the fear of the Lord, and he became the second man after the greatest king of that age, whereas the wise men were nearly put to death had not the prophet Daniel rescued them by interpreting the king's dream.
"Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith" [17]

* This is a reminder of what we said before, that vegetables are not agape (`agapy`) in themselves, but meals must be practiced with love. The middle way is the good way in everything, and especially at banquets. Excesses are in fact dangerous; humility is good, and whatever avoids pressing need is humble. Natural desires have their limits in inner satisfaction.

St. Clement of Alexandria * "Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith" (Prov 15:17). We often prefer simple, economical hospitality from hosts who receive us with a good conscience - but who have not the means to offer more - to those who, with arrogant words lifted up against the knowledge of God (2 Cor 10:5), seduce us to learn something foreign to the Father of our Lord Jesus (Mt 5:17).

Origen * Be content with what you have, and do not allow your condition to be improved by harming your neighbor. You will find your way of living in the simplicity of innocence. He who has his own goodness knows nothing of laying an ambush for others. He is not inflamed with the desire of the covetous man, who gains his profit at the expense of virtue and out of greed. Therefore he must recognize his blessings, and so the poor man becomes truly happy, since he lives in righteousness in a way better than all the treasures of the world, for "better is little with the fear of the Lord than all great treasures without fear"... May we use our talents to seek grace and obtain salvation, and not to deceive others who have done us no harm at all.

* When someone invites hungry guests to dinner who have a ready appetite for eating, then even if he sets a humble table it appears plentiful in the eyes of the guests, who fall upon the dishes with great desire. In the same way, with regard to your spiritual appetite, do not hold back if we set before you a poor and lowly table, offered in an ordinary way before your goodness.

This is also what a wise man observed when he said: "Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith" (Prov 15:17), suggesting that love gives a different point of view, so that ordinary things appear rich in its eyes, and scraps appear as nobility and generosity.

St. Basil the Great * Good is hospitality with vegetables. I will make clear what (Solomon) says. For the one who fears the Lord and delights in the benefits of men, it is better to have little than to have much. Truly, delight is not in abundance (of goods), but rather abundance is in delight.
St. John Chrysostom
"A wrathful man stirreth up strife: but he that is slow to anger appeaseth strife" [18]

Haste in anger is the natural fruit of pride, for the proud man cannot bear anyone who wounds his feelings with an insult, or with what seems to him a robbing of his rights, so the fires of anger are kindled in him and it is hard for him to quench them, and anger turns into strife and agitation. But the humble man longs to win every soul whatever the cost, and if a quarrel arises he soothes it through gentle speech.

When the anger of King Saul was kindled against David he tried to kill him, and he could not bear his son Jonathan's defense of David, so that he hurled the spear at him to smite him (1 Sam 20:33). Saul was determined to kill David, but when Saul fell into David's hand he did not touch him, but cut off the skirt of Saul's robe, and he could not bear even that, since his heart smote him for it. And gently he called after Saul, and stooped with his face to the earth, and bowed himself (1 Sam 24:8). And he said: "Behold, this day thine eyes have seen how that the LORD had delivered thee today into mine hand in the cave: and some bade me kill thee: but mine eye spared thee; and I said, I will not put forth mine hand against my lord; for he is the LORD'S anointed" (1 Sam 24:10). Saul lifted up his voice and wept, and said to David: "Thou art more righteous than I... the LORD reward thee good for that thou hast done unto me this day."
"The way of the slothful man is as an hedge of thorns: but the way of the upright is a highway" [19]

While the sluggard thinks that he rests by not working, behold, a hedge of thorns grows up within him as well as around him, so he finds no peace in his depths. But he who walks uprightly and diligently, with all the opposition he meets, finds his way made smooth. Troubles are turned to work on his behalf.

The first, with every slackness, finds all matters in his life becoming entangled, so his life becomes a chain of weariness that comes upon him. The second, since he knows the way and perceives his goal in life, goes up from step to step. And if he stumbles on the way, he rises with greater strength in joyful hope.
Since David did not know laziness, he sang, saying: "For by thee I have run through a troop; and by my God have I leaped over a wall" (Ps 18:29).

* When they turn aside from the royal road they are unable to reach the city to which we must come on our journey, and they lose their direction. The Preacher says: "The labour of the foolish wearieth every one of them, because he knoweth not how to go to the city" (Eccl 10:15)... I mean the heavenly Jerusalem, the mother of us all (Gal 4:26).

St. John Cassian * There are those who are called lazy in the Book of Wisdom, who cover their way with thorns, and count zeal in keeping the commandments of God as harmful to the soul, who object to the apostolic commandments, who do not eat their bread by toil but go around to others, and make idleness the rule of life. Then there are the dreamers, who count the deceptions of dreams more trustworthy than the teachings of the Gospels, and call fantasies revelations. Besides these there are also those who dwell in their houses, whom others consider unsociable and wild, not knowing the commandment of love and not knowing the fruit of longsuffering and humility.
St. Gregory of Nyssa
"A wise son maketh a glad father: but a foolish man despiseth his mother" [20]
This proverb came similar to what is in (Proverbs 10:1).

And as was said before, the wise son refers to the believer in whom his heavenly Father rejoices, and receives him as an heir of the Father, an heir with Christ. But the foolish man, who relies on his own opinions in arrogance, despises the Church his mother, counting himself wiser, more understanding and more spiritual than the Church.

21 Folly is joy to him that is destitute of wisdom: but a man of understanding walketh uprightly. 22 Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established.
"Folly is joy to him that is destitute of wisdom: but a man of understanding walketh uprightly" [21]

The foolish man, lacking understanding, finds his delight in evil and in his irresponsible, foolish conduct, but the man of understanding walks uprightly in the fear of the Lord, and rejects wicked pleasures, amusement and jesting.
"Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established" [22]

The wise man does not rely on his own opinion alone in important matters, but listens to those who have knowledge and experience. Perhaps for this reason the Lord sent His disciples and apostles two by two, that they might take counsel together, and share in preaching and worship.
23 A man hath joy by the answer of his mouth: and a word spoken in due season, how good is it! 24 The way of life is above to the wise, that he may depart from hell beneath.
"A man hath joy by the answer of his mouth: and a word spoken in due season, how good is it!" [23]

A fitting answer at the right time, in a fitting manner, and within sound limits gladdens the heart of the speaker and the heart of the listener, and leaves no room for a man to regret what he has said.

Here he stresses the manner of answering and the choice of the right time. For a sound answer at the wrong time may do more harm than silence and not answering. And also a wrong answer at the right time may cause a disaster!
"The way of life is above to the wise, that he may depart from hell beneath" [24]
Since the wise man enjoys true life, he lives always in ascents, rising from glory to glory (2 Cor 3:18), and at the same time avoids descending downward into hell.

Life knows no standing still: it is either ascent toward the heavenly things or descent toward hell. Some compare it to one who swims in the middle of a river: either he completes his course to cross to the shore, or he stops swimming and drowns.
Before man are two ways: the way of life, which knows no idleness, or the way of death.

* He who pursues perfection, clings to the ascent to heaven, and looks to the path on high cannot rest and stop at one height, thinking that he is complete in his work and no longer needs to ascend to another step, but he hastens daily to rise higher, until death opens the door for him to reach the harbor of the saints. I say to you, lover of virtues, it is good for you to think and meditate about advancing forward. And it is fitting for you to reckon that there is a greater way of life than yours. If you thought that you had climbed by virtue as far as you should have climbed, your striving would be in vain, and you would begin to descend because of the pretension that steals over your soul, and fall from the beauty of humility.

* I cry out with all my strength: if you find a place farther than yourself, flee to it, and if you find a place within you, withdraw to it. Do not cease to flee, and do not rest from running until you attain that for which Christ attained you (Phil 3:13).

St. Mar Jacob of Serugh * Growth takes place gradually from childhood to maturity and perfection in Christ. For faith increases and grows by the work of the divine Holy Spirit. Accordingly, the strongholds of evil thoughts are gradually broken until they are entirely demolished.
St. Macarius the Great

25 The LORD will destroy the house of the proud: but he will establish the border of the widow. 26 The thoughts of the wicked are an abomination to the LORD: but the words of the pure are pleasant words. 27 He that is greedy of gain troubleth his own house; but he that hateth gifts shall live.
"The LORD will destroy the house of the proud: but he will establish the border of the widow" [25]

It is not said of God that He resists any particular class of men except the proud (1 Pet 5:5). Here he affirms that He uproots them as from their very roots, since they bear the spirit of the devil, who by his pride wanted to set himself up as a god to be worshipped, to whom all creation would submit.

He who resists the proud, who rely on their abilities, their powers and their authority, takes care of the borders of the widow, which many covet in order to rob her of her rights and seize her possessions. He is the Judge of the widows, the Father of the fatherless, and the Defender of the wronged, the persecuted and the humiliated.
"The thoughts of the wicked are an abomination to the LORD: but the words of the pure are pleasant words" [26]

If God hates the sacrifices and offerings presented by the wicked who persist in their evils, then it is fitting for them to give up their evils and their defiled thoughts, which the Holy One cannot bear.
God hates evil thoughts, and delights in the words of His holy children, and receives them as pure, acceptable thanksgiving hymns, well pleasing to Him.
* If the evil word is an abomination to the Lord your God, how much more the evil word that denies (the faith) and openly proclaims another god, and the evil oath.

* We are not harsh toward those who repent. Rather, the wicked are wicked to themselves, for whoever is ignorant of instruction hates himself. Yet we must seek healing for them in every possible way, even for the person who has turned completely aside and no longer feels his evils, but is drunk with an intoxicant more dangerous than wine, the intoxicant that arises from the darkness of evil.
Origen "He that is greedy of gain troubleth his own house; but he that hateth gifts shall live" [27]

The house signifies the Church. He troubles it who turns it from its spiritual mission to commercial business, or from its holiness, as Achan the son of Carmi troubled all the people of God (Josh 7:25).

Perhaps he refers here to judges and witnesses, since love of money sometimes plays a grave role in those of them who are perverted, so that they judge or bear false witness for the sake of gifts or bribes offered to them, with no regard for the feelings and fates of the wronged.
"The heart of the righteous studieth to answer: but the mouth of the wicked poureth out evil things" [28]

The righteous man is not hasty in speech, but gives his heart or mind the opportunity to study the matter so as to give a wise and truthful answer. The wicked, however, speak rashly without thought or deliberation, because what concerns them is their material or moral gains.
The righteous man fears the Lord, not men, so he weighs every word with all care, lest he anger God or wrong anyone.
"The LORD is far from the wicked: but he heareth the prayer of the righteous" [29]

St. Peter the Apostle quoted the Psalmist's saying: "For the eyes of the Lord are over the righteous, and his ears are open unto their prayers: but the face of the Lord is against them that do evil" (Ps 34:15-16; 1 Pet 3:12). Truly God hears everything and sees everything, but the wicked are not worthy to be the object of God's knowledge, His sight and His hearing. They become as though far from Him, for there is no fellowship between the Holy One and evil!
* Wretched is the man who has masks for evil, and happy is the man who has many masks for goodness.

* "The wicked are like the dust which the wind scatters" (Ps 4:1). The Holy Scripture says that the wicked man will be wretched, so that he will not be even as the dust of the earth. For dust seems to have no existence, yet it surely has a kind of existence in itself... It is scattered here and there and has no one place, but the wind sweeps it away, and it has no power to resist. The same is true of the wicked man. As soon as he denies God, the breath of Satan sweeps him away into error and casts him wherever it wishes.
St. Jerome * God will receive those who repent, and will punish those who remain in their sins.
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem
"The light of the eyes rejoiceth the heart:
and a good report maketh the bones fat" [30]

Painful news spoils a person's peace and takes away his inner joy, and affects even his bodily health. But joyful news in the Lord refreshes the soul, and strengthens the bones of man, that is, his inner temple, and affects even his health.

The expression "fatness of the bones" is contrasted with "dryness of the bones," and it suits countries that depend on rain: if drought occurs the land loses its prosperity, famine befalls it, and it may be struck by diseases. So fatness of the bones signifies prosperity, refreshment and an abundance of good things.
31 The ear that heareth the reproof of life abideth among the wise. 32 He that refuseth instruction despiseth his own soul: but he that heareth reproof getteth understanding.
"The ear that heareth the reproof of life abideth among the wise" [31]
The first word in the Ten Commandments is "Hear," so he who is careful to listen to the voice of truth is qualified to join the choir of the wise.
Listening in a spirit of obedience is bound up with wisdom.
"He that refuseth instruction despiseth his own soul: but he that heareth reproof getteth understanding" [32]

The proud man who does not accept discipline does not despise his counselors but despises himself, and treats his eternity lightly. But he who receives words of criticism with great attention gains understanding and knowledge.

* O the happiness of him who puts his will to death, and leaves the management of his soul to the one whom God has given him as father and teacher, for his place will be at the right hand of Jesus Christ the Crucified.
St. John Climacus * Satan sows evil in people by means of their hatred of guidance, and then they fall like leaves.

* If a man seeks counsel he discovers the plans of the enemy. And if he submits to guidance, Satan flees and will not be able to spread his nets. Therefore he always urges others not to submit to guidance and not to seek it.
St. Dorotheus of Gaza
"The fear of the LORD is the instruction of wisdom; and before honour is humility" [33]

He concludes his discourse in this chapter with the fear of the Lord, which the humble receive, so that they obtain discipline and wisdom, and God honors them as He does men. It is as though the first and last lesson is to seek the fear of the Lord in a spirit of humility, so that we learn from God, who lifts up the humble.
* Humility is good at all times, and it delivers those who draw near to it from every distress.
