The fruits of humility are many, and it begets many good things. From it perfection is born, and through it Noah was proved righteous before God and He saved him, as it is written that God said to him: "For thee have I seen righteous and perfect in thy generation" (see Gen 7:1).

St. Aphrahat * He wants us not to seize leadership for ourselves, but to reach the lofty heights through humility... O the greatness of humility, for (the humble soul) wins the indwelling of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.
Fr. Theophylact * Humility lifted up Moses, but the proud were swallowed up by the earth.
* Put on humility at all times, and it makes you a dwelling place for God.
* Clothe yourself, my brother, with humility at all times, for it clothes your soul with Christ who gives it.
St. John Saba
Carry me, that I may rejoice in You, O Wisdom of God!
* That I may possess You, O All-Compassionate, and enjoy long-suffering.
No wounding word will come out of my mouth to stir up the fires of wrath.
But it will be seasoned with the salt of Your Holy Spirit.
You will awaken in my soul, as in the souls of those who hear, the spirit of joy.
* Let my mouth be opened, and let my tongue speak what You pour into my heart.
Let every word come forth for the edification of my soul and the edification of my brethren, and let there be no place for foolishness on my tongue.
* As I speak I see You looking with love upon my words as upon my heart!
Your glances lift me up as to heaven.
Your eyes crush me with surpassing love.
* My tongue will utter only words of peace, for, being upright, it is sanctified by You and becomes like a tree of life, from which I pluck fruit for my soul!
Carry me by Your love, and discipline me according to Your mercy.
For You are my Father, all-wise and all-tender.
You shepherd me in Your wonderful pastures, You uphold me with Your rod and Your staff.
So I turn neither to the right hand nor to the left.
* I look into my depths, and I see You dwelling in them.
I see You as my treasure, which no one will take from me.
I see You shining upon me with the light of knowledge.
And You receive every act of worship from me as a pleasure to You.
You grant me Your righteousness that I may live by it, You fill me with heavenly joy, and my face becomes ever cheerful by the grace You give!
* You have turned my heart into a perpetual feast!
A feast of love toward You, and toward humanity.
* I see You ever at work in my life, removing from my heart the thorns of sloth and the briers of slackness.
You grant me the spirit of constant diligence, and growth without ceasing!
* That I may work by You and with You, I always seek the guidance of Your Holy Spirit.
And I bow in obedience to Your bride, the Holy Church.
By You I am humbled, for You are meek and lowly in heart.
* I was a widow for a long time, but You received my soul as Your bride, for You are the Judge of the widows and the support of the weak.
* Finally, what do I ask except that You grant me Your fear.
By Your fear I seek the wisdom that is with You.
By Your fear every loftiness and pride within me is brought down.
By Your fear my wilderness becomes a delightful garden, ever bearing the fruit of Your Holy Spirit!

entries.section: 1. The Lord working in His believers

paragraphs.text: 1 The preparations of the heart in man, and the answer of the tongue, is from the LORD. 2 All the ways of a man are clean in his own eyes; but the LORD weigheth the spirits. 3 Commit thy works unto the LORD, and thy thoughts shall be established. 4 The LORD hath made all things for himself: yea, even the wicked for the day of evil.
"The preparations of the heart in man, and the answer of the tongue, is from the LORD" [1]

God sanctified freedom of will, and gave the rational creature the right of choice. It is man's right to choose the way, that is, the preparation of the heart and the intention, but it is God who grants the possibility and the power, even the possibility of answering with the tongue.
Without God man can do nothing, but He does not work in man by compulsion; rather, He leaves to him the choice of the way.

The prophet Jeremiah says: "O LORD, I know that the way of man is not in himself: it is not in man that walketh to direct his steps" (Jer 10:23). Even the human will, though we have received the right of choice, we need the grace of God that we may have strength of will, as the Apostle Paul says: "For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure" (Phil 2:13).

* Certainly, as it is written: "The preparation of the heart in man, and the answer of the tongue, is from the LORD" (Prov 16:10), some err from the way through lack of understanding, thinking that the preparation of the heart - that is, the beginning of goodness - belongs to man without the help of divine grace. Far be it from the children of the promise to understand it so.
* The horse does not tame itself, and neither can man do this. There is urgent need for man to tame the horse, and in the same way for God to tame man.

St. Augustine * God does not compel us, nor does the grace of the Spirit force our will, but God calls us and waits for us to come forward to Him in complete freedom, and when we draw near He grants us all His help.
* God does not compel those who do not want Him, but He draws those who want Him.
* God does not bind our desires or our will by His gifts, but no sooner do we begin and show readiness than we find Him offering us many opportunities for salvation.

* The Creator made our nature master of itself. In His mercy He always grants us His help, and He knows what is hidden in the depths of the heart. He entreats us, counsels us, forbids us and warns us against evil conduct, but He imposes nothing on us by force. He offers the suitable remedies, leaving the whole matter to the decision of the patient himself.
* We are masters; it is in our power to make every member of ours an instrument of evil or an instrument of righteousness.

entries.section: 1. The Lord working in His believers

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom "All the ways of a man are clean in his own eyes; but the LORD weigheth the spirits" [2]

Since the fall of man, man has come to justify his behavior and give himself excuses, and to think that he is walking as is fitting, even if he realizes that what he does is wrong or a crime that he commits, but he reckons that circumstances have driven him to it. Therefore it was said: "The imagination of man's heart is evil" (Gen 8:21). "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?" (Jer 17:9).

But if man accepts God's work in him, then he realizes that God's balances and reckonings are true, and he casts the blame on himself, not on the circumstances around him or on others, or on God Himself. For God does not err in His reckonings.

God grants His believers to enjoy the perception of His balances, not to crush them with grief and bitterness over their conduct, but to draw them to Himself, and so lift them up and sanctify them, and even glorify them.

Many of the Fathers of the Church, such as St. Clement of Alexandria and St. Basil the Great, called man to know the truth about himself, his inner depths, so that he may come to know God, who seeks his salvation, and to dwell in him.
* "Contemplate, then, yourself," until you reach the beholding of God.

* The Holy Scriptures warn you to pay great attention to yourself. So do not care for the body, nor for what is bound up with the body, such as health and beauty, pleasure and long life. Likewise do not pay great attention to wealth, glory and power, and all that is bound up with earthly life. But care for yourself above all things. For this is your precious treasure. Adorn it with the virtues, cleanse it from sin, and beautify it with the adornment of virtue, which is the most beautiful adornment. Contemplate well this thought: the body passes away and perishes, but the soul is immortal.

entries.section: 1. The Lord working in His believers

paragraphs.text: St. Basil the Great "Commit thy works unto the LORD, and thy thoughts shall be established" [3]

The Psalmist says: "Commit thy way unto the LORD; trust also in him; and he shall bring it to pass" (Ps 37:5). If the Lord shatters the plans of the wicked against God and against the believers, on the other hand He gives assurance to His humble believers. He is a support to them in their plans and works as long as they are according to His divine will.
* The humble person shows us what is upright in no easy way. For the penitent person will not boast of great things. But God does not wish to know the works of the proud.

St. John Chrysostom * We were commanded to show our ways to Him, and to make them go toward Him, ways that become straight not by our own efforts but by His help and mercy. Therefore it is written: "Make thy way straight in my eyes," or as it stands in other copies: "Make my way straight in thine eyes," so that what is straight in His eyes may appear straight in mine. And Solomon says: "Open thy works before the Lord, and He will direct thy thoughts," for our thoughts are directed only when we meet before the Lord, as to a firm rock that is not shaken, and everything we do we attribute to Him.

entries.section: 1. The Lord working in His believers

paragraphs.text: St. Jerome "The LORD hath made all things for himself: yea, even the wicked for the day of evil" [4]

Though all the heavenly and earthly creation glorifies God the Creator who cares for His creation, yet He did not create it out of need of someone to glorify Him, but created it because of His goodness, His love and His giving to others.

He proclaims all the more His love and care on the great day of the Lord, when the spiritual believers enjoy the eternal inheritance, while the wicked are judged by their own evil to eternal destruction.

By saying: "He made all things for himself," the believer feels his value, that God created him for Himself, not to profit from him, nor out of need of him, but because He loves him, wants to bring him into His embrace, and to have him belong to Him, so that He says: "I am the God of Abraham..."
The believer feels that he is not a person among a throng of human beings numbering billions, but a man of God, very dear to Him, and cared for by Him personally.

A man often thinks that the law of the world is chaos and lawlessness, and that the law of the jungle and violence prevails. But in the midst of all that seems as if God's eyes do not watch over men, and as if God does not care about their conduct, there is a divine plan that is surely being fulfilled, and with certain success at the appointed time.

* These things... though in appearance they point to one aim and one end (for they urge us to keep away from unseemly things), yet they differ among themselves in loftiness. For faith and hope are more fitting for those who have not yet acquired the love of virtue as they aim toward goodness. But love belongs to God, and to those who have received within them to be in the image and likeness of God. For God alone does good neither out of fear nor out of desire for a word of thanks or the receiving of a reward, but does good simply for the love of goodness. This is as Solomon says: "The LORD hath made all things for himself" (Prov 16:4). By His goodness He pours out good on the worthy and the unworthy, for He is not moved to anger by faults, nor affected by the passions of men's sins, since He is always wholly good and unchangeable.

Fr. Cherimon * God is good, perfectly good, He alone, and since you are His image it is fitting for you to be good. He is generous to all, so you ought to be generous, avoiding greed, and not begrudging your neighbor anything material that passes away, for this is the greatest calamity and folly.
Fr. John of Kronstadt
"Every one that is proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD:
though hand join in hand, he shall not be unpunished" [5]

Those who walk in a spirit of pride isolate themselves from God, who in His humility created man, set him up as king, and gave him authority over the earth. Man's loftiness makes him lose his attachment to God, the source of all good things, and puts himself in the position of an adversary of God, and he thinks he is able to enter into contention with Him as an equal, and so he is not unpunished.

* Nothing is more foreign to the mercy of God, and nothing sends to the fires of hell like the tyrant of pride. If we possess it within us our whole life becomes defiled, even if we practice chastity, virginity, fasting, prayer, almsgiving and any virtue. Scripture says: "Every one that is proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD." So we must examine this loftiness of soul, and cut off this cancer, if we want to be pure and be delivered from the punishment prepared for Satan.

St. John Chrysostom * It is shown with clear firmness, by examples and testimonies from Holy Scripture, that the sin of pride, although it is late in its order (among the sins), is the first of sins and faults, and it is not put to death by the virtue opposed to it (humility), and at the same time it destroys all the virtues, and tempts not only ordinary and simple people, but even more those who stand at the summit of courage.

For this reason the Apostle speaks of this spirit... and likewise the blessed David, although he was most careful of the storehouses of his heart to the point that he dared to address God, from whom the secrets of his conscience (his inner secrets) are not hidden, as in Ps 130 (131):1-2; Ps 100 (101):1-2. Nevertheless, since he knew the difficulty of watchfulness even for the perfect, he did not rely on his own efforts, but prayed to God and asked His help, so that he might come out victorious from the blows of his enemy, saying: "Plead my cause, O LORD, with them that strive with me. Take hold of shield and buckler, and stand up for mine help" (Ps 35:1-2). And because he feared and trembled lest he fall into what was said about pride, he therefore says: "God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble" (Jas 4:6), "Every one that is proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD: though hand join in hand, he shall not be unpunished" (Prov 16:5).

St. John Cassian * We read of a thing like this in the book of Chronicles concerning Joash king of Judah. When he was seven years old Jehoiada the priest called him to become king, and by the testimony of Holy Scripture he was praised for all his works during the life of the aforementioned priest, but we hear of him after the death of Jehoiada how he was puffed up with pride and was delivered over to a more shameful state. "Now after the death of Jehoiada came the princes of Judah, and made obeisance to the king. Then the king hearkened unto them. And they left the house of the LORD God of their fathers, and served groves and idols: and wrath came upon Judah and Jerusalem for this their trespass" (2 Chr 24:17-18). It was said a little later: "And it came to pass at the end of the year, that the host of Syria came up against him: and they came to Judah and Jerusalem, and destroyed all the princes of the people from among the people, and sent all the spoil of them unto the king of Damascus. For the army of the Syrians came with a small company of men; and the LORD delivered a very great host into their hand, because they had forsaken the LORD God of their fathers. So they executed judgment against Joash. And when they were departed from him, (for they left him in great diseases,)" (2 Chr 24:23-25).

Behold, you see how the lust of pride delivered him to shameful lusts of uncleanness because he was puffed up with pride and allowed himself to be worshipped as a god, as the Apostle says: "For this cause God gave them up unto vile affections... God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do those things which are not convenient" (Rom 1:26, 28), and because Scripture says: "Every one that is proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD" (Prov 16:5). He who is puffed up with ever-increasing pride of heart is delivered over to great disgrace and shame, to be deceived by them.

So when he is humbled he must know that he has been soiled by the uncleanness of the flesh and the knowledge of unclean lusts, a thing he refused to know when he was in the pride of his heart. Also this shameful corruption of the flesh can expose the hidden defilement of the heart which was bound to it through the sin of pride, as though the visible corruption of his body could prove his pollution which he did not see before, so that he knows that he has become unclean through the pride of his spirit.

St. John Cassian * Yes, those who speak the words of God before God understand that they have received the words of teaching from God, and so they must seek to please God and not to please themselves. Likewise they must listen to the saying of Scripture: "Every one that is proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD" (Prov 16:5). It is clear that when these seek their vainglory by exploiting the word of God, they usurp the right of God, the Giver and Bestower, for they do not fear to rob of praise those who have received instruction in holy things. Let them hear also what Solomon says to teachers: "Drink waters out of thine own cistern, and running waters out of thine own well. Let not thy fountains overflow outside, nor streams of water in the streets; let them be thine own alone, and not strangers' with thee" (Prov 5:15-17). When the teacher examines the depths of his heart and listens to what it says, he drinks from his cistern. And he drinks of the running waters from his well if he is moved by being watered from the spring of the Word. And when he added: "Let not thy fountains overflow outside, nor streams of water in the streets," he means that the shepherd should drink first and only then water others with teaching. The overflowing of the fountains outside is nothing other than the pouring out of teaching like water with power into others. And "streams of water in the streets" means the distribution of the divine word among great crowds of hearers, each according to his character. And because vainglory thrusts itself in as the word of God extends to the knowledge of many, the fitting saying came: "Let them be thine own alone, and not strangers' with thee." In this connection Wisdom calls the evil spirits "strangers." The prophet wrote of the tempters, saying: "For strangers are risen up against me, and oppressors seek after my soul" (Ps 54:3). Therefore he says that the streams of water in the streets should be yours alone, and this means that "it is necessary for the shepherd to go out to teach like streams in the streets, but he must not ally himself with the unclean spirits through conceit. We must not take enemies as partners in the service of the divine word." We must therefore spread our teaching far, that it may extend, without being tempted by any desire for vain praise.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 3. Love of God and of men

paragraphs.text: "By mercy and truth iniquity is purged: and by the fear of the LORD men depart from evil" [6]

By saying "by mercy and truth" he urges us toward repentance, or return to God, who is all-merciful, and in whom is all truth. We return to Him, and enjoy the fellowship of His attributes, and our iniquities are forgiven us by the precious Blood.

The fear of the Lord leads us in the way of truth, so that we turn neither to the right hand nor to the left, but remain firm in righteousness, as He is the Truth, the Giver of righteousness and holiness.

* The Holy Spirit speaks in the Holy Scriptures and says: "By alms and faith iniquity is purged" (cf. Prov 16:6), certainly not those sins that were committed before, for these are forgiven by the Blood of Christ and His sanctification.

And again he says: "Water will quench a flaming fire; and alms maketh an atonement for sins" (Sir 3:33). Here he makes clear that just as the fire of hell is quenched by the water of salvation, so by almsgiving and righteousness the flame of sins is put out (for those who believe in the Blood). Since in Baptism the forgiveness of sins is given once for all sins, the continual work without interruption - following the example of Baptism - grants the mercies of God again.

The Lord also taught us this in the Gospel, for when it was pointed out to Him that the disciples were eating without washing their hands, He answered, saying: "Did not he that made that which is without make that which is within also? But rather give alms of such things as ye have; and, behold, all things are clean unto you" (Lk 11:40-41). He teaches the washing of the heart, not of the hands, and that rather the uncleanness of the inside is to be removed, not the filth of the outside, and that when the mind is purified, then a man begins to cleanse his body. And as He counsels us how to wash and purify, He said that giving alms is necessary.

He who is tender teaches us and urges us to show compassion. For since He seeks the salvation of those for whom He offered such a sacrifice, He also pointed to those who, after receiving the grace of Baptism and committing sin, can be cleansed anew.

St. Cyprian the Martyr * Also with mercy and faith offenses are blotted out, for "by mercy and truth iniquity is purged" (Prov 16:6). And often this comes through our longing, striving and labor for the salvation of those who were saved by our warnings and exhortation, as Scripture says: "Let him know, that he which converteth the sinner from the error of his way shall save a soul from death, and shall hide a multitude of sins" (Jas 5:20).
Fr. Pinufius * My beloved... many times I remind you and confess to you what astonishes me greatly in what is recorded in Holy Scripture, and which I must often call to your attention.

I beseech you to consider what our Lord Jesus Christ said about Himself, that when He comes on the Day of Judgment, at the end of the world, He will gather all the nations before Him, and divide men into two parts: one part on His right hand and the other on His left.

He says to those on the right: "Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world." But to those on the left He says: "Depart from me... into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels."

Inquire into the cause of this great reward or this dreadful punishment... Why do the first inherit the Kingdom? "For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat." And why do the others go into the eternal fire? "For I was an hungred, and ye gave me no meat"...
The Lord did not say to these: "Come, inherit the Kingdom, for you lived pure, you deceived no man, nor wronged a poor man, nor encroached on anyone's borders, nor deceived anyone by an oath"...
But He said: "I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat." O the pre-eminence of almsgiving over all the other virtues, for the Lord did not point to all of them but to it alone!

Likewise He says to the others: "Depart into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels," and although there are many things He could raise against the wicked when they ask Him: "Why do we go into everlasting fire?" yet He does not answer them: "Why do you ask thus, you fornicators and murderers and deceivers and temple-robbers and blasphemers and unbelievers?"... But He says to them: "For I was an hungred, and ye gave me no meat."

I see that you marvel as I do, and truly it is a marvelous thing, for it is written: "Water will quench a flaming fire; and alms maketh an atonement for sins," "Shut up alms in thy storehouses, and it shall deliver thee from all evil. Therefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable unto thee, and visit thy sins with alms" (cf. Sir 3:33; 9:15).

There are many testimonies from the divine inspiration in which appears how great are the benefits of charity in quenching sins and removing them, therefore charity will be attached to those whom God is about to judge, nay rather, it will crown them. It is as though He says to them: It is not difficult for Me to find a cause against you to condemn you when I examine you and weigh you accurately and scrutinize your works, but enter the Kingdom, for I was an hungred and you gave Me meat; you will enter the Kingdom not because you have not sinned, but through your charity you have removed your sins.

Likewise, as if He were saying to the others: Depart into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels... It is not because of the sins you think of, but because I was an hungred and you gave Me no meat; had you turned away from these evil deeds of yours, and turned to Me, you would have been saved from all your crimes and sins by your charities. For "Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy" (Mt 5:7). But now depart into everlasting fire, "for he shall have judgment without mercy, that hath shewed no mercy" (Jas 2:13).

St. Augustine * Because you have not had mercy on others, no mercy shall be shown to you either, and because you shut the door of your house against the poor, God will not open to you the door of His Kingdom...
If you have fled from mercy, mercy flees from you. And if you have rejected the poor, He who became poor out of love for you rejects you.
St. Basil the Great

7 When a man's ways please the LORD, he maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him. 8 Better is a little with righteousness than great revenues without right. 9 A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps.
"When a man's ways please the LORD, he maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him" [7]
True goodness, which is the fruit of the work of God's grace in man, has the power to love even enemies and win them to our side, so long as we offer it for the glory of God.

It was not possible for Laban to do evil to Jacob, for God Himself appeared in a dream of the night, "and said unto him, Take heed that thou speak not to Jacob either good or bad" (Gen 31:24). As for Esau, who wanted to kill him, it was said of him: "Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept" (Gen 33:1-4).

* Wonderful is the goodness of the Lord. When God saw that Laban had inclined to make war on the good man and to enter into conflict with him, He said to him, as one reviewing his intention by the word: Take heed lest you become guilty by evil words against Jacob. Do not try to trouble Jacob even with a word, but take heed to yourself. Review this evil attack on your part. Control your anger. Control your raging thoughts, refrain from troubling him even with a word. I ask you to notice the compassions of God, for instead of commanding Laban to return to his place He directed him not to utter harsh or violent words against the good man. Why did this happen on earth? That the truly good man might learn, by truth and by experience, how far God cares for him.
St. John Chrysostom "Better is a little with righteousness than great revenues without right" [8].

If a man's income is bound up with exploiting his brethren, it is bound up with the sin of cruelty, and he loses peace of heart, and so feels no happiness. For man's happiness does not rest on man's material possibilities, or his position or his authority, but on his union with the Holy One, and his enjoyment of the blessed life.

For the sake of a good conscience, and of present peace, and of the blessedness to come eternally, it is better for a man to gain a little to live on, by a lawful way, than to gain much by the evil ways of the world.

Let us not judge a man by his outward appearance, but according to his inner conscience. And let us strive to attain the virtue and happiness that come from works of righteousness and goodness. And would that we all - rich and poor - would imitate Lazarus, for this man endured the trials of virtue not once or twice or three times but many times, and I mean how he was poor and sick and had no one to help him, and was cast down at the door of a house that could have given him rest and relieved him of all his troubles, but did not give him a single word of comfort, and he saw the man who neglected him enjoying such luxury, and not only living in the enjoyment of this luxury, but also living in evils without suffering any trials or distress, and he did not look at or care for any other poor man like Lazarus, nor bring rest to himself with any thought of the resurrection. And besides these misfortunes he had a bad reputation among the crowds of people because of the trials that befell him. And not for a day or two or three, but all his life he saw himself in this state and saw the rich man in the opposite.
What excuse shall we have when this man bore all these calamities at one time and with such courage, if we do not bear even half of this?

* The fornicator or adulterer or thief, not only when he is accused, but even when he hears of others accused of the same crimes, imagines himself in the same punishment for his sins, and so takes a lesson from the punishment of others. Another has been condemned, but this one who has not been condemned is troubled because he dared to commit the same sins, and this also in the case of good works, when some receive praise and honor, those who have done the same good works rejoice and are glad, imagining themselves in this same honor. Do you think there is anyone more wretched than this sinner who, when he sees others accused, slips away to hide? And on the other hand, is there anyone happier than the righteous person when he sees other righteous men honored? For he rejoices and is glad, remembering his own good deeds amid the joy and exultation over the others.
St. John Chrysostom "A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps" [9].

Man's heart is moved with a strong desire to think about achieving what is in his intention. With all the freedom of will that man has, he will not be able to move without God's care or God's permission. God created man a rational being, not that man should conceal this gift, but that while he plans he should lean on the breast of God and trust in Him, yet not in lack of thought or lack of movement toward work. As the Apostle Paul says: "Now God himself and our Father, and our Lord Jesus Christ, direct our way unto you" (1 Thess 3:11).

* Do we still dare to boast of free will and insult the blessings of God, the Giver of gifts, if the chosen vessel (Paul) writes plainly: "But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us" (2 Cor 4:7)?
St. Jerome * Paul did not work in order to receive grace, but he received grace in order to strive.
* How then can God's commandment be fulfilled, even with difficulty, without His help, since unless the Lord build the house, they labor in vain that build it.

St. Augustine * Paul wishes to remind us that we are not saved merely by our receiving God's free grace. Rather we must prove that we want to receive this free grace. The children of Israel received it, but they proved themselves unworthy of it and so were not saved.
Origen

entries.section: 5. The obligation of the king or leader

paragraphs.text: 10 A divine sentence is in the lips of the king: his mouth transgresseth not in judgment. 11 A just weight and balance are the LORD'S: all the weights of the bag are his work. 12 It is an abomination to kings to commit wickedness: for the throne is established by righteousness. 13 Righteous lips are the delight of kings; and they love him that speaketh right. 14 The wrath of a king is as messengers of death: but a wise man will pacify it. 15 In the light of the king's countenance is life; and his favour is as a cloud of the latter rain. 16 How much better is it to get wisdom than gold! and to get understanding rather to be chosen than silver!
"A divine sentence is in the lips of the king: his mouth transgresseth not in judgment" [10]

It is fitting for the king or leader to realize his responsibility toward the people, for he is like one who represents God, and he must observe justice in his decisions, and seek not his personal advantage but the advantage of the people. It is fitting that he not make light of the word that comes out of his mouth.

entries.section: 5. The obligation of the king or leader

paragraphs.text: "A just weight and balance are the LORD'S: all the weights of the bag are his work" [11]
However great a man's precision and honesty, it is hard for him to put things in their right place exactly, therefore the balance of truth belongs to the Lord.

What does he mean by the weights of the bag? Perhaps he means the bag kept in the temple, in which are the exact weights by which the balances of men are regulated. Or perhaps the "bag" here refers to the bag that merchants carried and in which they put gold and silver and other metals that they acquired in the course of their trade.

If merchants are bound to honesty in their balances, and so is every believer, how much more the king, to whom it is fitting to represent God in his leadership and care of the people, so that he keeps to justice, especially with balances.
It is not fitting for merchants, nor for leaders, especially the king, to separate their honesty in dealing with others from their worship of God, who is righteous and just, and without blame.

It is not fitting for a man to cheat in the balances, measuring with two measures, one by which he measures for his loved ones and friends and family and himself, and another by which he measures for strangers and those who oppose him!

entries.section: 5. The obligation of the king or leader

paragraphs.text: "It is an abomination to kings to commit wickedness: for the throne is established by righteousness" [12]

Let the king know that his throne is established not by his military or material or popular resources, but by divine righteousness. It is fitting for him as a king not only not to practice evil - and this is within his power - but to count even the mere thinking of it a defilement he cannot bear. He hates evil whether it comes from the people or from his palace or from himself personally.

By this the king becomes a shadow of the Lord Christ, the Son of David, King of kings. Of whom it was said: "And in mercy shall the throne be established: and he shall sit upon it in truth in the tabernacle of David, judging, and seeking judgment, and hasting righteousness" (Isa 16:5).

entries.section: 5. The obligation of the king or leader

paragraphs.text: "Righteous lips are the delight of kings; and they love him that speaketh right" [13]

Just as the king (or leader) is bound not only not to commit evil, but to hate even the mere thinking of evil, whether for himself or for those subject to him, so it is fitting for him to rejoice in those who speak the truth and to love those who speak uprightness.
How hard it is for those who occupy high positions, whether in society or in the Church, not to be deceived by words of flattery coming from those around them or from the people!

The splendid example of this is the role played by Bishop Flavian to calm the Emperor Theodosius when the people of Antioch assaulted his statues and rebelled against him. On the advice of the priest John Chrysostom, the bishop traveled eleven hundred kilometers until he reached Constantinople to say to the Emperor: [Your crown, O lord of Rome and of the world, is splendid, and is a proof of your worthiness, but it signifies the generosity that conveyed it to you. As for the crown of your humanity, the credit for it goes to your wisdom alone. Men admire the glittering jewels on your brow. But how great will be their admiration of the victory you win over your heart... If you pardon the Antiochenes you will gain great glory that will not fall away with the passing of the ages... You will bring great crowds into the Christian religion, for they will say: Look at the Christian religion. It has quenched the wrath of a man who has no equal in the world!]

entries.section: 5. The obligation of the king or leader

paragraphs.text: "The wrath of a king is as messengers of death: but a wise man will pacify it" [14]

If it is the duty of the king not to think evil, and not to be affected by words of praise, but to seek words of truth and love upright words, then it is the duty of the people to realize that the king is a man who has his weaknesses, and in his hand is authority. If anyone provokes him he is exposed to death. It is fitting for a man to be wise and pacify the king, giving honor to whom honor is due.
The Apostle Paul says:
"Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God: and they that resist shall receive to themselves damnation.
For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil. Wilt thou then not be afraid of the power? do that which is good, and thou shalt have praise of the same" (Rom 13:1-3).
"I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men;
For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty. For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Saviour" (1 Tim 2:1-3).

* Pray for kings (and rulers) (1 Tim 2:2), and for authorities and princes, pray for all who persecute you and hate you, and for the enemies of the Cross, that your fruit may be manifest to all, and that you may be perfect in Him (Christ).
St. Polycarp the Martyr * We pray to the eternal God, the true God, the living God, for the health of our rulers...

It is fitting for them to realize, as men, from whom they received their authority, that they have learned from the One who gave life itself. They are convinced that He is the only God, and on His power they depend completely...

To Him we Christians lift up our eyes and spread out our hands, for we are innocent, with our heads uncovered, for we have no need to be ashamed, and finally without anyone to urge us, for we pray from the heart and always make supplication for all our emperors. We ask for them a long life, a quiet empire, a secure dwelling, strong armies, a faithful senate, and a world at peace, and everything that this man and Caesar desires.

entries.section: 5. The obligation of the king or leader

paragraphs.text: Tertullian "In the light of the king's countenance is life; and his favour is as a cloud of the latter rain" [15]

To please the king in the Lord makes him joyful, and his countenance gives life, as though he were raining upon a dry land. The latter rain is the rain that falls before the harvest, without which the earth does not bring forth a worthy yield.

If the pleasure of the king gives life to those subject to him, how much more the favor of the King of kings. As the psalmist says: "In thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore" (Ps 16:11).

* Let us worship Him as the God of those who believe in His becoming man. For what profit is there in saying of Him that He is a man and not God, or what salvation do we have if we refuse to confess His humanity together with His divinity? Let us confess His presence, for He is both King and Physician. For Jesus the King, having become a Physician, girded Himself with the linen of our humanity and healed what was sick. The perfect Teacher of infants became an infant among them (Rom 2:20), that He might give wisdom to the foolish. The Bread of heaven came down to earth that He might feed the hungry!

* The following statement has come in the Gospel: "He that believeth not the Son shall not see life; but the wrath of God abideth on him" (Jn 3:36). The Father is angered when the only-begotten Son is despised. For a king is grieved by the mere insult to one of his soldiers. If a king is grieved merely because one of his soldiers is insulted, then if someone despises his only son, who can quench the wrath of the father on account of his only son?!

entries.section: 5. The obligation of the king or leader

paragraphs.text: St. Cyril of Jerusalem "How much better is it to get wisdom than gold! and to get understanding rather to be chosen than silver!" [16].

To enjoy heavenly wisdom is better than all earthly riches. For wisdom adorns the soul and keeps the body from evil, so that the whole man may live enjoying God the Word, or the wisdom of the eternal God. Gold, on the other hand, gives the body a temporary beauty, or is used to acquire what sustains and nourishes the body; but the body will surely die and leave the gold behind, whereas wisdom accompanies man even in the life to come.
Spiritual understanding, the perception of the mysteries of God, and the knowledge of the depths of the divine commandment are better than silver.

* As gold is better than silver, so wisdom is loftier than prudence. The first concerns knowledge, and the latter the interpretation of what is hidden, so that you may interpret the dwellings of wisdom as the churches or the dwellings of the saints in heaven. But wisdom itself is Christ.
St. Didymus the Blind
"The highway of the upright is to depart from evil:
he that keepeth his soul keepeth his way." [17].
The course of the upright, or their general way, is to walk without turning to the right or to the left; nothing can draw them away, neither self-righteousness or pride, nor lusts and pleasures.
When a person keeps himself, that is, takes care of his inner depths and is occupied with his eternal salvation, he keeps the uprightness of his way in the Lord, until he enjoys the divine embrace.

18 Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall. 19 Better it is to be of an humble spirit with the lowly, than to divide the spoil with the proud. 20 He that handleth a matter wisely shall find good: and whoso trusteth in the LORD, happy is he.
"Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall" [18]

He who exalts himself falls. When Herod put on his royal apparel and sat upon his throne... the people shouted: "It is the voice of a god, and not of a man" (Acts 12:22). Immediately the angel of the Lord smote him, because he gave not God the glory, and he was eaten of worms and died.

* We ought not to think that a person stumbles and goes down into grief by a sudden fall; rather, he descends into a hopeless fall either by being deceived from the beginning, during his training, through a wrong start, or he slips from his good spiritual state gradually over a long period because of mental negligence, so that the errors increase little by little. For "pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall" (Prov 16:18). It is like a house that does not fall suddenly all at once, but some defect occurs in the foundation over a long period, or it results from the neglect of its inhabitants for a long time, so that some seepage (or defect) occurs, and after this the fortified walls collapse gradually. For "by much slothfulness the building decayeth; and through idleness of the hands the house droppeth through" (Eccl 10:18); this is also what happens to the spirit.
Father Theodore * "Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall" (Prov 16:18).

Some people boast that they are the sons of rulers, and of their ability to bring down some priests from their priestly ranks; such people magnify themselves and boast for trifling matters that have no profit behind them, and therefore there is not the least reason for this self-exaltation of theirs... And there are those who boast that they have obtained what they call a privilege, Promotion, which enables them to strike off the heads of people: "the glory of these people is in their shame" (Phil 3:19). Others boast of their wealth, not true riches, but earthly wealth... All these things do not deserve even to be taken into consideration, and it is not fitting for us to boast of any of them.

The things that give us the right to exalt ourselves and boast are to boast that we are wise, or to boast (with discretion) that for ten years, for example, we have not approached bodily pleasures and lusts, or have not approached them since childhood; or again when we boast of bearing chains on our hands for the sake of the Lord Christ. These are things that call for boasting with justice; but even these things also, if we judge with our reason in truth, we find that it is not for us to exalt ourselves or boast of them.

The Apostle Paul had what could call him to boast because of the visions, revelations, miracles and signs, and because of the sufferings he bore for the sake of the Lord Christ, and because of the churches he established in many places of the world. In all this he had what could call him to boast, and according to the outward, visible things that call for boasting, the boasting of the Apostle Paul would have seemed natural to people; yet, since it was dangerous for him to boast, even about those things, the Father in His mercy, as He gave him those visions, also gave him, out of compassion for him, a messenger of Satan to buffet him, lest he be exalted; and for this reason Paul besought the Lord three times that it might depart from him, and God answered him: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness" (2 Cor 12:7-9).

Origen * Shall we praise hospitality? Shall we admire brotherly love, conjugal love, virginity, feeding the poor, singing psalms, keeping vigil in prayer all night long, and repentance? Do we humble the body by fasting? Do we dwell with God through prayer? Do we subject the lower element in us to the higher, that is, the dust to the spirit, as is proper if we judge rightly our nature, which is a mixture, like an alloy, of the two? Do we make life a meditation on death? Do we master our passions, remembering the loftiness of our second birth? Do we tame our proud and rebellious dispositions? Or our haughtiness that goes before a fall (Prov 16:18)... and our unrefined laughter, our uncontrolled eyes, our greedy ears, our immoderate talk, our wandering thoughts, or anything in us that the evil one can seize and use against us, so that death enters through the windows (Jer 9:21), as the Scripture says, by which windows are meant here the senses.
St. Gregory of Nazianzus "Better it is to be of an humble spirit with the lowly, than to divide the spoil with the proud" [19]

Humility of spirit grants a spirit of unity and harmony with the lowly, so the Lord declares His presence in their midst and grants them His grace. Pride, on the other hand, may bring great spoils and gains together with the proud, together with temporal honor, but a person loses his friendship with God and enslaves himself to the devil.

St. Augustine sees that the role of the believer in this life is to ascend as upon a tower whose top reaches heaven. This tower, rising from earth to heaven, needs the digging of foundations and a descent into the far depths of the earth. The higher the building rises, the more it needs the foundations to go down to greater depths. So whoever wants to build a tower whose top is in heaven needs to practice a deeper and deeper humility. Without the foundations of humility the tower of our spiritual life collapses, and instead of ascending to heaven with our humble Christ, our souls are completely shattered!

* Let us count the cost of the spiritual tower of towering height, and consider this carefully beforehand... Let us first take our faults clearly into account, so that we dig and remove the corruption and the refuse of the lusts, so that we may lay the strong foundations of simplicity and humility upon the solid ground... or rather, the foundations are laid upon the rock of the Gospel (Lk 6:48); by this the tower of the spiritual virtues rises, and is able to stand firm and rise to the heights of heaven in complete safety, unshaken.
Father Isaac "He that handleth a matter wisely shall find good: and whoso trusteth in the LORD, happy is he" [20].

A person may enjoy understanding and the ability to manage; he walks with understanding in the affairs of his temporal life, and receives good things, success, honor and esteem from others. But he who fears the Lord and trusts in Him receives the blessed, happy life, that is, we experience the earnest of the heavenly things.

* The upright person recognizes that when sorrows, tragedies or troubles come upon him, they are by the good will of God, and so he accepts them. But the one with a crooked heart looks at them with sorrow. He agrees that he is a sinner, but says that there are many worse than he who are happy.
The upright heart accepts everything that happens to it, saying: "The Lord gave, the Lord has taken; let Him do what pleases Him; blessed be the name of the Lord."

Troubles come from the Lord (by His permission). They are a punishment for the wicked and a chastening for the son. If you want to be a son, do not expect to escape sufferings, for He chastens every son whom He receives. Every son? Without exception?
Listen, the only-begotten Son alone is without sin, and yet He suffered.
He bore our weaknesses; the Head bore the members of the body in His person.
As a man He entered into His sufferings in sorrow, that you may rejoice.
He entered into bitterness that you may receive consolation. He said: "My soul is sorrowful unto death; but let not my will, but thy will be done, O Father."
St. Augustine

21 The wise in heart shall be called prudent: and the sweetness of the lips increaseth learning. 22 Understanding is a wellspring of life unto him that hath it: but the instruction of fools is folly. 23 The heart of the wise teacheth his mouth, and addeth learning to his lips. 24 Pleasant words are as an honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones.
"The wise in heart shall be called prudent: and the sweetness of the lips increaseth learning" [21]
The heart among the Jews corresponds to the mind among the Greeks. So whoever is wise and balanced in his thinking enjoys the respect of others and their esteem for his personality.

But whoever mixes this wisdom and balance with the sweetness of the tongue increases in learning, meaning that he becomes able to deal with others, so he benefits from their work and experience, and they reciprocate in the same way.

* It was said of Abba John of Qolzum - because he lived for some time beside Qolzum, that is, Suez - that because of his great humility he carried the whole wilderness of Scetis on his little finger. How did he do that?

The elder answered: "In the old copies it is recorded that he carried it toward his will, for with discernment, knowledge, old age and humility he was greatly adorned with cheerfulness, and he met with joy all the brethren who came to him at any time to reveal to him their battles and thoughts. The meaning of this saying is that they obeyed his thought in all that he wished and said and commanded.

At that time Abba Macarius of Alexandria was the head of the monastery, and St. John drew all the monks of Scetis to his will by the life-giving word that came out of his mouth, as he taught and preached to all the brethren."
The Paradise of the Fathers "Understanding is a wellspring of life unto him that hath it: but the instruction of fools is folly" [22]

The spirit of understanding and discernment overflows with blessings upon the believer, as though he carries within him a spring that overflows upon him with life. His thoughts make him grow and advance. But the fool is not benefited by a good word or by chastening, for he insists on not learning.

* People are usually called "rational," though the word "rational" is misused. The rational are not those who study the sayings and writings of the wise early Fathers, but those whose souls are rational, able to distinguish between what is good and what is evil. They avoid what is evil and harmful to the soul, and wisely care for what is good and profitable for the soul and practice it with great thanksgiving to God.
These alone are truly those whom we must call "rational"...

We become worthy to be called human when we are characterized by reason (according to the previous meaning); if reason (in this sense) is not present, we do not differ from the dumb animals except in the shape of our limbs and the gift of speech.
Therefore, let the rational man know that he is immortal, hating the shameful passions which are the cause of the death of men.
St. Abba Anthony the Great "The heart of the wise teacheth his mouth, and addeth learning to his lips" [23]

The writer gives great importance to the heart (or mind), that is, to the inner man; if it becomes holy, it translates this holiness practically through his lips, so his words come forth uprightly, and he enjoys continual edification.

* When the rational person examines himself, he sees what he must do, and what is profitable for him, and what is akin to his soul and leads it to salvation, as he also sees what is foreign to the soul and leads it to destruction, and in this way he avoids what harms the soul as something foreign to it.
St. Abba Anthony the Great "Pleasant words are as an honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones" [24]
The words of the godly person carry three characteristics.
The first is that they share the characteristic of the word of God, of which the psalmist speaks, that it is as the honeycomb (Ps 19:10).

Second, they do not stop at winning others and the growth of the spirit of love and friendship and the dispelling of the spirit of anger, but carry a special sweetness within the soul of the speaker himself.

And finally, together with their pleasantness and sweetness, they are profitable, for they heal the bones, which are the frame of man himself. It is as though words full of grace are profitable from every side, to the speaker and to the hearers, to the soul as to the body.

* You who love learning and long to listen, receive once more the holy words, and delight yourselves with the honey of wisdom, for so it is written: "Pleasant words are as an honeycomb, sweet to the soul" (Prov 16:24). For the work of the bees is very sweet, and benefits the soul of man in many ways; but the divine, saving honey makes those in whom it dwells skillful in every good work, and teaches them the ways of spiritual progress.

St. Cyril the Great * Be slow and dull toward idle talk, and wise and knowledgeable in listening to the words of the saving holy Scriptures. Let listening to worldly tales have a bitter taste in your mouths, but let the conversations of the saints be as the honeycomb.

St. Basil the Great * The sea is the Holy Scripture, which carries in it deep meanings and the secret depths of the prophets. Many rivers flow into this sea. Joyful and pure are these streams. These springs are calm and overflow with eternal life (Jn 4:14). There are also words that are delightful as the honeycomb (Prov 16:24), gentle conversations that water souls with the sweetness of the moral commandments. The streams of the Holy Scripture differ, and you know what you should drink first, then second, then last.

St. Ambrose The Roman senator Paulinus of Milan describes to us, concerning his friend St. Ambrose, bishop of Milan, that his father, who was also called Ambrose and was administering the provinces of Gaul, saw a swarm of bees entering and leaving the mouth of his little son, the infant Ambrose, as he lay in swaddling clothes with his mouth open. The father, his wife and his daughter feared for the child, but they watched the sight in astonishment. The swarm set out and rose high into the air until it disappeared completely. The father said in terror: "If this child lives, he will surely be of great importance." The senator comments, saying: [For the Lord was at work during the childhood of His servant so that the words might be fulfilled: "Pleasant words are as an honeycomb," for this swarm of bees was implanting the honeycomb for his works which came later, which bear witness to the heavenly gifts and direct the minds of the people from earthly things to heavenly things.]

25 There is a way that seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death. 26 He that laboureth laboureth for himself; for his mouth craveth it of him. 27 An ungodly man diggeth up evil: and in his lips there is as a burning fire. 28 A froward man soweth strife: and a whisperer separateth chief friends. 29 A violent man enticeth his neighbour, and leadeth him into the way that is not good. 30 He shutteth his eyes to devise froward things: moving his lips he bringeth evil to pass. 31 The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness.
"There is a way that seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death" [25]
We have already spoken of these deceptive ways that seem straight to a person but lead him into eternal death (Prov 14:12).

Here the wise man warns us against relying on personal judgment without the counsel of God, and enjoying the experience of the godly who went before us on the way. Scripture warns us against man's reliance on his own thought, for it is said: "In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes" (Judg 17:6; 18:1; 21:25).

* Likewise, when the monk is eager to long for a holy priestly office, under the pretext of teaching people and love of winning souls, he (Satan) by this draws us away from humility and from strictness in our life.

Thus he presents to us all the things that stand in the way of our salvation and do not suit our work, but he hides them under a cover, or veils them with a veil of compassion and piety, so that he may easily deceive those who lack skill and care.

They counterfeit the coinage of the true king, for they show these works as full of compassion, but they were not minted by those who have the right to do so, that is, they do not agree with the mind of the fathers of the universal Church, and they do not obtain them from the public office assigned to issue them; rather, they are minted by stealth through satanic deception, and they slip them to the unskilled and the ignorant...

Although at the beginning they appear useful and necessary, afterward they begin to penetrate into the soundness of our work and weaken the whole structure of our aim in several ways. Therefore it is good that these thoughts be cut off and removed from us, as though they were a diseased member which, though it seems necessary, is harmful to us. For it is better for us to be without this member of some commandment, that is, not to carry it out, and to remain in peace and safety and enter the Kingdom of Heaven so, than to sin against all the commandments through the deception of Satan, who offers us to carry out some commandment, and by means of it deprives us of our strict order and arrangement, and so there comes to us a loss exceeding in importance any later harm, and it drives all our former striving and the whole body of our works into the burning of the fire of Gehenna (Mt 18:8).

It is said of these kinds of deception, "There is a way that seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death" (Prov 16:25). And also, "He that is surety for a stranger shall smart for it..." (Prov 11:15). For Satan deceives us by taking on the appearance of holiness.
Father Moses "He that laboureth laboureth for himself; for his mouth craveth it of him" [26]
This proverb urges us to work diligently, whether in our daily work for temporal needs, or in spiritual work to satisfy the inner hunger.

The literal translation is "The soul that labors (strives) labors for itself." When a person feels hunger, his mouth urges him to work diligently, by the sweat of his brow, that he may eat and be satisfied.
"An ungodly man diggeth up evil: and in his lips there is as a burning fire" [27]
* Do not be one fought with the tongue. Let everyone bless you.

St. Anthony the Great * An elder said: The tongue is full of fire, and it defiles the whole body, so let him who loves his life have pity on his tongue. Guard your lips, O man of God, and bridle your tongue, and you will profit by all your labors, for he who keeps his tongue has many honors. Blessed is he who rules over his tongue, for his granaries (that is, his storehouses) are filled with good things.

* An elder said: If the movements of your tongue are abundant, the pure movements have been quenched in your heart; but if your tongue is silent and your heart boils with pure movements, blessed are you, for its movement by the Spirit lifts you to the calm of life. Silence your tongue that your heart may speak, and silence your heart that the Spirit may speak in it.
The Paradise of the Fathers "A froward man soweth strife: and a whisperer separateth chief friends" [28]

He has already spoken of the sweetness of the mouth of the wise man and what the words of grace offer to him and to those around him for the edification of all. Now he speaks of the words of the ungodly man, who, though he offers honeyed words, they are like a burning fire, destroying himself and those around him. The wicked man utters lies, kindles the fires of strife, and also corrupts friendships by his words.

By saying "diggeth up" he indicates that if he does not find what he can say of lies and deceptions, he takes it upon himself to dig in the earth and toils to find a terrible lie to utter. If Scripture indicates that the kingdom of the devil is under the earth, then it is as though the wicked man digs by his free will to meet always with the enemy of good, the liar, who teaches him lying and deceit, so that he bears his image as his son.
"A violent man enticeth his neighbour, and leadeth him into the way that is not good" [29]
By the violent man he means the man of violence, who finds his pleasure in the troubles of others.

* When a person deals with another out of malice, it (rebounds upon him) involuntarily. And it happens thus: whoever deprives (his brother) of something deprives himself of the same thing, even against his wish. So also whoever insults another falls under the judgment of those who are insulted. Whoever wrongs another falls under the judgment of those wronged, and those who blame others fall under the judgment of the blamed. Those who despise others fall under the judgment of the despised. And those who lie fall under the judgment of those slandered. I am not enumerating here; I say in brief that everyone who does wrong falls under the same judgment. The holy Scriptures bear witness to this when they say: "Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein: and he that rolleth a stone, it will return upon him" (Prov 27:26)... And it says also: "Is God unrighteous who inflicts wrath?!" (Rom 5:3).
St. Mark the Ascetic "He shutteth his eyes to devise froward things: moving his lips he bringeth evil to pass" [30]
Whoever commits sin in intention, closing his eyes to fall into wicked daydreams, or biting his lips from inner anger, practices evil.

The godly person closes his bodily eyes for a while, asking God to open his inner sight so that he may enjoy the vision of God's mysteries and glories, and he desires that all humanity share with him in this gift. But the wicked man scrutinizes his brother with his eyes and does not care about the injustice or distress he suffers, and shuts his lips like one who wants to take revenge!
"The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness" [31].

If gray hair has its dignity, it does not rest upon the color of the hair, nor upon the number of years, but upon the righteousness which he has lived and experienced. Old age cannot cause the righteous man to lose his vitality in righteousness, and his striving for the crowns. And as Caleb said: "And now, lo, I am this day fourscore and five years old. As yet I am as strong this day as I was in the day that Moses sent me: as my strength was then, even so is my strength now, for war, both to go out, and to come in" (Josh 14:10-11). And it was said of Moses: "And Moses was an hundred and twenty years old when he died: his eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated" (Deut 34:7).

* One day Abba Ammon went to visit (Abba Sisoes) and found him grieved over his coming from the wilderness. He said to him: Father, it is not good for you to grieve, because you have come near to the dwelling place of the brethren, for your body has become weak and you are no longer able to do those works that you want in the wilderness.

When Abba Sisoes heard these words, he looked at Abba Ammon sharply and answered him with anger, saying: What is this that you are saying to me, Abba Ammon? Was not the freedom of thoughts that I had in the wilderness sufficient to take the place of all works? And as for you also, Ammon, who understand life and the results of freedom of thought, and who are not subject to the necessity of wandering and disturbance of thought, nor are hindered by old age or weakness, tell me what can you do in the wilderness in advanced age? And even if I am not fit for the works of the body because I have become weak through my old age, I have more ability to accomplish the works of thought than I had in my early manhood.
The Paradise of the Fathers
"He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city" [32]

There is no greater strength than for a person, by the grace of God, to control his emotions, impulses and passions. Whoever rules over his anger is reckoned better than the mighty, and whoever rules over his depths and thoughts is greater than a king who governs a city.

* If you are angry, be angry with yourself, for thus you are stirred and do not sin. For whoever is angry with himself, since he is quickly stirred, ceases to be angry against others. But whoever wishes to justify his anger burns the more and quickly falls into sin. And as Solomon says: "He that controlleth his anger is better than he that taketh a city" - for anger misleads even the brave man.

St. Ambrose * The taking of cities is a small victory, for the places you conquer are outside us; the attaining of a greater victory is accomplished by patience, for a person conquers himself and subjects himself to himself when humility leads him to bear with others.

* Let the one who is not meek listen to the saying of the Holy Scripture: "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city." (Prov 16:32). Victory over cities is of less importance, for what is subdued here is something external; but victory through meekness is a far greater act, for it is the mind that conquers and rules itself by itself when meekness compels the mind to control itself inwardly.

Let the wrathful understand what the Truth says to His elect: "In your patience possess ye your souls" (Lk 21:19). The manner of creation is truly a marvelous matter, in that the mind governs the soul, and the soul rules over the body. But the soul loses its control over the body if the mind does not rule over it. Therefore the Lord shows us that meekness is the guardian of our states and also teaches us that by meekness we can possess ourselves. And so we realize the gravity of the sin of lack of meekness (anger) when we see that by it we lose our very being (our existence).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD." [33]

Perhaps he means that if a disagreement is found between two wise persons, and they cannot reach a decision, they pray and seek the will of God, then cast a lot, and the flood accepts the result of the lot.

In the division of the Promised Land the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: "Notwithstanding the land shall be divided by lot: according to the names of the tribes of their fathers they shall inherit. According to the lot shall the possession thereof be divided between many and few" (Num 26:55-56).

The lot was used to discover Achan, who disobeyed the Lord and took spoil and hid it (Josh 7:16-18), and the sailors were able to discover Jonah's disobedience to God (Jon 1:7). And in choosing a disciple in place of Judas, the disciples cast lots, and it fell upon Matthias (Acts 1:23-26).
* "The Apostle explains in (Acts 1:23-26) that if we use it (the casting of lots) with absolute faith, together with prayers, it will clearly reveal the will of God."

Origen Some see that after the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the Church there was no longer any need for the lot; rather, by prayer and fasting the men of God consult together under the guidance of His Holy Spirit to know His divine will.
Who is there to care for me but You!
* My soul blesses You for Your surpassing love.
You set me in Your image and likeness, and gave me freedom!
In the fullness of my freedom my depths cry out to You:
Take over my life and lead me.
There is none to sanctify me but Your Holy Spirit.
Nor any to justify me but You, nor any to open his arms to me but the holy Father!
O Holy Trinity, You are everything to me!
* You gave me mind and heart, but who sanctifies my scales but You.
Without You all the standards of my soul are disturbed.
Without You I cannot distinguish truth from falsehood!
Tame my soul with all its powers, and my body with all its members.
* Lead my thoughts, my intention and my conscience, so that my depths may walk in the spirit of uprightness.
And the light of truth shines within me!
* What shall I offer You? What shall I render to You for Your love?
You do not ask for sacrifices or offerings, and You have no need of praises and hymns of glory!
But in Your love You ask for my whole heart!
Take possession of me, that I may possess You, O Goodness itself!
* Break into my stony, haughty heart, that it may melt with Your love and be crushed in humility by Your grace!
May it be filled with love for You and for all humanity.
May it bear Your fear, so that it turns neither to the right nor to the left.
* Declare Your dwelling within me, so that the enemy of good may not come near me.
Indeed, may even my enemies be at peace with me!
* May my soul be satisfied by Your dwelling, so that it desires nothing but Your righteousness!
Fill me with the spirit of power, that I may carry within me the authority of the Spirit.
Every word that comes out of my mouth has its power, because You keep my mouth by Your power.
Every thought that passes through me will not dwell in me without Your command.
My heart is turned into a throne like the heavenly one.
And my words and deeds proceed in a manner worthy of Your Kingdom!
* Your dwelling in me leads my feelings, so I give honor to whom honor is due.
And I submit to the authorities with joy of heart!
* I ask nothing of men!
But I respect every person, and esteem every gift!
I desire that the whole earth become heaven!
And men angels!
* My depths cry out to You:
Grant all humanity the wisdom that sits by Your throne..
Grant all understanding and enlightenment, that all may perceive the riches of Your surpassing divine providence!
* When shall I see all men filled with love?
Their mouths dripping honey, and their souls filled with sweetness and pleasantness?
They walk in You, O true Way, so that no one is deceived by the devil's crooked ways.
All work in the spirit of love.
And injustice and violence have no place, nor lying any room among us!
* Sanctify all, O Longsuffering One, that all may become kings and priests to God Your Father.
To You be glory and thanksgiving, O Maker of good things!
To You be praise, O You who care for all Your creation!
"Better is a dry morsel, and peace therewith, than an house full of sacrifices with strife" [1]

It is clear that he is speaking of a church community "full of sacrifices." If the Church of the Old Testament was occupied with many kinds of sacrifices, among them the peace offering (Lev 3:1-17), which is "a sweet savour unto the LORD" (Lev 13:5, 16), the subject of God's pleasure is the reconciliation of man with his Creator as with his brethren, that is, practical love.

Thus it is fitting for every believer, when he offers a sacrifice of thanksgiving to God, that God will not be pleased with it as long as he carries in his heart hatred toward his brother. Often a person, a family or a church is occupied with enormous activities, but without inner peace; it is fitting for the person to withdraw for a while, to sit quietly with God, to draw from the divine love and to have his heart overflow with love for the salvation of all humanity.

God drew Moses out of the midst of Pharaoh's palace, with all its activities, banquets and possibilities, to live in a barren wilderness for 40 years, enjoying a dry morsel and peace with God, rather than living in Pharaoh's palace amid abundant feasts with strife.

And Elijah withdrew to the brook Cherith (1 Kgs 17), and left everyone suffering drought for three years and a half, that all might experience the dry morsel and be reconciled to God as to themselves, rather than enjoy good things with strife.

Let us withdraw for a while from being occupied with the many church activities, to sit with God as members of the household of God, so that we may enjoy peace with Him, and this peace may be reflected on our relationship with our brethren, and even on the church activities themselves.

The Apostle says: "Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ" (Rom 5:1). "Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord" (Heb 12:14).

* True peace is from above. As long as we are bound to the body, we bear a yoke of many things that weary us. Seek peace, then, and be freed from the troubles of this world. Acquire a quiet mind and a calm, untroubled soul, not stirred by the passions and not drawn by false teachings, and so defy the acceptance of their enticements, that you may receive "the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts" (Phil 4:7). Whoever seeks peace seeks Christ, for He Himself is our peace, who makes the two one new man (Eph 2:14), making peace through the blood of His cross, whether on earth or in heaven.
St. Basil the Great * In the house of God, in the Church of Christ, men dwell with one mind, and continue in harmony and simplicity.

* They continue together in prayer, declaring earnestly and in agreement in their prayers that God dwells with those who are of one mind in the house. Only those who are in agreement in their prayers enter the divine house.

* God has commanded us to be peacemakers, in unity and of one mind in His house... and He wants us, since we have been born again, to continue thus. Since we have become children of God, we remain in the peace of God, and since we have the one Spirit, we have also the one heart and the one mind.
God does not accept the sacrifice of the quarrelsome, but commands him to leave the altar and first be reconciled with his brother, for God is pleased with the prayers of the peacemaker.

St. Cyprian the Martyr * For the Lord makes men of one mind to dwell in a house. Hence love alone can endure without disturbance among those who have one purpose and one mind, who together want and refuse the same things.
Father Joseph

entries.section: 2. The wise man enjoys the inheritance

paragraphs.text: "A wise servant shall have rule over a son that causeth shame, and shall have part of the inheritance among the brethren" [2]

He compares a wise man who knows how to manage matters well with a son who behaves badly. Because of the wisdom and faithfulness of the servant, a man may allow him to be a partner with his sons in the inheritance, as one of the members of his household, while he may give little to the foolish son who is unable to act well.

It was in the mind of Abraham to give all that he had as an inheritance to his faithful and wise servant Eliezer (Gen 15:2), had God not given him Isaac. Abraham trusted the servant and entrusted to him all the affairs of his house, whereas Absalom the son rebelled against his father David, and sought nothing less than his neck.
"The fining pot is for silver, and the furnace for gold: but the LORD trieth the hearts" [3]

Afflictions and sufferings for believers are like the fining pot and the furnace for purifying gold and silver. As the psalmist says: "For thou, O God, hast proved us: thou hast tried us, as silver is tried. Thou broughtest us into the net; thou laidst affliction upon our loins. Thou hast caused men to ride over our heads" (Ps 66:10-12). As the Lord says to the house of Jacob: "Behold, I have refined thee, but not with silver; I have chosen thee in the furnace of affliction. For mine own sake, even for mine own sake, will I do it: for how should my name be polluted? and I will not give my glory unto another" (Isa 48:10-11).

The goldsmith knows the degree of heat required for the gold in his hands, and the length of time he allows the gold in the fining pot. His eyes remain fixed on the gold in the fining pot, occupied with nothing else, until he pours it out of the pot, pure from impurities. So God will not allow us to be tried beyond what we can bear, but knows perfectly what is for our purity and edification, and His eyes remain in the midst of the affliction, caring for our sanctification and our purification from every impurity.

* We know that even the saints, God permits their bodies to fall under the authority of Satan and many calamities to come upon them, and this is on account of slips (for their chastening), because the divine mercy cannot endure that there be in them any filth or defilement until the day of judgment, so He purifies them from every impurity, presenting them to eternity like refined gold or silver, no longer in need of purification. For God says: "And purely purge away thy dross... and take away all thy tin... afterward thou shalt be called, The city of righteousness, the faithful city" (Isa 1:25-26). And also, as silver is tried in the fining pot and gold in the furnace, so the Lord trieth the hearts (Prov 17:3). And also "for whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth" (Heb 12:6).
Father Serenus * How glorious are sufferings! By them we are made like His death!

As the refiner of gold throws the piece of gold into the furnace to endure the fire for a while until he sees that it is purified, so God permits humanity to be tested by afflictions until it is purified and obtains great benefit... Let us not be troubled or despair when trials come upon us. For just as the refiner of gold knows the time that the gold should be left in the furnace, and takes it out at the appointed time, and does not leave it any longer in the fire lest it be spoiled and burned, how much more does God know this. So when He sees that we have been purified more, He releases us from our trials lest we be cast down and cast out because of the increase of our evils.

When something comes upon us that we did not expect, let us not murmur nor let our hearts faint, but let us bear with God, who knows these things exactly, so that He may test our hearts by fire as He pleases; therefore He does this with a purpose, for the benefit of those who are tried. For this reason the wise man commands us to submit to God in all things, for He knows perfectly when to bring us out of the furnace of evil (Wisdom of Joshua 1:1-2).
Let us submit to Him continually, and thank Him constantly, bearing everything with contentment, whether He grants us blessings or offers us chastenings. For the latter are a kind of blessing.
