For the physician is not only a physician when he allows us to bathe (in the baths)... or to go to the delightful gardens, but also when he uses the scalpel and the knife!
And the father is a father not only when he caresses his son, but also when he disciplines and punishes him...

And since we know that God is more tender than all physicians, it is not for us to inquire into His dealings, nor to demand an account from Him about them, but He does what seems good in His eyes. We do not distinguish whether He releases us from trial or chastens us, for by either way He wishes to restore us to health and make us partners with Him, and He knows our various needs, and what suits each one of us, and how, and in what way we must be saved.
Let us follow Him wherever He commands us, and not think much whether He commands us to walk an easy and smooth way or a hard and rough way.

St. John Chrysostom * If you are gold, why do you fear the fire, since in the furnace the dross is burned and you come out pure? And if you are wheat, why do you dread the threshing, though you do not appear as what you are except by it, when the "chaff" is removed from you and your origin and honor appear?
St. Augustine
"A wicked doer giveth heed to false lips; and a liar giveth ear to a naughty tongue" [4]

When the heart conceals evil within it, the ears are ready to hear the voice of the enemy of good, that is, the lip of iniquity and its deceptive words; but if the heart is upright, it knows the voice of the enemy of good and refuses even to converse with him. In other words, it is fitting for us not to blame Satan, who casts his nets to catch us, but to blame our hearts, which have turned aside and become ready to respond to the devil's tricks and to take pleasure in his evil thoughts.

In the same way, when the false prophets prophesied falsely and the priests ruled wickedly, the wicked people responded to them: "The prophets prophesy falsely, and the priests bear rule by their means; and my people love to have it so" (Jer 5:31). A person finds pleasure and enjoyment when he meets those like himself, and responds to them. The liar is pleased with the company of liars, and the adulterer responds from the depths of his being to the conversations of adulterers... and so the sinner finds what he can justify himself with and set his conscience at ease by sharing with those who practice the same sin, and on the other hand the wicked support one another in practicing evil.
5 Whoso mocketh the poor reproacheth his Maker: and he that is glad at calamities shall not be unpunished. 6 Children's children are the crown of old men; and the glory of children are their fathers.
"Whoso mocketh the poor reproacheth his Maker: and he that is glad at calamities shall not be unpunished" [5]

God permits the existence of the poor and needy among humanity so that man may practice his tenderness and love toward his brother; the rich man needs to give, and the poor man gives thanks for the gift of giving which God grants to the rich, so that both groups live in a spirit of love, agreement and harmony together, and mutual respect.

It is fitting for the rich man not to despise the poor, for many of the poor are richer than the rich, since by faith they possess within them the Lord Christ, the treasure of knowledge and all learning, and they cherish God's fatherhood to them as a precious treasure, and surpassing eternal glories are prepared for them. Whoever mocks the poor despises these free divine gifts offered to all.

* In the Church a person is rich if he is rich in faith, for the believer possesses a whole world of riches. Is it strange that the believer owns the world, since he possesses the inheritance of Christ, which is more precious than the world? "Ye were redeemed with the precious blood" - this is certainly said to all, and not to the rich alone.

St. Ambrose * "Whoso mocketh the poor reproacheth his Maker." Why? Because God is the Creator of the poor. He who is cruel, without humanity, so that he laughs instead of being bound to compassion, since he who sins thus is punished for it. This person perishes because he sins against God's high providence and wisdom.

St. John Chrysostom If God permits a person or a nation some calamity or affliction, whoever rejoices at the calamity of another falls himself and finds no support from heaven, because he did not have mercy on his brother. The sin of Edom was that it rejoiced over its brethren when they fell into captivity for their chastening (Obad 12-16).

St. Ambrose, while he was a bishop, feared lest, having become a Christian and been ordained a bishop, he might perish by condemning some sinner, so he always remembered his weaknesses and set them before his eyes, not to despair but to be tender toward sinners. He says:

[I know that I was not worthy to be called a bishop, for I had devoted my life to the world, but by Your grace I have become what I am. And I am in truth the least of all bishops, and the lowest in worthiness. Do not permit him who was lost before his call to the priesthood to be lost when he has become a priest.

First grant me to know how to weep with all my inner being over those who sin. This is the greatest virtue, for it is written: "Thou shouldest not have rejoiced over the children of Judah in the day of their destruction; neither shouldest thou have spoken proudly in the day of distress" (Obad 13). Grant me always, when I learn of the sin of a fallen man, to suffer with him, and not to rebuke him haughtily, but to grieve and weep, for in weeping for another I weep for myself, saying: "She hath been more righteous than I" (Gen 38:26).]
"Children's children are the crown of old men; and the glory of children are their fathers" [6]

There is nothing that gladdens heaven itself like the family that bears the icon of heaven, where every member sees practically in the other members his glory, honor and riches. The old man does not utter a wounding word against the new generation (his children's children), not even in his thought, but sees in them his crown and glory. And the young man does not despise the former generation (his parents), but honors it in a spirit of obedience.

Practical love and mutual respect turn the home into heaven, and the family into the household of God, and all touch the promise of the Lord Christ: "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them" (Mt 18:20). And where the Lord Christ dwells, all gather together as in heaven from all nations, tongues, tribes and peoples, from all cultures and all ages, and there is no problem of a gulf between generations, but each one sees the reflection of Christ's splendor in the others.
* It is said, "Children's children are the crown of old men; and the glory of children is their father." Our glory is the Father of all, and the crown of the whole Church is Christ.
St. Clement of Alexandria

entries.section: 6. Let the believer's speech be befitting

paragraphs.text: "Excellent speech becometh not a fool:
much less do lying lips a prince." [7]

Some differ in the translation of the Greek word translated here "excellent"; some translate it in the sense of loftiness or sublimity, and others say that it carries the sense of haughtiness and pride. If it is not fitting for the fool to utter lofty and glorious things, then all the more it is not fitting for a noble, a ruler or a leader to bring forth a lying word from his lips.

When Saul prophesied among the prophets, "the people said one to another, What is this that is come unto the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?" (1 Sam 10:11), this became a proverb spoken when a fool utters lofty things. But the opposite proverb is, in the opinion of some, Abraham, the father of fathers, who denied that Sarah was his wife, for his great station and position made this behavior unbecoming to him (Gen 20:1-13).

entries.section: 7. Giving is the law of the house of love

paragraphs.text: 8 A gift is as a precious stone in the eyes of him that hath it: whithersoever it turneth, it prospereth. 9 He that covereth a transgression seeketh love; but he that repeateth a matter separateth very friends.
"A gift is as a precious stone in the eyes of him that hath it: whithersoever it turneth, it prospereth" [8]

If the gift is bound with inner love and humility, it has its own value in the eyes of the one who receives it. The Holy Scripture distinguishes between a gift and a bribe (Prov 17:24); the first is to win a spirit of love and affection, while the second is to pervert the ways of justice, or to obtain things to which we have no right, that is, unlawful things.

Jacob's gift to Esau removed the anger and the desire for revenge from Esau (Gen 33:4), and Jonathan's gift to David revealed the attachment of his soul to him, and his love for him as his own soul (1 Sam 18:1-4).

entries.section: 7. Giving is the law of the house of love

paragraphs.text: "He that covereth a transgression seeketh love; but he that repeateth a matter separateth very friends" [9]

We begin every congregational, family or individual (personal) prayer by offering a sacrifice of thanksgiving to God, the Maker of good things, "for He has covered us." If the Holy One, who cannot endure sin, covers us in order to lift us up with the spirit of hope from our sins, and brings us into His sanctuaries, how fitting it is for His children also to imitate Him, and cover their brethren in order that they may enjoy the holy life. "Charity shall cover the multitude of sins" (1 Pet 4:8; compare Prov 10:12).

Covering others does not mean flattery or indulgence toward sin, but in a spirit of love, humility and meekness it is necessary to pray for the fallen, that God may cover them and us when we always return to Him. It is also possible to speak quietly with the fallen without wounding their feelings.

Perhaps among the most beautiful examples of speaking with sinners is the prophet Jonathan and his dialogue with David the king and prophet for his repentance, where he spoke with him secretly, away from the eyes of others, and with his frankness and firmness he opened before him the doors of hope (2 Sam 12).
But whoever "repeateth a matter" (gossip), that is, publicizes the fallen, going about exposing their sins before others, destroys love!

* "Ye are the salt of the earth" (Mt 5:13). The properties of salt are many: it makes the insipid delicious, removes the moisture that produces stench, and firms what is soft. So you, draw people and firm up their softness, and warn them lest they incline to hypocrisy.

As salt preserves itself and others without corruption and stench, so you be concerned for the souls of the sons of men lest they stink in sin. He called love salt by saying: "Ye are the salt of the earth," that is, you are the love of the earth. So you must be lovers of all people, and be at peace with one another.

Ibn al-Salibi * It was said of St. Macarius that he became, as it is written, an earthly god; for as God covers the world, so Abba Macarius covered the faults of his brethren which he saw as though he did not see them, and the things which he heard as though he had heard nothing.

* It was said of St. Macarius that a cherub accompanied him from the day he began his ascetic life in the wilderness, strengthening him and giving him power to endure asceticism, and he grew in this every day, advancing in adornment with virtue, so that his good reputation spread throughout the whole Roman Empire and the regions of the East, for in truth he drew everyone to himself for the sake of the practical Gospel life, because of the fragrant aroma of his lofty ascetic labors, until he snatched a multitude of people from perdition so that they obtained eternal life. And our Lord Jesus Christ granted him the gift of seeing the sins of people like oil placed in a glass vessel, and he covered them all, imitating God.

The Paradise of the Fathers * Guard your ears from hearing talk of gossip and backbiting, so that your hearts may be pure, for if the ears hear unclean talk, the purity of the heart cannot be kept without defilement.

St. Macarius the Great * Nothing is worse for a person than condemnation, for from it he advances to evils and falls into evils; for he who condemns his brother in his heart speaks of him with his tongue and examines his works and conduct, and leaves off looking at what would amend himself, and busies himself with what does not concern him instead of what does concern him, and from here arise contempt, gossip, blame and reproach, and then the divine help forsakes him and he falls into the very thing for which he condemned his brother.

Gossip is for a person to tell of the personal sin that his brother has done, saying that he did such and such. But condemnation is for a person to tell of a bad character trait his brother has, saying that he is a thief or a liar or the like, so he judges him as continuing in this trait and not giving it up, and this is a very grave matter.

Therefore the Lord likened the sin of condemnation to the beam, and the sin condemned to the mote, and on that account the tax collector was justified despite his iniquities and the Pharisee was condemned for having condemned another, despite his almsgiving, fasting and prayer and his thanking God for that.

For judging God's creation befits God and not us, and the condemnation and justification of each one belongs to God alone, for He alone knows the secret of every man and his public affairs, and the judgment that is due in every matter and on every person.

St. Dorotheus * By gossip the serpent seduced Eve and brought her out of Paradise, and Adam with her; so exactly like the serpent, whoever falls upon his companion destroys the one who listens to him, and his own soul is not saved.
Abba Sisoes

entries.section: 8. Accepting rebuke and benefiting from it

paragraphs.text: 10 A reproof entereth more into a wise man than an hundred stripes into a fool. 11 An evil man seeketh only rebellion: therefore a cruel messenger shall be sent against him.
"A reproof entereth more into a wise man than an hundred stripes into a fool" [10]

The wise man always seeks his spiritual growth and progress in everything; therefore he does not resist a word of rebuke or constructive criticism. But the fool always thinks that he is right, wiser and more understanding than everyone. The first benefits from gentle, purposeful words of rebuke, and the second is not affected even by stripes, for he is rebellious and stubborn, stiff-necked and haughty.

An example of this is Pharaoh, upon whom fell not a hundred stripes, but the ten plagues, each more severe than the one before; and yet, even if he was affected for moments, he returned to the hardness of his heart and his stubbornness. He did not benefit from the plagues until the last moments of his life, when he threw himself with his army into the waters so that all died by drowning!
We should not wonder if God often permits trials for His saints, as though they were a rebuke He offers them as wise men ready to listen to His divine voice during the trials.

It is said that Father Hilarion went to St. Abba Anthony when he was about 15 years old, and for only two months he contemplated his manner of life and his dignified conduct, his diligence in prayer, his humility in dealing with his disciples, his strictness in rebuking, and his counsels.
* Must one who rebukes someone tell him the reason for rebuking him?
If you do not tell him, how can he amend his condition?
If you do not show the wounded man his wound, how will he be healed?

Therefore it is better to tell him; but if the souls are weak and cannot hear, we try to tell them in a veiled way and take their weakness into account, just as wine is given to the sick diluted with water, but to the healthy pure wine; so if you find him able to hear, it is better to make him aware of his mistake.
If, when you rebuke someone, you yield to anger, you are thereby satisfying your own passion (that of sin), and you must not destroy yourself in order to save others.

entries.section: 8. Accepting rebuke and benefiting from it

paragraphs.text: St. Macarius the Great "An evil man seeketh only rebellion: therefore a cruel messenger shall be sent against him" [11]

Here he speaks of the "rebellious evil man," for there are wicked people who fell into evil because of weakness or because of circumstances surrounding them; these need tenderness with gentleness and kindness together with frankness.
But the rebellious evil man needs a cruel messenger, because he does not accept the word of gentle, tender rebuke.

The Lord says through the prophet Isaiah: "Wash you, make you clean; put away the evil of your doings from before mine eyes; cease to do evil; learn to do well.. Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool. If ye be willing and obedient, ye shall eat the good of the land: but if ye refuse and rebel, ye shall be devoured with the sword: for the mouth of the LORD hath spoken it." (Isa 1:16-20)
"Let a bear robbed of her whelps meet a man, rather than a fool in his folly" [12]

To enter into a dialogue or dispute with the rebellious evil man is of no avail, for meeting a ravening beast whose young have been taken from it, such as the bear, is easier than meeting a foolish fool in a state of fury.
Always flee from every person who does not cease from arguing in his speech.
* If the soul withdraws from all debate, confusion and disturbance, the Spirit of God enters into it, and the one that was barren becomes fruitful.

Father Pimen But the wise friend is longsuffering in his discussions, * Abba Anthony was wise, of a brilliant mind, perceiving the reality of people with a penetrating insight, so that those who came to him were filled with amazement to find that he had perceived them as they truly were, despite his seclusion and his distance from people. And his speech was seasoned with heavenly salt, so that his hearers felt a heartfelt joy at the spiritual perfection he had attained, which endeared souls to him and drew hearts to him.

Likewise Abba Anthony was distinguished by patience and endurance in discussion, listening to everything said to him and answering it with all balance, so it is no wonder that it was said that God had set him up as a spiritual physician for his countrymen and for all who gathered around him.
St. Palladius
"Whoso rewardeth evil for good, evil shall not depart from his house" [13]
If it is not fitting for the believer to meet evil with evil, what if he meets good with evil? Such a person will not have evil depart from his house, or his family, or his grandchildren.
"The beginning of strife is as when one letteth out water: therefore leave off contention before it flows out." [14]

Negligence over a small spark from a match can kindle fires that spread to burn forests reaching thousands of acres. And negligence over a slight wound can multiply and lead to the death of the whole man. And a small breach in a trench, if neglected, can cause a flow of abundant water that cannot be faced. So if we neglect a sudden anger, and the sun goes down upon our wrath, it is difficult to recognize the bitter consequences in our life on earth and our eternity. Therefore the Lord Christ commands us: "Agree with thine adversary quickly, whiles thou art in the way with him" (Mt 5:25). And the Apostle commands us: "Let not the sun go down upon your wrath" (Eph 4:26).

The days of our sojourning are few, short and evil, so let us not waste them in strife. As Abba Aphrahat says: [It is fitting for those who draw near to God to look to Him alone, and take refuge in Him with such piety, so that they pay no heed to insult, even if they are wronged tens of thousands of times.]

* He who is wrathful is devoid of longsuffering and love; he is quickly troubled by trifling words, and stirs up strife over a petty, worthless matter, and wherever he has no place he throws himself in... Who does not lament for such a one? He is rejected by God and men.
St. Ephrem the Syrian

entries.section: 12. Justice is the law of the house

paragraphs.text: "He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both are abomination to the LORD" [15]

It is said: "Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness; that put bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter!" (Isa 5:20). If God is the Truth, then whoever exchanges truth for falsehood, good for evil, and light for darkness is like one who has denied God Himself, the greatest Good and the eternal Light. So to acquit the unjust and to condemn the innocent is an insult directed against God Himself.
16 Wherefore is there a price in the hand of a fool to get wisdom, seeing he hath no understanding? 17 A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
"Wherefore is there a price in the hand of a fool
to get wisdom, seeing he hath no understanding?" [16]
Why does the fool hold a price in his hand? Does he want to buy wisdom or acquire it with money? While his heart is not in wisdom, and he does not seek it for its own sake.

This is the position of some rich men whose children refuse to learn, and they think they are able to use their wealth and money to get their children into colleges. They may be able to buy academic degrees by one means or another, but their children's hearts do not seek learning or knowledge, and do not care about progress!
"A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity" [17]

The true Friend is our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lover of all humanity, who came as a physician for the sick to heal them, and not to condemn them or despise them. And He was born bodily, that is, became incarnate and became man for adversity, that is, to bear the Cross for the sake of the whole world! It is said of Him:
"Having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end" (Jn 13:1).
"Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world" (Jn 1:19).
"I came not to judge the world, but to save the world" (Jn 12:47).
"And he is the propitiation for our sins: and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world" (1 Jn 2:2).
"They that are whole need not a physician, but they that are sick" (Mk 2:17; Lk 5:13).
"Henceforth I call you not servants; for the servant knoweth not what his lord doeth: but I have called you friends" (Jn 15:15).
"He hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows" (Isa 53:4).

* When Jesus is attacked for mingling with sinners and choosing a despised tax collector as His disciple, one of them asks: What benefit can be reached from this? Only the salvation of sinners! The blame of Jesus for mingling with sinners is like blaming a physician for condescending and toiling to find substances with a difficult smell for the healing of the sick.

St. Gregory of Nazianzus * Since there is no perfect righteous man, Christ did not come to call those who are not here (in the world), but the present multitudes of sinners with whom the world is filled, remembering the psalmist's saying: "Save, Lord; for the godly man ceaseth" (Ps 12:1).

St. Jerome * He showed them that in His present coming into the world He did not come as a judge but as a physician, and did what a physician must practice, by mingling with those who are in need of healing.
St. Cyril the Great
"A man void of understanding striketh hands, and becometh surety in the presence of his friend" [18]

The wise man often warns against rushing to pledge oneself as surety for another without counting the cost and the means of repayment (Prov 6:1-5; 11:15). Paul became surety for Onesimus, and was ready to pay the debt himself (Phlm 18-19). Judah also became surety for Benjamin (Gen 42:17; 44:32). But our Christ, knowing our inability to pay the debt, paid it in advance on the Cross, so that by living faith we might have the right to enter into the divine embrace.

His Holy Spirit who dwells in us also intercedes for us, presenting the surety which the Lord paid on the Cross for whoever accepts His love and responds to it. "Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them" (Heb 7:25).

"The Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered. And he that searcheth the hearts knoweth what is the mind of the Spirit, because he maketh intercession for the saints according to the will of God" (Rom 8:26-27).
"Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us" (Rom 8:34).
* When the Holy Spirit sees our spirit wrestling with the flesh, and the spirit withdrawing to the flesh, the Holy Spirit stretches out His hands and helps us in our weakness.

Origen Here we wish to make clear that some Fathers see that the intercession of the Holy Spirit here does not mean the essence of the Holy Spirit, but the grace of the Holy Spirit dwelling in us, and the love that has come to us by the Holy Spirit, who directs the prayers of the believers so that they ask for themselves and for their brethren according to the will of God, and what is for their benefit. St. Augustine calls this divine grace "the gift of prayer."

19 He loveth transgression that loveth strife: and he that exalteth his gate seeketh destruction. 20 He that hath a froward heart findeth no good: and he that hath a perverse tongue falleth into mischief.
"He loveth transgression that loveth strife: and he that exalteth his gate seeketh destruction" [19]

The rebellious man finds pleasure in strife, and satisfaction in foolish, unconstructive argument, and in his rebellion he exalts himself and prides himself on his opinions like one who raises his gates high, so he destroys himself by himself.
"He that hath a froward heart findeth no good: and he that hath a perverse tongue falleth into mischief" [20]
What a person sows with his twisted heart and his changeable tongue he does not reap good, but evil.
The twisted heart cannot offer a holy, upright tongue, but a deceitful, changeable tongue, by which he loses his friends and provokes his enemies, and causes himself countless troubles.
"He that begetteth a fool doeth it to his sorrow: and the father of a fool hath no joy" [21]
There is no bitterness that befalls a person like having a foolish and senseless son (or daughter), so that joy cannot steal into his heart.

* God is called Father, and God's love for humanity is called mother, and it is the cause of the divine Incarnation and His suffering for us. Although God is our Father, He does not rejoice in one who has received adoption without having knowledge of the divine wisdom and knowledge, and who commits evil. But the prudent son pleases his mother, that is, God's love toward humanity. It is she who brings us to God the Father as undernourished (hungry) children longing for strong spiritual food. This is accomplished so that His Son - Jesus Christ - who became like a brother to us (Hab 2:17), may make us citizens of His kingdom, by word and deed, and also our mother the Church, who was betrothed to God the Father by the Holy Spirit. She bears sons and daughters to Him eternally. And those who learn heavenly wisdom and knowledge please God our Father and His Church our mother. But she grieves and laments over the unlearned who do not want to repent and be saved, but prefer to continue in evil.
Origen

entries.section: 16. The fountain of joy in the house of love

paragraphs.text: 21 He that begetteth a fool doeth it to his sorrow: and the father of a fool hath no joy. 22 A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones.

entries.section: 16. The fountain of joy in the house of love

paragraphs.text: "A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones" [22].

There is nothing that breaks down the body of man like gloom, anxiety and bitterness of soul. But if the heart is filled with the joy of the Spirit, the soul rejoices, and its rejoicing is reflected even on the health of the body.

Offering a sacrifice of joy, thanksgiving and praise daily, day and night, turns the believer into something like a rejoicing angel, who defies not only sickness but even bodily death! The believer repeats: "For thou hast delivered my soul from death, mine eyes from tears, and my feet from falling. I will walk before the LORD in the land of the living" (Ps 116:8-9).
* Every gospel brings joy for a good reason.

Origen * He did not fear but rejoiced to see him, because in him is the love that casteth out fear (1 Jn 4:18). He did not say: "He rejoiced because he saw," but he said: "He rejoiced because he sees," believing under all circumstances, and rejoicing in the hope of seeing with understanding. "And he saw it, and was glad"... If those whose bodily eyes were opened by the Lord rejoiced, what joy was his who saw with the eyes of his soul the ineffable Light, the Word who dwells (in the Father), the splendor that dazzles the minds of the godly, the Wisdom that does not fall, God abiding in the Father, and at the same time saw Him coming in the flesh without withdrawing from the bosom of the Father? All this Abraham saw.
St. Augustine
"A wicked man taketh a gift out of the bosom to pervert the ways of judgment" [23]

Often the bribe (a gift with a wrong intention) blinds the eyes of those in authority, so they pass unjust judgments. Therefore it is not fitting to offer a bribe to obtain what we have no right to, nor to accept a bribe from anyone, lest we turn aside from truth and justice.

24 Wisdom is before him that hath understanding; but the eyes of a fool are in the ends of the earth. 25 A foolish son is a grief to his father, and bitterness to her that bare him. 26 Also to punish the just is not good, nor to strike princes for equity. 27 He that hath knowledge spareth his words: and a man of understanding is of an excellent spirit. 28 Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise: and he that shutteth his lips is esteemed a man of understanding.
"Wisdom is before him that hath understanding; but the eyes of a fool are in the ends of the earth" [24]

What occupies the mind of the wise and godly man is the knowledge of God and the heavenly mysteries, that he may walk by it, with it and to it. But the fool has no aim. His eyes roam right and left without purpose, so he can never come to the knowledge of the truth (2 Tim 3:7; 4:3-4).

"Wisdom is God's revelation of Himself to us; we acquire it, and so we carry divine wisdom and heavenly knowledge. St. Augustine sees that wisdom is the ability to taste spiritual realities, and enjoying the truth leads to the glory of God and worshiping Him with the fear of sons. St. John Chrysostom sees that wisdom is the Gospel, that is, the enjoyment of God's joyful plan of salvation. Knowledge, on the other hand, is departing from evil (Job 28:28), and offering the word of salvation to men.

St. Clement of Alexandria sees that the aim of the spiritual man who has knowledge (the Gnostic) is to know God (the Truth) and see Him face to face, that is, to pass over to the perfection of knowledge of divine things through faith, and this through the experience of a pure life and constant contemplation. If we have passed from paganism to faith, it is fitting for us to pass from faith to knowledge, to see God and know Him. This knowledge is a divine gift that we receive through the Son, by receiving Him and being made like Him; that is, through purity of heart we behold God and perceive what seems to others imperceptible.
* Gnosis, which is the knowledge and perception of present, future and past things as certain and trustworthy matters, is granted and declared by the Son of God, who is "Wisdom."
St. Clement of Alexandria A foolish son is a grief to his father, and bitterness to her that bare him." [25].

The wise man often repeats such a statement, affirming that negligence in guiding children reflects bitterness and grief upon the parents, as happened with Eli the priest, who, because of his negligence in bringing up his two sons, saw the two sons killed, the people defeated, and their father die.
"Also to punish the just is not good, nor to strike princes for equity" [26]
The perversion of justice on the part of a ruler, leader or judge, causing loss to an innocent person or insult to an upright noble, is a detestable thing.
"He that hath knowledge spareth his words: and a man of understanding is of an excellent spirit" [27]
The wise man, with all the knowledge he has, has few words, and they have their weight, their dignity, and also their clear purpose.
* Let your words be measured, reckoned by yourself, knowing that you will give account to God for what comes out of your mouth, including jesting or a word that is not for edification.
St. Pachomius * Whoever seeks to know what the will of God is seeks wisdom, and shows himself prudent.

Whoever curtails his words to enter into knowledge - if one seeks wisdom, desiring to learn something about wisdom, while another does not seek wisdom, since he does not want to learn anything about wisdom, and even prevents his relatives from doing this, the first is more prudent than the latter.
St. Hippolytus of Rome "Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise: and he that shutteth his lips is esteemed a man of understanding" [28]

Since fools and the foolish are marked by much speaking, without reckoning or purpose, and it is very hard for them to confess their folly, therefore if they keep silent they are counted wise, and if they close their lips they are considered men of understanding.

* As in a house when the door is shut, the members hidden in it are not known, so in general we say, if a fool holds to keeping his composure (in silence), it does not appear whether he is wise or foolish. This happens as long as he does not practice a work that reveals what is in the mind of that silent one... And it was said of Solomon: "A fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise."
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Let the Kingdom of love be established within me!
* Let Your temple be established in my depths, the spacious house of love, to embrace all in it.
What sacrifice shall I offer You, and what offering shall be smelled as a sweet savour, but the sacrifice of praise and the offering of love?
Grant me Your love, that my heart may be filled with Your surpassing peace!
I will enjoy peace with You and with Your creation beloved to You.
* Break into my heart, O Beloved, for it is Your house, most dear to You.
You deposit in it from the treasures of Your knowledge and Your mysteries, so that I may truly become a heavenly storehouse!
* That I may live with You, O Crucified One.
That I may find sweet the fellowship of Your sufferings, and receive the honor of being crucified with You!
For there is no way to fellowship in Your glories except by accepting Your sufferings with joy and rejoicing!
* Your dwelling in me establishes Your righteousness within me.
Let evil have no place in my heart, nor lying any room on my lips!
I enjoy Your sublime mind, so I honor every poor man, and do not despise anyone.
I do not rejoice at anyone's calamity, but desire to bear his burdens!
I see You transfigured in the lives of my fathers, and my soul exults.
And I look to You working in the new generation, and I am filled with hope.
* My heart is opened to give to all.
As for the bribe, my soul abhors it!
I see You covering over me, so I desire to cover over my brethren.
Not a word of slander goes out from my lips.
* I feel Your tenderness in Your hands, even in the midst of my pains and tribulations.
I sense the warmth of Your fatherhood amid all events.
My heart is always drawn to You, Your gifts overwhelm me!
* I come to know You, O Truth, so I do not confuse light with darkness, nor mix righteousness with evil!
I possess You, O Wisdom of God, and ignorance flees from my depths.
I possess You, not with money, but by responding to Your love.
I possess You by the blood of Your Cross, You who suffered and bore the shame, to grant me the blessed, glorious life!
* I possess You, and my heart is turned into a joyful feast.
My soul exults in You, and my body is sanctified by Your grace.
And my insight is drawn up into Your heavens.
And I draw from Your mysteries without limit!

1 He that separateth himself seeketh his own desire; he is enraged at every counsel. 2 A fool hath no delight in understanding, but in the uncovering of his own heart. 3 When the wicked cometh, then cometh also contempt, and with ignominy reproach.
"He that separateth himself seeketh his own desire; he is enraged at every counsel" [1].

The Apostle Jude speaks to us of these separatists who in pride exalt themselves above their brethren, and seek to fulfill their desires and pleasures. "These are they who separate themselves, having no spirit (they do not have the Holy Spirit)" (Jude 19). These separate themselves from the divine truth and the holy congregation for the glory of themselves or to satisfy their desires, and not for the glory of God; these are stubborn, fanatical for their own ideas.
What occupies the thought of these separatists is to display their skill or intelligence or work, and not the edification of their souls and their progress, even in their study of the word of God.

These who separate themselves for the sake of their pleasures reject true wisdom, unlike those who separate themselves from evil and from sharing the wicked in their evils, for the sake of their purity in the Lord through their Church membership. As the Apostle Paul says: "Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you, and will be a Father unto you, and ye shall be my sons and daughters, saith the Lord Almighty" (2 Cor 6:17-18).
* These (separatists) are those who divide the believers from one another, under the influence of their unbelief. They cannot distinguish holy things on the one hand from dogs on the other.
St. Clement of Alexandria * The enemy of unity has no share in the love of God. Those who are outside the Church do not have the Holy Spirit.
St. Augustine It is fitting for the believer to separate himself from evil itself, not only by not committing it, but by not allowing his thought to converse with it.

* Some brethren asked an elder concerning the two previous sayings, saying: "If a man does not complete unclean thoughts, do they become void?" The elder said: "He means not only that he should not carry them out in his body, but also that he should not discuss them, for Abba Poemen taught that thoughts are not accomplished in deed except by negotiating with them and obeying them; so if a man abandons the cause and occasion that leads to the deed, he is freed from the thoughts and overcomes them, and so after a time of striving his heart is purified, his mind is enlightened, he is delivered from the sicknesses and rejoices in God."

* Abba Ammon of "Raithu" asked Abba Poemen about the unclean thoughts and vain desires that assail a man, and Abba Poemen said to him: "It is Satan's part to sow them in us, but our part is not to accept them."

Paradise of the Fathers * My children, flee from sin and endure unto death in keeping the Lord's commandments, and do not accept the counsel of the enemy to break any commandment however small, for the breaking of any commandment, small or great, angers God. I want your souls, my children, to be a perpetual dwelling place for God, so that you always think well of your neighbor, and none of you remembers evil against his brother or is moved with hatred against him, for the heart that thinks of evil and hatred cannot be a dwelling place for God.
St. Macarius the Great "A fool hath no delight in understanding, but in the uncovering of his own heart" [2]

If he who separates himself to satisfy his desires does not accept wise counsel, but relies on his own opinion alone, then he finds no pleasure in understanding; his pleasure is rather to carry out what is in his heart. Such a fool does not accept dialogue, and does not care for what profits him and what edifies others.
* In all that you do take counsel for yourself, for it is written: "It is folly to act without counsel" (cf. Prov 15:22), and if anyone asks you answer him, otherwise silence is better.

Abba Poemen * Some brethren with laymen visited Father "Felix" and begged him to say a word to them, but the elder remained silent. When they pressed him for a long time he said to them: "Do you want to hear a word?"
They said: "Yes, Father."

He said to them: "There is no more speech in these days, for when the brethren used to ask the counsel of the elders and do what was told them, God inspired the fathers with what to say; but now, because they ask and do not do what they hear, God has withdrawn the grace of speech from the elders, and they find nothing to say, because there is none who does, for the Psalmist says: "The LORD looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see if there were any that did understand, and seek God" (Ps 14:2).
When the brethren heard this they sighed and said: "Pray for us, our father."
Paradise of the Fathers "When the wicked cometh, then cometh also contempt, and with ignominy reproach" [3]

As the wicked fool clings to his opinion and refuses dialogue, he brings upon himself shame and reproach. For since he despises the opinions of others, others find no pleasure in him. But he who respects others and values their thoughts, and converses with them in love and in humility, the Holy Spirit of God, who works in the humble, gives him honor in the eyes of his brethren and those around him.
If sin is a reproach to any people (Prov 14:34), it is the shame of every man who insists on committing it. Sin is the way that brings down peoples as well as individuals to the shame of the pit.

When the hand of Pashur the son of Immer the priest was stretched out to smite Jeremiah the prophet and put him in the stocks, the divine sentence was issued against him that he be filled with fear and terror at what would befall him and his loved ones, and that they would fall into the Babylonian captivity, and there be buried in disgrace and shame (Jer 20:1-6).

* Believe this with piety and steadfastness: God does not forsake a person unless the person has indeed forsaken God. And although a person commits grave sins once and twice and three times, God continues to seek him, as the prophet says that by his returning he lives (Ex 33:11).

In any case, as he continues in his sins, despair is brought upon him by the multitude of his sins, and hardness occurs because of the despair. While inspired people despair because of their sins since they are small, these slight offenses increase, and crimes are even added to them, and they become a heap that swallows them, and when this happens what is written is fulfilled: "With the wicked cometh reproach."

Fr. Caesarius, Bishop of Arles * It is written: "When the sinner cometh into the depth of evil, he behaves with contempt" (Prov 18:3). They (the wicked) do not believe, as you see, so that what they have done cannot be forgiven them, and by this stone of despair they sink into deeper depths than they were in.

St. Augustine * When the wicked fall into the depths of evil, they lose all sense of decorum." It is a terrible thing, as you see, beloved, it is a terrible thing to fall between the teeth of Satan, I mean that the soul becomes like one who has fallen into a net, and like a wild boar falling into a snare of mire, caught by pleasure, it returns to its evil habits, and loses the full sense of the foul smell of sin. Therefore we must wake up and take heed, so that we do not allow an evil devil to find an entrance from the beginning, and put a cloud over our mind, and blind the keen insight of our understanding, as though he robbed us of the light of the sun, so that we do not see the rays of the Sun of righteousness, and so we fall into the pit.

St. John Chrysostom * The wicked mind is always in pain and weariness, for it either suffers calamities that come upon it or fears that they will come upon it from others. While it plans against relatives it is the more in terror that its relatives may plan against it... Even when it is at peace it suspects the plans which it deals with craftily, reckoning that there is no man who deals with it faithfully.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* The more these grave sins increase, the more the soul grows accustomed to them, and makes light of them. For it is said: "When the wicked has reached the depth of evils, he thinks of them with contempt."
Fr. John of Damascus

4 The words of a man's mouth are as deep waters, and the wellspring of wisdom as a flowing brook. 5 It is not good to accept the person of the wicked, to overthrow the righteous in judgment. 6 A fool's lips enter into contention, and his mouth calleth for strokes. 7 A fool's mouth is his destruction, and his lips are the snare of his soul. 8 The words of a talebearer are as sweet morsels, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly. 9 He also that is slothful in his work is brother to him that is a great waster.
"The words of a man's mouth are as deep waters, and the wellspring of wisdom as a flowing brook" [4]

When the Spirit of God dwells in the true believer in our Lord Jesus Christ, rivers of living water flow from his belly (Jn 7:38); this is the wellspring of wisdom that will never run dry. God reproached His people of old, saying: "For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water" (Jer 2:13).

* The word in the heart of man is deep waters, and a river and a flowing spring. Solomon means by deep waters "abundant waters." Many rivers can always overflow instead of one river. Or he says: they contain what is hidden and deep in them. Just as waters cannot be measured, so the word in the heart of the person who lives in the Lord is without limit. Therefore he uses "the word" in connection with knowledge. This is the person in whose heart a spring of water has gushed forth at the words of Jesus. He (Solomon) speaks of it as flowing, raining on the fields and watering them, so that they become fruitful.
St. John Chrysostom "It is not good to accept the person of the wicked, to overthrow the righteous in judgment" [5].

Since God wishes the Church to be an icon of heaven, and men to be ambassadors for Him, He insists on no partiality in judgment, so it is not permissible to justify the wicked, and fabricate charges against the righteous just; both are an abomination to the Lord, the just Judge. It is stated in Deuteronomy: "And I charged your judges at that time, saying, Hear your brethren, and judge righteously between every man and his brother, and the stranger that is with him. Ye shall not respect persons in judgment; but ye shall hear the small as well as the great; ye shall not be afraid of the face of man; for the judgment is God's" (Deut 1:16-17).

* Those who hear cases must judge with justice, and not accept bribes at the expense of the innocent, "for a gift doth blind the eyes of the wise, and pervert the words of the righteous" (Deut 16:19). Lest while seeking money they lose the soul. No one gets unjust gain without a just loss coming upon him. Where there is gain there is loss; the gain is in the money chest, but the loss is in the conscience.

Fr. Caesarius, Bishop of Arles This is what the Jewish people committed when they lifted up the face of the wicked Barabbas, for nothing but to condemn the Lord of glory, Jesus the Righteous, to crucifixion unjustly.
"A fool's lips enter into contention, and his mouth calleth for strokes" [6].

The lips of the fool (the foolish man) have no work but to call for the stirring up of contentions, so if the mouth of the righteous is a fountain of living waters, anointed with the anointing of the Holy Spirit, quenching the fires of anger, and pouring peace and coolness on stormy souls, then on the contrary the mouth of the fool is a source of troubles and disturbances, finding pleasure in stirring up quarrels and disputes.
"A fool's mouth is his destruction, and his lips are the snare of his soul" [7]
These contentions which the mouth of the fool stirs up in the lives of those around him recoil upon him, so that he suffers destruction, and falls into the nets he set for his brethren.
"The words of a talebearer are as sweet morsels, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly" [8]

The talebearer presents his words as a sweet morsel, so some find pleasure in listening to him, perhaps as a kind of amusement or to flatter the talebearer, but the listener suffers from these words, for they go down as into the chambers of his belly, and he does not know deliverance from their poisons.

* Abba Mark said: "Everything you say about your brother behind his back and cannot say in front of him is slander and defamation, and every concern that does not lead to the good of worship is a worldly concern."
* (Abba Isaiah) was asked what slander is, and he answered: "It is ignorance of the glory of God and hatred of others."
Paradise of the Fathers "He also that is slothful in his work is brother to him that is a great waster" [9].
Just as the wasteful or prodigal man squanders his money and spends it in the wrong places, so the careless or lazy or slack man squanders his precious time, counting it as dust of no value.

* Likewise, if strong hands do not try to carry the good works they have begun to the point of perfection, then mere slackness in diligence does not agree with what was accomplished at the beginning. Therefore Solomon says: "He also that is slothful in his work is brother to him that is a great waster" (Prov 18:9).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
10 The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe. 11 The rich man's wealth is his strong city, and as an high wall in his own conceit.
"The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe" [10]

Taking refuge in the name of the Lord is entering the divine fortress, in which he who accepts God's work in him takes shelter. But the unrepentant wicked man does not profit from the name of the Lord, because he uses it not for the edification of his soul, but for the accomplishment of earthly aims. As it is written in the Book of Acts: "Then certain of the vagabond Jews, exorcists, took upon them to call over them which had evil spirits the name of the Lord Jesus, saying, We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preacheth... And the evil spirit answered and said, Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are ye? And the man in whom the evil spirit was leaped on them, and overcame them, and prevailed against them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded" (Acts 19:13-16).
* The word "Jesus" is glorious and worthy of all worship and adoration. It is the name which is above every name.
Origen * The Head suffered in the place of a skull. What a great prophetic name! The same name reminds you to think of the Crucified One as not a mere man. He is the Head that has the power.

St. Cyril of Jerusalem * "Tell me, O thou whom my soul loveth." I call You so, because Your name is above every name (Phil 2:9). It is ineffable, and not comprehended by the human mind. Therefore Your name reveals Your goodness, and my relationship with You is spiritual.
St. Gregory of Nyssa "The rich man's wealth is his strong city, and as an high wall in his own conceit" [11].

While the true believer fortifies himself in the name of the Lord as in an impregnable stronghold, and clings to it as his treasure and his riches that satisfy his soul, the heart of the unbelieving rich man is bound to money, imagining that it gives him security and peace and satisfies all his needs forever. But soon wealth leaves its owner, or the man leaves it to depart from the world naked. As the Lord Christ says: "But woe unto you that are rich! for ye have received your consolation. Woe unto you that are full! for ye shall hunger" (Lk 6:24-25). As He also said: "How hard is it for them that trust in riches to enter into the kingdom of God! It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God" (Mk 10:24-25).
"Before destruction the heart of man is haughty, and before honour is humility" [12].

It is fitting for the believer to fix his eyes on God's gifts to him, for what he receives of spiritual or practical or material abilities, gifts and possibilities are holy gifts, so he thanks God and glorifies Him. As Mar Isaac the Syrian says: "There is no gift without increase except that which is without thanks." But he who counts what he has as the work of his own hands, denying the favor of God and His grace, loses himself as he may lose what is in his hands.
Humility is the fixing of the eyes on God who dwells in us, so we realize that through Him we enjoy everything and without Him we become nothing at all.

* Observe the tree, how it first inclines downward (the root) so that it may go upward. If it strikes its root down into the soil, it can raise its top toward heaven. Is it not through humility that you seek to rise? Without humility you will not reach the heights. Do you want to grow in the air without a root? Such is not growth but collapse.
St. Augustine
"He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him" [13]
The wise man often warns us against hasty judgments caused by rashness, by much speaking and by not listening to others.
How can we give a sound answer without listening carefully to the question put to us?
How can we win the one we speak with without attending to him with care?

The Word of God, who calls us to listen, came down to us to reveal that He listens to our petitions, and His longing to enter into dialogue with us. The Lord Christ listened to the Samaritan woman with long-suffering and gentleness without wounding her feelings. And He listened to the thief on the right who had formerly reproached Him. And He entered into dialogue with Abraham before the burning of Sodom and Gomorrah. And He called us: "Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD" (Isa 1:18).
"The spirit of a man will sustain his infirmity; but a wounded spirit who can bear?" [14]

If a member of the body is struck by an illness it can be cured, but if the soul is broken by despair or anxiety or pride and so on, the whole man is shattered, and needs the intervention of the hand of the Creator Himself to heal him and raise him up anew.

In the days of Nehemiah the walls of Jerusalem were broken down and its gates burned with fire, and also the walls of the hearts of the people and their inner gates were shattered. They needed a divine intervention, so all the people gathered themselves together as one man into the street, and Ezra the scribe read the Law from the morning until midday (Neh 8:3), and the ears of all the people were attentive unto the book of the Law, and Ezra blessed the LORD, the great God, and all the people answered, Amen, Amen. Nehemiah and Ezra the priest and the Levites that taught the people said: "Be not sorry: for the joy of the LORD is your strength" (Neh 8:10). Men, as sinners, need the presence of the word of God in their midst, and even within them, so that His joy becomes our strength!
There is no danger that strikes the being of man like deadly gloom, and there is no power that lifts up his whole being like the joy of the Spirit and the gladness of the divine presence.
* To hope in God from God, this is to love God, the possessor of grace.
* Hope drives man toward eternity, toward the future, in practical faith, and perseverance with joy and gladness amid sufferings.
* Let us listen and rejoice in hope even if the present is a life not loved but endured, for you will have strength to bear all its trials.
* We rejoice in hope, looking to the rest to come, so we walk with gladness amid the troubles.
St. Augustine * What is the hope of the Gospel but Christ? For He is our peace, who works all these things... and whoever does not believe in Christ loses everything.

* Hope is certainly like a strong rope let down from the heavens that helps our spirits, lifting him who holds it firmly above this world and the trials of this evil life; but if a man is weak and lets go of this holy cable, he falls at once, and is choked in the pit of evil.

* Nothing makes the soul so courageous and so fond of venturing as hope! And before we obtain the things we hope for, it gives us a reward, namely: "patient in tribulation." Before we obtain the things to come, you enjoy in the present life a great good through trials, for you become a patient and proven man...

Love makes things easy, and the Spirit helps, and hope enlightens, and trials refine you, making you proven, able to bear everything nobly, and with all this goes a very great weapon, which is prayer.

St. John Chrysostom * Hope lifts itself more firmly in God with regard to the hard things that a man suffers for God's sake. The joy of the reward in eternity cannot be gathered unless it is first sown here in godly sorrow. The Psalmist says: "He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him" (Ps 126:6). So Paul says: "For if we be dead with him, we shall also live with him: if we suffer, we shall also reign with him" (2 Tim 2:11-12). Likewise he warns his disciples, saying: "We must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God" (Acts 14:22).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"The heart of the prudent getteth knowledge; and the ear of the wise seeketh knowledge."[15]

The Lord Christ says: "Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled" (Mt 5:6). The more the believer possesses the righteousness of Christ the more his thirst and hunger for it increase, and he keeps drawing from the overflow of His surpassing grace until he meets Him face to face. So he who possesses knowledge becomes prudent, with a thirst for ever more, and his ear thirsts to listen to knowledge without weariness. Therefore the Apostle Paul says: "Forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before" (Phil 3:13).

16 A man's gift maketh room for him, and bringeth him before great men. 17 He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him. 18 The lot causeth contentions to cease, and parteth between the mighty. 19 A brother is more impregnable than a fortified city, and quarrels are like the bar of a castle.
"A man's gift maketh room for him, and bringeth him before great men" [16]
The wise Solomon is passionately fond of giving: the giving of the heart and the soul, as well as the giving of feelings and sentiments, the giving of practical, self-sacrificing love.

Giving is offered to the poor and needy and despised, as giving is offered to the family, and offered in love to superiors as to subordinates, and offered to those who bear a quarrel or a misunderstanding concerning the man. But the main line in the gift is not its material value, nor is it for the purpose of bribery, but in expressing love and submission and gratitude.

The world needs to take, and the Church needs to give. She gives the fruits of the Spirit: love, joy, peace... For a man's smile, welling up from the depths of the heart by the work of the Holy Spirit of God, is far more precious than many material gifts!
And giving solves many problems and quarrels without resorting to courts and judgment.
"He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him" [17]

The giving of the heart removes many quarrels, but many resort to the court to settle disputes. It is fitting for the judge or leader to listen to both parties. When he listens to him who comes first and complains he thinks he is in the right in his case, but he is bound to examine the matter with the other party, even if a man is confident in the truthfulness of the first. For each party looks at the matter from his own viewpoint, justifying his conduct, casting the blame on the other party.
It is neither wise nor just to pass a judgment, even in our mind, without examining the matter from all sides.

* He who accuses himself at the beginning of his speech is righteous (cf. Prov 18:17). Behold, you see that confession has a very effective power to correct faults. So denying the crime after committing the sin is worse than the sins themselves.
St. John Chrysostom "* If the righteous man is prepared to accuse himself, how much more the sinner?

* If the Apostle made such a confession (1 Cor 15:9), how much more is it fitting for the sinner to confess? Scripture says: "The righteous man accuses himself when he begins to speak" (cf. Prov 19:17).

St. Jerome * Let us tremble at the majesty of His ineffable appearance and at the voice that unceasingly proclaims the praise of that invisible Being. And let us be filled with fear and trembling, falling on our faces for fear before Him. Let us realize our earthly nature, knowing the foundation of the dust from which we are, that we may share the prophet's saying with feeling and a contrite heart: "Woe is me!" (Isa 6:5). Let us uncover our sins and condemn ourselves sharply, as it is said: "He that is first in his own cause seemeth just" (Prov 18:17).
Martyrius - Sahdona "The lot causeth contentions to cease, and parteth between the mighty" [18]
The use of the lot was spoken of earlier (Prov 16:33). In ancient times they resorted to the lot when discussions reached a dead end, as the only way to settle disputes.

Because of her sin Jerusalem was left in ruin and there was not even one to cast a cord or a lot to decide disputes (Mic 2:5). Now that we have enjoyed the Holy Spirit of God, He has become our leader and trainer that we may come to know the truth, and accept the will of God with joy. God Himself "trains (guides) the meek in the truth, and teaches the meek His ways" (Ps 25:9).
"A brother is more impregnable than a fortified city, and quarrels are like the bar of a castle" [19]

Friendship is a strong support for a man, so if two friends lose love and enter into quarrel, they are like those who have lost their fortress, and lost the stronghold of love, and both parties lose the gift of friendship. The dispute began between Judah and Israel in the days of Jeroboam the son of Solomon, and it could have been healed by gentle words of love, but pride on both sides led to destructive results throughout the ages, and the two kingdoms lost the blessing of unity and love.

* There the Lord gives the blessing, where? In such a dwelling, in such harmony together, in such agreement in dwelling together, in fellowship. This is a blessing and the opposite of this is a curse. Someone praises this by saying: "Three things my soul desires... the agreement of brethren, and friendship between neighbors, and a husband and wife who agree" (cf. Sir 25:1-2). Another writer points to the power of that by a riddle in words: [If two lie down they keep warm, and a threefold cord is not quickly broken] (cf. Eccl 4:11-12). Here both the delight and the strength appear clearly, showing the truth of the great delight that befalls those who sleep together, and the great strength brought to those who work (together). Again, a brother who helps a brother is a strong city (cf. Prov 18:19). And Christ said: "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them" (Mt 18:20). Now nature itself requires this, for even at the beginning of the creation of man God said: [It is not good that man should be alone] (cf. Gen 2:18).
St. John Chrysostom

20 A man's belly shall be satisfied with the fruit of his mouth; and with the increase of his lips shall he be filled. 21 Death and life are in the power of the tongue: and they that love it shall eat the fruit thereof.
"A man's belly shall be satisfied with the fruit of his mouth; and with the increase of his lips shall he be filled" [20]

The holy tongue is a fountain of deep waters (Prov 18:4), which can water the soul, turning its wilderness into a fruitful garden, and it is a holy garden overflowing with good things for its owner and for those around him, so his depths (his belly) are satisfied and he feeds his brethren with love.
"Death and life are in the power of the tongue: and they that love it shall eat the fruit thereof" [21]
By the tongue we sow either love that gives life, or quarrels and disputes that bring death. There is not a word we utter that does not bear fruit, even if it is passing.
* Beware of the babbling tongue and of ears eager to hear the news. Do not belittle others, and do not listen to one who belittles another.

* The garrulous old woman, and the old man who speaks fables, and the sophist in his words, all these confiscate the Holy Scriptures, and tear them to pieces, and they may teach with them without learning them.
* The more the tongue sins, the more wretched it becomes!

St. Jerome * How can the body be a sacrifice? Do not let your eye look at anything evil, and it becomes a sacrifice indeed (Mt 5:29; 6:22; 18:9). May your tongue not utter a defiled word, and it becomes an offering. And let your hand not do a wicked thing, and it becomes a whole burnt offering. But even this is not enough, for we are also bound to practice good works (2 Tim 2:21). The hand is bound to give alms, and the mouth to bless those who curse it, and the two ears to find time to listen to the reading of Holy Scripture. These are the firstfruits of all works.

St. John Chrysostom The sanctification of the tongue is accomplished not only by the sanctification of the words that come out of it, but by the sanctification of silence, when it lets holy works speak in the language of love and tenderness, and their words reach the hearts of the hearers.

* Abba Poemen said of Abba Nesteros that he was like the bronze serpent that Moses the prophet lifted up for the healing of the people, for he possessed every virtue, and without speaking he healed everyone.
Paradise of the Fathers
"Whoso findeth a wife findeth a good thing, and obtaineth favour of the LORD"[22]

Not every wife (or husband) is from God, but he who commits his life into the hand of the Lord, and seeks what is for his edification and the edification of the community, the Lord guides him to the holy wife (or husband), and the family becomes a Church pleasing and beloved to the Lord, the object of His delight.
* There is nothing more precious, and nothing more precious can be found, than for a man to be loved by his wife and to love her!

Scripture says: "A wife who agrees with her husband" (as one of the three blessings that the wise man mentioned) (Sir 25:1-2), for where this (love) exists there is wealth and prosperity overflows, and where this is absent nothing else avails, but all things go in a wrong way, and life becomes misery and anxiety.
Let us seek this before everything!
He who seeks money seeks nothing. Seek what endures!
Do not seek a wife from among the rich, lest the excess of wealth on her side cause arrogance.
It is fitting for us not to seek a wife for her wealth, but to seek her as a partner for us in life for the sake of the household management, that she may be a helper for the begetting of children.
God gave woman not to bring money but to be a helper!

* Husband and wife are one as wine and water are one when mixed together. Just as an unbelieving partner corrupts the believer. For this reason he who is not yet married must take all care either not to marry at all or to marry in the Lord.
Origen
"The poor useth intreaties; but the rich answereth roughly." [23]

The rich man often relies on his possessions, and speaks in a spirit of loftiness like one who leans on his wealth, but it is fitting for him to realize that the Lord Himself listens to the supplications of the wronged poor man and his hidden cries.
"He that multiplieth friends destroyeth himself: but there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother." [24]

The wise man fears a multitude of unwise friends, who waste his time, but while showing love to all, especially colleagues, a man must choose a spiritual friend who will be closer than his brother according to the flesh.

* Imagine a circle from whose center rays or lines go out. The farther the lines get from the center the farther apart they are from one another... and on the contrary, the nearer they come to the center the nearer they come to one another. Suppose that this circle is the world and the center of the circle is God. And the lines from the center to the circumference or from the circumference to the center are the way of the life of men; we find the same thing, for as the saints move within the circle toward the center, wishing to draw near to God, each of them draws near to the other.

St. Dorotheus * Let us befriend the righteous and live with them for long periods, not that others may reckon us saints like them, but with the aim of imitating them and receiving their blessing. For the friendship of those who strive kindles the heart with zeal and striving. But let us realize that they are men, liable to fall, and not gods immune from error, so that if they err we do not err like them nor despair of our own salvation!

* Just as those who sit with sellers of musk and fragrant perfumes acquire sweet scents, so we ought to keep company with the wise and the teachers and the masters of virtue, to follow their example in good things.
St. John Chrysostom
Let me live in Your house and separate myself from evil!
* What refuge have I but You? In Your house I dwell and with Your children I enjoy You.
I live in the spirit of love and unity, and so enjoy Your salvation.
And I separate myself from evil and vanity.
My heart is wide open to all men, but I have no fellowship with shattering corruption!
* In Your house I accept wise, holy counsel.
I enjoy the dialogue of love with my brethren.
And I feel the work of Your Holy Spirit in Your Church.
* Your Holy Spirit, the Giver of unity and wisdom, leads Your Church.
He turns our tongues into rivers of deep waters, and a wellspring of true wisdom.
* Your Church is the icon of heaven!
And Your people are the ambassadors of Your kingdom.
Grant righteousness and justice to become the law of every member in her.
And grant every heart to bear no hatred and ill will, so that there is no place for quarrel in her.
Nor for a wounding word to come out of the lips of any of her members.
Let slander not creep in among them.
Let all work in the spirit of strength, not of failure.
Let all be in the spirit of earnestness, knowing no slackness or sloth.
* You are the Church's capital, her wealth and her fortress.
Your name is sweet, the Giver of strength and victory.
In the spirit of humility Your children hide in You.
They glorify You, and You glorify them!
They honor You, and You honor them!
They are filled with the spirit of hope, for You are a Father full of tenderness, wise and almighty!
* Grant me the spirit of true wisdom.
By Your wisdom I do not enter into quarrel, but by love and giving I win, if possible, all men!
* I have learned how to take refuge in You in Your Church.
And I flee to You from every error and evil!
And I walk in everything according to Your good pleasure.
Finally, let my house arise as a holy Church for You, so that I with my family become the object of Your delight!

entries.section: 1. Between the way of truth and the crooked way

paragraphs.text: 1 Better is the poor that walketh in his integrity, than he that is perverse in his lips, and is a fool. 2 Also, that the soul be without knowledge, it is not good; and he that hasteth with his feet sinneth. 3 The foolishness of man perverteth his way: and his heart fretteth against the Lord.
"Better is the poor that walketh in his integrity, than he that is perverse in his lips, and is a fool" [1].

He compares a man who is materially poor yet walks in uprightness, seeking the life of perfection, with a man who boasts of the wealth and knowledge he has while he is a fool. For wisdom, or uprightness in life (godliness), or perfection, is better than the riches of the world.
Faith consists of many things, and reaches perfection in many ways. It is like a building constructed of many pieces of skillful work, rising to the summit.

* Know, my beloved, that stones are laid in the foundations of a building, and the whole structure rises upon the stones until it is complete. So our Lord Jesus Christ, the chief Stone, is the foundation of all our faith. Upon Him faith is founded. Upon Him the whole structure of faith stands until it is completed.

For the foundation is the beginning of the whole building... Its structure cannot be shaken by the waves, nor harmed by the winds, nor brought down by the storms, because the building is raised upon the rock of the true Stone.
If I have called Christ the Stone, this saying is not of my own; the prophets foretold it before me and called Him "the Stone."
St. Aphrahat * I will not be content with anything moderate remaining in you, but I long for you to rise high in everything and to be perfect in every matter.

St. Jerome * It is written: Blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked. Blessed is the man whom You chasten and teach out of Your law. Blessed are they who are not defiled in the way.
Blessed are those who trust in You.
Blessed is the people whose God is the Lord.
Blessed is he who does not judge.
Blessed is the man who fears the Lord (Ps 1:1; 94:12; Sir 14:1-2; Ps 112:1)...

Do you not see how the divine laws proclaim everywhere the blessedness, not of the rich, nor of the nobles, nor of those who hold glory, but of him who acquires virtue? For what is required of us is the foundation. If you plant this as a root, then not only the easy, honored, and glorious life will be your delight, but even enmities, calamities, insults, shame, and torments, all of these without exception will gladden you!
And just as the roots of trees are bitter in themselves, yet produce sweet fruits, so sound sorrow brings superabundant happiness...
And as I always say, it is not the nature of things but our own disposition that makes us sorrowful or joyful.

entries.section: 1. Between the way of truth and the crooked way

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom "Also, that the soul be without knowledge, it is not good; and he that hasteth with his feet sinneth" [2]

He criticizes the man who is stripped of knowledge and who, in his zeal, hastens in his decisions or moves without understanding or wisdom. For it befits a man to be wise and to deliberate in his decisions, and not to move before he has thought with balance.

entries.section: 1. Between the way of truth and the crooked way

paragraphs.text: "The foolishness of man perverteth his way: and his heart fretteth against the Lord" [3].

Being stripped of heavenly wisdom leads a man into the crooked way, and in his self-assurance and his clinging to his own thought, his heart frets against the Lord Himself. A clear example of this is Saul of Tarsus. He was brought up at the feet of Gamaliel, a teacher of the Law, and was a Pharisee zealous for the traditions of his fathers, the honor of his people, and the keeping of the Law, perhaps reckoning himself the most righteous man in the world after his teacher; yet in ignorance he blasphemed God, persecuted the Church of Christ, and slandered the believers, as he himself later confessed.

* When they hear Christ declaring in the Gospel, "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest," at once they cast off the weight of their sins and realize what follows: "For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light" (Mt 11:28, 30).

So the way of the Lord is restful to him who keeps His commandment. But if, through some wearisome neglect, we bring sorrows and toils upon ourselves, we exert great effort following a crooked way to keep the commandments of the world, and on this way we make the yoke of Christ heavy and His burden hard, as the passage says: "The foolishness of man perverteth his way: and his heart fretteth against the Lord" (Prov 19:3). And when it is said, "The way of the Lord is not equal," He answers, "Is not my way equal? are not your ways unequal?" (Ezek 18:25).

In truth you can discern how much easier the yoke of Christ is, and how much lighter His burden, if you compare the sweet, fragrant flower of virginity and the purity of chastity with the filth of defiled, foul-smelling lust, and if you compare the quiet and stillness of the monks and their distance from the dangers and losses that occupy the minds of people in the world, with the cares of wealth and its gnawing disturbances, full of anxiety...
Father Abraham * We should admonish the wrathful in one way, and the gentle in another.

We must tell the wrathful that when they neglect to purify their souls, they rush recklessly into many errors, even ones they do not intend, for it is clear that recklessness drives the mind to where it neither wills nor desires to go.

In such a case, those who fall into recklessness do deeds whose end they do not perceive, and they will repent of them when they acknowledge having done them. And when the ungentle act under the influence of passions, they do so contrary to their nature, and they scarcely perceive the error they have committed. And when they do not resist mental disturbances, they overturn the good things they could have done in a state of clarity of mind. By sudden emotion they destroy what they have built by continuous, long-extended labor. Even the virtue of love, which is the mother of all virtues, hides itself because of anger, for it is written: "Love suffereth long, and is kind" (1 Cor 13:4). Therefore, if love is lacking, gentleness is lacking. And because of the lack of gentleness, teaching, which is the nursing of the virtues, vanishes, for Scripture says: "The discretion of a man deferreth his anger" (Prov 19:11).

For to the extent that a man lacks gentleness, he appears to chafe at teaching, and in truth he cannot acquire what is good through teaching if he has not learned in his own life how to bear the evils of others with a calm mind and quietness.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 2. The love of money corrupts life

paragraphs.text: 4 Wealth maketh many friends; but the poor is separated from his neighbour. 5 A false witness shall not be unpunished, and he that speaketh lies shall not escape. 6 Many will intreat the favour of the prince: and every man is a friend to him that giveth gifts. 7 All the brethren of the poor do hate him: how much more do his friends go far from him? He that followeth after sayings, they are his.
"Wealth maketh many friends; but the poor is separated from his neighbour" [4]

In (vv. 4-7) the wise man highlights how the love of money has corrupted life in the world, giving examples of this. The first is that people, often in partiality, seek the favor of the rich and covet their friendship, while they flee from clinging even to their poor relatives. Man has given money an estimation that exceeds the feelings of friendship, affection, and love.
