"My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons. For if there come unto your assembly a man with a gold ring, in goodly apparel, and there come in also a poor man in vile raiment; and ye have respect to him that weareth the gay clothing, and say unto him, Sit thou here in a good place; and say to the poor, Stand thou there, or sit here under my footstool: are ye not then partial in yourselves, and are become judges of evil thoughts? Hearken, my beloved brethren, Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom which he hath promised to them that love him?" (Ba 2:1-5)

* There is no great without the small, nor small without the great, but we are bound to one another for the benefit of all. Let us take the body as an example: the head cannot exist without the feet, nor the feet without the head, "nay, much more those members of the body, which seem to be more feeble, are necessary" (1 Cor 12:21-22), and useful to the whole body. Yes, all the members work in harmony and are joined to one another in perfect obedience for the well-being of the whole body.

In this way we also keep our Christian body in its perfection, each of us submitting to his fellow according to his own particular gift. The strong must care for the weak, and the weak must respect the strong. The rich supports the poor, and the poor gives thanks to God who gave him one to support him. The wise man does not show his wisdom in words but in good deeds. The humble man does not boast of his humility but leaves others to bear witness for him. The chaste man likewise does not boast, knowing that his self-control is a gift from another (God). We must love the brethren from the heart, those who were created from the same matter from which we were created.

St. Clement, bishop of Rome The rich and wise man does not squander his wealth, but gains friends with it. As the Lord of glory says: "Make to yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness; that, when ye fail, they may receive you into everlasting habitations" (Lk 16:9).
For money is a gift that can be holy if it is used well, and can be evil if it is used for display, arrogance, and indulgence in pleasures and lusts.

* Wealth is not property; it is not possessions, but a loan for use. For how can you claim it as possessions when, at your death, whether you wish it or not, everything goes to others, and they in turn leave it to others again? We are all wanderers... Ownership in reality is nothing but a word; we are all owners, but of the possessions of other people... So wealth is not ours, and possessions are not property but a loan. Virtue alone is able to depart with us and accompany us in the world above.
* Is not the earth and its fullness God's? If then our possessions belong to the common Lord of all, they belong also to our fellow servants. The possessions of the Lord are common to all.

* If you grieve over some wealth, you profit nothing. If it is because of sickness, you gain nothing, but your grief only increases. I have heard many, after long experience, blaming themselves and saying: What benefit did we gain from our grief (over money or health, etc.)? I have only harmed myself.

entries.section: 2. The love of money corrupts life

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom "A false witness shall not be unpunished, and he that speaketh lies shall not escape" [5]

As he speaks of the misuse of money, or the love of money, he points to false witness and lying, whose motive is often material gain or partiality toward the rich and those in authority, and disregard for the rights of the poor and the oppressed.
Queen Jezebel hired false witnesses against Naboth the Jezreelite in order to seize his field after killing him! She killed and inherited!
* Everyone must give great attention lest "lying" rob him, for the liar is not united with God.
The liar is a stranger to God. And Holy Scripture says that the liar is of Satan, since he is "a liar, and the father of it" (Jn 8:44).
Thus Satan was called the father of lies, but the Truth is God, for He Himself says: "I am the way, the truth, and the life" (Jn 14:6).

Do you not see, then, how we become strangers to God through lying, and with whom we are united (through it)?! Therefore, if we truly wish to be saved, we must love the truth with all our strength and all our zeal, and guard ourselves from every lie, lest it separate us from the Truth and the Life.

entries.section: 2. The love of money corrupts life

paragraphs.text: Father Dorotheus "Many will intreat the favour of the prince: and every man is a friend to him that giveth gifts" [6]

Just as the love of money draws many to befriend the rich, so preoccupation with personal interests draws many to befriend the nobles who hold authority and to flatter them. But the Lord Christ came to befriend sinners, the despised, and the needy (Lk 15:1). The Apostle James criticized the Church when it behaved with partiality toward the rich (Jas 2:1-6).

* Let us strip the noble women of their ornaments and the masters of their slaves, and you will notice that these will not differ in any way from slaves bought with money, neither in their manner of walking, nor in their features, nor in their speech. Rather, they resemble in everything those who are subject to them. And if they differ from them in anything, it is only that they are weaker in build and less strong than the others (the slaves), because they were brought up in a luxury that exposes them to sickness.

entries.section: 2. The love of money corrupts life

paragraphs.text: St. Clement of Alexandria "All the brethren of the poor do hate him: how much more do his friends go far from him? He that followeth after sayings, they are his" [7]

Not only strangers and friends withdraw from the poor man, but even relatives and brothers according to the flesh. They ignore him. Our rich Christ, the Giver of riches, became poor, that through His poverty He might enrich us (2 Cor 8:9). So we find our happiness in meeting Him through His poor brethren, and we are enriched by His love which He pours into us, so that we love everyone, especially the needy, without waiting for a reward!

entries.section: 3. Wisdom and the salvation of the soul

paragraphs.text: "He that getteth wisdom loveth his own soul;
he that keepeth understanding shall find good" [8]

In our study of the Book of Wisdom we saw how the wise man links wisdom with righteousness: the man who is wise in the Lord enjoys divine righteousness, so he fears God and loves humanity. But how can he fear God unless he perceives the truth of his precious soul, the object of God's love and passion? And how can his heart open to others unless he discovers the kingdom of love that exists within him? The wise man cannot separate his care for his own depths from his care for others.

He who acquires God's wisdom does good to his inner depths, for he perceives God's care for him and His esteem of him. Thus he keeps God's commandment with understanding, and the commandment keeps him, and his depths guard him like a precious treasure.
Wisdom restores to man his true inner dignity before God as before himself, before he receives any honor from men.
He who sows wisdom by the Holy Spirit of God enjoys its fruit, by receiving countless good things from the work of the Savior.
"A false witness shall not be unpunished, and he that speaketh lies shall perish" [9]

A man bears false witness, that is, he speaks a lie, and so causes harm to the righteous, either to obtain a bribe or material gain, or to win the favor of a rich man, a friend, or a relative. But the lie will surely be exposed, and God's grace forsakes him, so he falls into troubles from which he does not escape. Finally he goes to where the devil, the father of liars, is, that is, to the darkness, and perishes eternally.

entries.section: 5. The luxury of the fool and the rule of the servant

paragraphs.text: "Delight is not seemly for a fool;
much less for a servant to have rule over princes!" [10]

Two grave matters in a man's life as in society: first, that a fool should live in luxury, even if he is of noble and rich origin, squandering the resources of society without benefit to himself or others, and temporal goods only increase his folly. And second, that a man who is a slave (to his lusts, or his possessions, or temporal honor), who has not tasted the sweetness of inner freedom, should occupy a position of leadership, so that his leadership becomes the humiliation of people, without compassion, kindness, or justice!
"The discretion of a man deferreth his anger; and it is his glory to pass over a transgression" [11].

He who has learned in the school of the long-suffering God, and responded to the Holy Spirit, and so received the fruit of love, if he becomes angry, prolongs his patience and controls himself, makes excuses for others, and does all he can to win the one who wronged him; and if he reaches the point of forgiving the one who wronged him, he has attained inner glory. He has fulfilled the divine commandment: "Agree with thine adversary quickly, whiles thou art in the way with him" (Mt 5:25).

* Do not think that anger is a matter to be made light of, for the prophet says, "My eyes are troubled (withered) with anger" (Ps 6:7). And surely one whose eyes are sick cannot look upon the sun. If he tries to see it, it hurts him and does not delight him.

St. Augustine * The deadly poison of anger must be uprooted from the depths of the soul, for if the spirit of anger remains and settles in our hearts, our minds are darkened and lose their power of sight, for anger strikes with blindness and a harmful darkness that makes spiritual vision impossible. We cannot make a right judgment in any matter, and good contemplation, which develops wisdom in us, becomes impossible; indeed, we cannot abide in what is good, or receive the true spiritual light, for it is written: "Mine eye is troubled with anger" (Ps 6:7).

And people may praise us as wise, but we shall not be wise if we persist in anger, for it is written: "Anger dwelleth at rest in the bosom of the fool" (Eccl 7:9) LXX. And it exposes us to the loss of the inheritance of eternal life. It may appear to us that we understand human nature and perceive its mysteries, but if anger remains in us, what is written is fulfilled in us: "Anger destroys the wise" (Prov 15:1) LXX. And anger deprives us of perceiving the "righteousness of God," for because of anger we lose discernment, and though people may say of us that we are holy and perfect, yet it is written, "The wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God" (Jas 1:20).

St. John Cassian * I asked God to make known to me the answer to your question, and He said to me: Cleanse your heart of all the thoughts of the old man and I will answer the question of your heart, for My gifts are in the pure and are given to them, and as long as your heart is stirred by anger, hatred, and the rest of the old passions, wisdom will not enter it.
If you desire to receive My grace and My gifts, cast out the foot of the enemy and drive him away from you, and My gifts will come to you...
He who longs for My gifts, let him follow in My footsteps, for I am like the lamb in whom there is no evil...
And although I commanded you to be gentle like doves, I find that you have taken for yourselves the cruelty of the passions.
Abba Barsanuphius

entries.section: 7. Winning those in authority in the Lord

paragraphs.text: "The king's wrath is as the roaring of a lion; but his favour is as dew upon the grass" [12]

Although the believer takes pride in belonging to God and is not afraid of people or of death, yet in a spirit of humility he is committed to submitting to those in authority in the Lord, giving honor to whom honor is due, and so he finds rest and spends his days in quietness and assurance, in all godliness and dignity (see 1 Tim 2:2). Some rabbis used to pray: "O Lord, bless the emperor, and keep him far from us."

If this is the believer's attitude toward a king or ruler, even if he is an unbeliever, what should his attitude be toward the King of kings and Lord of lords? He is the Lion who came out of the tribe of Judah; He came for the salvation of humanity, not for its judgment. But He will come on the Day of Judgment, and the souls of the true believers will rejoice, while the wicked will count it the day of His great wrath: who is able to stand before Him?

Tertullian says: [Therefore, concerning the honors due to kings and emperors, we have sufficient text that it befits us to be in complete obedience, according to the commandment of the Apostle, "to be subject to principalities and powers" (Titus 3:1); but the limit of obedience in this is that we keep ourselves apart from the worship of idols. We have in this also the example of the three youths, who, while obeying King Nebuchadnezzar, disdained to offer honor to his image and did not accept to worship it... So also Daniel was subject to Darius in all things, steadfast in his duty so long as it was far from the foundation of his faith (Dan 6).]
A foolish son is the calamity of his father: and the contentions of a wife are a continual dropping. 14 House and riches are the inheritance of fathers: and a prudent wife is from the Lord.
"A foolish son is the calamity of his father: and the contentions of a wife are a continual dropping" [13]

How wretched is the house that includes a foolish son and a contentious wife. Often the two agree together; for where there are quarrels in the family, the children become loose, and try to play a dangerous role between the parents, to show each of them that they are on his side, and so they win affection and benefit by obtaining concessions, and the sense of obligation and responsibility is removed from the children.

* If the Apostle commands us to care for others more than for ourselves, and if we are counted at fault when we neglect what is for their benefit, shall we not be much more at fault if this concerns those who are close to us?

The Lord will say to us: "Was it not I who gave these children a place in your family? Was it not I who entrusted them to your care, and made you masters, guardians, and judges over them? I gave you complete authority over them. I handed them wholly into your hands for their upbringing.

You will tell me that they did not want to bow their necks to the yoke, and that they cast it off. But this could have been avoided from the very beginning. It was fitting for you to bow their little souls under the yoke of obligation, to accustom them to it, to teach them this, and to bandage the wound at the beginning of its opening.

It was fitting for you to pull up the tares when they began to appear around the plants, and it was not fitting for you to wait until their roots deepened, so that it became impossible to control and tame the passions by strengthening them (the children) gradually during their formation and growth.

St. John Chrysostom Calm, constructive dialogue is beneficial for the family, in which each party respects the others and does not cling to his own opinion, so that the children learn the spirit of holy dialogue. But quarrels, strife, anger, and the withdrawal of one from another cause the home to lose the presence of the Lord Christ in their midst, and corrupt the spirit of godliness in all, fathers and children, and instill in the new generation the spirit of rebellion and clinging to one's own opinion.

He likens the contentious wife to drops of water that fall continually without stopping. The husband, like the children, feels that they are in a house from whose roof drops of water fall without ceasing, so that they do not know how to work or rest or sleep, finding no dry place in the house to take refuge in.
From the words of St. Gregory of Nazianzus in praise of his parents:

[Behold, the good shepherd is the fruit of the prayers of his wife and her guidance, and he learned from her his ideal pastoral life. With power he fled from the worship of idols, and afterward the demons fled from him.. They became equal in prudence and splendor, zealous, supporting one another, flying above all...

They had two bodies, but it was as though the two bodies had been turned into one spirit, even before their dissolution... They possessed everything and lacked nothing. They rejected wealth, and so became rich in honor...

I say only one word about them: that in right and justice each of them was appointed for his own kind. He was appointed an ornament for men, and she an ornament for women, not only an ornament, but also an example of the virtuous life.]
"House and riches are the inheritance of fathers: and a prudent wife is from the Lord" [14]

A man inherits a house, lands, or money from his parents, but the wise wife is a divine gift, which the Lord gives to him who truly lives in the spirit of godliness, and has a sound view of the meaning of marriage, and asks God to guide him and choose for him. When the will is submitted to the Lord, the Lord provides the wife or the husband according to what He sees for the salvation of the whole house.
God has holy sons and daughters, dear to Him, whom He wishes to give to the one who asks in submission to His will, and He gives him or her what suits the person.
How beautiful it is for a man to offer God a daily sacrifice of thanksgiving for the gift of the life partner whom he received from God's hand!

* When the Apostle spoke of marriage and virginity he said: "But every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that" (1 Cor 7:7). He says that marriage is a gift. For it is written: "A wife is given to a man from the Lord" (Prov 19:14), but this gift is not a spiritual gift in a strict sense, for there are many things that can be called gifts from God, such as wealth, bodily strength, physical beauty, and temporal authority. These gifts too are from God, and as Daniel says: "He removeth kings, and setteth up kings" (Dan 2:21).
Origen
"Slothfulness casteth into a deep sleep; and an idle soul shall suffer hunger" [15]

Many do not realize the value of work and commitment, nor the value of time, and that negligence in work, wasting time, and lack of commitment are all things that corrupt a man's spiritual, social, psychological, and bodily health, and make him lose even what he has received, and he gives account for all this!
The Apostle says: "Redeeming the time, because the days are evil" (Eph 5:16); "Walk in wisdom toward them that are without, redeeming the time" (Col 4:6).
* What we often gain through zeal, laziness destroys, and what hesitation loses, diligence restores.
St. Gregory of Nazianzus

16 He that keepeth the commandment keepeth his own soul; but he that despiseth his ways shall die. 17 He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the Lord; and that which he hath given will he pay him again.
"He that keepeth the commandment keepeth his own soul; but he that despiseth his ways shall die" [16]

He who keeps the divine commandment, the commandment keeps him eternally. In obedience to the commandment is the delight of love for God, a tasting of the blessing of obedience, and enjoyment of victory over death in Christ, the Giver of victory. But he who treats the commandment lightly treats God Himself lightly, and casts himself into the pit of eternal death.

* We ought to look to God's commandments when they are read, or when memory recalls them, as one who looks in a mirror, as the Apostle James says. Such a man wishes to look at God's commandments as in a mirror and is not confused, for he chooses not only to be a hearer of the commandments but also a doer of them. Therefore he desires that his ways be directed toward keeping God's statutes. How are they directed except by God's grace? Otherwise he finds in God's law not a source of joy but a source of confusion, if he chooses to look at the commandments and not do them.

St. Augustine * He who keeps one commandment and leaves others has betrayed all the commandments, for he insults God, who commanded them and bound them to one another. For He who said, Do not commit adultery, said also, Do not steal; if you steal you become a debtor to the whole law; but he who is careful of all the commandments will not be ashamed on the dreadful day of judgment.
Anthimus, bishop of Jerusalem "He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the Lord; and that which he hath given will he pay him again" [17].

He links the keeping of the commandment with mercy, especially toward the poor. For the Creator of the poor counts every kindness shown to the poor as offered to Himself personally, and considers it a loan that He repays doubled. David the psalmist says: "I have been young, and now am old; yet have I not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread. He is ever merciful, and lendeth; and his seed is blessed" (Ps 37:25-26).

* Hold fast, then, to asking Him for the debt, for it is not fitting that we leave Him and ask repayment from another besides Him, for He sees in what you do an error, as though He says to you: Why do you do this, and with what ingratitude do you accuse Me? Do you claim that I am poor, so that you intend to take the debt from others? Do you lend to (the one God) and then ask another to repay this loan? For though it is man who received the loan, it is God who commanded you to give to him, and His will is that He Himself be the debtor in the fullest sense of the word; and in truth the Lord gives you manifold opportunities to recover the debt from Him at all times and in all places. So do not let this opportune moment slip from you so easily, nor squander this abundant generosity by asking for the debt from those who have nothing. For what purpose do you show mercy to the poor? What? Was it not I who said to you, Give? Did you not hear that from Me, that you should recover your gifts from Me? Did I not say, "He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the Lord" (Prov 19:17)? And you have lent to God, so put this debt on His account, even if He does not repay you the whole debt now. Well, He does that for your good also. What a debtor! Not like many who simply wish to pay back what they borrowed; rather the Lord arranges everything, to invest it securely, because it is a loan given to the Lord. Therefore, as you see, He repays some of it here and defers the debt for the rest.
St. John Chrysostom
18 Chasten thy son, for there is hope in him; but let not thy soul be set upon his death. 19 A man of great wrath shall suffer punishment: for if thou deliver him, yet thou must do it again.
"Chasten thy son, for there is hope in him; but let not thy soul be set upon his death" [18]

In a spirit of hope a man disciplines his son with firmness mingled with tenderness and love. But violent, extreme punishments bear the guilt of murder, and also provoke the children and drive them to stubbornness, so that discipline is not for reform but for destruction.

In discipline a constructive dialogue must be entered into, so that the son understands what is behind the discipline, and the father understands what is behind his son's conduct, so that he does not discipline in haste and emotion. Loose liberty and violent severity are both ruinous and destructive to children as to the family.

King Saul, in his anger, instead of open dialogue with his son Jonathan, aimed the spear at him to smite him (1 Sam 20:33), and so the son lost his confidence in his father and withdrew from him in heart.
* God bears all the weaknesses of men, but He will not allow the perpetual murmurer to be left without discipline.
St. Mar Isaac the Syrian "A man of great wrath shall suffer punishment: for if thou deliver him, yet thou must do it again" [19]

Some link this proverb with the one before it, and interpret it thus: if the son is of great wrath, he must be disciplined or punished with wisdom and deliberation until he ceases from anger; if he is not disciplined he will repeat this emotion and fall under a bitter punishment, that is, he will punish himself by himself. It is as though whoever is not disciplined by his parents will discipline himself, or as it is said: "He whom his parents do not discipline, time disciplines."
20 Hear counsel, and receive instruction, that thou mayest be wise in thy latter end. 21 There are many devices in a man's heart; nevertheless the counsel of the Lord, that shall stand.
"Hear counsel, and receive instruction, that thou mayest be wise in thy latter end" [20]

Some see this proverb as the key to the whole book: the call to accept counsel so that the believer may become wise. Fools despise counsel, but the wise man accepts counsel with joy, and thinks seriously about rebuke or reproof, and even about the discipline that comes upon him, because he loves to learn and to benefit from the experience of others.
"There are many devices in a man's heart; nevertheless the counsel of the Lord, that shall stand" [21]

Often a man wavers in his thoughts; what he accepts now he may reject after a few minutes, or the reverse. He may listen to many counselors and be seized by a kind of confusion and disturbance. But when he takes refuge in God, who alone knows the truth and who loves His creation, He gives true, successful, and steadfast counsel.
"The adornment of a man is his kindness: and a poor man is better than a liar" [22].

The adornment of the spirit is well known: it is love, tenderness, and mercy with giving. The spirit is adorned by removing all selfishness, so as to expand and contain others within it. Along with this practical love the spirit must be truthful with itself; if a man is unable to give a certain gift, let him be frank and excuse himself for his poverty or inability, and not promise others while he knows he is unable to carry it out.

With complete frankness Peter declared to the lame man his inability to give material gifts, but he offered him something greater, for he said to him: "Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk" (Acts 3:6).
"The fear of the Lord tendeth to life:
and he shall abide satisfied; he shall not be visited with evil" [23]

He who fears the Lord and reveres Him takes refuge in Him and shelters in Him as his refuge and fortress. He lives in safety, lacking nothing. He feels that all things work together for good. He ever sings the song of victory, saying with the Apostle Paul: "In all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us. For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Rom 8:27-29). Thus he who fears the Lord rejoices, for his soul is watered from the springs of God's love, and is satisfied from the heavenly table.
* The great good is not to possess money, but to acquire the fear of the Lord and all the means of godliness.

St. John Chrysostom * If anyone wishes to obtain the love of God, let the fear of the Lord be in him, for fear begets weeping, and weeping begets strength. And when all these are fulfilled in the soul, the soul begins to bear fruit in everything. And when God sees these good fruits in the soul, He smells them as the fragrance of sweet incense, and rejoices in it, He and His angels, and satisfies it with joy, and keeps it in all its ways until it reaches its place of rest without any harm coming to it.
When Satan sees the great heavenly Guardian surrounding the soul, he is afraid to approach it or attack it because of this great power.
Therefore acquire this power so that the demons tremble before you, and your works become easy, and you delight in the divine work, for the sweetness of God's love is sweeter than honey.

Truly many monks and virgins in the communities have not tasted this divine sweetness and have not acquired the divine power, supposing that they have received it, despite their lack of striving. But he who strives for it will surely receive it through the divine mercies, for God is no respecter of persons.

So whoever wishes to have God's light and power must despise the honors of this world and its defilement, hate all the things of the world and the pleasure of the flesh, and purify his heart of all evil thoughts. And he offers God fasts and tears night and day without relenting as pure prayers; then God pours that power upon him.
Strive to obtain this power, that you may do all your works with ease and facility, and have great boldness before God, and He will give you all that you ask.
St. Anthony the Great
"A slothful man hideth his hand in the dish, and will not so much as bring it to his mouth again" [24]

The wise man portrays the lazy man with a sumptuous table set before him, full of foods; he stretches out his hand and puts it in the dish, but from his great laziness and desire for sleep and drowsiness, he finds it hard to lift his hand to put the food in his mouth. He prefers to suffer hunger in his slackness rather than stretch out his hand with food to eat and be satisfied. So many do, for God sets before them a delicious table in Holy Scripture, the food of the soul, but in slackness and laziness they do not benefit from the opportunity offered them to eat and be satisfied.
"Smite a scorner, and the fool will become shrewd; and reprove one that hath understanding, and he will understand knowledge" [25]

If the scorner is left to practice his contempt for the commandment or for others without rebuke or discipline, he finds justification for his conduct, unconcerned about the consequences of his evils. But as for firmness with the scorner, even if the person himself does not benefit from it, others will benefit, for they fear lest punishments come upon them. And the man of understanding, when he is rebuked for a mistake he committed, benefits from the rebuke, for he always wants to learn and to grow in every good work.

26 He that wasteth his father, and chaseth away his mother, is a son that causeth shame, and bringeth reproach. 27 Cease, my son, to hear the instruction that causeth to err from the words of knowledge.
"He that wasteth his father, and chaseth away his mother, is a son that causeth shame, and bringeth reproach" [26]

The rebellious son ruins his father, squandering his wealth and possessions to fulfill his pleasures and lusts. In his stubbornness he loses all tenderness, even toward his mother, and drives her away, thus staining the family with shame and disgrace. The rebel thinks that by this shameful conduct toward his parents he is exercising his right to freedom and breaking all restraints, and he does not know that he is practicing recklessness and laxity, and his life ends in scandal and destruction.
If rebellion against a ruler or king drives its perpetrator to being killed or executed, what then will be the punishment of the tyrant who rebels against God and His commandment?

St. Augustine says that by rebellion some of the heavenly beings lost their position and descended to eternal destruction, and no longer had the right of fellowship with the angels. Whereas (by obedience) man receives a promise that after the resurrection he will be equal to the angels.
"Cease, my son, to hear the instruction that causeth to err from the words of knowledge" [27]

The wise man offers his advice or commandment to the rebellious son, who embraces the principles and philosophies of license and rebellion, counting error away from the truth and indifference to the spiritual life as a call to practice freedom. The wise man asks him to carry the spirit of discernment, to walk in the light and reject the darkness. Let him stop his ears against misleading teachings, in order to listen and submit to the divine truth.
"A base witness scorneth the truth: and the mouth of the wicked devoureth iniquity" [28].

When the wicked man bears false witness against his neighbor, he drives himself into a chain of evils and the practice of injustice and violence, and counts his mouth, which swore falsely and testified lies, a workshop of iniquity.
"Punishment is prepared for scorners, and stripes for the back of fools." [29]
The scorners who treat the divine holy things lightly cast themselves into grave punishment, and are beaten as ignorant and foolish men.
The day of the Lord is surely coming, and judgment will truly fall on the wicked; the pleasures of sins are temporary, but their punishment is eternal!
St. John Chrysostom depicts for us the great day of the Lord on which the judgment takes place and the wicked are tried, saying:

* All things will be astonishing in the extreme and filled with terror and trembling. Even the angels themselves will be seized by fear, not only the angels but also the archangels, thrones, dominions, principalities, and powers. We read: "And the powers of the heavens shall be shaken" (Mt 24:29). For fellow servants will be asked to give an account of their lives on earth. If a single city is judged before the rulers of this world, all people tremble, even those who are out of danger; how much more if the whole world is summoned before such a Judge, who needs no witnesses nor proofs, but without all this brings up deeds and words in a form seen by those who commit sins and those who are ignorant of them, is it not natural that all the powers be astonished and tremble?
St. John Chrysostom
Grant me to walk in the way of truth!
* Grant me to be united with You, O divine Truth, that I may walk in the truth, and not turn to the right hand or to the left.
* I live by You in perfect freedom, so that no wealth, whatever its value, enslaves me.
I see You as my treasure and my riches.
Nothing occupies me except meeting You in Your glories.
Where my soul with my body shall enjoy eternal glories.
* I possess You, O Truth, so that lying finds no dwelling in me.
And ignorance does not creep into my depths.
And anger does not dominate my feelings.
* I love You and am occupied with You; I give honor to whom honor is due, and I honor every person, whatever his age or position.
* You are manifested in my depths, and make of me a temple for You.
And You declare Your presence in my family, so that it becomes a rejoicing heavenly church, whose canon is love, humility, and continual giving.
* Your Spirit kindles my heart with sacrificial love.
I work and give without ceasing.
I know neither deceit nor malice.
* I fear You as a son subject in love to his father.
I revere You lest I wound Your feelings.
I accept every discipline from Your hands, trusting in Your wisdom and care!
"Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise" [1]
Here for the first time we find a commandment warning against intoxicating wine, and the wise man returns to warn on other occasions (Prov 23:20-21, 29-35; 31:4-5).

Despite the medicinal benefits of wine, and though it is a holy creature, the enemy of good found no difficulty in drawing millions toward addiction to wine and drunkenness, and the destruction of their spiritual, psychological and physical lives. When Noah became drunk he was uncovered, and fell into shame, and when Lot became drunk he lay with his two daughters.

The destructive fruits of drunkenness are evident in all societies, and yet many are drawn to it, if not openly, then in secret. Wine mocks the man who drinks it excessively, and treats him with contempt, and the strange thing is that it makes him a fool, so that he mocks those around him, and they mock him.
* Above all, the monk must forbid gatherings with women and the drinking of wine, for wine and women drive even the wise to fall (Sir 19:2).

St. Basil the Great * A brother was warred upon by his thoughts to leave his monastery, so he told Abba Anthony about it, and the elder said to him: "Go, sit in your cell and pledge your body to the walls of your cell and do not leave it, and let the thought go wherever it wishes, only do not allow your body to go out of the cell... It will say to you: 'Drink a little wine like the blessed Timothy' (1 Tim 5:23); answer it also: 'Remember the sons of Jonadab who kept the commandments of their father' (Jer 35:6).

* Nothing renews the soul that has grown old like the fear of God and pure prayer and continual meditation on the words of the Lord, with supplying the soul with the provision of prayer, and persistence in vigils, and not excess in drinking water. In truth the monk must be abstemious in drinking water as he is completely abstemious in wine, for just as the tree that is watered with water is the only one that is laden with fruit, so also the body that is filled with water becomes soft and sluggish, and from softness comes slackness and sloth, and slackness begets drowsiness, and from drowsiness luxury is begotten, and so little by little the sicknesses of the soul increase and cast us into the depth of hell, and our bodies become a dwelling place for unclean spirits and our thoughts enslaved to shameful passions.

St. Anthony the Great * For it is certain that the souls of sinners are like different springs: the gluttons and lovers of wine are like springs that have been defiled, and the greedy and the swindlers are like springs full of frogs...
St. Paphnutius
"The fear of a king is as the roaring of a lion:
whoso provoketh him to anger sinneth against his own soul" [2]
It is fitting for us to acknowledge the authority of those in leading positions, especially the king or president, and to submit to every human ordinance for the Lord's sake (Rom 13:1; 1 Pet 2:13).
He who provokes the king sins against his own soul, for his anger is poured out upon those who oppose him and trouble him.

He who walks in godliness does not fear the ruler, for the Apostle says: "He that resisteth the power resisteth God, and they that resist shall receive to themselves damnation. For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil. Wilt thou then not be afraid of the power? do that which is good, and thou shalt have praise of the same: for he is the minister of God to thee for good" (Rom 13:2-4).
"It is an honour for a man to cease from strife: but every fool will be meddling"[3]
Nothing pours glory and honor and dignity upon a man like his gentleness and long-suffering. "Let your moderation be known unto all men" (Phil 4:5).

The wise man keeps away as far as he can from quarrels and disputes for the sake of his inner peace, and in order to practice positive, edifying works, and leaves the work to be the witness for the truth, and turns opponents into friends, but the fool is pleased with disputes, and sports in them.
* He who seeks peace seeks Christ, for He is our peace (Col 1:20), who makes both one (Eph 2:14), making peace by the blood of His Cross whether on earth or in heaven.

St. Basil the Great * Do not place enmity in your heart against any man, and do not hate him who is hostile to his neighbor nor condemn his enmity, and do not be angry with a brother who is angry with his neighbor, for this is true peace: that you encourage yourself with this thought: affliction continues for a short time, while peace is eternal by the grace of God the Word.
Abba Moses
"The sluggard will not plow by reason of the cold; therefore shall he beg in harvest, and shall not be given" [4]

The sluggard looks for any pretext to find himself an excuse not to work; he neglects his field while his neighbors spare no effort to cultivate their fields. And when harvest time comes, the neighbors are busy harvesting their fields, while he begs from them their leftovers and they do not give him.

The plowing season in the Middle East is November and December, so the sluggard excuses himself that it is winter and he cannot bear the cold, so it is no wonder that when the harvest season comes he finds his field without fruit.

* The slothful must be exhorted in one way, and the venturesome in another. The slothful must be persuaded not to lose the doing of good by putting it off, and the venturesome must not spoil the merits of their good deeds by a haste that lacks the deliberation of watching for the right times for these deeds.

Let the slothful realize that unwillingness may prevent doing, at the fitting time when this desire comes, the good we are able to do. The dull mind, when it is not moved by true zeal at its appointed time, entirely loses every sense of desire to do good, for this negligence grows and increases strongly, but without our feeling it. Therefore Solomon says plainly: "Slothfulness casteth into a deep sleep" (Prov 19:15).

The slothful man, although he may be awake with true feelings, yet his sloth increases negligence, and therefore it was said that sloth casts a man into a deep sleep. For when the striving in doing good ceases, he begins gradually to lose the sense of true feelings. It was well added to this passage: "and an idle soul shall suffer hunger" (Prov 19:15), for when the soul neglects itself and is not restrained by force, and does not direct its effort toward heavenly things, worldly desires harm it, and so when it ignores the bonds of discipline, it rather loses its way as it pursues pleasures, therefore also it is written in the Book of Proverbs on the tongue of Solomon: "The desire of the slothful killeth him" (Prov 21:25).
For this reason the Truth Himself teaches us that the house becomes clean when the evil spirit goes out, but when it remains empty he returns to it with other spirits to take possession of it.

The sluggard usually neglects what he ought to do, imagining obstacles and groundless fears, and he rests on excuses he invents because of his inertia and dullness. To these Solomon truly says: "The sluggard will not plow by reason of the cold; therefore shall he beg in harvest, and shall not be given" (Prov 20:4). Those who do not labor in works of righteousness now will reap nothing (in the summer), and this means that when the burning sun of judgment appears he will beg to enter the Kingdom but in vain.

Therefore Solomon says also: "He that observeth the wind shall not sow; and he that regardeth the clouds shall not reap" (Eccl 11:4). The wind is nothing but the temptations of the evil spirits, and the clouds that it drives are nothing but the calamities in which the wicked involve us. Yes, the winds drive the clouds when the blows of the evil spirits move the wicked, and so he that observeth the wind shall not sow, and he that regardeth the clouds shall not reap, for those who fear the temptations of the evil spirits and the injustice of the wicked do not now sow good seed, and do not afterward reap the holy reward.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"Counsel in the heart of man is like deep water; but a man of understanding will draw it out" [5].

The man of wisdom and counsel is patient, and listens, and stores up in his depths, so his heart becomes like a deep well in which true knowledge is stored. But fools, being by nature talkative, ascribe to the wise man ignorance and folly because of his few words. But as soon as he draws, that is, draws up the waters of knowledge at the right time, as from the well of his heart, all realize that he is a man of understanding.
* Do not do any work in the time of your repentance without counsel, and you will pass the days of your life in all rest.
Abba Isaiah * A monk must take counsel from a wise man, and not let the counsel of a fool dwell in his heart.
St. Hyperechius the Priest

6 Most men will proclaim every one his own goodness: but a faithful man who can find? 7 The just man walketh in his integrity: his children are blessed after him. 8 A king that sitteth in the throne of judgment scattereth away all evil with his eyes. 9 Who can say, I have made my heart clean, I am pure from my sin? 10 Divers weights, and divers measures, both of them are alike abomination to the LORD. 11 Even a child is known by his doings, whether his work be pure, and whether it be right. 12 The hearing ear, and the seeing eye, the LORD hath made even both of them.
In these proverbs [6-12] we see a living picture of the wise, godly man, who walks in purity and wants to live perfect.
"Most men will proclaim every one his own goodness: but a faithful man who can find?" [6]
Many people think they are good, but how great is the difference between what a man sees from outside and the true inner reality.

How hard it is to find a man who is faithful and sincere with himself. It is fitting for us not to be deceived by men's praise of us, for no one knows a man except the spirit of man. We must examine ourselves by the light of the Spirit of God, so that we are enlightened and sanctified by Him.
"The just man walketh in his integrity: his children are blessed after him" [7]

The just man is not deluded by men's praise of him, nor shaken by the biting blame and criticism of others; what concerns him is the perfection which God gives him as an inner treasure, which he enjoys, and offers as an inheritance to his children, who benefit from his prayers for them, and imitate him.
Fathers teach their children by practical life and conduct and secret prayers for them; that is better than presenting them with advice and instructions in words.

Children can touch the work of God in the lives of their fathers, as they also discover their hypocrisy and deceit if they put on a false appearance. The hearts of children can penetrate the hearts of their fathers, and come to know their secrets and uncover the truth of their relationship with God!

* Do not count one who is changeable and weak as father of your children, but it is fitting for you to make the eternal, unchangeable God father of your spiritual children. Entrust to Him your wealth which you want to save for them. Make Him a guard over them and a guarantor and keeper of them by His divine power, against all the misfortunes of time. For when you commit it into the hand of God no one takes away its ownership, nor does the public treasury seize it, nor does judicial injustice touch it, but the inheritance is safe when it is kept under the guard of God.
By this you furnish your dear heirs with the beatitudes of the future.

This is what fatherly affection dictates to you concerning the care of your heirs, relying on the saying of Scripture: "I have been young, and now am old; yet have I not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread." And its saying: "The just man walketh in his integrity: his children are blessed after him" (Prov 20:7).

Therefore if you do not care to guide your children and keep them in faith and godliness you do not deserve to be called a father but are a traitor father, you who are more careful of their earthly possessions than of their heavenly possessions, so you commend them to Satan and not to Christ. Thereby you sin two sins, and commit a double crime:
a. You have not furnished your children with the help of God their Father.
b. You teach them to love their possessions more than Christ.
St. Cyprian the Martyr "A king that sitteth in the throne of judgment scattereth away all evil with his eyes" [8].

When the wise king sits on the throne of judgment he is able by the glances of his eyes to sift the wicked, and separate them from the righteous. Here the wise man warns the wicked against trying to deceive the king the judge, for he will surely discover their deceit, and they add to their evils a new evil, lying to the king. This is true of the weak earthly king when the spirit of wisdom is given him and he wants to practice justice, so what of the King of kings when He comes on the clouds to judge the living and the dead? Everything is open before Him, even the hidden thoughts and the intents of the heart!

Origen believes that at the resurrection men are divided into two parts: the righteous who are saved, and the wicked who deserve judgment. The latter will be filled with grief befitting the life and works of those who made light of the Lord's commandments while in this life, and cast off all fear of judgment, and practiced uncleanness and covetousness.
The learned Origen says that the judgment will take place at the end of the world, and then the decisive distinction between the good and the wicked will be made.

* On the day of judgment, there is no doubt that the good will be separated from the bad, and the righteous from the wicked. And to every soul, through the judgment of God, a place will be assigned fitting its worth and desert, if God wills."
Origen * Since (God) sees everything, and hears everything, let us fear Him and abandon the evil works that spring from unclean lusts, so that His mercy may protect us from the judgment to come.
St. Clement of Rome "Who can say, I have made my heart clean, I am pure from my sin?" [9]

If the wicked cannot be justified before a human king, which of men can be justified before the King of kings? Who can keep himself free from error? Whoever thinks himself pure without sin, deceives himself and the truth is not in him. Here there is urgent need of Him who by His blood can wash us from our sins. "These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb" (Rev 7:14). Truly "They are all gone aside, they are together become corrupt; there is none that doeth good, no, not one" (Rom 3:12).
* Then let us, beloved brethren, know that gift of healing that belongs to the divine mercy, we who cannot be found without wounds in respect of conscience.

Let not a man flatter himself, imagining that his heart is pure and circumcised, relying on his own righteousness, reckoning that his wounds need no medicine, when it is written: "Who can say, I have made my heart clean, I am pure from my sin?!" (Prov 20:9), and it is said in the epistle of John: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us" (1 Jn 1:8). If there is no man without sin, and he who says he is without sin is proud or foolish, then how tender is the divine mercy, for we know that there are still wounds in those who are healed even after they have received healing; for this reason healing medicines have been provided to heal the wounds that arise anew!

St. Cyprian the Martyr * Therefore all the saints grieve with daily sighs for this weakness of their nature. And while they search out their wandering thoughts and the hidden things of their consciences and their deep retreats they cry out in supplication: "And enter not into judgment with thy servant: for in thy sight shall no man living be justified" (Ps 143:2), "Who can say, I have made my heart clean, I am pure from my sin?" (Prov 20:9). And also: "For there is not a just man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not" (Eccl 7:20). And also: "Who is aware of his inadvertent sins?" (Ps 19:12). And so they realized that man's righteousness is sick and imperfect and always needs the mercy of God, so that one of them, after seeing the seraphim on high and discovering the heavenly secrets, said: "Woe is me... for I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips" (Isa 6:5). I think he would not have felt the uncleanness of his lips unless it had been granted him to perceive the purity of true, complete perfection by the vision of God, so that he suddenly became aware of his uncleanness of which he had been ignorant before and the uncleanness of those around him... including in his general supplication not only the company of the wicked but also the company of the good, saying: "Behold, thou art wroth; for we have sinned: in those is continuance for ever, and we shall be saved; and we are all as an unclean thing, and as filthy rags" (Isa 64:5-6).
Abba Theonas * "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us" (1 Jn 1:8).

What sermon can declare the swarm of sins of the soul and of free will. He says: "From within proceed evil thoughts" (Mk 7:21; Mt 15:19). And he adds a list of the thoughts that defile us. If the nets of sins are spread around us on every side through all the senses and the inner movements of the soul, who can boast that his heart is clean, as Wisdom says (Prov 20:9) LXX? Or as Job testifies to the same thing: "Who is clean from stain?" (Job 14:4) LXX? The stain that touches the purity of the soul is sensual pleasure, which mingles with human life in various ways through soul and body, by thoughts and senses and deliberate movements and bodily behaviors.
Then whose soul is pure of this stain?
How can anyone be found who is not struck by conceit and trodden under the foot of pride?
Who has never been shaken by sinful hands, and whose foot has never run to evil?
Who has never been corrupted by the wandering of his eyes toward corruption or his uncontrolled ears?
Who has never been engaged in tasting with pleasure, and whose heart has never been moved by vain affections?
St. Gregory of Nyssa "Divers weights, and divers measures, both of them are alike abomination to the LORD" [10].

He who carries purity within him, and walks in the way of perfection, his measures become true and faithful, so that he does not measure for one man with one measure, and for another with another measure. The holy God hates deceit in measures and weights and standards, and so His holy children in Him cannot bear deceit, whatever its motives.
He has already spoken of deceit with balances (Prov 11:1; 16:11), and will speak of them again (Prov 20:23).
* Take heed, my children, for the salvation of your souls and return to the Lord with a repentance pure from deceit, and with weeping and supplication confess your shortcomings.

St. Macarius the Great * My son, do not show your word to one who does not know it. Make all men your friends, but do not make them all your counselors, but first of all take for yourself a trial (that is, a test). Do not make all men friends, and if they become your friends do not trust all of them, for the world is established in craftiness. But make for yourself one brother who fears the Lord, and cleave you to God alone like a child with his father. For men altogether walk in deceit, except a very few of them; and the earth is full of vanity and toils and griefs. So if you, my son, love to live in quiet do not mingle with those who busy themselves with vanity. And if you come to be in a midst where there is a mingling with many, be as one who is not mingled with them if you love to please God.
St. Anthony the Great "Even a child is known by his doings, whether his work be pure, and whether it be right" [11].
Not only adults, but even little children are known for their purity and uprightness by their practical conduct, as in the case of the little boy Samuel in the temple (1 Sam 3:18-21).
"The hearing ear, and the seeing eye, the LORD hath made even both of them" [12].

If all are not justified, since they need the divine work to cleanse them, sin crept into us and is not the Creator's making. God created the ear to listen to the commandment and the eyes to behold heavenly things, all His creation is good. Evil entered into us by our will, where we accepted the counsel of the devil.
"Love not sleep, lest thou come to poverty;
open thine eyes, and thou shalt be satisfied with bread" [13]

The wise man often warns us of sloth, for when a man practices it spiritual poverty comes upon him as well as social and material poverty. He loses everything and becomes poor, and finds nothing to satisfy him. But he who labors and watches, for him the night turns into day, fulfilling the commandment of the Apostle: "Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light" (Eph 5:14).
The watchful heart awaits the coming of the Lord Christ with joy.
* The watchful eye purifies the mind, and much sleep darkens the soul.
* Much sleep causes forgetfulness, and watchfulness purifies the memory.
St. John Climacus
"It is naught, it is naught, saith the buyer: but when he is gone his way, then he boasteth!" [14]

The deceitful buyer belittles the qualities of the goods, claiming that they are poor so that he may be able to buy them at a low price. And when he attains his end he rejoices that he was able to deceive the seller, boasting of it before his family and friends.
"There is gold, and a multitude of rubies: but the lips of knowledge are a precious jewel." [15]
The word of truth that comes from true knowledge is more precious than gold and a multitude of rubies.
"Take his garment that is surety for a stranger: and for strangers take a pledge of him." [16]

The wise man has already warned the believer against rashness in becoming surety for a stranger whom he does not know, and who cannot pay the creditor what he has guaranteed, so that he loses even his garment that covers him. It is fitting for the believer to be careful in reckoning the cost, and not to decide to stand surety for anyone hastily, and without study and deliberation.
"Bread of deceit is sweet to a man; but afterwards his mouth shall be filled with gravel"[17]
Lying and deceit may succeed, and men may be pleased with it, but soon the truth is exposed, and they look at the liar's mouth as though it were full of gravel.
* Lying is the destruction and absence of love, and perjury is the denial of God.
* He who has acquired the fear of the Lord has put lying away from him, for he has his conscience as an upright judge.
St. John Climacus
"Every purpose is established by counsel: and with good advice make war" [18]

The Lord Christ asks us not to be rash, but in every decision we must first count the cost. "Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand? Or else, while the other is yet a great way off, he sendeth an ambassage, and desireth conditions of peace" (Lk 14:31-32).
"He that goeth about as a talebearer revealeth secrets: therefore meddle not with him that openeth wide his lips" [19]

He who engages in talebearing against a person, showing kindness to his face while disfiguring his image before others, is a deceitful man who knows no love. It is not fitting for us to trust such a flatterer, nor to listen to his words.

* I heard some slandering their neighbor, and I rebuked them. And the doers of evil answered me, defending themselves by saying that they were doing this out of their love and concern for the one they were slandering. And I said to them: "Stop such love, otherwise you give the lie to him who said: 'Whoso privily slandereth his neighbour, him I used to cast out' (Ps 101:5). For this is the kind of love that God accepts."
* Judging others is a shameless usurpation of an authority that belongs to God alone; condemning a companion is the destruction of the soul.
St. John Climacus
"Whoso curseth his father or his mother, his lamp shall be put out in obscure darkness" [20]

He who dishonors his parents finds his light put out, and darkness surrounds him. For even if the parents err it is fitting for the children to cover over them, as Shem and Japheth did when Noah was uncovered because of his drunkenness (Gen 9:23).
"An inheritance may be gotten hastily at the beginning; but the end thereof shall not be blessed."[21]
Hoarding wealth by an unlawful way causes a man to lose the blessing of the Lord (Prov 21:6; 28:20).

* When these burn with the desire to be filled and satisfied with every kind of wealth and quickly, to these Scripture says: "He that maketh haste to be rich shall not be innocent" (Prov 28:20), and it is clear that those who strive to increase their riches by effort do not care to avoid sin, and imitate the birds when they watch greedily for the earthly bait.

They do not realize that they are being choked in the snares of sin, and they long for worldly gains, and ignore the loss they will suffer in the future; these must hear Scripture that says: "An inheritance may be gotten hastily at the beginning; but the end thereof shall not be blessed" (Prov 20:21).

This life is in truth a beginning, so that in the end we may enter the land of the chosen. For when we desire riches here by love of evil, we strip ourselves of the eternal Fatherly inheritance. To those who wish to gain much and are able to achieve all they desire, Scripture says: "For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?" (Mt 16:26). It is as though the Truth were saying plainly: "What does a man gain if he can gather everything around him and curse his own soul?"

And the desire of the wicked plunderers is usually quickly corrected when they are assured by admonition that this life is passing and perishing. We remind those who persevere in being rich in this world that their wealth will not last long and swift death will surprise them to strip them of all that they gathered by evil means. For so they carry with them to judgment an accusation of robbery. Let them contemplate examples of men whom they used to curse. They examined their consciences and were ashamed, because they were imitating persons whom they had formerly cursed for committing the very same evil deeds themselves.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"Say not thou, I will recompense evil;
but wait on the LORD, and he shall save thee." [22]

The believer feels that his whole life is in the hand of the Lord his God, so he does not avenge himself, nor even desire vengeance on his opponents through others, but desires their salvation, and believes that God turns all things to his good and theirs. The Apostle says: "Recompense to no man evil for evil. Provide things honest in the sight of all men. If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men. Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord" (Rom 12:17-19).
"Divers weights are an abomination unto the LORD; and a false balance is not good" [23]
It has been spoken of before (Prov 20:10).
"Man's goings are of the LORD; how can a man then understand his own way?" [24]

Man cannot by his own understanding, nor by his personal effort, recognize the way of truth and walk in it. He needs a divine intervention, the grace of God. The prophet Jeremiah says: "O LORD, I know that the way of man is not in himself: it is not in man that walketh to direct his steps." As he also says: "O LORD, correct me, but in truth; not in thine anger, lest thou bring me to nothing" (Jer 10:23-24).
God is ready to guide His children and lead them and uphold them: "I will instruct thee and teach thee in the way which thou shalt go: I will counsel thee, mine eye shall be upon thee" (Ps 32:8).

It was not possible for Moses or any other of the prophets to walk the way without God's leading him. He often assured him: "I will be with thee" (Ex 3:12), "Now therefore go, and I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt say" (Ex 4:12).

* These things which God has commanded will not be accomplished except as a gift from the Giver of the commandments and by His help, for it is in vain that we ask for them if we are able to accomplish them without the help of His grace.

St. Augustine * To the Lord belong the firstfruits (the beginning of the work) and the achievements (its completion). That I may begin to walk in the way I must be called, for: "Man's goings are of the LORD; how can a man then understand his own way?" (Prov 24:20). And that I may not turn aside from the straight ways and may not walk in a crooked way, I say by way of wish: "O that my ways were directed to keep thy statutes!" For I do not keep Your statutes unless my ways are under Your guidance and management.

Origen * Do we still dare to boast of free will and insult the blessings of God, the Giver of gifts, if the chosen vessel (Paul) writes plainly: "But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us" (2 Cor 4:7)?

St. Jerome * Who is it that writes in hearts? It is God who writes with His finger in all consciences the natural law which He gave to the human race. In it we begin and receive the seeds of truth to enter by it into the depth. These seeds, if we take care to sow them, bring forth in us good fruits in Christ Jesus.
Origen * It was Paul's custom to ask that the grace of Christ be with those to whom he wrote.
Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrus
"It is a snare to the man who speaketh rashly, saying, It is holy, and after the vows to make enquiry!"[25]
It is not fitting for us to be hasty in judging that a thing is holy without examining it and inquiring into it, just as it is not permitted to be hasty in vowing.
Jephthah was hasty in his vow, and offered his only daughter as a sacrifice (Judg 11:30-40).
"A wise king scattereth the wicked, and bringeth the threshing wheel over them" [26]

The wise king removes the wicked from his palace, and surrounds himself with faithful men who love truth and righteousness, so he is assured of their loyalty as of their counsel, and can rely on them in many matters. By this the king, like the kingdom, enjoys a kind of stability.

What we say of the king and the temporal kingdom applies also to the Kingdom of God which He establishes in our souls, for in order to enjoy this Kingdom we must leave no trace of evil and corruption in us. We cannot practice good unless we cease from evil, for there is no fellowship between light and darkness, and between Christ and Belial.
The Apostle Paul demanded of the Church of Corinth that they remove the wicked person from among them, lest he be a corrupt leaven that corrupts the whole lump!
"The spirit of man is the candle of the LORD, searching all the inward parts of the belly" [27]

God gives the spirit of man the light of knowledge, "For what man knoweth the things of a man, save the spirit of man which is in him?" (1 Cor 2:11). The Spirit is here called "the candle of the Lord," giving light not of itself, but by the work of God in it, therefore he did not say: "the light of the Lord" but His candle. Through the spirit God speaks with man, and draws him to Himself, and reveals to him His secrets.
"They conceive woe, and bring forth iniquity, and their womb prepareth deceit" (Job 15:35) [Vulgate].
(Man) conceives woe when he devises evil things, and brings forth iniquity when he begins to carry out what he devised.
By indulging in envy he conceives woe, and by uttering slanders he brings forth iniquity.
It is a great evil when the wicked man strives to show others as wicked, so that he himself may seem holy, by showing others as unholy.

* We must bear in mind that the title "belly" or "womb" is used in Holy Scripture to mean "the mind." It was said of Solomon: "The candle of the LORD is the ways of men, searching all the inward parts of the mind (understanding)" (Prov 20:27).

By the title "womb" is meant "the mind." For just as offspring are conceived in the womb, so thought is generated in the mind. And just as flesh is found in the belly so are thoughts in the mind. So the womb of the hypocrite prepares deceits, for he always conceives in his mind great evils against his neighbors, proportioned to his aims regarding himself, to appear innocent before all men.

* The pains of the body are a great grace which the sick man must realize, for they cleanse from iniquities, and restrain the sins that may be committed. Likewise the mind suffers from wounds hard to bear that dominate it from outward blows. Therefore Holy Scripture says: "The bruises of a wound are cleansing to the wicked, and stripes reach the chambers of the belly" (Prov 20:30). Yes, the bruises of wounds cleanse from evils; that is, the pains of purification cleanse from evils, whether in thought or deed. Bellies usually denote minds, because as bellies consume food the mind takes in cares by contemplating and thinking on them. We learn that the mind is denoted by the belly from the passage that is written: "The spirit of man is the candle of the LORD, searching all the inward parts of the belly" (Prov 20:27), that is, that the candle of divine inspiration enters into the human soul and enlightens it, revealing it to itself as a mirror. For before the coming of the Holy Spirit the soul used to sport with iniquities, but it did not know how to appraise their dangers.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"Mercy and truth preserve the king: and his throne is upholden by mercy" [28]

Nothing gives stability to the king's throne like the work of mercy and holding fast to truth. By this he becomes like the Lord Christ, who offered His mercy to the whole world by the Cross, and gave us Himself as the Truth.
* Nothing makes us equal to God except doing good (mercy).

* Let us bring ourselves and our children and all that are ours to the school of mercy, and let a man learn it above all things, for mercy is man... Let us count ourselves as not alive if we do not yet show mercy!

* This is the work of God... God created the heavens and the earth and the sea. Great are these works and worthy of His wisdom! But none of these has the power to draw human nature to Him like His mercy and His love for mankind!

* Charity (mercy) is like the highest of crafts, and a protector of him who practices it. It is dear to God, and always stands by Him asking Him on behalf of those who desire it, if we practice it in a way that is not mistaken...!
It intercedes even for those who hate, great is its authority even for those who sin!
It looses bonds, and scatters darkness and quenches fire, and kills the worm, and removes the gnashing of teeth.
Before it the gates of heaven open with great assurance, and it enters as a queen and none of the doorkeepers at the gates dares to ask her who she is, but all receive her at once.
So also is the case with mercy, for she is in truth a true queen, who makes men like God. She is winged and light, with golden wings on which she flies, greatly delighting the angels.
St. John Chrysostom
"The glory of young men is their strength: and the beauty of old men is the grey head"[29]

* The work of wisdom is righteousness, for she turns her gift from the stubborn and unbelieving to the believers, the obedient people of God. In any case it is useful here to observe carefully this remark: [Wisdom is known by her works] (cf. Mt 11:19).

St. Hilary, Bishop of Poitiers * "Wisdom is with the grey hairs, and understanding with length of days." That is because we acquire wisdom by study, and learning is planted in the mind by the lessons of men. But with God it is otherwise, for He Himself is Wisdom in His person, and it is He who teaches the lessons of wisdom.
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem
"The blueness of a wound cleanseth away evil: so do stripes the inward parts of the belly." [30]

Discipline is the mark of sonship, for the father cares for the edification of his legitimate son, and does not care for bastards (illegitimate children): "But if ye be without chastisement, whereof all are partakers, then are ye bastards, and not sons." And as St. John Chrysostom said: [If lack of discipline is a mark peculiar to bastards, then it is fitting for us to rejoice in discipline as a sign of the legitimacy of our sonship.]

* A father does not discipline his son if he does not love him, and the good teacher does not correct his pupil unless he sees in him signs of obtaining the promise. When the physician withdraws his care from a sick man, this is a sign of his despair of his healing.

St. Jerome * Yes, "the bruises of a wound are cleansing to the wicked, and stripes reach the chambers of the belly." That is, when we are struck from outside, we are called in silence, tormented, to remember our sins and see them with our eyes. And in the measure that we suffer outwardly, in that measure we grieve inwardly over our deeds. So the outward wounds of the body coincide with the secret sufferings that cleanse the chambers of the belly completely. Grief over hidden wounds heals the malice of evil deeds.

We must exhort the sick man to keep the virtue of gentleness, and to consider how great were the torments that our Savior bore at the hands of those whom He formed. And how grievous and dreadful were those insults, how many were the blows on the pure face at the hands of mockers. All this while the Savior was every day snatching souls from the captives in the grip of the ancient enemy. And while He was washing us with the water of salvation, He did not wipe His face of the spittle of the treacherous. He bore in silence our insults to free us from eternal torment through His role as Mediator, He bore the blows to grant us immortal glory with the choirs of angels. And while He saved us from the reproach of sins, He did not fear to expose His head to the thorns. He accepted the bitterness of gall in His thirst that He might make us drink the sweetness of the eternal water. And when they offered Him worship in mockery He kept silent, and offered on our behalf the worship of love to the Father although He is equal to Him in essence. And although He is the Life, He passed over to death so as to prepare life for the dead. Why then should it be hard for man to receive the divine blows for his evil deeds, if God bore such evil as this in return for His good deeds? And who is that wise and prudent man who denies kindness because suffering has struck him, while the Savior who lived without sin was not spared the beating of the whips?
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Let Your wisdom lead me in all the paths of life!
* Let me be drunk with Your love, so that I do not seek the pleasures of the body.
My mind is lifted up with my heart to behold Your mysteries!
So my body does not seek the wine of this world.
And I do not enslave myself to any addiction!
* By Your wisdom I respect every man, I submit to the authorities by Your fear.
And I give honor to whom honor is due.
Fear will not occupy my heart, for I carry Your fear, the giver of joy!
* I possess You, for You are my peace.
Peace dwells within me, and I enjoy reconciliation with heaven, and I long for the whole earth to become heaven, its law true peace.
* My God... You are working on my behalf until now.
How can I open a door to sloth and slackness?
How can I deliver my life through sloth to the enemy of good?
* Let me work by You until I meet You.
Grant me the spirit of humility, so that I seek for myself a counselor who upholds me by Your Spirit.
I see You working in the humble, and delighting in those who walk in the spirit of obedience.
* Expose me before myself, lest I be exposed on the great day of the Lord.
Let me not be occupied with men's praise or blame.
But let me take shelter in Your mercy and Your righteousness.
Who is justified before You?
Your grace covers me!
* Your grace sanctifies my concepts, so that I enjoy true standards.
My senses and my feelings and all my conduct are sanctified by You.
My soul keeps watch to work on behalf of Your Kingdom.
I walk in the spirit of wisdom and balance.
The truth works in me, so that I do not know lying.
I love all, and do not practice talebearing against anyone.
I respect all the members of my family.
And I show compassion to every man.
I accept all discipline from Your hands!
And You work all things for the edification of my soul.

1 The king’s heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will. 2 Every way of a man is right in his own eyes: but the LORD pondereth the hearts. 3 To do justice and judgment is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice. 4 A haughty look and a swelling heart, the light of the wicked, is sin.
The king’s heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will [1].

On the last night of the kingdom of Babylon, the prophet Daniel wanted to reveal to King Belshazzar that God is behind the rise of every kingdom, and that He has a special plan for the life of every king. This is the God whose house’s vessels Belshazzar had defiled (Dan 5:1-4), so he said to him: “O thou king, the most high God gave Nebuchadnezzar thy father a kingdom, and majesty, and glory, and honour...” (Dan 5:18, etc.).

All kings, the pious and the wicked, believers and unbelievers, will not move without God’s permission or will. Many of them think that they are able to work on a worldwide level, such as Pharaoh of Egypt, the kings of Assyria and Babylon, the Caesars of Rome, Alexander the Great and Napoleon Bonaparte. They did not know that they could not act without God’s permission. They declared, openly or secretly, their independence from God. This is what many leaders, and indeed many of the people, feel: that they do as they please. We need to celebrate daily our declaration of dependence on Almighty God, and not our independence from Him.

Esther realized this and cried out with her people, and the Lord moved the king’s heart, as is told throughout the whole book, especially when the king’s sleep fled from him and he read in the book of the records of the chronicles what Mordecai had done, and events moved on behalf of the people of God (Dan 6).
The hand of God moved Cyrus the Persian, for it is said: “Thus saith the LORD to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have holden, to subdue nations before him...”

If this is God’s work even with wicked kings, how much more is His role in the lives of His believers, as He says to the prophet Jeremiah: “Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee, and I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations” (Jer 1:5).

As the One who weighs the hearts, He is the only physician specialized in mending the heart and renewing it. Therefore we cry out to Him at the beginning of the prayer in every hour: “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Ps 51).

Who is the king whose heart is in the hand of the Lord? 1. The righteous leader: every righteous leader feels that his leading role does not rest on attaining a certain position, whether at the level of society or the Church, or work or the family, etc., but is realized when he acquires within himself a kingly heart, by his union with the Lord, the King of kings. The leader walks in humility and surrender in the hands of God, who directs his heart, his mind, his feelings and his sensations. His leading role is in truth walking according to the will of God, his Leader. 2. The wicked leader: some see that God permits him in order to discipline the wicked who are subject to him and to prove the children of God, so God uses him for edification. In this way his heart is in the hand of the Lord. This is as was said of Nebuchadnezzar and other kings who humbled the people of God in order to discipline them, so that Nebuchadnezzar, the pagan and wicked, was called the servant of the Lord. 3. Every holy soul is counted in the eyes of God a queen or a king, as the beloved St. John says: “And hath made us kings and priests unto God and his Father” (Rev 1:6). The wise man says: “The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God” (Wis 3:1).

* Surrender your soul into the hands of the Lord. Not only when you depart from the body, but also when you are in the body, it is in the hands of the Lord, even if you do not see it, nor see its source, nor the place of its arrival. It is in you and with the Lord. Therefore “the king’s heart is in the hand of the Lord,” who leads it and rules over it. The heart is also full of the Spirit, for the spirit is the governing part in the soul, and it is the power of the soul.
