But the slanderer falls recklessly by his deeds, from which he will not escape or come out.
St. Ambrose * The conduct of the monk must be pure, and he must not be a mockery to wicked women. For the woman who walks with flattery in the midst of houses is an arrow of the tempter.

St. Hyperechius the Priest * Abba Gerasimus met a naked woman in the wilderness. When she saw him she hid from him. He wanted to speak to her, and she hid behind a rock and spoke to him. He said to her: “How long have you been in this wilderness?” She said: “Fifty years.” He said to her: “And what was your food?” She said: “The Creator does not lose what He has created.” He said: “And what have you seen in this wilderness?” She said: “I have seen nothing but Christ and His works and His deeds.” He said to her: “In what is salvation found?” She said: “In your leaving what you are in.” He said to her: “And what is that?” She said: “Your being occupied with weeping over your sins is better than your asking a woman about what does not benefit you.” He said to her: “You have spoken truly,” and he made a prostration (metanoia) and departed.
Paradise of the Fathers Foolishness is bound in the heart of a child;
but the rod of correction shall drive it far from him [15].

The wise man asks parents to discipline their children with wisdom and understanding, so that they may not be bound to foolishness. The “rod” does not necessarily mean bodily punishment, but taking a firm stand joined with parental love and clarity of purpose, namely that the child not deviate from the straight way fitting for the children of God. Discipline with wisdom does not provoke the son under discipline to resentment and anger or a sense of injustice, but leads him to discover his follies and to seek wisdom. The wise man says in another place: “A reproof entereth more into a wise man than an hundred stripes into a fool” (Prov 17:10).

It is noticed that Solomon does not care only about outward behavior, but concentrates his attention on the heart, saying: “Foolishness is bound in the heart of a child.” So he seeks the healing of the heart, even if by the rod of correction.

* One of the Fathers said: “There is nothing better than this commandment: not to despise any of the brethren, for it is written: ‘Thou shalt in any wise rebuke thy neighbour, and not suffer sin upon him’ (Lev 19:17). If you know that your brother is in error and do not tell him so that he may know his error, his blood will be required at your hands; but if after the rebuke he persists in the sin and remains in it, he dies in his sin. How good is rebuke when it is done with love and humility, and not with reproach and contempt.”

Paradise of the Fathers * He who quibbles in the face of discipline drives away from himself the fatherly mercies. He who murmurs against trials has them multiplied upon him. He who is not disciplined here and crushed by trials is tormented there without mercy.

St. Isaac the Syrian * Rejoice that God visits you, and keep this blessed saying on your lips: “The Lord hath chastened me sore: but he hath not given me over unto death” (Ps 118:18). Even if you are iron, the fire has burned the rust off you, and if you are righteous and fall ill, you will go from strength to strength. And remember what is written: “If so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together” (Rom 8:17).
St. Amma Syncletica * She was asked: “How should a person rebuke?” She said: “As a father rebukes his son, and as the physician’s purpose is to heal the sick.
* And she was also asked: “How should rebuke be received?” She said: “As a child receives the discipline of his father and the sick man the treatment of his physician.”

St. Basil the Great * Let us receive trials as we receive medicines from the physician so that we may be saved, and as we receive discipline from the father so that we may be trained. For this reason the wise man said: “My son, if thou come to serve the Lord God, stand fast in righteousness and godliness, and prepare thy soul for temptation” (Sir 2:1).

St. John Chrysostom * Once again, after a long time, love compels me to strike you with the rod of Christ, which is for discipline and rebuke, so that the word of Scripture may be fulfilled in us: “Faithful are the wounds of a friend” (Prov 27:6), and what follows. And again, if we discipline you, do not faint, but remember the saying: “My son, despise not thou the chastening of the Lord, nor faint when thou art rebuked of him: for whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth” (Heb 12:5-6). But even if I rebuke you, you are not ignorant of the Apostle’s saying: “Reprove, rebuke, exhort” (2 Tim 4:2).
St. Barsanuphius and his disciple John He that oppresseth the poor to increase his riches, and he that giveth to the rich, shall surely come to want [16].

The wise man condemns two practices carried out for the purpose of acquiring gain or increasing resources: oppressing the poor, and giving gifts or bribes to the rich for the sake of material advantage or to obtain honour and authority. Both are hateful, even if they achieve temporary success, for they remove the Lord’s blessing from the man, and he comes into spiritual and material want.
Many have become poor through their oppression of the poor or their generosity in giving to the rich, not out of love but to obtain vain glory!

entries.section: 7. Resorting to the counsel of the wise

paragraphs.text: 17 Bow down thine ear, and hear the words of the wise, and apply thine heart unto my knowledge. 18 For it is a pleasant thing if thou keep them within thee; if they be fixed together upon thy lips. 19 That thy trust may be in the Lord, I have made known to thee this day, even to thee. 20 Have not I written to thee excellent things in counsels and knowledge, 21 That I might make thee know the certainty of the words of truth; that thou mightest answer the words of truth to them that send unto thee?
Bow down thine ear, and hear the words of the wise, and apply thine heart unto my knowledge [17].

Solomon felt the value of wisdom and went on at length in praising it, especially in the book of Wisdom (Wis 7-9), counting it better than the throne and the scepter (Wis 7:8), and than wealth (Wis 7:8), as well as than health and beauty, and even than visible light, for it is the source of sciences and knowledge, a reflection of the divine light (Wis 7:17 etc.), and he asked that it be the companion of his life (Wis 9). It is the bride who bestows glory, the immortal one, who sits on the heavenly throne. He wishes that the whole world might enjoy union with the wisdom of God.
* The monk ought to take counsel from a wise man, and not let the counsel of a fool dwell in his heart.

St. Hyperechius the Priest * Brother, the Holy Bible says: “Do all things with counsel” (Prov 24:6), and “Do nothing without counsel” (Sir 32:24). When you acted without counsel, but by your own will, you were not struggling with your mind. For there is none who does not need counsel except God alone, who created wisdom; but when you sought to cut off your passion according to God and to attain humility, and to take me, your very little brother, as a guide, you stirred up the envy of Satan, the enemy of good, who envies all people continually.

* Submit yourself to a teacher, that he may discipline you with mercy. “Do nothing without counsel” (Sir 32:19) even if things seem good to you, for the light of the demons finally becomes darkness. If you hear or think or see anything that leaves even a little disturbance in your heart, know that it is from the demons.

St. Barsanuphius * In Jerusalem there was a virgin who was shut in for six years, wearing sackcloth, and her asceticism was excessive, and she never ate anything pleasant. The Fathers forbade her this, but she did not listen to anyone’s counsel, and so she was stripped of God’s help because of her arrogance and self-admiration; the guardian of her chastity departed from her, and she fell a hideous fall. She brought in to her a man who used to serve her, and fell into sin with him. This calamity came upon her because she made the purpose of her asceticism to be show, and not for the love of God, and she thought herself better than many. When pomp took hold of her, she fell into the hand of the devil.

Paradise of the Fathers Everyone needs the counsel of a wise father of confession or a wise guide, even the solitary monk, however long his experience in the holy life and in fellowship with God. In the discourse of St. Gregory, head of the hermits of Cyprus, who departed at the end of the fourth century, he directs the attention of the hermits to the danger of a man relying on his own wisdom and not seeking the counsel of his father in a spirit of humility, for in this there is a hindrance to the practice of all the virtues and their uprooting, since the demons are given authority over him.

* Hear me, my brethren the monks, and guard this way of life, in which the salvation of your souls and their life is hidden and kept: Do not rely on your wisdom or on your knowledge, but follow in humility the counsel of your fathers, for doubt is a hindrance to all the virtues and uproots them, and is like a prison that binds all its disciples in ignorance, for they think that they will enter the Kingdom of Heaven without many afflictions.

* Because of their disobedience to the counsel of their spiritual fathers and their exhortation, the demons stripped them of the work of the holy virtues and filled them with all that Paul spoke of, for they thought that without the love of God and the keeping of His commandments they could attain and take for themselves the divine rest and the joy that is given to the hermits for their active labor.

entries.section: 7. Resorting to the counsel of the wise

paragraphs.text: St. Gregory, head of the hermits of Cyprus For it is a pleasant thing if thou keep them within thee; if they be fixed together upon thy lips [18].
He asks the hearer to treasure wisdom in his heart, and as we said before, the “heart” among the Jews is equivalent to the “mind” among the Greeks, and both mean the inner man.
Wisdom is kept in the heart and fixed upon the lips, so that the person has no other speech than what proceeds from the inner wisdom.

entries.section: 7. Resorting to the counsel of the wise

paragraphs.text: That thy trust may be in the Lord, I have made known to thee this day, even to thee [19].
No one enjoys true wisdom without relying on the Giver of wisdom.

entries.section: 7. Resorting to the counsel of the wise

paragraphs.text: Have not I written to thee excellent things in counsels and knowledge [20].
The wise man affirms that what he writes is not mere human wisdom, nor the fruit of human experience alone, but that he writes excellent things concerning our fellowship with God.

The literal translation of the Hebrew text is: “Have I not set it before you in three ways” or “a third time.” The text in the Septuagint is: “You describe the matters to yourself in three ways according to the breadth of your heart.”

* He who opens his heart with purity contemplates the words of God in their practical, physical and theological meanings. Therefore the whole body of Scripture can be divided into three parts: ethical, physical and theological. The book of Proverbs corresponds to the first part, Ecclesiastes to the second, and the Song of Songs to the third.

St. Evagrius * Just as human beings consist of body, soul and spirit, so the Holy Bible consists of the body of the letters, from which the ignorant person benefits, and which is called “the manual teaching.” The second consists of the soul, which is a higher meaning, understood by one who is more learned. And it also contains a spirit, which is the highest and the most spiritual contemplation, which the perfect speak and understand.

entries.section: 7. Resorting to the counsel of the wise

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom That I might make thee know the certainty of the words of truth; that thou mightest answer the words of truth to them that send unto thee? [21].

If the wise man in his love offers the light of divine truth and wisdom to the one who asked him, he requires the asker in turn to offer it to the one who sent him. Wisdom is offered to every person, to Solomon himself, to the one who came as a messenger to ask him, and to the one who sent this messenger.
Wisdom is a deposit of love; keeping it does not lie in hiding it, but in a man’s longing that all his brethren may enjoy it, offering it faithfully.
22 Rob not the poor, because he is poor: neither oppress the afflicted in the gate: 23 For the Lord will plead their cause, and spoil the soul of those that spoiled them.
Rob not the poor, because he is poor: neither oppress the afflicted in the gate [22].

Cases were heard at the gate of the city, and perhaps the choice of the courts of justice at the gates of the city carries a symbol that no unjust man, usurper or evildoer may enter the city. Here he gives a warning to the ruler and the judge and those who share with them in the courts of justice, against those who rob the poor man of his right and wrong him for the sake of the rich or those in authority.
For the Lord will plead their cause, and spoil the soul of those that spoiled them [23].

There is the Judge of judges and King of kings who specializes in defending the wronged, especially the poor and needy, who have none to inquire after them. He pleads their cause against the unjust judges, and judges the unjust with what they judged unjustly against others, so He spoils the spoilers. It is as though he who robs the needy man and presses upon him is robbing himself and pressing upon his own depths, as it is said in Obadiah: “As thou hast done, it shall be done unto thee: thy reward shall return upon thine own head” (Obad 15).

* “As thou hast done, it shall be done unto thee” (Obad 15). Such is the order of nature, that each one receives the same treatment with which he treats others, and the recompense is returned to him exactly equal to the deeds he practices.
St. Cyril the Great

entries.section: 9. Keeping company with an angry man

paragraphs.text: 24 Make no friendship with an angry man; and with a furious man thou shalt not go: 25 Lest thou learn his ways, and get a snare to thy soul.
Make no friendship with an angry man; and with a furious man thou shalt not go [24].

The wise man looks upon anger and wrath as a dangerous plague whose infection can spread quickly, so he warns us not to be in the company of an angry man, or even to walk with a furious man on the road. “Evil communications corrupt good manners” (1 Cor 15:33).

* To live among those who are without conscience and who are deceivers in their regard for keeping the commandments is dangerous, as is clear from Solomon’s following words: “Make no friendship with an angry man; and with a furious man thou shalt not walk, lest thou learn his ways, and get a snare to thy soul.

entries.section: 9. Keeping company with an angry man

paragraphs.text: St. Basil the Great Lest thou learn his ways, and get a snare to thy soul [25].

Let a man not rely on himself, thinking that friendship with an angry man and walking with a furious man cannot affect his conduct, for being lenient with oneself and accepting fellowship with the furious is a snare that a man sets for himself.

entries.section: 10. Wisdom in going surety for others

paragraphs.text: Be not thou one of them that strike hands, or of them that are sureties for debts [26].

entries.section: 10. Wisdom in going surety for others

paragraphs.text: If thou hast nothing to pay, why should he take away thy bed from under thee? [27].

Here he returns to repeat in the book his warning against being careless in going surety for the debts of a person or of reckless people, for because of this surety a man may lose even his bed on which he sleeps. We were warned before in Proverbs 6:1 and 17:18, and I have already commented on this warning.

Pope Gregory (the Great) used this warning while writing on pastoral care: it is fitting for superiors and leaders to care for the salvation of those under their leadership, lest their blood be required of them, as being sureties for them or responsible for them.

* We must therefore offer exhortation to subordinates, lest they receive a severer punishment if they are not justified even in their personal capacity; as for superiors, let them beware lest they be judged because of the faults of their subordinates, even if they are indifferent to their own deeds.

We must exhort the flock to care for itself, for the greater this care, the less it is entangled in caring for others. Likewise we must exhort the others (the shepherds) to fulfil their responsibility for the flock with wisdom, without neglecting their responsibility for themselves.

Scripture says to those who are slothful in caring for their own affairs: “Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise” (Prov 6:6). But to the other comes the fearful warning in the words of Scripture: “My son, if thou be surety for thy friend, if thou hast stricken thy hand with a stranger, thou art snared with the words of thy mouth, thou art taken with the words of thy mouth” (Prov 6:1-2). It is clear that he who goes surety for his friend takes upon himself the responsibility for the soul of another person by guaranteeing his conduct, and if he strikes his hand with a stranger, the mind is occupied with a new responsibility, and likewise when he is snared with the words of his mouth, and taken with the words in him, for if he speaks good words about those for whom he is responsible, he must needs watch over the subject of his speech. The speech is snared in his mouth because there is an urgent necessity that he rein himself in with prudence, lest negligence and slackness creep into his life, which would not agree with his teaching. Accordingly Scripture adds to the previous words the good exhortation: “Do this now, my son, and deliver thyself, when thou art come into the hand of thy friend; go, humble thyself, and make sure thy friend. Give not sleep to thine eyes, nor slumber to thine eyelids” (Prov 6:3-4). For the shepherd who has taken the responsibility of others upon himself, as an example by his life, must be on guard not only for himself but must labor to raise up the brethren of his flock.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set [28].

This can be understood as an affirmation of the commandment given by Moses the prophet (Deut 19:14), where he required every tribe, when receiving its portion in the land of promise, not to remove the landmarks of its boundaries and so seize from the fields or lands of the surrounding tribes. It is a commandment to every believer to be faithful in his dealings, not to cheat in the scales, and not to seize the right of his neighbor or relative. It can also be interpreted spiritually, as we saw before, namely that we keep the deposit of the faith, that is, the Tradition concerning the doctrines of the faith, without change.

Origen and other Fathers see in this commandment that what we received from the early Church concerning the canonical books of the Holy Bible and the Creed are the ancient landmarks set by our fathers under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, which we must preserve.

* We do not allow the faith or the Creed, defined by our holy fathers assembled in the days of the Council of Nicaea, to be shaken by anyone, nor do we entrust ourselves or others to replace a word of what they set down, or to tamper with a letter of it. For we remember him who said: “Remove not the landmark which thy fathers have set.”
St. Cyril the Great Some see that moving the landmark is to transgress the limits of the virtues, so that they turn into vices.

* He who moves the boundary of godliness turns it into superstitious beliefs or into evil. And he who moves the boundary of courage changes it into recklessness or cowardice. In the same way this applies to the other virtues as well as to doctrines and other matters of the faith.
This also concerns the teaching about the Holy Trinity. For whoever denies the divinity of the Holy Spirit denies Baptism, and whoever calls others gods brings in a whole temple of pagan gods.
St. Evagrius
Seest thou a man diligent in his business?
He shall stand before kings;
he shall not stand before mean men! [29]

A renewed and repeated call to a life of striving and faithfulness in family life, work and worship, so that we may hear the divine voice: “Thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.” The diligent man stands with boldness before the King of kings, to enjoy the divine embrace, but the slothful man’s portion is with the mean, that is, the unfaithful demons.

* Cursed is he who hides the wheat at the time of sowing (see Prov 11:26), for the divine parable [of the talents (Mt 25:14-30)] requires us not to neglect the gift or hide it without increasing and multiplying it, or else we shall justly be cast out as wicked murmurers. On this basis the Lord praised those who multiplied their talents, saying: “Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord (Mt 25:23).

* There is a commandment from the Apostle to his disciple that obliges him not to let the grace given to us be idle and without profit. And he affirms, saying to him, not to neglect the gift given to him. For he that tilleth his land is satisfied with bread, but the way of the slothful man is full of thorns. And the Spirit warns us not to fall into this (sloth), saying: “Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns” (Jer 4:3). And the prophet shows the end of such sloth, saying: “Cursed be he that doeth the work of the Lord deceitfully” (Jer 10:48). For the servant of God must be diligent and careful. Yes, rather he must be fervent as fire, so that when he crushes the fleshly lusts with a fervent spirit he may be able to draw near to God, whom the saints call “a consuming fire.”
St. Athanasius the Apostolic
For my sake You became poor, that You might make me rich!
* Let me possess You, who for my sake became poor; in You I become rich, so my soul lacks nothing, for You are my virtue and my wealth!
* In You I look upon all humanity, and I see all as the work of Your hands; all are born naked, and go out of the world naked; You are the glory and honour of man!
* The storms of evil blow, and I take refuge in You, O Rock of ages.
I clothe myself with Your humility, and You pour Your splendor upon me.
You keep me from the thorns of the world and the snares of the enemy.
* In the waters of Baptism I put on the garment of sonship; I became a child ascribed to You.
Let me receive all discipline and training from Your hands,
so that I may grow and enjoy true maturity.
* I flee from strife and contention, and let malice have no place in my heart.
You grant me peace and purity of heart; You give grace to my lips, so that they overflow with the honey of Your love.
You open my inner sight, and pour into me the knowledge of love.
* In You I go out to work with all diligence, for You are always working for my sake.
No enticement draws me, as long as You fill all my depths!
* I will not close my hand to the poor, nor wrong a hired servant, nor bribe a rich man for material benefit or to obtain honour!
* Let me possess Your humility, and so submit to the counsel of the wise,
and not rely in pride on my own opinion!
* My depths cry out to Your wisdom:
Welcome to your house!
And my lips are silent, so as to speak only according to your counsel.
* Grant me Your tenderness, that I may be merciful to all.
Let me not mock a poor man or rob him of his right, nor despise a needy man and wrong him.
For You are the Father of all, the Judge of the wronged, and the defender of those who have none to inquire after them.
* In my companionship with You, I do not walk with an angry man in his way, nor do I find rest with a murmuring, furious man.
I will not accept walking on a road in which You are not.
And I will lean on no one but Your breast!
* You grant me Your wisdom, so I bear the spirit of discernment, and do not confuse virtue with vice!
Nor do I mix light with darkness.
* Who gives me the spirit of faithfulness but You? Who supports me in my striving but You?
In You I am faithful in everything!

entries.section: 1. Etiquette of sitting at a ruler’s table

paragraphs.text: 1 When thou sittest to eat with a ruler, consider diligently what is before thee: 2 And put a knife to thy throat, if thou be a man given to appetite. 3 Be not desirous of his dainties: for they are bread of lies.
When thou sittest to eat with a ruler, consider diligently what is before thee [1].

Many rejoice that they find favor with the ruler, enter with him into an almost familial relationship, and share with him at his table. But it is fitting for a person, however firmly his relationship with the ruler is established, to recognize his limits; if he sits with him at the table, let him consider that he is in the presence of a ruler, and not take advantage of his love, but give honour to whom honour is due (Rom 13:7).

St. Evagrius sees that if a person must be careful when he sits with a ruler, then all the more must he be careful when he reads the Holy Bible as the royal table, contemplating it in a spiritual, intellectual way, for understanding it in a literal way does not give us the truth. Many of the Fathers see that this table is the table of the Eucharist.

* “When thou sittest to eat with the ruler, understand with discernment what is before thee.” Christ has already been proclaimed as the Ruler; His table and food are the words of His teaching about the eternal good things. He who understands with discernment what Jesus teaches by His works and words stretches out his hand, which means his works, and begins to show that he imitates Christ, becoming humble, peaceable, loving to all, patient in trials. He who does not do this, but instead looks eagerly toward the pleasures of the world, must cease to desire temporal goods, which are the mark of the vain life, and whoever loves them will not enjoy the eternal possessions.

St. John Chrysostom * What is the “table of the one in authority (the ruler)” but the mind of him who said: “I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me” (Phil 4:13), “when I am weak, then am I strong” (2 Cor 12:10)? On the table of this pure man of authority, that is, in his heart and in his mind, bread is offered to the Lord.
If you sit at the table of this Apostle who has authority, it is that you may understand with discernment what is set before you, that is, understand spiritually what he says.

Origen * The Holy Scriptures alert us to partake with discernment of the table when we are invited to eat at the table of a rich man. I can say that the table of the Holy Bible, which belongs to the Rich One, is set before us. We enter a garden filled with roses; here a rose, there a lily gleaming with whiteness; in every place there are many kinds of flowers.

St. Jerome * What is “the ruler’s table” but the table from which we partake of the Body and Blood of Him who gave His life for us? And what is sitting but approaching in humility? And what is considering and understanding the things set before you but being made worthy to receive so great a grace as this?
* You are approaching the table of the ruler. You who are believers know to what table you are approaching. To what royal table you are approaching.
What is set before you is not a table made by the skill of cooks. Christ Himself sets His table, and He satisfies you. Be poor, and you will receive your fill.

* Certainly it is a great table, where the Lord of the table Himself is the feast. No one feeds his guests with himself as food. But Christ the Lord did this, being Himself the Host, and Himself the food and drink.

entries.section: 1. Etiquette of sitting at a ruler’s table

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine And put a knife to thy throat, if thou be a man given to appetite [2].

It is fitting for a person not to be gluttonous, but to eat in order to live, and not to live in order to eat and take pleasure in food. How much more when he sits at the table of a ruler, for his sitting with the ruler is loftier and more delightful than the desire for food.

If this is so with regard to sitting with a ruler, how much more when you are in the presence of the King of kings and Lord of lords, for there is no pleasure of food or drink, or preoccupation with luxurious clothing, or luxury, or frivolous laughter that should draw us away from the sweetness of sitting with Him.

* Hear then, my beloved, to whom I write, I mean what concerns the hermits, monks, virgins and saints. Above all it is fitting for the man upon whom the yoke has been placed to be firm in his faith. And as I wrote to you in the first epistle, he must be zealous in fasting and prayer, fervent in the love of Christ, humble, meek and wise. Let his speech be calm and cheerful, and his mind sincere toward all. Let him weigh the words he utters, and make a fence for his mouth that turns it away from harmful words, and let him keep entirely away from frivolous laughter.
May he not love showy clothing, and it is not fitting for him to grow his hair long and adorn it and anoint it with perfumes.
May he not run after banquets, nor wear luxurious clothes.
Let him not presume to drink more wine.

entries.section: 1. Etiquette of sitting at a ruler’s table

paragraphs.text: St. Aphrahat Be not desirous of his dainties: for they are bread of lies [3].

Daniel and his three young companions give us living examples of not desiring the king’s dainties. For since they did not indulge themselves in the dainties, “God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom: and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams” (Dan 1:17).

* There is no limit to the gluttony practiced by these people. Truly, in the constant invention of a multitude of new sweets and the search for recipes for foods, they are ruined amid pastries and honey cakes and sweets...
A man of this kind (a glutton) is nothing but a huge mouth... But as for us, who seek the heavenly food, we must control our bellies and keep them under the watch of heaven.

St. Clement of Alexandria * Beware of gluttony! Do not be bound to your appetite, for it drives the fear of God out of the heart and modesty out of the face, makes a man captive to perishable, base passions, and leads the mind astray from God. Let your eating be for the sustenance of the body and not for appetite, make it weak (feeble) a little, and tire it much with prostrations (metanoia).
Abba Anthony the Great * Do not go to the feasts of the saints and eat and drink and make merry, for it was gluttony that drove Adam out of Paradise.
St. Abba Isaiah * The beginning of all goodness is spiritual love, followed by humility and the love of poverty and the cutting off of familiarity. But the ruin of the soul is the love of the belly.

St. Abba Pishoy * Eating with appetite is desiring to take food not for the need of the body but because of gluttony. But if a man sees that for a right motive (such as the health of the body) he prefers, for example, green vegetables to dry legumes, this is not for the sake of appetite but because they are lighter (that is, easier to digest); then the case is different.
John, disciple of St. Barsanuphius

entries.section: 2. Freeing the heart from the desire for wealth

paragraphs.text: 4 Labour not to be rich: cease from thine own wisdom. 5 Wilt thou make thine eyes fly toward it, and it is not? for it maketh itself wings; as an eagle it flieth toward heaven.
Labour not to be rich.
Cease from thine own wisdom [4].

Some reckon it to be prudence or wisdom for people to spend all their effort or energies to become rich, so they gather money greedily and not from inner satisfaction. These make wealth a god to whom they bow in worship, just as gluttons make their bellies gods. Both labor without rest, and the world uses them instead of their using it.
Wilt thou make thine eyes fly toward it, and it is not?
for it maketh itself wings.

entries.section: 2. Freeing the heart from the desire for wealth

paragraphs.text: As an eagle it flieth toward heaven [5].

The wise man likens the greedy to those who set up wings for wealth, not that it may fly with them to rest, but that it may fly away from them and vanish, so that they do not find what they had gathered. Whereas the contented man who uses the world well carries the two wings of the Spirit to fly as it were to heaven, while the labor of the greedy man’s hands flies away from him, and he is left cast down in the world in dire want!

When Gehazi, the disciple of the prophet Elisha, was enslaved by the love of money, he ran after Naaman the Syrian to take something from him (2 Kgs 5:2), and he received double what he asked, but Naaman’s leprosy clung to him and to his seed also (2 Kgs 5:27). And when Achan the son of Carmi coveted a goodly Babylonish garment and two hundred shekels of silver and a wedge of gold (Josh 7:21), the wrath of God came upon the whole people because of him.
* You cannot live according to God if you love money and earthly pleasures.

St. Abba Isidore * Listen to me, my brother, and bear with an opinion from me that may profit you: you are tempted by the demon of covetousness and the love of money, for I have seen it in you; but if you accept my advice and drive it out of your heart, you will complete the work of God perfectly in this place, and in the end you will be glorified, and God’s chastisements will not come near you. But if you do not listen to me, you will fall into what Gehazi fell into, because his disease is in you!

* I tell you, my son, that every evil work is in these two things: fornication and the love of money, although fornication is very evil, and after a little while a man turns his face away from it and is disgusted by it because of its foul smell. But the love of money comes from hoarding, and when it comes it is sweet to you, because it is greedy and insatiable; for this reason a man must seal the doors of the church of the wilderness and the doors of the dead with fear of the powers of this age, for in truth certain men will arise who search and inquire into the inheritance of those who sleep, forgetting what is written: “If riches increase, set not your heart upon them” (Ps 62:10) LXX, and this is what the Apostle speaks of: “The love of money is the root of all evil” (1 Tim 6:10).
St. Macarius the Great

6 Eat thou not the bread of him that hath an evil eye, neither desire thou his dainty meats: 7 For as he thinketh in his heart, so is he: Eat and drink, saith he to thee; but his heart is not with thee. 8 The morsel which thou hast eaten shalt thou vomit up, and lose thy sweet words. 9 Speak not in the ears of a fool: for he will despise the wisdom of thy words.
Eat thou not the bread of him that hath an evil eye, neither desire thou his dainty meats [6].

While we love all humanity from all the heart, this love must be in the Lord, practiced in a spirit of wisdom, so that it is for our edification and the edification of others. But whoever befriends the wicked to share their pleasures and lusts, drives his life toward destruction.

* Wise is he who forbids us to eat in the company of an envious man, and in his reference to this company at the table, this applies also to every other social relationship. Just as we must be careful in material matters that can easily catch fire, and keep as far from the fire as possible, so it is fitting for us to refrain as far as we can from forming friendships in all circles in which the envious are members. By doing this we keep ourselves out of range of their spears. For we are caught in the troubles of envy only when we draw near to it.
St. Cyril the Great For as he thinketh in his heart, so is he.
Eat and drink, saith he to thee; but his heart is not with thee [7].

The wise man calls us to flee from the table of the wicked man, for while he offers you food and drink he carries no true love within him; rather, what concerns him is the cost of the table he has set before you, or how he can exploit the offering of the feast to push you toward evil, The morsel which thou hast eaten shalt thou vomit up, and lose thy sweet words [8].
When a person discovers that the wicked friend offers his table but not his heart, and that his honeyed words hide bad feelings, he cannot stand the food offered to him but vomits it up.
* Do not corrupt the commandment of God for the sake of anyone’s friendship.

St. Anthony the Great * If you have a friendship with one of the brethren, and your mind reproaches you that your association with him harms you, cut yourself off from him. And I say this, beloved, not so that you may hate people, but so that you may cut off the causes of vice.
St. Ephrem the Syrian * Let us follow the friendships that are according to the Spirit, for they are strong and hard to dissolve, and not the friendships that are formed around the table.

St. John Chrysostom * Do not bind yourself in friendship with any person except your poor brethren; do not hasten to any person for him to do you good, but hasten to God alone and care for His service, for it is He who gathers you into the bowels of His fatherhood. But as for you, beware of familiarity with people, and let all your familiarity be only between you and God. Do not hasten to any person to enjoy rest in your familiarity with him; do not presume upon his dwelling, and do not stay with him without receiving an order to do so, lest you be a burden to him. My brother, if you wish to be at rest all your life, and to have your thoughts united with God every hour, beware of familiarity with people.
St. Macarius the Great Speak not in the ears of a fool: for he will despise the wisdom of thy words [9].

The foolish man who persists in his folly in stubbornness stops his ears from listening to any counsel, so it is fitting for the wise man not to waste his time giving him advice. As the Lord Christ says: “Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you” (Mt 7:6).

* We can understand “that which is holy” and “pearls” as one thing, called holy because of the obligation not to corrupt it, and pearls because of the obligation not to despise it. For a man corrupts what he does not wish to keep whole, and despises what he reckons trifling and base. Therefore a despised thing is said to be trampled under feet. The Lord says: “Give not that which is holy unto the dogs,” because dogs rush upon a thing to tear it, even if this thing cannot be torn, corrupted or defiled. Let us then consider what these violent and fiercely hostile opponents of the Spirit desire. They desire to destroy the truth, which cannot be destroyed. But swine differ from dogs, for they do not attack to tear with their teeth, but they defile the thing by trampling it with their feet in recklessness... Let us then understand that the “dogs” signify the opponents of the truth, and the “swine” those who despise it.

St. Augustine * Take care lest you be led into teaching while you are young, and go astray through vainglory, and do not teach what you have learned by experience, more than by reading, to those who have been defiled to the end (that is, the reckless), so that what the wise man Solomon declared is fulfilled, who said: “Speak not in the ears of a fool: for he will despise the wisdom of thy words” (Prov 9:23). And “Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you” (Mt 6:7). It is fitting for us to hide the secrets of the spiritual meanings from people of this kind, so that we may truly sing: “Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee” (Ps 11:119).
Father Nesteros
Remove not the old landmark; and enter not into the fields of the fatherless [10].
For their redeemer is mighty.
He shall plead their cause with thee [11].

Whoever wrongs widows, orphans, the weak and those unable to defend themselves defies God Himself, their Creator and living Redeemer. He pleads their cause, defends them, and restores their rights to them.

Queen Jezebel killed poor Naboth the Jezreelite and inherited his vineyard (1 Kgs 21), and she thought that there was no one who could defend him, but the dogs ate her in the very field of Jezreel that she had seized (2 Kgs 9).

12 Apply thine heart unto instruction, and thine ears to the words of knowledge. 13 Withhold not correction from the child: for if thou beatest him with the rod, he shall not die. 14 Thou shalt beat him with the rod, and shalt deliver his soul from hell.
Apply thine heart unto instruction, and thine ears to the words of knowledge [12].

Kail and Deiltesch see that this proverb is a summary or echo of what is stated in (Prov 22:17-21), and as for the word “instruction” here, in their opinion it refers to discipline, whether from God or from human beings in moderation.

This advice is general, directed to the old as to the young, to those who need to learn and to those who are already learned. We all need God’s plan and His dealings with us even when they seem firm, just as we need guiding fathers, so that we may incline our ears to the words of knowledge in a spirit of humility.

In the discourse of St. Gregory, head of the hermits of Cyprus, he likens this holy knowledge to the yoke (the part of the plow that is placed on the neck of the ox); without it the soil of the heart will not be plowed to bear the fruits of the Spirit.

* The yoke with which these holy farmers toil is the holy knowledge, composed of three divine virtues, namely love, fasting and prayer, or faith, hope and love, and the furrow in which this plow goes to cleave the earth is the humility beloved of God, before which all ranks of the demons tremble, that virtue into which the demons have not been able to enter.
St. Gregory of Cyprus * God will give you knowledge so that you may know Him.
St. Stephen of Thebes * The foundation of the monk’s life is true knowledge, and the monk’s ignorance darkens himself.

Of St. Hyperechius the Priest * One pilgrim met another pilgrim in the wilderness of Sinai and asked him: “By what is salvation attained?” He said: “By knowledge of the truth of things, and working according to the truth.” He said to him: “Is he who does not know not saved?” He said: “He is not saved.” He said: “And what is knowledge?” He answered: “That the servant know the truth about his Creator, and from what He created him, and what his end will be. For if he knows that, he will not disobey Him, but will work to please Him throughout his life.” He said: “You have spoken truly,” and then departed.
Paradise of the Fathers * If a man knows that he is transgressing the commandment, he shows one proof of knowledge, and he who knows corrects himself.
St. Barsanuphius Withhold not correction from the child: for if thou beatest him with the rod, he shall not die [13].
Thou shalt beat him with the rod, and shalt deliver his soul from hell [14].
Discipline with wisdom and love benefits children, for though they suffer a little for a time, it keeps them from falling into the pit.

God in His fatherhood to us disciplines us, not out of vengeance but out of kindness toward us and compassion on us for our edification, for the wise man says: “For whom the Lord loveth he correcteth; even as a father the son in whom he delighteth” (Prov 12:3). Firmness in fatherhood differs from the cruelty that lacks fatherhood, for it springs from sincere love.
We must bear in mind that before we discipline, our heart must be enlarged with love, as St. Augustine says: [Rebuke must be preceded by mercy, not by anger.]

* Correction by discipline, as their names (that is, correction and discipline) imply, is blows that have their effect upon the soul, so that they restrain sin, guard against death, and lead those enslaved by vice to self-control.

St. Clement of Alexandria * Just as little children who are neglectful in learning become more alert and obedient after being punished by their teacher or trainer, and just as they do not listen before they are beaten, but after feeling the pain of the beating they hear and respond as though their ears had been newly opened, and progress takes place in their memory, so also with those who neglect the divine teaching and lightly resist the commandments. For after they experience God’s correction of them by discipline, the commandments of God, which were always known to them yet which they neglected, are received with great readiness, as with newly washed ears.
St. Basil the Great * Fathers, teach your children in the Lord, and bring them up with discipline and the knowledge of Christ, and teach them fitting trades, lest they be accused of idleness...
Do not be afraid to rebuke them and teach them with authority, for you do not kill them if you teach them, but you love them.

entries.section: 6. The righteous son makes his father’s heart rejoice

paragraphs.text: My son, if thine heart be wise, my heart shall rejoice, even mine [15].

entries.section: 6. The righteous son makes his father’s heart rejoice

paragraphs.text: Yea, my reins shall rejoice, when thy lips speak right things [16].

After speaking of the necessity of disciplining children, lest the children think that in this there is a kind of disdain of the fathers for them, or contempt for their thinking, or stifling of their breath, he gives us his personal experience with regard to his own sons. He rejoices in their wisdom, and his heart exults in their success through the uprightness of their lives.

These are Solomon’s feelings toward his children; how much more are the feelings of God and His joy in the wisdom of His children. He gives His children wisdom, and then boasts in their wisdom and the uprightness of their hearts.
Here he urges children not to be angry when they fall under the divine discipline or the discipline of their parents.

And why do we speak of the joy of God and of parents in children upright in heart, when even the angels rejoice in them, as appears from the vision of St. Abba Anthony at the departure of St. Abba Paul.
* The crucified monk who dies every day acquires great grace, for the angels rejoice in him when he is received into the Kingdom of Heaven.

* How great is the joy of the angels when they see a sinner enter the Kingdom of Heaven by his repentance! And how great is the delight of the saints when they find a sinner turning back from his error! So after you imitate their faith, seek diligently the joy that follows it.

St. Hyperechius the Priest * (On the meeting of Abba Anthony with Abba Paul) Abba Anthony returned by the same road by which he had come, longing to see Abba Paul before he gave up his spirit to Christ, but on his way he saw a company of angels and in their midst St. Paul as they were taking him up, and they were praising and saying:
“Peace upon your meeting with the saints, O Paul, man of God.
The angels rejoice with you. You will be glad in the heavens.
You have left the darkness behind, and gone forth to the Paradise of bliss.
You have left sorrow behind for the joy that has no end.
You have left weeping behind, and you will go on to eternal joy.
For you have become blessed in your generation, and your memory is through the passing of the ages.
You are a man of God; blessed are you, and again blessed.”

Paradise of the Fathers * They said to him (to Abba Anthony): “What is the meaning of the Apostle’s saying: ‘Rejoice in the Lord’?” He said: “If we rejoice in doing the commandments, this is rejoicing in the Lord. Let us rejoice in fulfilling the commandments of the Lord and in the success of our brethren, and let us guard ourselves from the joy of the world and from laughter if we want to be of the Lord’s own. For He said that the world will rejoice, and you will weep (Jn 16:20), and He said that woe is to those who laugh and blessed are those who weep (Lk 6:21, 25). And it is not written that He ever laughed, and it is written that He grieved and His eyes shed tears (Jn 11:35).
Paradise of the Fathers

entries.section: 7. Holding fast to the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: 17 Let not thine heart envy sinners: but be thou in the fear of the Lord all the day long. 18 For surely there is an end; and thine expectation shall not be cut off.
Let not thine heart envy sinners: but be thou in the fear of the Lord all the day long [17].

Some envy the wicked who prosper, but whoever enjoys the fear of the Lord realizes that the success of the wicked is temporary and does not last, and that if they do not return to the Lord they perish. But whoever places his hope in the Lord in a spirit of godliness and the fear of the Lord will surely be rewarded in due time.

* Three things make the heart rejoice: distinguishing good from evil, thinking about a matter before it is carried out, and keeping away from cunning. And three things enlighten the mind: doing good to him who has wronged you, patiently enduring what befalls you from your enemies, and ceasing to look with envy at him who is ahead of you in the world.
St. Abba Arsenius * Just as fire dries up the moisture of wood and burns it, so the fear of the Lord, when it dwells in a man, dries up his flesh and withers his bones.

* There is nothing that rises above the fear of the Lord, for it rules over everything, and by the fear of the Lord everyone departs from all evils. Let us therefore acquire this fear for ourselves, let us turn away from everything that God does not want, and test and keep everything that pleases Him, and do nothing that grieves Him, and know that everything we do He beholds, and nothing is hidden from Him.

St. Macarius the Great * In our time we do not find anyone who asks: Who is it that fears the Lord? But rather: Who is the senior by the laying on of hands? And if they say: So-and-so is senior, they say to him: It is fitting for you to sit at the head of the table. And no one remembers the words of the Savior when He pronounced woe on the scribes and Pharisees.

entries.section: 7. Holding fast to the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: St. Aphrahat For surely there is an end; and thine expectation shall not be cut off [18].

At the same time that the wise man warns us not to envy the wicked for the progress, success or abundance of goods they have attained, because these are temporary things, he asks us to fix our eyes on the hope of obtaining the eternal inheritance, true success and lasting victory. For the true believer, hope opens the doors of heaven before his eyes, so he lives rejoicing under all the circumstances of life, however harsh they may seem. He is confident in the riches of God’s grace and the possibility of enjoying a life of victory.

* Do not be fainthearted, O monk who labors in the virtues, and say in your heart: My enemies have caught me for nothing like a bird. Know that the victory of Jesus is with you at all times, and cry out with joy, and say: The Lord is my help; whom shall I fear? Knock at the door of His tenderness, and He will answer you quickly. Ask Him your petition in faith, and He will give you His mercies many times over, and do not say: I cannot work.
* What dries up all the crops of Satan is prayer with hope in God.

* If the demon of dejection comes upon them (the believers), let them be comforted by the promises of our Lord, and look to the hope of the riches of the Spirit, and surrender themselves to the promises of joy. By this the sorrows of dejection will pass from them with God’s help, and His joy will dwell in their souls.

* Flee from the counsels of the demon of dejection and from the cutting off of hope, and listen with love to these discernments that we have set down for you: Christ is merciful, so seek Him with all your hearts, and be strengthened, and He will heal the pains of your bodies and the sicknesses of your souls. Do not fear, O laborer, and do not tremble at the threats of the demons. For they are scattered before the power of virtue. You who have been overcome by the demons, work and live, and do not cut off your hope.

If you have sinned like the thief, cry out to our Lord: “Remember me,” and you will live; or if you have fallen like the harlot, go out in search of the mercy of our Lord and you will find it. Do not fear, and do not rest from seeking mercy. Flee from thoughts of cutting off hope.
St. Gregory of Cyprus

19 Hear thou, my son, and be wise, and guide thine heart in the way. 20 Be not among winebibbers; among those who destroy their own bodies: 21 For the drunkard and the prodigal shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags.
Hear thou, my son, and be wise, and guide thine heart in the way [19].

In the spirit of tender fatherhood the wise man declares that he does not seek to deprive his son of anything, but that when he forbids him to be addicted to wine or to excess in bodily pleasures, it is only in order that his son may walk with wisdom in the straight way, for the good of his body, soul and spirit.
He warns him against the company of drunkards and those immersed in excess and pleasures, for the company of the wicked impels one to share in their evils.
Be not among winebibbers; among those who destroy their own bodies [20].
For the drunkard and the prodigal shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags [21].

St. Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, sees that it is fitting for the believer to obey the commandment of the Lord Christ to put off the old garment (Mk 21:2), the tattered garment worn by him who is drunk with wine and by the harlot (Prov 21:23), in order to put on the new garment, the garment of purity and immortality, after the likeness of the garment of the Lord Christ in which He appeared at His Transfiguration. * The Fathers said: “Where there is wine drinking... there is no need for a demon.”

* An elder said: “It is good for your name to be found written in the houses of the poor and widows and the weak, rather than found written in the houses of wine sellers. And it is good for your mouth to smell foul from the severity of fasting, rather than for its smell to be that of wine.”

* The monks were celebrating one of the feasts in Scetis, and they gave one of the elders a cup of wine, and he refused it, saying: “Take this death away from me.” When the others who were eating with him saw what he had done, they too refused to take any wine.
Paradise of the Fathers * Above all the monk must avoid gatherings with women and the drinking of wine, for wine and women make even the wise fall (Sir 19:2).
St. Basil the Great
Hearken unto thy father that begat thee, and despise not thy mother when she is old [22].

It was said of the Lord Christ: “Though he were a Son, yet learned he obedience by the things which he suffered” (Heb 8:5). And we, as members of His body, when we are united with Him, are rightly counted obedient, since we bear fellowship in His features. On the other hand, we understand obedience not as servility and humiliation or a diminishing of our worth, but as union with Christ, who obeyed the Father while being one with Him in essence, and obeyed St. Mary and St. Joseph, who were the work of His hands. Thus we understand true obedience as union with the Lord Christ and maturity.

* The Scripture says, “He was subject unto them.” To whom was Jesus subject? Was He not subject to His parents? As the Son of Man He was subject to both of His parents (St. Joseph, His father according to the Law, and St. Mary, His mother)...
Let children learn their commandments: which are obedience and submission to their parents. For the world was subject to Christ, and Christ was subject to His parents.
St. Augustine
Buy the truth, and sell it not; also wisdom, and instruction, and understanding [23].

* May we hunger for righteousness and be filled (Mt 5:6) from the table of His Kingdom. Let us be the salt of the truth, so that we do not become food for the serpent. Let us clear our seed of thorns, so that we may bring forth fruit a hundredfold (Lk 8:7-8).
Let us set our building upon the rock (Mt 7:24), so that it is not shaken by winds and waves.
Let us be vessels unto honour (2 Tim 2:21), so that the Lord may seek us for His use.
Let us sell all that we have and buy for ourselves the pearl (Mt 13:46), and so be enriched.
* Let us gird our loins with truth, so that we are not found weak in the battle.
St. Aphrahat

entries.section: 11. The parents’ joy in the righteous son

paragraphs.text: The father of the righteous shall greatly rejoice: and he that begetteth a wise child shall have joy of him [24].

entries.section: 11. The parents’ joy in the righteous son

paragraphs.text: Thy father and thy mother shall be glad, and she that bare thee shall rejoice [25].

When the life of Saul of Tarsus changed and he enjoyed the new holy life, he says: “And they glorified God in me” (Gal 1:24). This is the attitude of the Church, which exulted in the life of Saul (the Apostle Paul), who became her son. In the same spirit the hearts of parents are filled with inexpressible joy when they see in their children the righteousness of Christ and the wisdom of God working in their lives, and their souls are refreshed, as they see that God has listened to their prayers for their children, sanctified their lives, and removed from them sinful habits that they used to practice.
My son, give me thine heart, and let thine eyes observe my ways [26].

The most that God wants from us is the heart. In the Old Testament the Law was given to us engraved on stones, that our stony hearts might catch something of the divine Law, or that the Law might leave its imprints on our hearts. And since this did not happen, the Gospel of the New Testament gave us a law carved by the Holy Spirit on our hearts. “I will put my laws into their mind, and write them in their hearts” (Heb 10:8). Therefore when the priest cries out: “Lift up your hearts,” the people sing exultantly: “We lift them up unto the Lord.”
* Within you is either the knowledge of the truth or ignorance, delight in virtue or in vice; by this we prepare our hearts either for the Kingdom of Christ or the kingdom of the devil.

Father Moses * If you do not give your soul, you lose it. Love itself speaks through wisdom, and tells you, in order to save you from a state of panic, as it is said: “Give me your soul.” If someone wants to sell you a field, he says to you: “Give me your gold,” and if it is something else he says to you: “Give me your copper,” “Give me your silver.” Now listen to what love says to you, speaking through the mouth of wisdom: “My son, give me thine heart.” What do you give it? “Your heart, my son.” Your heart was evil when it was with you, when you kept it for yourself. You were drawn this way and that as by dolls and trifles and the lusts of destructive love. Cast your heart away from all this. Where are you drawing it? Where are you putting it? Wisdom says: “Give me thine heart.” Make it mine, and you will not lose it.
St. Augustine
For a whore is a deep ditch; and a strange woman is a narrow pit [27].
She also lieth in wait as for a prey, and increaseth the transgressors among men [28].

There is no virtue greater than purity and cleanness, so that a person sees in the other sex brothers or sisters, whom he respects as persons, and not as objects for the satisfaction of his evil lusts. Therefore it is fitting for a person to flee from stumbling, lest he fall into adultery, even in thought or even in dreams, or later in moments of his weakness. The enemy of good wishes, if possible, to corrupt the purity of every person, even if he is a hermit ascetic.

* Solomon compares the love of such a woman to a deep pit. She calls the one who loves her lame when she sees that he has lost all his possessions (that is, she mocks him and the poverty that has befallen him because of her). And she does not stop at this, but opposes him with all her effort without ceasing and causes his collapse, and mocks him, and causes him many troubles, things which words cannot describe.

St. John Chrysostom * Woe to the unjust, for his wealth flees from him and an unquenchable fire meets him. Woe to the negligent, for they wish for the time they neglected and do not find it. Woe to the lover of fornication, for he goes out from the king’s wedding feast in shame. Woe to the deceiver and the drunkard, for they are condemned with murderers and adulterers. Woe to him who respects persons, for the shepherd will deny him and the wolves will devour him.
St. Nilus of Sinai * If we keep the right faith and keep the body from fornication and the tongue from slander, then by the grace of God we are prospering according to this age.

Abba Palla * A brother asked an elder about thoughts of fornication, saying: “What shall I do about the thought of fornication that troubles me?” Father Copres of Alexandria answered, saying: “Cast yourself down in prayer before God, for if we had no thoughts we would be mere animals. Just as the enemy works for what is his, so let us work for what is ours. Let us stand in prayer and let us care for our faith, and let us endure, for enduring with patience is itself a victory. And if a man does not strive he will never be crowned. For there are champions in the world who win in spite of their wounds, and although two persons may wound one person many times, if he can endure the blows he can triumph over the two who struck him. Observe what degree of endurance those who work for trade in this world possess! So you too endure, and God will fight against your enemies on your behalf while you remain quiet.”

Paradise of the Fathers * The demon of fornication stirs up bodily lust, and launches his attack on the ascetics, and strives to make them abandon their asceticism, sowing in their souls that this asceticism of theirs is of no use.
And if he is able to defile the soul, he begins to prepare it to speak some (evil) talk and to listen to it, so that it seems as though the (evil) deed itself is present before their eyes.

* The demon of vainglory is opposed to the demon of fornication. And it is not possible for the two to fight the soul together. For one promises honour and dignity, and the other brings shame. Therefore if one of them draws near to you and begins to trouble you, call to mind the thoughts you were exposed to from the opposing demon; and if you succeed in what the proverb says about driving out a nail with a nail, know that you are on the way to being without passion (free from lust), if you prove that your mind is able to drive away the counsels of the demon concerning human thoughts.
But of course, if you are able to drive away the thought of vainglory by humility, and the thought of fornication by chastity, this is a sign that you are “free from passion.”

Try also to do this with all the demons and their opposites, and ask God to help and assist you, so that you may drive away the enemies by the second method (resorting to humility and chastity, etc.).
St. Evagrius of Pontus

29 Who hath woe? who hath sorrow? who hath contentions? who hath distress? who hath wounds without cause? who hath redness of eyes? 30 They that tarry long at the wine; they that go to seek mixed wine. 31 Look not thou upon the wine when it is red, when it giveth his colour in the cup, when it goeth down smoothly. 32 At the last it biteth like a serpent, and stingeth like an adder. 33 Thine eyes shall behold strange women, and thine heart shall utter perverse things. 34 Yea, thou shalt be as he that lieth down in the midst of the sea, or as he that lieth upon the top of a mast. 35 They have stricken me, shalt thou say, and I was not sick; they have beaten me, and I knew it not: when shall I awake? I will seek it yet again.
Who hath woe?
who hath sorrow?
who hath contentions?
who hath distress? who hath wounds without cause?
who hath redness of eyes? [29]
The wise man presents us with six brief questions, and the answer to them comes in the following verses, which give a terrifying description of the life of the drunkard.
They that tarry long at the wine; they that go to seek mixed wine [30].
Look not thou upon the wine when it is red, when it giveth his colour in the cup, when it goeth down smoothly [31].

* With reference to the redness of the eyes, a sign of death, it is clear that the bubbling of wine is indeed death to the Word and to reason. It proclaims his death to the Lord. When a man forgets the motives that urge him to seek the true life, he is drawn down toward corruption. Therefore, for a good reason, the Teacher who cares for our salvation strictly forbids us: “Be not drunk with wine.”

St. Clement of Alexandria * Understand this, brethren: every drunkard makes the habit of drinking an inner leprosy in the soul, for the soul of the drunkard is known to be like the body of the leper. Therefore whoever wishes to be free from the sin of drunkenness, which kills the soul and weakens the body, must drink little. Whoever does not keep this rule is hated by God and an object of men’s mockery.

* Those who want to be like this (drunkards) try in a wretched way to find an excuse for themselves. They say: My friend will be upset if I do not give him what he wants to drink when I invite him to a banquet. [But I say to you,] let there be no friend of yours who wants to make you displeasing to God, for he is an enemy to himself as well as to you. If you make yourself like other drunkards, you will have a man as a friend, and God as an enemy to you.
Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles At the last it biteth like a serpent, and stingeth like an adder [32].

Drunkenness is one of the great plagues that afflict humanity, and causes it misery. Though all recognize its danger, it nevertheless attracts many and leads them astray. The wise man likens it to a poisonous serpent that a man embraces and it destroys him.
* It was said of Abba Paphnutius that he did not drink wine even when he was ill.

* Brethren asked an elder: “What is the meaning of Abba Sisoes’ saying that the third cup is from Satan?” The elder said: “That is because he knew that excess is the cause of all sins: abuse, striking, fornication and the rest of the passions. Therefore we must avoid drinking wine not only because of the passions, but also because of the relaxation it brings into our hearts, so that the demons find the opportunity to draw us into sin and deprive us of the blessedness that our Lord promised to those who mourn. The hermits withdrew in order to mourn at all times and to labor in every work, for with much sorrow they are able to keep their souls from the deceit of the demons and the multitude of battles; so how could they drink much wine that gladdens their hearts and looses their seals, and fall into the sins of drunken laymen?!”
Paradise of the Fathers Thine eyes shall behold strange women, and thine heart shall utter perverse things [33].

Drunkenness inflames in a man bodily lusts that cause him to lose his purity and the uprightness of his life. It also stirs in his depths a state of disturbance and imbalance, which is often reflected even in his conduct, so that he loses his balance.

* Whoever allows himself to drink wine cannot escape the assault of thoughts and the ugliness of deeds, for when Lot was compelled by his two daughters and became drunk with wine, it was easy for Satan to cause him to fall into the ugly act of fornication.

Abba Isidore * An elder said: “Wine stirs up the desire for procreation and gladdens the heart (humanly), and dispels sorrow (in a soulish, bodily way), as the wise Solomon said: ‘Give strong drink unto him that is ready to perish, and wine unto those that be of heavy hearts. Let him drink, and forget his poverty, and remember his misery no more’ (Prov 31:6-7).’”
Paradise of the Fathers: "Yea, thou shalt be as he that lieth down in the midst of the sea, or as he that lieth upon the top of a mast" [34].

The drunkard resembles a man lying down in the midst of the waves of the sea, or resting his head on the top of a mast; he will find no rest and feel no security, although he often justifies his resort to drunkenness as an escape from the problems and troubles that pursue him.
He says: "They have stricken me, and I was not sick.
They have beaten me, and I felt it not.
When shall I awake? I will seek it yet again" [35].

* The early Fathers found the drinking of wine very hard, because it makes the old men like children without knowledge, and stirs in the young men an inclination to evil desire, and the ascetics hate it because of the grievous war of fornication.

* Abba Isaiah was asked: "If a brother compels me to drink a cup of wine with him in his cell, is it good for me to go with him?" He answered: "Flee from the drinking of wine, and you will be safe as the gazelle is safe from the beast. For many, because of this matter, have been driven to fall through their thoughts."
Paradise of the Fathers: * Do not love wine, lest it deprive you of the good pleasure of God. Love the poor, that you may be delivered in the time of distress.

St. Abba Moses the Black: * When we are struck with blindness we cannot see in ourselves anything but grave offenses, supposing that we need only be clean of those offenses alone which the laws of the world condemn. And if we see that we have been freed from them for a while, we think that we have become entirely without sin... So we do not see the many stains that gather together within us, and consequently we do not remove them by saving contrition, nor do we grieve when thoughts of vainglory befall us, nor do we weep over our prayers which we offer in great slackness and lukewarmness. Nor do we count the wandering of our mind during the chanting of the Psalms and prayers as a fault. Nor are we ashamed of our imaginations of many things which we would be ashamed to utter or practice before men, and which are laid bare before the divine sight. Nor do we cleanse the corruption of defiled dreams with abundant tears... Nor do we believe that any loss befalls us when we forget God, thinking of corrupt earthly things. Thus the words of Solomon apply to us: "They have stricken me, and I was not sick; they have beaten me, and I felt it not."

Abba Theonas: * I am not presenting to you my own opinion, but I recall the opinion of the blessed Anthony, with which he put to shame the sloth of a certain monk who was overcome by indifference... When a man came to him and said that this order of asceticism was not perfect, declaring that he sought a greater virtue for man, practicing what belongs to the perfect life alone in a manner beyond what is fitting for the dwellers of the wilderness, then the blessed Anthony asked him about the place where he lived, and when he told him that he lived with his relatives, boasting of their help to him, freed from every care and daily labor, devoting his life to reading and prayer without ceasing and without distraction of spirit, at once the blessed Anthony said to him: Tell me, my dear friend, do you grieve at their griefs and misfortunes, and rejoice at their joys?

The man confessed that he shared with them in that, then the elder said to him: "You must know that you will be judged in the world to come for the community with which you live, thus sharing with them in their gain and loss, their joy and sorrow"...

And when he was not persuaded by this, the blessed Anthony went on to say: This kind of life and this indifference not only drive you to the loss mentioned before, even though you do not feel it now, as it is written in the Book of Proverbs: "They have stricken me, and I was not sick; they have beaten me, and I felt it not" (Prov 35:23), and as it is said in the prophet: "Strangers have devoured his strength, and he knoweth it not: yea, gray hairs are here and there upon him, yet he knoweth not" (Hos 9:7), but they also draw your mind unceasingly toward temporal things, and change it according to circumstances. Likewise, as they offer you the fruit of their hands and supply you with provisions, they thereby deprive you of carrying out the commandment of the blessed Apostle, for when he gave his last charge to the leaders of the Church of Ephesus he assured them that, despite his being occupied with his holy duties of preaching the Gospel, he was working for his own needs and the needs of those who were with him in the ministry, saying: "Yea, ye yourselves know, that these hands have ministered unto my necessities, and to them that were with me" (Acts 34:20). And that you may see how he did this as an example for us, he says in another place: "For yourselves know how ye ought to follow us: for we behaved not ourselves disorderly among you... Not because we have not power, but to make ourselves an ensample unto you to follow us" (2 Thess 7:3, 9).

Abba Abraham: * Those whom sexual desire assails and overcomes must break the earthly bonds, for when they are occupied with them immoderately, they are not aware of the arrows of sin that may pierce them. Therefore the drunken man, who has lost consciousness, says by the tongue of the prophet Solomon: "They have stricken me, and I was not sick; they have beaten me, and I felt it not: when shall I awake? I will seek it yet again" (Prov 23:35).

The mind rests and sleeps without any cares to trouble it, and feels no pain, even when it is struck. This happens when it cannot see before it the evils that surround it, nor is it aware of those it has committed. Evils crowd upon this soul, and it does not feel the allurements of vices, nor does it even want to rise to defend itself. At the same time it wishes to be awake only in order to find wine again. That is, being weighed down with a weak and wavering sleep that does not allow it to watch over itself and guard itself, it tries to awake only to plunge into the cares of this world and be drunk with its pleasures.

It sleeps at the time when it ought to be awake and watchful, and when it awakes it does not pursue what it ought, but other worldly matters. For this reason it was written before: "Yea, thou shalt be as he that lieth down in the midst of the sea, or as he that lieth upon the top of a mast" (Prov 23:34).
The man who neglects the wars of iniquities that rise against him, as though they were waves beating against mountain peaks, sleeps heavily in the midst of a sea of worldly trials.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Grant me to become in Your image!
* Sitting with rulers calls for reverence and attentiveness; let me sit at Your feet, O King of kings, and listen to Your sweet voice.
Let me enjoy the table of Your love, and long for Your eternal goods.
The world with all its pleasures becomes tasteless, for the sweetness of eternity surrounds me.
* My soul is broken within me as I sit with You at Your table.
You host me, and give me Your Body and Blood as food for my soul!
What love is greater than this!
* I will not sit with Your holy Book without You, for You are the Word of God who satisfies souls.
Your Holy Spirit is the giver of enlightenment.
I see You transfigured in Your Book, I draw from the overflow of Your glory, and my whole being is drawn toward Your heavens.
* When my soul is satisfied, gluttony flees from me.
I see life as better than food.
I eat that I may live, and I do not live that I may eat!
Life with You has its delight!
* Grant me, with Daniel and his companions, not to desire the delicacies of this world, so that Your wisdom becomes my desired food.
Grant me not to spoil my energy with greed and the love of riches, so that wealth does not become a god to me in place of You.
* Give me the wings of a dove, that I may fly and be with You in heaven.
Lest my heart be absorbed in the love of possessions, and every possession fly away, and I lose my life!
* Grant me to love everyone, yet not to enter into fellowship with an envious man, nor to share his feasts and delicacies.
Grant me friendships with spiritual people, that I may cleave to You the more, and learn much from them.
I see You transfigured in my friendship with Your children.
Embrace me with them in Your bosom.
* Teach me with whom to speak and give counsel, and when to speak, and what to say.
For I fear for myself, lest I be a lover of teaching and of much talking.
Grant me the spirit of discernment, O heavenly Wisdom of God!
* May You shine with the light of Your knowledge in my depths.
I know You, my Creator and Savior, and I know my weakness, so I cleave to You!
I know my sin, so I flee to You, O Forgiver of sins.
* Let Your hand be stretched out and discipline me, but do not deliver me to death.
There is none who loves me like You, and none who cares for my salvation and my eternity like You.
Count me as a little child, in need of Your fatherhood and tenderness, and in need of Your chastisements.
* If the hearts of our fathers rejoice in our wisdom, and their inmost parts exult in the uprightness of our life, how much more are You pleased with us, O heavenly Father, wonderful in Your love?
* Fix Your fear in my flesh, that I may walk in what pleases You, and turn aside from all that You do not desire.
I long for Your eternal Kingdom, and I seek no temporal glory!
My soul rejoices as it hopes to depart to You.
And it is not entangled in the troubles and cares of life.
Let me always enjoy Your victory, and delight in the answer to my petitions.
* Let me walk by Your Spirit with commitment, and be drunk with Your Spirit, not with the wine of the world.
* My holy Savior, in humility You obeyed St. Mary Your mother and Joseph the carpenter.
Grant me to share in Your obedience.
Grant me to be girded with truth, and to walk in wisdom, discipline, and understanding.
* Lord, receive my heart, engrave Your law upon it, and establish Your Kingdom in it.
Let no base desire draw near to it, and no evil pleasure attract it.

entries.section: 1. A warning against envying the wicked

paragraphs.text: 1 Be not thou envious against evil men, neither desire to be with them. 2 For their heart studieth destruction, and their lips talk of mischief.
Be not thou envious against evil men, neither desire to be with them [1].

The success and arrogance of the wicked have often raised questions in some about divine justice, and have sometimes even stirred people's envy and jealousy of them, as though brute force were always above the right, injustice above justice, and darkness stronger than light. It is no wonder, then, that it is said: "But as for me, my feet were almost gone; my steps had well nigh slipped. For I was envious at the arrogant, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked. For there are no bands in their death: but their body is fat. They are not in trouble as other men; neither are they plagued like other men. Therefore pride compasseth them about as a chain; violence covereth them as a garment. Their eyes stand out with fatness: they have more than heart could wish. They scoff and speak wickedly concerning oppression: they speak loftily. They set their mouth against the heavens, and their tongue walketh through the earth" (Ps 73:1-9). But the psalmist discovered that the wicked are "like the green herb" that soon wither (Ps 37:1).
