This the Holy Scripture confirms and repeats again and again; we content ourselves here with the following passages:
"The wicked man travaileth with pain all his days, and the number of years is hidden to the oppressor" (Job 15:20).
"The wicked in his pride doth persecute the poor: let them be taken in the devices that they have imagined" (Ps 10:2).
"Break thou the arm of the wicked and the evil man: seek out his wickedness till thou find none" (Ps 10:15).
"Many sorrows shall be to the wicked: but he that trusteth in the LORD, mercy shall compass him about" (Ps 32:10).
"Evil shall slay the wicked: and they that hate the righteous shall be punished" (Ps 34:21).
"For yet a little while, and the wicked shall not be: yea, thou shalt diligently consider his place, and it shall not be" (Ps 37:10).
"The curse of the LORD is in the house of the wicked: but he blesseth the habitation of the just" (Prov 3:33).
"His own iniquities shall take the wicked himself, and he shall be holden with the cords of his sins" (Prov 5:22).
"As the whirlwind passeth, so is the wicked no more: but the righteous is an everlasting foundation" (Prov 10:25).
"The righteousness of the perfect shall direct his way: but the wicked shall fall by his own wickedness" (Prov 11:5).
"The righteous is delivered out of trouble, and the wicked cometh in his stead" (Prov 11:8).
"The wicked earns the wages of deceit, but to him that soweth righteousness, the wages of faithfulness" (Prov 11:18).
"A wicked soul destroys him who has it, and makes him a laughingstock to his enemies" (Sir 6:4).
"The eye of the covetous man is not satisfied with his portion, and the injustice of the wicked wearies his soul" (Sir 14:9).
"Are there yet in the house of the wicked the treasures of wickedness, and the scant measure that is accursed?" (Mic 6:10).
* ["But as for me, my feet were almost gone; my steps had well nigh slipped. For I was envious at the arrogant, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked" (Ps 73:2-3).]

What brought him near to slipping was his envy of the ungodly, when he saw the doers of good and those committed to justice in a narrow living, hardship, and distress, while the wicked and malicious were in comfortable living, in ease and delight, so that even in their death there is nothing that troubles or distresses them. And if sickness comes upon them, their pain is light and not severe as it comes upon the good and those of virtue.
Father Anthimus of Jerusalem: * I observed the sinners, and I found them in peace (Ps 73:3).
What peace? A temporary, worldly, dissolute, and earthly peace.
I saw those who do not serve God receiving what I desire in order to serve God, and my feet slipped, and my steps had almost slipped...
Observe that these men are proud and undisciplined; observe that the ox is prepared for slaughter and is allowed to sin freely, and to break what it wants until the day of its slaughter comes.

entries.section: 1. A warning against envying the wicked

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine: For their heart studieth destruction, and their lips talk of mischief [2].

The first fruit of evil is the corruption of the heart, as it turns to violence and the love of plunder, so that true love does not dwell in it, and consequently it is unable to see God, the divine Love! Evil corrupts the heart and the lips are corrupted with it, so that if they utter sweet words they are mixed with the poison of mischief, that is, of evil. Their wicked tongues often reveal what their hearts hide of evils toward others.

3 Through wisdom is an house builded; and by understanding it is established: 4 And by knowledge shall the chambers be filled with all precious and pleasant riches. 5 A wise man is strong; yea, a man of knowledge increaseth strength. 6 For by wise counsel thou shalt make thy war: and in multitude of counsellors there is safety. 7 Wisdom is too high for a fool: he openeth not his mouth in the gate. 8 He that deviseth to do evil shall be called a mischievous person. 9 The thought of foolishness is sin: and the scorner is an abomination to men. 10 If thou faint in the day of adversity, thy strength is small.
Through wisdom is an house builded; and by understanding it is established [3].
If the Lord Christ is the wisdom of God, then our spiritual house is founded on the Lord Christ, the true Wisdom.
The building of the house of wisdom continues in this life until we reach our heavenly Jerusalem, so the wise, the learners, and the understanding do not cease seeking more.
St. Hippolytus calls on us to build walls around wisdom so that it may stand and not be shattered.
* Open the door of Your treasure to us, O Lord, when we offer the prayers of our supplications. Let our prayers serve as an ambassador for us, reconciling us with the Godhead.
O all you wise, take heed; O you learners, seek understanding and knowledge, for you are learners and wise.

St. Mar Ephrem the Syrian: * Fence it about with holy thoughts, for you need a greater defense, since there are many things that threaten such a possession with dangers. But if we are able to fortify it, if there are virtues within our power that increase the knowledge of God, these will be bulwarks for it, such as practice of it, study, and the whole chain of virtues.

St. Hippolytus: * If anyone wishes to understand the houses as good works, then every good work is the house of its owner. Those who hear the words of Jesus and do them... build their foundation upon the rock (Mt 7:24). Since virtue as a whole is one, he who strives in it builds his house, setting it upon the rock, upon the word of God who is not defeated, that is, upon Christ.

St. Didymus the Blind: * (Solomon) calls Christ wisdom and understanding. And the house is the Church (of Christ) which He builds, and He fills its storehouses with every kind of precious and splendid wealth; its storehouses are the hearts of those who believe in Christ and live in imitation of Him. These hearts abound with goodness in thoughts, words, and deeds. For this reason they are made worthy of eternal blessedness.
St. John Chrysostom: And by knowledge shall the chambers be filled with all precious and pleasant riches [4].

God, who is all-wise, created man in His image and likeness so that he might build his inner being, especially his mind, emotions, and feelings, upon divine wisdom, true knowledge, and the truth of the Gospel, so that the holy temple of the Lord is established within him. And his depths are turned into a storehouse bearing the treasures of knowledge that cannot be valued! As our teacher the Apostle James says: "But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy. And the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace of them that make peace" (Jas 3:17-18).

St. Jerome sees that everything diminishes with time, even spiritual practices such as asceticism, fasts, moving from one place to another to seek spiritual benefit, hospitality to strangers and giving, and perseverance in prayer; for as the body grows weak with advancing age these exercises lessen, but wisdom increases always and is not broken by advancing age.

The person who clings to divine wisdom does not fear time, nor illness, nor the unknown future; he is in constant growth in wisdom, discernment, learning, and knowledge, increasing in radiance and light, and even in inner strength and authority.

* This is the discernment which is called not only "the light of the body" but also "the sun," as the Apostle says: "Let not the sun go down upon your wrath" (Eph 4:26). It is also called "authority," since Scripture does not permit us to do anything without it: "He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls" (Prov 25:28).

And in it wisdom dwells, and understanding and knowledge reside, and without it our inner house is not built, and we cannot gather the spiritual wealth that is ours, for it is said: "Through wisdom is an house builded; and by understanding it is established: and by knowledge shall the chambers be filled with all precious and pleasant riches" (Prov 24:3-4).

And it is the "perfect food" on which the perfect feed in growth and health, for it is said: "But strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil" (Heb 5:14).

And its importance and necessity for us appear in proportion to the importance of the word of God and its power, for it is said: "For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart" (Heb 4:12).
Abba Moses: A wise man is strong; yea, a man of knowledge increaseth strength [5].
For by wise counsel thou shalt make thy war: and in multitude of counsellors there is safety [6].

If wisdom is the foundation for building the inner house, and is the precious treasure of the soul, then it is also the secret of the soul's true dignity and strength, as it is behind victory and salvation. The wise believer is in constant war against the devil and his hosts, resisting them with heavenly wisdom, and with humility in the counsel and direction of his spiritual fathers.
* Perhaps (Solomon) warns us not to rush into war without deliberation. He says: Look, when you take a decision, is it not profitable that wisdom be in the midst of the matters?
St. John Chrysostom: Wisdom is too high for a fool.
He openeth not his mouth in the gate [7].

The foolish man, who persists in his evil, does not accept counsel and is unable to attain wisdom. Therefore when the time comes for his trial before the divine court (justice was administered at the gates of the cities), he is silent, he openeth not his mouth in the gate, for he has nothing with which to justify his folly. He is like one who enters the wedding without a wedding garment, and when he was asked about it he "was speechless" (Mt 12:22). "Then said the king to the servants, Bind him hand and foot, and take him away, and cast him into outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth" (Mt 22:13).

How wonderful! Because of our folly we stand at the gate silent, unable to justify ourselves; so the Word of God Himself came incarnate, and He, the Holy and Righteous One, entered in our place to be tried, bearing our sins. "He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth" (Isa 53:7). He kept silent to give us Himself, that we may speak by Him, and be counted before the Father as righteous, with the right to enter His throne!

When we are summoned, not to the gate of the city for trial before the men of justice, but to the gate of the great judgment, we cannot open our mouths to defend ourselves. But thanks be to the Lamb of God, who did not open His mouth at His trial, that the gates of heaven may be opened before us on the great day of the Lord.
* By the Cross He paid our debts.
By the Cross He gladdened Paradise, whose closed gates were opened.
By the Cross He shut the gates of Hades and its bars, that those who believe in Him might not enter it.
By the Cross He crushed the ancient serpent, and made void its deceit.
By the Cross He restored to woman her dignity.
By the Cross the evil times came to an end, and the joyful age of grace was opened.
By the Cross He removed from Adam and Eve and their descendants the garments of shame, and gave them the garment of surpassing glory.
St. Mar Jacob of Serugh: He that deviseth to do evil shall be called a mischievous person [8].
The thought of foolishness is sin: and the scorner is an abomination to men [9].

Since wisdom plays the role of builder of the spiritual house [2], and grants wealth, dignity, strength, victory, and salvation (5-6), folly or evil, on the contrary, demolishes, corrupts, and causes ridicule. Man loses his spiritual, moral, social, and eternal being. He becomes a corrupt leaven, corrupting whoever clings to him or mingles with him. And he emits the odor of death, loathsome and foolish.

The fool treats the Holy One and His holy things lightly, like Pharaoh who asked scornfully: "Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice?" (Ex 5:2). And as Belshazzar the king of Babylon did, who, "whiles he tasted the wine, commanded to bring the golden and silver vessels which his father Nebuchadnezzar had taken out of the temple which was in Jerusalem; that the king, and his princes, his wives, and his concubines, might drink therein... They drank wine, and praised the gods of gold, and of silver, of brass, of iron, of wood, and of stone" (Dan 5:2-4). And since the fool treats the Holy One and holy things lightly, he himself becomes an object of ridicule, even before himself, as happened with Belshazzar, for "the king's countenance was changed, and his thoughts troubled him, so that the joints of his loins were loosed, and his knees smote one against another" (Dan 5:6).

St. Gregory of Nyssa sees that the difference between wisdom and folly is exactly like the difference between light and darkness. Darkness in truth has no being, but is the absence of light; so folly has no being, but is a deprivation of wisdom. Evil has no being, but is the absence of goodness.

* There is nothing in common between the wise person and the fool, whether in human expressions or in divine rewards. For in human works the end surprises all, while they think they are still at the beginning. But the destiny of the wise person will not share in the portion of the fool.

St. Gregory the Wonderworker: * Darkness is folly, through which we fall into sin, not seeing the truth. And knowledge is the light we obtain, which makes ignorance vanish, and also grants us pure vision.
St. Clement of Alexandria: If thou faint in the day of adversity, thy strength is small [10].

The day of adversity is the thermometer that reveals to man the truth of his strength. For the wise man, the man of God, may faint with Elijah the prophet, who "requested for himself that he might die; and said, It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life; for I am not better than my fathers" (1 Kgs 19:4). But the hand of God raised him up, and God entered into a dialogue with him, and his life at that time ended with his ascent to heaven in a chariot of fire. But as for the fool, adversity exposes the truth of his weakness, and the man himself drives himself to ruin.
He who thinks of evil or folly has taken part in sin, if not in deed or word, then in thought. This participation corrupts a man's mind and heart, and even his life.
* The knowledge of evil is not blamed; rather, participation in evil is blamed.
St. Ambrose

11 If thou forbear to deliver them that are drawn unto death, and those that are ready to be slain; 12 If thou sayest, Behold, we knew it not; doth not he that pondereth the heart consider it? and he that keepeth thy soul, doth not he know it? and shall not he render to every man according to his works?
Deliver them that are drawn unto death, and those that are ready to be slain.
Forbear not [11].

The wise man did not ask us to examine those who are led to death, for that is the work of judges and rulers. But if an opportunity is found to rescue someone from death, or from distress, we must not refrain from the work of love.
He did not specify the nationality of those whom we rescue in their distress, nor their religion, nor their conduct, since we ought to support all mankind with wisdom and love as much as we can.

* (Solomon) did not say: "Inquire out of curiosity, and find out who these are." Yet most of those led to death are wicked. This is love in general. For he who does good to a friend does it not for God's sake, but he who does good to one he does not know does it for God alone.

St. John Chrysostom: * You must therefore learn compassion for those in distress, and not terrify those exposed to the danger of deadly despair, nor burden them with harsh words, but correct them with quiet, deep words of consolation. For wise Solomon says: "Deliver them that are drawn unto death, and those that are ready to be slain. Forbear not" (Prov 24:11). And be like our Savior: "A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench..." (Mt 21:20).
Abba Moses: If thou sayest, Behold, we knew it not; doth not he that pondereth the heart consider it? and he that keepeth thy soul, doth not he know it?
And shall not he render to every man according to his works? [12].

These two verses point to a person's obligation to rescue the innocent man as long as it is within his power. It was among the common customs in Syria and Palestine at that time that when one of the criminals was taken to trial, a herald would go before him on the road announcing his crime, so that if anyone had information in favor of this accused person, he would come forward. If someone came forward, the person's trial would be reopened in the court, and his case file opened anew. If someone withheld a true piece of information that could acquit the person, he was counted as one who had killed him, because he hid from the court a truth and caused the person to be put to death unjustly.

In the parable of the Good Samaritan, the Samaritan cared for the wounded Jew and saved him from death, while the priest and the Levite were counted as having committed a crime against this wounded man, because they did not care to rescue him.

This concerns those led to bodily death; how much more is the responsibility of the believer when he sees millions of souls exposed to eternal destruction in the fire of Gehenna, and does not come forward to pray, fast, or counsel for their rescue; rather he shares with Cain the murderer of his brother, saying: "Am I my brother's keeper?"

* (The Lord) teaches us that the man who went down (from Jerusalem to Jericho) was neighbor only to the one who wished to keep the commandments and prepare himself to be a neighbor to everyone who needs help.
Origen: * Some think that their neighbor is their brother, from their family, from their relatives.

Our Lord teaches us who the neighbor is, in the Gospel, in the parable of the man who went down from Jerusalem to Jericho... Everyone is our neighbor, so we must not harm anyone... We are neighbors, all people are neighbors to all people, because we have one Father.
St. Jerome

13 My son, eat thou honey, because it is good; and the honeycomb, which is sweet to thy taste: 14 So shall the knowledge of wisdom be unto thy soul: when thou hast found it, then there shall be a reward, and thy expectation shall not be cut off.
My son, eat thou honey, because it is good; and the honeycomb, which is sweet to thy taste [13].

Honey of the bees was among the sweetest foods to the Jews, and Solomon used it to warn us against the honeyed words of the adulteress (Prov 5:3). Again, the praise others give a man is counted as honey, which if we eat much of it burdens the stomach (Prov 25:27). Solomon also calls us to moderation in everything, for he who eats too much honey has his stomach stuffed and vomits it (Prov 25:16). He whose soul is satisfied has no need of, and cannot bear, the honey of men's praise of him (Prov 27:7).

The unfaithful woman's lips drop honey, but whoever unites with her is led by her to the ways of bitter death. But the Lord Christ carries us with Him on the way of the Cross, and leads us to the joy of His resurrection and its glories.

There is no sweetness for the soul better than divine wisdom, for it was said of the Lord Christ, the wisdom of God: "His mouth is most sweet: yea, he is altogether lovely" (Song 5:16), and it was said of Him, "and the desire of all nations shall come" (Hag 2:7).
* The Lord Jesus knows how the soul of man, that is, the rational mind created in His image, cannot be satisfied except by Him alone...

He knows that He has been revealed and that He is hidden. He knows that in Him what is hidden has been declared. He knows all this. The Psalm says: "How great is the multitude of thy sweetness, O Lord, which thou hast hid for them that fear thee, which thou hast wrought for them that hope in thee" (Ps 31:19) LXX.
Your sweetness is great and manifold, which You have hidden for those who fear You...
To whom will You open it? To those who hope in You.
A two-sided question has been raised, but each side resolves the other...
Are those who fear and those who hope different?
Are not those who fear God the very ones who hope in Him...?

To the Law belongs fear, and to grace hope... The Law warns the one who relies on himself, and grace helps the one who trusts in God... We hear the Law. If there is no grace, you hear the punishment that comes upon you... Let him cry out: "O wretched man that I am!" (Rom 7:24). Know yourself as defeated, let your strength be in shame, and say: "O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?"... Thus the Law warns the one who relies on himself.

Look, here is a man relying on himself, trying to strive; he is prostrate, enslaved, and taken captive. Whoever has learned to rely on God, while the Law continued to warn him not to rely on himself, is now upheld by grace, as he relies on God. In this confidence he says: "Who shall deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord" (Rom 7:24-25) [Vulgate].
Now look at the sweetness, taste it, delight in it. Hear the Psalm: "Taste and see how sweet the Lord is" (Ps 34:8) [Vulgate]. He becomes sweet to you, as He delivers you.
You were in the bitterness of yourself, when you relied on yourself. Drink the sweetness, and receive thus the zeal of the great abundance.
St. Augustine: So shall the knowledge of wisdom be unto thy soul.
When thou hast found it, then there shall be a reward, and thy expectation shall not be cut off [14].
He who possesses the Lord Christ, the wisdom of God, enjoys the eternal inheritance and fellowship in glory; his hope is not cut off.

* Since it comes to this, that one must take everything from within the river or the valley, and rejoice in it, we say that our Lord Jesus Christ is compared to a river, in whom we find every delight and enjoyment in hope, and in whom we rejoice with a spiritual, divine joy.
St. Cyril the Great: * How wretched I am?!
My God... when will this corrupt nature leave me, and Your perfect power work in me?!
My God... how delightful are solitude, stillness, truth, and purity, all of which are Yours! But I amuse myself with noise, clamor, vanity, and vice!
I return, and what more shall I say?! You are the true Good, merciful, holy, just... but I am wicked, self-loving, sinful, unjust...!
You are the light, but I am darkness!
You are life, but I am death!
You are the Physician, but I am sick!
You are joy, but I am sorrow!
You are the true Truth, but I am real vanity, like any man on earth!
In what language do You want me to speak to You, my Creator?! I beseech You to be pleased to listen to me. I am the work of Your hands, and my destruction is a fearful thing!
I am Your creature, and behold I die! I am the work of Your hands, and behold I slide down toward nothingness!

If I have existence, You are the One who gave me existence, "Thy hands have made me and fashioned me" (Ps 119:73). Your hands that were nailed to the Cross, let them give me peace; for will You despise the work of Your hands?!
Ah! I look upon Your deep wounds, for You have engraved my name in Your hands! Read my name and save me!
My soul that groans before You is the work of Your hands. Create in me a new creature; this is Your work. Therefore it does not cease to cry out to You, saying: "O Life, give me life again!"
It is the clay of Your hands, wrapping itself around You, beseeching You to restore to it its first beauty!
Forgive me, my God, since You have permitted me to speak with You. For who is man that he should speak with the Lord his Creator?!
Yes. Forgive me! Forgive my boldness! Forgive Your servant who dared to raise his voice before his Master!

Necessity knows no law! Pain drives me to speak with You! The calamity that has befallen me makes me call the Physician because I am sick! I seek the light because I am blind! I search for life because I am dead! And who is this Physician, Light, and Life but You?!
O Jesus of Nazareth, have mercy on me!
St. Augustine

15 Lay not wait, O wicked man, against the dwelling of the righteous; spoil not his resting place: 16 For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again: but the wicked shall fall into mischief. 17 Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, and let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth: 18 Lest the LORD see it, and it displease him, and he turn away his wrath from him. 19 Fret not thyself because of evil men, neither be thou envious at the wicked; 20 For there shall be no reward to the evil man; the candle of the wicked shall be put out. 21 My son, fear thou the LORD and the king: and meddle not with them that are given to change: 22 For their calamity shall rise suddenly; and who knoweth the ruin of them both?
Lay not wait, O wicked man, against the dwelling of the righteous.
Spoil not his resting place [15].

What is the dwelling of the righteous but the divine embrace? And what is his resting place, his true place of repose, but fellowship with God? The wicked lies in wait for the righteous, setting many snares for him, that the righteous may fall into one of them, and not return to the divine embrace, and lose his fellowship with God. The wicked finds his pleasure in leading the righteous astray, and in ruining his own soul by falling with him into iniquity.

This statement seems addressed to the wicked, that he may not lie in wait to catch the righteous, for he toils in vain, because God is the defender of the righteous and his savior. But since the wicked does not listen to the voice of God, the address is in truth directed to the righteous, that he may not fear the wicked nor be troubled by him, whatever his plans and resources, because God Himself fortifies His children against the wicked and their evil deeds.
For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again.
But the wicked shall fall into mischief [16].

If the wicked exert all their effort to catch the righteous in the snare of evil, then God for His part opens the doors of hope before mankind, so that everyone who falls, however many times he falls, may seek salvation and find it in his hands. But the wicked, who exerts all his effort to lay stumbling blocks before the righteous, himself stumbles, while the righteous are saved and crowned.

* The words "seven times" are used to express every kind of affliction by which a man collapses in the eyes of men. And the words "riseth up again" mean that the man benefits from all these afflictions.

* When evils come upon the wicked they fall by them. And when evils come upon the righteous, God strengthens them, and raises up all those who have fallen (Ps 145:14), all who belong to Him, for "God resisteth the proud" (Jas 4:6).

St. Augustine: * By the help of God we can and must not commit grave sins, but there is no righteous person who does not sin, and we will not be able to live without little sins. We are always disturbed and tormented by these sins as by flying insects buzzing around us. Often sins creep in through thoughts, desires, conversations, or actions, as something unavoidable, through weakness and because of forgetfulness, if a man thinks of grave sins. Therefore we must not make light of our sins because they are small, but let us fear them because they are many. Drops of rain are small, but because they are many they fill rivers and flood houses, and sometimes by their force move mountains.

Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles: * A Christian is said to "rise up" in two senses: the first is when he is freed in this world by grace from the death of vices, and continues justified by God, and as the great Solomon in wisdom said: "A just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again." The second is in the general resurrection, where the righteous enjoys the eternal rewards.

Cassiodorus: * This speaking of the forgetting of former sins, I mean the principal sins condemned by the Mosaic Law, the inclination to which has ended and has been removed from us by a good life, and for which repentance has been completed. But as for the other (lesser) offenses, of which it was said: "For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again" (Prov 24:16), repentance for them does not end, because whether through ignorance or forgetfulness or thought or speech or mere desire or necessity or weakness of the flesh or uncleanness in a dream... into these things we often fall every day without our will or with it. For such sins David the prophet prays to the Lord, and asks to be cleansed from them and forgiven for them: "Who can understand his errors? cleanse thou me from secret faults" (Ps 19:12). And the Apostle also says: "For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do" (Rom 7:19). Therefore he sighed, saying: "O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" (Rom 7:24).

We fall into these sins easily as though by the very nature of things, so that despite our alertness and watchfulness toward them, we cannot avoid them altogether. This is what made one of the disciples whom Jesus loved cry out, saying: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us" (1 Jn 1:8).
Father Pinufius: Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, and let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth [17].

It befits the believer to be after the pattern of God, who maketh His sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust. Let the believer's heart be widened with love even toward those who oppose him.

The Apostle Paul says: "For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son" (Rom 5:10). If God reconciled us after we bore a spirit of enmity against Him, let us return this love to Him in those whom He loves, that is, in all mankind.
Whoever rejoices at his enemy's fall and whose heart is glad at his stumbling is counted as an opponent of God Himself, who seeks the salvation of all.

* He who rejoices in the misfortunes of others grieves God, as Solomon says. In any case, the Jews were not rejected for the sake of the Gentiles, but rather because they refused to give the Gospel the opportunity to be preached to the Gentiles. If you boast against those in whose root you were grafted, you insult the people who received you so that you might turn from evil to good. You will not continue in this if you were grafted in and remain firm in it.
Father Ambrosiaster: Lest the LORD see it, and it displease him, and he turn away his wrath from him [18].

The eyes of the Lord observe what is in our hearts, and if He sees in a heart joy at the calamities and disasters that befall another, God's wrath turns from the one under discipline to the one who gloats over him, as happened with the sons of Edom who gloated over Israel after their captivity, and the prophet Obadiah recorded his book especially because of this attitude, to highlight the gravity of gloating over those on whom discipline falls. "But thou shouldest not have looked on the day of thy brother in the day that he became a stranger; neither shouldest thou have rejoiced over the children of Judah in the day of their destruction; neither shouldest thou have spoken proudly in the day of distress. Thou shouldest not have entered into the gate of my people in the day of their calamity; yea, thou shouldest not have looked on their affliction in the day of their calamity, nor have laid hands on their substance in the day of their calamity; neither shouldest thou have stood in the crossway, to cut off those of his that did escape; neither shouldest thou have delivered up those of his that did remain in the day of distress. For the day of the LORD is near upon all the heathen: as thou hast done, it shall be done unto thee: thy reward shall return upon thine own head" (Obad 12-15).

* We must not be puffed up by our victory, therefore he warns us, saying: "Lest when thou hast eaten and art full, and hast built goodly houses, and dwelt therein; and when thy herds and thy flocks multiply, and thy silver and thy gold is multiplied, and all that thou hast is multiplied; then thine heart be lifted up, and thou forget the LORD thy God, which brought thee forth... from the house of bondage (sin)" (Deut 8:12-14). Likewise Solomon says in Proverbs: "Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth (that is, at your victory over sin and Satan), and let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth: lest the LORD see it, and it displease him, and he turn away his wrath from him" (Prov 24:17-18), that is, lest God see the pride of your heart and no longer attack him (defend you against sin), and thereby forsake you, so that the lust you had previously overcome by the grace of God overcomes you.
Father Serapion: Fret not thyself because of evil men, neither be thou envious at the wicked [19].
For there shall be no reward to the evil man.
The candle of the wicked shall be put out [20].

He repeated the same commandment as in verse 1 and in Proverbs 23:17, because God knows how hard it is for man to accept it, although he realizes how great its blessings are for him and how God is pleased with its fulfillment.

It is not fitting for us to envy the wicked for their circumstances, for time quickly passes and the wicked stand in judgment, their lamps having been put out, and their destiny is outer darkness. They have no share in the eternal inheritance and no place in the bosom of God...

By the putting out of the lamp of the wicked is meant the destruction of their children, for what they gather of the wealth of injustice and store up for their offspring is quickly scattered, and their offspring lose the divine blessing, if they walk in the evil way of their fathers. But the righteous man leaves blessing as an inheritance to his children according to the flesh as well as according to the Spirit, if they walk in the holy way of their father.

Here we notice God's wonderful regard for man. God offers man, however great his evils, opportunities and possibilities that he might shine like a star in the midst of heaven; but the wicked rejects the divine light by his evil will, and so every trace of light in him is put out.
My son, fear thou the LORD and the king.
Meddle not with them that are given to change [21].
Truly, the fear of the Lord and submission to Him are followed by submission, in the Lord, to those in authority.

The man of God does not meddle with those given to change, that is, he does not take part with those who rise in rebellion, nor cooperate with the schemers, who find their pleasure in revolts and intrigues against civil or church leaders.

* "My son, fear thou the LORD and the king," that is, fear Christ the true God, and the king, or Solomon means by the king one who rules himself before ruling others. "Be not disobedient to either of them." Truly, whoever does not honor the king chosen by God insults God.
St. John Chrysostom: For their calamity shall rise suddenly; and who knoweth the ruin of them both? [22].

Whoever acquires the fear of the Lord within him, along with the boldness he gains before God, and his freedom from fear of men however high their positions, and even from fear of death, nevertheless in a spirit of deep humility fears God and seeks His pleasure and approval, and he respects those of social standing, not in servility and humiliation, but in a spirit of contentment and in order to live a life full of peace. He does not meddle with those given to change, that is, those without fixed principles, who incline toward intrigues and revolts.

It is regrettable that even within the Church there are those who love biting criticism and resisting every church arrangement and order; they gather for themselves the wrath of God, and calamities await them.

The man who rebels against God and the leaders reaps for himself an inner rebellion; his body rebels against his spirit, and his emotions rebel against his mind, so that he carries within him bitter calamities. And while he thinks that he is seeking to reform society and the Church, he finds himself dissolute, and loses his harmony even with himself.

23 These things also belong to the wise. It is not good to have respect of persons in judgment. 24 He that saith unto the wicked, Thou art righteous; him shall the people curse, nations shall abhor him: 25 But to them that rebuke him shall be delight, and a good blessing shall come upon them. 26 Every man shall kiss his lips that giveth a right answer.
These things also belong to the wise. It is not good to have respect of persons in judgment [23].

By saying "These things also belong to the wise" he reveals that he recorded what precedes as one unit, which began by asking for the fear of the Lord and ended with the obligation of the fear of the Lord and obedience to the leaders. And what appears in the rest of this chapter is considered something like an appendix dealing with four important matters in the life of the believer, namely: no partiality, counting the cost, abstaining from false witness, and not being slothful. Perhaps these are considered an introduction to the next collection of proverbs.

He warns us against respect of persons, for whoever fears God does not fear men, and shows partiality to no one because of kinship in the flesh, or wealth, or honor, or one in authority. For in true humility he seeks the truth and proclaims it.

It befits rulers and civil leaders, as well as spiritual ones, to hold to this principle, as it befits every believer to hold to it, even if he does not have a leadership position in the eyes of society.

In the story of Susanna, which is in the addition to Daniel, there is a wonderful picture of the young Daniel, who boldly did not fear the two elders who had led astray all those around them; and courageously he rescued Susanna, who was falsely accused, and exposed the two elders for their corruption.
He that saith unto the wicked, Thou art righteous; him shall the people curse.
Nations shall abhor him [24].

Because of fear of the wicked, some flatter him and justify his actions, and even regard him as righteous. But when the truth is uncovered, people shun this deceiver at the expense of the truth, and the person brings a curse upon his own head.
Many contemporary societies have been struck by this blow, justifying the errors of some wicked people, and sometimes even praising them as though they were good and heroic deeds.
Perhaps the address here is to leaders and men of the judiciary, who for one reason or another justify the errors of some criminals at the expense of the poor and wronged classes.
But to them that rebuke him shall be delight, and a good blessing shall come upon them [25].

In contrast to those who show partiality to the wicked and call them good, we find others who discipline the wicked, whether by rebuke or by corporal punishment; these the people will surely respect when everyone confirms the corruption of the wicked, and how the judges or rulers restrained them from practicing their evils, so blessings come upon them.
* "But to them that rebuke him shall be delight, and a good blessing shall come upon them" (Prov 24:25).

I choose that the Lord visit my sins and correct my offenses here in this world, so that Abraham may say to me there what he said about poor Lazarus in his conversation with the rich man: "Son, remember that thou in thy lifetime receivedst thy good things, and likewise Lazarus evil things: but now he is comforted, and thou art tormented" (Lk 16:25). For this reason, when the Lord rebukes and disciplines us, we must not be ungrateful. Let us then understand that our rebuke in the present time is so that we may receive consolation in the future. As the Apostle says: "But when we are judged, we are chastened of the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world" (1 Cor 11:32). For this reason Job also accepted all his sufferings willingly, saying: "What? shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?" (Job 2:10).
Origen: Every man shall kiss his lips that giveth a right answer [26].

He who gives upright judgments without partiality is honored and trusted, and is the object of the admiration and love of many. The kissing of the lips here refers to respect through love, not fear, and the kiss in the East is still known in this sense. As it is said in the Psalm: "Kiss the Son, lest he be angry" (Ps 2:12).

The kiss is also used as an acknowledgment of a person's justice and wisdom, and of trust in him and submission to him. Pharaoh said to Joseph: "Thou shalt be over my house, and at thy mouth shall all my people kiss" (Gen 41:40).
Prepare thy work without, and make it fit for thyself in the field;
and afterwards build thine house [27].

The wise man calls us to count the cost, so that we build the house only after preparing the work: we choose the suitable site for the house, choose the kind and size of the buildings, calculate their cost, and see whether we are able to complete the work. As the Lord Christ Himself says: "For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it? Lest haply, after he hath laid the foundation, and is not able to finish it, all that behold it begin to mock him, saying, This man began to build, and was not able to finish" (Lk 14:28-30).

The Old Testament gives us an example of those who began to build the tower of Babel so that its top might reach to heaven, carrying obstinacy and resistance against God; since they did not count the cost, they did not finish the work (Gen 11:9).

* Scripture says: "Prepare thy work for thy departure, and make it ready in thy field." Now I think that "thy departure" means our going out from this world and leaving it. "What man is he that liveth, and shall not see death? shall he deliver his soul from the hand of the grave?" (Ps 89:48). For man's nature was condemned in Adam and fell into corruption, because in folly he disobeyed the commandment given to him.
St. Cyril the Great: * Whoever values the safety of his soul takes care not to be in danger, by keeping his freedom from sin, so that he may preserve for himself the benefit of his former good works.

The Canons of the Apostles: * Let us count the cost of the spiritual tower of towering height, and examine it deeply and carefully beforehand... Let us take into consideration first the faults plainly, and dig and remove the corruption and the refuse of the passions, so that we may lay the strong foundations of simplicity and humility upon the solid ground of our living breast, or rather the foundations are laid upon the rock of the Gospel (Lk 6:48); thus the tower of spiritual virtues rises, and is able to stand and to rise to the heights of heaven in complete safety and without being shaken.

Father Isaac: * It is a day of shouting and trumpet (Zeph 1:16). It is a day of grief and sighing for those who have not prepared their works well for the road, that is, for their departure from the body to meet God profitably.
St. Wissa
Be not a witness against thy neighbour without cause; and deceive not with thy lips [28].
Say not, I will do so to him as he hath done to me:
I will render to the man according to his work [29].

Returning evil for evil, or revenge, strips man of the life of purity and corrupts holiness, especially if he gives false testimony against his brother with the intention of taking revenge on him, even if this brother had previously testified falsely against him. For evil is not resisted with evil. A man's truthfulness and the holiness of his life are things that must not be touched, whatever the motive. The Apostle says: "Recompense to no man evil for evil" (Rom 12:17).

When the believer realizes that God embraces him, upholds him, solves his problems, and defends him, he does not avenge himself, but leans on God's breast. The Apostle commands us: "Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord" (Rom 12:19).

The man of God desires to see those who trouble him turn back from the evil they practice and be sanctified. This he cannot attain by avenging himself, but by leaving the matter in the hands of God, who is able to renew the heart and sanctify the soul.

* The utmost desire of the injured man is to see vengeance; this God accomplishes for him in its fullest measure on condition that he does not try to avenge himself. Leave it to God to follow up the injuries that have befallen you.
St. John Chrysostom

30 I went by the field of the slothful, and by the vineyard of the man void of understanding; 31 And, lo, it was all grown over with thorns, and nettles had covered the face thereof, and the stone wall thereof was broken down. 32 Then I saw, and considered it well: I looked upon it, and received instruction. 33 Yet a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep: 34 So shall thy poverty come as one that travelleth; and thy want as an armed man.
I went by the field of the slothful, and by the vineyard of the man void of understanding [30].

The wise man called us to a life of continual striving by saying: "Cast thy bread upon the waters: for thou shalt find it after many days" (Eccl 11:1). For our faith in the Lord grants us springs of water of His Holy Spirit flowing from our bellies (Jn 7:38); we enjoy His divine help, and feed on Him as the bread of life if we cast out works of love toward God and toward our neighbor, and He returns it to us as surpassing heavenly love.
Origen sees that a man does not enjoy the light of knowledge while in slackness and sloth, but enjoys wisdom and knowledge through practice and diligence.

* Do not think that wisdom comes before its being enacted in works, but works must come first, and wisdom be sought afterward... He says: "Sow to yourselves in righteousness" (Hos 10:12)... and after that you can do what follows: "enlighten yourselves with the light of knowledge."
Origen: And, lo, it was all grown over with thorns, and nettles had covered the face thereof, and the stone wall thereof was broken down [31].
Then I saw, and considered it well.
I looked upon it, and received instruction [32].

The wise man has previously warned us against sloth (Prov 6:10-11; 20:4). Here he presents a precise picture of the field and vineyard of the slothful man, and one's soul grieves for the owner of the field and the vineyard, for the ruin, drought, thorns, and thistles that befall them only reveal the destruction and ruin that has befallen the heart of their owner.
The nettle is a kind of thorn that abounds in abandoned regions (Isa 34:13; Hos 9:6). And the bramble is the thorn tree.
And even if a man has no need of money, sloth corrupts his inner life, shatters his personality, and removes from him the taste of life, so that it becomes tasteless and aimless.
Yet a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep [33].
So shall thy poverty come as one that travelleth; and thy want as an armed man! [34].

When the time of work comes, the slothful man sleeps, and thinks there is rest and happiness in this, but he is surprised by poverty running swiftly to fall upon his possessions as well as upon his mind and heart, so that his inner energies are shattered, and want invades him like an armed man who takes him captive.
May I possess You, O Wisdom of God!
* In You, O Wisdom of God, my whole life is built; upon You my soul is established as a holy building; I truly become a temple in which Your Holy Spirit dwells.
He fills it with treasures of wisdom, learning, and knowledge. * According to Your promise You become a wall of fire surrounding my whole being.
So the fiery darts of the enemy cannot pass through to me.
You are the fortress of my life, You and the One who works in me; I bear Your righteousness, and I am fortified by Your grace.
* In You I become like a tree planted by the rivers of water, bearing much fruit, whose leaf does not wither.
The wicked are deprived of union with You, so they become like chaff in the wind; they take pride in their abilities, capacities, and strength, and plan to destroy the wise.
But soon they perish, and the righteous wise are saved.
In You I grow constantly; time cannot break my depths, nor sickness corrupt my strength, nor events take from me the spirit of wisdom and the treasures of learning and knowledge.
In You I go from victory to victory.
And I experience the glory of salvation day by day.
I enter the battles of the devil fortified in You!
* I stand before the court in silence.
What shall I answer? And how shall I defend myself?
I confess that I deserve eternal death!
But You came forward on my behalf.
And You, the Judge and the Holy One, were silent and did not open Your mouth!
You were silent, O holy Word of God, that in You I may speak, and in You be justified, and in You claim the right to enter the heavenly glories.
You did not open Your mouth at Your trial, that You might open for me the door of Paradise which I closed by my sins.
* By Your silence You granted me the power of the word, You granted me wisdom as an eternal light that death cannot extinguish.
If distress comes upon me, however severe, my strength will not fail, for You are my strength!
The distress that crushes the fool proves me and bears witness to Your grace working in me.

* May I possess You, so that my heart is widened with love, and I love everyone, even those who oppose me, for You loved me while I was an enemy, and reconciled me with the Father by Your precious Blood.
Grant me to return love for love, so that I do not cease to support every afflicted person, whatever his nationality, religion, or conduct.
May I love everyone for Your sake, O Lover of all mankind!
* May I possess You, O Desire of the nations, whose mouth is most sweet, and who is altogether lovely.
You are the sweetness of my soul.
You are its joyful satisfaction!
Without You I have no life.
You are my hope, You are the Physician of my soul!
You change me from corruption to incorruption.
You raise me from the death of sin that I may enjoy the experience of the power of Your resurrection and its joy.
When all shut their doors before me, I find Your opened side waiting for me, and Your divine embrace welcoming me.
And Your heavens await my coming!
* Grant me love toward all mankind, so that my heart does not rejoice at the fall of an enemy of mine among men, for I have no real enemy but the devil himself.
As for men, they are all my brothers.
Gladden my heart with their salvation and success.
* Remove evil from the wicked, so that their lamp is not put out.
Sanctify their lives, so that they seek not what belongs to the world, but what belongs to Your eternal Kingdom.
* Grant me the spirit of the fear of the Lord and godliness.
That I may not fear any man, and in a spirit of humility not take part in rebellion or biting criticism!
But let me not praise a wicked man for his wickedness, nor show partiality because of kinship or profit.
* Receive the building of my inner house, for no human hand can establish it, but Your divine wisdom lays its foundations and raises it up.
It rises even to heaven, and enjoys Your dwelling in it!
* Work, O Wisdom of God, in me, and work even in those who oppose me.
For what I desire is the salvation of all!
* Grant me Your fiery Spirit who is ever at work, so that I do not slacken or grow careless, nor seek sleep and sloth!
But in You let me become a burning spiritual coal!
These are also proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied out: [1]

These proverbs were collected under the guidance of the Holy Spirit of God. Three centuries after the death of Solomon, some scribes "copied them out," that is, transcribed and transmitted them in writing. They were called the men of Hezekiah, and the Septuagint calls them "the friends of Hezekiah."

Hezekiah was a good king, a man of peace and reform; in his reign there was progress in the fields of art and literature, and the leaders and the people took interest in religious life. For where there is a good leader, the people enjoy a holy character and care for their salvation.

We learn from 2 Chr 29:25-30; 31:21 that Hezekiah took care to restore the order that the prophet David had set for the service of the temple, and God rewarded him for his concern for the movement of religious reform by the discovery of this collection of proverbs after it had remained hidden for three centuries. This was like the discovery by the men of the good Josiah of a copy of the Law (2 Chr 34:14-16).
Some see that this addition was made under the guidance of such men as Isaiah, Hosea, and Micah.

2 It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter. 3 The heaven for height, and the earth for depth, and the heart of kings is unsearchable. 4 Take away the dross from the silver, and there shall come forth a vessel for the finer. 5 Take away the wicked from before the king, and his throne shall be established in righteousness. 6 Put not forth thyself in the presence of the king, and stand not in the place of great men: 7 For better it is that it be said unto thee, Come up hither; than that thou shouldest be put lower in the presence of the prince whom thine eyes have seen.
It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter [2].

It befits the king to realize that the things of God, His wisdom and His plan, cannot be penetrated to their depths as they are. As the Apostle Paul says: "O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out! For who hath known the mind of the Lord? or who hath been his counsellor?" (Rom 11:33-34; Deut 29:29). The things of God cannot be searched out, for He alone knows the secrets of Himself, but the king is obliged to search out every matter to which he puts his hand or which he seriously considers, so that his decision may be sound. For the glory of the king is not in his authority and his commands, but in searching out matters in the spirit of wisdom.

When the king realizes that the things of God cannot be searched out, he is filled with the fear of the Lord, and takes into account that there is One higher than the high, who is above all, so he is obliged in all his conduct to fear God and revere Him.

Since God has made the believing man a king with authority, he is obliged to search out the matter, that is, to practice everything after a deep study of the word of God and knowledge of the will of God, so that he may become an object of His pleasure. The Lord Christ says: "Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me" (Jn 5:39). And the Apostle says: "Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth" (2 Tim 2:15).

* Consider what is said in the Psalms: "Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, I cannot attain unto it" (Ps 139:6). And Solomon says: "It is the glory of God to conceal a thing" (Prov 25:2). For this reason I have often decided to stop and not write. Believe me, this is what I did. But lest I cause you disappointment, and lest my silence lead those who asked me into ungodliness, and they give themselves up to dispute, I pressed myself to write briefly what I now send to your holiness.

Pope Athanasius the Apostolic: * Even if all minds gathered together to search together, and tongues cooperated to speak together, as I have said, no one will be able to reach a satisfactory conclusion in this matter.
St. Basil the Great: The heaven for height, and the earth for depth, and the heart of kings is unsearchable [3].

With the height of the heavens, man has been granted to examine the stars through the science of astronomy, and with the depth of the earth he has been granted to examine the treasures in its interior, such as minerals, petroleum, and so on; but the heart of the true believer united with God cannot be searched out; for the Lord Christ Himself says: "the kingdom of God is within you" (Lk 17:21). And the Apostle says: "ye are the temple of the living God; as God hath said, I will dwell in them, and walk in them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people" (2 Cor 6:16). Who then can search out the kingdom of God, and know the details of His temple in which the Holy Spirit dwells?
Take away the dross from the silver, and there shall come forth a vessel for the finer [4].
Take away the wicked from before the king, and his throne shall be established in righteousness [5].

The purifying of silver from dross allows the silversmith to form a precious silver vessel, and the removal of evil from the heart makes of it a temple for the Spirit of God, the Giver of sanctification. And the removal of wicked counsellors from before the king establishes his throne in righteousness. This is what Solomon did, as he condemned the doers of evil around him before beginning his kingly work (1 Kgs 2).

This is also what will happen on the great day of the Lord, when the King of kings comes and crushes the devil and his kingdom, and casts him with his hosts and followers into the lake burning with fire, to declare His eternal heavenly kingdom, and be glorified in His elect forever.
In the same spirit it befits the Church to cast out the wicked one, and remove the corrupt leaven, lest it leaven the whole lump.

This is also what the believer experiences in his daily life, where the roots of evil must be plucked out while good is planted by the work of divine grace. As the psalmist says: "Depart from evil, and do good; and dwell for evermore" (Ps 37:27).

* Why is it said: "Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the LORD" (Ps 118:1)? Scripture here specifies "who walk," not "who have walked," those who walk in the doing of good and find their delight in doing it... As for those who flee from evil... they cannot be praised if they manage to avoid sin once or twice, unless they are able to cut it off from their lives completely... If we want what is good, let us begin by avoiding evils... "Depart from evil, and do good" (Ps 37:27): the Psalm sketches for us the way of virtue... with knowledge and skill... For departing from evil is the beginning of good... If perfect virtue were demanded from the beginning, you would draw back before you began.
St. Basil the Great: Put not forth thyself in the presence of the king, and stand not in the place of great men [6].
For better it is that it be said unto thee, Come up hither; than that thou shouldest be put lower in the presence of the prince whom thine eyes have seen [7].
It befits the believer not to push himself to appear before rulers, nor to desire to sit with them in order to obtain the honor of men.

When the palaces of emperors and great men were opened to the men of the Church by the conversion of Constantine to the Christian faith, there was another race to flee to the wilderness to enjoy sitting with God in the stillness of the wilderness, as St. Abba Anthony the Great did.

The Lord Christ says: "When thou art bidden of any man to a wedding, sit not down in the highest room; lest a more honourable man than thou be bidden of him; and he that bade thee and him come and say to thee, Give this man place; and thou begin with shame to take the lowest room. But when thou art bidden, go and sit down in the lowest room; that when he that bade thee cometh, he may say unto thee, Friend, go up higher: then shalt thou have glory in the presence of them that sit at meat with thee. For whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted" (Lk 14:7-11).

The pride that drives man to present himself in the presence of the great shatters man's life before himself as before others, and deserves God's rebuke. But whoever is humbled in his depths with sincerity and devotion, God exalts. As St. Mary said: "He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree" (Lk 1:52).
If he who pushes himself to obtain vain honors and glories from the world deserves blame, what of the believer who pushes himself in spiritual and religious fields seeking temporal glory?
* Let the proud seek earthly kingdoms and love them, but "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."

* The Lord sat in the house of a proud Pharisee (Lk 7:36), as I said, He was in his house but not in his heart, but He did not enter the house of the centurion, and yet He possessed his heart (Mt 8:8).

Zacchaeus also received the Lord in his house and in his heart (Lk 19:6). As for the centurion's faith, it was praised because of his humility, for he said: "I am not worthy that thou shouldest come under my roof." The Lord said: "Verily I say unto you, I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel" (Mt 8:10), this according to the flesh, for according to the Spirit he is an "Israelite." Christ came to the Israelites according to the flesh, that is, to the Jews, seeking first the lost sheep among this people, taking His body also from this people. He said: "I have not found so great faith." We can measure the faith of men as men judge it, but the Lord, who sees what is within, and whom no one deceives, bore witness to the heart of this man as he listened to words of humility and announced a word of healing.
* As soon as you become proud, you immediately lose what you have received.
St. Augustine: * Humility is granted to each person according to the degree of his greatness. Pride is harmful to everyone. It seeks to corrupt, through themselves, those who are great!
St. Jerome: * What madness! Does not this proud man know that his glory passes away and evaporates like a dream, and that greatness and authority are nothing but a deceptive mirage?
St. Basil the Great
Go not forth hastily to strive, lest thou know not what to do in the end thereof, when thy neighbour hath put thee to shame [8].

The Lord Christ gives us a practical example in life concerning not hastening to enter into quarrels or battles with others. He says: "Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand? Or else, while the other is yet a great way off, he sendeth an ambassage, and desireth conditions of peace" (Lk 14:31-32).

King Josiah committed this error; although he did that which was right in the sight of the Lord (2 Kgs 22:2), yet when Pharaoh Necho king of Egypt went up to fight against Assyria, King Josiah went up to fight him, although Pharaoh had not gone up to fight Josiah. He entered a battle at Megiddo which ended in his death (2 Kgs 23:29-30).

It befits the believer not to throw himself into battles which he could have avoided. For this reason our Lord asked us that when persecution comes in a city we flee to another, not out of fear of death, nor in cowardice and servility, but that we may not push ourselves into temptation.

* He leaves us peace as He departs, and He will give us His peace when He comes at the end. Peace He leaves us in this world, and His peace He will give us in the world to come. He leaves us His peace, and as we dwell in it we defeat the enemy.
He will give us His peace when there are no more enemies to fight and we reign as kings.
Peace He leaves us so that we may also love one another here, and He will give us His peace when we are beyond the possibility of strife.

Peace He leaves us so that one may not judge another in what is a secret to each, while we are on earth; He will give us His peace when He "will make manifest the counsels of the hearts: and then shall every man have praise of God" (1 Cor 4:5). Yet in Him and from Him we receive peace, whether that which He leaves us as He goes to the Father or that which He will grant us when He brings us to the Father.

And what does He leave us when He ascends from us but His presence, which He will not withdraw from us? For He is our peace, who hath made both one (Eph 2:14). Therefore He becomes our peace, whether when we believe that it is He, or when we see Him as He is (1 Jn 3:2).

For if, while we are still in this corrupt body which weighs down the soul and we walk by faith, not by sight, He does not leave those who depart while they are absent from Him (2 Cor 5:6-7), how much more, when we attain that vision, will He fill us with Himself.

* The peace He leaves us in this world can more fittingly be called our peace than His peace. For since He is utterly without sin, there is in Him no element of strife itself. But the peace that is ours is that in the midst of which we still say: "Forgive us our debts" (Mt 6:12)... It is not the perfect peace, for we see another law in our members, warring against the law of our mind (Rom 7:22-23).
St. Augustine
Debate thy cause with thy neighbour himself; and discover not a secret to another [9].
Lest he that heareth it put thee to shame, and thine infamy turn not away [10].

Not only is it unfitting for us to hasten to enter a quarrel with our neighbor, but we must also, before resorting to the courts or to the entry of a third party for reconciliation, meet with him in secret, and speak with him in a spirit of brotherhood, so that he feels that we seek reconciliation in a spirit of love, and not by justifying ourselves and exposing him.

The entry of a third party or resort to the courts may oblige him to reveal matters we did not know, and so we become a scandal. The Lord Christ commands us: "Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother. But if he will not hear thee, then take with thee one or two more, that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established..." (Mt 18:15 etc.).

* Solomon often refers to a "friend" and "friendship." So it is fitting for us now to look at what he means by friendship. He says that grace and friendship set free. Also the Savior says in the Gospels to the Jews who believed on Him: "If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed; and ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free" (Jn 8:31-32). Again Paul says: "Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law" (Gal 3:13); so if friendship sets free, then Christ is the truth and the friendship. For this reason all who acquire the knowledge of Christ are friends to one another. For this the Savior calls His disciples friends (Jn 15:15), John the Baptist is the friend of the bridegroom (Jn 3:29), and so is Moses (Ex 33:11), and all the saints. And by virtue of that friendship alone the friends are friends of one another.
St. Mar Evagrius

11 A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver. 12 As an earring of gold, and an ornament of fine gold, so is a wise reprover upon an obedient ear. 13 As the cold of snow in the time of harvest, so is a faithful messenger to them that send him: for he refresheth the soul of his masters. 14 Whoso boasteth himself of a false gift is like clouds and wind without rain.
A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver [11].
Some see that the discussion here is of apples beautiful in form, golden in color, set in a dish of silver. It is a wonderful sight! So is the wise word spoken at its proper time.
Ruth spoke with Boaz in words full of grace and at the proper time, and there was fulfilled for her what she had not dreamed of, that the Lord Christ should come from her seed.
And Abigail spoke wise words with David at the time of his fury, and he praised her and listened to her (1 Sam 25:32).
It is not enough that we speak the truth, but we must realize how to present it, and when to speak it and to whom.

How much we need wisdom to be our nature in our inner being, joined to our conduct and words outwardly, that is, that we bear the holiness of the inner man and also the holiness of the body with its senses, feelings, gifts, and all its energies and conduct. This wisdom (or knowledge or understanding) is a divine gift.
* The Holy Spirit, in whom are all kinds of gifts, gives to some the word of wisdom.
* Through the guidance of the Spirit man comes to the knowledge of the nature of all things.
* Send out thy light (Ps 3:43); this light sent from the Father to the mind of those called to salvation is understanding through the Spirit, who leads them to be enlightened by God.
Origen: * There is no knowledge without faith, nor faith without knowledge. The Son is the true Teacher.
St. Clement of Alexandria: As an earring of gold, and an ornament of fine gold, so is a wise reprover upon an obedient ear [12].

If the rebuke comes from a wise man who bears a spirit of love and tenderness, this rebuke is counted as an ornament and an earring of gold on the ear, that is, his rebuke is counted a precious and beautiful gift.

The Second Book of Chronicles gives us a wonderful example in the rebuke of the prophet Oded to the army coming from Samaria, where he told them that the wrath had reached heaven because they had taken captive their brothers of Judah. And indeed they returned the captives after honoring them, and provided them with their needs (2 Chr 28:9-15).
As the cold of snow in the time of harvest, so is a faithful messenger to them that send him: for he refresheth the soul of his masters [13].

It was the custom of reapers in the Middle East to put snow in their drinks during the summer harvest to refresh them, so that they could do their work in the midst of intense heat. So the trusted messenger refreshes the souls of those who sent him, since they have no doubt of his faithfulness.

Faithfulness is an essential element in dealings within any society; the faithful husband, and also the wife, the superior and the subordinates, these and others, when they are faithful in providing the information required of them, refresh society, like snow that refreshes one suffering from intense heat.

And on the great day of the Lord we hear the divine voice: "Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord" (Mt 25:21).
* The steward who mismanages the affairs of his master and loses his possessions fears to face him; on the contrary, the steward who always manages his master's affairs well meets him with joy.

St. Jerome: * When your turn comes in the service, add to your bodily work a word of counsel and loving consolation for those you serve, so that your service, seasoned with salt (Col 4:6), may be acceptable.
Do not allow another to practice what is rightly entrusted to you, lest the reward be taken from you and given to another, so that he is enriched by your wealth while you are put to shame.
Carry out the obligations of your service with gentleness and care, as one who serves Christ. For the prophet says: "Cursed be he that doeth the work of the LORD negligently" (Jer 48:10).

Fear, as though the eyes of the Lord were upon you, for deviation comes from negligence and disregard, even if the work being done seems lowly to you. The work of service is a great work, which leads to the Kingdom. St. Basil the Great: Whoso boasteth himself of a false gift is like clouds and wind without rain [14].

When a place suffers drought and then a cloud appears, everyone eagerly awaits that it will pour down rain instead of the suffering of drought, and if the cloud is scattered without dropping rain, the people fall into a state of frustration and disappointment. Such is the state of him who boasts, asserting that he gives a gift, and does not fulfill what he promised.

When the Apostle Jude wrote about the teachers who promise their hearers to present the truth of the Gospel but are unable to carry out what they promise, he quoted what is in this verse, and wrote of them that they are "clouds they are without water, carried about of winds; trees whose fruit withereth, without fruit, twice dead, plucked up by the roots" (Jude 12).
By long forbearing is a prince persuaded, and a soft tongue breaketh the bone [15].

Two important things are required in dealing with others, namely long-suffering or slowness to anger, and the gentle, kind word. By long-suffering we quench the outburst of others' anger without our being kindled with anger, and thus we can, at the proper time, converse calmly and give others the opportunity to review themselves.

And by the kind word we break the anger of another. Perhaps among the most beautiful things in the Old Testament is David's attitude toward King Saul. Saul went down to the wilderness of Ziph with three thousand chosen men of Israel to seek David and kill him (1 Sam 26:2). And when David found Saul with his army commander and the people lying around him, Abishai asked to strike Saul and kill him at one stroke, but David refused; rather he took the spear that was at his head and the cruse of water and crossed over to the top of the mountain at a distance, and rebuked Abner for not guarding the king. Saul knew David's voice and said: "Is this thy voice, my son David?" (1 Sam 26:17). David said to him: "for the king of Israel is come out to seek a flea." And Saul, after he had reflected, said: "I have sinned: return, my son David: for I will no more do thee harm... behold, I have played the fool, and have erred exceedingly..."

* There is nothing that surpasses love, and consequently there is nothing lower than anger. We must not concern ourselves with anything, however useful and necessary it may seem, in order to avoid the anger that causes disturbance, and we must not be troubled by matters, even those we consider not essential, in order to preserve the calm of love and peace without lack, for we must realize that nothing is as destructive as anger and vexation, and nothing as profitable as love.

Father Joseph: * A brother asked an elder: I want to be martyred for God. He answered him: "Whoever bears with his brother in the time of distress, he has become as one inside the furnace of the three youths."
The Garden of the Monks: * If a person becomes angry as a man, he puts an end to the anger as a Christian.

* The word that comes out of the mouth goes out like a stone thrown by the hand; it is far from being recalled or controlled... Therefore one must reflect on what will be said before the speech goes out. For after it has gone out, reflection on it is in vain.
St. Jerome
Hast thou found honey?
eat so much as is sufficient for thee, lest thou be filled therewith, and vomit it [16].

Eating food in moderation is beneficial for health and spiritually, while excess in eating is harmful. So it is with all the needs of the body: excess in them is destructive to the body as well as to the soul. There is no sin in food as long as it is taken with thanksgiving and moderation.
Lack of control of the belly turns the sweetness of honey into nausea of the stomach. And lack of control of the tongue turns your wise words away from achieving their purpose.

* Yet I do not mean that we should not think of God at all times, and there is no need for my opponents to attack me with this argument, since they are always ready to attack, for we ought to remember God more often than we breathe, indeed I may say that we ought not to do anything else but that, and I am of those who hold the principle which commands us to "meditate day and night" (Ps 1:2), to declare the Lord "evening, and morning, and at noon" (Ps 55:17), to "bless the LORD at all times" (Ps 34:1), or as Moses said, "when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up" (Deut 6:7), or when we do anything else, and by this remembrance of God we become pure, and so I am not against the continual remembrance of God, but against the continual discussion of theology, and I do not oppose theology, as though it were something against godliness, but I oppose discussing it at an unsuitable time, and I am not against teaching theology, except when it exceeds the limit, for fullness and surfeit, even of honey with all its sweetness, cause vomiting (Prov 25:16), and for everything there is a time, as I see and as wise Solomon sees, and what is good is not good if the time is not suitable; flowers are quite out of season in winter, and men's clothes do not suit women, nor women's clothes men. Excessive laughter is not fitting during mourning, nor weeping at a drinking party. If all these are unsuitable because they are at an unsuitable time, shall we neglect choosing the suitable time only in discussing theology, though observing the suitable time for this discussion is of the utmost importance?

St. Gregory of Nazianzus: * As moderation and abstaining from extravagance are usually the children of contentment, if a man is accustomed to it he does without everything that is superfluous and unnecessary, so that there may be no deviation or falling into temptations, being content with what is necessary and needful for health and for the blessed life according to the teaching of the heavenly Word, to whom be glory. Let the clothing of women be simple, neat, and well-formed, and there is no harm in using fine fabrics, those that are not suitable for men, but without wounding their modesty, and leading them to extravagance. And clothing must suit age, person, build, nature, and conduct, for the divine Apostle counsels us by saying: "But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof" (Rom 13:14).
St. Clement of Alexandria
Withdraw thy foot from thy neighbour's house; lest he be weary of thee, and so hate thee [17].

Again he speaks of moderation in everything, even in our relations with our relatives. With our great love for them, we must set limits in our conduct, so that we do not poke our nose into their lives, nor ask them about personal matters, nor be curious about their lives and conduct; and we set limits to our visits, and the length of the visit, however welcoming they are to us.
Let us lengthen our time of meeting God in secret and speaking with Him, and let us lessen as much as we can our meeting with people and speaking with them.
* As for the apostles and prophets, act according to the teaching of the Gospel, thus:
Receive every apostle who comes to you as the Lord (Mt 10:40).
But he must not stay more than one day, and if need be he stays another day; if he stays three days he is a false prophet.
The Didache
A man that beareth false witness against his neighbour is a maul, and a sword, and a sharp arrow [18].

False witness or slander of a person resembles a hammer with which a man strikes the minds of others, or a club that crushes what is beneath it, or a sword or an arrow that destroys. But the believer, even if he is attacked by slander, counts this as permitted by God to discipline him, prove him, and gain the one who slandered him.
