When Shimei the son of Gera cursed David, and was throwing stones at him and at the servants of the king and the mighty men around him, Abishai said to the king: "Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? let me go over, I pray thee, and take off his head" (2 Sam 16:9). But the king, who was fleeing from the face of Absalom his son, said: "So let him curse, because the LORD hath said unto him, Curse David. Who shall then say, Wherefore hast thou done so?" And David said to Abishai and to all his servants: "Behold, my son, which came forth of my bowels, seeketh my life: how much more now may this Benjamite do it? let him alone, and let him curse; for the LORD hath bidden him" (2 Sam 16:11).

* He who is struck with a stone goes to a physician, but sharper than a stone are the blows of slander (the defaming of reputation). As Solomon says: false witness is war with a club and a sword and a sharp arrow" (see Prov 25:18), and its wounds can be healed by truth alone. If truth is destroyed, the wounds become worse and worse.
St. Athanasius the Apostolic
Confidence in an unfaithful man in time of trouble is like a broken tooth, and a foot out of joint [19].

The man who gains an important position of work and is trusted, and is a traitor, is exposed, and is counted as broken teeth and dislocated feet. Instead of helping others he becomes a cause of troubles and unrest. The most serious example of this is Judas, who was chosen as a disciple, and was entrusted with the treasury, and behold, he betrays his Master.
* The disciples heard that their Teacher would be killed by the Jews and were pained, and heard that one of them would betray Him and were troubled.
I wonder who goes out from the choir of our Lord's light, and goes and mingles with the darkness in great terror.
I wonder who leaves the company of the sun of fair rays, and walks in the way full of clouds and darkness.
Who is this lamb who turned himself over and became a wolf, and began to bite the good Shepherd?
Policy forced Peter to deny the Son, but no one forced Judas to betray... And when Judas asked: Is it I? the Lord answered him: Thou hast said. As one who says to him: No one forced you.

If you say: Why did He who knows all choose him when He knew he was a deceiver...? He chose him when he was good and pure and there was no fault in him, for he was gentle and upright. And after He chose him, being worthy and full of goodness, he changed and destroyed his goodness and became rejected...
The Son of God promised Judas the throne, and when he denied Him, He brought him down and left him to the gallows...
Where do you leave your throne and your glory, O chosen one? Who will give you a high throne like yours...?
The sick whom You healed weep bitterly over you; the lepers whom You cleansed bow because of your fall.
Tremble, you who are set apart, at deceitful kisses, for by one deceitful kiss the Son of God was hung on a tree.
The devil who taught Judas to betray his Teacher came back and taught him to hang himself, so that by both he might inherit the Hades for which he was qualified.
St. Jacob of Serugh
As he that taketh away a garment in cold weather, and as vinegar upon nitre, so is he that singeth songs to an heavy heart [20].

The consolation of the sorrowful is not accomplished by offering him one of the songs, even if he loves it, nor by asking him to sing as the Babylonians did. They asked the Israelites in the land of captivity to praise for them with one of the songs of the Lord. As the psalmist says: "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion. We hanged our harps upon the willows in the midst thereof. For there they that carried us away captive required of us a song; and they that wasted us required of us mirth, saying, Sing us one of the songs of Zion. How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?" (Ps 137:1-4).

The Apostle says: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep" (Rom 12:15). And the wise man says: "A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance" (Eccl 3:4).

Whoever does not consider the feelings of the sorrowful and heavy of heart, and instead of sharing his sorrow sings, is like one who takes off the clothes of a man suffering from bitter cold, thus doubling his distress, or like one who put vinegar on nitre, so that it reacts with it and foam is produced.

* I suffer and grieve with our fellow believers who fell and denied the faith during the bitterness of persecution; they draw away a part of our hearts with them, and have caused us a similar grief by their wounds.
St. Cyprian: * Our sufferings have thus reached the ends of the inhabited world; when one member suffers, all the members suffer with it.
St. Basil: * General sharing in everything, in good things and in sorrowful ones, is the only way to attain the perfection of fellowship.
St. John Chrysostom
21 If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink: 22 For thou shalt heap coals of fire upon his head, and the LORD shall reward thee.
If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink [21].
The Apostle Paul quoted these two verses, except for the last clause, from the Septuagint (Rom 12:20).

The man of God offers love with the gift, and kindles a fire of love on the head of the one who troubles him, turning his anger and fury into friendship and love. The Lord Christ commanded us: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you" (Mt 5:44).
For thou shalt heap coals of fire upon his head, and the LORD shall reward thee [22].

When we give the hungry enemy food and the thirsty drink, we must aim at his repentance, longing that he share with us our life full of love for God and men. This repentance is kindled in his heart with inner fires according to the good pleasure of God. But some give food and drink with the aim of pride and of belittling the enemy or making a fool of him; this is not fitting for the believer.

* The Apostle Paul teaches us in perfect clarity that almsgiving is offered to everyone, for he says: "As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith" (Gal 6:10). This is quite clear enough that in works of this kind priority is given to the righteous (in giving).. This does not mean that we close our hearts toward others, even toward sinners, and even toward those who hold a hostile attitude toward us. Christ Himself says, above all: "Love your enemies, do good to them which hate you" (Lk 6:27). This matter did not pass in silence in the Old Testament; you see that we read in it: "If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink," a text which the Apostle used in the New Testament (Rom 12:20).

* This (scriptural) statement seems to command the committing of a crime or the practicing of a vice. But it is symbolic speech guiding us to share in the sufferings of the Lord... Scripture says: "If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink." This, without doubt, commands tenderness, but the continuation is: "For thou shalt heap coals of fire upon his head"; you may think that it commands a crime of malice. Do not doubt that it is a symbolic expression. For while it can be interpreted in two ways, one inclines toward harm, and the other interpretation inclines toward good love which calls him to leave harm and cling to tenderness, so you understand the coals as the fiery laments of repentance by which a person's pride is healed and he grieves that he is an enemy to the one who soothes his distress.
St. Augustine
The north wind driveth away rain: so doth an angry countenance a backbiting tongue [23].

It befits us not to welcome or encourage the one with a slanderous tongue who gnaws at people's honor and criticizes others in their absence, but to meet him as with a frowning face. Thus he does not go on with his destructive talk.

The Book of Proverbs repeats the necessity of peace and love in the family (Prov 21:9) and among friends, because it is a grave matter, without which the family, like society, turns into an unbearable hell.
It is better to dwell in the corner of the housetop, than with a brawling woman and in a wide house [24].

* We have been commanded to love our neighbor as ourselves, therefore the first obligation of man under God's economy is to love his wife and children. By this saying I wish to assure you that you know that the responsibility of the man, as of the woman also, is their household.

Since God has set up this order in mankind itself, husbands and wives and children, it is reasonable that we should fulfill the law of love in the home first. Above all, who has more opportunity to experience our love, our peace, and our long-suffering than those who live with us? Whom must we seek to love first, besides those whom we can serve and care for the more?

Yes, we may take care of everything for our families for their material comfort and possessions, but if we fail to offer them the love of God, the Apostle shows the truth of our hearts, that it is worse than unbelievers (1 Tim 5:8). He says this to awaken our understanding, that God desires heavenly peace to rule our homes, flowing from those in charge in love toward those who are called to obey in love.
In order to manage our households, those who give orders must do so in godliness, and not with hardness of heart, or with a kind of authority without understanding or tenderness...
The righteous man, that is, he who lives by faith, is like a traveler heading toward the heavenly city, and those who give directions and commands in truth serve those who appear to be commanded...

As you exercise authority, do not fall into pride because of your position, but rather exercise spiritual authority in your homes. You are ruled by the love of God, which encourages, hopes, believes, and will never fail (1 Cor 13).
St. Augustine: * "That they may teach the young women to be sober, to love their husbands" (Titus 2:4).

The Apostle says that the older women are to advise the young women to love their husbands, because the chief of the goods of the household is that the wife be in agreement with her husband. If this happens there is no evil at all. For how can there be no peace when the body agrees with the head...? If the head is in peace, who can remove or prevent peace...? This is more useful to the household than money, nobility of birth, and power...
By love all resistance vanishes; if the husband is a pagan he quickly accepts the faith, and if he is a Christian he becomes better.

Did you see how Paul, who works with all his effort to draw us away from worldly things, gives great attention to what concerns the state of the household? For if households are well managed, spiritual things find a place, and without a sound household spiritual things are ruined...

For when a woman is married to an unbelieving man and is not virtuous, it is impossible that God not be slandered because of her, but if she is adorned with preaching she wins honor from her preaching and her good works.

Let the women whose husbands are harsh or unbelieving hear and be disciplined, so that they may lead them to good worship. For if you do not win him or persuade him to share with you in the upright teachings, you close his mouth and do not let him blaspheme the Christian religion. And this is not a simple matter, for the religion is praised because of our conduct.

St. John Chrysostom: * He who marries knows how rarely we find a wife without these faults, therefore the great orator Varius Geminus said well: "The man who does not quarrel is a bachelor." In truth: "It is better to dwell in the corner of the housetop, than with a brawling woman and in a wide house." If a house shared between husband and wife makes the wife proud, and she shows contempt toward the husband, what if the wife is the richer, and the husband a refugee in her house!
St. Jerome
As cold waters to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country [25].

What is the good news but the coming of the Lord Christ Himself, the Word of God, who is able to satisfy the soul and water it with the waters of His love? He causes to spring forth within it a fountain of living water, and it in turn waters many by the work of His Holy Spirit in it and in them.

* Scripture says: "As cold waters to a thirsty soul," so is the knowledge of our Lord Jesus, the giver of life to the mind that loves knowledge. Therefore let us draw from the holy springs, the living, life-giving waters, the rational spiritual waters. Let us take what quenches our thirst and not stop drinking. For in these matters there is a constant need for instruction beyond imagination, and greed is highly praised.
St. Cyril the Great
A righteous man falling down before the wicked is as a troubled fountain, and a corrupt spring [26].

The soul of the righteous and upright man is filled with distress when he finds himself obliged to submit to a wicked, corrupt man, and he is like a traveler who sees a spring of water and runs to it to drink, and behold it is full of filth, or finds a fountain and finds it full of algae.
It is not good to eat much honey: so for men to search their own glory is not glory [27].
Excess in taking honey harms the stomach and causes nausea in a person; such is the state of the man who lives not to serve others with love and in true inner humility, but seeks his own glory.

St. John Chrysostom was moved before the long-suffering of the Lord Christ even in His dealing with the devil during the temptation, for he says: [He was neither angry nor aroused, but with extreme gentleness He argued with him a second time from Scripture... teaching us that we overcome Satan not by working miracles, but by endurance and long-suffering, so that we do nothing for the sake of boasting and vainglory.]
* Just as Christ "took upon him the form of a servant" (Phil 2:7) and overcame Satan by humility, so in the beginning man fell through pride and vainglory by the deceit of the serpent?

St. Macarius the Great: * Nothing is acceptable to God like a man's counting himself the last of all; this is the first principle of practical wisdom, for the humble man, wounded in his heart, does not love vainglory, nor is he wrathful, nor does he envy his neighbor, nor does he resort to any lust.

St. John Chrysostom * Let us put a stop to this senseless and vain arrogance, which springs from vainglory, the root of pride. For the desire to dominate others, and the strife to attain it, rightly makes a man blameworthy, although he is not entirely without what deserves praise. For eminence in virtue deserves esteem (honour), but those who wish to attain this must be humble in mind, having humble feelings, not seeking to be first, and this through their love for the brethren. This is what the blessed Paul wants in us, when he wrote: "in honour preferring one another" (Rom 12:10). The saints are made worthy of these feelings, and by them they are glorified, for they make our godliness toward God honoured, tear the net of the devil's malice and shatter his many snares, deliver us from the pit of corruption, and make us perfect in likeness to Christ the Saviour of us all. Listen how He sets Himself before us as an example of the humble mind and of the will that does not seek vainglory, when He says: "Learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart" (Mt 11:29).
St. Cyril the Great
A city broken down, and without walls, is the man who hath no rule over his own spirit [28].

He who does not control himself, how can he control his household or those under him? The wise and virtuous man first takes care to control his inner depths, so that he is like a fortified city, into which the enemy of good cannot steal and devour him.

* Those who are addicted to much talking must observe carefully how far they are from the straight path when they plunge into a flood of words. The mind behaves like water. When we enclose water with a fence, it rises to higher levels, ascending to the height from which it came down. But when we let it go and the fence is broken down, it is scattered in every direction and runs through all the lower levels. So in truth all excessive speech is lost like water when it is freed from the watch of silence, and the mind is carried through many channels and wanders, and thus loses the power by which it could return inwardly to self-knowledge, for it is scattered by much talking and chatter, and turns aside from the places of secret contemplation in the heart. And here the mind exposes itself to the wounds aimed by the enemy who lies in wait for it, because it has not surrounded itself with a fence of vigilance. So it is written in Proverbs: "A city broken down, and without walls, is the man who hath no rule over his own spirit" (Prov 25:28).

The citadel of the mind that has no wall of silence is exposed to the arrows of the enemy, and when speech issues from the walls of the citadel and strikes them, it is exposed to the enemy openly, and he overcomes it without toil, for the talkative mind is defeated when it fights itself by its own much speaking.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
May Your Spirit lead me in the royal way!
* O Your wondrous love, O King of kings!
You desire to raise up from mankind kings and leaders.
You reveal to them Your mysteries, which no human mind can search out.
You give them Your Spirit, the Giver of wisdom, so that they do not walk in the way without wisdom.
They examine matters and remove the dross, and become vessels of silver, bright and honoured.
* In Your presence we draw from the overflow of Your humility, so that we may walk in the spirit of true humility, and pride or vainglory may not steal into our thoughts.
* By You we are bound to live in peace, if possible, with all.
We wish to be reconciled with everyone, O You who reconciled the earthly with the heavenly, the people with the peoples, and the soul with the body!
* Sanctify our inner depths together with our words and our conduct...
that we may not utter a word out of its place.
and that our tongue may not run loose in speech without restraint, but that we may offer our words as apples of gold in a vessel of shining silver!
By You, let no word come out of our mouths without the fragrance of love breathing from it!
* Grant us the spirit of faithfulness in little as in much.
May we be faithful in our words and our conduct, and faithful in our promises.
May we not bear false witness in revenge, nor betray anyone, whatever his conduct toward us.
* Grant us fellowship in Your longsuffering!
Then anger will not rise up in us without restraint, and our tongue will not slip into wounding words.
* Grant us the spirit of moderation in everything.
May we eat moderately, so that we do not vomit what we have eaten, even if it is honey.
May we not overdo our visits to our brethren!
* Let our hearts groan with the groans of the hearts of our brethren.
And let us share the joy of those who rejoice in the Lord.
Let us love even those who oppose us, and provide for them all their needs as far as we can.
Thus we shall heap coals of fire of repentance on their thoughts, and they will join us in love in Your Kingdom!
* Let Your peace dwell in our hearts, let love fill our homes, and let our earth be turned into Your heavens!
You are the good heavenly news!
Your coming down to us became cold water, quenching our thirsty souls!
Come, O holy One from heaven, and dwell in our hearts, that our inner depths may become Your fortified city!

1 As snow in summer, and as rain in harvest, so honour is not seemly for a fool. 2 As the bird by wandering, as the swallow by flying, so the curse causeless shall not come. 3 A whip for the horse, a bridle for the ass, and a rod for the fool's back. 4 Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest thou also be like unto him. 5 Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own conceit. 6 He that sendeth a message by the hand of a fool cutteth off the feet, and drinketh damage. 7 The legs of the lame hang loose: so is a parable in the mouth of fools. 8 As a bundle of precious stones in a heap, so is he that giveth honour to a fool. 9 As a thorn goeth up into the hand of a drunkard, so is a parable in the mouths of fools. 10 As an archer that woundeth all, so is he that hireth the fool, or hireth the deceivers. 11 As a dog returneth to his vomit, so a fool returneth to his folly. 12 Seest thou a man wise in his own conceit? there is more hope of a fool than of him.

This chapter begins by speaking about the fool, and as we have already seen in our study of the Book of Wisdom as in the Book of Proverbs, "fool" does not mean one who suffers from an incapacity of mental ability, but the foolish man, that is, the wicked one who does not walk in a spirit of uprightness, and so sports in sin, rejecting true wisdom. The fool may be educated and highly cultured, but as the Psalmist says: "The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God" (Ps 14:1).
The Hebrew word corresponding to "fool" is translated "dull-witted."
As snow in summer, and as rain in harvest, so honour is not seemly for a fool [1].

Snow is useful in its proper time, that is, in winter, but harmful if it falls in summer; and rain is useful after the sowing, but destructive if it falls during the harvest. So the fool does not know the proper time for his thoughts, his words and his conduct, and so he acts without discretion and destroys himself.

The foolish man, though he desires vainglory and temporal honour, when he obtains a position of leadership and comes to have authority and honour, the honour destroys him, as snow destroys when it falls in summer at harvest time, or as heavy rains pour down during the harvest. He does not know how to use authority and to order affairs in their proper place, and as the Psalmist says of him: "Nevertheless man being in honour abideth not: he is like the beasts that perish" (Ps 49:12).

St. Basil sees that the work of the serpent, that is, of Satan, is to corrupt our nature, so that we do not look upward but bow down like the animals toward the dust, seeking earthly things. Therefore he counsels us, saying: [For the head of the beasts looks toward the earth, but the head of man was created to look toward heaven, and his eyes are directed upward; therefore it befits us to seek what is above, and with our insight to pierce through earthly things.]

* How do you see the form of four-footed creatures? Their head is bent toward the earth, and they look to their belly, searching for the things that give them pleasure. But you, O man, your head is raised toward heaven, and your eyes look to the heights. So if you are defiled by the lusts of the flesh, and are enslaved to the pleasures of the belly and the lower pleasures, then by this [you draw near to the irrational animals and become like them] (Ps 59:14).

I set before you the care of another matter that befits you: seek the things that are above, where Christ stands (Col 3:1). Rise above the passing accidents of this perishing world, and learn from the make-up of your body, and make it a rule for your life: your city is heaven, your true homeland is the Jerusalem above, and your fellow citizens are the firstborn, whose names are written in the heavens.
St. Basil the Great As the bird by wandering, as the swallow by flying, so the curse causeless shall not come [2].
The foolish man hastens to pour curses on others without cause...

But he who does not trust in God's providence fears these curses and thinks that they will destroy him. But he who relies on God and takes refuge in Him knows that they are only hollow words dissipated in the air, like the bird that flies before a man and does not harm him, and like the swallow that flies and disappears from before a man's face. These curses harm the fool, and do not harm those on whom he pours them. Goliath the giant poured out curses, but they struck him, and he was killed by the hand of the boy David, and came to shame and disgrace. Rabshakeh and Sennacherib poured out curses against the good king Hezekiah and his people, and destruction fell upon their army, and God was glorified in King Hezekiah.

* "As the birds and the sparrows by flying, so the curse causeless shall not come." Again Solomon says: "He that uttereth a slander, is a fool" (Prov 10:18). But he is like the bee, which as to its strength is weak, and when it has stung someone loses its sting and becomes a burden; so in the same way every injury you practise against another is brought upon you.
Apostolic Canons A whip for the horse, a bridle for the ass, and a rod for the fool's back [3].

When a man surrenders his life to God, the Lord leads him in his way, giving him the spirit of wisdom and understanding, and as the believer fixes his eyes on the Lord, the Lord fixes His eyes on him. But he who rejects God's counsel becomes without understanding, and the Psalmist counts him as an animal, for understanding or reason is what distinguishes us from the irrational animals. In Christ Jesus, the Wisdom of the Father, we are raised to be like the angels of God, and by withdrawing from God we lose even our humanity!

Unruly and stubborn horses need a whip to restrain their wildness, and the hasty ass that does not perceive its way needs a bridle to restrain and direct it; so the fool is marked by wildness and haste without wisdom, and needs the rod of rebuke and tribulations to keep him from stubbornness. It is said in the Psalms: "Be ye not as the horse, or as the mule, which have no understanding: whose mouth must be held in with bit and bridle, lest they come near unto thee" (Ps 32:9). Though it is easy to tame the horse and the ass, it is hard to tame the fool.

* With bit and bridle He restrains the jaws of those who do not come near to You, for under the pressure of circumstances, as you said, they necessarily bow their necks to God, even against their will.
St. Cyril the Great Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest thou also be like unto him [4].
It befits the wise man not to come down to the level of the fool and fight him with his own mocking manner, and descend with him from the spirit of calm, reason and wisdom.

* Your flight will be good if you do not answer the fool according to his folly. Your flight is good if you direct your steps away from the features of the foolish. Truly a person can quickly go astray if the leadership is evil; so if you want your flight to be good, remove your ways from their words.

* David was accustomed not to answer the enemy who provoked him, the sinner who was angry with him. He says: "But I, as a deaf man, heard not; and I was as a dumb man that openeth not his mouth" (Ps 38:13). Again it is said in another place: "Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest thou also be like unto him." The first duty is that you have a true measure for your speech; by this you offer a sacrifice of praise to God. So pious fear appears in the reading of the Holy Scriptures. By this parents are honoured. I know well that many speak because they do not know how to practise silence. A person is always silent when speech is not profitable. The wise man, when he wishes to speak, takes into consideration what he says, and to whom he addresses the speech, also where and at what time he speaks.

St. Ambrose * (From the words of his sister St. Macrina) It is better for a man to remain silent about such questions, and to look with consideration upon their folly and undignified arrogance, which is not worthy of an answer, since the divine words forbid us, saying: "Answer not a fool according to his folly." And the fool, according to the prophet, is "he that says there is no God" (Ps 53:1).
St. Gregory of Nyssa Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own conceit [5].

These two verses (4, 5) seem to contradict each other, but in fact they complement each other. For it does not befit us to answer the fool or the foolish man according to his folly, that is, with discussion and dialogue that carries a spirit of mockery and scorn, that is, according to his style, for then we ourselves would have descended to his base level instead of raising him out of it. So let us not meet his sarcasm with sarcasm, nor imitate the spirit of recklessness he carries. Rather, let us answer him in a spirit of firmness and seriousness, for our edification and his.

The people were bound by the command of King Hezekiah not to answer Rabshakeh, who despised God (2 Kgs 18:36), and by this they fulfilled the counsel of the wise man in verse 4. But Nehemiah answered Sanballat firmly, when he wished to destroy the work of building, saying to him: "There are no such things done as thou sayest, but thou feignest them out of thine own heart" (Neh 6:8), and he refused to enter into a dialogue with him as Sanballat requested: "Come now therefore, and let us take counsel together" (Neh 6:7).

When a man asks about contradictions in the Holy Bible, if the person seeks it in order to mock, then the dialogue with him turns into foolish arguments; but if he is serious in seeking to know, then dialogue is necessary, as the Apostle Peter says: "Sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear" (1 Pet 3:15). The same is true if the dialogue is with an atheist who denies the existence of God: the decision to engage in dialogue or not depends on our perception of the questioner's intention. By refusing to answer we take care not to slip into his folly, and by our reply to him we wish to preserve him from the folly that has mastered him.

* It befits us to learn well to know our faith, so that when anyone asks us about it we may be able to give a fitting answer, and to do so with meekness and in the fear of the Lord. For he who does this does it as though God Himself were present, hearing him.

St. Didymus the Blind * The Apostle tells us to be ready to answer everyone who asks us, to explain our faith to him; so if an unbeliever asks me the reason for my faith and hope, and I perceive that he cannot accept it unless he believes, I give him the same reason, so that he may see how absurd it is for him to grasp it without believing.
St. Augustine * He who decides to do this is not doing something new, nor offering some new explanation, but rather is showing those who ask about his faith in Christ what it is.
St. Cyril of Alexandria He that sendeth a message by the hand of a fool cutteth off the feet, and drinketh damage [6].

A man errs when he sends a message with a foolish messenger, for he is like one who has cut off his own feet and become unable to move, or like one who has chosen to drink from a cup of poison or injustice, which brings him ruin and destruction. So the wise man requires us to choose the right messenger when we send a message to someone. He had already counselled us in this: "As the cold of snow in the time of harvest, so is a faithful messenger to them that send him: for he refresheth the soul of his masters" (Prov 25:13).
The legs of the lame hang loose: so is a parable in the mouth of fools [7].
A parable coming from the mouth of the fool is of no use, like the legs of a lame man, which do not support him in moving, unless they are a burden to his body.
As a bundle of precious stones in a heap, so is he that giveth honour to a fool [8].

He who honours a fool with words of praise is like one who throws precious stones on a heap, or strikes with them from a sling. For he who uses precious stones in a sling has misused the precious stones and at the same time does not know how to use the sling.

When the people praised Herod, the proud and foolish king, saying: "It is the voice of a god, and not of a man" (Acts 12:22), immediately the angel of the Lord smote him, because he gave not God the glory, and he was eaten of worms and died. He who gives honour to a fool only hands him a weapon with which to destroy himself.
As a thorn goeth up into the hand of a drunkard, so is a parable in the mouths of fools [9].

He who hands a branch full of thorns to a drunken man causes harm to him and to those around him; so the parable that comes out of the mouth of the fool, when he occupies the position of a teacher, condemns him, and neither he nor those around him benefit from it, because of their stumbling in him. The drunken man does not feel pain in the moments of his drunkenness, so he waves the branch full of thorns, and hurts himself and those around him with it, while he laughs mockingly. He does not know in the moments of his drunkenness how to use what is in his hand.

The word of the Lord came by the mouth of Jeremiah the prophet against Shemaiah: "Because that Shemaiah hath prophesied unto you, and I sent him not, and he caused you to trust in a lie... Behold, I will punish Shemaiah the Nehelamite, and his seed" (Jer 29:31-32).

* The sin of all men is not taken away by the lamb, if they do not grieve and repent until it is lifted from them. It is like the thorn, which is not only planted, but takes deep roots in the hands of everyone who has become a drunkard because of evil and lost his dignity. And this is like the saying in Proverbs: "The thorn grows in the hand of the drunkard." What more fitting thing should we say about the greatest disaster that befalls him who receives such a plant (the thorn) into his soul? For he who adds evil in the depths of his soul to such a degree must be cut off by the living and active word of God, which pricks him more than a two-edged sword, and is more able to burn than any fire (Heb 4:12; Sir 48:1), that fire which reveals the thorn.
Origen As an archer that woundeth all, so is he that hireth the fool, or hireth the deceivers [10].

It befits a man to choose well those who work with him or on his behalf, because hiring foolish men or passers-by to carry out important tasks is a serious matter. For he is like one who shoots arrows without awareness or aim. He hits others, and he also pierces himself without knowing it.
As a dog returneth to his vomit, so a fool returneth to his folly [11].

Those who return to a life of evil, leaving fellowship with God, find their last state worse than their first. The Apostle Peter says: "For it had been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness, than, after they have known it, to turn from the holy commandment delivered unto them. But it is happened unto them according to the true proverb, The dog is turned to his own vomit again; and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire" (2 Pet 2:21-22).

How hideous is sin! The sinner finds pleasure and delight in its filth, while the souls of others loathe it. It is a grave disease, which makes the one it strikes a sick man who loves the sickness. This is the state of one who turns back from sin for a time through intellectual conviction, without seeking the help of God and His grace, which renews his thought, his heart and all his depths. But he who throws himself by grace into the divine bosom hears the divine voice: "My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me: and I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand" (Jn 10:27-28).
A lamb may fall into the mud, but it will not rest until it is washed of it; but the pig, after it is washed, throws itself into the mud and finds its happiness in the filth.
St. Cyril of Alexandria sees that this proverb applies to the heretics who invent defiled heresies, and open their mouths against the divine glory and "speak perverse things" (Acts 20:30).

Father Hilary, Bishop of Arles, sees that St. Peter refers here to those who received Baptism after confessing their faith in Christ Jesus, but then returned and left Him, so that they became like the dog that returns to its vomit.

* Do you not know that those who do not care about their salvation, and who waver between taking care of it and falling recklessly into the net of Satan, are compared in the Holy Bible to dogs? Remember the saying: "He who leaves his sin and then returns to it is like the dog that returns to its vomit."

St. John Chrysostom * While we were in this state full of anxiety, we could not make a decisive decision beneficial for our salvation. Rather, with our sighs we were in bitterness, rebuking ourselves for our rashness (in giving the promise), hating the defect of our nature, feeling the weight of the matter, for which we had no other way under the pressure of those who hindered us from what was for our benefit and good, by demanding from us a promise to return quickly. And we wept because we had done this under the fault of this defect of which it was said: "As a dog returneth to his vomit, so a fool returneth to his folly" (Prov 11:26).

Father Joseph * These things are suffered, without doubt, by men of the priesthood and by monks and virgins who are proud, disobedient and lukewarm. In the beginning of their life they renounce the ways of this world, and with a fervent spirit flee to the holy service of religion, and by the grace of God they are delivered from all sins. But afterwards, because of their negligence and sloth, they are not filled with zeal, and are not filled with spiritual graces by God's help, and the vices that left them find them empty, and return with other vices worse than they, and compel them to return to their vomit. Then what is written is fulfilled: the dog that returns to his vomit is hated, and so is the sinner who returns to his sin.
Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles Seest thou a man wise in his own conceit?
there is more hope of a fool than of him! [12]

The man who thinks himself wise shuts himself in, so he does not accept anyone's counsel and does not seek to learn, and by his pride he perishes. One may hope more for the fool who realizes his folly that he will learn and be saved from his foolishness than for one who thinks himself wise. Therefore the Apostle says: "Be not wise in your own conceits" (Rom 12:16).

It is as if what is more dangerous than stupidity is pride, self-reliance on one's own opinion, and a man's deceiving himself, so that he asks neither wisdom from God nor counsel from anyone. He is like the sick man who thinks he is in health and has no need of a physician, or the sinner who thinks himself righteous and has no need of the Saviour.
* It is pride that turns a man back from wisdom, and so folly takes its place when wisdom is abandoned.
St. Augustine * They increase in their error by claiming to be wise while they show themselves to be fools.

Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrrhus * There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, a person who is wise in his own eyes, and it is more dangerous that a person who does not know his own ignorance should undertake the responsibility of teaching others.
St. Gregory of Nazianzus * The person who is conceited is foolish in his ignorance, and cannot know the wisdom of God, since he clings to his foolishness, counting it wisdom.

Origen * It is no light error for a man to count himself wise, and to refer all matters to his own judgment... Paul directed this very rebuke to the pagan philosophers: "Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools" (Rom 1:22). This is the cause of their folly. The writer of the Book of Proverbs for his part says: "Seest thou a man wise in his own conceit? there is more hope of a fool than of him." Again, it is Paul who gives this counsel: "Be not wise in your own conceits" (Rom 12:16).
* Because they think themselves exalted, and do not have enough patience to walk in the way which God commands them, they become absorbed in a way of thinking that has no meaning.
St. John Chrysostom

13 The slothful man saith, There is a lion in the way; a lion is in the streets. 14 As the door turneth upon his hinges, so doth the slothful upon his bed. 15 The slothful hideth his hand in his bosom; it grieveth him to bring it again to his mouth. 16 The sluggard is wiser in his own conceit than seven men that can render a reason.
The slothful man saith:
"There is a lion in the way; a lion is in the streets" [13].
He has already spoken about the danger of sloth and its work in a man's life (Prov 13:4; 15:9; 19:15; 20:4; 21:25-26; 24:30, 34).

The first mark of the sluggard is that he offers excuses for his laziness, with a mistaken feeling that dangers surround him if he moves to work. So he finds in idleness rest for himself, calm for his soul, and safety for his life from the lions and cubs that await him. It is as though they had no work except to watch for him to go out to work and then devour him. But the man who works in the Spirit of the Lord does not fear; rather he opens the lion's mouth to rescue a lamb as the boy David did, and tears a lion in the way as Samson did.
As the door turneth upon his hinges, so doth the slothful upon his bed [14].

Doors still turn on a pivot; they move round upon themselves and do not move from their place. So the sluggard thinks that he is always moving and working, while he remains in his idleness as on his bed, of no use even to himself. He lacks the spirit of ambition and the sense of his mission.
The sluggard does not carry a creative spirit that tends to renewal and innovation.
The slothful hideth his hand in his bosom; it grieveth him to bring it again to his mouth [15].

The sluggard reaches the point of stretching out his hand to the dish to eat, and finds it difficult to lift it to put the food in his mouth. He prefers to remain hungry rather than move his hand to eat!

We hear of this in some tribes in tropical regions, when the heat becomes intense, and a person feels a severe kind of sluggishness, and sees before him free food such as bananas and other fruits, and finds it hard to stretch out his hand to pluck a fruit and eat!
Some see that this proverb applies to one who feels that the weather is bitterly cold, so he puts his hands in his bosom to warm them, and does not think of taking them out even to eat.
It also applies to some lazy people who pretend to be helpless and unwell in order to ask for alms, and do not want to work.
The sluggard is wiser in his own conceit than seven men that can render a reason [16].

By his idleness and loss of resolve the sluggard thinks he is wiser than those who work, for he does not exhaust his body or his mind, but lives as one without care! He thinks idleness is economy of health, and not working is wisdom!

* The ant is a very small creature, but it ventures to accomplish things beyond its strength. It is not dragged to work like a slave. Rather, without compulsion, and in the freedom of foresight, it takes care of the provision for the coming day. Holy Scripture counsels us to imitate the perseverance of the ant: [Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wiser than she] (cf. Prov 6:6). The ant has no land to till. Yet without a leader urging it on, it takes care to store up food. Whatever harvest it gathers into its store is a harvest it gathers from the remains of your works, while you may be in want and it needs nothing. There are no granaries set apart for the ant, no guards hard to pass, no grain stores that may not be touched!

St. Ambrose * Why must we speak of how great the evil in sloth is, if the Apostle states plainly that he who does not work shall not eat (2 Thess 3:10)? For if daily bread is necessary for everyone, so work is essential according to each person's strength. The Lord links sloth with evil, saying: "Thou wicked and slothful servant" (Mt 25:26)... We have reason to fear lest this fault stand against us on the day of judgment, for He who gave us the ability to work requires us to work according to our capacity.

St. Basil the Great St. Augustine gives us a symbolic interpretation of the ant's striving and of our duty to imitate it: if the ant gathers food in the summer season, when it is hot, and feeds on it during the winter in the cold, so it befits us to be diligent in reading the Holy Bible in the time of our spiritual warmth. Let us strive to work while it is summer, so that when the time of trial comes upon us, and we feel a kind of spiritual coldness, our souls may feed on what we enjoyed in the time when our hearts were kindled by the Spirit.

entries.section: 3. Meddling in what does not concern us

paragraphs.text: He that passeth by, and meddleth with strife belonging not to him, is like one that taketh a dog by the ears [17].

The wise man has already counselled us to flee as far as we can from disputes, even those that concern us, and to resort to reconciliation instead of entering the courts. How much more should we not interfere in quarrels to which we are not a party, lest we be like one who seizes the ears of a savage dog, and expose ourselves to harm. This does not mean that we refuse to make peace between the quarrelling, but that we refuse partiality, and entering as a party into a quarrel that does not concern us. In the Septuagint it says: "like one who takes a dog by the tail," for the dog turns round and bites him.
As a mad man who casteth firebrands, arrows, and death [18].
So is the man that deceiveth his neighbour, and saith, Am not I in sport? [19]

The wise man warns us against deceitful dealings with relatives, which cause them harm, after which the person laughs mockingly and says: I was only jesting with them. People's lives are not a plaything in our hands, to be mocked with recklessness. He who does this is counted as a madman who throws burning coals at others, or strikes them with arrows, and causes their death.

St. John Chrysostom says: [To lure them on (Herod the Magi), he pretended piety, hiding the sword behind it. He painted the appearance of simplicity over the malice of his heart. This is the way of all evildoers, for they plot in secret to wound others, and so pretend simplicity and friendship.]

20 Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth. 21 As coals are to burning coals, and wood to fire; so is a contentious man to kindle strife. 22 The words of a talebearer are as sweet morsels, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly.
Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth [20].

Gossip adds fuel to the fire of strife, and if it is not found the flames die down and go out, for where there is no fuel or wood the fire goes out. It is said: "The whisperer defileth his own soul, and is hated wheresoever he dwelleth" (Sir 21:31).
* If you hear someone slandering another, flee from him as you would flee from a poisonous serpent, until he is ashamed and learns not to speak so again.

St. Jerome * What does it mean that we abstain from eating meat, while we do not abstain from eating the flesh of our neighbour by gossip and backbiting? And what does it mean that we fast from food, while we do not abstain from evil thoughts, fornication, malice and hatred?

St. Basil the Great * Abba Macarius said: "Guard your ears from hearing words of gossip and slander, that your hearts may be pure, for if the ears hear unclean talk, it is not possible to keep the purity of the heart without defilement."

* Abba Mark said: "Everything you say about your brother behind his back, and cannot say in front of him, is gossip and slander, and every concern that does not lead to the good of worship is a worldly concern."

* Abba Shishoi said: "By gossip the serpent deceived Eve and brought her out of Paradise, and Adam with her; so exactly like the serpent is he who falls upon his companion, for he destroys the one who hears him, and his own soul does not escape."
Abba Isaiah was asked what gossip is, and he answered: "It is ignorance of the glory of God, and hatred of others."

* An elder said: "What you hate for yourself, do not say to another. You hate him who gossips about you (that is, who condemns you), so do not gossip about anyone. You hate him who lies to you, so do not lie to another. You hate him who curses you, so do not curse anyone. He who has ears, let him keep these words, and they will suffice him."
The Paradise of the Fathers As coals are to burning coals, and wood to fire; so is a contentious man to kindle strife [21].

The wise Solomon calls us to settle dispute and strife at the beginning of its outbreak (Prov 17:14; 30:32-33). If possible, let us not enter into discussions and arguments that may inflame the situation (Prov 20:3).

Some incline to spread the spirit of peace (Prov 12:20), while others find their pleasure in strife (Prov 22:10; 26:21). There are also people who are at rest in no situation: whether they are angry or laugh, they have no rest (Prov 29:9).
God counts the peacemakers as His sons (Mt 5:9), and wisdom likewise calls us to meekness and to freedom from factions (Jas 3:13-14).

There are people like the coal that is thrown into burning embers so that it burns more fiercely, or like the wood thrown into the fire so that it blazes more. These are the stirrers-up of strife wherever they are found. They are not occupied with the word of God, the Giver of peace, even if they recite it and preach it much.
The words of a talebearer are as sweet morsels, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly [22].

Often the talebearer uses honeyed words, and pretends friendship and concern for the one he speaks with, and so casts the bitterness of gossip into the innermost parts of the belly of his hearer, where it settles in his depths and inflames the spirit of anger and resentment in him.

* Feigned patience often provokes anger more cleverly than speech does. And by harmful silence it increases the insults of others more than speech provokes them, and the wounds of enemies are borne more easily than the flattery of mockers, full of craftiness, of which it was well said by the prophet: "To bind his princes at his pleasure" (Ps 22:105). And in another place it is said: "The words of a talebearer are as sweet morsels, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly" (Prov 22:26). Here applies the saying: "Their tongue is as an arrow shot out; it speaketh deceit: one speaketh peaceably to his neighbour with his mouth, but in heart he layeth his wait" (Jer 8:9). In any case he deceives others, for "A man that flattereth his neighbour spreadeth a net for his feet" (Prov 5:29).
Father Joseph * Do not slander any man, lest God hate your prayer.
St. Abba Anthony the Great

23 Burning lips and a wicked heart are like a potsherd covered with silver dross. 24 He that hateth dissembleth with his lips, and layeth up deceit within him; 25 When he speaketh fair, believe him not: for there are seven abominations in his heart.
Burning lips and a wicked heart are like a potsherd covered with silver dross [23].

He who hides behind an appearance of love, friendship and concern for others and utters words of gossip carries an evil heart, and has lips burning with the fire of hidden evil. This man resembles a potsherd, a fragment or shard of a clay vessel, of no value, covered with a thin layer of silver full of dross. He seems to be something precious and shining, while in truth he is utterly worthless and of no use.

Perhaps he means here that the lips of the gossip are burning as though with a radiant fire, and sweet words come out of them, but in truth they come from a malicious, wicked heart. He is a hypocrite!
He that hateth dissembleth with his lips, and layeth up deceit within him [24].
The hater thinks how to conceal what is in his depths of his hatred behind deceptive words, but his inward part or his depths carry deceit!

* Do not cover up the sin you have committed. Refuse to answer back, and do not think evil in your heart against him who angers you or hates you. Do not be quick to anger. Beware of speaking empty talk, and do not hear it from others so as to retain it, but let your speech be in remembrance of God the Most High and in seeking His forgiveness.
* Do good to everyone, and if you cannot, love everyone, and if you cannot, at least do not hate anyone, and none of this will be possible for you as long as you love the things of the world.
St. Abba Anthony the Great When he speaketh fair, believe him not: for there are seven abominations in his heart [25].

The hypocrite is skilled in a sweet voice and gentle words, but he is not to be trusted, for his heart is full of seven abominations, that is, abominations without number, for the number 7 signifies perfection, or multitude in number (Prov 24:16).
* My son, do not be a hypocrite or a liar.

St. Abba Anthony the Great * A brother asked Abba Poemen: "Who is the hypocrite?" The elder said to him: "The hypocrite is he who teaches his neighbour something that he himself does not strive to do. It is written: 'And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye? ... Thou hypocrite, first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother's eye'" (Mt 7:3-5).
The Paradise of the Fathers * When you sit in your cell, my son, do not be like the hypocrites. Do not grow weary of prayer, and you will be heard.

* Do not be a hypocrite. Rather seek the word of the Lord from the man of God. For the Lord said by the prophet: "And they come unto thee as the people cometh, and they sit before thee as my people, and they hear thy words, but they will not do them: for with their mouth they shew much love, but their heart goeth after their covetousness" (Ezek 31:33).
Abba Paul of Tamwah

26 Whose hatred is covered by deceit, his wickedness shall be shewed before the whole congregation. 27 Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein: and he that rolleth a stone, it will return upon him. 28 A lying tongue hateth those that are afflicted by it; and a flattering mouth worketh ruin.
Whose hatred is covered by deceit, his wickedness shall be shewed before the whole congregation [26].

There is nothing hidden that will not be revealed, so he who hides his hatred and resentment behind a glittering appearance will not endure; rather his malice will be exposed before the whole community, and he will come to disgrace.

* The contentious man who does not rest from strife is the one who is not content with the first quarrel but rises up in anger anew. But the one who, on the contrary, is not a contentious man, when his anger is kindled, returns to himself at once, blames himself, and asks forgiveness from his brother with whom he was angry, and so the strife in him is calmed because he has condemned himself and been reconciled with his brother, and the struggle will find no place in him, as I have said.

But the wrathful man, in whom the strife is not calmed, and who, when he is angry, does not condemn himself but his anger rises all the more without his ever repenting of his anger, and is not even content with what he said in his anger but adds to it; this one is called a contentious man, and anger is not calmed within him, because malice, bitterness and malignity follow anger. May the Lord Jesus Christ save us from the fate of such people and grant us the portion of the meek and the humble!
St. Zosimas Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein: and he that rolleth a stone, it will return upon him [27].

The cross that Haman prepared for Mordecai, he himself was hanged upon. And the plan that the enemy of good devised to get rid of the Lord of glory, Jesus, caused him to lose his authority and shattered his kingdom. With the measure we measure, it shall be measured to us.

The den that the wicked prepared for Daniel, they fell into it, they and their families. And as the Psalmist says: "His mischief shall return upon his own head, and his violent dealing shall come down upon his own pate" (Ps 7:16); "The heathen are sunk down in the pit that they made: in the net which they hid is their own foot taken... the wicked is snared in the work of his own hands" (Ps 9:15-16). "They have digged a pit before me, into the midst whereof they are fallen themselves" (Ps 56:6).

* "Whoso diggeth a pit for his neighbour shall fall therein." This happened at that time, when they wished to destroy (Jesus) in order to hide His preaching, but the opposite happened. His preaching was refreshed by the grace of Christ, while all their plans came to nothing and perished. Rather they lost their country, their freedom, their security and their worship, and were deprived of all honour and glory, and became slaves and captives. And since we know these things, let us not make plans against others, learning that by doing this we make the sword sharp against ourselves, and wound ourselves more than we wound others.
* It is a sign of God's tender love that He makes those who set snares fall into them, so that they cease from striving and from devising plots against their brethren.
St. John Chrysostom A lying tongue hateth those that are afflicted by it; and a flattering mouth worketh ruin [28].

He closes the chapter with a warning against the lying tongue that harms others and hates them, and likewise against the mouth that flatters another while the man plans the ruin and destruction of the one he speaks with. We may say that what the wise man aims at here is that we face the truth of our depths with complete frankness, and not cover what is in the heart of hatred and malice with a deceitful smile, or words of flattery, or lying and deceit.

* Lying is foreign to us, whether its subject is grave or slight, and even if someone lies with the intention of reaching some kind of good, this lie is nevertheless not commendable, for the Saviour says that lying comes from the evil one (Mt 5:37; Jn 8:44).
St. John of Asyut * Do not allow the spirit of lying to be found in you, lest the Lord deliver you to destruction.

* If you surrender your heart to him in false dreams, he grows more firmly rooted in vain thought, until he leads astray all who receive the spirit that loves the word of which it was written: "When he speaketh a lie, he speaketh of his own: for he is a liar, and the father of it" (Jn 14:8).
Abba Paul of Tamwah
Gather me into the company of Your children!
* My heart rejoices in Your surpassing love.
You loved us and came down to us, to embrace all mankind in love, and to make all of them Your sons.
* Let me avoid the company of fools, who in their stubbornness persisted in resisting You!
I confess to You my ignorance, but You enlighten my depths with Your wisdom.
You give me understanding and wisdom, so that I desire nothing but to be in Your image, and to speak Your words!
No word of cursing will come out of my mouth, but only the words of blessing that are from You.
* Give me wisdom, that I may know when to speak and when to be silent.
Then I shall not go down with the stubborn fools, nor be provoked and bear the same marks as they.
But I shall walk in wisdom, and bear witness to You by Your work within me!
Let me avoid the company of the lazy, for in Your embrace I shall not know idleness.
You and the Father work for the sake of the whole world.
In Your love work in me and through me for the sake of Your Kingdom.
* Let me avoid the company of the stirrers-up of strife.
You came down to us to reconcile us with Your Father.
You gave us fellowship with the heavenly ones, You raised up from every tribe and people a holy people for Yourself; why then strife, when You are Peace itself.
O that I might possess You, and my heart be filled with peace; O that I might possess You, and the serpent not cast his malice into my mouth or my heart.
O that I might possess You, and my words be sanctified; I shall find no taste for gossip, no place in me for lying, and no need for the violent word.
Rather, let my words be salted with the salt of Your Holy Spirit!
Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth [1].

The past has gone by and will not return, and the future we do not know whether it will come upon us in this world or whether we shall pass away before it comes, but the moment we are living is ours. Through the present we benefit from the past, with its good things as well as our mistakes, and through it we work for the future, whether we are found in this world or the other. In this way we boast in the present day and sanctify it to the Lord, and live every moment of our life rejoicing.

By becoming accustomed to postponing to tomorrow, often the tomorrow in which we are to work never comes, because with every tomorrow we postpone to the tomorrow that follows it. Some say: "Postponing till tomorrow is a thief that steals a man's life."

The Holy Bible calls us not to postpone, especially concerning the salvation of our souls: "behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation" (2 Cor 6:2). "To day if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts" (Heb 3:7-8). Felix the governor trembled when he heard Paul reason of righteousness, temperance and judgment to come, and instead of taking a decision to repent, he said: "Go thy way for this time; when I have a convenient season, I will call for thee" (Acts 24:25), and Felix did not get a convenient season to call for him until he died.
He who walks in the way of postponing to tomorrow will not reach a dwelling in which to settle.

* Let us not postpone to tomorrow, for we do not know what the next day may bring forth. And let us not say: "We shall overcome this habit little by little," for this thing will never come to an end. Therefore, to nullify this excuse, let us say: "If we do not amend the practice of swearing oaths today, we shall not postpone it to later, when countless matters press upon us. For we shall certainly die, and be punished, and lose all that we have. Let us not give Satan the benefit of our loitering, nor of the practice of delay," for if the Lord knows your soul to be fervent, He Himself also stretches out a hand of help to change your life.

St. John Chrysostom * Behold, the days are buried like the dead. Yesterday we buried yesterday, and behold, today we are advised that it will also profit. Weep then over yesterday which no longer exists, and raise your voice over today because it will pass as well. Behold, the days snatch you away, and life flees.
When the evening buries you, the morning raises you up.
It puts you to death daily so that you may know that you will die.

* The life of yesterday has fled from you, and behold, the life of today is swift to pass. Whether you are awake or asleep, the night does not stop on its course, and the day does not rest from completing its journey.
This life of yours is being plundered, so plunder from it the benefit.
Do not rely on the morning because it is bright, if your mind is not enlightened by God so that it may dawn.
Do not think that the evening is for rest, as long as your soul is tormented by the pains of evils.
* As you have driven repentance away with various excuses until now, awaken your will to drive away sin day after day, until victory meets you like wealth meets the poor man.

* Please God as you have pleased the world. Grow rich by poverty, as you grew poor by riches. Seek detachment as you sought possessions. Take your mind out of the world and direct it to God, as you took your soul out from God and behind the world.
* Until today you were not king of yourself, but a slave of the world. Be king of yourself, and serve it.
* If a thief robbed you, you would wail, while your life is being stolen from the life of God and you do not grieve over it. (Letter 43)

St. James of Serugh * Let us return to Him, beloved, and not postpone our amendment to the end of our life. Let us listen to the prophet who says: "Make no tarrying to turn to the Lord: and put not off from day to day" (Sir 5:7). For you "knowest not what a day may bring forth." Why do you postpone, O man, from day to day, when today may be your last day?
Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles
Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth; a stranger, and not thine own lips [2].

If a man is struck with the love of praise he loses the spirit of humility, and the grace of God forsakes him. Those who praise you may be sincere in their praise, but no man knoweth the things of a man, save the spirit of man which is in him (1 Cor 2:11). A man knows the truth of his weaknesses, stumblings and falls, and if God in His love covers him, then at least let him reject in his inner self the praise of men.
Many praise us today and blame us tomorrow, so he who is pleased by men's praise today loses his peace tomorrow.

* If I seem arrogant to you, it is because I bear witness to myself. For every man, when he wishes to bear witness to himself, seems haughty and proud; therefore it is written: "Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth."

St. Augustine * No one crowns himself, for this man who heaps praise on himself is rightly mocked, since it is written: "Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth; a stranger, and not thine own lips." But although hypocrites may remain undiscovered and receive honours from men, he says: "but God knoweth your hearts." For the Judge cannot be deceived; He sees the depths of our mind, and knows who is the true contender, and who steals by fraud the honour rightly due to another.

St. Cyril the Great * Our souls are a holy bride for the immortal Bridegroom, and the wedding is the divine Mysteries... So give heed to yourself, keeping your bridal chamber undefiled, and long to receive the heavenly Bridegroom, Christ the King, so that on the day of His coming He may make His abode in you with His Father, and you may have great praise before the angels and the holy archangels, and enter Paradise with great joy.
St. Mar Ephrem the Syrian

entries.section: 3. Dealing with the wise and the fool

paragraphs.text: 3 A stone is heavy, and the sand weighty; but a fool's wrath is heavier than them both. 4 Wrath is cruel, and anger is outrageous; but who is able to stand before envy? 5 Open rebuke is better than secret love. 6 Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.
A stone is heavy, and the sand weighty; but a fool's wrath is heavier than them both [3].

The foolish or stupid man has no fear of the Lord in him, and does not walk in a spirit of godliness; if he is angry he loses his awareness, and acts with great violence without discrimination, so his wrath is heavier than stone and sand. Therefore it befits the wise man not to converse with him or confront him during his anger, but to keep silent and flee from his face. When Saul was angry with David without cause, the king lost his awareness, and called his son Jonathan, who loved David, "thou son of the perverse rebellious woman" (1 Sam 20:30), and could not bear to call David by his name, but called him "the son of Jesse," and "the son of death" (1 Sam 20:31), and determined to kill him by every means.

entries.section: 3. Dealing with the wise and the fool

paragraphs.text: Wrath is cruel, and anger is outrageous; but who is able to stand before envy? [4]

The wise man warns us against the stealing of envy into our hearts, for although wrath is heavier than stone and sand, it is like a short-lived storm, and anger is also like a sweeping flood, that is, nothing can stand before it; but envy dwells in the heart and reigns over it, even if its outward manifestations disappear.

* The envious man does not count the disasters that befall him a trial; his trial is the good that befalls another, and conversely success for him is not that he should be happy but that trials should befall another. The envious man grieves to see the good works of men, and is glad at the disasters that befall them. It is said that the birds of prey that devour dead bodies are destroyed by a sweet smell (perfume), for their nature agrees with what is evil and corrupt. And anyone who falls under the control of this disease (envy) is destroyed by the happiness of his relatives and neighbours, but if he sees an evil trial he flies to it and puts his crooked beak into it and brings out the hidden disasters.

St. Gregory of Nyssa * Envy is hard to heal, because when its causes are sought it grows worse. It looks for external causes and not the inner truth, and its severity increases by rendering services and gifts to the envious man, because, as Solomon himself says: "he stands before the envious" (Prov 4:27). The more the other (the envied one) succeeds in submission and humility, or in the virtue of patience or generosity, the more the pricks of the other's envy increase, for he desires nothing but the destruction and death of the envied one.

Father Piamoun * Contentiousness and envy are born of vainglory, for if a man seeks the glory of men he bears a grudge against him who works and succeeds and is glorified, and envies him, and humility is the cure for that.
St. Abba Poemen * He who has found envy has found with it Satan, who brought it into being from of old.

entries.section: 3. Dealing with the wise and the fool

paragraphs.text: St. Mar Isaac the Syrian Open rebuke is better than secret love [5].

If there is true love, the believer should care for the salvation of those he loves, and be frank with them. He criticizes them, but in a spirit of love without wounding their feelings. He shows them their faults, without exposing them.

* It is certainly clear that hidden sin contributes to the death of the sick person, for the sting of death is sin (1 Cor 15:56) as the Scripture says, and also: "Open rebuke is better than secret love." May no one hide a sin out of courtesy to another, lest the killing of the brother take the place of brotherly love.

St. Basil the Great * Rebuke is good, and is often better than silent friendship. Even if you think the friend himself has been hurt, rebuke him, and if the bitterness of correction wounds his mind, rebuke him and do not fear. For friendship must be sincere and steadfast in love.

St. Ambrose * We who were driven out from the original happiness of Paradise because of our boldness in desiring pleasures must return through bearing hardships with humility; we, the fugitives through our evil doing; there we did what is contrary to justice, here we suffer for the sake of justice.
St. Augustine * It befits us to rejoice when we are counted worthy of divine discipline.

Tertullian * If God disciplines those whom He loves, and He disciplines in order to correct, then it befits the brethren, especially the priests, not to hate but to love those who discipline them, so that they may correct them, for God foretold through Jeremiah, pointing to our present time, saying: [And I will give you pastors according to mine heart, which shall feed you with discipline] (cf. Jer 3:15).

entries.section: 3. Dealing with the wise and the fool

paragraphs.text: St. Cyprian the Martyr Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful [6].

Wounds that come from a loving and wise heart, which knows what to rebuke and when and how far, these wounds are faithful and profitable. But he who wishes to win those around him, so he flatters them and takes part with them in their occasions without caring for their salvation, his conduct is counted as deceitful kisses in which there is neither faithfulness nor sincere love.

In perfect love the Apostle Paul differed with his friend St. Peter, and withstood him for the sake of the truth of the Gospel, as St. Barnabas also differed... but he bore hatred toward no one; rather the Apostle Paul's rule was pure love.

* Not everyone who forgives is a friend, nor everyone who strikes an enemy. For "Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful." Peter was wounded, and Judas kissed. But the kiss condemned Judas, for it carried the poison of betrayal, and the wound that Peter suffered was healed, for he washed his fault with tears.

St. Ambrose * When you rebuked me so that I should not tell the truth, did I not say to you: "I love you more than those who flatter you. In rebuking you I care for you more than all who show you respect?" Did I not also say to you: "Faithful are the wounds of friends rather than the deceitful kisses of enemies" (Prov 27:6). Had you yielded to my wounds, their kisses could not have led you to destruction, for my wounds work for your healing, but their kisses push you to a disease hard to cure.

St. John Chrysostom * Who is this friend whose wounds are better than the kisses of an enemy? The answer is clear to anyone who knows the mystery of salvation. For the true, steadfast friend does not cease to love us even while we are still enemies, but the enemy (the devil) is treacherous and violent. He subjects us to death though we have not harmed him.
St. Gregory of Nyssa

7 The full soul loatheth an honeycomb; but to the hungry soul every bitter thing is sweet. 8 As a bird that wandereth from her nest, so is a man that wandereth from his place. 9 Ointment and perfume rejoice the heart: so doth the sweetness of a man's friend by hearty counsel.
The full soul loatheth an honeycomb; but to the hungry soul every bitter thing is sweet [7].
Great hunger opens a man's appetite for food, and gives him an enjoyment and taste of it which he does not find when he is full.

People's indulgence in various kinds of food has made them lose their taste for food, so many try to be inventive in kinds of food, in order to attract the man of today to food, even if it is not healthy for them.

When we feel hunger for the word of God as food for the soul, we eat it and ruminate on it and meditate on it with delight. Perhaps the wise Solomon wishes to bring out the practical truth that the rich man, with his huge wealth and sumptuous foods, is not as happy as the poor man eating simple food, for he finds delight in it. The rich man often finds bitterness or unhappiness in what is sweet, while the poor man finds sweetness in what seems bitter!

* For although the telling of holy matters is often repeated, the mind that feels a thirst for true knowledge is never disgusted by its fullness, but every day receives the word as something new that it needs. In any case it often listens to it with great eagerness, and speaks of it. And repetition, for him, confirms him without weariness in the knowledge he already has.

This is the sign by which a mind is known to be cold and arrogant, that it receives the remedies of the words of salvation with contempt and carelessness, although they are offered with zeal and great earnestness, and that is because "the full soul loatheth an honeycomb; but to the hungry soul every bitter thing is sweet" (Prov 7:27).

So if these things are taken with care, and stored up within the soul, and sealed with the seal of stillness, they become like wine sweet to the taste, which gladdens the heart of man, and are aged by being stored long in the thought with steadfast patience, and a delightful fragrance comes out of the vessel of the heart, and it becomes a perpetual spring that overflows with the depths of experience in abundance, and is like watered channels. Virtue pours out abundant streams as from the deep well of your heart.

Father Nestor * Do not let the delights of the rich, by worldly measures, entice you, as though they were something useful. They delight in the art of cookery for their pleasure; but you women, surpass their excessive foods by fasting and moderation in eating, for the Scripture says: "The full soul loatheth an honeycomb" (Prov 27:7).

* Do not be deceived by the delights of the world's wealth, as though it contained something useful for vain pleasure. The worldly esteem the art of cookery, but you surpass their abundance of food with fasting and cheap food. It is written: "The full soul loatheth an honeycomb" (Prov 27:7). Do not be filled with bread, and you will not desire wine.
St. Syncletica As a bird that wandereth from her nest, so is a man that wandereth from his place [8].

The pure man is marked by a spirit of contentment and a life of thanksgiving, and so feels a kind of satisfaction and stability despite his struggle and striving and continual progress and growth in everything. But the unbeliever is not satisfied even if the whole earth is given to him, and will not rest, and feels no stability, for he is always murmuring. He is like a bird that forsakes its nest, and so is exposed to dangers.

The Apostle says: "But the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal" (1 Cor 12:7). "But now hath God set the members every one of them in the body, as it hath pleased him" (1 Cor 12:18). Therefore it befits the believer to recognize the gift that has been given him by God, and to kindle it with joy and faithfulness, without boasting over one who does not have the same gift, and without envying one who he thinks has a higher and greater gift than his own.

What is the nest that the bird leaves and so goes astray, but the embrace of God opened to us through the Cross, to which His Holy Spirit carries us, and in which we settle in a spirit of exultation? Demas left this nest, of whom the Apostle Paul said: "For Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world" (2 Tim 4:10).
The man sanctified to the Lord lives in this world as in heaven, and because of him peace comes upon those around him.

* Blessed is the city of Alexandria, of which you are the patrons! And the cities of Sodom would not have perished and turned to ashes if ten righteous had lived in them, and the other cities would not have been overturned if they had kept among them such holiness as yours. And the Holy Bible tells how the friends of the most godly Job, who were the objects of wrath (from God), were saved by his merit: "My servant Job shall pray for you: for him will I accept: lest I deal with you after your folly" (Job 42:8).

* What virtues adorn your lives, so dear to God! What a bright crown these virtues make! How great with you is perseverance in good works! The peace that reigns over you is by virtue of your distance from vices, and of the humility which is the sign that Christ reigns over you, which Satan lost from the beginning.

It was my bounden duty to write to you and tell you this, since it is written: "The memory of the just is blessed" (Prov 10:7), and the praise of the righteous gladdens the people (see Prov 29:2). So when some remember you, it is natural for them to incline to praise you.
St. Abba Serapion, Bishop of Thmuis * Hate your belly and the needs of this world and evil desires and honours, as though you did not yet exist in this world, and you will acquire peace.

St. Abba Anthony the Great * May the peace that comes from the Lord overflow in you beyond all measure, that heavenly peace that raised the light above the world. That which the prophets proclaimed and of which the righteous spoke, and which the angels announced with glad tidings.
