Have mercy on me and forgive me, for I am a sinner!
* Grant me the spirit of uprightness and faithfulness.
Then Your grace will uphold me all the more, and keep me from all the trials of life.
Grant me simplicity of heart, that I may not waver between the ways.
* Take away from me the spirit of cheating and deceit, for I do not seek what belongs to the world but what is Yours!
I walk in the spirit of truth, and am bound only by Your good pleasure and approval.
May my eyes be satisfied by looking to You, and my heart satisfied from the treasuries of Your love!
* Let me hold to the truth for the sake of Your good pleasure; let me not show partiality to any man, nor fear anyone, but speak the truth mingled with the spirit of love.
I respect all and honor everyone, but without flattery.
* Let me hold to the spirit of meekness and humility.
So that through You I may be a peacemaker.
I flee from every atmosphere of strife.
And I find no rest in a spirit of contention.
You are our peace and the rejoicing of our hearts.

entries.section: 1. The righteous and the concept of authority

paragraphs.text: 1 He, that being often reproved hardeneth his neck, shall suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy. 2 When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn. 3 Whoso loveth wisdom rejoiceth his father: but he that keepeth company with harlots spendeth his substance. 4 The king by judgment establisheth the land: but he that receiveth gifts overthroweth it. 5 A man that flattereth his neighbour spreadeth a net for his feet. 6 In the transgression of an evil man there is a snare: but the righteous doth sing and rejoice. 7 The righteous considereth the cause of the poor: but the wicked regardeth not to know it. 8 Scornful men bring a city into a snare: but wise men turn away wrath. 9 If a wise man contendeth with a foolish man, whether he rage or laugh, there is no rest. 10 The bloodthirsty hate the upright: but the just seek his soul. 11 A fool uttereth all his mind: but a wise man keepeth it in till afterwards. 12 If a ruler hearken to lies, all his servants are wicked.
He, that being often reproved hardeneth his neck, shall suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy [1].

Wise Solomon has already praised the rebuke that comes from a heart full of fatherhood or brotherhood, sincere in its love and faithful in its concern for the one it rebukes. He considered such rebuke better and more profitable than honeyed words and than praise given in a spirit of flattery. But if the rebuke comes from a hard neck or an arrogant soul, it does not offer a remedy, but causes wounds that cannot be healed and fractures that cannot be set.

On the other hand, rebuke, even if it comes from a loving heart, and even from God Himself, if a person hardens his heart, becomes a cause of his judgment and not of his healing. This is what happened to many, such as Pharaoh in the days of Moses the prophet, Ahab and Jezebel in the days of Elijah, and many of the kings of Israel after the division.
* Judge, O bishop, with authority like that of God. But whoever repents, receive him to yourself, for God is the God of mercy.
Rebuke the one who sins, and teach with cheerfulness the one who does not wish to return to you.
Didascalia, chapter 3 * There must be true standards for our words and teachings, so that they may not take on the appearance of excessive leniency or exaggerated harshness.

* In this office it does not befit the shepherd to be harsh and violent, nor to be too lax, lest in the first case he be like one with unjust authority, and in the second like one who without cause dishonors the office he has received.

entries.section: 1. The righteous and the concept of authority

paragraphs.text: St. Ambrose When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn [2].

The righteous often resort to firmness and not to laxity with the reckless and the negligent, while the wicked may not care about what their subordinates do. But the righteous leader, with all his firmness, pours a spirit of joy upon the community, whereas the wicked leader causes groaning and bitterness for his subordinates.
* At the birth of the saints joy spreads among all, for it is a blessing to everyone.

* There is a special joy at the beginning of the conception of the saints and at their birth, for the saint does not only gladden his family, but becomes a cause of the salvation of many. This phrase (Lk 1:14) teaches us to rejoice at the birth of the saints.
St. Ambrose * I will offer you proof of what I say in the case of a king.

Saul the son of Kish did not covet kingship, but was only seeking his donkeys. He went to Samuel the prophet to ask him about the donkeys, and the prophet told him of God's calling for him to set him up as king. Yet Saul did not hasten to accept, but drew back. But when he used his authority as king in an evil way, this authority that was given to him by God, was his drawing back enough to protect him from the wrath of God who had granted him this kingship? Was he able to say to Samuel when he rebuked him: Did I rush and hasten to accept authority? I wanted to live as one of the common people in a life full of peace and without disturbance. But it was you who compelled me to accept. If you had left me in my simple (lowly) state, I would not have fallen into all these stumblings, but I would have remained unknown among the people, and consequently I would not have been sent to this battle, and God would not have entrusted me with the war against Amalek... and so I would not have sinned.
But such excuses are feeble; they are not merely feeble but dangerous, for in truth they kindle the wrath of God.

For whoever thinks of himself that he is not responsible for error, because he has received a work that the common people have not received, is like one who protests the love of God as a reason for his own personal errors.

St. John Chrysostom * Let a man know his own measure, so that no one may dare to take for himself the office of shepherding while vice still dominates him and causes his condemnation. For one whom iniquities have corrupted ought not to intercede for the iniquities of others.
Father Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 1. The righteous and the concept of authority

paragraphs.text: Whoso loveth wisdom rejoiceth his father: but he that keepeth company with harlots spendeth his substance [3].

The Book of Proverbs invites us to enter into a relationship of love with wisdom: "Love her, and she shall keep thee" (Prov 4:6), and here it says: "Whoso loveth wisdom rejoiceth his father" (Prov 29:3). And in the Book of Wisdom it is said: "I became a lover of her beauty" (Wis 8:2). He enters, as it were, into a spiritual wedding relationship!

Whoever enters into friendship with harlots squanders his wealth and ruins his life. Therefore the Apostle advises us: "Flee also youthful lusts" (2 Tim 2:22). He also says: "What? know ye not that he which is joined to an harlot is one body?... But he that is joined unto the Lord is one spirit" (1 Cor 6:16-17). Whoever is joined to a harlot loses everything, but whoever is joined to the Lord enjoys unity with Him, and the heavenly Father rejoices in him as his parents rejoice in him.

* If anyone obeys Solomon and takes true wisdom as his companion and the partner of his life, of whom he says: "Love her, and she shall keep thee" [exalt her, and she shall promote thee] (cf. Prov 4:6, 8), he prepares himself for this love, keeping the wedding garment pure, rejoicing in this wedding, so that he may not be cast out, since he is wearing what is fitting for one who is married. It is clear that the longing for this kind of wedding is shared by men and women alike. For the Apostle says: "There is neither male nor female" (Gal 3:28), and Christ is all to all human beings. The aim of the true lover of wisdom is to cling to God, the true Wisdom, the incorruptible Bridegroom, and so he has the love of true wisdom, that is, of God.

St. Gregory of Nyssa * In my opinion the picture of the soul that longs to keep the blessed tradition without losing a single point sometimes runs like this: "When a man loves wisdom, he rejoiceth the heart of his father." Wells that are constantly used supply us with purer water, but wells from which no one draws become foul. Use makes iron brighter, and disuse makes it produce rust. In general, use (work) makes souls and bodies healthy.

entries.section: 1. The righteous and the concept of authority

paragraphs.text: St. Clement of Alexandria The king by judgment establisheth the land: but he that receiveth gifts overthroweth it [4].

Bribery corrupts the foundations of laws and destroys the land, so we must hate it as an enemy of ours (Prov 15:27). It corrupts justice (Prov 17:23). By a bribe a person can reach the great (Prov 18:16), and win their favor (Prov 19:6), but it causes disputes and robs a person of his peace (Prov 21:14).

The righteous King of kings alone came to turn our earth into heaven, and to grant the leaders to enjoy fellowship with Him, so that they may establish truth, justice and righteousness. But whoever seeks gifts as a bribe, and whose heart clings to material things, corrupts the judgment.

* No one was able to know Wisdom, for "no man knoweth the Son, but the Father; neither knoweth any man the Father, save the Son, and he to whomsoever the Son will reveal him" (Mt 11:27). Therefore He revealed Him to John, since Wisdom was with the Apostle, and he spoke not what was according to his own thought, but what Wisdom had poured into him: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God" (Jn 1:1). In truth death could not hold her, for Wisdom said: [O death, where is thy victory? O death, where is thy sting?] (cf. 1 Cor 15:55).

entries.section: 1. The righteous and the concept of authority

paragraphs.text: St. Ambrose A man that flattereth his neighbour spreadeth a net for his feet [5].
Although everyone needs words of encouragement, if praise turns into flattery as a kind of courtesy, adulation or amusement, it is like a net spread out into which the person falls.
* "The righteous shall chasten me with mercy, and reprove me: but let not the oil of sinners anoint my head" (Ps 140:5).

The oil of the sinner is the expressions of flattery and fawning; these the prophet hates greatly. He loves that the righteous man should rebuke him and discipline him with sternness and mercy, and does not want praise with hypocrisy and partiality. For fawning and adulation profit a person nothing, but increase his ignorance and iniquity and his persistence in them...

God said through the prophet: "O my people, those who call you blessed lead you astray" (Isa 3:12), that is, those who praise you and speak of you with tales out of hypocrisy and deceit only deceive you and destroy you utterly. But those who rebuke you and counsel you do you a great kindness.

* (Laxity toward sinners) is not a virtue but a weakness. It is neither love nor meekness but neglect; indeed it is cruelty toward those souls that are overlooked, so that they perish without being warned of their ruin.

entries.section: 1. The righteous and the concept of authority

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine In the transgression of an evil man there is a snare: but the righteous doth sing and rejoice [6].

It is fitting for us to distinguish between the fall of the wicked and the fall of the righteous. The first falls, and surrenders to the fall, and so is shattered, but the second, even if he falls, rises. Therefore even after his fall he sings and praises God, who forgives sin and rescues souls from corruption. The language of the wicked is frustration and despair; the language of the righteous is hope, joy and rejoicing in the Lord.
* ["Jesus answered them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin" (Jn 8:34).]
He is a servant, would that it were of a man, but of sin!
Who is not terrified before such words? May the Lord our God grant us, you and me, that I may speak in fitting terms about this freedom, seeking it, and that I may avoid that bondage...

What a wretched bondage! When human beings suffer from wicked masters, they seek by all means a change of master. What does the servant of sin do? To whom does he present his request? From whom does he seek salvation...?
Where does the servant of sin flee? For he carries (his mistress, that is, sin) wherever he flees. The evil conscience does not flee from itself; there is no place for it to go.

Indeed he cannot withdraw from himself, for the sin he commits is within him. He commits sin in order to obtain some bodily pleasure. But the pleasure passes and the sin remains. What he delights in passes, and the sting remains behind it. What an evil bondage...!
Let us all flee to Christ, and appeal against sin to God as our Savior.

Let us ask to be sold, so that He may save us by His blood. For the Lord says: "Ye have sold yourselves for nought; and ye shall be redeemed without money" (Isa 52:3). You shall be saved without a price on your part; so says the Lord, for He paid the price, not with money but with His blood, otherwise we would have remained needy slaves.
* This world is without doubt the valley of tears in which a man sows while weeping. It supports you to continue in your faith. In any case, explain what this book means by the seed that we sow now.
It is the good works which God has ordained for each one of us to walk in (Eph 2:10). And He planned for us to perform them by the power of His Spirit in the midst of the toils of this troubled life.

Whoever learns to practice the work of God in this world, this valley of tears and toils, becomes joyful like the diligent farmer who sows the seed even in the death of winter; can the cold winds and harsh weather keep him from his work? Certainly not! So it is fitting that we look at the troubles of this life. Amusements are thrown in our way by the evil one, with the aim that we may turn aside from the good works which we were created to do. See what the Psalmist says: "He that goeth forth weeping..." Truly he finds reason for weeping; each one of us finds it. Yet we must go on, practicing the good works of God along our way.
How wretched we would be if we had been called to work earnestly only to weep, without looking for any fruit of our labor. How wretched we would be if we found no one to wipe away our tears.

But we know that the Holy Spirit works that we may continue planting in the midst of our tears. For through the Psalmist the Spirit promises us that we shall return astonished with joy! We bring the fruit of our labor as an offering to Him.

entries.section: 1. The righteous and the concept of authority

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine The righteous considereth the cause of the poor: but the wicked regardeth not to know it [7].

Since the righteous is occupied with his brethren, he hears the voice of the poor, responds to his groans, and recognizes his complaint. But the wicked shuts his heart upon the "ego," and seeks only what he thinks is for his personal benefit; thereby he loses true knowledge.

* Mercy is a universal virtue, and the basic principle that must be practiced everywhere and by every age, so that neither the Pharisee nor the soldier nor the farmer is exempt from it... neither the rich nor the poor, for all are called to give to those who have not, because mercy is the perfection of the virtues.

entries.section: 1. The righteous and the concept of authority

paragraphs.text: St. Ambrose Scornful men bring a city into a snare: but wise men turn away wrath [8].

The scornful man counts his success in stirring up differences among those around him, appearing as one who wishes to reconcile them and spread peace among them, or who works for their benefit, as Demetrius the silversmith did, who made silver shrines for Diana (Acts 19:23-41). But the wise man finds his peace in the peace of his brethren; he turns away wrath from himself, as he turns it away from his brethren, so that all may live in the true peace of God.

* St. Nilus of Sinai made a comparison between these two measures of virtue in the cases of the blessed Moses the prophet and his brother Aaron: the rite of covering the chest and the heart with the priestly breastplate, which Aaron performed when he entered the Holy of Holies, represented the state of the person who, though angry in his heart, suppresses this anger by struggle and prayer. But the state of the person who has no anger at all in his heart, because he has reached perfection by his victory over the passions and demons, St. Nilus compares with what was said of Moses the prophet, saying: "Moses the prophet offered the breast as a sacrifice, because the soul dwells in the heart, and the heart in the breast."

And wise Solomon says: "Wise men turn away wrath" (Prov 29:8), and the Scripture says regarding Aaron: "And thou shalt make holy garments for Aaron thy brother for glory and for beauty. And thou shalt speak unto all that are wise hearted, whom I have filled with the spirit of wisdom, that they may make Aaron's garments to consecrate him, that he may minister unto me in the priest's office... a breastplate, and an ephod, etc. And thou shalt put in the breastplate of judgment the Urim and the Thummim; and they shall be upon Aaron's heart, when he goeth in before the LORD" (Ex 28:2-4, 30). This teaches us monks that it is fitting for us to cover the anger of the heart with good, humble, quiet thoughts, and not to allow anger to rise to the throat, where the tongue exposes the stench of this anger.

* Abba Moses said: "He who humbly bears a word of injustice or reproach for the sake of Christ completes his martyrdom, and he who becomes poor for God's sake, God provides for him, and he who shows his weakness before God or becomes foolish for His sake, God makes wise."

Paradise of the Fathers * When the peace of the mind is struck by anger, it grieves and tears it, like one who falls into confusion, so that it is not in harmony with itself, and loses the power of its inner harmony. Let us then take into consideration how grave the sin of anger is, by which we lose gentleness, the likeness to the image of the Most High. By anger wisdom is driven out, and we are left in complete ignorance of what to do and how to do it.
St. Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 1. The righteous and the concept of authority

paragraphs.text: If a wise man contendeth with a foolish man, whether he rage or laugh, there is no rest [9].

It is hard for a fool to realize his errors and confess them, for he is always stiff-necked in his opinions, thinking that he is right in everything. So if a wise man tries to guide him, whether with firmness or gentleness, he will not accept his guidance and advice.

entries.section: 1. The righteous and the concept of authority

paragraphs.text: The bloodthirsty hate the upright: but the just seek his soul [10].

The violent, hard-hearted person who sheds blood hates the upright man, because the latter condemns him, if not openly then through his conduct, which pricks the conscience of the wicked. The first example in the life of mankind is therefore Cain, who killed his brother Abel, for no reason except that he offered a sacrifice acceptable to God (Gen 4:5). But the person who loves virtue finds rest in the upright man and clings to him.
* Sitting with those who are not wise shatters the heart, and conversing with the virtuous is a sweet spring.

* Do not descend to the slack, or you will put yourself in the lowest rank, but let your converse be with lovers of good, that you may dwell with them on high. Therefore let your abode be bravely in the places where there is the highest knowledge. Go to the city of light, and do not descend to the sinners.

entries.section: 1. The righteous and the concept of authority

paragraphs.text: St. Isaac the Syrian A fool uttereth all his mind: but a wise man keepeth it in till afterwards [11].

The foolish man is ready to look for any reason to rage and be furious against others, without regard for the consequences of his wrath. But the wise man is patient, and even if he is stirred within himself over some act, he does not hasten until he calms down, and examines the situation with deliberation and without agitation.

Haman was foolish and stupid, for he found a reason to kill an entire people because he imagined that one of the members of this people did not honor him and bow down to him as to a god. But King David wisely looked for a reason to calm himself against his opponents, so he refused to take revenge on King Saul, and he listened to Abigail and praised her because she kept his hand from shedding the blood of her husband Nabal.

* We ought to restrain every movement of anger and soften it under the guidance of discernment (wisdom), so that we may not rush headlong in blind fury, of which Solomon said: "A fool uttereth all his mind: but a wise man keepeth it in till afterwards" (Prov 29:11). That is, the foolish man blazes up with the passion of anger to avenge himself, but the wise man, because of the maturity of his counsel and his gentleness, extinguishes anger little by little and rids himself of it.

The Apostle says something similar: "Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord" (Rom 12:19). That is, do not allow your hearts to be confined in the narrow straits of impatience and cowardice, so that when any violent storm of anger rises you cannot bear it, but let your hearts be wide, receiving the waves of angry words into the wide streams of love, which "beareth all things... endureth all things" (1 Cor 7:13). Thus your minds will be enlarged with longsuffering and patience, and in it will be the depths of faithful counsel that faces the smoke of anger and destroys it.

The phrase can be understood in the following sense: we give place to anger to the extent that we submit with a humble and quiet mind to the passion of others, and bow to the impatience of those who are in turmoil, as though we deserved every kind of wrong (as a discipline for us).

But those who distort the meaning of the perfection of which the Apostle speaks, interpreting giving place to wrath as keeping away from a person at the time of his anger, seem to me by this not to cut off the causes of anger but to stir up the motives of strife. For unless we immediately set right the anger of our neighbor with a correction full of humility, keeping away provokes the neighbor all the more...

Solomon speaks of such a matter, saying: "Be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry: for anger resteth in the bosom of fools" (Eccl 7:9). And "Go not forth hastily to strive, lest thou do something to the other when thy neighbour hath put thee to shame" (Prov 25:8). By this he does not blame haste in quarrel in the sense that he praises delayed quarrel.

In the same way we must understand the saying: "A fool's wrath is known in his day: but he that covereth shame is prudent" (Prov 12:16), for it does not mean that the wise man stores up the outburst of anger secretly, but it blames the rash outburst of anger... He must hide the outburst for this reason, that while he leaves it for a time the spirit of anger subsides forever. For this is the nature of anger: when room is left for it (that is, when we do not hasten with it) it weakens and perishes, but if anger is exposed in a state of turmoil it burns more and more.

Hearts must be enlarged and opened so that they are not confined in the narrow straits of cowardice and filled with increasing anger, and become able to receive the commandments of God by what the prophet calls "largeness of heart" or "surpassing largeness." For the prophet says: "I will run the way of thy commandments, when thou shalt enlarge my heart" (Ps 119:32). For slowness to anger is wisdom, which we learn by the clear sayings of the Holy Bible. For "He that is slow to wrath is of great understanding: but he that is hasty of spirit exalteth folly" (Prov 14:29). Therefore the Holy Bible says of the person who asked the Lord for the gift of wisdom: "And God gave Solomon wisdom and understanding exceeding much, and largeness of heart, even as the sand that is on the sea shore" (1 Kgs 4:29).

Father Joseph * Let the one who is not gentle listen to the saying of the Holy Bible: "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city" (Prov 16:32). Victory over cities is of less importance, because what is subdued here is something external, but victory by means of gentleness is a far greater act, because it is the mind that conquers and rules itself by itself, when gentleness compels the mind to control itself inwardly.

Let the angry man understand what the Truth says to His chosen ones: "In your patience possess ye your souls" (Lk 21:19). The way of creation is indeed a wonderful matter, for the mind governs the soul, and the soul rules the body. But the soul loses its rule over the body if the mind does not rule over it. Therefore the Lord shows us that gentleness is the guardian of our states, and teaches us also that by gentleness we can possess ourselves. Thus we understand the gravity of the sin of lack of gentleness (that is, anger) when we see that by it we lose our very being (our existence).

Let the angry hear what Solomon says: "A fool uttereth all his mind: but a wise man keepeth it in till afterwards" (Prov 29:11). It is through the impulse of anger that the spirit is entirely laid bare, and it inclines to anger more quickly, because wise inner discipline is not available. But the wise man holds back and leaves future matters to care for themselves. And when someone wrongs him he does not rush to take vengeance at once, because by his forbearance he desires not to lose the others, although he truly knows that all things will be punished by a just judgment on the last Day of Judgment.

On the other hand, we should exhort the gentle man not to let his heart be grieved by what he suffers outwardly. For this great sacrifice which such persons offer without any hindrance ought not to be spoiled by any infection of inner malice. For even if people do not see their grief, the searching divine eye sees it.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 1. The righteous and the concept of authority

paragraphs.text: If a ruler hearken to lies, all his servants are wicked [12].

The wicked ruler or leader in any community represents a focus that includes wicked people who share his evil, and by their evil counsel they push him all the more toward evil. When Jeroboam and all Israel asked Rehoboam the son of Solomon to lighten the yoke upon them, he consulted young men who were not wise, and answered: "My little finger shall be thicker than my father's loins... my father chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions" (2 Chr 10:10-11), and the kingdom was divided, and ten tribes withdrew from him.
* A foolish counselor is a blind guard, and a wise counselor is a fortress of confidence.
St. Isaac the Syrian
13 The poor and the deceitful man meet together: the LORD lighteneth both their eyes. 14 The king that faithfully judgeth the poor, his throne shall be established for ever.
The poor and the oppressor meet together.
The LORD lighteneth both their eyes [13].

By the oppressor here he means the usurer who exploits the poor, who lends to the poor at interest without regard for their circumstances and capabilities. It would have been fitting for him to realize that the One who gave the poor man the light of life is the very One who gave him the same light. For God is the source of life of both, and it is He who will judge between them.

* You have begun to belong to a great family, and by this kinship all become brothers: master and servant, commander and soldier, rich and poor. Christians have earthly fathers of different ranks and classes, some of them noble and some despised, and yet they all call upon one heavenly Father, they all say: "Our Father which art in heaven." Have they understood that they are brothers? Let the master not disdain to regard his servant as a brother, looking to our Lord Jesus who granted him to be a brother to him.
By love alone the children of God are distinguished from the children of the devil.
* By love alone the children of God are distinguished from the children of the devil.

A man can be baptized and born again, but let him look into his heart and see whether he loves his brother; then he can truly say: "I am a son of God." Otherwise, even though he has received the mark of the sacrament, he is no better than a deserter from the army and a vagabond.
St. Augustine The king that faithfully judgeth the poor, his throne shall be established for ever [14].
The one who judges with justice and cares for the poor and needy is upheld by divine providence, so his kingdom is established, and blessing comes upon his children and grandchildren.

* Let us sow those good seeds generously, so that we may reap generously in due season. Now is the time for sowing, where I ask you not to neglect it, so that in the time of harvest we may gather the fruits of what we have sown here, and enjoy the tender compassion from the Lord.

* If you invite a friend, he continues to thank you until the evening, but friendship lasts for a time and ends very quickly, and does not equal what it cost you in expense. But if you invite a poor or maimed person, the thanks does not spoil, for God remembers it for you eternally, He will not forget it, since He Himself becomes your debtor.
St. John Chrysostom

15 The rod and reproof give wisdom: but a child left to himself bringeth his mother to shame. 16 When the wicked are multiplied, transgression increaseth: but the righteous shall see their fall. 17 Correct thy son, and he shall give thee rest; yea, he shall give delight unto thy soul. 18 Where there is no vision, the people perish: but he that keepeth the law, happy is he. 19 A servant will not be corrected by words: for though he understand he will not answer. 20 Seest thou a man that is hasty in his words? there is more hope of a fool than of him. 21 He that delicately bringeth up his servant from a child shall have him become his son at the length. 22 An angry man stirreth up strife, and a furious man aboundeth in transgression. 23 A man's pride shall bring him low: but honour shall uphold the humble in spirit. 24 Whoso is partner with a thief hateth his own soul: he heareth cursing, and bewrayeth it not. 25 The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe. 26 Many seek the ruler's favour; but every man's judgment cometh from the LORD. 27 An unjust man is an abomination to the just: and he that is upright in the way is abomination to the wicked.
The rod and reproof give wisdom: but a child left to himself bringeth his mother to shame [15].

Parents who do not care for the upbringing of their child ruin his soul and shatter his character, and he becomes a shame and disgrace to them. Rebuke and discipline given with wisdom and love support the child to enjoy wisdom.
Eli the priest neglected the upbringing of his two sons, so they perished and he perished with them, and the ark of the covenant was lost from the people, and the army was defeated.
* Discipline (or rebuke) is a sign of loving care, and it leads to understanding.

The Teacher shows this rebuke when He says in the Scripture: "How often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!" (Mt 23:37). And the Scripture also says: "They went a whoring after idols and stones, and offered their burnt offerings to Baal." It is a great proof of His love, for although He knows the shame of those who rejected Him and that they ran far away from Him, yet He urges them to repent. And Ezekiel says: [But thou, son of man, be not afraid to speak to them; perhaps they will hear] (cf. Ezek 2:6). And He says to Moses: "Go and tell Pharaoh to let my people go. But I know that he will not let them go." Here both things appear: His divinity, which is shown by His foreknowledge of what will happen, and His love, by giving them the opportunity to choose repentance for themselves. And in His care for the people He rebuked them through Isaiah, saying: "This people honour me with their lips, but their heart is far from me" (Isa 29:13). And He says also: "But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men" (Mt 15:9). Here His loving care shows their sins and salvation side by side.
St. Clement of Alexandria When the wicked are multiplied, transgression increaseth.
But the righteous shall see their fall [16].
The wicked think that they are successful and have obtained authority, but soon righteousness prevails, and the righteous see the wicked fallen.
* Just as the saint is the temple of God, so the sinner makes of himself a tomb.

St. Jerome * Those who are not saints die in their sins, but the saints repent of them. They bear their wounds and recognize their errors. Then they go to the priest seeking a remedy, or seek cleansing by the bishop.

Origen * Although the servants and friends of God avoid the sins that lead to death, and practice many good works, we do not believe that they are without trivial sins, for God does not lie, where it is said: "No infant whose life is one day upon the earth is without sin." The blessed John the Evangelist, who is without doubt no less than James in worthiness, added to this: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us" (1 Jn 1:8). Moreover, we read in another place: "For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again" (Prov 24:16).
Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles Correct thy son, and he shall give thee rest; yea, he shall give delight unto thy soul [17].
Whoever disciplines his son finds rest in due time, and reaps joyful fruits and delights that gladden the soul.

* A father does not train his son if he does not love him, and a good teacher does not correct his pupil unless he sees in him signs of obtaining the promise. When the physician withdraws his care from a patient, this is a sign of his despair of his healing.

* Which is better: that we enter a battle (of discipline) for a time and carry stakes of thorn (skewers of stakes), and have weapons with us, and are wearied by carrying heavy shields, so that afterward we may rejoice through victory, or that we remain slaves forever, because we could not endure for a single hour?
St. Jerome Where there is no vision, the people run wild: but he that keepeth the law, happy is he [18].

By vision is meant inner insight, true seeing, and knowledge of the word of the Lord. As it is said: "And the word of the LORD was precious in those days; there was no open vision" (1 Sam 3:1). But the leader who responds to the word of the Lord and keeps the commandment, his eyes are opened and he enjoys a blessed life that is reflected on those whom he guides and shepherds.
* The Scriptures (the Holy Bible) are an ocean in which you find the hidden pearl.
So the interpreter must dive into the water to bring it out.
The mind dives into the Scriptures, brings out the pearl, and shows it to the merchants.
And the mind dives into the Torah, and seizes the divine pearl.
And the tongue offers it to the hearers, saying: Fasten the daughter of light in your minds as an adornment for yourselves.

St. Jacob of Serugh * It is very beneficial to read the Holy Bible, for it makes the soul wise, directs the spirit toward heaven, moves a person to thanksgiving, destroys the desire for earthly things, and lets our minds constantly contemplate the other world.
St. John Chrysostom A servant will not be corrected by words: for though he understand he will not heed [19].

The Septuagint has "the stubborn servant." The stubborn person, full of malice, cannot have his affairs set right by gentle, kind speech, for he needs some firmness. For even if he realizes the gravity of his conduct, he does not care, because of his stubbornness.

Some see that in our stubbornness we often need God's firmness and His disciplines for us, as He did with Jonah when he insisted on disobedience, so God allowed the sea to rage against him and for him to be thrown into the sea, and at the same time He prepared a great fish for him and rescued him.

* By saying: "A servant will not be corrected by words," (Solomon) does not command that (the servant) be left to himself, but counsels the means that must be used for correction. Otherwise he would not have said: "Will not be corrected by words." For he says in another place that not only the servant but also the undisciplined son must be corrected by beating, and so he bears great fruit. For he says: "Thou shalt beat him with the rod, and shalt deliver his soul from hell" (Prov 23:14).
St. Augustine Seest thou a man that is hasty in his words?
There is more hope of a fool than of him [20].
Wisdom requires slowness in speech, so that we speak only after listening to the other party, and weigh matters with deliberation before we utter a word.

Jephthah was hasty in uttering his vow, and so he sacrificed his only daughter (Judg 11:21). Herod was hasty in his promise to his brother's daughter, and so he killed St. John the Baptist (Mt 14:8-11). King Saul was hasty in his judgment, and almost killed his son Jonathan had it not been for the intervention of the people (1 Sam 14). The Apostle James advises us: "Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath" (Jas 1:19).

* As long as a man lets himself talk on without restraint, the gravity of silence flees from him, and he loses the safe keeping of himself. Therefore it is written: "The work of righteousness shall be quietness" (Isa 32:17). So Solomon says: "A city broken down and without walls is the man who hath no rule over his spirit in speech" (Prov 25:28) [Vulgate]. He also says: "In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin" (Prov 10:19). And the Psalmist bears witness to this, saying: "A talkative man shall not be established on the earth" (Ps 140:11), and indeed the value of a true statement is lost when it is spoken without discernment...

A true statement is against the wicked, if it aims at the benefit of the good... But the wicked cannot hear good words with patience, ignoring the reform of their lives, so they attach themselves to words in order to answer others.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Beware of the chattering tongue and the ears eager to hear news. Do not belittle others, and do not listen to one who belittles others.

* The garrulous old woman, the old man who speaks fables, and the sophist in his words, all these seize the Holy Scriptures and tear them into pieces, and they may teach with them without having learned them.
St. Jerome He that delicately bringeth up (pampereth) his servant from a child shall have him become grateful at the length [21].

Whoever pampers his servant from his youth, that is, spoils him, and does not bind him to obligations and the sense of responsibility and work, in the end he becomes "grateful," that is, the master is obliged to be very grateful to his servant. Some translate it "he becomes a son," that is, he inherits his possessions as a son. Though our father Abraham esteemed the person and services of Eliezer of Damascus, he could not bear that he should inherit him in place of having a son of his own.

This proverb can be interpreted as a call not to pamper the body, since it is a servant of the soul and its slave, and not a master over it who moves it with fleshly lusts and pleasures. This is what led the Apostle Paul to say: "I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection" (1 Cor 9:2).

The Lord Christ called us to be counted children of God, although we are His servants. Therefore the free love of God, His surpassing grace and His wonderful works with us call us not to be proud even if we do what is right, but to say "We are unprofitable servants" (Lk 17:10).

* When Israel was formed from its childhood and was surrounded and pampered with delights and luxury... "he waxed fat, and grew thick," until (the Israelites) finally fell into captivity among the Gentiles. The man who is pampered in his childhood is handed over to slavery.
St. Ephrem the Syrian An angry man stirreth up strife, and a furious man aboundeth in transgression [22].

The angry man causes quarrels and strife, so it is fitting for us to flee from anger and fury, lest we fall into hatred and enmity. It is also fitting for us to avoid the angry man, especially when he is angry, and not to answer his anger with anger. The elder son in the parable of the compassionate father and the prodigal son became angry, and so he insulted his father, wronged his brother, and deprived himself of entering his father's house (Lk 15).

* Whoever is angry is empty of longsuffering and love, quickly troubled by trivial words, and stirs up strife over a small, paltry matter, and wherever he has no place he throws himself in... Who does not mourn for such a man? He is despised by God and men.

St. Ephrem the Syrian * An elder said: He whose brother quarrels with him, and his heart is not grieved, has become like the angels. If he quarrels with him and then returns at that very hour and reconciles with him, this is the work of strugglers. But the one who grieves his brethren and is grieved by them, and holds on to malice in his heart, is obedient to Satan and opposes God, and God does not forgive his offenses unless he forgives his brethren.
The Garden of the Monks A man's pride shall bring him low: but honour shall uphold the humble in spirit [23].

When the proud man is puffed up he falls, and when the humble man walks in a spirit of meekness he receives honor from God and men. As St. Mary said: "He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree" (Lk 1:52).
* It is clear that excessive boasting was among the marks of the false apostles.

* Haughtiness together with sin is a great calamity... If the one who does good loses his labor if he is puffed up, how great is the iniquity of him who adds to his sins the sin of haughtiness? For such a one cannot practice repentance.
St. John Chrysostom * As soon as you become proud you immediately lose what you have received.
St. Augustine * Whoever loves humility acquires many gifts through humility.
When you seek mercy, you find it in the humble, for humility is the dwelling place of righteousness.
Teaching is found with the humble, and knowledge is the springs of their lips.
Humility begets wisdom and understanding, and the humble acquire prudence...
Sweet is the word of the humble, and his face is radiant, and he laughs and rejoices.
Love is beautiful among the humble, and they know how to manage with it.
The humble fast from all evils, and their faces shine with the goodness of their hearts.
The humble man speaks and his speech is fitting, and his lips laugh, yet the sound of his laughter is not heard...

The humble man is humbled, but his heart is lifted up to the heights above. Where his treasure is, there are his thoughts. The eyes of his face look to the earth, and the eyes of his mind to the heights above.
St. Aphrahat Whoso is partner with a thief hateth his own soul.
He heareth cursing, and bewrayeth it not [24].

Whoever shares with the thief what he has stolen, even if he did not carry out the act of theft, shares in his crime, and falls with him under the sentence. It is dangerous to share in the sins of others, in one way or another, or to cover for them, without urging them to repent and turn back from their evil. The Law pronounced judgment against one who conceals stolen goods (Lev 5:1). And John the Apostle says: "If there come any unto you, and bring not this doctrine, receive him not into your house, neither bid him God speed: for he that biddeth him God speed is partaker of his evil deeds" (2 Jn 10-11). And Paul the Apostle also says: "Neither be partaker of other men's sins" (1 Tim 5:22).
The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe [25].
It is fitting for us to fear God and not to fear men, and as St. Arsenius asks us to be servants of one Master, and not to enslave ourselves to many masters.

The Apostle Paul says: "For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ" (Gal 1:10). The Lord Christ says: "And I say unto you my friends, Be not afraid of them that kill the body, and after that have no more that they can do. But I will forewarn you whom ye shall fear: Fear him, which after he hath killed hath power to cast into hell" (Lk 12:4-5).

The reason for fearing men and not God is the saying of the Lord Christ: “For they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God” (Jn 12:43). Fear of men may lead to denying the Lord Christ, as Peter did before the maid. It may also lead to a kind of lying, as Abraham did when he denied that Sarah was his wife (Gen 26:7).
* Why are you afraid, O Christians?
Christ speaks: “It is I; be not afraid.”
Why are you disturbed by these things? Why are you afraid?
I told you beforehand that these things would surely happen... “It is I; be not afraid. Then they willingly received him into the ship” (Jn 6:21).

When they knew Him and rejoiced, they were freed from their fears. “And immediately the ship was at the land whither they went.” An end was found at the land, from the region of water to the region of solid ground, from agitation to steadfastness, from the way to the goal.
St. Augustine * It is the will of God not to deliver you from fears, but to urge you to despise them, for this is greater than being delivered from them.

* What does this roughly mean? If the one who punishes me is a man, his punishments do not wholly condemn the one who falls under them. I can plead before him and prove to him that he is unjust, but because You are God this is impossible.
St. John Chrysostom Many seek the ruler’s favour; but every man’s judgment cometh from the LORD [26].

It is fitting for the believer to give honor to whom honor is due, and so to submit in a spirit of love, but not at the expense of his faith, remembering the great day of the Lord when he will enjoy his eternal rights. But if he fears men he seeks the face of the ruler, that is, the favor of his superior or master or ruler at the expense of his faith and the salvation of his soul.
An unjust man is an abomination to the just: and he that is upright in the way is abomination to the wicked [27].

The righteous cannot bear the way of injustice, so he hates in the unjust man his violence and cruelty toward his brethren. And the wicked cannot bear the uprightness of the righteous man’s heart and conduct, because he feels that it condemns him and exposes his corruption, even if it does not confront him.

* The Apostle says: “What communion hath light with darkness?” Where there is a decisive contradiction, there can be no reconciliation between light and darkness. The person who shares in both together contributes nothing, because of their opposition and the contradiction of the one to the other at the same time in his common life. His faith extends the bright side, but his dark habits extinguish the lamp of the mind.
St. Gregory, Bishop of Nyssa
Turn my depths into a fountain of joy!
* Grant my heart to be enlarged with Your love, to rejoice in You, and to spring forth joy for others.
Let me bear the spirit of wise friendship, full of love.
Let my conduct carry neither excessive leniency nor exaggerated seriousness.
* Your Holy Spirit leads my life, and You rejoice in me as Your son.
Let me walk in the spirit of uprightness, and let Your righteousness reign over my life.
Let my hand not reach out to wrong, so that I desire no gift from anyone, and my mouth utters no word of flattery.
* I confess my weaknesses to You, but even if I fall I rise.
I do not give in to despair, but am filled with hope through Your Cross, O Forgiver of sins.
* My ears hear with You the sighs of my brethren, and my soul is poured out with them and cries out to You:
You are the hope of him who has no hope, You are the judge of the wronged and the suffering.
You are the Father of the fatherless, and the helper of those who have no one to inquire after them.
* Grant me the spirit of wisdom, so that I may be a peacemaker, and anger may not creep into my heart.
Rather let me rejoice in the peace of others, even of those who oppose me.
* Let me befriend Your children who love You, so that I learn much from them, and receive the blessing of their prayers for me.
Let me love even the wicked, and hate evil and abhor it.
Let me seek the salvation of the wicked, that they may enjoy the sweetness of fellowship with You.
* Let Your hand reach out to work in me.
For You are all love even in Your discipline.
Your rod and Your staff give me Your wisdom.
And Your firm care keeps me in Your bosom.
The enemy cannot snatch me from between Your hands.
* Your hand turns my heart from a tomb into a holy temple.
The enemy of good made of me a gloomy tomb.
Your Spirit turns me into a joyful heaven.
* Grant me true insight, so that I may see You, O Lover of all mankind.
Let me keep Your Law, for it is the delight of my heart.
It is my guide on the way of my pilgrimage.
* Be a keeper of my mouth and a guard of my lips.
So that I may be swift to hear, and deliberate in speaking.
* Grant me the spirit of humility, so that I may obtain Your mercy.
By humility the treasures of Your knowledge are opened to me.
By humility I enjoy Your wisdom.
By humility my face shines with Your light, and Your joy fills my heart.
By humility I find Your love and the love of my brethren sweet.
By humility Your Holy Spirit lifts up my heart, to enjoy its heavenly treasure.

1 The words of Agur the son of the God-fearing woman of Massa. The oracle of this man to Ithiel, to Ithiel and Ucal: 2 Surely I am more brutish than any man, and have not the understanding of a man. 3 I neither learned wisdom, nor have the knowledge of the holy. 4 Who hath ascended up into heaven, or descended? who hath gathered the wind in his fists? who hath bound the waters in a garment? who hath established all the ends of the earth? what is his name, and what is his son’s name, if thou canst tell? 5 Every word of God is pure: he is a shield unto them that put their trust in him. 6 Add thou not unto his words, lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar. 7 Two things have I required of thee; deny me them not before I die: 8 Remove far from me vanity and lies: give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me: 9 Lest I be full, and deny thee, and say, Who is the LORD? or lest I be poor, and steal, and take the name of my God in vain. 10 Accuse not a servant unto his master, lest he curse thee, and thou be found guilty. 11 There is a generation that curseth their father, and doth not bless their mother. 12 There is a generation that are pure in their own eyes, and yet is not washed from their filthiness. 13 There is a generation, O how lofty are their eyes! and their eyelids are lifted up. 14 There is a generation, whose teeth are as swords, and their jaw teeth as knives, to devour the poor from off the earth, and the needy from among men.
The words of Agur the son of the God-fearing woman of Massa.
The oracle of this man to Ithiel.
To Ithiel and Ucal [1].

We know nothing about Agur except what is mentioned in this chapter; we do not know his clan nor the tribe to which he belongs. As for Ithiel, a name whose meaning is “God is with me,” and Ucal, a name whose meaning is “the able,” perhaps they were friends of his, or two persons receiving instruction at his hands.

If we take the symbolic interpretation, the writer is Solomon the “Preacher,” the son of the godly David. And he writes a prophecy to everyone who wishes to be united with the Lord Christ as Immanuel, or God with us, or Ithiel, the Almighty, that is, Ucal. The repetition of the word Ithiel is to highlight the importance of the prophecy concerning the coming of Christ so that we may enjoy being with God. Perhaps its repetition points to His coming to the Jewish people as well as to the Gentiles.

As for the repetition of the name, mentioning it twice, it is because the number 2 points to love in the Holy Bible: the widow paid two mites, that is, she offered her whole heart; the good Samaritan paid two denarii to the innkeeper to care for the wounded man, that is, he offered his love; and in the sacrament of marriage the two become one by holy love. Thus we come to know the surpassing divine love by our union with the Almighty Savior Immanuel.
Surely I am more brutish than any man, and have not the understanding of a man [2].

Solomon the wise, who sought Wisdom as a companion for himself (Wis 8), feels the need of a constant thirst for her, so he counts himself a dull man, without understanding, until he enjoys perfect union with Wisdom.

* Ignorance is always accompanied by impetuosity, and leads people to attach great importance to their evil imaginations. Thus the victims of this disease think of themselves as great, and reckon that they are possessors of a knowledge which no one can attain. They seem to forget what Solomon says: “Be not wise in thine own eyes” (Prov 3:7), that is, according to your own individual judgment....
St. Cyril of Alexandria I neither learned wisdom, nor have the knowledge of the holy [3].

In true humility Solomon the wise, as he stands before God the Holy One, feels that he has not yet learned wisdom, nor yet known the Holy One. And he remains so until he meets the Wisdom of God face to face and enjoys the vision of the Holy One in eternal glory.

The more a man enjoys wisdom, the more his longing for her increases, and he counts himself as one standing on the shore of wisdom, seeking to enter into its depths. From the intensity of his longing for her he thinks that he is dull, lacking in wisdom and very far from her.

* Thus Solomon was the wisest of all (1 Kgs 3:12), whether in his own days or before them, and God gave him largeness of heart, and an abundance of contemplation, more than the sand; for the more he entered into the depths of the great wisdom, the more he felt its great height. And he declared how wisdom is very far from him (Eccl 7:23).

St. Gregory of Nazianzus * It is not mere human wisdom that Solomon claims for himself, he who says: “God teaches me wisdom,” and also “All my words are from God,” ascribing to God everything he utters.
St. Gregory of Nyssa Who hath ascended up into heaven, or descended?
Who hath gathered the wind in his fists?
Who hath bound the waters in a garment?
Who hath established all the ends of the earth?
What is his name, and what is his son’s name, if thou canst tell? [4].

A wonderful question that Solomon the wise presents through the shadows, for he saw with the eye of prophecy the divine Word, the Wisdom of God who is in heaven, bowing the heavens and coming down to save man and to give him Himself. He is the One who in His discourse with Nicodemus said: “And no man hath ascended up to heaven, but he that came down from heaven, even the Son of man which is in heaven” (Jn 3:13). And it was said of Him: “Now that he ascended, what is it but that he also descended first into the lower parts of the earth? He that descended is the same also that ascended up far above all heavens, that he might fill all things” (Eph 4:9-10).
That Heavenly One accomplished our salvation on the Cross and descended into Hades to bring up those who had died in hope, and to bring them in as captives into Paradise.

“Who hath gathered the wind in his fists?” Here he affirms His authority and His power to save, for He is the Almighty who gathers the wind as in His fists, and binds the water as in a garment, and establishes all the earth. Wherever man is found, whether in the air with the wind, or in the midst of the waters, or at the ends of the earth, God is able to gather him to Himself and care for him and accomplish his salvation. As the Lord Christ Himself says: “For God so loved the world... that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life” (Jn 3:16).

As for his saying: “What is his name, and what is his son’s name, if thou canst tell?” the answer comes at the Incarnation of the Wisdom of God, who came to tell us of the surpassing mystery of the Father. He says: “The only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him” (Jn 1:18), as He also says: “No man knoweth the Son, but the Father; neither knoweth any man the Father, save the Son, and he to whomsoever the Son will reveal him (Mt 11:27).”

* Do you believe that God sustains His creation and is able to do everything? Allow suitable works to follow your faith, and then He will hear you. Do not think of seizing the winds in the grasp of your hands, that is, of faith without works.
St. Ephrem the Syrian Every word of God is pure.
He is a shield unto them that put their trust in him [5].

The wise man affirms that every word of Scripture is pure and perfect because the Holy Bible is inspired by God (2 Tim 3:16). He who accepts it and trusts in it enjoys divine protection, and finds in its words a shield for his protection, a refuge and a fortress.
* The eating of bread is heaviness and sloth; but the word of life raises wings for the soul that it may fly with them.
St. Jacob of Serugh * He who trusts in the power of the Gospel trusts in God who makes it possible. He who has not received power from God cannot boast in the Lord, since he seeks his own glory.
Ambrosiaster Add thou not unto his words, lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar [6].
The words of God are perfect, they need no addition, they satisfy the soul and water it, and bring it into the divine glories. What we need is to enjoy the gift of a sound understanding of it.
* Nothing good comes from anyone other than God, especially the understanding of the Holy Scriptures.
* God guides those who listen to Him through the whole Holy Bible and through those who work, by means of his deepening.
* Although the whole Law is spiritual, the spiritual meaning is not known to all, but to those who have been given the grace of the Holy Spirit in the word of truth and knowledge.
* If you need the help of God at all times... we always need the Holy Spirit in order to understand the Holy Scriptures. Now is the time for Him to help me and show me the meanings of His words.
Origen * By accepting the Gospel a man becomes perfect after having walked according to the Law.
St. Clement of Alexandria Two things have I required of thee; deny me them not before I die [7].
Remove far from me vanity and lies.
Give me neither poverty nor riches.
Feed me with food convenient for me [8].
Lest I be full, and deny thee, and say,
“Who is the LORD?” or lest I be poor, and steal, and take the name of my God in vain [9].

What the wise man desires all the days of his life until the moment of his departure is to enjoy God Himself, so he does not ask for riches, lest his heart be occupied with them instead of the Giver of riches, and does not ask for poverty, lest because of his need he sin in one way or another. In other words, what occupies the wise man is his fellowship with the Holy One, and not riches nor poverty.

The believer fears to become like Jeshurun, of whom it was said: “But Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked: thou art waxen fat, thou art grown thick, thou art covered with fatness; then he forsook God which made him, and lightly esteemed the Rock of his salvation” (Deut 32:15). Rather he wishes to say of the Apostle Paul: “I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content... I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need” (Phil 4:11-12).

God alone knows what is suitable for each man, and what supports him in his salvation, for some are proved by the money which God gives them, so that they practice works of love and giving, and some are proved by need and by accepting it with thanksgiving and joy in the Lord.
Agur does not ask for riches nor poverty, not because they are evil, but lest he misuse them, for evil is in man’s conduct and his evil intention, and not in riches, nor in poverty.
* If riches and poverty are from the Lord, how can poverty or riches be evil?

St. John Chrysostom * Let the poor man be on his guard as well as the rich, for there are temptations for the man of poverty as for the man of wealth. As the wise man says: “Give me neither poverty nor riches.” He tells you how you can obtain these. It is enough for a man to have what is sufficient, because the rich man tends to burden his mind with cares and confusion, just as he fills his stomach with rich foods. Therefore the wise man asks to have what is necessary and suitable... to avoid the temptations of the world, so that the poor man may not despair, nor the rich man be haughty.

St. Ambrose * Solomon says: Give me neither poverty nor riches, give me only what is necessary and sufficient, “lest I be full, and deny thee,” and say: Who sees me? or being poor I steal and deny the name of my God; thus riches represent surfeit, and poverty represents the complete deprivation of the necessities of life, and sufficiency is a state of freedom from want and without excessive abundance. Sufficiency differs according to the bodily condition and present needs... Each condition needs special care to find a good table without exceeding the limits of real needs.

St. Basil the Great * Surely you see that this sufficiency is not desired for its own sake, but to secure the health of the body and clothing fitting to a man’s dignity, which allows a person to live with others respected and honored.
St. Augustine Accuse not a servant unto his master, lest he curse thee, and thou be found guilty [10].

It is fitting for the believer to take into account the circumstances of those with whom he deals, so that if a servant wrongs him he does not accuse him to his master, lest he deal harshly with him, and his soul groan within him, and his groaning reach the ears of God.
There is a generation that curseth their father, and doth not bless their mother [11].
The word “generation” here, as in the three following phrases, is meant to indicate a certain period of time, as the Lord Christ said of the Jews: “An evil and adulterous generation” (Mt 12:39).
Here the wise man warns us against insulting parents and not seeking their blessing.

The book of Proverbs often speaks of the family. When children walk in wisdom they bring joy to their parents (Prov 10:1; 15:20; 17:21, 25; 19:26; 23:24-25). It is a great disaster for children to lose their respect for their parents (Prov 23:22; 30:7), and to insult them (Prov 20:20), and to squander their money with bad friends (Prov 28:7; 29:3), and to rob their parents (Prov 28:24). Early discipline of children trains them to respect their parents and to appreciate parental love (Prov 13:24; 19:18; 22:15).
There is a generation that are pure in their own eyes, and yet is not washed from their filthiness [12].

He continues his discourse about the corrupt generation that insults parents and does not honor them, saying that it is a proud generation that does not look at its faults in order to be purified from them, but in a spirit of arrogance thinks that it is pure and better than the generation before it, that is, the generation of its parents.
* In any good work you do for your little brethren remember that your Master is the one who did it with them first. Listen and tremble, never take pleasure in your humility...

Perhaps this phrase provokes laughter in you, as though humility were calling you to be puffed up. Do not be astonished if humility makes you puffed up, for if this happens it shows that your humility is not genuine. How and in what way does this happen? When a man practices it to win the favor of men, not of God. When we practice it in order to be praised and counted great in the eyes of men. For this is from Satan.
Those who are puffed up because they are not proud please themselves by their humility and their high estimation of themselves...

Have you done a work that springs from humility? Do not boast of it, lest you lose all merit in it. For so it was with the Pharisee. He boasted of himself because he gave his tithes to the poor, and by this he lost the honor of the work. But it was not so with the tax collector, nor with Paul who said: “I know nothing by myself; yet am I not hereby justified.” He humbled himself by every means and was humble even when he had reached the summit...

When it occurs to your mind that you admire yourself because you are humble, remember your Master. Remember to what degree He humbled Himself, then you will not admire yourself nor ever praise yourself.
St. John Chrysostom There is a generation, O how lofty are their eyes! and their eyelids are lifted up [13].

The secret of its not realizing its sins is that it is an arrogant generation that lifts up its eyes and its eyelids, that is, they speak with impudence in contempt of their parents and advisers, and even of the friends around them.
There is a generation, whose teeth are as swords, and their jaw teeth as knives, to devour the poor from off the earth, and the needy from among men [14].

The fruit of corruption and pride and contempt of others is the loss of divine grace, and the turning of the heart to extreme violence, so that they become like beasts of prey, their teeth deadly swords and their jaw teeth sharp knives. They practice their violence against the poor and needy who are unable to defend themselves.

entries.section: 2. The two daughters of the horseleach

paragraphs.text: 15 The horseleach hath two daughters, crying, Give, give. There are three things that are never satisfied, yea, four things say not, It is enough: 16 The grave; and the barren womb; the earth that is not filled with water; and the fire that saith not, It is enough. 17 The eye that mocketh at his father, and despiseth to obey his mother, the ravens of the valley shall pick it out, and the young eagles shall eat it.
The horseleach hath two daughters, crying, “Give, give.” There are three things that are never satisfied.
Yea, four things say not, “It is enough” [15].

The horseleach (aluwqaah) means the bloodsucker. It is a voracious worm which eats and is not satisfied. Its two daughters are a symbol of its traits: it does not cease to suck blood without stopping. Perhaps the two daughters point to the love of money and the lust of the flesh.
Calmet sees that it points to greed, and that its two daughters are the love of money and covetousness.
Some see that it is the name of a woman who was known to him personally as well as to the public, and who had two daughters of bad reputation for their covetousness and corrupt morals.

Some rabbis see that the horseleach points to the fate and destiny that befalls man, or the inevitability of death, and that this fate and destiny has two daughters, the Garden of Eden and Gehenna, or Paradise and Hades. The first receives the righteous and the second the wicked.

Bochart also sees that the horseleach points to fate and destiny, and that its two daughters are the tomb and Hades, the first receiving the body at the death of man, and the second receiving the soul.
The Talmud sees that the horseleach points to Hades and that its two daughters are temporal authority and heresy.
Many of the Fathers of the Church see that the horseleach is understood to mean the authority of Satan.

He presents to us four things that are not satisfied, as symbols of the wicked heart, which deprives itself of God, the source of its satisfaction, so that whatever it asks and takes it remains in a state of emptiness and does not feel content. The wicked seeks money and bodily pleasures as two daughters that he embraces, but without satisfaction.

* The soul of man comes to vanity if it is occupied with the things of the world and concentrates on the needs of the body. Every day we wake up to eat and drink, and yet no one is satisfied so as not to hunger or thirst. After a short while we pursue gain daily and are seized by limitless greed, “the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing”! He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver... There is no limit to toil, nor profit in abundance... all things exist already and there is nothing new under the sun, but all is vanity.

St. Ambrose * Who can hide from himself what this riddle means? “The horseleach has three daughters, dear beloved ones, yet she is not satisfied, and with the fourth she is not satisfied when you say: Enough: the grave, and the love of a woman, and the earth that is not satisfied with water, and the fire that does not say, Enough.” The horseleach is the devil, and the daughters of the devil are dear and beloved, and they are not satisfied with the blood of the slain: the grave and the love of a woman and the dry earth and burning by heat.” He does not speak of a fornicator or a fornicatress, but of the love of a woman who is generally charged with being greedy. Remove it outside, and it bursts into a blaze of fire, abundantly; it is not satisfied; it makes a man’s mind feeble, and seizes all thought in order to feed lust.

St. Jerome * “The horseleach has three daughters, dear beloved ones.” Her daughters are presented to sin, daughters of fornication and murder and idolatry, these three do not satisfy her, for she is not satisfied. By destroying man with these deeds, sin does not change but grows continually. As for the fourth, she will not be persuaded to say Enough, that is, it is an unbridled lust... Just as the body is one and has many members, so sin is one, and contains within itself many lusts by which it casts its nets for men.

entries.section: 2. The two daughters of the horseleach

paragraphs.text: St. Hippolytus The grave; and the barren womb; the earth that is not filled with water; and the fire that saith not, “It is enough” [16].
The four things are:

A. Hades, which opens its mouth to swallow the dead, and will not stop doing so. It will not feel that it has been filled with the souls of the dead and so be content with those who have entered it. So the greedy man’s heart snatches up the love of money, and the more he obtains the more his thirst for more increases. St. Augustine likens him to one who suffers from dropsy: the more water he drinks the more he feels that he needs more without being satisfied. Or to one who drinks salt water which cannot quench the thirst of the thirsty.

B. The barren womb: perhaps he means by this the woman who loves evil with everyone and does not seek children, but seeks bodily pleasure; she will not feel that it is enough. Rather the practice of sin arouses her all the more.

Many a person thinks that he needs to practice the sinful bodily relationship in order to obtain satisfaction from it, but the truth is that it does not satisfy man’s needs but makes him thirstier for it, despite his feeling of distress after the sinful practice.

C. The sandy earth which absorbs water quickly, so that it is not fit for cultivation, but remains dry despite the rain that has fallen on it. So the love of money and bodily pleasures does not yield useful fruits.

D. The fire that does not say, “Enough”: whenever fuel is cast into the fire its flame increases, seeking to burn more and more, and the fire cannot feel a kind of contentment as long as fuel is cast into it.

entries.section: 2. The two daughters of the horseleach

paragraphs.text: The eye that mocketh at his father, and despiseth to obey his mother, the ravens of the valley shall pick it out, and the young eagles shall eat it [17].
It is known of ravens and eagles that they attack their prey, whether a dead carcass or a living bird, by pecking at the eyes.
So he who despises his parents loses his inner insight and stumbles in the darkness; he cannot see the light of divine truth, nor enjoy the vision of the heavenly glories.
* “The eye that mocketh at his father, and despiseth the old age of his mother,” that is, he who blasphemes God (his Father)... for the ravens coming from the caves pick out the eye of happiness.
St. Hippolytus

18 There be three things which are too wonderful for me, yea, four which I know not: 19 The way of an eagle in the air; the way of a serpent upon a rock; the way of a ship in the midst of the sea; and the way of a man with a maid. 20 Such is the way of an adulterous woman; she eateth, and wipeth her mouth, and saith, I have not done wickedness.
There be three things which are too wonderful for me, yea, four which I know not: [18]
The way of an eagle in the air; the way of a serpent upon a rock; the way of a ship in the midst of the sea; and the way of a man with a maid [19].

He tells us of the seriousness of adultery, that when a man falls into it once and again he feels that it is a natural bodily need, in which there is no sin. As the Scripture says: “They drink iniquity like water.” This is how some justify this sin, saying that it is a natural necessity like eating and drinking and sleeping, which a normal person cannot fail to practice.

The one who commits the sin thinks that no one has seen him, and that he gives no account for it. The Preacher concludes his book by saying: “For God shall bring every work into judgment, with every secret thing, whether it be good, or whether it be evil” (Eccl 12:14).

The wise man likens the position of the adulterer who does not care about what he commits to three examples: the way an eagle takes in the air, which no one can determine precisely, and the way of a serpent that goes upon a rock, and also the traces of a ship in the sea after it has passed; so the wicked man who commits sin tries to hide every trace of it, so that no one may trace it.

* If the house is founded upon a rock no harm will befall it. For there is no “way of a serpent upon a rock” (Prov 20:9)... The house falls if Christ is not its foundation. But the truly wise man builds his house upon a rock. This is the way in which the Lord built His Church upon the rock with a hedge and strength. This is the reason that the gates of hell shall not prevail against it (Mt 16:18). All the persecutions that come upon that house become as nothing. The house is built upon the rock.

Origen * Just as the serpent cannot leave a mark upon the rock, so Satan could not find sin in the body of the Anointed One. For the Lord says: “The prince of this world cometh, and hath nothing in me” (Jn 14:30).

And just as the ship sailing in the sea leaves no trace behind it, so the Church which lives in the world as in a sea removes the hope that is upon the earth, for it keeps its life in heaven, and since it holds its way here for a short time, no one can follow its tracks...

“Three things are too wonderful for my understanding, and the fourth I know not: the traces of an eagle flying,” that is, the ascension of Christ, and the ways of a serpent upon a rock, that is, Satan finds no trace of sin in the body of Christ, and the ways of a ship crossing the sea, that is, the ways of the Church, which is in this life as in a sea, and which is directed by her hope in Christ through the Cross, and the ways of a man in his youth, that is, the ways of the One who was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin.

St. Hippolytus * The gates of Hades cannot prevail against the rock upon which Christ builds the Church, nor against the Church, just as the way of a serpent upon a rock, according to what is written in Proverbs, cannot be found. Now if the gates of Hades have prevailed over anyone, such a one cannot be a rock upon which Christ builds the Church.
Origen Such is the way of an adulterous woman.
She eateth, and wipeth her mouth, and saith,
“I have not done wickedness” [20].

* This is the conduct of the Church which believes in Christ, for after committing adultery with the idols she renounced Satan, and was cleansed from her sins, and received forgiveness; then she affirms that she will not commit evil.

St. Hippolytus * “Such is the way of an adulterous woman; when she is washed she says: I have not done wickedness.” It is clear that this was said of her who was washed in the fountain, and does not remember the vices of her sins, but takes upon herself the virtue of preaching, and removes her stains with the living water, so that she no longer looks upon her sin, but rushes on in burning zeal. In a way she says that she does nothing evil now but has become an apostle of the truth, by forgetfulness she renounces her evil and preaches chastity through her consecration. This is the power of Christ the Lord, for even the sinner who is washed in His waters becomes renewed to virginity, and forgets what he did before. And by his new birth he proclaims the innocence of childhood, and does not know the sins of youth, and although he was formerly an adulterer because of the corruption of sin, he now becomes a virgin because of his faith in Christ.

Father Maximus, Bishop of Turin * Who is worthy to be burned now by this fire in his heart, so as not to be burned by it on the last day? I will describe to you who is the man who has this fire within his heart: imagine with me that two men each committed a sin of the same kind, say for example the most abominable kind of adultery. And that one of them felt after committing it no kind of remorse or grief or emotion about his sin, but as it was said in the book of Proverbs of the adulterous woman: “She eateth, and wipeth her mouth, and saith, I have not done wickedness” (Prov 30:20). Look also at the second sinner; after committing his sin he could not bear it, and it was his conscience that punished and rebuked him, and he was tormented in his heart, unable to eat or to drink, fasting not by choice but because of the pains and torment of repentance. Imagine with me this man who “was bowed down to the end and went mourning all the day long, and his heart was filled with burning, and there is no health in his flesh” (Ps 38:6-7), and his sin does not cease to rebuke and reprove him. Compare this man with the first man who does not care about his sin and does not feel it: which of them do you prefer? Which of them, in your opinion, can have hope in the Lord? The man who repented of his sin is of course the one who has hope, for the more he is burned by the fire of punishment the more he becomes worthy of mercy. A period of punishment suffices him such as the Apostle Paul decreed for the man who committed adultery and then repented and grieved over his sin, because the punishment was beneficial to him, for the Apostle Paul imposed the punishment upon him, and when he saw that his grief was great and sufficient, he said: “Lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow. Wherefore I beseech you that ye would confirm your love toward him” (2 Cor 2:7-8).

Let each one of us examine his conscience, and see what sins he has committed, so that when he knows that he ought to be punished, he may then ask God that the fire that came to Jeremiah, and also upon the two disciples at Emmaus, may come to him, so that he may not be delivered on the last day to the eternal fire, for if he sins here on earth and does not care about his sin and the divine fire does not work in him, his destiny in the end will be the eternal fire.
Origen
