entries.section: 4. Four things that cannot be borne

paragraphs.text: 21 For three things the earth is disquieted, and for four which it cannot bear: 22 For a servant when he reigneth; and a fool when he is filled with bread; 23 For an odious woman when she is married; and an handmaid that is heir to her mistress.
For three things the earth is disquieted, and for four which it cannot bear: [21].
For a servant when he reigneth; and a fool when he is filled with bread.

entries.section: 4. Four things that cannot be borne

paragraphs.text: For an odious woman when she is married; and an handmaid that is heir to her mistress [22].
* For three things the earth is disquieted (moved), that is, by the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. “And for four which it cannot bear,” that is, by the last coming of the Savior...

The disquieting of the earth means the changing of the things that are on the earth. Sin, which by its nature is a slave, reigned over the body of the mortal people. Truly, it reigned once in the days of the Flood, and again in the days of the people of Sodom, where it was not content with the land that was subject to it, but stirred up violence against strangers. And the third time in the case of hateful Egypt, for although it obtained Joseph who distributed food to all, lest they perish of famine, it did not repay his kindness well, but persecuted the children of Israel. The handmaid who is heir to her mistress is the Church of the Gentiles, for although she was a slave and a stranger to the promises, she drove out the free master, the synagogue of the Jews, and became the wife of Christ and His bride.

All the earth was moved by the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and the fourth it cannot bear. For He came first with the receivers of the Law, and second with the prophets, and third with the Gospel, where He declared Himself openly, and in the fourth He will come as Judge of the living and the dead, where all creation will not be able to bear His glory.

St. Hippolytus After presenting four examples of things which are hard to trace, he presents four others of hateful things which are hard to bear, to reveal that earthly man, although he loves sin and finds pleasure and attraction in it, cannot bear its consequences. These examples are:

A. A servant when he reigneth: perhaps he means the servant who betrays his master the king and assassinates him in order to occupy the throne of the kingdom. He had already likened him to the sweeping tempest and the sweeping rain (Prov 28:3). Kings in ancient times were often exposed to coups and assassinations, sometimes by one of their servants, as Eutropius attempted in the days of St. John Chrysostom.

It is often reported in history of people in lowly positions who, when they took over rule, became more violent than others. They wrong the poor and needy all the more, ignoring what they themselves had been.

B. A fool when he is filled with bread: that is, the poor and foolish man, when he obtains much of the good things, forgets his poverty, supposing that his sudden riches give him honor and authority over others.

C. An odious woman when she is married: this means one who was full of spite and desire for revenge, hated by all those around her. For if she marries, instead of rejoicing and being pleased with her husband so that they may live together in peace, she enters into disputes and strife with him and robs him of his peace.

D. An handmaid that is heir to her mistress: in the Septuagint it came: “A handmaid that has taken the place of her mistress.” Perhaps he means a maidservant who wins the affections of her master. For she uses every means to oppose her mistress and her children so that the master may divorce his wife and marry the maidservant and not care for his children. Thus ruin comes upon the family.

24 There be four things which are little upon the earth, but they are exceeding wise: 25 The ants are a people not strong, yet they prepare their meat in the summer; 26 The conies are but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks; 27 The locusts have no king, yet go they forth all of them by bands; 28 The spider taketh hold with her hands, and is in kings’ palaces.
There be four things which are little upon the earth, but they are exceeding wise: [24].
He presents a third set of four examples marked by wisdom despite their small size and man’s contempt for them, and they are:

* Four are the smallest on the earth, and they are wiser than the wise: the ants have no strength, yet they prepare their meat in the summer. In the same way the Gentiles prepare for themselves eternal life by faith in Christ with good works. The conies are a feeble folk, and make their houses in the rocks. And it can be said that the Gentiles are built upon Christ, the spiritual Rock, who becomes the cornerstone. The spider, which feeds itself with its hands, and can be easily caught, dwells in the strongholds of the rich, meaning that the thief, with his hands stretched out on the cross, rested on the cross of Christ, and dwelt in Paradise, the stronghold of kings: the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. The locusts have no king, and yet they move in orderly ranks as under one leader. The Gentiles have no king, for sin reigned over them, and now that they believe in God they are engaged in a heavenly battle.
St. Hippolytus The ants are a people not strong, yet they prepare their meat in the summer [25].

A. The ant: despite its smallness it is marked by diligence and care for the future with precise order and collective work. Ants store food in the summer so as to find food in the winter. So it is fitting for man to be diligent in his daily work as in his spiritual life, for what he does today supports him tomorrow.
God provides the ant with its food, but on its part it is bound to work diligently.
So it is fitting for the Church to work together under the leadership of the invisible Head, in a spirit of love and unity, without divisions or strife (1 Cor 3:3; 1:10).

* Be prudent and provide yourself with what is in the future in heaven. Be wise, and follow the ant, as the Scripture says: “Store up in the summer, lest you hunger in the winter.” The winter is the last day, the day of tribulation, the winter is the day of transgressions and bitterness. Gather what can be found for you in the future. If you do not do so you will perish, being neither prudent nor wise.
St. Augustine The conies are but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks [26].

B. The coney: according to the Law it is reckoned among the unclean animals because it chews the cud, but does not part the hoof (Lev 11:5). It is a small animal resembling the rabbit and of its size, and because its round feet are soft it cannot dig a hole for itself, so it takes refuge in the rock, sheltering in it (Ps 104:18). It points to the sinful man, for he cannot establish for himself a refuge in which to hide, but he must hide in Christ the true Rock (1 Cor 10:4), and so find rest and satisfaction and peace.

* Here (Solomon) points to those who have no strength, and yet store up treasures for eternal life by their good works... And the rock is in truth the refuge of the coney that lives in it. He says: You also, though you are weak, run toward the rock of true faith, and by it you recover life.

The man who enjoys works enters the Kingdom. Therefore he says: Do not despair of the Kingdom of Heaven because of the weakness of your faith, but believe in the promises, hasten to the works that you have been commanded. Christ is the Lion, and in truth all rational beings are reckoned a flock in relation to Him. (Jeremiah) says: “I am a child” because of the natural lightness of movement; it was said of the lion that he walks without hindrance.

St. Didymus the Blind * It befits the mind to cleave to this phrase continually, and so be strengthened by its constant use and unceasing meditation on it, and in this way drive away from itself all other rich thoughts, disdaining them... content with the poverty of this single phrase. And thus it reaches with the utmost speed the beatitude mentioned in the Gospel, which occupies the first place among the beatitudes, for He says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Mt 5:3).

And when a man becomes exceedingly poor with such poverty, the saying of the prophet is fulfilled in him: “Let the poor and needy praise thy name” (Ps 74:21). Truly what poverty is greater than for a man to know of himself that he has no strength with which to defend himself, seeking daily help from the generosity of another. And so he knows that every moment of his life depends on divine providence... and so he cries out to the Lord daily: “But I am poor and needy; yet the Lord thinketh upon me” (Ps 40:17).

Thus, through spiritual illumination, he ascends to the knowledge of God from many sides, and is nourished by high holy mysteries, as the prophet says: "The high hills are a refuge for the wild goats; and the rocks for the conies (the hedgehog)" (Ps 104:18).

This applies fully to the meaning we are presenting, for he who walks in simplicity and innocence harms no one, content to strive to protect himself from the harm of his enemies. He is like a spiritual hedgehog who always arms himself, fortified in the rock of the Gospel, that is, sheltered by remembering the sufferings of the Lord... And it is said in the Book of Proverbs of this spiritual hedgehog: "The conies (hedgehogs) are but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks" (Prov 30:26)..
Abba Isaac The locusts have no king, yet go they forth all of them by bands [27].

C. The locusts: despite their small size and great number, they go forth from country to country, and even from kingdom to kingdom, without a visible leader; one locust does not crowd another, as though all were soldiers in an ordered army. The locust is called the army of God, which God uses for chastisement (Joel 2:25).

* Although the locust has no king, as the Scripture says, it moves like a well-ordered army in a single line; but men, although they were created rational by God, are unable to govern themselves with good management or to accept the plan of God with patience as a king.
Origen The spider taketh hold with her hands, and is in kings' palaces [28].

D. The spider: some may wonder that the wise man speaks of the spider in kings' palaces, but in many countries, even advanced ones, the rich leave the spider in the upper halls of their palaces as a sign of good luck.

In any case, the spider has a sponge-like sac under each of its feet containing a sticky substance, by the secretion of which it can hold its prey fast with its feet (usually flies and some insects). What a man is sometimes unable to drive away, such as small insects, the spider can capture. Likewise it is fitting for the believer to make his dwelling like the spider in heaven (the royal palace), and to trust by faith in Christ who protects him from the insects.

29 There be three things which go well, yea, four are comely in going: 30 A lion which is strongest among beasts, and turneth not away for any; 31 A greyhound; an he goat also; and a king, against whom there is no rising up. 32 If thou hast done foolishly in lifting up thyself, or if thou hast thought evil, lay thine hand upon thy mouth. 33 Surely the churning of milk bringeth forth butter, and the wringing of the nose bringeth forth blood: so the forcing of wrath bringeth forth strife.
There be three things which go well, yea, four are comely in going: [29].
For the fourth time the wise man presents four things or creatures marked by strength.

* Three are comely in stepping, and the fourth is perfect in his going. They are the angels in heaven, the saints on earth, and the souls of the righteous under the earth. But the fourth is God, the Word incarnate, who passed in honor through the womb of the Virgin, renewing the creation of Adam, passed through the gates of heaven, and became the firstfruits of the resurrection and an ascent for all.
St. Hippolytus A lion which is strongest among beasts, and turneth not away for any [30].

A. The lion: it is marked by boldness and courage, for it does not retreat backward. The true believer becomes, in Christ Jesus, the Lion that comes out of the tribe of Judah (Rev 5:5), a lion in truth, not by himself but by his Christ. So he says: "For when I am weak, then am I strong" (2 Cor 12:10). And he says: "I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me" (Phil 4:13). As was said in the previous group, he is like the feeble cony dwelling in the rock, whom no one will harm, and like the spider that makes its house in the high ceilings of kings' palaces.
A greyhound; an he goat also; and a king, against whom there is no rising up [31].

B. The greyhound: the word in the Hebrew is "girded about the loins." It is a figurative name for an unknown animal; some thought it to be the hunting greyhound, which pursues its prey with great speed until it brings it back, and others thought of other animals.

In any case, it is fitting for the believer to be girded about the loins; he will not cease to work with all his strength until he achieves his goal. So he says with the Apostle Paul: "Brethren, I count not myself to have apprehended: but this one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus" (Phil 3:13-14). Thus he will not cease to gird his loins, a sign of constant work together with purity and chastity, until he enters the heavenly glories. And as the Apostle says: "Let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us, looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God" (Heb 12:1-2).

Girding the loins was also a mark of slaves, so that their garments would not hinder them from serving. If the Word incarnate became a servant and girded Himself to wash the feet of mankind, it is fitting for us to make ourselves servants to all, if possible, that we may gain the more.

C. The he goat: among its characteristics is that it goes before the flock and leads it, tends to climb rocks, and refuses to stay in the low valleys. So God created man to live always with a spirit of leadership, confident in the grace of God and taking pride in the work of God, in humility.

The children of God are not at rest in the low valleys; they lift up their eyes to the high mountains, from whence cometh help from the Lord, who made heaven and earth (Ps 121:1-2). The psalmist says: "The high hills are for the wild goats" (Ps 104:18). The believer lives in the heavenly places!

The he goat is offered as a sin offering (Lev 16); it is a type of the heavenly Lord Christ, who offered Himself as a sacrifice of atonement for the world. The believer finds his life in union with the Savior.

D. The king against whom there is no rising up: the believer, since he has fellowship with the King of kings, is counted a king possessing authority, whom the devil, with all his forces, cannot crush.
If thou hast done foolishly in lifting up thyself, or if thou hast thought evil, lay thine hand upon thy mouth [32].
Surely the churning of milk bringeth forth butter, and the wringing of the nose bringeth forth blood: so the forcing of wrath bringeth forth strife [33].

Agur ends his discourse with a warning against anger. After presenting, in the preceding fourth group, examples of great and mighty heroes, he warns us against misusing strength and turning it into destruction by falling into anger.

If our calling is honored in Christ Jesus, it is fitting that we not exalt ourselves in arrogance, lest we be counted fools, and that we beware of every word that comes out of our mouths bearing haughtiness and arrogance, for we must lay our hands upon our mouths, so that they utter only what befits us as children of God who bear the meekness of Christ and have the spirit of humility.
As the churning of milk brings forth butter, and the pressing of the nose causes bleeding, so the forcing of wrath brings forth nothing but strife and quarrels.

* "The churning of milk bringeth forth butter." Churn it with faith in the two Testaments of Christ, and you will find the commandments to be as it were milk. As soon as you are refreshed by them, they are turned into whole, saving bread.

St. John Chrysostom * An answer from the Elder himself to the two of them also, when they wished to press the brothers with the whole rule at one time: I say to you, my son and my brother: I wrote to you before about long-suffering, and now I say: "Milk, and it will be butter, but if you press the udder with your hand, it brings forth blood" [(Prov 30:33) according to the Septuagint]. And St. Paul says: "Unto the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might gain the Jews... etc." (1 Cor 9:20), and afterward he says: "I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some" [(1 Cor 9:22) according to the text], for if a man wishes to bend a tree or a vine, he bends it gradually and it does not break, but if he pushes it suddenly and violently, it breaks at once... Understand what I say to you!
St. Barsanuphius and his disciple John
Let Your Wisdom Overflow upon Me
* Grant me to perceive my folly, so that I may take refuge in You, O All-Wise, and You will pour out Your wisdom upon me, and my soul will rejoice in divine knowledge and true understanding.
You are the teacher of wisdom, You are the satisfier of the soul, You are the sanctifier of the heart!
* Why do I seek You outside myself, as though You were far from the one You love?
You are within me, nearer to me than myself!
Reveal Yourself in my depths, so that my heart may become a holy temple for You, and my soul may be secure, taking refuge in You.
* By Your wisdom let me not desire riches, lest they distract me from You.
Nor let me ask for poverty, lest my hand be stretched out to wrongdoing.
Be Yourself my wealth and my satisfaction!
* Grant me a heart that has compassion on all.
And with tenderness, let it enjoy wisdom and purity in humility.
* Do not allow my soul to be greedy like Sheol, which is never satisfied with receiving the dead.
Nor like a barren womb that seeks only a pleasure without profit.
Nor like sandy ground that no water will satisfy, however much there be.
Nor like a fire whose flame increases the more as fuel is added without sufficiency.
* Grant me to know my sins, and to confess them.
Let me not hide my weaknesses, lest I become like the way of an eagle in the air, which leaves no trace.
Nor like the way of a ship in the midst of the sea.
* Grant me wisdom together with tenderness.
So that I may not be like a violent servant who enjoys authority.
Nor like a fool when he is filled with meat, nor like an odious woman when she is married.
Nor like a handmaid who seduces her master and humiliates her mistress.

* Let me learn wisdom even from the smallest creatures, like the diligent ant, and like the cony that dwells in the rocks, and like the swarms of locusts ordered like a great army, and like the spider that dwells in the palaces of kings.
With You I fight the enemy, the devil, for the salvation of my soul and the salvation of my brothers.
So I will be bold like the lion, swift in movement like the greyhound, and I will bear a spirit of leadership like the he goat in the midst of the flock.
And the care of a king who loves his people.
1 The words of Lemuel, king of Massa, which his mother taught him: 2 What, my son? and what, the son of my womb? and what, the son of my vows?
The words of Lemuel, king of Massa.
Which his mother taught him: [1].
This chapter presents to us the proverbs recorded by Lemuel, king of Massa, which his mother taught him. Who, then, is Lemuel?
A. Some scholars see him as a king over a tribe called Massa and not over Judah, an unknown king, whom the Spirit of God guided to write these proverbs.

B. Since there was no king of Judah by this name, some see that Solomon himself is meant. Some see that the word "Massa" may mean a certain place. Others see that it means "a teaching," which is the subject of the divine announcement or inspiration. On this view his mother is Bathsheba, who, by the Spirit of God, gave her son the king guidance about how he ought to conduct himself, especially at royal banquets, and what he must take care of in choosing his wife.

Some see that the writer of this chapter is King Solomon. God gave Solomon a new name, "Jedidiah," which means "beloved of the LORD" (2 Sam 12:25), whereas Lemuel means "dedicated to the Lord," and this was probably the name by which his mother called him from his birth. Many men, especially those in high positions, are ashamed to mention the name their mothers called them in their childhood. But Solomon cherishes this name, because his wise mother chose for him a name that reminds him of his role in life, whenever anyone called him while he was still a child.

Perhaps whenever she called her son by this name she lifted her heart to God to sanctify him and consecrate him to Himself, that he might be truly like his father David, of whom God testified that his heart bore the image of God's heart.
What, my son?
And what, the son of my womb?
And what, the son of my vows? [2].

The repetition of the word "what" three times here is to stress the importance of what she says, for she longs for her son to have an upright conduct and a holy life, since he became king while still a young man, and she feared for him lest he go astray.

"The son of my vows": after she gave herself to David in sin, and the son of her sin died, she longed that God would give her a holy son in whom was the fear of the Lord. She repented and was sorry for what had come from her, and the Lord gave her this son, "and the LORD loved him" (2 Sam 12:24). "And he sent by the hand of Nathan the prophet; and he called his name Jedidiah, because of the LORD" (2 Sam 12:25).

entries.section: 2. The king's flight from evil pleasures

paragraphs.text: 3 Give not thy strength unto women, nor thy ways to that which destroyeth kings. 4 It is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink wine; nor for princes strong drink: 5 Lest they drink, and forget the decree, and pervert the cause of all the afflicted. 6 Give strong drink unto him that is ready to perish, and wine unto those that are bitter of soul. 7 Let him drink, and forget his poverty, and remember his misery no more. 8 Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of every orphan. 9 Open thy mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy.

entries.section: A. A warning against wicked women

paragraphs.text: Give not thy strength unto women, nor thy ways to that which destroyeth kings [3].

The mother warns her son the king against wicked women, lest she lose him his royal authority; for this shatters the bodily, psychological and spiritual powers. Moreover, corrupt lusts deprive us of the divine presence, so that we do not enjoy God, our strength and our song! Thus the Church our Mother, the Queen who sits at the right hand of the King of kings, warns us against the spirit of fornication, lest we lose the mark of royalty, and our souls fall under the slavery of lusts.

The mother gives her son the king a warning not to corrupt his powers through women who destroy kings. As the Lord's commandment came concerning the king: "Neither shall he multiply wives to himself" (Deut 17:17).

Solomon listened to the voice of his wise mother in his youth, but afterward he married many women, using human wisdom to win the kings around him, despising divine wisdom, and the result was that his wives turned away his heart from the Lord. Though he repented and was sorry afterward.
It is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink wine; nor for princes strong drink [4].

"Wine" as a substance is a good gift if it is used as medicine or in its proper place, as St. Paul asked his disciple Timothy to drink a little wine because of the illnesses that afflicted his stomach.

Bathsheba counsels her son to rule himself first before he rules the people, warning him against indulgence and excess in drinking wine and strong drink, lest he fall into what Noah fell into, even after he triumphed over the waters of the flood, saved his family, and enjoyed the new earth. He gave himself over to drinking and was uncovered, and was in shame and disgrace.

* The wine of the flesh does not gladden the heart of man, but gains mastery over him and produces madness. Truly it is written: "It is not for kings to drink wine." The Apostle also writes that it is good neither to eat flesh nor to drink wine (Rom 14:21), and yet he told us that wine gladdens the heart of man. This means the spiritual wine, which if anyone drinks he becomes at once sober.
St. Jerome Lest they drink, and forget the decree, and pervert the cause of all the afflicted [5].

When a man seeks his own pleasures by indulging in drinking wine, he forgets his obligations and responsibilities toward the salvation of his own soul, as well as toward those under him whom he shepherds. He forgets his role as a leader who is concerned to examine the people's cases with justice and to lift injustice and humiliation from them. For the king's role did not stop at the political role of the country, but he also exercised the legislative, judicial and executive authority. If wine robs the will, how can he support the oppressed?

* Who in the world does not know that drinking wine without moderation, beyond what is necessary, is a rush toward dissolution, a road to a man's laxity, an injury to the young, a disfigurement of age, a shame to women, a poison that leads to madness, an aid to wantonness, a destruction of the soul, a killing of understanding, and an estrangement from virtue? From it spring base merriment, bitterness without cause, tears without meaning, pride without foundation, shameful lying, longing for false illusion, expectation of violent and terrible threats, fear without cause, lack of caution about what is truly fearful, envy without need, exaggerated familiarity, and the promise of impossible things - this without mentioning the improper bowing of the head, the trembling, the walking with a heavy head -... and the unbalanced movement of the limbs, and the bending of the neck that can no longer support itself on the shoulders, where the muscles of the neck waste away through wine.
St. Gregory of Nyssa Give strong drink unto him that is ready to perish, and wine unto those that are bitter of soul [6].

This wise mother reckons that he who is excessive in drinking is called one ready to perish and bitter of soul. As though in some mockery she says: Let wine (and strong drink) be given to him who is ready to perish and bitter of soul, that perhaps he may forget for a while the destruction and bitterness in which he is, without removing his ruin or the bitterness of his soul.

* Hear what the Holy Scripture says: "Give strong drink unto him that is ready to perish, and wine unto those that are bitter of soul" [6]. Truly wine can lighten pains and sorrow, and draw the clouds from the brow, and as the psalmist says: [Wine that maketh glad the heart of man] (cf. Ps 104:15). How then does wine cause drunkenness? For wine cannot play this role and that in a contradictory way.

Without doubt drunkenness does not come from wine, but from misconduct. Wine was given to us for no other purpose than the health of the body, but this purpose is lost by its misuse. Hear also what the blessed Apostle writes to Timothy: "Use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thine often infirmities" (1 Tim 5:23).

This is the reason for which God formed our bodies in a moderate and useful size, so that we might be content with little. By this He teaches us that He created us to suit another (heavenly) life. We are not worthy of this (other) life, and during the time in which He has postponed it, He does not allow us this excessive pampering, for a small cup of wine and a single loaf of bread suffice to satisfy the multitudes.

God, the Lord of all creation, made man to require less food than the animals, and made his body small to declare to us by this that we are hastening on our way to our other life, and nothing else than that. It is said: "Be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess," for it does not save but destroys, not the body alone but the soul also.
* Certainly drunkenness arises not from wine but from excess. Wine was given to us for no other purpose than the health of the body, but this purpose also is hindered by immoderate use.
St. John Chrysostom Let him drink, and forget his poverty, and remember his misery no more [7].

* The wisest man, that is, Solomon, tells you: "Give strong drink unto him that is ready to perish, and wine unto those that are bitter of soul. Let him drink, and forget his poverty, and remember his misery no more" (Prov 31:6-7). That is, those who have come into the distress of grief and sorrow because of their past deeds, support them abundantly with the joys of spiritual knowledge, like "wine that maketh glad the heart of man, and oil to make his face to shine, and bread which strengtheneth man's heart" (Ps 104:15). These he corrected by the strong drinking of the word of salvation, lest they be drowned in continual sorrow and fall into the despair that leads to death, lest they be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow (2 Cor 2:7). But as for those who are still in coldness and indifference, not struck by sorrow of heart, of these we read: "The talk of the lips tendeth only to penury" (Prov 14:23).

Father Nestor * There is a good remedy for sorrow with (Solomon), for he commanded that wine be given to the sorrowful, and says to us who work in the vineyard: "Give your strong drink"... the wine that maketh glad the heart of man (Ps 104:15).

Let one entrust to the others this unmixed strong drink, which is not measured by cups, and it is the word of God; by this our sorrow is turned into joy and gladness, by the grace of the only-begotten Son of God.
St. Gregory of Nyssa * Abba Pimen used to say: "The Spirit of God does not enter the house in which there are delights and pleasures."
* Some brothers told Abba Pimen about a brother who does not drink wine, and he said to them: "Wine is not for monks, for there is nothing in it that is useful for the dwellers in the monasteries."

Brothers asked an elder: "What is the meaning of the saying of Abba Pimen that wine is not for monks?" The elder said: "Because wine stirs the desire for procreation, and gladdens the heart (humanly), and drives away sorrow (in a soulish, bodily way), as the wise Solomon said: "Give strong drink unto him that is ready to perish, and wine unto those that are bitter of soul. Let him drink, and forget his poverty, and remember his misery no more" (Prov 31:6-7)."
Paradise of the Fathers
Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of every orphan [8].
Open thy mouth.
Judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy [9].

It is fitting for the king not to open his mouth to drink and become drunk, but to open his mouth for those who are unable to defend themselves, that is, the dumb, and for those who have no power, as though they were orphans; he opens his mouth with justice to defend the oppressed who have no one to inquire after them.

10 Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies. 11 The heart of her husband doth safely trust in her, so that he shall have no need of spoil. 12 She will do him good and not evil all the days of her life. 13 She seeketh wool, and flax, and worketh willingly with her hands. 14 She is like the merchants' ships; she bringeth her food from afar. 15 She riseth also while it is yet night, and giveth meat to her household, and a portion to her maidens. 16 She considereth a field, and buyeth it: with the fruit of her hands she planteth a vineyard. 17 She girdeth her loins with strength, and strengtheneth her arms. 18 She perceiveth that her merchandise is good: her candle goeth not out by night. 19 She layeth her hands to the spindle, and her hands hold the distaff. 20 She stretcheth out her hand to the poor; yea, she reacheth forth her hands to the needy. 21 She is not afraid of the snow for her household: for all her household are clothed with robes. 22 She maketh for herself embroidered coverings; her clothing is silk and purple. 23 Her husband is known in the gates, when he sitteth among the elders of the land. 24 She maketh fine linen, and selleth it; and delivereth girdles unto the Canaanite. 25 Strength and honour are her clothing; and she shall rejoice in time to come. 26 She openeth her mouth with wisdom; and in her tongue is the law of kindness. 27 She looketh well to the ways of her household, and eateth not the bread of idleness. 28 Her children arise up, and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praiseth her: 29 "Many daughters have done virtuously, but thou excellest them all." 30 Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised. 31 Give her of the fruit of her hands; and let her own works praise her in the gates.

This section is a poem of 22 verses, arranged according to the Hebrew alphabet (alef, bet, gimel, dalet, he, vav). The first letter of each verse follows the order of the letters, so that it might be easy for the Jew to memorize the whole passage by heart.

He has already spoken of the believer as a dignified king, who controls himself and rules himself before he rules others, who does not fall under the humiliation of bodily lusts and drunkenness with wine, but, living in dignity, is able to practice his royal life in his depths as well as in his dealings with his brothers. Now he speaks of the believer as a virtuous bride who is made worthy of the heavenly wedding, who cannot be valued by any price!
The mother gave her discourse to the king so that he might understand how to choose the wife who will help him, esteem her above all the treasures of the world and honor her, and thank God for her.

The description given here of the virtuous woman in those days still suits the woman who is kindled with the Spirit of God in all ages and in all countries, if we grasp it in its spirit and not in a literal way.

entries.section: A. Virtuous: her price is far above rubies

paragraphs.text: Who can find a virtuous woman?
For her price is far above rubies [10].

The mother presented a living picture not only of the virtuous woman, but rather also of the virtuous husband, and of every devout believer. For the virtuous person in general, woman or man, child or youth or elder, cannot be valued by any price.
It is a wonderful picture which every person can imitate, since it expresses the human soul longing to be a heavenly bride, and striving to achieve this by divine grace.

It may be said that if the harlot, of whom the wise man often warns us, is folly, then the virtuous woman here is the wisdom to which we long to cleave. For the wise man says of her: "I loved her and sought her from my youth, and I desired to take her for my bride, and I became a lover of her beauty" (Wis 8:2).

Perhaps the first mark of the soul, the bride of Christ, is her awareness of the esteem in which her heavenly Bridegroom holds her; for if He is the pearl of great price (Mt 13:46), then since she acquires Him and is united with Him, she becomes through Him of surpassing price. She is the heavenly bride, the Queen seated at the right hand of the King, the daughter of the King, God the Holy One, the body of Christ, a partner in eternal glory!

It is fitting for the believer to fix his eyes the more on the gifts of the Savior to him, and on his awareness of God's esteem for him; thus he does not fall into despair because of his sins, nor does hopelessness come upon him, but his life is turned into a sacrifice of thanksgiving to God who forgives sins, who acquired him by His precious blood (1 Cor 6:20).

* When Solomon described in a poetic way the spiritual marriage of the one who enters into a close relationship with wisdom, he points to many ways by which our union with virtue is achieved, and says: "Honour her, and she shall embrace thee" (Prov 4:8) LXX.

St. Gregory of Nyssa * [In his praise of his mother during the lament over his father according to the flesh] I heard the Holy Scripture say: "Who can find a valiant woman?" And also that she is a gift from God, and that a good marriage is arranged by the Lord. Those outside have the same thought also - if the saying truly comes from them - namely: there is no greater gift to a man than a good wife, and nothing worse than for the opposite to happen. It is impossible for anyone to be happier than my father in this matter. For I believe that if anyone, from the ends of the earth and from the whole human multitude, were to seek to arrange the best possible marriage, and to establish a union more virtuous and harmonious than this, it could not be achieved. For the best of the men and the best of the women were united, so that their marriage was a union of virtue rather than a union of bodies. And although they surpassed all others, they were always contending with one another in virtue, and neither could outdo the other.

St. Gregory of Nazianzus * The Catholic Church was preached not only after the coming of our Lord and Savior, beloved brethren, but from the beginning of the world; she was prefigured in many forms, rather in hidden mysteries. In truth the Catholic Church existed in holy Abel, and in Noah, and in Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and in many saints before the coming of our Lord and Savior. In truth Solomon says of her: "Who can find a virtuous wife?" What does he mean by saying "who can find"? Here we find the understanding of the difficulty concerning the hardness of finding her. This bold woman is the Church.
Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles

entries.section: B. The one in whom her husband trusts

paragraphs.text: The heart of her husband doth safely trust in her, so that he shall have no need of spoil [11].
Many women can seize the praise of people, but the true praise is that which comes from those closest to her, such as the husband and the children.

The wise woman is trusted by her husband, so he leaves all the affairs of his house for her to manage, and is happy with her, as with her wisdom and her good management, and feels that she is for him a "spoil" that cannot be valued by any price.

Since the soul trusts in the heavenly Bridegroom and leans on His breast, He returns this trust to her with words of praise, trusting in her, and counts her His beloved, greater than any spoil. He has no need of spoil, because she asks of Him no spoil; she asks of Him nothing but union with Him, and with Him she asks for nothing.

* The divine Solomon, in his teaching of wisdom, I mean in his Book of Proverbs, praises the woman who takes care of her house and loves her husband, in contrast to her who roams outside, without restraint in a shameful manner, hunting precious souls with licentious words and ways. But this woman manages her house well, and with courage attends to her womanly duties; her hands hold the staff of the spindle, and she prepares two garments for her husband, and takes care of the food of her servants, and welcomes her friends at a generous table... with other details in which (Solomon) sings, praising the humble woman who works diligently.
St. Gregory of Nazianzus
She will do him good and not evil all the days of her life [12].
Her husband's happiness is always before her eyes; with sweet words she offers works full of kindness. She does good without mixing it with any evil.

In her godliness she does not cease to do good, striving all the days of her life. She does not look to the future to rest from her work, for her rest is in doing good to the last breath. She is careful to profit from every moment of her life, for every second of her life has its value; she wastes not a second on what is of no benefit.

The bride who is united with the Doer of good things, who went about doing good, goes about with Him and by Him and in Him to do good all the days of her life. There is no place for evil in her heart or her thought or her feelings or her senses!

By saying: "She will do him good and not evil all the days of her life," he means that the wife's faith returns to what Eve was with her husband before the fall, when the Lord God said: "It is not good that Adam should be alone; I will make him a help meet for him" (Gen 2:18).

* Was he who received the grace of the Spirit in need of any other helper? How much more will he need help in the future, he who fills the body of Christ? At that time man was created in the image of God, but now He has united him with God Himself. At that time man was commanded to have dominion over the fish and the animals, now He gives us Paradise to dwell in. Now He opens to us the gates of heaven. At that time man was formed on the sixth day... now he is formed on the first day from the beginning and in the light.

St. John Chrysostom * God in His goodness gave man a helper, and there was nothing not good in his portion. For God said that it is not good that man should be alone. He knew perfectly well what a blessing the race of Mary would offer him (Adam), and the Church.

Tertullian * Scripture says that woman was created as a helper for man, so that by spiritual union she might bear spiritual offspring, that is, good works for the divine praise; while he rules, she obeys. He is governed by wisdom, and she is governed by the man. For Christ is the head of the man, and the man is the head of the woman (1 Cor 11:13).

* "The heart of her husband doth safely trust in her." Certainly he trusts, and he teaches us also to be confident. Behold, you see that the Church has been entrusted to the ends of the earth, among all the nations, from sea to sea. If she does not persevere and endure to the end, the heart of her husband does not trust in her... Thus she plunders the world, and spreads through it everywhere...
"She will do him good and not evil all her life." This is the reason why this lady plunders the nations: she works for the good of her husband, not out of necessity...

At all times she does good, not harm, not to herself but to her husband. "That they which live should henceforth not live unto themselves, but unto him which died for them, and rose again" (2 Cor 5:15).
St. Augustine
She seeketh wool, and flax, and worketh willingly with her hands [13].

The virtuous, wise woman knows neither idleness nor laziness, but strives and works with all her energy, and finds her delight in the labor of love which she offers to her family with all willingness. She works at many things so that she need not buy anything as far as possible. She does not buy ready-made clothes, but spins with her hands from the wool of her flock or from the flax of her field, in order to provide her husband with clothes made by her hands. In other words, she finds her pleasure in constant work with joy and gladness of heart. In Jewish, Greek and Roman societies, women of the upper classes worked with their hands for the family, not out of need, nor for lack of workers or hired servants, but noble women found delight in household work. It was the custom in the East for women to spin wool and flax, and she felt her responsibility to prepare clothing for the whole family. They took pride that the clothes of their husbands and sons were made by their own hands.

* Those who wish to be equal to Sarah are not ashamed to perform services and to help travelers, especially those on foot. For Abraham said to her: "Make ready quickly three measures of fine meal, knead it, and make cakes upon the hearth" (Gen 18:6). And it is said: (And Jacob saw) Rachel the daughter of Laban his mother's brother, and the sheep of Laban" (Gen 29:9). The Holy Scripture contains countless examples of diligent labor and of their doing the work and training in it, without need of others.
St. Clement of Alexandria Some of the Fathers offer a symbolic interpretation of the wool and the flax here.

* Wool signifies something bodily, and flax something spiritual. This interpretation is taken from the order of dress. For the underclothes are of flax, and the outer garments of wool. Therefore wool signifies something bodily, since it results from a mixing or union, whereas flax comes from the earth without bodily pleasure, and so it seems to represent chastity. Indeed, according to the commandment of the Law, the priests of the Old Testament used linen girdles as a symbol of chastity.

Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles * The sacred text compares the housewife to a weaver of wool and flax... I think that wool means something that concerns the body, and flax something that concerns the spirit. I venture to offer this guess from the order of our underclothing, for our underclothes are of flax, and the outer ones of wool. Now whatever we do in the body is public, and what we practice in the spirit is private. Now he who works in the body and not in the spirit may seem good while he is worthless, whereas he who works in the spirit and neglects what is according to the body (that is, does not work) is reckoned frankly as idle.
St. Augustine She is like the merchants' ships.
She bringeth her food from afar [14].

The wise Solomon compares the virtuous woman to the merchant at work with his ship coming from afar loaded with goods, especially provisions and the necessary food, while he exports other goods without stopping. She is like the Apostles who come into the world with glad heavenly tidings as spiritual provision that satisfies souls.
She riseth also while it is yet night, and giveth meat to her household, and a portion to her maidens [15].

The virtuous woman is glad to begin her day before dawn, and prepares food for the family. She offers herself as an example to her maidens, who imitate her, so they rise very early to help her with joy and gladness of heart.
She considereth a field, and buyeth it: with the fruit of her hands she planteth a vineyard [16].

The virtuous woman works to support her husband, so that when she finds a suitable opportunity she multiplies her husband's possessions by buying fields and planting vineyards. She "planteth a vineyard" to find wine to use as medicine, and to offer to the temple.
If vineyards point to joy, then she will not cease to spread the spirit of joy in the life of all the members of the family.
She works at many things so that she need not buy anything as far as possible.

* The text speaks of the Church as a virtuous soul ("she considereth a field, and buyeth it"), who acquires the tree of knowledge and the tree of life, knowledge like the law, and life like the Word. For she who came from the side of Christ, and was found by her Bridegroom to be a woman with a sound mind and strength, keeps the faith of her Bridegroom, as she awaits His second coming from heaven.
Origen She girdeth her loins with strength, and strengtheneth her arms.
She perceiveth that her merchandise is good [17].

Her much movement and variety of work give her body strength and vigor, so that it is like a constant bodily exercise [17]. In her work she cares not merely for abundance of production but for its quality, that it may be good, and so she gains a good reputation.

Girding the loins points to readiness for service in the spirit of humility; for the virtuous woman serves all the members of the family without slackness, but in a spirit of strength, with a gentle arm, without complaint or murmuring.

* "She girdeth her loins with strength, and strengtheneth her arms." She is strong (courageous) in truth. Let us see now whether she is not also a servant, and with what godliness she serves, and with what readiness! She girds her loins to keep the repeated blows of bodily lusts from breaking into the path of her work, and thus she avoids treading on the hems of her long garments as she hurries in her work. Here lies the chastity of this lady, as she is girded with the girdle of the commandment, and always ready for good work.
St. Augustine Her candle goeth not out by night [18].
A sign of constant watchfulness and care. While everyone sleeps she remains in tender, watchful motherhood, especially if she has children.

Since she delights in her family work and her service to all, she does not put out her lamp by night, but it remains always lit, for she is in a state of constant vigil. Like her Lord she becomes a light to the world. As a daughter of light, she knows no darkness.
She layeth her hands to the spindle, and her hands hold the distaff [19].
She uses her hands in spinning, and asks no help from another.

The distaff is the head of the spindle by which she holds the thread in spinning. She is always at work; she not only clothes her household, but also shares in meeting the needs of the poor and needy.

* Concerning this spindle, let me say what the Lord allows me. For all this work of spinning wool is not wholly foreign to men. Listen to what he means by saying: "She layeth (grasps) her hands to the spindle." One may say "to the distaff of the spindle." It was not said "the spindle" without reason, for the spindle seems to mean spinning, and spinning means the good works of the chaste woman, the housewife who is hard-working and careful...

Look at these two instruments for spinning wool: the spindle and the distaff. The wool is wound around the distaff, and drawn out and turned by spinning as a thread, and then passes to the spindle... So your good work is on the spindle and not on the distaff. What is on the distaff is what you will do, and what is on the spindle is what you are doing now. Now see whether you have anything on the spindle, and where your arms must take hold.
St. Augustine

entries.section: E. Her mercy to the poor

paragraphs.text: She stretcheth out her hand to the poor; yea, she reacheth forth her hands to the needy [20].
The virtuous wife bears the nature of continual giving, without return, and with joy.
* Brothers, let us not be ashamed to practice the holy works of wool. If anyone has a full storehouse, let all these things be on the distaff; let them pass to the spindle.

It remains on the left as long as it does not give to the poor, but as soon as it begins to practice almsgiving it turns to the right side, and becomes a work that accomplishes the making of a garment.

entries.section: E. Her mercy to the poor

paragraphs.text: Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles She is not afraid of the snow for her household: for all her household are clothed with robes (purple) [21].

The virtuous woman is not troubled when winter comes, nor does she fear the snow, for she spins for her family the woolen clothes they need, enough for warmth. And the Church, as a mother who cares for her children and is concerned that their hearts be kindled with divine love, does not fear for them the days of spiritual coldness, when trials come upon them.

The word "purple" in the Hebrew, אַרְגָּמָן (argamān), does not mean merely the purple-red color, for the color does not give warmth, nor is it suitable for work, but it means that it is dyed twice, or a garment of two layers (with a lining), which gives warmth. It is also in the Vulgate "duplicibus," that is, "double."
* When Solomon gave a summary of the manifold grace of the Church, he added: "For all who are with her are clothed with double garments."

St. John Cassian * These are good things where the cloth of the priestly garment is used as a symbol of the Law or the Church, for she makes two garments for her husband, as it is written, one the garment of work, and the other the garment of the Spirit, woven together with the threads of faith and works.
St. Ambrose She maketh for herself embroidered coverings.

entries.section: E. Her mercy to the poor

paragraphs.text: Her clothing is silk and purple [22].
The virtuous woman makes embroidered coverings, that is, carpets which she lays on the floor for the comfort of her household and guests, or special coverings for the family.

She wears white linen garments (silk) and costly purple; the first points to her cleanness and purity through receiving the righteousness of Christ, and the second also points to the royal nature which she enjoys.

entries.section: F. Because of her, her husband is honored among the elders

paragraphs.text: Her husband is known in the gates, when he sitteth among the elders of the land [23].

He who chooses a virtuous wife receives honor for his prudence and balance, as well as for his wife, who gains a good reputation in all circles. The peace of his house and his good management prepare him to be among the elders to judge well in the cases of others.

The wisdom of the virtuous woman is reflected in the life of her husband, for the building up of the house and adorning it with the righteousness of Christ makes her husband fit to be a dignified judge, who has his standing at the gates of the city where the courts are held.

entries.section: F. Because of her, her husband is honored among the elders

paragraphs.text: She maketh fine linen, and selleth it; and delivereth girdles unto the Canaanite [24].

The virtuous woman does not make shirts for her family only, but also makes shirts which she sells for the benefit of the family. She also makes girdles which she offers for sale to those who come in distant caravans.
She points to the Church, which is clothed with the righteousness of Christ and bears witness to Him, and so offers to strangers the possibility of enjoying the same righteousness.

entries.section: F. Because of her, her husband is honored among the elders

paragraphs.text: Strength and honour are her clothing; and she shall rejoice in time to come [25].

Since the virtuous woman enjoys spiritual righteousness, and her inner man is renewed day by day by the Holy Spirit of God, she does not fear the future, for she is in a faithful hand, and under the Spirit of God, who is able to overcome all difficulties.
She puts on our Lord Jesus, and hides in Him, and so she bears His splendor within her, which the world has no power to take from her.

entries.section: F. Because of her, her husband is honored among the elders

paragraphs.text: She openeth her mouth with wisdom; and in her tongue is the law of kindness [26].

Grace is poured out on the lips of the virtuous woman, so she always works on behalf of the Kingdom of God, as Priscilla did with her husband Aquila when they instructed Apollos in the Holy Spirit, of whom he had not heard before (Acts 18:26).
By the spirit of wisdom together with gentleness the virtuous woman builds up many souls.

* Mercy is found on the tongue of (Jesus), as He teaches the Law with mercy, as it is said of wisdom: "She bears on her tongue the law and mercy." Do not fear that you cannot fulfill the Law; flee to mercy.

* "She openeth her mouth with wisdom, and puts a rule (law) on her tongue," so she praises creation as creation, and the Creator as Creator, and the angels as angels, and the heavenly beings as heavenly, and the earthly as earthly, men as men, and animals as animals. There is no mixing, and nothing out of order, and she does not take the name of the Lord her God in vain, nor does she ascribe the nature of the creature to the Creator. She speaks of everything with an orderly method, so she does not set the lesser things above the more important, nor bring down the more important to the lesser.
St. Augustine

entries.section: G. Her care for her household

paragraphs.text: She looketh well to the ways of her household, and eateth not the bread of idleness [27].

Her serious care for her household obliges every member of the family to perform his role diligently in his relation with God and his relation with the rest of the family, especially the wife or mother. She works for them, and so she finds them vying in working for her.
She teaches that idleness leads to vice, therefore every member in the house has his work, that they may eat of the sweet bread of work, not the bread of sloth and idleness.

With the gentleness of her speech and the kindness of her conduct she remains watchful over the salvation of her household, working with all her strength for the building up of all, and she knows no slackness or idleness in this work.

* Our Lord Jesus Christ says: "The workman is worthy of his meat" - not everyone at all and however it may happen, but only the doer (Mt 10:10); and the Apostle Paul commands us to labor and work with our hands the thing which is good, that we may have to give to him that needeth (Eph 4:28). From this it is clear that we must work diligently, for it is not lawful for us to take worship as a pretext for idleness and for escaping office. Rather we must make it a subject of striving and many labors and patience in tribulations, that it may be granted to us also to say: "In weariness and painfulness, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst" (2 Cor 11:27). Such a course profits not only for the mortification of the body, but also for the practice of love of neighbor, that we may support needy brothers and provide them sustenance by our hands, according to what the Apostle taught in the Book of Acts, saying: "I have shewed you all things, how that so labouring ye ought to support the weak" (Acts 20:35). And again: "Rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth" (Eph 4:28). And so you will deserve to hear His words: "Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world: for I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink..." (Mt 25:34).

And I have no need to describe to you the gravity of the evil of idleness, when the Apostle commanded plainly: "If any would not work, neither should he eat" (2 Thess 3:10); for just as daily bread is necessary for every man, so toil according to his ability is necessary for him. Solomon did not write in vain in praise of the diligent woman: "She eateth not the bread of idleness" (Prov 31:27), and the Apostle also said of himself: "Neither did we eat any man's bread for nought; but wrought with labour and travail night and day, that we might not be chargeable to any of you" (2 Thess 3:8), although he had authority as a preacher of the Gospel to live of the Gospel (1 Cor 9:4, 14); indeed the Lord joins idleness with wickedness when He said: "Thou wicked and slothful servant" (Mt 25:26). Moreover, the wise Solomon not only praised the worker in what we have mentioned (Prov 31:27), but also rebuked the sluggard by comparing him with the lowest of the animals, saying: "Go to the ant, thou sluggard" (Prov 6:6). Therefore we must fear lest we too be rebuked in the day of judgment, because He who gave us the ability to work requires of us works suited to this ability. For He said: "To whom men have committed much, of him they will ask the more" (Lk 12:48).

And since some shrink from work on the pretext of prayers and the chanting of psalms, such people should know that there is a special time for everything, as the Preacher said: "To every thing there is a season" (Eccl 3:1).

* We must therefore work as far as possible, to share resources with those who lack them... There is no excuse for the lazy man who lives in idleness while he is able to work. Let him imitate those fish that cross the seas in a wonderful way in search of food.
St. Basil the Great

entries.section: H. Her honor and her outlook full of hope

paragraphs.text: Her children arise up, and call her blessed.
Her husband also, and he praiseth her [28].

This watchfulness over the salvation of the household may at times cause a kind of temporary distress, but soon all discover - young and old, the sons and the husband - that her presence in the house, her prayers, her vigils, her fasts for them and her prostrations (metanoias) are priceless treasures! So her children call her blessed, and her husband praises her.

Since she cares for the upbringing of her children, they see in their home a living icon of heaven, their souls rejoice, and they respect their mother and call her blessed. They carry within them the fear of the Lord and obedience to the divine commandment, with gentleness and kindness even in speaking with their mother.

* The religious wife is blessed. Let her praise the fear of the Lord; give her of the fruit of her lips, that her husband may be praised in the gates. Again: "A virtuous woman is a crown to her husband" (Prov 12:4). And also: [Many women built a house] (cf. Prov 14:1). You have learned what great commandments the prudent and loving wife receives from the Lord God.

entries.section: H. Her honor and her outlook full of hope

paragraphs.text: Canons of the Apostles Many daughters have done virtuously, but thou excellest them all [29].

The Church of the New Testament surpassed, in her inner glory, the people of God of old, for it was said that the least in the Kingdom of Heaven is greater than St. John the Baptist (Mt 11:11). It was also said to the men of the New Testament that the Fathers and prophets desired to see what they see and to hear what they hear, and did not enjoy it as they do (Lk 10:24). The Church of the New Testament also surpassed the devout among the ancient Gentiles who walked according to the natural law.
St. John Chrysostom sees that the Church of the New Testament occupies the position of the devil before his fall, so she is counted as one of the greatest heavenly orders.
And St. Mary, the Mother of God, as the first and most perfect member of the Church, since the divine Word became incarnate of her by the Holy Spirit, surpassed those in heaven and those on earth.

Who is this who surpassed all the daughters who have done virtuously, but St. Mary, to whom the preceding characteristics apply, together with her enjoyment of the riches of the surpassing grace of God, since she bore the Word of God within her without the seed of man?!
* There is none like the Mother of God, for while dwelling on earth you became the mother of the Creator.
(Paralex) the Hymn of Blessing

entries.section: I. Her wisdom and inner beauty

paragraphs.text: Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised [30].

The true beauty of the virtuous wife does not lie in her outward features and delicacy, but in her fear of the Lord. For the fear of the Lord, when it reigns over the heart, reflects a divine beauty upon the soul that increases in splendor with time.

The beauty of the body is vain; sickness can spoil it and pains can shatter it, and by death it passes away completely. But the fear of the Lord is the refuge in which the soul takes shelter to live in a beauty that gives pleasure to God and the heavenly beings and also to men.

The virtuous wife is wise in all her conduct; every word that comes out of her mouth is weighed by the judgments of wisdom. She is prudent not only in her behavior but in her counsel to others. The law of love and kindness is engraved on her heart, declared in her words. Her heart is satisfied with what she enjoys of the earnest of the other life, and her hands work on behalf of heaven.

Outward beauty is deceitful, for it passes away with time, but the godliness of the virtuous woman increases in splendor with time, and reaches perfection in the great day of the Lord. It is said: "The king's daughter is all glorious within" (Ps 45).

The soul that receives the Lord Christ as her spiritual Bridegroom enjoys true beauty, for He pours His splendor upon her. Her all-beautiful Bridegroom says to her: "And thy renown went forth among the heathen for thy beauty: for it was perfect through my comeliness, which I had put upon thee, saith the Lord GOD" (Ezek 16:14). So the beauty of the bride is only a reflection of the beauty and splendor of the Bridegroom upon her.

* "Behold, thou art fair, my love; behold, thou art fair; thou hast doves' eyes" (Song 1:15). You are fair and strong because you are made like him whom the song presents: "in thy glory and thy majesty" (Ps 45:4); you hear from your companion: "Forget also thine own people, and thy father's house; so shall the king greatly desire thy beauty" (Ps 45:10-11).
St. Jerome * It is fitting for the wife to follow her husband if she sees him standing beside God (Gen 18:11).

entries.section: I. Her wisdom and inner beauty

paragraphs.text: Origen Give her of the fruit of her hands; and let her own works praise her in the gates [31].

In the great day of the Lord the good works of the Church in the Lord will come forward to bear witness to her righteousness, and stand at the gates so that the heavenly beings may honor her for her faithfulness in her love for her heavenly Bridegroom and her patience in bearing witness to Him.
The Queen, the Heavenly Bride!
* You created my soul in Your image and likeness.
And You gave it dominion over the earthly creation.
You put all things under its feet.
In folly it clung to evil, and spoiled what it had received.
And in negligence it became drunk with the pleasures of the world.
Who can remove evil from me but You, O You who alone are good!
Who can turn me back from the drunkenness of this world, except the drunkenness of Your love?
* May I acquire You, O pearl of great price.
I hide You in my heart, the weak vessel.
And I enjoy Your manifestation within me, so that my soul becomes through You a heavenly queen, and Your Spirit prepares me as a bride adorned with heavenly things.
* Let me lean on Your breast, trusting in You, and You will strengthen me, and I will become through You a place of every confidence.
* You dwell within me by Your Holy Spirit, and I become a temple for You and a holy throne.
The enemy will not dare to creep in while You are within me.
Nor can sin draw me away while You are in my depths!
By You I am justified, and without You I am condemned!
* Let Your hands strengthen me, that I may work.
Laziness will not creep in upon me, for I find delight in working by You and with You and for You.
And You, the Creator of all, work for my sake; how then shall I not work for Your Kingdom?
* Grant me fellowship in Your attributes, that my heart may be filled with love and tenderness.
Let my soul groan with the groans of every heart.
And let my depths cry out with the cries of every sufferer.
Let me see the whole world as my beloved home.
I long to serve all, and let my hands be spread out in prayer for all.
* You are the All-Beautiful.
Your indwelling pours into the soul a beauty that does not fade!
Your manifestation shines with light within me!
